teachings.title: A New Relation to Time and Space
teachings.summary: Pregnancy alters our familiar relationship with time and space, moving us from active 'doing' to becoming the space where an energetic essence takes physical form. This profound shift invites us to consider our own origins before physical existence.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

“When the energy of Heaven meets the energy of earth, Birth and death appear. Between birth and death, Life appears.”

Pregnancy engenders a profoundly new experience of time and space. As adults, we have already learned a great deal about time and how long things take. We understand the time required to finish a school year, build a house, or bake a loaf of bread. So much of our lives revolves around the length of time it takes to bring a goal or idea to fruition. Our everyday minds connect a meaningful use of time with doing. We commit ourselves to something—a project, a recipe, a program, a skill—that requires our time and energy, trusting that if we stay the course, we will see a result.

### Core Teaching

Pregnancy brings forth a fundamentally different connection to doing and time. Regardless of how it is set into motion—whether entirely unexpectedly or as the result of a deeply intentional focus—once pregnancy happens, we enter into a new dimension. Instead of us using time, time is using us. Even though there is nothing active for us to do, a human being is being developed through time. It takes about forty weeks before the concept of 'us' manifests into a fully formed baby, ready to emerge into the world.

Similarly, when we think about space, we often think about the objects that take up space. We look around and see things—the chair, the dishes in the sink, the computer. Our eyes are drawn to these forms, followed quickly by the thoughts they inspire about what we need to do. We mostly focus on the forms around us and what they represent, forgetting that before, after, and surrounding all the “things” of our lives, is space.

The one form or thing we are most connected to, in terms of taking up space, is our own body. Yet, mostly we move through life with little awareness of the inner workings of our bodies, treating them more like a piece of equipment we expect to function adequately until something goes wrong. 

With pregnancy, the status quo of living in our bodies is changed. The very space we take up becomes altered. We come to realize our space, the most personal space we know, is suddenly being shared. Familiar and automatic functions change, and then there is movement—kicks and bumps and lumps. There is something alive in here: something that is in us, but isn’t us. 

With the start of pregnancy, the energetic essence of us begins to take physical form. Pregnant parents become the vehicle necessary to bring the ethereal “nothing” of our pure potential into the something of us as a physical being. Conception and pregnancy are when we become embodied, literally, by energies winnowed out of infinite possibilities. Drawn together out of the vast, unexplainable soup of potential, comes the etheric, energetic, cosmic whomever we will become.

### What to Notice

Notice how you typically relate to time. Is it a resource you are trying to manage, use, or conquer through 'doing'? Observe how this active relationship with time contrasts with the passive, unfolding nature of gestation, where time works upon us rather than us working upon it.

Notice also your relationship with your own physical space. Do you treat your body as a piece of equipment, only paying attention when it falters? What shifts when you consider your body as the sacred space where the infinite once gathered itself into your specific, unique form?

### Reflection

The idea that we already were—that there was an existence of an “us” that preceded our physical form—is something we might have considered but often have trouble relating to. And yet, what were we before we began to come into this beingness? How did we emerge with our individual personalities, our gifts, and our deficits-in-waiting? 

Could it be that there was an energetic “me” prior to conception that fit itself seamlessly into the genetic blueprint of the combined egg and sperm? Could it be we are energetic essences already in existence, anticipating this earthly life, streaming in from the infinite to become ourselves?

### Practice

Find a quiet place to sit comfortably and take a few deep, grounding breaths. Bring your awareness away from the objects and 'things' around you, and instead notice the space that surrounds them. Then, gently bring your attention inward to the space of your own body. Rather than thinking of what your body needs to do, simply feel it as a vessel. Imagine the time before you were physically formed, the vast potential from which your specific essence was drawn. Allow yourself to rest for a few minutes in the feeling of being an energetic essence that was lovingly gathered into physical form. You do not need to figure it out; just allow the mystery of your own beginning to be present with you.

### Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's *Elevating Your Origins to Love*, exploring the profound shifts in our relationship to time and space that occur as energetic potential becomes physical reality.

teachings.title: Discovering the This and the That
teachings.summary: Explore the profound transition from the fusional consciousness of the womb into the vast world of separation and differentiation. By observing the natural fascination of a child, we can better understand our own early journey of discovering boundaries, identity, and the beautiful yet daunting reality of standing as a separate self.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

There is a remarkable period in early childhood when the world opens up in a spectacular explosion of diversity. If you have ever spent time with a toddler around eighteen months of age, you may have witnessed this extraordinary phase of development. It is a time when the young mind is completely fascinated by absolutely everything. Through their fresh and eager eyes, the universe is no longer a blur of sensations but a rich tapestry of distinct objects, colors, and meanings. Every single thing, from the grandest tree to the smallest piece of carpet fuzz, holds importance and is worthy of discovery. This boundless curiosity is not just a charming phase of growing up; it is the fundamental process through which we all begin to make sense of our existence and our place within the vastness of life.

### Core Teaching

In our earliest beginnings, before we are propelled into the world, we exist in what can be described as a fusional consciousness within the womb. In that state, there is no separation, no boundary between self and other, and no distinction between this and that. It is a state of complete oneness. However, as we emerge into the world, it takes time for our developing brains and senses to gradually attune to the infinite variety of stuff that surrounds us. 

We begin by noticing broad categories—perhaps the discovery of cars. Soon, those categories refine into ever-finer distinctions: the difference between a van, a jeep, and a taxi. Then comes the contrast between cars and trucks, buses, motorcycles, and bicycles. We begin to recognize colors, identifying the red car, the white truck, and the yellow school bus. Eventually, we make the profound leap of connecting these distinct objects to the people we love, recognizing, for instance, a grandparent's specific blue car. Birds differentiate into crows, eagles, and seagulls; food becomes bananas, steak, quinoa, and carrots. 

Out of this massive, turbo-speed absorption of differentiations emerges the most important distinction of all: the realization of ourselves. We come to understand that we are not our mother. We are not our father, our brother, our sister, or the bird flying in the sky. We stand separate. This realization of individuality is a monumental milestone. It is both incredibly powerful and undeniably daunting. Suddenly, we are faced with the reality of our own separateness, and an innate, urgent drive kicks in, telling us that we had better figure out this life thing as fast as we can.

### What to Notice

As you reflect on this early stage of human development, notice how the process of differentiation continues to echo throughout your adult life. The way we categorize, separate, and define our world has its roots in this very early need to understand our environment and establish our identity. Notice if there are areas in your life where the feeling of separateness feels empowering, allowing you to express your unique individuality. Conversely, pay attention to the moments when this separateness feels daunting or isolating. 

The sudden awareness of being an individual, distinct from the caregivers who once represented our entire universe, can leave a lasting imprint on our nervous system. It is completely natural to carry a blend of awe and apprehension about our independence. By noticing these internal responses, we can bring a compassionate awareness to the parts of ourselves that are still trying to navigate the complex balance between autonomy and connection.

### Reflection

Take a moment to pause and turn your attention inward. Consider the incredible journey you have made from that early state of fusional consciousness to the complex, differentiated individual you are today. How does it feel to acknowledge the sheer effort and brilliance your young mind employed to make sense of the world? 

Reflect on your current relationship with the concept of separateness. Are there ways in which you might be holding onto a fear of standing alone, perhaps rooted in that early, daunting realization of being separate? Or perhaps you have built such strong boundaries that you sometimes miss the underlying interconnectedness of all things. Invite a gentle curiosity into these reflections, honoring the child within who had to figure out so much, so quickly.

### Practice

For this practice, invite yourself to step into the world with the fresh, fascinated eyes of a toddler. Set aside ten or fifteen minutes to simply observe your surroundings without the usual filters of adult familiarity. Pick a room in your home or step outside into nature. Allow yourself to notice the distinct qualities of the objects around you—the texture of a leaf, the specific shade of a fabric, the way light reflects off a surface. As you do this, silently name the distinctions you see, appreciating the "this" and the "that" of your environment. 

As you practice this mindful observation, gently remind yourself that just as every object has its unique place and meaning, so do you. You stand as a distinct and beautiful expression of life. Breathe into the awareness of your own individuality, holding it not as a daunting separation, but as a powerful and necessary step in your ongoing journey of growth and connection.

### Source Note

This teaching is derived from the foundational concepts explored in Susan Drury's work, offering a reflective adaptation of the profound transitions we experience as we grow and discover our unique place in the world.

teachings.title: Elevating Generations Through Love
teachings.summary: By extending compassion back through our ancestral lines, we can untangle the inherited pain and unspoken tensions that shape our families. This practice of loving restoration allows us to see our parents and grandparents not as the source of our wounds, but as individuals carrying their own unresolved griefs.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

Our parents were not the origin of everything that went wrong in our lives. They were the heirs to the unhealed griefs, losses, sorrows, and traumas of their own parents, who in turn inherited the burdens of the generations before them. When we consider this long lineage of pain, a profound question arises: What might happen if we lovingly revised these stories, tracing compassion back through the generations?

## Core Teaching

Childhood memories often hold moments of sharp disconnection that lodge deep within us, quietly eroding our sense of safety or lovability. We may recall instances of sudden anger or rejection from a parent, internalizing these events as a reflection of our own worth. However, when we revisit these painful memories through the lens of love, a wider perspective often emerges.

We may begin to see the heavy burdens our parents carried—the unspoken tensions, the grasping demands of their own parents, and the unresolved confusion that created a minefield in their family homes. The sternness or distance we experienced might not have been about us at all. It may have been the only way they knew how to manage their own profound discomfort, or the result of keeping themselves on a tight leash simply to survive the dynamics of their own upbringing.

When we look beyond our own childhood wounds, we can see the broader landscape of our ancestors' struggles. We might recognize a grandmother's grasping demands born of feeling excluded and abandoned, or a grandfather's withdrawal stemming from his painful inability to fulfill those endless needs. 

## What to Notice

Notice the temptation to hold family members accountable for their behavior without considering the context of their own dashed hopes and confusion. It is natural to feel hurt by their actions, but as we expand our awareness, we can observe how they, too, were drowning in disappointment. Pay attention to the tight straitjackets of resentment and the thick walls of separation that have been constructed over generations.

As you bring love to these historical dynamics, notice if those walls begin to crumble. Observe if the frozen moments of pain and misunderstanding start to thaw, allowing for a new vision of connection and resolution to take shape in your mind's eye.

## Reflection

Consider a painful memory from your childhood where you felt rejected or misunderstood by a parent. What unspoken tensions or unresolved conflicts might they have been carrying from their own parents? How does viewing their behavior through a lens of inherited pain shift your understanding of that moment?

Reflect on the possibility that the distance or anger you experienced was not a reflection of your lovability, but rather a manifestation of their own internal struggles and the heavy legacy of their family history.

## Practice

Find a quiet place to sit comfortably, close your eyes, and allow yourself to enter a space beyond time and space. Bring to mind a difficult memory involving a parent or family member. As you observe the scene, consciously extend love from your heart to all those involved, including your younger self. Visualize the heavy burdens, the unspoken tensions, and the rigid walls of separation dissolving. In your mind's eye, see these family members standing taller, moving closer to one another, and stepping into a deep embrace of resolution and restoration. Allow yourself to be included in this healing circle, feeling the ancient wounds shift and the age-old energies of separation bridge into love.

## Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's personal story of revisiting a painful childhood memory and extending love to her father and grandparents, ultimately transforming her understanding of their shared history.

teachings.title: Meeting Your Parents
teachings.summary: This guided practice invites you to shift from outer doing to inner awareness, gently observing your thoughts and physical sensations. From a place of safety and receptivity, you are encouraged to envision your parents with fresh eyes, discovering new dimensions of their complex humanity beyond childhood perceptions.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

Begin by sitting quietly and closing your eyes. Turn your attention inward, moving deep into your body. Allow yourself to become aware of any sensations you may be experiencing right now. Notice any physical feelings. Notice any emotions. Remain very open and present to whatever is coming forward, adopting a receptive, even welcoming attitude.

If your mind is noisy, be present to that as well, but without buying into the thoughts. The beta brain state is all about doing—solving problems, reviewing so-called mistakes, trying to find better ways to do things in the outer world. But now, we are deliberately turning away from this outer world. We are consciously shifting our focus and brain waves into a kind of inner awareness: an inner perception of the vast, complex world that is always alive and active within us.

## Core Teaching

Become more and more focused on your sensations and what you are perceiving within yourself. Notice the emotions you may be experiencing. Notice the thoughts that may come forward, and notice what your thoughts are saying.

Be present, but don't identify yourself with your thoughts. It is so easy for us to believe our thoughts are "us," that they make us who and what we are—but that is not true. Our thoughts are simply energy that we can reinforce and make more solid, or we can let them flow along without giving them any further emphasis.

As you continue to simply observe and focus your consciousness on whatever is happening within yourself right now, invite your breath to slow down a bit. Invite the inhales to come a little deeper into your body. Observe, invite, and allow the breath in more deeply without any force or insistence. Step back from trying to *do* anything; simply invite, observe, and follow. Spend a few minutes just inviting the breath in more deeply, and following what happens.

## What to Notice

Now, in your mind's eye, invite a memory of your parents—either your mother or father, or both—to come forward. Invite them with the intention of understanding something you hadn't previously been aware of. Something you misunderstood, misinterpreted, or just didn't know about them.

Take your time here. If you feel some trepidation about this, ask that it be something small, something easy, something you are completely ready to see and now understand from a place of safety and kindness.

If that feels impossible, if your memories and feelings of a parent are too much to even approach, then be kind to yourself and only do what feels appropriate right now. Back off whenever you have gone far enough.

Continue to let your breathing be slow and gentle, with no forcing of anything, no "doing." You are simply receptive and open, allowing memories to come forward in a new light. In a new understanding. In discovering something you have been seeking for a long time, and are now ready to experience in the fullness of a more expansive truth.

## Reflection

As a child, you had a limited perspective. Your understanding of the world, of humans, of the immensity of the human experience, was but an infant's grasp. So many things we little ones misunderstood, so many things we misinterpreted, so many things were beyond our mind's ability to comprehend in a fuller way.

There is no shame in this; it is simply part of our journey. Yet how often do we get stuck in a memory that only contained the partial story, that couldn't encompass the larger picture, the ever-changing, ever-dissolving, and rebuilding of reality?

Look carefully and closely at your parent. Look into their eyes. Notice their expression. Notice things about them you have never noticed before. What are they concerned about in this moment? What are the burdens that could be weighing them down? What are the cares and concerns they are trying to figure out? What are the dreams and desires, the deeper purpose they are trying to fulfill for themselves in the world?

As you continue to look at them, perhaps you begin to feel what might have been true for them at that moment. If you find yourself thinking the same thoughts about them that you have always thought, deliberately disengage from those thoughts; keep yourself open. What would it feel like to see a new aspect or perspective of them? There is likely much more to them than you have realized before, so remain present and curious. And remain kind—to them, and to yourself.

Perhaps breathe consciously into your heart area as you remain present. If you notice even the smallest thing about them in a new way, be open to it—and to your inner sensations and feelings. It can be a shock to see someone we thought we knew in a new light; it can feel discombobulating, as though the reality you have always believed in is suddenly dissolving. That is okay. Go ahead and let it dissolve, let the sands shift. Stay present to whatever you are experiencing, without shutting anything down. Simply allow a new reality to come forward, a new understanding about your parents.

Stay present to your emotions. Perhaps you are feeling very uncomfortable, in pain, or not wanting to stay with this. Or perhaps you are feeling a lightness and a new sense of freedom. Whatever you are feeling, stay present and allow things to shift and move as they flow. You are exploring a new possibility. Allow it to take whatever shape it wants. Be gentle and kind to yourself, to all parts of this experience right now.

When you feel you have reached a conclusion—or simply must move along and return to the outer world—try to sit for another minute and allow whatever you have learned or seen to remain present a bit longer. Often, we need to simply be quiet for a minute to allow a new integration within us. This process will, of course, continue—and it is helpful if you can return to this new awareness again and again over the next few days and weeks, further aligning its new truth into your experience.

## Practice

For many of us, giving a new understanding some creative expression can be a powerful way to further integrate our evolution and growth. Perhaps you would like to draw or dance an expression of what you have experienced. Perhaps you would like to write about it. The more you can expand the fullness of this new understanding in different ways, the more it will become alive in you. These changes will ripple further out within you, and eventually into your ongoing experience. Let your imagination, your creativity, even the movement of your body, enliven whatever you have discovered. Energize your new understanding and give it space to expand. Like pregnancy itself, allow the new potential you have discovered to morph and grow roots. To expand beyond your old, cramped perceptions into something spacious and light. Allow this expansiveness its full expression—through writing, dancing, music, art, or in whatever way you are moved to manifest—and continue to fill out the pictures and memories you have of your parent or parents. They were so much more than you realized, their existence so much fuller, more complicated. While we may have fixed our parents in our minds like a bug to a board, perhaps you now have a sense of their own continual processing and changing. Of other possibilities within them, still available for you.

## Source Note

Adapted from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* by Susan Drury.

teachings.title: Rooting Our Humanness
teachings.summary: Our preliminary education begins in the womb, where our developing nervous system absorbs our mother's experiences and emotions. By acknowledging and welcoming the complex feelings we may hold about our origins, we can begin to see our earliest challenges as integral parts of our own hero's journey.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

We float in the womb, in the sea of our mother’s moment-to-moment experiential reality. Our fetal nervous system absorbs her infinite feeling moments, long before we have language to describe our awareness. The world begins its subtle influence upon us, chemical signals express delivered courtesy of the placenta and amniotic fluid. Signals, regardless of what they transmit, we received from our earliest development.

## Core Teaching

The preliminary education of an earthly life dovetails with the development of our bodies as we gestate within the mother. No matter how welcomed and loved, every being growing into a human body will experience a nine-month-long apprenticeship in humanity, filtered through their expanding cellular network.

Neuroscientists have discovered that a certain amount of our mother’s stress accelerates our physical and mental development. We seem meant to be exposed to stress for our own benefit. Perhaps this preliminary exposure to the human experience is as important a part of our gestation as the delivery of nutrients and the removal of waste. By the time we enter the world, we have been neurologically pre-wired, jump-started by mother and all she is living, as it streams through our sensory awareness.

It’s something to consider that parts of ourselves were set in motion by the very circumstances, experiences, and situations our parents, especially our mothers, had during the nine months we grew within her. And in turn was she affected during her gestation by her mother. And her by the mother before. And before her. All the way back through our human origins it goes, one mother at a time. We are compilations of the history of humankind itself, silently passed on within the infinite wombs that have gestated all humanity.

It appears we humans are meant to be messed around with, to feel the entire spectrum of emotions, to explore and stumble and encounter hardship and stress right from the beginning. To learn about what does and doesn’t feel good. To be indoctrinated into a worldview that reflects the history and experience of the family into which we are born.

## What to Notice

Notice what your thoughts are about your mother. About her mothering of you, whether as a child or even today. Regardless of how wonderful or terrible she might have been, many of us will have mixed feelings about her. We know too much, we swam in her waters — so to feel pure, unconditional love may be a challenge!

Often the best way to soothe confused feelings regarding our mothers is first to simply acknowledge and normalize them — even welcome them, as they have usually been relegated to the basement of our psyches, wallowing in a murky sea of anger, resentment, sadness, confusion, or guilt.

## Reflection

What to do if you believe your mother was not in the best way during your pregnancy? What to do if you know or suspect that she went through difficult or traumatic events while you were gestating within? How to approach your own earliest beginnings with the intention of finding something good or beneficial for yourself, even though you might have preferred a very different pre-birth environment?

Remember that each of us has come to live, in one capacity or another, a hero’s journey — where hardships are necessary parts of the adventure. Where confusion and even pain are signposts that we are in the vicinity of a challenge specific to us.

## Practice

What would it feel like to touch those places of painful energies and simply embrace yourself as both the child as well as the adult you are today, despite the complexity of feelings you may have about your mother? What would it be like to open yourself in a compassionate welcoming of what seemed to have gone wrong, and simply be willing to consider this was all part of your hero’s journey? Take a moment to gently hold these possibilities. If you encounter difficult emotions, please give yourself permission to pause, breathe, or seek support if needed.

## Source Note

Derived from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* (2023) by Susan Drury, pages 76-78.

teachings.title: The Newborn Brain
teachings.summary: Explore the profound difference between the practical, problem-solving beta brain state of adults and the unified, present-moment delta state of infants. This teaching offers insight into our earliest transition into the world and how early sensory impressions shape our nervous systems.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

As adults, we spend the vast majority of our waking hours operating in the beta brain frequency. This is the practical, problem-solving, in-the-world state of mind where we figure out how to get things done—doing our jobs, putting dinner on the table, and juggling the multitude of demands that life asks of us. The beta frequency works lightning-fast to process what we think we know so that we can project how things will unfold going forward. Without this highly useful frequency, the basic nuts and bolts of our lives would never come together; we could not build a house, organize a government, or maintain order. Yet, while the beta frequency is entirely necessary to bring a sense of structure to the world, it is not particularly creative.

Because the beta brain relies heavily on past experiences to assess what will happen in the future, it often lacks the bandwidth to imagine new potential or expect new possibilities. It perpetually draws from the same pool of information—what it already knows, or thinks it knows. Consequently, we tend to repeat a lot of personal history while in the beta state of mind, because every decision, response, or reaction stems from conclusions our brains have already made about life. This day-to-day energy is busy doing, fixated on an outer world of separate things that need to be controlled and problems that need to be solved.

### Core Teaching

In stark contrast to the adult's beta state, very tiny babies operate mostly in the delta frequency. In this state, there is little awareness of an outside world or of anything separate at all. Infants live in a perpetual present moment of pure sensory experience, completely free of language, assessments, or critical thinking. They arrive from a state of fusion within the womb, still unaware of the earth in all its dense diversity and the complex requirements of being a human in a body.

The early days, weeks, and months of life serve as a profound transition time. During this period, infants remain highly connected to that fusional oneness, even as profound adjustments begin to take place. Their little bodies, brains, nervous systems, immune systems, and hormonal systems are all just starting up. Bit by bit, their focus begins to shift from the source waters of unity to the external world.

Here lies a fundamental mismatch: while these newly born beings live in the unified consciousness of delta vibrations, their parents are mostly operating in beta. Parents are focused outwardly on solving problems, paying rent, attending to jobs, caring for other children, and managing a wide array of responsibilities. Although the baby’s entire world is their moment-to-moment sensory experience, the parents are decidedly not in that same state.

While mothers are designed—hormonally, chemically, and neurologically—to fall in love and devote body and soul to supporting this helpless little being, life does not always work out perfectly. Births can be difficult, leaving the mother recovering from injury or trauma. She may have other children, need to return to work, or find herself limited by life circumstances in fulfilling the twenty-four/seven needs of a newborn. Wherever we come from, we are all new to planet earth at first, emerging tiny, immature, dependent, and clueless, born to humans who are still figuring things out for themselves.

### What to Notice

Notice the profound difference in reality between an infant and an adult. No matter how dedicated and loving parents may be, they are living in a fundamentally different head space than their baby, burdened by the wide range of demands the external world continually imposes upon them. This gap in frequency and awareness is simply a part of our design—it is how we humans make our way into the world.

When you observe your own tendencies to stay locked in a beta state of problem-solving and control, recognize that this is a learned survival mechanism. Notice also if you have any vague sensory impressions related to your early days. Often, the moments that tend to stand out or linger in the body are the ones that were not entirely comfortable—the experiences that our developing nervous systems took in but could not completely process, leaving some remaining red flags stuck in place.

### Reflection

Reflect on your own typical state of mind. How much of your day is spent in the beta frequency, repeating history and relying on past conclusions to navigate the present? Consider the infant's delta state of unified, present-moment awareness. How does it feel to recognize that your earliest experiences of the world were shaped by a profound difference in consciousness between you and your caregivers? 

If you hold uncomfortable sensory impressions from your early life, can you hold them with compassion, understanding that your nervous system was simply doing its best to process an overwhelming new world? Recognizing this inherent mismatch is not about placing blame, but about understanding the very human conditions of our arrival.

### Practice

Take a few moments today to consciously step out of the beta brain frequency. Find a quiet space where you can sit comfortably and close your eyes. Allow yourself to drop beneath the need to figure things out, solve problems, or plan for the future. 

Instead, invite a taste of that early, present-moment sensory awareness. Notice the feeling of the breath moving in and out of your body, the weight of your physical form against the chair, and the simple fact of your existence in this exact moment. If feelings of vulnerability or vague discomfort arise, greet them gently. Remind your nervous system that you are safe now, and that it is okay to soften the beta mind's grip on control. Practice resting in the simple awareness of being, honoring the sensitive, feeling nature that has been with you since your earliest days.

### Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's book, *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power*, specifically exploring the transition from the unified consciousness of the newborn to the practical, problem-solving mind of the adult.

teachings.title: What’s Your State of Mind?
teachings.summary: Our everyday beta brain state helps us function by relying on past assumptions, often formed in early childhood. While useful for practical tasks, this state can keep us stuck; opening to deeper dimensions allows us to perceive more creative and beneficial potentials for reality.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

Try on this thought: What our eyes perceive as solid is actually a vibrating, morphing, continually coming together and moving apart of both waves and particles. Within a flash, our senses interpret and hold a particular picture of what we think of as “reality.” However, in another dimension, this reality is anything but static. Although our thought-forms will continue to hold reality in a particular fixed pattern for us until we look in a different way, there are other potentials ever ready to be perceived.

## Core Teaching

Our everyday waking state, often referred to as our beta brain state, is focused on how to negotiate life in the outer world. It operates almost exclusively through interpretations and assumptions made from the past. Many of these foundational assumptions were developed during our early "theta" years—the time in childhood when our physical senses and emotions first interpreted reality based on early experiences. 

Even though our current environment and the people in it are now vastly different, our beta mind still uses these past assumptions of reality in its projections and decisions about the future. It relies on this historical data to determine how we should show up in the world today.

## What to Notice

There is nothing inherently wrong with this functional state. As long as our beta version of reality keeps us functioning and not harming ourselves or others, it serves an important purpose. It is the practical frequency through which we feed ourselves, keep a roof over our heads, perform assigned tasks, complete exams, and drive safely on the roads. We need this state to navigate the practical demands of daily life.

However, it is not our most creative or evolutionary state. Often, relying solely on this frequency keeps us stuck in a less satisfying version of reality based on our past, rather than envisioning ever-deeper, more beneficial potentials for ourselves and our world. 

## Reflection

Consider how often your current reactions are based on old assumptions. Are there areas in your life where you feel stuck in a repeating pattern? This might be an indication that your beta mind is relying on outdated interpretations of reality. Recognizing this is the first step toward opening up to new potentials. Just keep that in mind as you continue your journey of exploration.

## Practice

Take a moment to pause and observe your current state of mind. When you find yourself reacting to a situation based on past assumptions, gently remind yourself that what seems fixed might actually be fluid. Take a deep breath and ask yourself if there is another way to perceive the situation. Allow yourself to entertain the possibility of a different, more beneficial potential unfolding. 

## Source Note

This teaching is derived from Susan Drury's *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power*, pages 27-28. It invites us to explore the fluid nature of reality and the impact of our early assumptions on our present state of mind.

teachings.title: Where Did You Come From?
teachings.summary: Explore the mystery of conception and the profound truth that your existence began as an unseen presence ready to manifest. Regardless of the circumstances surrounding your arrival, you are a unique expression of gathering energy that met a human spark.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

When we consider our beginnings, it is natural to focus on the human story—the circumstances, the relationships, the timing. Often, the narrative of our conception is not the idealized fairy tale of a loving partnership perfectly prepared to welcome a child. It can be unexpected, sudden, and deeply human in its imperfections. My own journey into motherhood began with a spontaneous, unexpected knowing—a sudden awareness that someone was coming in, even when medical odds and life circumstances suggested otherwise.

### Core Teaching

Pregnancy happens, and who really knows how? Whether parents are mentally or financially ready, whether they are in a stable relationship or not, somehow the moment lines up. Regardless of how we react to the result, conception brings us into the realm of profound mystery: the creation of something out of nothing, the manifestation of a new and unique human being.

How does a new person come into the world? While stories often portray it happening through a loving relationship ready and waiting to bring forth a child, that is hardly the standard experience for everyone. Countless lives are conceived and brought into the world through circumstances that might be considered less than ideal. And yet—we come! Even when we aren't always wanted or able to be cared for by the parents whose bodies provide the entrance. Something happens, and the readying energy comes on in.

This truth points to a deeper reality about your own existence. You were already an energy, a vibration, a consciousness even, an unseen presence ready to be manifest. Even before you began to become *you*, there was a power, a potential gathering of energy, of forces readying to move into the realm of something tangible. When the opportunity came, when the energy was ignited and met with a human spark, you began.

### What to Notice

Notice any stories or beliefs you hold about the circumstances of your own conception and birth. Pay attention to how these narratives might shape your sense of worth or belonging. Notice if there is a tendency to judge your beginnings based on human standards of readiness or appropriateness, rather than recognizing the profound mystery of your manifestation.

### Reflection

Consider the idea that you were an unseen presence ready to manifest, regardless of the human circumstances surrounding your conception. How does it shift your perspective to view your existence not merely as a biological event, but as a gathering of energy and potential that met a human spark? What might change if you embraced the mystery of your arrival?

### Practice

See if you can feel this truth for yourself. Take a few moments to sit quietly and breathe deeply. Imagine yourself as that gathering energy, a vibration readying to move into the physical realm. Allow yourself to sense the power and potential that existed before you even had a form. Acknowledge the profound mystery of your existence, honoring the truth that your arrival was a manifestation of energy meeting a human spark, bringing forth the unique human being you are today.

### Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power*, focusing on the mystery of conception and the unseen presence that precedes our physical manifestation.

teachings.title: To Be—or Not?
teachings.summary: Susan Drury reflects on the uncertainty and vulnerability of pregnancy, touching upon the delicate balance between life and loss. She invites readers to consider their mother's experience of pregnancy and how those early energies might have shaped their own development.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

In a first pregnancy, everything feels unknown and foreign. It can be a strange combination of disconnection and deep connection, alternating back and forth between outer and inner worlds. When something unexpected happens, like a sign of potential complication, we are ushered into another aspect of expectant motherhood: the fear that something threatens this precious, yet still tentative, new life.

### Core Teaching

Our fears are not unfounded. They have their history in our mothers, our grandmothers, the lineage linking one mother to the next. The history of uncertainty around childbearing has inspired huge developments in maternal care and medical assessments. As humans, we hate to have uncertainty; we lose sleep or feel uneasy when we can’t know something to be okay. But no matter how far our medical abilities progress, there is something about this process that remains beyond our control.

Birth is always intimately connected to what we call death. The coming and the going remain two sides of the same coin. Miracle and mystery, something seems to come forward, but then recedes back into nothingness. When losses happen, the confusion, sadness, disappointment, and even embarrassment can never be underestimated. A baby in the womb is like a second heart whose beating has grown out of our own. When something goes amiss, there is a loss that cannot be measured or made up. There is a grieving that must be done.

### What to Notice

Notice the energies and emotions that arise when considering the vulnerability of life. Reflect on the lineage of mothers and the shared history of uncertainty and fear. Observe any tendencies to blame oneself or seek control in situations that are inherently beyond human control. 

### Reflection

Hopefully, we come to a time of laying down any guilt or railing at the unknown. What was becoming manifest had gone as far into the process as it was going to go. In the move toward new life, something always remains beyond our human control.

### Practice

Take a moment to reflect on your mother's experience of carrying you. Consider what she might have been going through, any fears she might have had, and the energies that were present during your gestation. Acknowledge the profound connection and the shared journey of navigating the unknown.

### Source Note

Adapted from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* by Susan Drury, pages 84-87.

teachings.title: Birthing Influences
teachings.summary: Explore the profound energetic template of birth and how the stories we hear shape our field of possibilities. This teaching invites reflection on the unique journey of your own birth and the deep communion between mother and child.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

When we are pregnant with new possibilities—whether a child, a project, or a new phase of life—we often seek information to understand what is taking shape within us. Like many women expecting their first child, I sought insight from books and stories to prepare for the unknown. In the midst of this preparation, a chance encounter in a midwife's waiting room opened a new pathway for me. A mother shared a story of a surprisingly swift and natural birth, contrasting sharply with the prolonged labors I had been told to expect. This unexpected narrative took root in my field of possibilities, overriding the fearful stories and laying down a new energetic pathway of communion between my baby and myself. I realized then that there are many ways for new life to emerge, and we have the power to consciously choose the influences we let shape our journey.

## Core Teaching

A woman's body is built around an energetic template designed to bring forth life. While not all women will or can give birth, and each has her own unique version of that template, the energetic blueprint remains a profound force. We were all born from a woman's body, transitioning from a hushed inner sanctum into a bright, chaotic world. This journey, enacted countless times across history, is always a miracle.

Your mother's body was more than a vessel; she was the yielder, the one who had to give over and let your development take its course. There was so much for her to anticipate, so much that remained unknown, requiring a deep trust in the body, the baby, and the design of life itself. Every mother has her own individual story of bringing uniqueness into the world. Every birth is a complete story, with a beginning, a middle, and an end, none of which can be fully foretold.

This teaching reminds us that the influences we absorb—the stories we hear and believe—shape our experiences. Just as that mother's story in the waiting room rewired my expectations, we too can seek out narratives that empower and satisfy us, trusting in the inherent wisdom of our own energetic blueprints.

## What to Notice

Notice the stories and influences you are currently allowing into your field of possibilities. Are they stories of struggle and fear, or stories of ease and empowerment? Pay attention to how these narratives affect your body, your energy, and your expectations for the future. Observe any resistance or openness you feel when considering the energetic template of your own birth and the unique story of how you emerged into the world.

## Reflection

Consider the stories you have been told about your own birth. How might those narratives have shaped your understanding of beginnings and transitions? Reflect on the ways you are currently "pregnant" with new ideas, projects, or phases of life. What influences are you inviting into these spaces, and how can you consciously choose stories that support your growth and empowerment?

## Practice

Take a few moments to find a quiet, comfortable space. Close your eyes and take a few deep, grounding breaths. Visualize the energetic blueprint within you, a template designed for creation and emergence. Imagine planting a new, empowering story into this fertile ground—a story of trust, ease, and miraculous unfolding. As you breathe, allow this new narrative to take root, feeling its supportive energy hum through your body. Carry this sense of possibility with you as you navigate the beginnings and transitions in your life.

## Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* (2023), Pages 93-96. The insights and reflections presented here are derived from the original text, honoring the author's compassionate and invitational tone.

teachings.title: Emerging Into the World
teachings.summary: Reflecting on the profound transition of birth, Susan shares her personal story of bringing her first daughter into the world. This teaching invites you to honor the intense, shared journey between mother and child, and to explore the energetic imprint of your own arrival.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

There is a profound, primal power in the act of giving birth—a process that, once initiated, takes over completely and carries us beyond the illusion of full control. Whether we approach it with excitement, impatience, or apprehension, the journey of bringing a new life into the world is an overwhelming transition. It is a shared passage, an intense collaboration between a mother's body and the emerging child.

### Core Teaching

Reflecting on the birth of my first daughter, I remember the elation of unexpected early labor. The painless contractions, the frantic rush to the hospital, the comical terror of a speeding taxi driver—it all felt like an adventure I was fully prepared for. But when the waters broke, everything narrowed. I went down the rabbit hole into the raw, all-consuming intensity of childbirth. It is an incessant rhythm of rising sensation, overwhelming peaks of endurance, and blessed relief, where time dissolves and the body works harder than it ever has before.

When there seems to be nothing left to give, you give once more. And then, suddenly, there is your baby. For me, the emergence of a daughter was a moment of profound confirmation—a meeting with an energy I had communed with for months, arriving exactly as I had somewhere always known she would. 

No matter how much medical science can ease discomfort or minimize trauma, birth remains a force of nature. It is a monumental transition that leaves an imprint. The circumstances of your own birth—whether peaceful, medicalized, or traumatic—may still be held energetically in your body's memories.

### What to Notice

Notice any physical sensations or emotional responses that arise when you think about the story of your birth. Does your body feel open and relaxed, or is there a subtle tightening? Observe if there are any deeply held beliefs about your arrival into the world, or how you transition into new phases of your life today. If the circumstances of your birth involved trauma or danger, recognize that these early experiences can leave energetic imprints. *Note: These reflective possibilities are offered for self-exploration and are not medical diagnoses or causes. Please seek qualified medical or therapeutic care for physical symptoms or treatment decisions.*

### Reflection

Do you know the story of how you entered the world? What kind of situation was your mother in, and how did the birth unfold? If you have been told stories of your emerging, consider how those narratives have shaped your understanding of yourself. If you know nothing about your birth, take a moment to simply honor the mystery of that great transition. Regardless of your current relationship with your mother, or whether she is still alive, consider the possibility that in the moments of your birth, her energy was entirely dedicated to bringing you forward safely into the world.

### Practice

Find a quiet space where you can sit or lie down comfortably. Close your eyes and take a few deep, grounding breaths. Place a hand gently over your heart or your belly. Bring your awareness to the simple, miraculous fact of your existence—that you emerged into this world through a monumental, shared journey. Visualize a soft, supportive light surrounding you, acknowledging the incredible transition you and your mother went through together. If you encounter feelings of pain, grief, or trauma during this reflection, please give yourself permission to pause, breathe, and seek the support of a trusted friend, therapist, or counselor. Honor your body's wisdom and the resilience it took to arrive exactly where you are today.

### Source Note

Adapted from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* (2023).

teachings.title: Needs Not Always Met
teachings.summary: Birth experiences, both our own and those we have with our children, can sometimes leave us holding feelings of loss, guilt, or regret. By recognizing these feelings and deliberately rescripting the narrative, we can free ourselves from the pain and embrace a more compassionate reality.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

The earliest days of life are often envisioned as a time of deep connection, where a newborn's needs are intuitively met with warmth and nourishment. We imagine the soothing relief of a mother's embrace immediately after birth, the flow of oxytocin creating a sweet sense of oneness, and the days spent floating safely together, sheltered from the external demands of worldly life.

Yet, this ideal is not always the reality. Sometimes, our beginnings—or the beginnings of our children—are marked by separation, medical intervention, or trauma. These experiences can leave lasting imprints, shaping how we relate to ourselves, our children, and our stories.

## Core Teaching

When we experience the profound sweetness of nurturing a child—the long, blissful minutes of connection and the unfolding of love—we may also begin to recognize and mourn the loss of that experience for ourselves. Stark imaginings of our own beginnings, perhaps in a hospital nursery far from our mother, can take on a painful reality in our minds.

Similarly, parents who have had painful or traumatic birthing experiences with their children often find feelings of loss or guilt clouding their memories. These feelings can affect not only how they remember the birth but also how they relate to their child going forward.

When this happens, it is easy to remain stuck in the belief that something went wrong, that we were cheated, or that we lost out on what should have been a better experience. We may look to blame something or someone for not achieving the perfect birth we desired.

However, the birth experience is only the beginning of our lives, our relationships, and our stories. The only thing that keeps us stuck in regret or loss is ourselves. We have the power to change our inner stories and our inner beliefs.

By finding something to appreciate in any part of our stories and deliberately rescripting the aspects we feel went wrong, we can stop recycling those hurts. When we decide to free ourselves from our regrets, a profound shift occurs: we also free everyone else who was part of that 'bad' story—our parents, our children, medical professionals, and even the divine. In doing so, we allow a more accepting and compassionate reality to come forward.

## What to Notice

Notice if there are any lingering feelings of loss, guilt, or regret surrounding your own birth or the birth of your children. Pay attention to the stories you tell yourself about these experiences. Are you holding onto blame or a sense of being cheated out of an ideal beginning?

Observe how these feelings might be influencing your present relationships and your sense of self. Acknowledge these emotions without judgment, recognizing them as a natural response to unmet needs or traumatic experiences.

## Reflection

Consider how your early experiences or the stories of your birth have shaped your inner beliefs. How might releasing the need for a 'perfect' beginning open you up to more compassion and acceptance?

Reflect on the power of rescripting your narrative. What might change in your life if you chose to focus on gratitude and healing rather than regret and blame?

## Practice

Set aside a quiet moment to sit with yourself in a comfortable space. Gently bring to mind any feelings of regret or pain associated with your own birth or the birth of your child. Acknowledge these feelings with compassion, understanding that birth trauma is a shared human experience. Breathe deeply into any areas of tension in your body. As you exhale, imagine releasing the story of what 'should have been.' Consciously offer love and forgiveness to yourself, and to anyone else involved in that experience. Affirm your intention to embrace a new, compassionate reality, allowing healing to flow through your past and into your present.

## Source Note

This teaching is adapted from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power* by Susan Drury.

teachings.title: Filling Gaps From Our Beginnings
teachings.summary: Our earliest beginnings, even those outside our conscious memory, can shape our underlying sense of safety and capability in the world. By gently exploring our unconscious wiring and the ways we respond to insecurity, we can begin a quiet dedication to discovering our own strength and restoring our sense of safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

Our entrance into the world is our first major transition, and it carries profound significance. For some, this passage is met with immediate warmth, connection, and the soothing flow of bonding. For others, the beginning is marked by separation, medical necessity, or a delayed connection with our caregivers. While we may retain no conscious or even shadowy memories of these earliest days, our bodies and nervous systems often hold the imprint of how safe and regulated we felt as we began our lives as separate human beings.

When those early gaps in connection and safety occur, they can leave subtle but enduring marks on how we perceive the world. We might unconsciously look for others to take control because we do not feel capable within ourselves, or we might retreat into the protection of stronger individuals—only to resent the control we have given away. These patterns are not flaws; they are our defense system doing its job to keep us safe. Yet, as we grow, we have the opportunity to revisit these gaps and offer ourselves the soothing and support we may have missed.

## Core Teaching

In our explorations of our inner world, we can sometimes access the pre-verbal psyche—the felt sense of our earliest days. This work is not about asking "why" something happened or getting caught in the details of the outer world. Instead, it is about turning inward, trusting the deeper currents of insight, and allowing whatever is ready to be revealed to unfold. When we do this, we may uncover surprising emotional residues, such as a deep-seated terror or helplessness that our neurology has held onto for years.

If we discover that our entrance into the world missed the crucial step of feeling safe and regulated, we can begin to understand how this perception has played out in our lives. We might see how an unconscious lack of trust in our own sufficiency has influenced our relationships and choices. But more importantly, we can recognize that these gaps can become the very impetus for our personal hero's journey. They urge us forward, fostering a quiet dedication to discovering our own security, our own safety, and our own ability to stand and move in the world.

## What to Notice

How do we know if we have remaining energies that automatically scream "danger" because our nervous systems free-fall too easily into threat? Regardless of where these origins come from, we can gather clues by observing what triggers us to feel insecure in our present lives.

Notice how you respond to new situations and to other people. Observe how easily you can believe in your dreams being realizable, and how much you are willing to give to yourself. Pay attention to how worthy you feel simply in being alive. If you notice—perhaps with a sinking sensation—that you easily feel fear or lose your sense of security, do not despair. Your defense system has been working diligently to protect you. It may just be wired to a higher pitch, needing conscious support to see life through the lens of possibilities rather than its dangers.

## Reflection

As you consider your own patterns of seeking safety or control, gently ask yourself how these strategies have served you in the past. What might shift if you were to offer your nervous system a little more soothing and conscious support today? Consider how the gaps in your own beginnings, whatever they may have been, might actually be the hidden drivers of your dedication to discovering your own strength.

## Practice

Take a few moments to settle into a comfortable position, allowing your breath to flow naturally. Bring your awareness to a place in your body where you feel a sense of grounding or neutrality. As you rest your attention there, gently offer yourself this thought: "I am safe in this moment, and I am capable of supporting my own well-being." If feelings of insecurity or fear arise, greet them with compassion, acknowledging that they are simply your defense system trying to help. Breathe softly into these spaces, offering them the warmth and reassurance they may have needed long ago. Allow yourself to rest in the possibility that you can cultivate your own inner safety, step by step.

## Source Note

This teaching is derived from *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power*, focusing on the ways our earliest experiences shape our nervous system and how we can consciously rewire our sense of safety and capability.

teachings.title: Why Are We Doing This?
teachings.summary: Understand the purpose of meditative exercises in reprogramming neural pathways. Explore early childhood experiences and the conclusions drawn from them before language developed.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

You may wonder what these meditative exercises are all about. In the hardware/software biological metaphor, it’s about moving away from the outer world/beta brain waves, and into the more spacious, intuitive alpha state of consciousness.

## Core Teaching

Remember that as our brains and nervous systems develop, they get trained into set patterns of neural pathways that become our automatic pilot of thinking/feeling/living. When we consciously access an alpha or even more spacious frequency of mind, it’s like getting our hands on our creative control panel.

In these states, we can begin to reprogram our inner software, and start generating more positive, empowering pathways. Expanding them further through writing, art, movement, or any mindful out-in-the-world activity, encourages our automatic pilot to flow more easily into these kinder realizations, and create more beneficial experiences for ourselves and others.

## What to Notice

Take a few minutes to think about what (if any) imaginings you may still retain from those early weeks and months of being in the world. Try not to judge whatever you perceive (if anything) as good or bad, nor do you need to go digging for deep, dark secrets. Just explore whatever you feel when you think about your first years of life. All babies and young children will experience some hurts, but it’s how those experiences were interpreted and laid down that affects us going forward.

## Reflection

Often when we have some feeling of limitation or pain that doesn’t seem related to anything, it can be harkening to a moment before we had language. Before we could name any experience, even as the energy of it slid right into our nervous system and began to broadcast a particular interpretation of life.

Perhaps that was the moment when Mother was taking a shower or Dad was distracted on the phone. Or they were having a terrible fight. Or just too exhausted to get out of bed and pick you up. So many reasons our early needs couldn’t be met in the moment, so many parents who want to be there, but don’t have their own resources to do it.

## Practice

Here is an interesting question: What kinds of conclusions about life or yourself or others, do you think you may have drawn from your very earliest days?

## Source Note

Derived from "Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power" by Susan Drury, Pages 129-130.

teachings.title: Discovering a Gap That Wasn't
teachings.summary: Explore how our assumptions about early childhood experiences might not align with our actual felt memories. By connecting with our deeper intuition, we may discover that times we assumed were lonely were actually periods of profound peace and safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

Perhaps you have heard some stories about your early days, months, or years that sound difficult. But it's a worthwhile consideration that some of the things you may assume caused you harm, actually didn't. Sometimes the experience wasn't perceived as frightening or lonely and caused no negative repercussions at all.

What have you heard about your first year on the planet? Were there circumstances you know happened that you assume caused you angst? Is your interpretation coming from felt memories, or based on stories others have told you? What if you have been projecting painful impacts that weren't your actual experience in those moments long ago?

## Core Teaching

In one of my classes, we were exploring a very early, pre-verbal experiential memory. Due to serious illness, one of the participants had had to spend several months in the hospital during his first year of life. His parents lived far away and weren't able to make the long drive every day due to work and commitments at home.

Now long grown and far down the road of raising his own children, the thought of his infant experience brought sadness. He imagined himself as a small baby alone, cared for by doctors and nurses in a sterile, impersonal environment. He imagined feeling forsaken—not because anyone was deliberately cruel, but because those were the circumstances he had to endure at a time when he was most helpless.

But then he closed his eyes, relaxed his body, and went into a more meditative frame of mind. When he allowed his deeper intuition and memory sense to go back, he had a very different experience. Rather than feeling the painful loneliness he had projected onto that time, instead he moved into a space of peace and rest.

Gone was any sense of isolation. In its place was an atmosphere of quiet, safety, and contentment. He was amazed to recognize that what he had projected as a painful gap was actually a time of nurturing.

This discovery completely transformed an experience he had assumed was harsh and lonely. Now came the realization he had never felt alone, never felt abandoned. Where once he had told himself a story of separation and vulnerability, the more deeply remembered experience was one of safety and protection.

## What to Notice

This is something to consider. During our earliest, pre-verbal days, our brains simply aren't interpreting what is happening in the same way adults do. And while an infant's brain and consciousness will certainly receive and absorb negative stimuli and retain impressions within their little nervous systems, the vibrational foundation of this tiny being is still highly connected to the beyond-time-and-space realms from which we came.

For sick or premature infants, a quiet, protected environment where their bodies are given the necessary support may be just right. Like an extended time in the womb, this is the space to delta-dream a little longer before they are ready and fully able to enter the world.

## Reflection

And for us now? When we go into a deep sleep at night, where do we go? We are still alive; we breathe, our hearts beat, but we are totally disconnected from the outer world—and we don't miss it. Nor do we remember where we went once we awaken. While we may remember some of our dreams, in our deepest sleep we willingly go behind a curtain that simply isn't available during our waking hours.

## Practice

Take a moment to breathe deeply and connect with your inner sense of safety. Allow yourself to consider an early experience you've been told was difficult. Without forcing any particular outcome, invite your deeper intuition to show you the felt sense of that time. You might discover, as the man in our class did, a profound sense of peace and protection where you previously imagined only vulnerability.

## Source Note

This teaching is drawn from "Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power" by Susan Drury, pages 131-133.

teachings.title: An Inherent Protection?
teachings.summary: Our early years can hold significant unremembered pain that our young minds shield us from to ensure our survival. As we grow into adulthood, we gain the capacity and maturity to eventually uncover, process, and transform these hidden layers of trauma into profound wisdom.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
### Opening

Sometimes, the absence of memory is itself a profound testament to what we have survived. When I reflect on my early childhood, I have almost no memories before the age of seven. While I cannot definitively know why, I conjecture that the major losses my family experienced during those years deeply impacted my parents, and consequently, me. Science suggests that when faced with traumatic stress, our brains can activate alternative pathways to store or suppress memories. It is possible that our own defense mechanisms create a kind of amnesia, an inherent protection designed to preserve our inner stability through experiences that would otherwise be unbearable.

### Core Teaching

The landscape of early childhood can be marked by profound grief that is absorbed rather than consciously remembered. In my own family, the joy of my third birthday—shared with the birth of my baby brother, Stuart—was shattered just three months later by his sudden and unexplained death. The profound shock and grief of that loss, followed by subsequent miscarriages and the traumatic premature birth and loss of another baby boy, created an atmosphere of profound sorrow. 

So often, for our own survival, our young minds and nervous systems simply have to take all the things we cannot process, put them into a room, and close the door. These unprocessed experiences become a layer within us, much like the rings of an onion, getting covered over with other layers as we grow more fully into our lives. We carry these hidden layers forward, protected from their immediate impact but still shaped by their presence.

### What to Notice

One day, years later, when we have cultivated sufficient space and maturity, those hidden layers may become exposed. This early, buried pain—a quiet timebomb ticking away—waits for the moment when we are finally ready to notice it, bring it out into the light, and decommission its power over us.

When buried pain and trauma begin to make their way into our awareness, it can feel dangerous and shocking. The child within us who lived through the original experience may suddenly come back on board, bringing with them old feelings of incapacity and helplessness. These feelings often rise up accompanied by intense waves of anger, resentment, shame, or grief. It is natural to feel completely overwhelmed and to wonder how we can possibly deal with such immense emotion.

### Reflection

What the child within us doesn't realize is that we have grown up since those early days. The situation, the environment, and the people around us have long since changed—and so have we. The adult you are today holds capacities, resources, and a depth of understanding that the child you were could not possess.

Trusting in our own capacity to find personal transformation and growth through anything we have lived is the essential first step. This trust does not minimize the pain of the past; rather, it honors our resilience and our ability to hold that pain within a larger container of awareness and self-compassion.

### Practice

Next is the willingness to accept—or at least imagine accepting—our past pain or trauma as a pathway for our growth. This takes time, patience, and profound compassion for yourself. When those old, overwhelming feelings arise, remind yourself that you are no longer the helpless child who had to shut the door to survive. You are the capable adult who can gently open that door. Breathe into the present moment, acknowledging the feelings without being consumed by them. Allow yourself the grace to process these layers slowly. And then, one day, you may find yourself finally able to digest what had previously felt toxic, allowing a deep hurt to become one more transformative influence in becoming the wise, whole person you came here to be.

### Source Note

This teaching is drawn from Susan Drury’s reflections on the protective mechanisms of early childhood memory and the eventual integration of buried trauma.

teachings.title: You Should Know Better
teachings.summary: Explore the lasting impact of the phrase "you should know better" and how it shapes our self-confidence. Discover how releasing the unrealistic expectation of innate knowledge can help restore your personal power and self-compassion.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## Opening

"You should know better!" Have you ever heard those words directed at you, or perhaps caught yourself saying them to someone else? Along with the equally confounding phrase "for your own good," these words can be profoundly confusing, especially for a child. The phrase carries a weight of expectation that assumes a level of understanding that simply may not exist yet. It suggests that knowledge is somehow innate or should have been acquired without explicit guidance. 

When we hear these words early in life, they often plant a seed of doubt. We begin to wonder if there is a universal manual for life that everyone else received, but somehow we missed. This early confusion can linger long after childhood has passed, echoing in our adult minds whenever we make a mistake or find ourselves in unfamiliar territory. The resonance of "you should know better" can create an inner environment where we constantly second-guess our instincts and doubt our inherent worth.

## Core Teaching

What a child knows about the world is actually very little. A child's mind is a blank canvas, devoid of the boundaries, definitions, and concrete walls that adults use to divide right from wrong or good from bad. Children do not understand the complexities of the adult world. They do not realize that their parents have entire lives, concerns, and histories that pre-date their arrival. They are not born knowing what is expected of them or what constitutes a good idea versus a bad one. They live life moment by moment, treating each experience as a grand experiment.

How each moment unfolds determines the kind of "knowing" a child absorbs. While their unique temperament and individuality influence how they adapt and learn, no one enters this world inherently knowing how to navigate life on this planet. No one comes in "knowing better." Yet, the dictate of "you should know better" is repeated throughout history, despite its irrelevance to the actual experience of a child who is still innocent of the universal knowledge adults assume they possess.

As adults, we may still carry a hidden expectation that we should know better, and we might find this expectation operating silently in various areas of our lives. The assumption that we lack knowledge we *should* possess can become a heavy burden. This burden casts a shadow over our sense of self-confidence and personal power, affecting how we relate to ourselves internally and how we navigate the world externally. Recognizing this pattern is the first step toward dismantling the unrealistic expectations we place upon ourselves.

## What to Notice

Notice the moments in your daily life when a quiet, critical voice whispers that you should have known better. Pay attention to the situations that trigger this feeling—is it when you make a simple mistake at work, when a relationship encounters friction, or when you are trying something new? Observe the physical sensations that accompany this thought. You might feel a tightening in your chest, a sinking feeling in your stomach, or a flush of embarrassment. 

Notice if there is a vague sense of inner guilt that arises, even when it is not tied to a specific action or event. This guilt often strikes a slightly sickening chord within, a remnant of early experiences where your innocent lack of knowledge was met with expectation or reprimand. Be curious about how this assumption—that you are somehow deficient in knowledge you should possess—impacts your confidence. Does it make you hesitate to speak up? Does it prevent you from taking risks or stepping into your power? 

## Reflection

Take some time to reflect on your earliest memories of being told that you should know better, or similar phrases that implied you were lacking in expected knowledge. How did those moments shape your understanding of yourself and the world? Consider how the innocence of your childhood perspective was met by the expectations of the adults around you. 

Reflect on the areas of your life today where you feel the shadow of this burden. Where do you hold yourself to an impossible standard of pre-existing knowledge? How might your life feel different if you could fully embrace the truth that it is okay to not know everything, that every moment is still an opportunity for learning and experimentation? Imagine what it would be like to release the guilt of not knowing and instead approach yourself with the same compassion you would offer a child who is simply trying to figure things out.

## Practice

This week, practice extending grace to yourself when you encounter a situation where you feel you "should have known better." When that critical voice arises, pause and take a deep breath. Acknowledge the thought without judgment, and then gently remind yourself, "I am learning, and it is okay not to know everything." 

Consciously choose to reframe the experience from a failure of knowledge to an opportunity for growth. If you make a mistake, treat it as a data point in your ongoing experiment of life, rather than a reflection of your worth or intelligence. You might even visualize yourself as that blank canvas, open and receptive to new information, free from the concrete walls of unrealistic expectations. By consciously replacing the heavy burden of "knowing better" with the lightness of curiosity and self-compassion, you can begin to reclaim your self-confidence and personal power.

## Source Note

This teaching is adapted from Susan Drury's *Elevating Your Origins to Love: A Guided Journey of Transformation, Healing, and Power*, focusing on the profound impact of the phrase "you should know better" and the importance of recognizing our inherent innocence and capacity for learning.
