teachings.title: Finding Your Authentic Rhythm: Transcending Thyroid Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan reframes thyroid imbalance as an embodied language about our internal timing, showing how patterns of slowing (safety, hiding) and speeding (worthiness-as-performance) are meaningful responses rather than failures. She invites readers to listen to the body's rhythm, use neuroplasticity to shift old stories, and cultivate a dynamic, compassionate relationship with rest and action. The piece centers curiosity, embodiment, and the chrysalis metaphor to honor necessary seasons of transformation.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Let me paint a picture for you.

And one of the most profound aspects is navigating our own internal sense of timing. Have you ever felt like you were running a race you didn’t sign up for, your heart pounding with a relentless urgency to *do more, be more, achieve more*? Or have you felt the opposite—a profound and heavy slowness, as if you’re moving through water while the rest of the world zips by in a blur, a little voice whispering that it’s safer to stay small, to stay quiet, to not take up too much space?

Most of us know both of these feelings. We oscillate between the frantic and the frozen, the rushed and the reluctant. This isn’t a personal failing. It’s a deep pattern, a story our bodies learn to tell. And so often, the physical storyteller of this very human drama is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the base of our throat—the thyroid.

I remember a particular winter years ago. The Vancouver rain felt relentless, and a deep, cellular slowness had settled into my bones. My energy felt thick, my creative well seemed not just dry, but frozen solid. A familiar and harsh narrative of self-criticism was beginning to brew, whispering that I *should* be doing more, writing more, seeing more clients. The world outside my window seemed to be humming with an energy I simply couldn’t access. One afternoon, I was watching a documentary about monarch butterflies. The film showed the chrysalis stage in intricate detail—the utter stillness, the complete dissolving of the caterpillar into a kind of cellular soup before the miraculous reforming could begin. I felt a pang of impatience, a judgment against my own stillness. And then, a deeper wisdom rippled through me, a quiet voice from my own body’s knowing. The chrysalis wasn’t doing nothing. It was in the midst of the most profound transformation imaginable. It was not on my timeline, or the filmmaker's, or the world's. It was on the timeline of life itself. In that moment, I felt a deep bow of respect for that sacred, soupy, messy, and utterly necessary stillness. And I felt a wave of compassion for my own body, for my thyroid, and for its quiet, insistent message to simply *be*.

## The Body’s Sacred Messenger

The thyroid is the master conductor of our metabolic rhythm. It sits at the base of the throat, a place the yogis call the *vishuddha* chakra, the center of expression and truth. It sends out hormones that tell our cells how quickly or slowly to burn fuel, how much energy to generate, how fast our heart should beat. It is exquisitely sensitive, a finely tuned instrument that responds not just to our physical needs, but to our deepest beliefs about safety, worthiness, and our place in the world.

When this delicate gland is thrown off balance, it’s not a malfunction. It is a message. It is the body, in its infinite wisdom, trying to communicate a story that we have perhaps been too busy, or too afraid, to hear. The patterns of imbalance are not pathologies to be eradicated, but invitations into a deeper relationship with ourselves. They are love letters from our own being, asking for our attention.

## The Pattern of Slowing: When Safety Means Hiding

For many, especially women, the thyroid learns to slow down. This is the pattern of hypothyroidism. On a physical level, it can manifest as fatigue that sleep doesn’t touch, a persistent feeling of coldness, hair loss, brain fog that makes words and thoughts feel just out of reach, and a general sense of sluggishness. It can feel like you’re trying to drive with the emergency brake on, a deep and frustrating inertia.

But what is the deeper story here? So often, this pattern is rooted in a belief that it is not safe to be fully seen, fully expressed, fully powerful. Perhaps somewhere in your childhood, your authentic, vibrant self—your loud laugh, your strong opinions, your boundless energy—was met with criticism, punishment, or dismissal. Maybe you learned that being quiet, agreeable, and small was the best way to secure love and belonging. Your nervous system, in its brilliant and protective wisdom, created a neural pathway: *Big energy is dangerous. It gets me into trouble. Slow down to be safe. Dampen your life force to survive.*

And so, the thyroid, listening intently to this deep, unconscious narrative, obliges. It dials down the metabolic fire. It’s not trying to sabotage you; it’s trying to protect you based on an old map. It’s a form of energetic hiding. The body creates a physical reality that matches the belief that you must not shine too brightly, lest you attract unwanted attention or be “too much” for others. It’s a profound act of love from a younger part of you, a strategy that has simply outlived its purpose. The fatigue becomes a weighted blanket, forcing you to retreat when all you really want is to expand.

## The Pattern of Speeding: When Worthiness Is a Performance

The other side of the coin is the pattern of speeding up—hyperthyroidism. Here, the thyroid is overactive, flooding the body with hormones that scream, *faster, faster, faster*. This can look like a constant, humming anxiety, heart palpitations that feel like a trapped bird in your chest, unexplained weight loss, insomnia, and a feeling of being perpetually “on” and unable to rest. It’s a state of relentless, wired exhaustion.

What is the story beneath this frantic pace? It is almost always a deeply ingrained belief that your worth is conditional. It is the story that you must earn your place through doing, achieving, and producing. The underlying fear is that if you stop, if you rest, your value will disappear. You will be seen as lazy, unproductive, and ultimately, unworthy of love. This isn’t just a personal belief; it’s a cultural one. We are marinated in a society that celebrates the “hustle,” the relentless drive, the cult of productivity.

The body internalizes this pressure. The nervous system gets locked in a sympathetic “fight-or-flight” state, and the thyroid becomes the engine of that perpetual emergency. It’s running the body ragged, not out of ambition, but out of a deep, existential terror of stopping. The belief is: *My worth depends on my accomplishment. I must speed up to be worthy.* Rest feels dangerous. Stillness feels like failure. And so you run, and run, and run, until the body simply cannot run anymore.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Transcending the Duality: Finding Your Authentic Rhythm

So what do we do? How do we heal this deep rift in our being? The answer is not to “fix” the thyroid. The answer is to change the story. The work is to transcend the duality of fast versus slow and come home to something far more nuanced, far more true: your own authentic rhythm.

This is where we bring in the beautiful concept of neuroplasticity—the brain’s ability to form new neural pathways. The old beliefs that “slow is safe” or “fast is worthy” are simply well-worn grooves in the brain. We can create new ones. We can teach our bodies and our beings a new truth, one of unconditional worthiness and inherent safety.

Finding your authentic rhythm is not about settling on a perfect, unchanging pace. It is about cultivating the capacity to listen inwardly, moment by moment. It’s a dynamic dance. There will be seasons for the quiet, inward work of the chrysalis. And there will be seasons for the joyful, expansive flight of the butterfly. Neither is better than the other. Both are essential parts of the whole.

Begin by noticing. Without judgment, simply notice your own rhythm. Are you rushing when you could be savoring? Are you holding back when you could be expressing? Place a hand on your throat, over your thyroid, and just breathe. Send it a little warmth, a little gratitude. It has been working so hard for you, telling a story it thought you needed to survive.

Transformation is not a race. The butterfly emerges when it is ready, not when it is forced. Trusting this timing is perhaps the most profound healing we can offer ourselves. It means releasing the belief that you must slow down to be safe *and* the belief that you must speed up to be worthy. It means finding the courage to simply be, in this moment, exactly as you are.

What would it feel like to trust the timing of your own becoming? To know that the moments of rest are just as valuable as the moments of action? To feel a sense of worthiness that is not tied to your output, but is inherent to your being? This is not a mental exercise; it is a felt sense in the body. It is the feeling of your feet on the earth, the gentle rise and fall of your own breath, the steady beat of your own heart.

This is the transcendent possibility held within the thyroid. It invites us to move beyond the frantic push and the fearful pull, and to find our own unique, sacred cadence. It is the rhythm of the soul, and it has been waiting patiently for you to listen.

It is the rhythm of you. Unrushed. Unforced. Finally, and fully, home.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: No Leg to Stand On: The Emotional Roots of Hip and Leg Pain
teachings.title: No Leg to Stand On: The Emotional Roots of Hip and Leg Pain
teachings.summary: Susan uses Rosalind’s story to show how chronic hip and leg pain can be an embodied message of emotional rigidity—unprocessed grief, fear, and long-held duty that harden tissues and nervous-system responses. She links neurobiology (amygdala, sympathetic arousal, psoas tension) with a compassionate, safety-first approach to unwinding patterns and reclaiming flexible stability through somatic listening and gentle nervous-system re-education.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman I’ll call Rosalind first came to see me folded in on herself. Not literally, of course, but her energy was. She moved with a profound stiffness, her hips so tight they seemed fused, her knees locking with every hesitant step. She told me about the pain—a deep, grinding ache in her right hip that radiated down her leg, making the simple act of walking a monumental effort. She’d been a dancer in her youth, she said, a wry, sad smile touching her lips. Now, the memory of that suppleness felt like a ghost from another life.

“I feel like I have no leg to stand on,” she whispered, and the truth of that statement hung in the air between us, shimmering with a meaning far deeper than just the physical.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We are built for movement, for flow, for the glorious, multidirectional dance of life. Our hips, with their incredible ball-and-socket joints, are designed for a full range of motion—forward, backward, side to side, and in rotation. They are our foundation, our ultimate grounding rods, the connection between our upper body and the earth. Our legs are the pillars that carry us forward on our journey. They are meant to be both stable *and* mobile, strong *and* flexible.

So what happens when that inherent suppleness turns to rigidity? When the fluid grace of our stride becomes a painful shuffle? The body, in its infinite wisdom, is never just a collection of mechanical parts. It is a sacred messenger, and symptoms are its language. This is not a punishment. It is a profound act of love from a body that is desperate to get your attention, to communicate a truth that the conscious mind has been too busy or too frightened to acknowledge. When the hips and legs begin to cry out in pain, it is an invitation to look deeper. To ask: Where in my life have I become inflexible? Where am I refusing to bend? What forward movement am I resisting?

## The Body as a Battlefield

For Rosalind, the answer was everywhere. She was carrying the weight of a difficult divorce, a demanding career where she felt perpetually unsupported, and the heavy responsibility of caring for her aging parents. Her life was a landscape of obligations, and she met them with a rigid, unyielding sense of duty. She was, in her own words, “holding everything together.”

Her body was simply reflecting her inner reality. Her hips, the center of her stability, had become a battlefield where her deep need for support clashed with her fierce, self-imposed independence. Her legs, meant to carry her forward with confidence, were locked in a pattern of resistance, terrified to take the next step into an uncertain future. Every ounce of unprocessed grief from her divorce, every wave of resentment from her thankless job, every pang of guilt related to her parents—it all had to go somewhere. And it went into her tissues. The emotional burdens she carried had become, quite literally, physical restrictions.

This isn’t just poetry; it’s neurobiology. When we experience chronic stress, fear, or emotional overwhelm, our amygdala—the brain’s smoke detector—sounds the alarm. This triggers the sympathetic nervous system, flooding the body with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline. It’s a brilliant, ancient survival mechanism designed for short-term threats. But when the threat is not a saber-toothed tiger but a toxic work environment or a painful family dynamic, the alarm never shuts off. This sustained state of high alert has profound physical consequences. The large, powerful muscles of the hips and legs—the glutes, the quadriceps, the hamstrings—are primary movers in the fight-or-flight response. They tense up, ready for action. The psoas, a deep and sensitive core muscle that connects the spine to the legs, is often called the “muscle of the soul” because of its intimate connection to our deepest feelings of safety and fear. In a state of chronic threat, it becomes chronically contracted, pulling the whole pelvic region into a state of guarded tension. The body is preparing for a battle that is being waged internally, and in doing so, it creates a prison of its own making.

These patterns, repeated over time, carve deep neural pathways in the brain. The body *learns* to be rigid. The brain *learns* to anticipate pain. The vibrant, responsive tissue that was designed for dancing becomes dense, dehydrated, and starved of life force. We literally lose our flexibility, not because we are getting older, but because we are holding onto old fears, old grievances, and old ways of being that no longer serve us.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Rigidity of Fear

Think of a time you felt truly safe and supported. Perhaps walking on soft grass, your feet connecting with the earth. Or the feeling of being held in a loving embrace. In those moments, your body is soft, open, receptive. There is a natural suppleness in your joints, a fluid ease in your breath. This is our natural state.

Rigidity, on the other hand, is the signature of fear. It’s the body’s attempt to brace against impact, to protect itself from perceived danger. I see this so often in my clients. The stories are different, but the pattern is the same. The man with sciatica who was taught as a boy that “men don’t cry.” The woman with knee problems who was the designated peacemaker in a chaotic family, never allowed to have needs of her own. For many of us, as it was for Rosalind, this pattern begins in childhood. The developing nervous system is like soft clay, imprinted by its early experiences. If we grew up in an environment where it didn’t feel safe to be vulnerable, to be soft, to express our needs, to simply *be*—we learned to create armor. We tightened our hips, clenched our jaws, and held our breath. We learned, on a cellular level, that stability required rigidity. That survival depended on not needing anyone.

But this is a profound misunderstanding of the body’s wisdom. True stability is not rigid; it is flexible. It is the ability to stay grounded and centered *while* moving with the changing rhythms of life. It is the willow tree that bends in the wind, not the oak that shatters. When we lose our physical flexibility, it is a sign that we have lost our emotional and mental flexibility as well. We are stuck in a fixed position, resisting the natural flow of our own life force.

Working with Rosalind, we began a gentle process of unwinding. This was not about aggressive stretching or forcing the body into submission. That would only have reinforced the pattern of struggle. Instead, our work was about creating a profound quality of safety. Through gentle touch, guided meditation, and deep listening, we invited the nervous system to shift from its sympathetic high-alert into a parasympathetic state of rest, digest, and repair. We brought a warm, compassionate awareness to the places that were holding on so tightly. We explored the stories held in the dense, fibrous tissues of her hips—the unshed tears of her divorce, the silent rage at her boss, the profound, bone-deep loneliness of feeling unsupported. We didn’t try to banish the pain. Instead, we honored it as a messenger. We listened to it. We asked it what it had to tell her. And in the safety of that compassionate space, the stories began to pour out, and the tissues began to soften.

## The Dance of Flexible Stability

Slowly, tenderly, something began to shift. As Rosalind began to acknowledge and release the emotional burdens she had been carrying, her body began to respond. The chronic tension in her hips started to soften. The locked-down muscles began to remember their capacity for release. It was a process of re-educating the nervous system, of creating new neural pathways that whispered *safety* instead of *danger*.

This is the transcendent possibility hidden within the pain of our hips and legs. It is the invitation to step beyond the old fears that have kept us locked in place. It is the call to reclaim our natural inheritance of flexible stability—to trust that we can be both strong and yielding, grounded and free.

Your body is built to stay in step with the music of your life, whatever its tempo, whatever its rhythm. It is designed to carry you through challenges with grace and to stand firm in your truth without becoming rigid. The journey from pain to possibility is not about fighting against your body, but about entering into a loving, conscious relationship with it. It is about learning to listen to its whispers before they become screams.

What would it be like to trust your foundation? To know, in your very bones, that you have a right to be here, that you are fully supported by the earth beneath you and the life force within you? What would it be like to allow your legs to carry you forward not with fear, but with a quiet confidence in the journey itself?

This is the dance of healing. It is slow, it is sacred, and it is available to every single one of us.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Stuck, Uncertain, Afraid to Step Forward: What Your Feet Know](/blog/feet-stuck-uncertain)
- [The Sacred Central Channel: What Your Spine Communicates](/blog/spine-sacred-central-channel)
- [Shame, Sexuality, and the Silencing of Creative Power](/blog/reproductive-shame-sexuality)

**More on Hips & Legs:**

- [When Flexibility Becomes Rigidity: What Your Hips Are Holding](/blog/hips-flexibility-rigidity)
- [Hips and Legs: The Foundation of Your Dance Through Life](/blog/hips-legs-dance-through-life)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

reflectionPrompts: When did you first notice stiffness or guardedness in your hips or legs? What was happening in your life then, emotionally or practically?
Bring attention to how you brace or hold in daily life (tasks, relationships, responsibilities). Where do you notice tension in your pelvis, hips, or legs when you imagine asking for support?
If your body could answer the question 'What do I need to take the next step?', what image, word, or sensation arises? What is one small, compassionate response you could offer to that answer?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a safe, quiet spot to sit or stand with feet on the ground. Close your eyes if that feels okay, and take 6–10 slow, connected breaths. On each exhale, imagine the hips softening a little and the weight of the body being supported by the earth; if comfortable, let your knees micro-bend or allow a tiny pelvic rock to invite release. Move only within comfortable limits—if you feel sharp pain, dizziness, or alarm, pause and rest. This is a gentle, complementary practice and not a substitute for medical or physical-therapy care; consult your healthcare provider if pain is severe, new, or persistent.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article includes themes of divorce, grief, long-term emotional burden, and childhood imprinting that may evoke strong feelings. You have permission to pause at any time and return when you feel steadier.

If the material brings up traumatic memories, overwhelming grief, or intense emotional distress, consider reaching out to a qualified therapist, physician, or a trusted support person for guidance and containment.

Somatic practices described are complementary. If you have acute, unexplained, or worsening pain, recent injury, or a medical condition affecting hips or legs, please seek assessment from an appropriate healthcare professional before starting new movement or bodywork practices.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Body as Messenger - Why Your Symptoms Are Speaking to You
teachings.title: The Body as Messenger - Why Your Symptoms Are Speaking to You
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to treat symptoms as communicative messages from the body’s deeper intelligence rather than random mechanical failures. Drawing on Taoist patience and somatic inquiry, she offers a compassionate framework for listening—using breath, curiosity, and metaphorical 'translations' of organs—while honoring the role of conventional medical care. The essay emphasizes nervous-system regulation, the holographic nature of symptoms, and the need for humility, community, and steady practice in decoding what the body is asking for.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You have been carrying a language all your life that you were never explicitly taught - a subtle, somatic dialect spoken by tissues, nerves and organs. It is a language that arrives before your first coherent thought, that remembers what words cannot hold, and that will not stop speaking until you finally lean in and listen. When a joint tightens, when your breath shortens, when a pattern of fatigue returns like a recurring guest, these are not random failures of machinery. They are messages from the deeper intelligence that lives in you. They are the body as messenger.

Think of symptoms as messengers from below your conscious awareness. They are not separate from you; they are you in a different register. Pain is not your enemy - it is information. Illness is not a punishment - it is an invitation. When you receive a twinge in your shoulder, an ache in your belly, a persistent cough, your organism is pointing to a pattern, an unmet need, a history that was never properly processed. If you treat only the outward manifestation, if you apply a salve to the skin while ignoring the story below it, the message will not be silenced. The body will continue to reflect the same truth until you investigate the source.

There is a Taoist way of hearing this wisdom. Lao Tzu reminds us that a process begins with a single step - "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step." Approach your symptom as the first step into a deeper conversation, not the last desperate problem to be fixed. The Tao does not hasten and yet everything is accomplished. Likewise your body does not rush toward healing; it invites you into a patient, persistent attentiveness that transforms over time.

You learned early how to survive. As a child you absorbed beliefs and paradigms like language - what to expect from others, what you deserved, how safety was earned. These early templates settled into your nervous system and became the scaffolding for how your body orients toward the world. When an emotion was unsafe to express, a place of the body learned to hold it. When needs were denied, a pattern of constriction or weakness developed. You are not to blame for these adaptations. They were brilliant, necessary responses. Yet they have become habits that continue to shape your physiology long after their original purpose has passed.

To understand the body as messenger is to understand the holographic nature of your form. Every part of you carries the whole. The way you digest an idea can mirror how you digest food. The mobility in your hips speaks to your flexibility in relationship. A thyroid imbalance can be both a metabolic event and a reflection of how you give and receive energy across your life. This holography means that a shift in one place has the capacity to reverberate everywhere else. When you restore mobility to a shoulder, you may also free a pattern of responsibility held in the chest. When you tend to a gut wound with curiosity and care, you may also open to previously inaccessible possibilities in your work or intimacy. Your physical systems are not isolated - they are conversations with the world and with the Self.

It is also true that treating symptoms without addressing the influences behind them often leads to return. A pain suppressed will migrate. A lack of attention to what ails the heart may become a systemic exhaustion. You may soothe the surface and delay the inevitable disclosure, but the deeper intelligence that speaks through your cells keeps asking to be heard. Symptoms do not punish you for ignoring them; they simply become more persistent and more creative in getting your attention until you finally take the time to investigate with tenderness.

What does investigation look like? It is not a frantic search for a miracle. It is practiced receptivity. It begins with your breath. Slow, deliberate inhalation brings you into presence. Your exhalation becomes the relinquishing of urgency. In that space between breaths you can place your hand on the area that troubles you and say, silently or aloud: I see you. I hear you. What is your message? This simple acknowledgment changes the field. Gratitude returns agency to the body. From that gentle place of alliance, you can listen without judgment.

Listening often requires translation tools. The work I offer, and the set of cards many of you already know, are simply maps - frameworks for decoding what the body is saying. They point toward underlying themes: the bladder that holds resentment about release, the breasts that reveal the architecture of nurture and self-mothering, the lungs that teach you about what you can inhale and what you cannot yet exhale. Each organ offers a metaphor and an invitation. When you lean into the inquiry beneath a symptom, you begin to perceive patterns that previously felt like random misfortune.

Take the bladder as an example. On the surface an infection or urgency may seem like a microbial event. Beneath that, the bladder can speak of a long habit of holding - emotions you were not allowed to release, shame around expression, the belief that letting go will result in loss. This organ teaches you about the tension between control and surrender. Its message, when heard, asks you to examine where you are withholding in order to be safe, or withholding because release felt punished in the past. When you honor what needs to flow and practice letting go within safe container, the physiological system can return to graceful function.

Consider the liver and gallbladder. Their anatomy is intimately tied to how you metabolize life - particularly the bitter, the unjust, the anger that has been left to crystallize. Gallstones are literal stones of bitterness - hardened residues of unprocessed indignation. To work with this is to develop metabolic courage - the willingness to metabolize resentment into learning, to practice discernment without destruction. The biochemical health of the liver reflects your capacity to transform what once hurt you into a medicine for future aliveness.

The immune system carries a particularly potent message. At its best it is a wise guardian - a constant teacher about boundaries, about what belongs to you and what does not. When the immune system becomes aggressive toward yourself, it reveals a profound fragmentation of identity - parts of you exiled and treated as foreign. Auto-immune illness invites you to bring those parts home. It asks you to tend the exile with tenderness and to re-integrate what has been split off through shame, secrecy, or trauma. Healing is not simply an act of defense; it is an act of reconciliation.

And then there is the nervous system - the swift highway of safety and threat that learned its rules often before you could speak. When your nervous system is locked into vigilance, chronic pain and anxiety become the language of that survival code. The nervous system keeps operating on old evidence unless you provide new evidence of safety. This is why somatic practices - slow breath, attending to sensations, safe touch, regulated movement - are so essential. They teach the nervous system new stories about being safe, about taking pleasure, about resting. Rewiring is not a betrayal of memory; it is an act of sovereignty where you choose new defaults that support your fullest life.

Illness as invitation is not a romanticization of suffering. There are-times when despite deep work, bodies remain afflicted. Some illnesses are part of a soul path that asks for endurance, empathy, or particular forms of presence that do not resolve with a cure. If this is your path, receive my compassion and my deepest respect. Your manifestation does not indicate moral failure. It indicates a mystery with purposes we may never fully understand. Even here your body continues to be a teacher - inviting you toward self-compassion, toward community, toward the embodied richness of being known and cared for.

When you begin the work of investigation, you need humility. You must allow yourself to not know. You must be willing to discover what you did not know that you did not know. The posture of inquiry is not the same as blame. It is an honoring of your complexity - a recognition that every pattern served you once and has an intent that is alive even when no longer helpful. Sit with curiosity. Be patient. The Tao teaches that "the softest thing in the universe overcomes the hardest thing in the universe." Gentleness often dissolves what force cannot.

The work of decoding is both personal and relational. Your body speaks about your relationships with others, with yourself, and with life. A repeated throat issue may be more than laryngitis; it may be an invitation to find voice, to say the truth that has been stifled by fear. Shoulder pain may be a literal compression of burdens you have carried for others. Knee pain may teach you about humility and about where your ego refuses to bend. These are not simplistic metaphors. They are precise reflections of how your inner life shapes tissue and cellular processes. When you integrate the story, when you make different choices in relationships and in how you relate to yourself, the tissue will often follow.

Your healing is an art of translation. You translate symptom into narrative without inventing moral meaning. You translate pain into instruction without making yourself wrong. You translate illness into invitation without glorifying suffering. This takes practice. It takes witnesses. It takes rituals of attention. It takes being taught how to hold a part of yourself with reverence. In community, the body feels safe to reveal. In solitude, the body learns the discipline of listening.

There will be moments of resistance. You may read an "inquiry" and feel anger, or grief, or the urge to run. These resistances are not obstacles to be shamefully bypassed. They are the exact doors you need to open. Resistance points directly to what needs care. When you meet resistance with compassion instead of judgment, you create a field that allows the message to unravel. Tears, tremors, or sudden memories may come - they are part of the body's clearing. Let them move. Witness them. Anchor them with breath and safe touch.

Part of this work is practical. You will still, at times, require medicine, surgery, or emergency intervention. You are not being asked to reject modern medicine. What you are invited into is a partnership: use appropriate clinical care while also opening to what the symptom is saying. Treat the immediate with clarity and tenderness and the root with curiosity and courage. When both domains are honored, you cultivate an integrated wisdom that supports lasting change.

Another practical aspect is formulating new habits that support the messenger. This means tending your sleep, retraining your nervous system with breath and movement, making dietary choices that honor your inner chemistry, creating boundaries that protect your heart and lungs from undue injury. It means having conversations with people who contributed to old patterns when that is safe and appropriate. It means saying no more often. It means receiving help. These are not small acts. They are the grammar of a life that listens to itself.

The body will tell the story until it is attended to. Often it will escalate until you finally do. It will shift the location, change the tone, or intensify the message so you cannot ignore its plea. Understand this without panic. This persistence is a form of devotion - your organism will not allow a crucial lesson to be missed. When you finally turn your attention toward that lesson, something shifts. Not always instantaneously. Not always perfectly. But the tide begins to move. Patterns that seemed immortal begin to soften. You find new options for action. You reclaim energy squandered on defending a past that no longer serves you.

At the end of the day, this is a conversation between two intelligences - the intelligence of the body and the intelligence of consciousness. Both have roles, both have dignity. Your task is to become an adept translator, to steward the field where those two intelligences meet. When you do, you learn a new ethics of being: you treat your form as a sacred messenger, you listen to the small signals before they become cries, and you create a life in which your body is not merely a problem to be solved but the most intimate ally in your journey toward wholeness.

May you cultivate the courage to listen, the patience to investigate, and the tenderness to receive what your body has been trying to say all along. May each symptom be met as an emissary and each healing as a deeper knowing. And may you remember, always, that this is not about perfection but about alignment - the slow, steady coming home into your own embodied wisdom. As Lao Tzu reminds us, the soft and yielding overcome the rigid. In your gentleness toward yourself, healing often finds its truest and most luminous path.

Blessings on your listening.

What is your message?” Notice sensations, images, words, or emotions that arise without judgment. If anything feels overwhelming, pause, return to the breath, and seek professional or trusted support as needed. This is a gentle, complementary practice and not a substitute for medical care.

teachings.sourceTitle: When Your Body Attacks Itself: Autoimmune Patterns and Self-Rejection
teachings.title: When Your Body Attacks Itself: Autoimmune Patterns and Self-Rejection
teachings.summary: This piece frames autoimmune illness as a profound somatic expression of self-rejection rooted in early survival strategies and attachment wounding. Susan invites readers to understand chronic inflammation and immune exhaustion as learned states of hyper-vigilance and depletion, and to practice compassionate inner diplomacy—welcoming exiled parts back into the definition of self through steady, embodied attention. The emphasis is on curiosity, non-blame, and gradual rewiring of threat responses rather than quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
>
> There is a practice I do every evening that has quietly transformed my relationship with myself.

We learn so early to divide the world into ‘me’ and ‘not-me,’ ‘safe’ and ‘unsafe,’ ‘good’ and ‘bad.’ It’s a fundamental survival mechanism, a blueprint handed down through generations, etched into our most primal neural pathways. Our very cells learn this language of borders and belonging. The immune system, in its profound wisdom, is the ultimate guardian of this internal territory. It is the master of discernment, the silent, vigilant network that patrols the frontiers of our physical being, asking of every molecule, every microbe, every cell: *Are you me?*
>
> For most of us, most of the time, this intricate dance of recognition and response happens far below the level of our conscious awareness. It’s a miracle we take for granted—the body’s innate capacity to protect its own integrity. But what happens when the guardian turns on the very kingdom it is meant to protect? What happens when the body’s answer to that fundamental question—*Are you me?*—becomes a confused and resounding *No*?
>
> This is the bewildering and painful reality of an autoimmune condition. It is the body attacking its own tissues—the thyroid, the joints, the skin, the gut—as if they were foreign invaders. It is the ultimate crisis of identity, a civil war waged at the cellular level. I have sat with so many beloved clients over the years, their bodies reeling from this internal betrayal. I see the exhaustion in their eyes, the deep ache of a system that can no longer find its way back to a state of peace. The body, in its infinite intelligence, is sending a message, a desperate plea for integration. It is reflecting a pattern of self-rejection so profound that it has become flesh.
>
> ## The Battlefield Within
>
> Think of chronic inflammation, so common in autoimmune patterns, as the body’s expression of a perpetually perceived threat. The alarms are always ringing. The soldiers are always on patrol. The body is locked in a state of high alert, burning through its precious life-force energy to fight a battle against… itself. It’s a state of hyper-vigilance that is utterly exhausting. This isn’t a design flaw. It’s a learned response. Somewhere along the way, often in our earliest moments of life, our nascent nervous system learned that the world—or even parts of our own inner world—was not safe.
>
> Perhaps we had a caregiver who was frightened or overwhelmed, and our own system mirrored that fear. Perhaps our authentic expressions of anger or grief were met with disapproval, and we learned to turn that energy inward, to reject those parts of ourselves as ‘unacceptable.’ We learned to create an ‘other’ within our own being. We learned to say *No* to our own life force. This is not a conscious choice, but a deeply ingrained survival strategy. The child, in her profound need for attachment, will sever connection with a part of herself before she will risk severing connection with her caregiver. And so, a part of the self is exiled, pushed into the shadows of the unconscious, where it becomes ‘not-me.’
>
> I remember a woman I worked with, a brilliant artist with rheumatoid arthritis that had painfully gnarled her hands. She spoke of a childhood where her creative impulses were seen as messy, impractical, and a waste of time. She became a lawyer, a ‘practical’ and ‘successful’ woman, but her hands—the very instruments of her soul’s deepest calling—were screaming in protest. Her immune system was attacking the joints in her hands, the physical embodiment of the creativity she had rejected. Her body was literally at war with her own artistry. We worked together for months, not to ‘fix’ her hands, but to welcome home the exiled artist. We made space for the messy, the impractical, the joyful expression of her creative soul. Slowly, gently, the inflammation in her hands began to subside. The war was not won; it was rendered obsolete.
>
> This is not about blame. It is never about blame. It is about compassionately illuminating the patterns that have brought us to this moment. Every pattern, no matter how painful, once served a purpose. Rejecting our messy, creative, emotional selves was a strategy for survival, a way to secure love and belonging in a world that felt conditional. But the body, in its unwavering honesty, always keeps the score. It remembers the parts of ourselves we have exiled. And it will continue to send us messages, in the form of symptoms, until we are ready to listen.
>
> [PROMO_SESSIONS]
>
> ## The Exhaustion of Defense
>
> If chronic inflammation is the body on high alert, then immune *deficiency* can be seen as the inevitable outcome of that prolonged war. It is the exhaustion that comes from constantly defending, from pouring all of our resources into maintaining the borders. The system simply runs out of energy. It becomes depleted, vulnerable, unable to mount an effective response to genuine threats.
>
> This is more than just a physical state; it is a spiritual and emotional one. It’s the feeling of being utterly spent, of having nothing left to give. It’s the soul-deep weariness that comes from a lifetime of holding parts of yourself at bay. The energy it takes to suppress your truth, to perform a version of yourself you believe is more acceptable, is immense. The body pays the price. I see this in clients who have spent decades in careers that stifle their spirit, or in relationships where they feel they must constantly shrink themselves to be loved. Their immune systems are often the first to wave the white flag, succumbing to every cold and flu that comes their way, as if to say, *I cannot fight anymore. I am done.*
>
> I recall another client, a man with a severe autoimmune skin condition that left him in constant discomfort. He was a successful executive, known for his calm and unflappable demeanor. But as we worked together, a different story emerged. He spoke of a childhood with a volatile, angry father, where the only way to stay safe was to become invisible, to show no emotion, to have no needs. He had become a master of self-containment, but his skin was erupting with the rage he had suppressed for a lifetime. His body was screaming the truth his mouth could not speak. The healing for him was not in a cream or a lotion, but in the slow, terrifying, and ultimately liberating process of allowing himself to feel his own anger, to give it a voice, to let it move through him without judgment.
>
> So, what is the way through? How do we begin to broker peace in this internal war? The journey begins not with a new battle, not with a new strategy to eradicate the ‘bad’ parts, but with a radical act of diplomacy. It begins with turning toward the parts of ourselves we have deemed unacceptable, the parts our body has learned to attack, and extending a hand of welcome.
>
> It requires us to ask, with genuine curiosity and boundless compassion: *What is the message you are carrying for me? What part of my own being have I refused to love?* It is a process of expanding our definition of ‘self’ to include all of it—the anger, the grief, the fear, the messy creativity, the inconvenient truths. It is about recognizing that these exiled parts are not enemies. They are our own life force, frozen in time, waiting to be reclaimed. This is the work of alchemy, of turning the lead of our suffering into the gold of our consciousness.
>
> This is the work of neuroplasticity in action. As we consciously and repeatedly turn toward these rejected parts with warmth and acceptance, we begin to rewire the ancient neural pathways of threat and defense. We create new patterns of safety and connection within our own nervous system. We teach the guardians at the gate that they can stand down, that the kingdom is finally at peace with itself. This is not a passive process. It is an active and courageous choice, moment by moment, to meet ourselves with love.
>
> ## A Benediction for the Body
>
> This is not a quick fix. It is a journey of profound devotion, a slow and gentle turning toward the self. It is the practice of meeting your own being with the same unconditional love you might offer to a frightened child. It is the work of a lifetime, a sacred pilgrimage back to the wholeness that has always been your birthright.
>
> So today, I invite you to place a hand on your heart. Feel the steady rhythm beneath your palm. And perhaps, just perhaps, you might whisper to the deepest parts of your being, to every cell, every tissue, every forgotten corner of your soul:
>
> *You are all me. You are all welcome. You are all loved.*
>
> May you have the courage to meet yourself with radical compassion. May you find the spaciousness to welcome home the exiled parts of your magnificent being. And may you remember, in your very bones, that you are not a battlefield. You are a sacred, unified whole, a radiant expression of life itself.
>
>

---

teachings.sourceTitle: A Practice for Releasing Anger and Restoring Liver Harmony
teachings.title: A Practice for Releasing Anger and Restoring Liver Harmony
teachings.summary: Susan reframes anger as a sacred messenger and offers a short, embodied protocol to help release held resentment and restore harmony to the liver-gallbladder system. The piece combines an active ‘Wood Chopper’ breath and movement, a hands-on liver meditation with green-light imagery, and a forgiveness visualization, plus a simple daily check-in to support ongoing integration.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I want to begin with a confession.

And one of the most profound aspects of this human experience is navigating the powerful, often overwhelming, energy of anger.

I remember a time, many years ago, when I was consumed by a rage so potent it felt like a physical presence in my body. It was a hot, bitter stone lodged just under my right ribcage, and its heat radiated through my entire being. I was angry at a situation I felt powerless to change, and the injustice of it all felt like a poison I was forced to swallow every day. My sleep was disturbed, my digestion was a mess, and a constant, low-grade headache became my unwelcome companion. My body, in its infinite wisdom, was screaming at me. It was my liver, the body’s master alchemist, crying out under the strain of metabolizing so much unprocessed rage.

We tend to think of anger as a “negative” emotion, something to be suppressed, controlled, or immediately banished. We’re taught to “calm down,” to “let it go,” to not make a scene. But what if anger isn’t the enemy? What if it’s simply a messenger, a powerful surge of energy designed to show us where our boundaries have been crossed, where our truth has been violated, or where a deep injustice is occurring?

Your liver, that incredible, resilient organ, is responsible for over 500 vital functions in your body. It’s a master metabolizer, breaking down not just the food you eat and the toxins you encounter, but the very experiences of your life. When you experience something that feels unjust, unfair, or enraging, it’s your liver and its partner, the gallbladder, that are tasked with processing that energetic and emotional load. When the load is too heavy, or when the anger is suppressed and left to fester, it can crystallize into what I call bitterness—a hard, dense energy that can manifest as physical symptoms, from digestive issues and fatigue to, in the case of the gallbladder, literal stones.

This isn’t just poetry; it’s a reflection of the deep connection between our minds, our emotions, and our physical bodies. Modern neuroscience is beginning to map the very neural pathways that confirm this ancient wisdom. When we repeatedly experience and suppress an emotion like anger, we strengthen the neural circuits associated with that pattern. The body learns that this powerful energy is unsafe to express, so it stores it away in our tissues, creating a state of chronic internal stress. But here is the beautiful, hopeful truth: because of neuroplasticity, our brains and bodies can change. We can create new neural pathways. We can learn to relate to our anger in a new way—not as a poison to be stored, but as a powerful life force to be honored, listened to, and moved through our systems with conscious awareness.

So, how do we begin to metabolize what we’ve been storing? How do we work with the body to release the grip of old anger and restore harmony to our liver and our entire being? It begins with creating a safe space within yourself to feel what you are feeling, without judgment. It begins with practice.

Here is a guided practice I offer to you, a gentle yet powerful way to begin this process of release and restoration. Find a quiet, comfortable space where you won’t be disturbed for at least 15-20 minutes.

## A Guided Practice for Liver-Gallbladder Healing

### Step 1: The Anger Release Breath

Begin by sitting or lying down comfortably. Close your eyes and bring your awareness to your breath. For the first few moments, simply notice the natural rhythm of your inhale and exhale.

Now, I invite you to gently bring to mind a situation that has been causing you to feel anger, frustration, or resentment. Don’t force it, just allow an image, a memory, or a feeling to surface. Notice where you feel this anger in your body. Perhaps it’s a tightness in your jaw, a heat in your chest, or a familiar ache under your right ribs. Just notice.

We will now use a specific breath to begin moving this energy. It’s called the Wood Chopper breath. On your inhale, reach your arms up overhead, perhaps even interlacing your fingers. As you inhale, imagine you are gathering up all of that hot, stagnant energy of anger into your arms. Then, on your exhale, you will forcefully swing your arms down as you make a loud “Ha!” sound from your belly. The exhale is sharp, audible, and comes from your diaphragm. You can bend your knees and fold forward as you do this.

Let’s try it. Inhale, reaching up, gathering the anger… and “Ha!” as you swing down. Inhale, gather it all up… “Ha!” Do this for at least 8-10 repetitions, or until you feel a shift in the energy. It might feel awkward at first, but allow yourself to be fully in the practice. You are giving your anger a voice and a way out.

After your last repetition, come back to a still, seated position. Place your hands on your lap and just feel. Notice the tingling, the vibration, the new sense of space you may have created.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

### Step 2: The Liver Meditation

Now, bring your right hand to your right side, just below your ribcage. This is the home of your liver. Let your hand rest there, a warm, comforting presence.

Close your eyes again and bring all of your awareness to this space beneath your hand. Imagine you can breathe directly into your liver. With each inhale, picture a beautiful, healing green light—the color of new spring leaves—flowing into your liver, bathing every cell in soothing, cleansing energy. With each exhale, imagine a murky, grey smoke leaving your liver, carrying with it all the old bitterness, resentment, and unprocessed anger.

Inhale the vibrant, healing green light… and exhale the grey smoke of what no longer serves you. Continue this for several minutes. You might whisper words of gratitude to your liver. *Thank you for working so hard for me. Thank you for processing so much. I am here with you now. You are safe.* Feel the warmth of your hand, the gentle rhythm of your breath, and the healing energy of the green light restoring your liver to its natural state of harmony and ease.

### Step 3: The Forgiveness Visualization

As you continue to breathe into your liver, allow your awareness to soften. Forgiveness is not about condoning harmful behavior. It is not for the other person. It is for you. It is the act of releasing the bitter poison of resentment from your own system so that you can be free.

Bring to mind the person or situation connected to the anger you’ve been holding. Imagine them standing before you. See them not as a monster, but as a soul on their own journey, with their own wounds and their own struggles. You don’t need to understand or excuse their actions. You are simply seeing them through the eyes of compassion.

Now, imagine a cord of energy connecting your liver to them. This cord may be thick and dark, pulsating with the energy of your anger and resentment. See it clearly. Now, from your heart, imagine you are calling forth a beautiful pair of golden scissors. These are your scissors of freedom. When you are ready, use these scissors to cut the cord. See it sever completely. The end attached to you retracts back into your body, where it is dissolved in the green light of your liver meditation. The other end retracts back to the other person. It is their energy, and you are no longer required to carry it.

Take a deep breath in, and as you exhale, whisper the words, “I release you. I set myself free.” Feel the profound shift as you reclaim your energy and your power. Stay with this feeling of freedom for a few moments.

## A Daily Practice for Liver Harmony

This deep practice is something you can return to whenever you feel the heat of anger rising. For daily maintenance, I recommend a simple morning practice. Upon waking, place your right hand over your liver, take three deep breaths, and send gratitude to this vital organ. This simple act of conscious connection can make a profound difference in how your body metabolizes the experiences of your day.

Anger is a sacred messenger. It is a fire that can either burn us from the inside out or fuel our transformation. By learning to listen to its message, to honor its power, and to move its energy with conscious practice, we can alchemize this potent force into a catalyst for profound healing and a deeper connection to our own truth.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Seeing with New Eyes: Vision Beyond Fear and Trauma](/blog/eyes-seeing-with-new-eyes)

**More on Liver-Gallbladder:**

- [The Alchemist of Anger: What Your Liver Is Processing](/blog/liver-alchemist-of-anger)
- [Gallstones of Bitterness: When Resentment Crystallizes](/blog/liver-gallstones-bitterness)

Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Walking Your Path: When Your Feet Finally Feel the Earth
teachings.title: Walking Your Path: When Your Feet Finally Feel the Earth
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to listen to the feet as intelligent messengers that hold both physical pain and life history. Through Catherine’s story of plantar fasciitis and a recent life upheaval, the article shows how gentle, grounded attention to the soles of the feet can create nervous-system safety, support neuroplastic change, and open small, meaningful steps forward. The emphasis is on curiosity, compassion, and the steady practice of returning to the body rather than quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I believe in the intelligence of the body the way some people believe in gravity — not as a theory, but as an undeniable, lived reality.

And sometimes, the most profound, most profound invitations to heal show up in the most ordinary of places. Our bodies, after all, are constantly speaking to us, and they rarely bother with small talk.

A woman I’ll call Catherine first came to see me with a pain so sharp in her left foot, she said it felt like walking on broken glass with every step. Plantar fasciitis, the doctors had told her. A common diagnosis for an uncommon level of suffering. They’d given her the stretches, the special inserts, the advice to rest. But the pain, a fierce and insistent messenger, refused to be silenced. It had a story to tell, and it was determined to be heard.

Catherine was an accountant in her late forties, a woman who had built her life on the solid ground of precision and predictability. Her world was one of spreadsheets and balanced budgets, of clear lines and known outcomes. But a recent, unexpected divorce had shattered that sense of order. Her path, once a clearly paved road leading to a comfortable retirement, had dissolved overnight into a dense, unfamiliar forest. She was, in her own words, “completely and utterly stuck.” She didn’t know which way to go, and so, her body had decided for her. It refused to move at all without screaming in protest.

Her feet, those incredible structures of twenty-six bones each, had become the repository for her fear. They held the story not just of the steps she had taken in her life—the confident strides into boardrooms, the patient pacing in hospital waiting rooms, the joyful dashes across sunny beaches—but of the one she was terrified to take now. The step into the unknown. The step into a life she had not planned.

This is what our bodies do. They speak for us when we have no words. They are the most honest storytellers we will ever know, faithfully recording every experience, every emotion, every unspoken fear. They are not betraying us with their pain. They are calling us home.

## The Stories Our Feet Tell

Our feet are our primary interface with the earth, the very ground of our being. They are our roots, our connection to the physical reality of our lives. When that connection feels fraught, when we don’t feel safe or supported, our feet are often the first to let us know. They are the foundation, and when the foundation is shaky, the entire structure feels unstable.

Think about it. Every step you have ever taken is recorded in the tissues of your feet. The joyful, bounding steps of childhood, chasing after a ball or a butterfly. The hesitant, shuffling steps of adolescence, navigating the treacherous terrain of high school hallways. The determined, purposeful strides of adulthood, marching toward a goal. The weary, heavy steps of grief, each one a monumental effort. They are all there. The entire history of your journey, with all its triumphs and sorrows, is held in the soles of your feet.

And so is the history of the steps you *didn’t* take.

The promotion you were afraid to ask for, convinced you weren’t ready. The love you were afraid to declare, terrified of rejection. The move you were afraid to make, clinging to the familiar. The truth you were afraid to speak, worried it would upset the peace. That fear of moving forward, of stepping onto a path that isn’t guaranteed, can manifest as physical pain. It can show up as bunions, as fallen arches, as the searing pain of plantar fasciitis. The body, in its infinite wisdom, creates a physical anchor to match the emotional one. If you *feel* stuck, your body will find a way to *be* stuck.

It’s a profound and sometimes frustrating conversation. But it is always, always an invitation. An invitation to listen more deeply, to get curious about the story the pain is telling. It’s not a punishment; it’s a communication from a deeper part of yourself, a part that remembers your wholeness.

For many of us, this pattern begins in childhood. When a child doesn’t feel that the ground beneath them is stable—emotionally or physically—when they don’t feel truly supported by the adults in their world, the neural pathways of the nervous system learn a particular lesson: *the world is not a safe place to stand*. The feet, in turn, learn to be tentative, to be braced, to be disconnected from the very earth that is meant to hold them. We learn to live in our heads, floating above the reality of our lives, because the ground feels too dangerous. This isn’t a conscious choice; it’s a brilliant survival strategy. The young nervous system, in its quest for safety, creates a pattern of disconnection that can last a lifetime, until we consciously choose to create a new one.

## Finding Your Footing

With Catherine, our work wasn’t about “fixing” her foot. It was about creating a sense of safety so profound that her nervous system could finally exhale, perhaps for the first time in her life. It was about gently, compassionately acknowledging the terror she felt about her future. We didn’t try to force the next step. Instead, we focused on the feeling of *this* step. Right here. Right now.

I invited her to simply stand, and to feel. To feel the texture of the floor beneath her soles. To feel the subtle shifts in weight as she breathed. To imagine roots growing from her feet, down, down, down into the rich, dark soil of the earth. Not as a visualization to achieve something, but as a sensory experience. A homecoming. An act of remembering her connection to something larger than her fear.

At first, it was excruciating. Her pain would flare, her mind would race. *This is silly. It’s not working. I’m still stuck.* This is the voice of the old neural pathways, the well-worn grooves of fear and skepticism. But slowly, session by session, something began to shift. The simple, repeated act of bringing gentle, non-judgmental awareness to her feet began to repattern her brain’s response. This is the beauty of neuroplasticity—the brain’s ability to change and form new connections. Her nervous system, so long on high alert (a state known as sympathetic dominance), began to register moments of safety. Moments of peace. It began to learn that it could shift into a state of rest and repair (parasympathetic). She was, in essence, teaching her body a new language.

> The body is not a problem to be solved. It is a sacred messenger, a wise and loving guide pointing you back toward wholeness.

This is the power of body wisdom. It bypasses the analytical mind, the part of us that wants to figure everything out, and speaks directly to the older, deeper parts of our being. It reminds our cells and our tissues of a truth our minds have forgotten: *you are supported*. The earth is here for you. You can rest your weight upon it. You don’t have to hold everything up by yourself.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

As Catherine began to feel more grounded in her body, she started to notice a change in her life. The overwhelming forest of her future began to look less menacing. A small trail, previously invisible, appeared. It wasn’t a superhighway. It was just a simple, narrow path leading toward a pottery class she’d always wanted to take. A small thing. An insignificant thing, her old mind might have said. But she followed it.

She decided to take a walk on it, literally. She went to a nearby park, and for the first time in months, she walked without the expectation of pain. She walked with the intention of feeling the earth beneath her, of receiving its support with every single step. She focused on the sensation of her heel landing, her arch flexing, her toes pushing off. A moving meditation.

She told me later, with tears in her eyes, that it was the first time she had ever truly felt the planet holding her. The sensation was so profound, so full of unconditional love, that it changed everything. Her pain didn’t vanish overnight. But its quality changed. It was no longer an enemy to be vanquished. It was a guide, a reminder to come back home to herself, to the present moment, to the feeling of her own two feet on the ground. The pain became a signal to check in: *Am I in my head? Am I holding my breath? Am I disconnected from the ground?* It became an ally in her healing.

## Walking Your Own Path

What is the story your feet are telling? What is the ground beneath you asking of you? Is there a step you are afraid to take? A direction you are afraid to move in?

Perhaps it’s an invitation to slow down. To stop running from the discomfort and to simply be with it. To feel the fear of the next step without needing to have the whole path mapped out. Our culture tells us to push through, to ignore the body’s signals. But true healing lies in the opposite direction. It lies in turning toward the sensation, with curiosity and with compassion.

Transformation is rarely a lightning bolt from the heavens. More often, it is a quiet, steady process of returning. Returning to the body. Returning to the breath. Returning to the simple, profound sensation of your own two feet, standing on the earth, right here, right now. It is in this returning that we find our true strength, our true stability.

Your feet are not just instruments for getting from one place to another. They are sensitive, intelligent, and deeply wise. They are the foundation of your dance through this life. Trust them. Listen to them. Let them feel the unwavering support of the ground that has been waiting for you all along. Let every step be a prayer, a declaration of your right to be here, to take up space, to walk your own sacred path, one grounded step at a time.

teachings.sourceTitle: Seeing with New Eyes: Vision Beyond Fear and Trauma
teachings.title: Seeing with New Eyes: Vision Beyond Fear and Trauma
teachings.summary: Susan explores how blurred or compromised sight can be a somatic signal of inner conflicts, fear, or unresolved pain rather than solely an optical problem. She invites a compassionate, courageous inquiry into what we are unwilling to see, describes the brain's role in shaping perception, and offers the possibility of reclaiming clear, compassionate vision by holding both pain and beauty together.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The word 'heal' comes from the Old English 'haelan,' which means to make whole. Not to make perfect. To make whole.

And sometimes, the most profound business of all is learning to see.

I remember a time, years ago, when my vision started to blur. Not in a gentle, out-of-focus way, but in a sudden, alarming refusal to see what was right in front of me. I was driving on a familiar road, the trees lining the highway like old friends, when the car ahead of me seemed to dissolve at the edges. Its brake lights became a smear of red, indistinct and hazy. I blinked, hard, convinced it was a momentary lapse. But it happened again the next day, and the next. The world, which had always been so sharply defined, was losing its edges.

My first stop was the optometrist, of course. He was a kind man with gentle hands who ran me through the usual battery of tests. “Your prescription has changed slightly, Susan,” he said, “but not enough to explain this kind of distortion.” He found nothing physically wrong. No glaucoma, no cataracts, no macular degeneration. My eyes, he assured me, were perfectly healthy.

And yet, I could not see.

It took me months of sitting with this strange new reality, this soft-focus world, to understand what my body was trying to tell me. It wasn’t a problem with my eyes. It was a problem with my *vision*. My physical sight was failing because my inner sight was in crisis. There was something in my life I was profoundly unwilling to look at, a truth so painful that my very cells had conspired to blur it out of existence.

## The Body’s Sacred Language

This is one of the deepest truths I have come to know in over thirty years of healing work: your body is a sacred messenger. Every symptom, every ache, every unexpected change is a communication. It is a love letter from your soul, asking you to pay attention. And the eyes, the proverbial windows to that soul, are perhaps the most eloquent communicators of all.

Vision problems, in my experience, almost always correlate with a conflict about what you are willing to see. When the world as you perceive it seems to take you away from love, from safety, from your own deepest truth, your eyes may literally begin to fail. It is an act of profound, if unconscious, self-protection. Your body, in its infinite wisdom, is trying to shield you from a view it has learned is unbearable.

Think about it. Nearsightedness, or myopia, often develops in children or young adults. From an energetic perspective, this can be seen as a pulling-in of one’s focus, a retreat from a world or a future that feels overwhelming or unsafe. The distant horizon is a blur because looking too far ahead is just too frightening. The immediate, close-up world is all that can be managed. Farsightedness, on the other hand, can emerge when the present moment is too painful to behold. The details of one’s immediate life—the bills on the table, the conflict with a loved one—are a blur, while the distant, imagined future is where focus resides. It’s a way of escaping the here and now.

These are not judgments. They are simply patterns. Your body is not betraying you. It is responding, perfectly and intelligently, to the signals it is receiving from your consciousness, from your history, from the neural pathways carved by your every experience.

## The Neuroscience of Seeing

Here’s a very good thing to know: you do not see with your eyes. You see with your brain. Your eyes are the exquisite lenses, the gates through which light and information enter. But the actual construction of the image, the interpretation of what it all *means*, happens in the three-pound universe of the brain. And that interpretation is never neutral.

Your brain is a prediction machine, constantly comparing incoming sensory data with a vast library of past experiences. When you look at a tree, you’re not just seeing a tree. You are seeing every tree you have ever seen, every story you’ve ever been told about trees, every feeling you’ve ever had while standing in the shade of a tree. All of this is layered onto your perception in a fraction of a second. This is the miracle of our neural wiring.

But what happens when that library of past experiences is filled with fear, with trauma, with the pain of not being seen or loved for who you are? The brain, in its fierce and loyal desire to keep you safe, will begin to filter your perception. It will highlight potential threats. It will interpret neutral faces as hostile. It will project old stories onto new situations. It learns to see a world that confirms its deepest fears. This isn’t a flaw; it’s a survival mechanism. But it can keep us locked in a prison of our own perception, unable to see the love, the beauty, the possibility that is also, always, right here.

My own blurred vision was a direct result of this. I was in a relationship that, on the surface, looked fine. But on a deeper level, my body knew it was a betrayal of my own soul. Looking clearly at the dynamic, at the subtle ways I was diminishing myself to keep the peace, was so terrifying that my brain and eyes colluded to say, “No. We will not see this.” It was easier to blur the world than to face the sharp, painful truth.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Courage to Look

The journey back to clear sight was not about a new prescription. It was about courage. The courage to sit in the blur. The courage to ask, gently, without judgment: *What am I not willing to see? What truth feels so dangerous that my body must protect me from it?*

This is the inquiry. It is not an interrogation. It is a tender turning-towards. It is bringing a compassionate curiosity to the patterns that run your life. You might begin by simply noticing, without trying to change anything.

> Notice when your vision feels sharpest, and when it feels most compromised. Is it around certain people? In certain situations? When you are thinking about certain topics?

> You might ask your eyes, directly, as if they were two beloved friends: *What do you long to see? What are you tired of looking at?*

> What would it be like to look at your life, your relationships, your challenges, not through the lens of fear, but through the lens of love? What new details might emerge? What might you see that you have been missing?

For me, the path to seeing clearly again involved learning to see beyond surface appearances. It meant looking at the person I loved and seeing not just the man in front of me, but the wounded child within him. It meant seeing his painful patterns not as a personal attack, but as his own soul’s cry for healing. And most importantly, it meant seeing myself with that same compassion. Seeing the part of me that had learned, long ago, that it was safer to be small, to be blurry, to not have sharp edges or clear needs.

When I could finally look at that truth, with love and without blame, the world began to come back into focus. The brake lights on the car ahead became crisp and clear once more. The leaves on the trees regained their distinct, intricate beauty. I had not healed my eyes. I had healed my vision.

## Seeing with the Eyes of the Soul

This is the transcendent possibility that lives within every one of us. To see with new eyes. To allow our physical sight to be illuminated by the light of a higher consciousness, a deeper wisdom. This is not about pretending the world is not, at times, a painful and frightening place. It is about developing the capacity to hold both the pain and the beauty, the fear and the love, in a single, unified field of vision.

It is about releasing the exhausting need to “keep an eye on” everything, to manage and control and predict. It is about trusting that you can handle what you see, because you are seeing it from a place of groundedness and inner resource. It is about knowing that beneath the often-frightening surface of reality, there is a deeper reality, a current of love that holds and sustains all things.

When you learn to see from this place, you are no longer a victim of your perception. You are a conscious creator of it. You can look upon the world, and upon yourself, with a clarity that is not harsh or critical, but infinitely kind. You see the patterns, the wounds, the fears… and you see the radiant, unbreakable soul that shines through it all. You see with the eyes of love.


---

**More on Eyes:**

- [When We Choose Not to See: The Courage of Clear Vision](/blog/eyes-courage-of-clear-vision)
- [Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision](/blog/eyes-emotional-roots-of-vision)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you have the courage to see what is true, the compassion to hold what you see with love, and the grace to allow your vision to be transformed.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

If you are experiencing new or worsening vision changes, please seek prompt evaluation from an eye care or medical professional—this practice is an invitation for inner noticing, not a substitute for medical care.
