teachings.sourceTitle: The Weight You Carry: What Your Shoulders Are Telling You
teachings.title: The Weight You Carry: What Your Shoulders Are Telling You
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to listen to the body’s signals—particularly the shoulders—as an entry point into understanding invisible burdens of responsibility and stress. The piece blends gentle anatomy, nervous-system framing, and a guided somatic inquiry to help discern which weights are truly ours to carry and which can be released. It emphasizes compassionate awareness, breath-based release, and the ongoing practice of sacred discernment.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A few years ago, I was walking home from my favorite little market on a crisp autumn day. The air had that specific, clean scent of woodsmoke and damp leaves, and the sun was casting long, golden shadows. My canvas bags were digging into my hands, heavy with the bounty of the season—a beautiful, bumpy squash, a bag of tart apples, a bundle of carrots with the dirt still clinging to them. I was trying to do it all in one trip, of course, telling myself it was efficient. As I shifted the load, trying to get a better grip, a familiar, deep ache bloomed across the tops of my shoulders. It radiated up my neck and down my arms, a sensation I knew with an old, weary intimacy. This wasn't just the weight of the groceries.

In that moment, the apples felt like obligations, the squash like unspoken anxieties. The carrots were a list of phone calls I needed to return. It was the weight of a long week, of holding space for my clients' profound and tender stories, of a conversation with a loved one that had left a residue of worry, of the endless, silent hum of things that needed *doing*. My body, in its infinite wisdom, was using the very literal weight of my market haul to get my attention. It was asking me to look at the much heavier, invisible load I was carrying.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We carry so much, don’t we? And so often, the burden settles in our shoulders. Have you ever noticed that? A tightness across your upper back after a difficult meeting. A sharp, pinching pain in your shoulder blade when you’re feeling overwhelmed by your to-do list. That feeling of being braced, as if for an impact that never comes. Your body is speaking to you. It’s telling a story about the weight you carry. And the shoulders… oh, the shoulders are profound, eloquent storytellers.

They are, in their very design, a paradox of strength and vulnerability. The shoulder girdle is the most flexible and mobile joint system in the entire body. At each shoulder, three bones converge—the clavicle (collarbone), the scapula (shoulder blade), and the humerus (upper arm bone)—creating a complex, shallow cradle. This incredible design is what allows us to reach, to pull, to push, to lift, to embrace. It is the gateway of our extension into the world. It’s how we offer a hand, how we hold our beloveds, how we literally shoulder responsibility.

And there it is. That word. *Responsibility*. For many of us, it has become a heavy, loaded thing. A synonym for burden.

## The Cradle of Responsibility

Think of your shoulders as the place where your purpose meets the world. They are the anatomical starting point for how you *do*, how you *act*, how you *give*. The energy of your heart, your intentions, your love—it all flows out through your arms and hands, but it must first pass through the gateway of the shoulders. They are the bridge between your inner world and your outer expression.

In the language of the body, we can even see a beautiful duality. The right shoulder is often associated with the masculine principle of doing, action, and protection in the external world. It’s the weight of your duties, your career, the pressures to provide or perform. The left shoulder is often connected to the feminine principle of being, of receiving, of carrying emotional and relational burdens. It’s the weight of caring for others, of feeling responsible for their happiness, of holding the emotional tenor of a family or a friendship.

When we are in alignment, this is a beautiful, dynamic dance. We carry our true responsibilities with a sense of purpose and strength. Our shoulders are broad, relaxed, and capable. We can reach out and engage with the world from a place of groundedness, and we can also know when to pull back, when to rest, when to receive. But most of us are not in alignment. We have taken on weights that were never ours to carry. We carry the expectations of our parents. We carry the unspoken needs of our partners. We carry the collective anxieties of the world. We mistake obligation for love and duty for purpose. And our shoulders begin to ache. They creep up toward our ears, tense and rigid. They become storehouses for everything we feel we *should* be doing, *should* be feeling, *should* be holding together.

This isn’t just a metaphor. It’s neuroscience. When your brain perceives a threat—whether it’s a looming deadline, a financial worry, or the emotional distress of a loved one—it doesn’t always distinguish it from a physical threat, like a predator on the savanna. It triggers the sympathetic nervous system, the body’s ancient fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline and cortisol flood your system. Your heart rate increases, your breath becomes shallow, and your muscles contract, preparing to act.

The trapezius muscles, those large, diamond-shaped muscles that span from your neck across your shoulders and down your upper back, are particularly responsive to this stress signaling. They tense up, ready for a fight that never comes, bracing for a blow that is purely emotional. Over time, with chronic stress and a feeling of being perpetually overwhelmed, this tension becomes the new normal. The fascia, the connective tissue that wraps around the muscles, begins to thicken and harden. The neural pathways that link “responsibility” with “threat” and “muscle contraction” become deeply grooved, like a well-worn path in the woods. Your shoulders are now, quite literally, carrying the physiological imprint of your perceived burdens. It becomes a form of muscle armoring, a physical shield against a world that feels too demanding.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Sacred Discernment

So what do we do? How do we set down a weight we’ve been carrying for so long we’ve forgotten it’s even there? It begins not with shrugging it all off in a fit of frustration, but with a gentle, compassionate inquiry. It begins with turning *toward* the sensation, not away from it.

Here is a practice, a way to begin the conversation. Find a quiet moment. Sit comfortably in a chair, with your feet flat on the floor. Close your eyes, or soften your gaze. Bring your awareness to your breath, just noticing the gentle rise and fall of your chest. Now, bring your attention to your shoulders. Don’t try to change anything. Just notice.

Are they tight? Are they aching? Is one higher than the other? Is the sensation sharp, or dull, or burning? Simply be with what is there, with as much kindness as you can muster.

Now, gently, ask the sensation a question. You can ask it aloud or in your mind. *“What is the weight you are carrying?”* And then listen. Listen with your whole being. Don’t search for an answer with your analytical mind. Wait for a word, an image, a memory to arise.

Perhaps the word is *“perfection.”* The weight of trying to do everything flawlessly.
Perhaps the image is of your mother’s tired face, and you feel the weight of her sadness that you took on as a child.
Perhaps the memory is of a time you felt you failed, and the weight is the shame you’ve carried ever since.

Whatever arises, just receive it. Breathe into it. *“Ah, so this is it. This is the weight.”* No judgment. No need to fix it. Just acknowledgment. This simple act of awareness is profoundly healing. You are bringing the light of consciousness to a place that has been held in the dark.

Here is a very good thing to know: *You do not have to carry it all.* Your purpose is not to be a beast of burden. Your purpose is to be a vessel of love, and love is not heavy. It is light. The work, then, is one of sacred discernment. It is the practice of parsing out what is truly yours to carry and what is not. Your true responsibilities often feel empowering. They align with your heart, they give you a sense of meaning, even when they are challenging. The false burdens, the ones we absorb from others or from our own conditioned beliefs, feel heavy, draining, and depleting. They create the chronic tension that speaks of a deep misalignment.

What would it be like to let some of that go? To consciously release the tension in your shoulders and, with it, the belief that you are responsible for holding up the world? You can do this with your breath. Inhale, and feel the support of the earth beneath you, the chair holding you. Exhale, and with a sigh, imagine the tension melting from your shoulders, flowing down your back and into the ground, where it can be composted and transformed. This isn't a one-time fix. It's a practice. A moment-by-moment choosing to release and trust.

This is not an act of selfishness. It is an act of profound self-love and wisdom. When you release the weights that are not yours, you free up an immense amount of energy. You create space. Your shoulders, no longer locked in a state of chronic tension, can rediscover their natural mobility. You can once again become that gateway of extension, reaching out into the world not from a place of heavy obligation, but from a place of authentic, purposeful love.

You can extend a hand to help, and know when to let go. You can hold another in an embrace, and not absorb their pain as your own. You can stand tall, your shoulders relaxed and open, a stable and graceful foundation from which you can offer your unique gifts to the world.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you feel the strength in your own sacred structure. May you have the courage to set down the weights that were never yours to carry. And may you extend your arms with the full, beautiful force of your loving purpose, feeling the lightness of being that is your birthright.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
keyThemes: Somatic awareness and mindfulness of physical sensations
Shoulders as metaphors and gateways for responsibility
Neuroscience of stress and muscle tension (fight-or-flight and the trapezius)
Distinguishing true responsibilities from absorbed burdens
Breath-based release and embodied inquiry
Cultivating boundary-setting and discernment
The practice of compassionate, nonjudgmental noticing
reflectionPrompts: Sit quietly and bring attention to your shoulders. What sensations, images, or words arise when you ask, “What is the weight I am carrying?” Stay with whatever surfaces for a few breaths—no need to fix or analyze.
List current responsibilities, roles, and relationships. Which ones feel energizing and aligned with your purpose, and which feel draining or like obligations you absorbed from others?

Recall a time when shoulder tension increased (after a meeting, an argument, or a caregiving period). What beliefs, expectations, or unmet needs were present then, and what small boundary or choice might shift that pattern?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a chair and sit with your feet on the floor. Soften your gaze and take three slow, grounding breaths. Bring gentle attention to your shoulders—notice tone, height, and any ache without trying to change it. Ask inwardly, “What is the weight you are carrying?” Wait for a word, image, or memory; receive it with kindness. On an exhale, let out a soft sigh and imagine a bit of tension flowing down into the ground. Repeat this cycle for 5–10 breaths, pausing at any time if you feel discomfort. This practice complements—but does not replace—professional medical or therapeutic care; if you have persistent or severe pain or feel emotionally overwhelmed, please consult a physician or qualified mental-health professional.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article references childhood burdens, shame, and emotional weight; these can bring up strong feelings. You are encouraged to pause the practice if it becomes distressing.
If the material triggers intense emotions, consider reaching out to a trusted therapist, counselor, or support person for containment and guidance.
The suggested somatic practices are gentle invitations; they are not a substitute for medical evaluation for persistent pain or for professional treatment of trauma-related symptoms.

teachings.sourceTitle: When Mind, Body, and Spirit Align: The Experience of Wholeness
teachings.title: When Mind, Body, and Spirit Align: The Experience of Wholeness
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to recognize the body as an anchor, the mind as a garden to tend, and the spirit as the open sky that holds both. Through simple somatic attention, mindful practice, and moments of stillness, she describes how these three dimensions can come into coherence, creating a lived sense of wholeness rather than a forced achievement. The piece offers gentle guidance toward integrating body, mind, and spirit through ongoing, compassionate practice.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
## The Body as a Gateway For so long, many of us have treated our bodies like machines. Vehicles to carry our brains around. We push them, ignore their signals, and resent their limitations. It is common to live almost entirely in our heads, in a world of ideas, plans, and anxieties. The body becomes just… background noise. Or worse, an inconvenience. Consider a common scenario: you might be sitting in a beautiful, peaceful place, yet your mind is a whirlwind. A work crisis, a looming deadline, a difficult conversation you need to have… thoughts can be like a swarm of angry bees. Your shoulders might be up around your ears, your jaw clenched, with a deep, familiar ache in your lower back. You are physically present, but your awareness is a million miles away. And then, a small, quiet voice might whisper from within. *What if you just… felt your feet on the ground?* It is such a simple thought, almost laughably so. But in a moment of grace, you might listen. You take a breath—a real breath, one that goes all the way down into your belly—and you bring your full attention to the soles of your feet. You feel the solid earth beneath them. The coolness of the grass. The subtle texture of the ground. And something shifts. The swarm of bees in your head doesn’t vanish, but it quiets. The tension in your shoulders eases, just a little. The ache in your back is still there, but it feels… held. In that simple act of turning attention from the chaos of the mind to the quiet, steady reality of the body, a door has been opened. You have stepped out of the frantic narrative and into the living, breathing present moment. This is the power of the body. It is our anchor to the now. It doesn’t lie, and it doesn’t get lost in hypotheticals. It is always, unfailingly, in the present moment. When we learn to listen to it, to inhabit it fully, it becomes the most incredible gateway to aligning our entire being. > The body is not a thing, it is a situation: it is our grasp on the world and our sketch of our project. - Simone de Beauvoir Our culture teaches us to disconnect from our bodies, to numb their messages with distraction and medication. But our bodies are speaking to us all the time, offering a constant stream of wisdom. That tightness in your chest? It might be unprocessed grief. That flutter in your stomach? It could be the thrill of a new possibility. That persistent headache? Perhaps it’s the strain of trying to control the uncontrollable. Neuroscience is now confirming what ancient wisdom traditions have always known: the mind and body are not separate. The vagus nerve, a superhighway of information running from the brainstem down into the abdomen, directly links our cognitive and emotional states with the functioning of our heart, lungs, and digestive system. When we are stressed and anxious, our bodies go into a state of high alert—the “fight or flight” response. Our heart rate increases, our breathing becomes shallow, and our digestion shuts down. When we are calm and feel safe, the parasympathetic nervous system takes over, allowing our bodies to rest, digest, and repair. By consciously working with the body—through breath, through movement, through mindful attention—we can directly influence our nervous system. We can guide ourselves out of the stress response and into a state of balance and coherence. This isn’t about “thinking positive thoughts.” It’s about engaging in practices that create a physiological shift. It’s about sending a message of safety and presence from the body back up to the mind. This is where true alignment begins. ## The Mind as a Garden If the body is our anchor to the present, the mind is the garden where our reality takes root. And for many of us, it’s a garden that has been left untended, overgrown with the weeds of old conditioning, fear, and limiting beliefs. We believe our thoughts are *us*. We identify with the constant chatter, the inner critic, the storyteller who is always spinning tales of lack and not-enoughness. We get so lost in the labyrinth of our own thinking that we forget we are not the thoughts themselves, but the awareness *behind* the thoughts. We are the sky, not the clouds that drift through it. Many people can spend decades trapped in the prison of their own minds. There is a tendency to become masters of intellectualization, able to analyze and dissect feelings until they are just lifeless concepts. One can explain *why* they are anxious, but not *feel* their way to peace. The mind, designed to protect, can become a cage. The turning point for many is discovering profound wisdom traditions like the Tao Te Ching. These philosophies don't offer complex strategies or ten-step plans. They offer a different way of being. They speak of *wu wei*, often translated as “effortless action” or “non-doing.” It’s not about passivity; it’s about moving with the natural flow of life, rather than struggling against it. > When you are content to be simply yourself and don't compare or compete, everybody will respect you. - Tao Te Ching, Chapter 8 This can be a revelation. The mind is often striving, comparing, competing. It can be a relentless engine of effort. The Tao invites a softening. A letting go of the need to control everything. A trust that there is a deeper intelligence at work, both within us and in the universe. This is where mindfulness and meditation become such powerful practices. They are not about stopping our thoughts—that’s impossible. They are about changing our *relationship* to our thoughts. We learn to observe them without judgment. We create a little space between ourselves and the mental chatter. In that space, we find freedom. We begin to see that our thoughts are just… thoughts. They are not ultimate reality. They are not commands. We can learn to tend the garden of our mind. We can gently pull the weeds of negative self-talk. We can plant the seeds of self-compassion and acceptance. We can water the flowers of gratitude and presence. This isn’t about forcing ourselves to be positive. It’s about consciously choosing where we place our attention. As the saying goes, “What you practice grows stronger.” When we practice observing our thoughts with kindness, we strengthen our capacity for inner peace. When we practice gratitude, we start to notice more and more things to be grateful for. We are not trying to silence the mind, but to befriend it. To transform it from a source of torment into a source of clarity and wisdom. ## The Spirit as the Sky And what of the spirit? This is the part of us that can feel the most elusive, the most abstract. We might associate it with religion, with dogma, or with something completely outside of ourselves. But spirit, as it can be known, is simply the vast, open, loving awareness that holds everything. It is the sky that holds the clouds of the mind and the landscape of the body. Spirit is the part of you that yearns for meaning, for connection, for something more than just the daily grind. It’s the part of you that is stirred by a piece of music, that feels a sense of awe looking up at a starry night, that knows, on a level deeper than words, that we are all connected. For many, spiritual life can feel separate from everyday life. It can be something done on certain days, or in certain places. It isn’t always integrated. It can feel like another box to check. The mind is busy, the body is tense, and the spirit is a distant concept. There is no alignment, only fragmentation. The bridge is learning to see the sacred in the ordinary. It is realizing that spirit isn’t “out there.” It is right here. It is the life force animating the body, the awareness illuminating the mind. It is the silence between our thoughts, the stillness beneath our restlessness. Quantum physics, in its own mysterious way, points to this interconnectedness. It tells us that at the most fundamental level, all of reality is a unified field of energy and information. The separation we perceive between ourselves and the world is an illusion, a trick of the senses. As the physicist David Bohm said, “The implicate order is the deeper and more fundamental order of reality.” We are not separate drops in the ocean; we are the ocean itself, expressing itself as individual waves. To connect with spirit is to connect with this underlying unity. It is to remember that you are a part of something vast, ancient, and intelligent. It is to trust the unfolding of your life, even when it doesn’t make sense to the rational mind. It is to listen to the whispers of intuition, the quiet nudges of your soul. How do we do this? By creating moments of stillness. By spending time in nature. By listening more than we speak. By asking bigger questions: *What truly matters to me? What is my heart’s deepest longing? How can I serve the whole?* Connecting with spirit is not about adding another “to-do” to your list. It is an act of subtraction. It is about letting go of the noise, the armor, the identities that are not truly you, so that the quiet, luminous presence of your own spirit can shine through. It is always there, my dear one, waiting with infinite patience for you to come home to yourself. ## The Experience of Wholeness So, we have the body, our anchor in the present moment. We have the mind, a garden we can consciously tend. And we have the spirit, the vast, open sky of our being. When these three are in alignment, something magical happens. It’s the difference between a discordant orchestra, with each instrument playing its own tune, and a symphony. Wholeness is not a static state of perfection. It is a dynamic, flowing dance. It is the feeling of being deeply, unapologetically yourself. The masks fall away. The need to pretend, to perform, to please—it dissolves. In its place is a quiet confidence, a sense of being grounded in your own truth. So many people describe a moment when it all clicks. Consider a person who has been a master of their professional life but feels utterly disconnected from themselves. They live in their head, in a world of strategies and goals. Their body is a source of chronic pain, and their spirit feels like a distant memory. Through gentle, patient work, they are invited back into their body through breathwork and somatic awareness. They work on befriending their mind through mindfulness, and they open to spirit through moments of quiet contemplation. One day, they might be walking on the beach, a place they’ve walked a thousand times before. But this time, it is different. They are not *thinking* about the beach. They are not planning their next step or worrying about the tide. They are just… there. They feel the cold sand under their bare feet, the sting of the salt spray on their face, the cry of the gulls in their ears. And for a moment, there is no separation. There is no ‘me’ walking on the beach. There is just… the walking. The beach. The being. They feel… whole. That is it. That is the experience. It is the collapse of the observer and the observed. It is the dissolution of the fragmented self into the unified field of the present moment. It is a state of profound coherence, where your thoughts, your feelings, your physical sensations, and your spiritual sense of connection are all singing the same song. This alignment is not something you achieve through force of will. You cannot strong-arm your way into wholeness. It is an act of surrender. It is the gentle, consistent practice of returning, again and again, to the wisdom of the body, the clarity of the befriended mind, and the vastness of the spirit. It is a journey of a thousand small steps, a thousand gentle course corrections. It is the most important journey you will ever take.

teachings.sourceTitle: Facial Pain and the Tension of Pretending
teachings.title: Facial Pain and the Tension of Pretending
teachings.summary: Susan explores how chronic facial tension and unexplained jaw pain can be the embodied result of lifelong emotional suppression and a ‘frozen’ expressive landscape. Using Claire’s story, she links early attachment patterns and neural processes to the phenomenon of facial armoring, and offers compassionate, somatic approaches—gentle touch, curiosity, and playful expression—to begin softening that armor and reclaiming expressive vitality. Healing is framed as gradual and tender work, not a quick fix.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman I worked with years ago—let’s call her Claire—came to me with debilitating jaw pain. It was a deep, unrelenting ache that radiated from her temples down to her chin, a constant thrumming that made it hard to eat, to speak, to think. She had been to doctors, dentists, specialists. They’d fitted her for mouthguards, prescribed muscle relaxants, suggested stress-management techniques. Nothing touched it. She carried a collection of diagnoses—TMJ, trigeminal neuralgia, myofascial pain syndrome—but no diagnosis had offered a key to relief.

As she sat across from me in the quiet of my healing room, what I noticed first was not the pain she described, but the incredible *stillness* of her face. It was a beautiful face, elegant and composed, but it was as if every muscle was frozen in a state of placid neutrality. She smiled, but the smile never quite reached her eyes. She spoke of her pain, but her brow remained perfectly smooth. It was a mask of serene control, worn so long and so tightly that it had fused to the flesh and bone beneath. Her face was a masterpiece of camouflage, a testament to a lifetime of carefully managing how she was perceived.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We learn so early to present a certain face to the world. A face that is acceptable, agreeable, strong, capable. A face that doesn’t betray the messy, vulnerable, contradictory truths of our inner lives. We learn to arrange our features into a performance, a carefully curated presentation of self that we hope will keep us safe, will win us love, will help us belong. But what is the cost of this performance? What happens to the life force, the unique, untamed vitality that gets hidden behind the mask? The body, in its infinite wisdom, always keeps the score. And sometimes, the bill comes due in the form of chronic, unexplainable pain.

## The Armor of a Frozen Face

The face is the mirror of the soul, the most recognizable part of us, the way we “face” the world. It is designed to be an exquisitely expressive landscape, with dozens of muscles capable of conveying the most subtle shifts in our internal state. But for so many of us, it becomes a battlefield. A place of immense, unconscious tension.

Think of the sheer effort involved in holding an unnatural expression for hours on end. The slight lift of the eyebrows to feign interest in a meeting that drains your soul. The polite smile held in place during a difficult family dinner. The clenching of the jaw to hold back an angry word you desperately need to speak. The tightening around the mouth to stop a sob from escaping when your heart is breaking. Each of these is a physical act, a muscular contraction. And when these contractions become chronic, repeated day after day, year after year, they become armor.

This was the heart of Claire’s pain. Through our work together, a story emerged. A story of a childhood where her sensitivity was seen as “too much,” where her fiery spirit was a problem to be managed. She was a child who felt everything deeply—the injustice of a playground squabble, the beauty of a sunset, the unspoken tension between her parents. But she learned, as so many sensitive children do, that her deep feeling was inconvenient, even alarming, to the adults around her. So she began to camouflage. She built a fortress of agreeableness, a smooth, unreadable facade to hide the parts of herself she believed were unacceptable. Her unique vitality—her passionate anger, her deep grief, her wild joy—was kept under lock and key. The tension in her face was the physical manifestation of a lifetime of holding herself in, of pretending. Her jaw was clenched against a lifetime of unspoken truths.

From a neuroscience perspective, this is not just a poetic metaphor. It’s biology. When we feel an emotion, the limbic system—the brain’s emotional center—sends signals to the facial muscles to express it. This is an ancient, hardwired process. When we suppress that expression, the prefrontal cortex—the thinking, managing part of the brain—sends a counter-signal, creating a state of conflict and tension in the muscles themselves. You are literally putting the brakes on a moving car. Dr. Allan Schore, a pioneer in interpersonal neurobiology, has written extensively on how early attachment experiences shape our capacity for emotional expression. If a child’s spontaneous expressions are met with rejection, neglect, or punishment, the neural pathways for that expression are pruned back. The child literally learns, on a cellular level, to freeze the muscles of the face to stop the forbidden feeling from showing. The body learns that expression is dangerous.

This creates what is sometimes called “facial armoring.” The chronic tension restricts blood flow, impedes lymphatic drainage, and traps metabolic waste in the tissues. The fascia, the connective tissue that wraps around the muscles, begins to thicken and harden. Nerves can become compressed. The result is pain. It can manifest as TMJ, as tension headaches, as trigeminal neuralgia, or as a generalized, mysterious ache like Claire’s. The body, in its profound wisdom, is sending a message. It is telling us that the mask has become too heavy, too tight. It is asking us to look at what we are hiding.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Soul’s Radiance

So what do we do? How do we begin to soften this armor, to let the life back into our faces? It can feel like a monumental task, like trying to dismantle a fortress with your bare hands.

It is not a matter of forcing or fixing. It is a gentle process of turning towards the tension with curiosity and compassion. It is about creating a safe space for the frozen history to thaw. It begins with the simple, radical act of paying attention, of becoming an archaeologist of your own inner landscape.

Here is a very good thing to know: your body is always on your side. The pain is not an enemy to be vanquished; it is a sacred messenger. It is the part of you that has refused to be silenced completely, the part that remembers the truth of who you are beneath the mask. It is a call home.

> The face leaks the truth through micro-expressions, a momentary flash of the soul’s weather. But what if we didn’t have to leak? What if we could simply allow?

When I work with clients on this, we often start with touch. Not an aggressive, probing touch, but a loving, receptive one. I invite you to try this. Find a quiet moment. Place your own warm hands on your jaw, your temples, your forehead. Not to manipulate or change anything, but simply to bring loving awareness to the area. To say, with your touch, *I am here. I am listening.* Feel the warmth of your palms, the gentle weight of your hands. Let it be a gesture of profound kindness to yourself.

As you do this, you might notice the subtle patterns of holding. The clenched jaw, the furrowed brow, the tight line of the mouth. Don’t try to relax it. That often just creates more tension, another layer of striving. Instead, just feel it. Acknowledge the incredible work those muscles have been doing, perhaps for decades, to keep you safe. Thank them for their service. You might even say, silently or aloud, “Thank you for holding so much for me. I see you. I appreciate you.” This simple act of acknowledgment can be profoundly transformative.

From there, you can begin to invite gentle movement. Imagine you are waking up a sleeping animal. You wouldn’t shake it awake; you would offer a gentle nudge. Open and close your mouth slowly, feeling the movement in the joint. Massage the hinge of the jaw with your fingertips, using small, slow circles. Explore the muscles of your cheeks, your forehead, the space between your brows. Let your touch be a question, not a demand. *What is here? What needs to be felt?*

Then, when you feel ready, you can play with expression. Making faces in the mirror—silly faces, angry faces, sad faces. It can feel incredibly vulnerable at first, but it is a way of reclaiming the expressive capacity of your face, of reminding the muscles that they are allowed to move. Stretch your mouth wide in a silent scream. Snarl like a tiger. Weep like a heartbroken child. Let the energy move. You are not performing for anyone; you are simply allowing the stored-up life force to have its expression in a safe container.

This is not about becoming a person who has no control over their expressions. It is about moving from a state of rigid, unconscious holding to one of conscious, flexible responsiveness. It is about having the capacity to be still and composed when you choose, but not being locked into it as a default. It is about allowing the authentic energy of your emotions to move *through* you, rather than getting stuck in the tissues of your face.

Beneath the surface of the persona, you are the radiance of sheer love. The work of healing is simply to dissolve the armor that obscures this light. To release the exhausting effort of pretending, and to allow the truth of your own beautiful, multifaceted soul to shine through your eyes, your smile, your very skin.

It is a journey of a lifetime, this process of becoming more fully ourselves. It asks for courage, for patience, and for a deep and abiding compassion for the parts of us that learned to hide. But the reward is a sense of freedom, of vitality, of coming home to the face that was always waiting for you beneath the mask. For Claire, the journey was slow, but as she learned to listen to her face, to welcome the feelings she had suppressed for so long, the pain began to recede. In its place, a new mobility emerged, a new expressiveness. Her smile finally reached her eyes. It was her own true face, and it was more beautiful than any mask.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

If you have a diagnosed facial or jaw condition, are in acute pain, or feel overwhelmed emotionally, pause this practice and continue working with your medical provider or a qualified therapist—this invitation is a gentle complement, not a substitute for professional care.

teachings.sourceTitle: Healing the Healer: When the One Who Gives Must Learn to Receive
teachings.title: Healing the Healer: When the One Who Gives Must Learn to Receive
teachings.summary: Susan explores the paradox many caregivers face: mastering the art of giving while resisting the necessity of receiving. She names the nervous-system reality—ventral vagal co-regulation—and offers a simple garden anecdote to show how being witnessed and allowed to receive can restore a depleted healer. The piece invites somatic attention to bodily signals and an embrace of receiving as an essential, courageous practice rather than a weakness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious paradox, this path of the healer. We spend our lives learning to hold space for others, to channel comfort, to be the steady hand in the storm. We become experts in the art of giving. But the journey inevitably leads us to a threshold we often resist with all our might: the moment we must learn to receive. If you are someone who has spent your life caring for others—as a therapist, a bodyworker, a coach, a doctor, a parent, a friend—this is for you. If you are the one people call in a crisis, the one who remembers the birthdays, the one who carries the emotional weight of your family or community… you know this path intimately. You know the profound fulfillment of service. And you likely also know the deep, quiet exhaustion that can settle in your bones when the well runs dry. ## The Sacred Imbalance We are taught, in a thousand subtle and not-so-subtle ways, that giving is virtuous. Noble. *Good*. And it is. To offer your presence and care to another is a sacred act. But we are rarely taught about the other side of that equation. Receiving is often framed as selfish, weak, or indulgent. We feel guilty asking for help. We feel like a burden when we have needs of our own. We tell ourselves, *I’m the helper, I should have it all together.* This creates a profound imbalance, not just in our relationships, but within our own nervous systems. From a neuroscience perspective, our capacity for connection and healing—for both ourselves and others—is governed by the vagus nerve. When we are constantly in a state of giving, of high-alert empathy and energetic output, we are living in a sympathetically-charged state. We are *on*. We are holding, doing, fixing. To truly replenish, to come back to a place of grounded safety and wholeness, we must activate the ventral vagal part of our nervous system. This is the state of rest, digestion, and—crucially—*co-regulation*. It’s the state that tells our bodies, *You are safe. You are held. You can let go.* And we cannot activate it alone. We are wired for connection. Receiving is the physiological mechanism for that replenishment. It is not a luxury; it is a biological necessity. ## The Gardener’s Hands I remember an afternoon last spring, I was in my garden, tending to the lavender and echinacea. My hands were deep in the cool, dark earth, the scent of the soil rich and alive. I was feeling that familiar, bone-deep weariness that comes from holding space for heavy stories all week. A client’s grief, another’s trauma, the quiet desperation in a third’s voice—it was all clinging to me like damp moss. My neighbour, a lovely woman in her eighties with the most brilliant white hair, leaned over the fence. “Susan,” she said, her voice gentle, “you look tired.” My immediate impulse was to deny it. To straighten up, smile brightly, and say, “Oh, I’m fine! Just enjoying the sun.” It’s the healer’s reflexive mask. But for some reason, that day, I couldn’t summon the energy. The mask felt too heavy. I simply nodded, my shoulders slumping. “I am,” I admitted, the words feeling foreign on my tongue. “I really am.” She didn’t offer advice. She didn’t try to fix it. She just stood there, her presence a soft, steady anchor. After a moment, she disappeared from the fence, and a few minutes later, she reappeared at my garden gate holding a steaming mug. “From my own garden,” she said, handing me a cup of lemon balm and chamomile tea. “Just sit for a moment, dear. The weeds can wait.” As I sat on the warm stone bench, the heat of the mug seeping into my palms, I felt a profound wave of emotion wash over me. It wasn’t just gratitude. It was a deep, cellular-level *surrender*. In that simple act of receiving—a cup of tea, a moment of quiet witnessing—my nervous system finally exhaled. I hadn’t even realized I was holding my breath. My neighbour, in her simple wisdom, had offered me the gift of ventral vagal co-regulation. She had healed the healer. ## The Tao of Receiving The Tao te Ching speaks beautifully to this balance. It reminds us that the valley, in its emptiness, is what makes the river possible. The hub of the wheel, in its nothingness, is what allows the wheel to turn. > We shape clay into a pot, > but it is the emptiness inside > that holds whatever we want. For years, I thought my job was to be the pot—strong, sturdy, holding everything for everyone else. I had forgotten that the *purpose* of the pot is not just to hold, but to be filled. And to be emptied. And to be filled again. The giving and the receiving are not two separate acts; they are the inhale and the exhale of a single, sacred breath. When we only exhale, we eventually collapse. To receive is to acknowledge our own beautiful emptiness. It is to declare that we are worthy of being filled. It is the ultimate act of trust—trust in others, trust in the universe, and trust in our own intrinsic value, which is not dependent on how much we do for others. So I ask you, my dear one, where in your life are you only exhaling? Where are you pretending to be fine when you are weary to your bones? Who in your life is standing at the garden gate, holding a cup of tea, waiting for you to be willing to receive it? Learning to receive is perhaps the most advanced and courageous practice for any healer. It requires us to dismantle the identity we’ve built around being the strong one. It asks us to be vulnerable, to be soft, to admit our own humanity. It’s a tricky business, this being human… and it’s even trickier when we try to do it all alone. Let your body be your guide. Notice the tension in your jaw, the tightness in your shoulders, the shallow quality of your breath. These are not signs of failure. They are loving messages from your body, whispering, *It’s time. It’s time to let go. It’s time to be held.*

teachings.sourceTitle: The Heart That Loves Itself First: Radical Self-Worth
teachings.title: The Heart That Loves Itself First: Radical Self-Worth
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe the heart as both a physical organ and an energetic center that must both receive and give. She traces how chronic one‑way giving creates emotional and bodily congestion—anxiety, resentment, exhaustion—and offers gentle, practical steps and mindset shifts to relearn receiving and replenish true self‑worth.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The body is not a machine. I know this seems obvious, but you would be amazed at how deeply the mechanical metaphor has embedded itself in our collective consciousness.

I remember a particular Tuesday in my late thirties. The rain was doing that thing it does in Vancouver, a relentless, grey sigh against the windowpane. I was sitting on the floor of my clinic office, my back against a bookshelf filled with worn spines of wisdom traditions and anatomy texts, a cup of long-cold tea forgotten beside me. I’d just finished with a client, a dear soul wrestling with a grief so profound it felt like a geological formation in the room. Her story was one of immense caregiving, of pouring herself into her family until she felt like a ghost in her own life. I had held the space for her, as I had for so many others, creating a sanctuary for her pain to be seen and honored.

And as the door clicked shut behind her, something inside me… collapsed.

It wasn’t a dramatic, shattering fall. It was a quiet, internal crumbling. A slow-motion implosion. My own heart felt heavy, thick, and exhausted. I had a sudden, visceral image of it as a faithful, tired pump, squeezing out the very last of its reserves. For whom? For everyone, it seemed. For my clients, my family, my friends, the world. For everyone but myself. The thought, when it landed, was not an accusation. It was just a quiet, devastating truth. My well was dry. And I was still trying to give water.

Have you ever felt that? That sense of profound, soul-deep depletion, a feeling that you are giving and giving and giving, while some essential part of you is quietly starving? It’s a particular kind of exhaustion that sleep doesn’t fix, a spiritual malnourishment that leaves you feeling hollowed out, even as you stand in a life that looks full from the outside.

## The Sacred Pump and the Great Imbalance

Here is a very good thing to know about your body, your sacred messenger. The heart is the first declaration of your existence. Before your brain sparked into its complex symphony, before your limbs were even buds, your heart was there. A rhythmic pulse in the quiet darkness of the womb, a tiny drumbeat announcing your presence. It is the central sun of your entire being, the energetic core from which your life force radiates.

And its physical function is a miracle of sacred engineering—a perfect, two-way pump. One chamber receives the deoxygenated blood, the body’s waste, the story of what has been used and spent. The other gives the fresh, oxygenated blood, the life force, the nourishment needed for every cell to thrive. It draws in, and it pushes out. In, and out. A constant, life-sustaining rhythm. Receiving and giving. It is a physical law written into the very muscle that keeps you alive.

So what happens when we override this fundamental law? What happens when we, through our beliefs and conditioning, turn ourselves into a one-way street? All giving, no receiving.

We create a toxic clog. The energy that is meant to flow *to* us, to nourish us, to fill our own sacred vessel, gets blocked. It backs up. And what does it become? It doesn’t just vanish. Energy never does. It transforms. It curdles into a thick sludge of anxiety, of unspoken anger, of crushing responsibility, of bitter resentment. We feel it as a tightness in our chest, a constant, low-grade hum of panic, a weariness that no amount of sleep can touch. We might snap at our loved ones, feeling a surge of inexplicable rage over something small, like a dish left in the sink. That rage is the blocked energy of the heart, screaming for its own needs. The anxiety is the fear that we will never, ever be replenished. The resentment is the soul’s deep knowing that this imbalance is fundamentally unjust.

For so many of us, especially those who feel called to heal, to help, to serve, this pattern is deeply ingrained. It’s a neural pathway carved by generations of conditioning, this belief that our worth is conditional upon our sacrifice. That to be a “good” person—a good mother, daughter, partner, healer—is to put ourselves last. We learn to ignore the chamber of the heart that is designed to *receive*. We cut off our own supply. And then we wonder why we feel so empty, so tired, so alone.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Heart’s Desperate Cry

Sometimes, the body has to scream to get our attention. A heart attack, from this perspective, is not a betrayal. It is not a failure of the body. It is the heart’s last, desperate attempt to be heard. It is a radical, life-or-death intervention, a demand to stop. To listen. To finally, *finally* pay attention to the profound imbalance that has been sustained for years, for decades.

Think of the physiology. The coronary arteries, the vessels that feed the heart muscle *itself*, become blocked. The very organ of giving is starved of its own supply. It is the most literal, physical manifestation of the energetic pattern. The body is always speaking the truth of the soul. It is the body saying, with all the force it can muster: *You cannot keep pouring from an empty vessel.*

I didn’t have a heart attack on my office floor that rainy Tuesday. But I felt the whisper of it. The deep, aching truth of it. My body was sending me the message in a way I could no longer ignore. The quiet collapse was my heart’s cry for help. It was a call to return to the fundamental law of my own being: the sacred balance of giving *and* receiving.

This isn’t about selfishness. This is about sustainability. It’s about recognizing that you are not an infinite resource. You are a sacred vessel. And that vessel must be filled. The love, the care, the compassion you so generously pour out to others must first be poured into yourself. Not just as a treat, not just on weekends, but as a constant, devotional practice. It is a prerequisite for authentic giving. Without it, what we are “giving” is often tainted with the poison of our own depletion—resentment, expectation, and the unconscious demand for payback.

What would it be like if you allowed yourself to receive? To be nourished? To be filled to the brim until you were overflowing? That overflow is what you have to give. It is radiant, it is abundant, and it is given without depletion, without resentment, without the toxic clog of self-neglect. It is the purest form of love.

## Filling Your Own Cup First

Learning to fill my own cup first was the most radical and transformative journey of my life. It meant unlearning a lifetime of conditioning that screamed, “Selfish! Uncaring! Not enough!” It meant sitting with the profound discomfort and guilt that arose when I chose to say “no” to others so I could say “yes” to myself. It meant disappointing people who were used to me being an ever-available wellspring. It meant redefining my entire sense of worth, detaching it from my productivity and my service.

It started small, almost imperceptibly. It started with five minutes of silence before my day began, before the demands of the world could rush in. Just five minutes of placing my hand on my heart and breathing. In and out. Receiving and giving. It started with buying myself a small bouquet of freesias, not for a special occasion, but just because their scent made my soul feel seen. It started with taking a walk in the woods without a destination, allowing my feet to lead me, rather than my mind. It started with the simple, revolutionary act of making myself a beautiful lunch and sitting down to eat it without the distraction of a book or a screen, just savoring the nourishment.

Slowly, painstakingly, I began to rewire those ancient neural pathways. I began to teach my nervous system, through repeated, gentle action, that it was safe to receive, that my worth was inherent and not earned. I began to truly understand, in my cells and in my bones, that my capacity to love others was directly proportional to my capacity to love myself.

A heart that loves itself first is not a closed heart. It is an open heart. It is a heart that has become a source-fed river, not a stagnant pond. It is a central sun, radiating warmth and light not because it *has* to, but because it *is* its nature. It gives freely, joyfully, from a place of infinite abundance, because it is, first and foremost, full.

This is the invitation for you, beloved one. To come home to your own heart. To honor its sacred rhythm. To have the courage to fill your own vessel, to nourish your own soul. And to discover the profound, world-changing power of a heart that loves itself first.

teachings.sourceTitle: Too Much to Stomach: When Life Becomes Indigestible
teachings.title: Too Much to Stomach: When Life Becomes Indigestible
teachings.summary: Susan frames the stomach as an alchemical organ and a messenger for our capacity to digest life’s experiences. The piece invites a compassionate, embodied inquiry into how chronic stress, unspoken emotions, and toxic inputs can show up as indigestion, reflux, or nausea, and offers a simple somatic practice to begin listening to bodily wisdom. It emphasizes relationship with the body over quick fixes and the possibility of rewiring gut–brain communication through attention and kindness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
What would it be like if you could meet yourself — all of yourself — with the same tenderness you would offer a frightened child?

We are asked to navigate a world of immense complexity, to open ourselves to love and loss, to joy and disappointment. And through it all, our bodies are our constant companions, our faithful barometers, speaking a language of sensation and symptom that is often far more honest than the stories our minds tell.

I remember a time, years ago, when my life was a whirlwind of activity. I was juggling a thriving practice, writing my first book, and caring for my young family. On the surface, everything was wonderful. I was doing work I loved, surrounded by people I cherished. But underneath, a quiet tension was building. It began as a subtle knot in my solar plexus, a feeling of being perpetually, almost imperceptibly, clenched. Then came the heartburn, a fiery whisper after meals that soon grew into a demanding roar. I, a healer who teaches others to listen to their bodies, was ignoring my own.

My stomach, it turned out, was trying to tell me something my mind refused to acknowledge. It was telling me that I had taken on too much. Not just too much food, but too much pressure, too many expectations, too much of the world’s relentless pace. My life, as it was, had become indigestible.

## The Alchemical Cauldron

Our stomach is a remarkable organ, an alchemical cauldron where the outer world is transformed into the inner. Through the potent crucible of hydrochloric acid, it breaks down the sustenance we consume, preparing it to be absorbed as life-sustaining energy. It is a process of profound surrender and transformation. What was once *other* becomes *self*. This is a miracle we participate in with every meal, a daily communion with life itself.

This physical process is a perfect mirror for our psychological and emotional digestion. Just as we take in food, we take in experiences, relationships, beliefs, and the energetic tenor of our environment. And just as our physical stomach must break down a meal, our energetic and emotional bodies must process these non-physical inputs. We are constantly being asked to digest life itself. We metabolize a harsh word from a colleague, the ambient stress of the evening news, the joy of a child’s laughter, the grief of a sudden loss. All of it enters the field of our being and asks to be processed.

But what happens when an experience is too much? When a loss is too sharp, a betrayal too bitter, a truth too difficult to swallow? What happens when the sheer volume of life’s demands—the relentless emails, the 24-hour news cycle, the pressure to perform—overwhelms our capacity to process it all?

This is when the stomach begins to speak. That feeling of having a “knot in your stomach” is not just a metaphor. It’s a physiological reality. Our gut is often called our “second brain,” and for good reason. It is lined with a network of neurons called the enteric nervous system, and it is in constant communication with the brain in our head via the vagus nerve. This gut-brain axis is a two-way street. When we are under stress, the brain sends signals to the gut, activating the body’s sympathetic nervous system—our “fight or flight” response. This shunts blood away from the digestive organs to the muscles and brain, preparing us for perceived danger. Digestion, a process of rest and repair, is put on hold. The stomach literally clenches, its secretions diminish, its rhythmic churning ceases. It is bracing for impact.

If this state becomes chronic, if we live in a perpetual state of low-grade stress, our digestive fire is dampened. We may experience indigestion, bloating, or a feeling of food sitting like a stone in our bellies. We have, quite literally, lost our capacity to take in the world and be nourished by it. The world starts to feel like a threat rather than a source of sustenance. We are running on empty, because the very mechanism designed to refuel us has been shut down.

## When the Body Says ‘No’

For many people I’ve worked with over the years, the stomach’s messages become more insistent over time. The gentle whispers of indigestion can escalate into the searing pain of an ulcer or the constant discomfort of acid reflux. These are not random malfunctions. They are the body’s desperate attempt to get our attention, to say, in no uncertain terms, *“This is making me sick.”*

An ulcer, a literal wound in the lining of the stomach or small intestine, often speaks to a place within us that feels gnawed away by worry, criticism (internal or external), or a situation that feels deeply corrosive. It’s the physical manifestation of an emotional state that is eating away at us. The very acid that is meant to transform nourishment into life force begins to break down the body itself. It’s a profound form of self-attack, mediated by the body’s own chemistry.

Acid reflux, or GERD, has its own story to tell. It’s often a sign of pressure—too much pressure from within. It can be the voice of swallowed anger, of unexpressed grief, of words that have been held back for so long they are beginning to burn their way up. It’s the body’s attempt to expel what it cannot contain. Nausea, too, is a powerful form of rejection. It is the body’s wisdom saying, *“I cannot take this in. This is toxic to me.”* This could be a toxic relationship, a toxic work environment, or a toxic belief system we’ve been force-feeding ourselves for years.

I once worked with a woman, a brilliant and compassionate lawyer, who suffered from debilitating nausea every morning before work. She had been to countless doctors, but no physical cause could be found. As we began to explore the landscape of her life, it became clear that her career, which she had pursued to please her father, was a profound betrayal of her own soul’s calling. Her body was rejecting, every single day, the life she was forcing it to live. The nausea was not the problem; it was the messenger. The cure was not a pill; it was the courage to listen.

I think also of a man who came to see me with chronic, burning indigestion. He was a peacekeeper, the one in his family who always smoothed things over. He had swallowed a lifetime of unspoken truths to maintain a fragile family harmony. His stomach was on fire with the words he’d never allowed himself to speak. The burning wasn’t just acid; it was the heat of his own silenced truth.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Inquiry: A Gentle Conversation with Your Stomach

It is a very good thing to know that your body is always, *always* on your side. Its symptoms are not a punishment, but a loving, if sometimes clumsy, form of communication. Your stomach is not your enemy. It is a sacred messenger, a wise alchemist pointing you toward a deeper truth.

So, I invite you to begin a conversation. This is not about diagnosing or fixing, but about listening with a new quality of attention. Find a quiet moment where you won’t be disturbed. You can lie down or sit comfortably, whatever allows your body to feel most at ease.

Close your eyes and bring your awareness to your breath. Don’t try to change it, just notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest and belly. Feel the support of the chair or the floor beneath you. You are held.

Now, gently place one or both hands over your stomach, over your solar plexus. Let the warmth of your hands be an offering of kindness. For a few moments, just breathe with your hands here. You are simply saying hello. You are making contact.

When you feel settled, I invite you to ask, silently, from your heart…

*Beloved stomach, what are you holding for me?*

And then, listen. Listen not with your ears, but with your whole being. You might perceive an answer as a feeling—a clenching, a fluttering, a warmth, a coldness. You might see an image in your mind’s eye. A word or a phrase might float into your awareness. It might be something you expect, or it might surprise you. Trust whatever comes.

Don’t rush to analyze it. Just receive it. Breathe with it. Offer it your compassionate presence.

Now, you can gently deepen the inquiry. You might ask:

*   What in my life am I finding hard to digest?
*   What experiences have I swallowed whole, without allowing myself to truly taste or process them?
*   Is there any unspoken anger, grief, or fear that is burning within me?
*   What nourishment am I truly, deeply hungry for?

Again, just ask, and then listen. Let the answers arise from the quiet wisdom of your body, not the busy chatter of your mind. Stay here for as long as it feels right. This is not about finding a quick fix. It’s about cultivating a relationship with your body built on trust and respect, rather than fear and control.

The neural pathways that link our gut and our brain are ancient and deeply ingrained. But the beautiful truth of neuroplasticity is that these pathways can be rewired. Every time you pause to listen like this, you are carving a new neural groove—a pathway of communication, compassion, and self-awareness. You are learning to respond to your body’s signals with kindness rather than frustration.

This is the path of transformation. It’s not about achieving a perfect, symptom-free body. It’s about developing the capacity to be with all of it—the comfortable and the uncomfortable, the sweet and the bitter. It’s about trusting that even the most challenging experiences contain nutrients for our evolution. It’s about becoming a masterful alchemist, capable of digesting the fullness of our human lives and transforming it all into the gold of consciousness.

Your body is not a problem to be solved. It is a sacred text, waiting to be read. Your stomach, with its fiery wisdom, is simply asking you to turn the page.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

If you are in crisis or feel unable to keep yourself safe, contact local emergency services or a crisis line immediately.

teachings.sourceTitle: A Practice for Spinal Freedom and Authentic Uprightness
teachings.title: A Practice for Spinal Freedom and Authentic Uprightness
teachings.summary: Susan invites a gentle, compassionate conversation with the spine, presenting it as both structural axis and messenger of emotional life. She frames posture as learned story rather than flaw and offers a short seated practice—spinal awareness meditation, gentle movements, and an integrity visualization—to cultivate a fluid, authentic uprightness. The emphasis is on listening, curiosity, and neuroplastic possibility rather than forcing a “perfect” posture.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember standing in front of a full-length mirror in a dance studio, many years ago. I was a young woman then, just beginning my journey into the body’s wisdom. The teacher asked us to simply stand and notice our posture. And what I saw… surprised me. My shoulders were slumped, my head pushed slightly forward, my lower back swayed in a deep curve. It was the posture of apology. A posture that was trying so hard to be good, to not take up too much space, to not be a bother.

It wasn’t *wrong*. My body, in its infinite wisdom, had found a way to hold me upright in a world that had often felt overwhelming. It was a strategy. But seeing it reflected back to me, I felt a sudden, sharp pang of longing. A longing for what? For an uprightness that felt less like a strain and more like a homecoming. For a spine that was not just a stack of bones, but a vibrant, alive channel of energy and truth.

It’s a tricky business, this human experience of being vertical. We are the only creatures who walk this way, with our heads balanced precariously atop this long, elegant, serpentine column. The spine. It is our central axis, our structural support, and our primary communication highway, connecting the brain to every single part of our being. It is, in so many ways, the architecture of our integrity.

## The Sacred Messenger

In my work with The Body Cards, the Spine speaks of this very thing—our relationship with our own integrity, our courage, and our flexibility. It is the literal “backbone” of our being. When we feel we have to bend over backward for others, our spine may curve in response. When we are rigid with fear, terrified of making a wrong move, our spine can become stiff and unyielding. When we feel defeated, when we’ve given up on our own truth, the spine can feel like it’s collapsing under an invisible weight.

These are not failures. They are communications. Your spine, like every part of your sacred body, is a messenger. It is constantly speaking to you, offering you the most profound feedback about your inner world. The tension you feel between your shoulder blades after a long day of carrying emotional burdens… the ache in your lower back when you feel unsupported in your life… these are not random pains to be ignored or medicated away. They are whispers from your soul, transmitted through the intricate neural pathways of your central channel.

Our posture is a learned language. The way we hold ourselves is a story written in tissue and bone, a story that often begins in early childhood as our sensitive nervous systems learn how to navigate the world. We learn to stand tall with pride, or to shrink in fear, or to brace against impact. These patterns become so ingrained, so automatic, that we mistake them for who we are. But they are not the whole story. They are simply the current shape of our energy.

And the beautiful, hopeful truth—a truth confirmed by the science of neuroplasticity—is that we can create new patterns. We can learn a new language of uprightness. We can consciously, lovingly, create new neural pathways that support a spine that is both strong *and* flexible, grounded *and* elevated. We can learn to stand tall in our truth, not with rigidity, but with a fluid, responsive grace.

## A Practice for Spinal Freedom

This is not about forcing yourself into a “perfect” posture. That is just another form of rigidity, another form of apology. This is an invitation to begin a gentle, compassionate conversation with your spine. It is a practice of listening, of sensing, and of allowing a new possibility to emerge from within. You will need a quiet space and a chair or cushion to sit on.

**Part 1: Spinal Awareness Meditation (10 minutes)**

Find a comfortable seated position. You can sit on the edge of a chair with your feet flat on the floor, or on a cushion on the floor with your legs crossed. Allow your hands to rest gently on your thighs.

Close your eyes, or soften your gaze toward the floor. Begin by bringing your awareness to your breath… not changing it, just noticing the gentle rise and fall of your chest and belly. Feel the air entering your nostrils, cool and fresh, and leaving, warm and soft.

Now, bring your gentle, curious attention to the base of your spine. Can you sense your tailbone, the very tip of this beautiful structure? Imagine it as an anchor, a grounding point connecting you to the earth beneath you. Don’t worry if you can’t “feel” it perfectly. Just bring your mind there, with softness.

Slowly, begin to travel your awareness up your spine, vertebra by vertebra. Move through the low back, the sacrum… noticing any sensations. Is there warmth? Tingling? Numbness? Tightness? Whatever is there, just notice it. No judgment. You are simply listening.

Continue your journey upward, through the gentle curve of your lumbar spine… past your kidneys… into the area behind your heart, the thoracic spine. This is an area where we hold so much. Grief, responsibility, the weight of the world. Just be with it. Breathe into whatever you find there.

Travel higher still, up through the neck, the cervical spine… this delicate bridge that holds your head. Feel the back of your skull, and imagine the very top of your spine meeting the base of your head. And then, imagine a single, fine, golden thread extending from the crown of your head all the way up to the heavens.

For a few moments, just sit here. Held between the earth and the sky. Aware of this entire channel, this river of energy and information. Noticing its curves, its strengths, its vulnerabilities. You are simply being with your spine, perhaps for the first time. You are listening to its story.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

**Part 2: Gentle Spinal Movements (5 minutes)**

When you feel ready, begin to introduce some gentle movement. Staying seated, place your hands on your knees. On an inhale, gently arch your back, allowing your heart to shine forward and your gaze to lift. This is a gentle spinal extension. Feel the front of your vertebrae opening.

On an exhale, gently round your spine, tucking your chin to your chest and drawing your navel back. Feel the back of your vertebrae opening, creating space. This is spinal flexion.

Continue this movement, flowing with your own breath. A gentle, cat-cow motion in your chair. Let the movement be slow, fluid, and delicious. This isn’t a workout. It’s an exploration. What does your spine want? How does it want to move? There is so much wisdom in its innate intelligence.

After a few rounds, come back to a neutral spine. Now, imagine you are growing taller from your seat. On an inhale, lengthen your spine. On an exhale, gently twist to your right, bringing your left hand to your right knee and your right hand to the chair behind you. The twist should originate from your mid-spine, not your neck. Keep both sit bones grounded. Breathe here for a moment, then gently unwind on an exhale. Repeat on the other side.

**Part 3: Integrity Visualization (5 minutes)**

Come back to your neutral, seated posture. Once again, bring your awareness to the full length of your spine, from tailbone to crown. Feel that connection between earth and sky.

Now, I invite you to call to mind a moment when you felt fully, authentically yourself. A moment you spoke your truth with clarity and kindness. A moment you stood your ground, not with aggression, but with a deep, quiet knowing. A moment you felt… integral.

It doesn’t have to be a big, dramatic moment. It could be a quiet conversation, a creative act, a simple choice. As you remember this moment, notice how your body feels. Notice your posture. Notice your spine. Can you feel a quality of energy that comes with that memory of integrity?

Breathe that quality into your spine. Imagine your spine as a channel for this energy of authentic uprightness. See it, feel it, as a column of light. It is not rigid or brittle. It is strong, yet fluid. It is radiant. It is your unique, divine axis. This is the feeling of standing tall in your truth.

## Your Daily Practice of Uprightness

This entire practice can take as little as fifteen minutes. You might choose to do it in the morning to set the tone for your day, or in the evening to release the tensions you’ve accumulated. It is a way of tending to your central channel, of reminding your nervous system that this new way of being—this authentic, fluid uprightness—is available to you now.

To stand tall in your truth is not an aggressive act. It is an act of profound self-love. It is the willingness to be seen, to be heard, and to take up your rightful space in the world. It is the embodiment of your own sacred authority. Your spine is the key. It is the path and the destination.

May you walk it with grace, with courage, and with infinite compassion for yourself and your journey.


---
