teachings.sourceTitle: Metabolizing Betrayal: Your Liver's Deepest Teaching
teachings.title: Metabolizing Betrayal: Your Liver's Deepest Teaching
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider the liver not only as a metabolic organ but as an alchemical processor of emotional toxins—especially betrayal, anger, and long-held resentment. Through client stories, neuroscience context, and a gentle somatic practice, she offers a path of presence, compassion, and incremental transformation rather than blame or quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Metabolizing Betrayal: Your Liver's Deepest Teaching

A woman I worked with years ago—we’ll call her Helena—came to me with a liver condition that had baffled her doctors. Her enzymes were perpetually elevated, she was fatigued to the bone, and a constant, low-grade nausea had become her unwanted companion. She had done everything “right,” she told me, her voice tight with a frustration that felt much older than her 40-odd years. She ate a clean diet, she didn’t drink, she exercised. Yet, her liver was crying out.

As we sat together in the quiet of my healing room, I asked her a question that wasn’t on any medical intake form. “Tell me about a time you felt deeply betrayed.”

Helena’s eyes, which had been fixed on a point just past my shoulder, suddenly met mine. And for the first time, I saw the deep, simmering anger she had been carrying. The story that tumbled out was one of a business partner who had not only stolen her ideas but had systematically dismantled her reputation, leaving her financially and emotionally bankrupt. The injustice of it was a palpable thing in the room—a bitter, metallic taste in the air. Helena had been forced to move on, to rebuild, but she had never truly processed the poison of that betrayal. Her liver, it seemed, was still trying to do it for her.

It’s a tricky business, being human. And one of the trickiest parts is what we do with the experiences that feel unforgivable. What do we do with the bitter pills of injustice, the searing pain of betrayal? We are told to forgive, to let go, to move on. But what if the body holds a different kind of memory? What if certain organs become the unwitting keepers of our deepest wounds?

## The Liver: Your Body’s Alchemical Genius

In the vast, intricate landscape of your body, the liver is the master alchemist. It is a metabolic powerhouse, performing over 500 vital functions, from filtering toxins in your blood to producing the bile necessary to digest fats. It is a resilient, regenerative marvel, the only organ in the body that can regrow itself from a small piece. It is, in essence, the great processor. It takes everything you ingest—food, drink, medication, air—and discerns what is nourishing and what is toxic, what to keep and what to eliminate.

But what we often forget in our mechanically-minded view of the body is that we ingest *experiences* too. We take in the energy of a harsh word, the shock of a sudden loss, the slow-burn of resentment. And the liver, in its infinite wisdom and tireless service, tries to metabolize these as well. It tries to process the energetic toxins of life, especially those that feel deeply, fundamentally *unjust*.

When we are steeped in feelings of anger, bitterness, and resentment over a long period, the liver can become overwhelmed. It’s as if we are asking this magnificent organ to continuously process a poison for which there is no antidote. The energy of these emotions, when left unexpressed and unresolved, can crystallize in the body. In the language of The Elevated Body system, the liver and its partner, the gallbladder, are the seat of our capacity to process anger and discern what is right for us. When this system is out of balance, we might see the physical manifestation of this emotional toxicity—gallstones, which I often think of as crystallized bitterness, or the kind of chronic inflammation and dysfunction that Helena was experiencing.

This isn’t about blame. It is never about blame. You are not broken. Your body has not failed you. On the contrary, your body, in its profound love for you, is sending you a message. It is communicating a deep truth that your conscious mind may have tried to override or ignore. The symptom is not the enemy; it is a sacred messenger, asking you to turn your attention inward.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Neural Pathways of a Grudge

Neuroscience now shows us what ancient wisdom traditions have always known: our thoughts and emotions have a physical impact on our bodies. When you repeatedly replay a story of betrayal, you are strengthening a specific neural pathway in your brain. The story becomes a well-worn groove, a default setting. Your nervous system learns to live in a state of high alert, perpetually scanning for the next injustice, the next threat. This creates a cascade of stress hormones that, over time, can be incredibly taxing on the body, and particularly on the liver, which has to process them.

Holding onto a grudge is not a sign of strength; it is a state of chronic stress. It is the body being held in a state of fight, a war that is being waged internally. The person who betrayed you may be long gone, but in the landscape of your own body, the battle rages on. The liver, in this scenario, is the battlefield.

I worked with another client, a man whose gallbladder was so full of stones he was in constant, debilitating pain. His story was one of a bitter divorce, where he felt his ex-wife had turned his children against him. He spoke of her with a venom that was startling. “I will never forgive her,” he would say, his jaw clenched. And his body was reflecting that refusal. His bile, the very substance meant to help him digest life, had turned to stone.

Healing for him didn’t begin with a lecture on forgiveness. It began with compassion. Compassion for the immense pain he was in. Compassion for the part of him that felt so deeply wronged, so profoundly betrayed. It began with creating a safe space for him to simply acknowledge the rage he was carrying, without judgment. To allow the anger to be there, to give it a voice, without needing it to be righteous or justified. Just to let it be seen.

## Metabolizing the Unforgivable

So what does it mean to metabolize betrayal? It doesn’t necessarily mean forgetting. It doesn’t mean condoning the actions of another. And it doesn’t even always mean forgiving, at least not in the Hallmark card sense of the word.

*Metabolizing is about transformation.* It is about developing the capacity within your own being to process the experience so that it no longer has a toxic hold on you. It’s about finding the nutrients in the poison. It’s an alchemical process of turning the lead of your pain into the gold of your wisdom.

How do we begin? We begin by turning toward the body. We begin by placing a hand on our own belly, over the space of our liver on the right side, and simply breathing. We begin by offering a different kind of message to this part of ourselves.

> *You can try this right now. Find a quiet space. Place your right hand over the lower part of your right ribcage. Close your eyes. Take a few slow, deep breaths. And then, silently or out loud, offer these words to your liver: “Thank you. Thank you for working so hard for me. I am here with you now. I am willing to help you process what has felt too heavy to carry alone.”*

Notice what happens. There may be a softening. There may be a wave of emotion. There may be nothing at all. The point is not to force an experience, but to open a dialogue. To shift the relationship from one of unconscious burden to one of conscious, loving partnership with your own body.

From this place of presence, we can begin to gently inquire. What is the story my body is holding? What is the injustice that still feels alive in my system? What would it feel like to allow even a tiny bit of space around this story? We are not looking for answers from the mind, which will only want to re-litigate the case. We are listening for the deeper wisdom of the body, the quiet whispers beneath the noise of the grievance.

This is the journey of healing. It is not a quick fix. It is a practice of returning, again and again, to a state of presence and compassion for yourself. It is the slow, sacred work of rewiring those ancient neural pathways of anger and creating new ones—pathways of resilience, of wisdom, of self-compassion. It is about realizing that your ultimate power lies not in changing the past, but in how you choose to relate to it in your present.

Your liver knows how to heal. It knows how to regenerate. Our work is to create the inner conditions—the emotional and energetic environment—that allow for that natural healing intelligence to flow. To stop feeding it the poison of old stories and instead, to nourish it with the frequencies of presence, compassion, and the willingness to let go, not for them, but for *you*.

May you find the courage to turn toward the parts of you that hold the deepest hurts. May you discover the alchemical power within you to transform even the most bitter of experiences into a source of profound strength and wisdom. And may you come to know, in your very cells, that you are worthy of a life free from the prison of the past.


---

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

Symptoms are reframed as communicative messengers rather than mere malfunctions, and the author offers a somatic, listening-based approach — becoming a conductor rather than a controller — to reweave fragmented parts through breath, touch and gentle sustained attention. Practical tools include hand-on-heart awareness, vocal toning, and the threefold inquiry of purpose, inquiry and transcendence to shift entrenched patterns. The essay names the social and relational dimensions of healing and encourages group containers that honor interior process.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The Web of Your Being - The Unified Field of Consciousness

There is a luminous intelligence that moves through you whether you notice it or not. It is not your thinking mind, nor is it merely the sum of organs and tissues. It is an invisible orchestration - a living, humming web in which each strand is both distinct and inseparable from the whole. When you come to know this web you begin to sense how every breath, every cell, every memory and every feeling is part of a single field of organization. The Taoists knew this intimacy with the subtle order of life when they wrote, "Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished." In that effortless accomplishment you glimpse how your body and consciousness coordinate without your conscious direction - and how your presence can transform the way that coordination unfolds.

The Miraculous Totality

Think of your body as a city and each organ, tissue, and system as a neighborhood with its own rhythm, language and needs. The nervous system sends messages like couriers. The heart pumps like a central station, moving energy and information through the arteries and veins. The immune system patrols like vigilant guardians. The digestive tract metabolizes experience into usable fuel. Yet the city is more than the activity of its neighborhoods. There is an underlying intelligence that knows where to send resources, when to repair infrastructure, and which neighborhoods need attention. This is the Web of Your Being - the unified field in which physiology, emotion, memory and spirit converse continuously.

What is most miraculous is that this web works without your explicit permission. You do not need to decide when your liver will metabolize a toxin or when your lungs will pull in life-giving oxygen. The systems coordinate with uncanny timing - a choreography that predates your conscious narrative. It is an intelligence that has nothing to prove and everything to maintain. It sustains you through the night while you sleep and renews cells without any dramatic fanfare. The body, in its quiet sovereignty, is closer to the Tao than the conceptual mind can be. There is great relief in accepting that some aspects of your life are already being held by this deep, invisible order.

Symptoms as Sacred Messengers

Every ache and every pattern has meaning. When you lived only in the realm of cause and effect you learned to treat symptoms as enemies to be eradicated. Modern medicine has given us miraculous tools to do so, and yet when symptom management becomes the sole focus you lose sight of the intelligence behind the message. Your body is a messenger - not a malfunctioning machine. Pain, inflammation, fatigue and chronic patterns are forms of language in the body-mind field. They are attempts at communication from parts of you that have been silenced, rejected or forgotten.

Imagine a nervous system that has been wired in childhood to assume danger. It keeps sending red alerts because, at one time, alertness saved your life. The body continues to act in fidelity to that truth. When the immune system identifies parts of you as foreign, it speaks to a history of alienation within your own psyche. A frozen shoulder can be a metaphor and a mechanical reality at once - an area of life you have stopped moving through because movement felt unsafe. The holographic nature of the body means that these messages are never isolated. A restriction in the hips alters your gait, your breath and even the quality of your relationships. Each symptom is a portal if you are willing to listen - a map that leads to an unseen architecture of belief and lived habit.

Fragmentation and the Cost of Disconnection

Many of us live with a quietly artisted fragmentation. You have known what it is to split: to carry one face for public performance and another for private survival, to hold terror in the tissues while the mind creates a soothing narrative, to be present in the world yet absent from your own body. Fragmentation is a survival strategy that becomes a chronic pattern when unexamined. It organises the Web of Your Being into compartments that do not talk, or that speak in poor translations. You may be brilliant at thinking your way through problems while your body holds grief as a tightness beneath the ribs. You may be generous and open in relationships yet carry a hidden instruction to shrink and not claim pleasure. Each split is an energetic toll. It drains resources, creates chronic inflammation, exhausts the immune system and blunts the aliveness you came here to know.

When parts of you stop being recognized by other parts, the immune system sometimes physically mirrors that alienation. Auto-immune responses are heartbreaking examples of inner exile. The body begins to attack what it no longer identifies as belonging to the unified field. In an even subtler way, chronic anxiety is the nervous system's long-term dedication to the state of being prepared for an imagined threat. Fragmentation blunts your capacity to hold complexity, to contain paradox, to receive life in both tenderness and challenge. Yet the medicine for fragmentation is not force but presence. The reconnection begins with listening - a gentle, persistent attention that invites estranged systems to remember their role within the whole.

You as Conductor - Not Controller

There is an exquisite distinction between being the controller and being the conductor. Control is coercive. It tries to micromanage the movements and outcomes. Conduction is musical - it invokes a subtle resonant authority that allows parts to express their intelligence while shaping the field through timing, cueing and relationship. The more you practice tuning your attention, the more you become a conductor of your own inner orchestra.

To step into this role you do not need to issue orders. You develop a sensitivity to timing and resonance. You cultivate a listening that is both embodied and spacious. You learn how to cue the breath, soften the neck, place a hand over an organ and listen for its story. You learn how to invite rather than to demand. The confluence of somatic presence, breath and intention alters the subtle field. The nervous system relaxes because it recognizes a new pattern - someone is present to hold its alarms without betraying panic. The heart relaxes because it senses a companion for its grief. The digestive system can take the time to digest not just food but experience when you provide a receptive container.

In practical terms you may find yourself pausing before you react to a symptom. You may place your palm over the area that feels loud with pain and speak in first person what the tissue needs to hear. You may imagine a slow exhale that invites the liver to loosen its clenched processing of old injury. These simple acts are not magical thinking. They are an invitation to the ancient intelligence within you to reform the patterns of flow. When you conduct with kindness and intention you are training the field to be more cooperative, more fluid and ultimately more joyful.

The Holographic Principle of Healing

Working with one part of you can change the whole. This is not metaphorical optimism but the holographic principle at work: each part contains the pattern of the whole. When you open a tender conversation with your hands, you may find your heart softens. Attending to the tightness in your throat can reveal a buried anger in the liver-gallbladder field. When you begin to allow the body to speak with dignity and curiosity, the ripples move outward and rearrange the matrix. This is why the practice of listening to one system - whether it is the thyroid, the lungs or the Web of Your Being itself - offers a portal to entire recalibrations of identity and habit.

Your ability to sense this holographic wholeness is also the path to deeper empathy. As you learn to re-member your own disowned parts, you become more capable of holding others without judgment. You stop assuming that a behavior is personal attack and begin to see it as an activation of a system doing its best. This recognition is not moralizing. It is compassionate intelligence. You can set boundaries and protect yourself without reentering the reactive patterns of exile and suppression that created the dissonance in the first place.

Practices for Aligning the Web

Begin where you are able. The most radical practice is often the simplest - a regular orientation to your breathing and to the felt sense of your physicality. When you return to your breath with curious attention you teach your nervous system that the present can be safe. When you place a hand at the heart or on the belly and breathe into the touch you expand the field of attention beyond the narrative mind. Use your voice as well. A low hum or soft tonal exhale creates sympathetic vibration through tissues and can release held patterns. I encourage you to speak the truth you most need to hear to the area of your body that feels loud. "I see you. I hear you. You are safe with me." These are not empty phrases. They are energetic commitments that the Web recognizes and begins to reorganize around.

Another potent practice is the threefold inquiry I have used with the Elevate Your Body To Love cards: purpose, inquiry and transcendence. This structured listening cultivates a kind attention that first acknowledges function, then invites story, and finally imagines the healed pattern as present reality. You can do this with any system: the lungs that feel constricted, the knees that will not bend, the shoulders carrying an invisible load. Start with the Purpose - what does this system do for you? Move into Inquiry - what feelings, beliefs or histories might be expressing themselves here? Stay with whatever arises without judgment. Finish with Transcendence - imagine and speak the pattern you wish to embody as if it already exists within your tissues. The Web does not distinguish between imagination and biochemistry. Your poised attention changes the quality of signaling and invites a new field to emerge.

When the Field Resists

There will be times when the intelligence within you appears stubborn. Patterns that have been woven for decades may resist your invitations. This is not failure. It is fidelity to the survival story that supported you in an earlier climate. Be gentle. The Tao Te Ching reminds us that yielding is often more powerful than force. "The soft overcomes the hard," the text suggests, and this is true for inner transformation as well. Persistence without coercion is the alchemy here. You return, again and again, with kindness and curiosity. You do the small practices of listening and presence. You find support when a system is burdened beyond your current capacity - from skilled practitioners, therapists, or medical care. The Web of Your Being will not be replaced by a single intervention. It will re-weave itself over time through consistent, tender attention.

Reweaving Community and Field

No web exists in isolation. You are an individual expression of an interwoven field that includes family narratives, cultural paradigms and ancestral patterns. The systems of your body reflect not only your personal history but also collective beliefs. When you heal, you shift the field for those around you. When you re-member your own fragmented parts, you model a different possibility for your family and community. This is why group processes can be so catalytic - the field is amplified and the shared resonance makes re-patterning faster and deeper.

Gather with others in containers that honor interior process. Share the stories of what is awakening within you without needing to fix anyone else. Listen without advising. In that sacred holding, your web finds new connections and your nervous system learns different rhythms of safety. The body remembers that it can trust not only the quiet of itself but also the responsive presence of others.

A Blessing for Your Web

May you learn to listen in the way a river listens to the rocks it flows over - attending to the outlines, aware of the resistance, yet always continuing in patient movement. May you become a conductor of your inner orchestra - not by forcing notes into alignment but by holding time and invitation so that each instrument may find its pitch. Remember that reweaving a life is not a project to be completed but a conversation to be sustained. Let the Tao guide you - allow gentleness to be your teacher and patience to be your ally. You are not broken. You are a living whole learning to remember itself. Trust the intelligence that keeps you breathing. Engage it with reverence. Let the web of your being sing.

teachings.summary: Susan reframes the immune system as a communicator of boundary and identity rather than solely a warrior, and offers consciousness-based practices to strengthen it through discernment and self-integration. The piece provides a guided Boundary Meditation, a Visualization of Radical Self-Acceptance (the Inner Council), and daily integration suggestions to help the nervous system shift from constant threat to clearer, loving discernment. These practices are presented as ongoing, accessible ways to cultivate resilience and inner safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There are moments in life when a profound thought arrives, unbidden, as the best ones often do. It can happen in a quiet moment of observation, when we least expect it.

This is often most true when we feel invaded. Many of us have experienced periods where it feels like everything is coming at us—an endless barrage of demands, a cacophony of distressing news, or even environmental sensitivities that feel like a personal affront. In these times, it is common to feel porous and undefended. The body, in its infinite wisdom, may respond in the only way it knows how: with illness. This can be seen as the immune system, the elegant, intricate guardian of our identity, screaming for our attention.

We’re taught to think of our immune system as a military operation. An army of cells, a battalion of antibodies, all waging war against foreign invaders. And on a purely biological level, there’s truth to that. It is a system of profound discernment, a constant dance of distinguishing *self* from *other*. It’s the gatekeeper of our physical being. But what if we’ve been looking at it through the wrong lens? What if the constant state of high alert, of attack and defend, is actually exhausting the very system designed to protect us?

Your body is a sacred messenger, and the state of your immune system is one of its most profound communications. When it’s in overdrive, as in autoimmune conditions, it’s a crisis of identity—the body, confused, begins to attack its own tissues. It’s the ultimate manifestation of turning against the self. When it’s deficient, it’s often a sign of profound exhaustion, of a spirit worn down from constantly defending its borders. Chronic inflammation, that slow burn beneath the surface, is the body living in a state of perpetual, low-grade threat. It’s a body that has learned the world is not safe.

But here’s a very good thing to know. The body’s wisdom is not just in its alarms, but in its capacity for transformation. We can shift the entire paradigm from one of attack and defense to one of discernment and integration. We can teach our nervous system, and by extension, our immune system, that not every “other” is a threat to be annihilated. That some influences are simply information. That some are even doorways into our highest growth. This is the beginning of strengthening your immune system through consciousness.

## The Boundary Meditation: A Guided Practice

This is not about building walls, but about cultivating a clear, resilient, and loving energetic boundary. It’s about teaching your system the difference between a firm “no” and a fearful one. Find a quiet place where you can sit comfortably, with your spine straight but not rigid, and your feet flat on the floor.

1.  **Ground and Arrive:** Close your eyes. Take three deep, slow breaths. With each exhale, feel your body settling more deeply into your chair. Feel the solid ground beneath your feet, the unwavering support of the earth. You are here. You are safe.

2.  **Sense Your Energetic Field:** Bring your awareness to the space around your physical body. Without trying to change anything, simply notice it. Can you sense a field of energy that extends a few inches, or even a few feet, from your skin? This is your personal space, your energetic boundary. It might feel fuzzy, or dense, or barely there at all. Just notice.

3.  **Define Your Space:** Now, with gentle intention, imagine you can define this space. Imagine a beautiful, permeable membrane of light surrounding you, about an arm’s length away in all directions—front, back, sides, above, and below. This is your sacred space. You get to decide what comes in and what stays out.

4.  **The Power of “No”:** Think of something or someone that feels draining or invasive to you. It doesn’t have to be a major trauma; it could be a demanding colleague or a negative news story. As you bring it to mind, notice what happens to your energetic field. Does it shrink? Does it harden? Now, from the core of your being, silently and firmly say, “No.” Feel the power of that word. It is not an act of aggression; it is an act of self-honor. Watch as your boundary of light becomes clearer, stronger, more defined. Nothing can enter without your conscious permission.

5.  **The Power of “Yes”:** Now, think of something that feels deeply nourishing. The warmth of the sun, the love of a pet, a beautiful piece of music. As you bring this to mind, silently and lovingly say, “Yes.” Feel your boundary become more permeable, more receptive. Imagine it has tiny, intelligent pores that can open to receive love, support, and beauty, while still maintaining their integrity. Practice this—the firm “no” and the soft “yes.” Feel the discernment in your very cells.

6.  **Return:** When you feel complete, bring your awareness back to your physical body. Wiggle your fingers and toes. Gently open your eyes. Carry this sense of your sacred, intelligent boundary with you as you move back into your day.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Visualization of Radical Self-Acceptance

So much of our immune system’s confusion comes from our own internal wars. The parts of ourselves we reject, judge, or try to exile become the “other” that the body is then primed to attack. Healing the immune system requires a radical act of inner diplomacy. It requires welcoming all of your parts home.

This practice is best done lying down, in a state of deep relaxation.

1.  **The Inner Council:** Once you are relaxed, imagine you are standing in a beautiful, safe, and sacred inner space. Before you is a large, round table. This is your inner council table. One by one, invite the different parts of yourself to take a seat. Invite the scared child. Invite the angry teenager. Invite the harsh inner critic. Invite the part that feels exhausted. Invite the part that is radiant and joyful. Leave no one out. See them all there, seated at the table of your consciousness.

2.  **Giving Voice:** Go around the table, and give each part a voice. Ask each one: *What do you need me to know? What do you need from me?* Listen without judgment. The inner critic might need to know it’s trying to protect you. The scared child might need a hug. The angry part might need to have its pain acknowledged. Simply listen. Receive their messages.

3.  **The Light of Acceptance:** Once every part has been heard, imagine a warm, golden light beginning to glow in the center of the table. It’s the light of pure, unconditional acceptance. See this light expand, gently and lovingly, to encompass every single part of you seated at the table. It doesn’t try to fix them or change them. It simply loves them. It says, *You belong. You are part of me. You are welcome here.* Feel the profound relief as the inner war comes to an end. There is no “other” here. There is only *self*, in all its beautiful, messy, glorious complexity.

## Daily Integration: A Practice for Life

This work is not a one-time fix. It is a practice, a returning, a cultivation of a new way of being. Here are a few ways to integrate this immune-strengthening consciousness into your daily life:

*   **Morning Boundary Check-In:** Before you even get out of bed, take 60 seconds to sense your energetic boundary. Re-establish your sphere of light. Set the intention for the day: “I will honor my sacred space. I will receive what nourishes me and release what does not.”

*   **“Self or Other?” Discernment:** Throughout the day, when you feel a charge of anger, fear, or overwhelm, pause. Place a hand on your heart and ask: “Is this mine, or is it someone else’s?” This simple question can stop you from absorbing the energetic static of the world around you.

*   **Metabolize Your Day:** At the end of the day, take a few moments to consciously metabolize your experiences. Breathe in, and acknowledge everything you encountered. Breathe out, and release any energy that is not yours to carry. Give thanks for the lessons, for the nourishment, and even for the challenges that are helping you grow.

Ultimately, the journey to a strong immune system is a spiritual one. It is the journey of coming home to yourself. It is the realization that you are not a fortress under siege, but a luminous, intelligent field of consciousness, capable of navigating this world with both strength and grace. It is the slow, beautiful, and life-long practice of learning to love all that you are.


---

teachings.sourceTitle: Inspiration and Expiration: The Spiritual Dimensions of Breath
teachings.title: Inspiration and Expiration: The Spiritual Dimensions of Breath
teachings.summary: Susan frames breath as a sacred exchange—inhale as receiving life/spirit, exhale as releasing what no longer serves—and uses Miriam’s story to show how shallow breathing often mirrors beliefs about worthiness and self-sacrifice. The piece invites gentle, compassionate attention to the body as messenger and presents breathwork as a supportive bridge between conscious intention and the autonomic nervous system. Emphasis is on listening rather than forcing change and on creating safe space for gradual unfolding.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A client, I’ll call her Miriam, came to me once, folded in on herself. Her shoulders were a soft curve around her heart, her head bowed, and her breath… her breath was a tiny, shallow whisper. She spoke in hushed tones, as if afraid to take up space, even with her own voice. She was a successful lawyer, a mother, a wife, a pillar of her community—and she was suffocating.

She told me about her life, a litany of responsibilities and achievements. But as she spoke, I wasn’t just listening to her words. I was listening to her body. And her body was telling me a story of profound exhaustion, of a life lived for everyone else, with very little air left for herself.

I asked her, gently, “Miriam, what would it be like to take a full, deep breath? Right now?”

Her eyes widened in something that looked like fear. She tried. I saw her chest attempt to rise, a small, hesitant movement, before it collapsed back in on itself. She couldn’t. It was as if an invisible band was constricting her ribs, a silent, powerful force holding her back from the very source of life itself.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We learn so early to hold our breath. We do it when we’re scared, when we’re concentrating, when we’re bracing for impact. We learn to make ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to want less, to need less. And our breath, the most fundamental rhythm of our existence, follows suit. It becomes shallow, constricted, a pale imitation of the powerful, life-giving force it is meant to be.

## The Sacred Exchange

The word ‘inspiration’ literally means ‘to breathe in spirit.’ Think about that for a moment. *In-spirit*. With every inhale, you are not just drawing in oxygen; you are drawing in life force, divine energy, the very essence of the universe. You are breathing in possibility, creativity, and the infinite, loving support that is always available to you.

And ‘expiration’? It means ‘the spirit leaves.’ With every exhale, you are releasing what is no longer needed. You are letting go of the old, the stagnant, the toxic. You are releasing thoughts, beliefs, and emotions that have served their purpose and are now ready to be transformed. It is a sacred exchange, a constant dance between receiving and releasing, between taking in and letting go.

But what happens when we don’t feel worthy of that full inspiration? What happens when, deep in our cells, we carry a belief that we don’t deserve to take up that much space, to receive that much life? Our breath becomes a reflection of that belief. It becomes shallow, timid, apologetic. We sip at the air, rather than drinking it in deeply. We hold ourselves in a state of perpetual, low-grade suffocation, wondering why we feel so tired, so anxious, so disconnected.

And what about the exhale? What happens when we are afraid to let go? When we cling to old hurts, old stories, old identities, because we don’t know who we would be without them? Our exhale becomes constricted. We hold on to the very things that are poisoning us, because the thought of releasing them feels even more terrifying. We become containers for stale, stagnant energy, and our bodies, in their infinite wisdom, begin to reflect that toxicity back to us through physical symptoms.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Body as a Sacred Messenger

Our bodies are sacred messengers, and the lungs are one of their most eloquent communicators. They are the intimate interface between our inner world and the external atmosphere. They are where the outside becomes the inside, where the world enters us and becomes a part of us. And they are where we, in turn, release ourselves back into the world.

When we experience issues with our lungs—whether it’s asthma, chronic bronchitis, or simply a persistent, shallow breath—it is an invitation to look deeper. It is an invitation to explore our relationship with life itself. Are we allowing ourselves to be fully inspired? Are we allowing ourselves to fully release what needs to be let go?

I worked with Miriam for many months. We didn’t focus on ‘fixing’ her breathing. Instead, we focused on creating a space of safety and compassion where her body could finally begin to tell its story. We explored the deep-seated beliefs she held about her own worth, the generational patterns of self-sacrifice she had inherited, the unspoken grief she was carrying in her heart.

Slowly, gently, as she began to untangle these knots, her breath began to change. It started as a flicker, a momentary deepening, a sigh of release. Then, one day, in the middle of a session, she took a deep, shuddering breath that seemed to start in her feet and travel all the way up to the crown of her head. Tears streamed down her face, tears of grief, of release, of homecoming.

“I’m here,” she whispered, her hand on her heart. “I’m finally here.”

## A New Possibility

Your breath is the most powerful tool you have for transformation. It is the bridge between your conscious mind and your autonomic nervous system, the gateway to the wisdom of your body. You cannot think your way into a new way of being. But you can breathe your way there.

When you consciously choose to deepen your breath, you are sending a powerful message to your nervous system: *You are safe. You are supported. You can relax.* You are creating new neural pathways, rewiring your brain for a state of calm and connection. You are reminding your body of its innate capacity for healing and wholeness.

This is not about forcing your breath, or striving for some perfect, yogic ideal. It is simply about paying attention. It is about bringing a gentle, loving awareness to the rhythm of your own life force. It is about noticing, without judgment, where your breath is constricted, and inviting it, with compassion, to soften and expand.

What would it be like, just for a moment, to allow yourself to be fully inspired? To draw the breath all the way down into your belly, to feel your ribs expand, to receive the full, abundant gift of this moment? And what would it be like to let it all go? To release the tension in your shoulders, the tightness in your jaw, the stories you have been telling yourself for so long?

This is the journey of healing. It is not a destination, but a process, a dance, a constant returning to the truth of who you are. And it all begins, and ends, with the breath.


---

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

teachings.sourceTitle: When the Body Whispers Before It Screams
teachings.title: When the Body Whispers Before It Screams
teachings.summary: Susan offers a personal account of how years of tuning out subtle bodily signals culminated in a severe break-through event that forced a deeper listening. She outlines the neuroscience of interoception and how childhood survival strategies can dim internal sensing, then offers gentle, practical invitations—small embodied practices and a compassionate curiosity toward symptoms—to rebuild trust with the body. The piece frames this work as patient, ongoing, and intimate rather than prescriptive.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
My grandmother had hands that told stories. Rough, warm, capable hands that could coax bread dough into rising and calm a crying child with a single touch.

We live so much of our lives in our heads—in the endless swirl of thoughts, plans, worries, and memories—that we can forget we even *have* a body. We can forget that this flesh, these bones, this intricate web of sensation and energy is the sacred vessel for our entire experience of being alive. We forget, that is… until it screams.

For me, the scream came on a Tuesday afternoon. I remember the quality of the light, the way it slanted through the window and illuminated the dust motes dancing in the air. I was reaching for a book on a high shelf, a simple, ordinary movement. And then—a searing, electric pain shot through the right side of my face. It was a lightning bolt of pure agony that buckled my knees and stole my breath. In that moment, there was no thought, no analysis, no past or future. There was only the raw, blinding reality of the pain. The official diagnosis, when it came, was trigeminal neuralgia, a condition some doctors grimly call the “suicide disease” for its brutal, unrelenting nature. But the deeper, truer diagnosis, the one that took me years to fully understand, was this: I had spent a lifetime ignoring my body’s whispers.

Before the scream, there were countless subtle signals, a whole chorus of whispers I had expertly trained myself to tune out. There was the persistent clenching in my jaw, a tightness I would only notice when I’d try to relax at the end of the day. There was the shallow breathing, the quiet hum of anxiety that I had long ago accepted as my baseline, my “normal.” There were the headaches I pushed through with caffeine and sheer will, the profound fatigue I overrode because there was always too much to do, and the quiet, persistent ache in my heart that I learned to expertly numb with work, with doing, with anything that would keep me from having to feel it. I was a master of overriding my body’s messages, of choosing my mind’s ambitious agenda over my body’s gentle, wise counsel. And eventually, my body, in its profound and desperate love for me, had no choice but to shout.

This progression from whisper to shout is a universal story, one I have witnessed in countless clients over thirty years of healing work. The body *always* communicates with us. It speaks in a language of sensation, of energy, of symptom and ease. It begins with a whisper—a subtle flutter in the chest, a fleeting ache in the shoulder, a quiet, persistent sense of “off-ness” about a person or a situation. It’s the gut feeling you ignore, the moment of fatigue you push past. If we don’t listen, the whisper gets a little louder. It becomes a persistent nudge—a recurring indigestion, a patch of eczema, a sleep that is no longer restful. It’s a pattern of discomfort we can no longer so easily dismiss. If we continue to turn away, to numb, to override, the whisper becomes a shout. The shout is the chronic condition, the debilitating pain, the diagnosis that stops us in our tracks. It is the body’s last-ditch effort to get our attention, to bring us back home to ourselves, to the sacred, unified field of our own being.

## The Neuroscience of Tuning Out

Why do we lose the ability to hear these subtle signals? It’s not a personal failing or a sign of weakness. For most of us, it’s a deeply ingrained adaptive response that begins in childhood. Our capacity to sense our internal state—the rich, ever-shifting landscape of our body—is a process called *interoception*. It’s the brain’s way of receiving and interpreting a constant stream of signals from within the body: from the heart, the lungs, the gut, the muscles. This network, largely carried by the vast and wandering vagus nerve, is the biological basis of our feelings, our emotions, and our fundamental sense of self.

When we are small, our survival depends entirely on the safety of our environment and the attunement of our caregivers. If that environment feels unsafe, chaotic, or overwhelming, or if our authentic feelings are met with disapproval, dismissal, or punishment, we learn a brilliant survival strategy: we disconnect from our internal world. If feeling our fear, our sadness, or our anger is simply too much for our little nervous systems to handle, we numb. We retreat into the relative safety of our minds. We dissociate from the raw, overwhelming, and inconvenient sensations in our bodies. This is not a conscious choice; it is a profound act of self-preservation, a testament to the incredible resilience of a child’s spirit.

The neural pathways that form the superhighway of interoception become faint, like country roads that have fallen into disuse. The volume on our internal awareness gets turned way, way down. We learn to live from the neck up, navigating the world through intellect and will, while the rich, nuanced wisdom of our bodies goes unheard. We become strangers to our own physical selves, until one day, the body has to scream to be heard over the incessant noise of our minds.

My journey with trigeminal neuralgia was a long, painful, and ultimately transformational process of learning to listen. It was a forced surrender, a complete dismantling of a lifetime of ignoring my body’s truth. It required me to get very, very quiet. To sit with the pain, not as an enemy to be vanquished, but as a messenger. *What was this pain trying to tell me?* I would ask, my hand gently on my cheek. *What part of me have I abandoned that is now crying out for my attention?* Slowly, painstakingly, I began to rebuild the connection. I started with the simplest of practices: feeling my feet on the floor. Noticing the subtle sensation of my breath moving in and out of my body. Allowing myself to feel the warmth of a cup of tea in my hands. These were not grand, dramatic gestures, but small, consistent acts of turning my awareness inward, of saying to my body, again and again, *I am here. I am listening.*

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Learning to Hear the Whispers Again

How do we begin to tune back into our body’s whispers? It is a gentle, compassionate process of re-establishing trust and communication. It is not about “fixing” yourself, for you have never been broken. It is about coming home. It is a practice of remembering the wisdom that is already encoded in you, a wisdom as ancient as the Tao itself, which reminds us: “The gentlest thing in the world overcomes the hardest thing in the world.”

Here are a few gentle invitations to begin:

**Practice Embodied Presence.** Choose one small, ordinary moment each day to be fully present in your body. It could be the sensation of water on your skin in the shower, noticing its temperature and pressure. It could be the feeling of your heart beating after you’ve walked up a flight of stairs, a steady rhythm of life within your chest. Or the simple, complex taste of your morning coffee. The practice is simply to notice, without judgment. Let the sensations be exactly as they are. This is the practice of inhabiting your own life, one moment at a time. It is a quiet revolution against the tyranny of the mind.

**Get Curious About Your Symptoms.** When you feel an ache, a pain, or a discomfort, see if you can meet it with curiosity instead of the habitual fear or resistance. Place a gentle hand on the area, a gesture of kindness. Breathe into it, imagining your breath could create a little space around the sensation. Ask it, softly, *What do you have to tell me? What do you need me to know?* You may not get an immediate, clear answer in words. The answer may come as an image, a memory, a feeling, or a color. The key is to shift from an adversarial relationship with your symptoms to a compassionate, inquisitive one. You are not fighting a battle; you are beginning a dialogue.

**Explore the Language of Sensation.** Your body speaks in sensation, not in sentences. To learn its language, you must become a student of its unique dialect. Begin to build a vocabulary for what you feel. Is the sensation sharp or dull? Hot or cold? Tingly, buzzy, or numb? Is it expanding or contracting? Does it have a color? A texture? A weight? The more you can name the nuances of your internal experience, the more you are strengthening those neural pathways of interoception. You are turning up the volume on your body’s whispers, making it easier to hear them.

**Follow the Wise Impulse.** Our bodies are constantly giving us impulses for what they need to find balance and regulation. A sudden urge to stretch your arms overhead. A deep, cleansing yawn. A desire to look out the window and rest your eyes on the sky. A feeling of thirst. So often, we override these small, wise impulses in the service of productivity or politeness. What would it be like to honor them? To allow your body to stretch when it wants to stretch? To drink when it is thirsty? To rest when it is tired? This is a radical act of self-love and a direct way to rebuild trust with your body. It is telling your body, *Your needs matter.*

The journey back to the body is not a linear one. There will be days when the whispers are clear as a bell, and days when all you hear is static. Be infinitely gentle with yourself. You are unlearning a lifetime of conditioning. You are re-wiring your brain and nervous system for safety and connection. This is profound, sacred work. It is the work of a lifetime.

Your body is not a machine to be fixed or an enemy to be conquered. It is a sacred messenger, a wise and loving ally on your journey of healing and transformation. It has been whispering to you all along, waiting patiently, with infinite love, for you to come home. May you have the courage to get quiet enough to listen. May you learn to trust the wisdom that flows in your own veins.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: When Life Falls Apart: Finding the Sacred in the Shattered
teachings.title: When Life Falls Apart: Finding the Sacred in the Shattered
teachings.summary: When life collapses, Susan invites readers to hold the shattered pieces with tenderness and curiosity rather than hurry toward fixes. She describes the body’s nervous‑system response to sudden loss, offers Kintsugi and Tao metaphors for repair and flow, and centers simple embodied attention as the first, sacred step toward renewal. The piece reframes breaking as an initiation that can reveal resilience, compassion, and new direction.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human existence. We spend so much of our energy building, striving, creating lives that feel solid, dependable. We lay the bricks of our relationships, pave the roads of our careers, and furnish the rooms of our identity with beliefs we hold as truths. And then, sometimes, in a breath, it all comes tumbling down. The ground gives way. The diagnosis is spoken. The person you love walks away. The career you built dissolves. It is a shattering. A terrifying, disorienting free-fall into the unknown. And in that moment, the world as you knew it is gone. What is left is just… pieces. I remember a time, years ago, when my own world fractured. I was sitting in my small garden, the one I had poured so much love and attention into, when the phone call came. A project I had dedicated years to, a community I had nurtured, had been dismantled by forces beyond my control. I remember the feeling of the sun on my skin, the scent of damp earth and jasmine, and then a sudden, hollowing cold that had nothing to do with the weather. Everything I had been working toward, everything I thought I *was*, seemed to have vanished. The future I had so carefully mapped had become a blank, terrifying page. In that moment, my body didn’t know what to do. It was a cascade of pure, primal activation. My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic bird trapped in a cage. My breath became a shallow, tight knot in my chest. This is the language of the nervous system in crisis. The amygdala, our brain’s ancient smoke detector, screams “DANGER!” and the whole system floods with cortisol and adrenaline, preparing for a fight or a flight that never comes. We are left vibrating with a terror that has no immediate physical threat to escape from. We are simply left in the rubble. For days, I just sat with the pieces. The anger. The grief. The profound, disorienting loss. It felt like the end. But then, slowly, something else began to emerge from the wreckage. A quiet space. A stillness I hadn’t known was possible. ## The Gold in the Cracks There is a beautiful Japanese art form called *Kintsugi*. When a piece of pottery breaks, it is not thrown away. Instead, it is meticulously repaired with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. The philosophy behind it is that the breakage and repair are part of the object’s history, not something to disguise. The cracks are not seen as imperfections, but as a beautiful, integral part of the story. The piece is more beautiful for having been broken. This is what can happen to us when life falls apart. We are not meant to be discarded. We are not meant to pretend the cracks aren’t there. The invitation, beloved one, is to find the gold. The sacred lives in the shattered places. It’s in the raw, aching vulnerability that we discover a strength we never knew we possessed. It’s in the quiet moments of surrender that we hear the whispers of our own deepest wisdom. > “The world is filled with suffering. It is also filled with the overcoming of it.” - Helen Keller When we stop fighting the reality of the break, when we finally lay down our weapons and just *be* with what is, we create the space for grace to enter. The gold is the compassion we learn to offer ourselves. It’s the resilience that is forged in the fire of our pain. It’s the new perspective that allows us to see what truly matters. ## Your Body, Your Anchor In these moments of collapse, it is so easy to dissociate, to float away from the intense sensations in the body. But our bodies, in their infinite wisdom, are our greatest anchors to the present moment. The healing doesn’t happen in the story we tell ourselves about the collapse; it happens in the felt sense of our own physical being. I invite you, my dear one, to place a hand on your heart right now. Feel the warmth of your own touch. Take a slow, deep breath and feel your belly soften. This is where the work begins. Not in figuring it all out, but in coming home to yourself, right here, right now. Your body has been holding the story, the tension, the grief. It also holds the key to your release. Neuroscience teaches us that gentle, mindful attention to the body can begin to down-regulate that hyper-aroused nervous system. By focusing on the physical sensation of our breath, or the feeling of our feet on the ground, we send a powerful signal to our amygdala that says, “In this moment, you are safe.” It is a practice. A slow, patient turning towards ourselves with kindness. ## The Wisdom of Water The Tao Te Ching speaks of the power of water. It is the softest thing, yet it can overcome the hardest. It does not resist; it flows. It yields, and in its yielding, it finds its way. > “The supreme good is like water, > which nourishes all things without trying to. > It is content with the low places that people disdain. > Thus it is like the Tao.” When our world shatters, we are asked to become like water. To stop struggling against the rocks and instead to flow around them. To be content, for a time, with the low places. It is in this surrender that we find our true power. It is not a passive giving up, but an active, courageous trust in the flow of life itself, even when we cannot see where it is leading. From the rubble of my own dismantled project, something new began to grow. The quiet space that opened up allowed me to hear a deeper calling, one that led me to the work I do today—work that is more aligned with my soul than anything I had planned. The shattered pieces of my old life became the fertile ground for a new, more authentic existence. The green shoots began to push through the cracks. Your breaking is not the end. It is an initiation. It is the painful, holy, and necessary unraveling of who you thought you were, so that who you truly are can emerge. The process is not easy, but it is sacred. And you don’t have to walk it alone.

teachings.title: Having a Backbone: Courage, Integrity, and Spinal Health
teachings.summary: Susan uses a client story about chronic lower back pain to explore how the spine reflects emotional patterns such as carrying others' burdens, fear of taking up space, and learned rigidity. She weaves somatic, neuroscientific, and metaphorical perspectives to invite a compassionate inquiry into posture, nervous-system holding, and the possibility of relearning strength with flexibility. The piece offers gentle prompts and a short embodied practice to reconnect with the spine as an axis for courage and integrity.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a moment in every healing journey — and I mean every single one — where the ground seems to fall away.

And one of the most profound aspects, I’ve found, is learning to stand tall in the world. Not just physically, but emotionally and spiritually. To have a backbone.

I remember a client, a lovely woman in her late forties, who came to me with chronic lower back pain. She had tried everything — physiotherapy, chiropractic, massage — but the pain persisted, a dull, constant ache that radiated down her legs. As we began to work together, a story emerged. A story of a lifetime of shouldering burdens that were not hers to carry, of bending over backward to please others, of a deep, unspoken fear of taking up space. Her spine, in its wisdom, was simply telling her story. It was collapsing under the weight of a lifetime of unspoken truths.

She told me about her childhood, about being the “good girl” who never caused any trouble. She learned early on that her value lay in her ability to anticipate the needs of others, to smooth over conflicts, to keep the peace at all costs. This pattern continued into her adult life, in her marriage, in her career, in her friendships. She was the one everyone relied on, the one who always said yes, the one who never complained. But underneath the surface of this capable, accommodating persona, a deep resentment was brewing. Her body was keeping the score.

Our spines are such exquisite messengers. They are our central channel, the sacred axis around which our entire being is organized. They are both a marvel of biological engineering — providing structural support, allowing for an incredible range of movement — and a conduit for the most subtle energies and information. The spinal cord, housed within the protective embrace of the vertebrae, is the superhighway of our nervous system, carrying messages between the brain and the body, between our inner and outer worlds.

When we experience issues with our spine, it is an invitation to a profound inquiry. It is a call to look at the places in our lives where we are not standing tall, where we are lacking in courage, integrity, or flexibility. The body, in its infinite intelligence, does not create pain to punish us. It creates sensation to communicate with us, to bring our attention to the places where we are out of alignment with our own deepest truth.

## The Language of the Spine

Think about the language we use. When someone lacks courage, we call them “spineless.” When we are carrying a heavy emotional load, we might find our shoulders rounding, our upper back curving, as if to physically brace against the weight. When we are rigid in our thinking, inflexible in our beliefs, our spine can become stiff and unyielding, a reflection of our inner state. And when we feel defeated, when we have given up on our own dreams, our spine can literally begin to collapse, a physical manifestation of a spirit that has lost its will to stand tall.

These are not just metaphors. These are the ways in which our bodies speak to us, in a language more ancient and more truthful than words. Our posture is a poem. It tells the story of our life, of our joys and our sorrows, our fears and our courage.

From a neuroscience perspective, we know that trauma and chronic stress can become locked in the body’s tissues. The fear response, mediated by the sympathetic nervous system, creates a cascade of physiological changes — muscles tighten, breath becomes shallow, the body prepares for fight or flight. When this state becomes chronic, when we live in a perpetual state of low-grade fear, our posture can become permanently altered. The body learns to hold itself in a defensive crouch, and the spine, our central pillar, is directly affected. The neural pathways that fire in response to perceived threat become well-worn grooves, and the body’s default setting becomes one of tension and contraction. The psoas muscle, the deep core muscle that connects the spine to the legs, can become chronically shortened, pulling the lumbar spine into a state of compression and creating the kind of persistent low back pain my client was experiencing.

But here is the beautiful truth: these patterns are not fixed. The brain and the nervous system are plastic, capable of changing and rewiring themselves throughout our lives. We can create new neural pathways. We can learn to release the old patterns of holding and tension. We can teach our bodies that it is safe to stand tall again.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Dance of Strength and Flexibility

True spinal health is not about rigidity. It is not about having a “stiff upper lip” or an unbending will. It is a dance between strength and flexibility, between the ability to stand firm in our convictions and the grace to yield and flow with the currents of life. A healthy spine is both strong and supple, a reflection of a spirit that is both grounded and free.

I’ve worked with people whose spines are ramrod straight, held in place by a fierce, unconscious effort. Often, this rigidity is a compensation for a deep-seated fear of falling apart. They have learned to control their environment, their emotions, and their bodies with an iron will. But this control comes at a cost. It cuts them off from the flow of life, from the ability to be spontaneous, to be vulnerable, to be truly intimate with themselves and others. Their bodies are braced for an impact that never comes, and the constant tension exhausts them.

Then there are those whose spines have begun to curve, to round forward under the weight of perceived burdens. This is the posture of the perennial caregiver, the one who carries the weight of the world on their shoulders. They have taken on the emotional baggage of their families, their communities, their ancestors. Their bodies have become a repository for unresolved grief, for unspoken resentments, for the heavy mantle of responsibility. They have forgotten how to receive, how to let go, how to allow themselves to be supported.

And then there are those, like my client, whose spines seem to be collapsing, losing their structural integrity. This is often the result of a profound sense of hopelessness, a feeling of having been defeated by life. They have given up on their dreams, they have lost faith in themselves, they have forgotten their own innate worth. Their bodies are expressing a deep spiritual fatigue, a longing to simply let go and be done with the struggle.

Whatever the pattern, the invitation is the same: to bring a compassionate, non-judgmental awareness to the story our bodies are telling. To listen with love to the messages of our spine.

So, I invite you to a gentle inquiry. What is the story your spine is telling? Where in your life are you being called to cultivate more courage, more integrity, more flexibility?

Perhaps you might begin by simply bringing your awareness to your spine. As you sit here, reading these words, can you feel the length of your spine, from the tailbone to the crown of your head? Can you imagine a current of energy flowing up and down this central channel, a river of light connecting earth and sky?

Notice any areas of tension or holding. Don’t judge them, don’t try to force them to release. Simply bring a gentle, loving awareness to them. Breathe into these spaces. Imagine your breath as a warm, healing balm, softening and melting any rigidity. With each inhale, imagine you are drawing in courage and strength. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing fear and tension.

What would it be like to allow your spine to be a little more fluid, a little more free? What would it be like to stand a little taller, to take up a little more space in the world? You might even try this as a physical practice. Stand up, feel your feet on the ground, and gently, vertebra by vertebra, begin to unfurl your spine, as if you were a fern frond opening to the sun. Let your head float up toward the sky. Feel the space between each vertebra. Feel the dignity and grace of your own uprightness.

This is not about forcing yourself into a “perfect” posture. It is about cultivating a loving, conscious relationship with your body. It is about listening to the whispers of your spine before they become screams. It is about reclaiming your birthright to stand tall, in all your unique and magnificent beauty.

Your spine is the axis of your world. It is the mast of your ship, the trunk of your tree. When you tend to the health of your spine, you are tending to the health of your entire being. You are saying yes to life. You are saying yes to yourself.


---

teachings.title: A Breathwork Practice for Lung Healing and Vitality
teachings.summary: Susan offers a gentle, invitational breathwork practice aimed at restoring ease and presence in the lungs, using conscious awareness, a three‑part breath, a grief‑release sequence with sound, and an expansion visualization. teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was sitting with a client recently—a lovely woman with a sharp, brilliant mind and a heart she guarded like a fortress. She spoke of a deep, persistent sadness that had shadowed her for years, a grief she couldn’t name but that sat heavy in her chest. As she spoke, I noticed it. The almost imperceptible catch in her breath. The way her inhales were shallow, tentative sips of air, as if she were afraid to take in too much. Her exhales were just as quiet, just as restrained.

Her body was telling the story her mind was still trying to understand. It’s a story I see so often in my practice, a narrative written in the subtle mechanics of breath. The story of the lungs is one of profound intimacy and vulnerability. They are our most direct connection to the world beyond our skin, the place where we literally take in life, and where we release what we no longer need. When this vital exchange is compromised, it speaks volumes about our inner state.

Our lungs are the most intimate interface between our inner world and the outer atmosphere. With every breath, we draw the outside in—not just oxygen, but the very energy, the *prana*, the life force of the world around us. And with every exhale, we release what is no longer needed, what is toxic, what is ready to be let go. It is the most fundamental rhythm of our lives, this sacred exchange. And yet, for so many of us, this rhythm is disrupted.

We hold our breath in moments of fear. We forget to breathe when we’re concentrating. We learn to breathe shallowly, cautiously, as children in environments where it didn’t feel safe to take up space, to be fully seen, to feel the full spectrum of our emotions. When we are navigating the depths of grief or the fog of depression, our breath becomes a mirror to our inner state—constricted, heavy, small. We feel, quite literally, suffocated by life.

But here is a very good thing to know: the breath, while mostly automatic, is also consciously accessible. This is a profound gift. It means we have a direct pathway to influence our own physiology and our own consciousness. By choosing to breathe more deeply, more consciously, we can begin to gently unwind the ancient patterns held in the body. We can signal to our nervous system that we are safe, right here, right now. We can create new neural pathways that support a state of calm and presence, rather than one of perpetual, low-grade anxiety.

This isn’t about forcing or striving, which so often comes from a place of feeling that we are not enough as we are. This is a gentler, more profound invitation. It’s about permission. It’s about creating a space of safety within your own being where the breath can naturally, organically, begin to deepen and expand. It’s about remembering, on a cellular level, that you deserve to take in the full gift of life. You are worthy of the oxygen, the energy, the inspiration that is your birthright.

## A Guided Practice for Your Lungs

This practice is an invitation to come home to your breath. Find a comfortable position, either sitting with a straight spine or lying down. Close your eyes if that feels safe. There is nothing to achieve here, only to notice.

### Part 1: Conscious Breathing

1.  **Simply Notice.** Without changing a thing, bring your awareness to your breath. Notice the sensation of the air entering your nostrils. Is it cool? Is it warm? Follow it as it travels down your throat and into your lungs. Notice the gentle rise of your chest and belly on the inhale, and the soft release on the exhale. Just watch for a few cycles. No judgment, no agenda. Pure awareness.

2.  **The Three-Part Breath.** Now, we’ll invite the breath to deepen. Place one hand on your belly and one on your chest. On your next inhale, imagine breathing all the way down into your belly, feeling your hand rise. Then, let the breath fill your ribcage, expanding it out to the sides. Finally, let the breath fill the very top of your chest, right up to your collarbones. It’s one smooth, continuous inhale in three parts: belly, ribs, chest.

3.  **The Releasing Exhale.** Exhale with a soft, audible sigh. Let it all go. The exhale is a full release, a letting go. Practice this three-part breath for a few minutes. Inhale belly, ribs, chest. Exhale with a sigh. Feel the rhythm, the expansion, the release.

### Part 2: The Grief Release Breath

The lungs are known in many wisdom traditions as the storehouse for grief. When we don’t allow ourselves to fully feel and process loss, the sadness gets trapped in the body, constricting the breath. This practice can help to gently move that stored energy.

> *A word of caution, beloved one: be gentle. If this feels like too much, return to the simple conscious breathing. You are in charge.*

1.  **Connect to the Feeling.** Bring to mind a sense of sadness or grief that you’ve been carrying. It doesn’t have to be a dramatic, capital-T Trauma. It could be the quiet grief of a friendship that has faded, a dream that didn’t come to pass, or simply the ambient sadness of the world. Just touch it gently with your awareness.

2.  **Breathe Into It.** As you continue with your deep, three-part breath, imagine that your inhale is moving directly into that place of sadness in your chest. Imagine the breath surrounding the grief with warmth, with compassion, with pure, loving presence. You are not trying to get rid of the feeling. You are simply breathing with it.

3.  **Exhale with Sound.** On your exhale, allow a sound to come out. It might be a sigh, a hum, a quiet sob. Let the vibration of the sound help to loosen the grip of the stored emotion. The sound is a vehicle for release. Inhale into the grief, surrounding it with love. Exhale with sound, letting it go. Continue for as long as it feels supportive.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

### Part 3: Expansion Visualization

After the release, it’s time to reclaim your space. It’s time to remember the truth of your own magnificence.

1.  **The Inner Light.** Return to your steady, deep breathing. Now, imagine a tiny spark of golden light in the center of your chest, right in the heart of your lungs. See it, feel it, sense it.

2.  **Grow the Light.** With every inhale, imagine that golden light growing brighter and larger. With each breath, it expands, filling your entire chest cavity. It’s warm, radiant, and full of peace. Feel your lungs expanding with this light, effortlessly, joyfully.

3.  **Breathe Beyond Your Body.** Now, imagine that with every inhale, you can draw this golden light in from the world all around you. And with every exhale, you can radiate this light out from your chest, out into the room, out into the world. You are a conduit for light. You are breathing in life, and you are breathing out love. Feel the spaciousness within you and all around you. You are not small. You are not constricted. You are vast.

## A Daily Practice

You don’t need to set aside an hour a day to feel the benefits of conscious breathing. The beauty of this practice is that you can integrate it into the moments of your life.

My invitation to you is this: three times a day, simply pause. Pause before you get out of bed in the morning, pause before you eat your lunch, pause before you drift off to sleep. And take three deep, conscious, three-part breaths. Inhale belly, ribs, chest. Exhale with a sigh of release. That’s it.

That’s the practice. It is a simple, profound act of self-love, a quiet revolution against the patterns of holding and constriction. It is a way of reminding your body, your nervous system, and your soul that you are here, you are safe, and you deserve to be full. Each conscious breath is a declaration: I am worthy of this life. I am open to receiving. I am willing to let go.

Your breath is your most constant companion, your most faithful guide. It is with you from your first moment to your last. By cultivating a conscious, loving relationship with it, you are coming home to the wisest part of yourself. You are tending to the sacred fire within your own lungs, and in doing so, you are illuminating the path to your own healing and vitality.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Your Heart: The First Declaration of Your Existence](/blog/heart-first-declaration)
- [The Silver Tongue and the Silent Scream: Two Sides of Vocal Wounding](/blog/vocal-cords-silver-tongue)

**More on Lungs:**

- [When You Cannot Breathe: Suffocation, Grief, and Your Lungs](/blog/lungs-cannot-breathe-grief)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

So be gentle with yourself, beloved. This journey of coming home to the breath is not a race. It is a slow, tender unfurling. Some days, the breath will be deep and full. Other days, it may feel shallow and tight. It’s all okay. It’s all part of the practice of being human. The goal is not perfect breathing, but a perfect compassion for wherever you find yourself. Your lungs have carried you this far. Trust their wisdom. Trust the sacred exchange. Trust that every breath is a new beginning.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe the spine as a sacred, communicative axis that holds both physical structure and deep emotional meaning.
