teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember standing in line at the grocery store a few years ago, after a long day of seeing clients. The fluorescent lights hummed overhead, the air thick with the scent of roasted chicken and cold metal. I was tired, a deep-in-my-bones weariness, and my shoulders were slumped forward, the familiar ache in my lower back a dull, insistent throb that had been my companion for years. I shifted my weight from one foot to the other, the worn linoleum cool beneath my sandals, trying to find a position of ease that just wasn’t available. And as I stood there, lost in the fog of my own fatigue, my eyes landed on a toddler in his mother’s shopping cart. He was sitting up so perfectly, his little back a study in effortless alignment, his head balanced like a flower on its stem. There was no strain, no effort. Just a pure, upright presence as he curiously watched the world go by.

And a question dropped into my awareness, soft as a whisper: *When did I forget how to do that?* When did I trade that innate, graceful alignment for the weight of the world on my shoulders?

It’s a tricky business, being human. We come into this world with these perfectly designed instruments, these bodies that know, deep in their cellular memory, how to be. And then… life happens. We learn to brace, to shrink, to puff up, to carry burdens that were never ours to hold. And no part of our body tells this story more profoundly than our spine.

Your spine is so much more than a stack of bones. It is your central axis, the mast that allows you to stand tall and meet the world. It is the architectural marvel that grants you both stability and grace, the literal “backbone” that speaks of courage and integrity. But it is also a river of information, a sacred central channel through which the intelligence of the universe flows, communicating constantly between the cosmos, your brain, and the vast, wise landscape of your body.

## The Pillar of Presence, The River of Light

Think about the sheer miracle of your spine. Thirty-three individual vertebrae, stacked in a beautiful, dynamic S-curve, creating a pillar that is both incredibly strong and exquisitely flexible. It’s designed to move, to bend, to twist, to dance. It holds you upright, allowing you, as a human being, to have your hands free to create, to hold, to comfort. This uprightness is a declaration of presence, a way of saying, *I am here*.

Nestled within this bony fortress is the spinal cord, the superhighway of your nervous system. It is a dense bundle of nerves, a river of light carrying trillions of messages every second. Your brain sends signals down this channel to orchestrate the complex symphony of your heartbeat, your breath, your digestion, your every movement. And just as importantly, your body sends signals *up* this channel to the brain, reporting on the state of your inner and outer worlds. Is it safe? Am I hungry? Is that texture rough or smooth? Is my heart aching?

This communication network is the physical home of your autonomic nervous system, the part of you that runs the show behind the scenes. Nerves branch out from between your vertebrae, connecting to every organ and system. When you perceive a threat—a car swerving, a critical email from your boss—it’s your sympathetic nervous system, the “fight or flight” response, that fires up. Your heart races, your breath becomes shallow, your muscles tense… and your spine often reflects this by becoming rigid, ready for action. Conversely, when you feel safe and at ease, it’s the parasympathetic nervous system, the “rest and digest” response, that takes over. Your heart rate slows, your breath deepens, and your spine can soften and lengthen. For many of us, our systems have learned that the world is not safe, and we live in a state of chronic sympathetic activation, our spines held in a state of constant, low-grade alarm.

This is not a one-way street. It is a constant, dynamic, and deeply intimate conversation. When we talk about “body wisdom,” this is the physical mechanism for it. Your gut feelings, your intuitive hits, your felt sense of a person or a situation—these are all messages traveling along this sacred central channel, whispering their truth to you long before your conscious mind has had time to analyze the data. The spine is the bridge between your thinking mind and your feeling body, between your earthly experience and your highest consciousness.

## When the Channel Carries Weight

Because this channel is so central, so vital, it is also where we register our deepest conflicts about our place in the world. Our spines are honest. They do not lie. They simply reflect the energetic and emotional loads we are carrying.

Do you feel the constant weight of responsibility on your shoulders? Your spine may begin to curve forward under the perceived load, your upper back rounding as if to physically hold it all. Have you been through experiences that made you feel unsupported, as if you had no one to lean on? Your lower back might ache with the strain of trying to be your own sole foundation. I worked with a client once, a lovely woman who had been the primary caregiver for her aging parents for over a decade. She came to me with debilitating sciatic pain, and as we worked together, it became clear that her spine was screaming what her heart couldn’t admit: she felt utterly alone in her duties and was terrified of collapsing under the pressure.

Sometimes, out of fear, we become rigid. We hold our backs ramrod straight, a posture of bracing against the world, terrified that if we relax, we will collapse. This inflexibility in the body mirrors an inflexibility in our minds and hearts, a resistance to the natural flow of life. We lose the spine’s natural, shock-absorbing curves, and life’s bumps and jolts land with much more impact. This rigidity is often born from a deep-seated belief that we must control everything to be safe, a pattern often learned in chaotic or unpredictable childhood environments.

And sometimes, we simply give up. The weight feels too heavy, the effort too great. We collapse into ourselves, our spines losing their integrity, a physical manifestation of a spirit that has lost its will to stand tall. This is not a failing; it is a sign of profound exhaustion, a body crying out for rest and a reconnection to purpose.

> “Your spine is the axis of your being, the staff of life itself. It is where your personal story and the story of the cosmos meet.”

These patterns are not your fault. They are intelligent adaptations. A curved spine might have been a way to appear smaller and safer in a childhood home. A rigid back might have been the only way to get through an overwhelming loss. Your body did what it had to do to survive. But now, you are no longer in that old story. You have the capacity to gently, lovingly, invite your spine back into its true nature: an axis of grace, strength, and fluid communication.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming Your Sacred Axis

Many ancient spiritual traditions understood the spine as the central channel of divine energy. In yogic traditions, it is the home of the *sushumna nadi*, the primary energetic pathway through which *kundalini*, the evolutionary life force, is said to ascend. The *sushumna* is the river, and the vertebrae are the locks and dams. When this channel is clear and open, our energy flows freely, and we experience a sense of connection, vitality, and purpose. We feel both grounded in our bodies and connected to a reality far greater than our individual selves. This isn’t some esoteric fantasy; it’s a felt sense of wholeness, of being aligned with life itself.

What would it be like to relate to your spine not as a source of pain, but as a sacred antenna? A channel for wisdom and light?

You can begin right now, just by bringing your awareness to it. As you sit here reading, can you feel it? Can you sense its length, from the anchor of your tailbone to the crown of your head? Can you imagine a current of light, a gentle energy, flowing up and down its length with your breath?

On your inhale, imagine drawing energy up from the core of the earth, a steadying, supportive force. Feel it rise through each vertebra, creating space and length.

On your exhale, imagine a soft, warm light pouring down from the cosmos, through the crown of your head, and cascading down your spine, releasing tension, dissolving old holding patterns, and reminding every cell of its inherent grace.

Here is another simple practice. Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. Place a small, rolled-up towel under your head if you need to. Simply lie there and bring your full, compassionate attention to the places where your spine makes contact with the floor. Notice the space under your lower back, the space under your neck. There is no need to change anything. Just notice. Breathe into these spaces. With each exhale, you might imagine your spine getting heavier, wider, releasing just one percent more of its holding into the support of the earth. Stay here for five minutes, just breathing and feeling. This simple act of awareness can begin to repattern a lifetime of holding.

This isn’t about forcing a “perfect” posture. It’s about cultivating a loving relationship. It’s about listening. Your spine is communicating with you in every moment. The ache in your lower back might be asking you to look at where you feel unsupported. The tension in your neck might be inviting you to release the burden of over-thinking.

By listening, you begin to restore the flow. You begin to embody the truth of your spine: that you are designed to be both strong and flexible, grounded and elevated, human and divine. You are designed to stand tall in the truth of who you are, supported by the earth beneath you and informed by the heavens above, with a river of light flowing right through the center of your being.

May you feel the unwavering support of your own beautiful backbone. May you trust the messages that flow through your sacred central channel. And may you stand in the world with the full, graceful, and courageous presence that is your birthright.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: What Your Childhood Taught Your Body
teachings.title: What Your Childhood Taught Your Body
teachings.summary: Susan describes how early life experiences are encoded in the body, shaping posture, breath, and chronic pain long after the original circumstances have changed. She invites a gentle, compassionate listening to these somatic memories and frames healing as a gradual, neuroplastic relearning that creates new experiences of safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
In the quiet hours before dawn, when the world is still and the mind has not yet begun its daily chatter, there is a space.

And so much of that business begins when we are very small, before we have the words to name our experience, before our conscious minds are fully formed to make sense of it all. We arrive as pure, open, receptive beings, and the world begins to teach us. It teaches us what is safe, what is dangerous, who we are, and how we must be to survive.

And where does this teaching land? Before it becomes a story, before it becomes a belief, it lands in the body.

I remember a client, a woman in her late forties, who came to me with chronic, debilitating shoulder pain. She had tried everything—physiotherapy, massage, acupuncture, pain medication. Nothing provided more than temporary relief. As we began to work together, dropping into the quiet space of her body’s wisdom, a memory surfaced. It wasn’t a dramatic, traumatic event. It was a small, repeated experience. She was the eldest of four children, and her mother, overwhelmed and exhausted, would often sigh and say, “You’re the oldest, you have to be the responsible one.”

In that moment, a pattern was encoded. The weight of that responsibility, the unspoken burden of holding the family together, landed squarely on her small shoulders. Her body learned to carry it, tensing the muscles, bracing for the load. Decades later, long after she had left home and her siblings were grown, her shoulders were still carrying that weight. The pain was not a defect. It was a message, a story from her childhood, held faithfully in her tissues all these years.

## The Body Remembers

The body is a profoundly intelligent and faithful archive. It remembers everything. While the conscious mind might forget or repress difficult experiences to protect us, the body holds the score. The field of neuroscience has illuminated this process, showing us how early life experiences, particularly those of developmental trauma, are not just psychological but are deeply *somatic*. They are encoded into our very biology.

When a child experiences a threat—whether it’s a loud noise, an angry parent, or a sense of abandonment—the nervous system instinctively reacts. The sympathetic nervous system, our “fight or flight” mechanism, floods the body with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline. The heart rate increases, breathing becomes shallow, and muscles tense in preparation to defend or escape. In a healthy, supportive environment, once the threat passes, the parasympathetic nervous system comes online to restore a state of calm and safety. This is called regulation.

But what happens when the threat is chronic? What happens when the environment is consistently unsafe, unpredictable, or emotionally barren? The child’s nervous system doesn’t have a chance to return to a state of rest. It learns that the world *is* a dangerous place. This chronic state of high alert becomes the new baseline. The body adapts. It might adopt a posture of collapse and submission, with rounded shoulders and a sunken chest, to appear smaller and less of a target. Or it might develop a rigid, braced posture, a kind of physical armor against anticipated attack. Breathing patterns become permanently shallow, limiting the intake of life force and suppressing overwhelming emotions. Muscle tension becomes chronic, a constant state of readiness for a danger that may no longer be present.

> “The body is the subconscious mind. Our physical postures, gestures, and mannerisms are the outward expression of our innermost thoughts and feelings.” — Candace Pert

These are not conscious choices. They are brilliant, adaptive strategies for survival. The body, in its infinite wisdom, does what it must to get us through. The problem is that these patterns, once wired into our neural pathways and embedded in our tissues, continue to run on autopilot long after the original circumstances have changed. We carry our childhood rooms within us—the tension, the fear, the unspoken grief—in the very architecture of our physical being.

This somatic encoding is the body’s native language. It is a form of memory that lives in the tissues, the organs, and the nervous system. It’s why a certain tone of voice can make your stomach clench, why a particular smell can transport you back to a forgotten moment of fear, or why you might find yourself bracing for impact in a perfectly safe situation. Your body is responding to an echo from the past, a deeply ingrained neural pathway that was laid down long ago as a matter of survival. It is not a flaw; it is a feature of your incredible resilience.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Discovering Your Own Embodied History

My own journey into this work was born from my body’s cries for attention. For years, I struggled with a deep, persistent tension in my jaw. I would wake up with a sore face, my teeth aching from clenching all night. Dentists offered mouth guards, but no one could tell me *why* it was happening. It was in the deep stillness of meditation that the answer began to surface. It came not as a thought, but as a felt sense—a visceral memory of being a little girl, biting back my words, swallowing my truth because it felt unsafe to speak. In my family, emotions were not welcome. The unspoken rule was to be quiet, be good, don’t make waves. And so, my jaw learned to clamp down on my own expression. It was a profound revelation. My body hadn’t betrayed me; it had been holding my unspoken story for me, waiting patiently for me to be ready to listen.

This is the sacred work of coming home to ourselves. It is the practice of turning towards the body not as a problem to be fixed, but as a wise and loving messenger. It is about cultivating a compassionate presence that allows these long-held patterns to be seen, felt, and heard without judgment. It is a profound act of self-reclamation, of gathering the exiled parts of ourselves and welcoming them back into the fold. It is the beginning of a new conversation, one where we learn to listen to the subtle whispers of the body before they become screams.

What is your body trying to tell you? Where in your body do you feel the echoes of your past?

Perhaps it’s in the tightness of your hips, holding the fear of taking your next step. Maybe it’s in your feet, which never quite felt the solid ground of support beneath them. It could be in your stomach, which learned to churn with anxiety, or in your lungs, which learned to hold their breath in anticipation of the other shoe dropping. These are not random symptoms. They are love letters from your past, invitations to a deeper healing.

## A Compassionate Approach

Working with these deep, early patterns is not about forcing them to change or trying to erase the past. That would be another form of violence. It is about bringing a new quality of attention to them—an attention infused with warmth, curiosity, and profound compassion. It is about creating a new experience in the present moment: an experience of safety.

When we can meet a tense muscle, a shallow breath, or a painful sensation with gentle awareness, something miraculous begins to happen. The nervous system, which has been on high alert for decades, receives a new signal. The signal is: *you are safe now*. *I am here with you*. *You don’t have to hold this alone anymore*.

This is the power of neuroplasticity. The brain and nervous system are not fixed. We can create new neural pathways. By repeatedly introducing experiences of safety, presence, and self-compassion, we can begin to rewire those ancient survival responses. The braced muscles can learn to soften. The shallow breath can learn to deepen. The body can learn, cell by cell, that the war is over.

This is not a quick fix. It is a journey, a slow and sacred unfolding. It requires patience and a willingness to be with what is, without needing it to be different. It is the practice of mothering ourselves, of giving our own bodies the gentle, attuned presence that they may have longed for in childhood. It’s about learning to offer yourself the soothing words, the gentle touch, and the unwavering acceptance that you may not have received. It is a radical act of love to place a hand on your own heart and whisper, “I am here. I’ve got you.” This simple act, repeated over time, can begin to mend the deepest of wounds.

Your body has been your most faithful companion. It has carried you through everything. It has held what your mind could not bear. It has done everything in its power to keep you safe. Now, we can turn towards it with gratitude. We can listen to its stories. And we can, together, teach it the beautiful, liberating truth that it is finally safe to come home.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Vocal Cords - The Vibrational Signature of Your Soul
teachings.title: The Vocal Cords - The Vibrational Signature of Your Soul
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard the voice as an embodied, holographic messenger: a physical instrument shaped by breath, anatomy and the nervous system, and an energetic threshold braided with early relational patterns. The piece names how survival-based responses to speaking can leave muscular and emotional imprints in the throat, and offers somatic and contemplative practices—from gentle hums to staged exposure—to rewire safety and reclaim authentic expression. The approach is both practical and spiritual, grounded in Taoist humility about the limits of language while encouraging gradual, tender reclamation of voice.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a place inside you where silence carries a weight and sound carries revelation. Your vocal cords are not merely tissues folded into the throat; they are an intimate instrument through which your inner truth meets the world. Each inhalation prepares a field, each exhalation becomes a message. When you speak, hum, laugh, sob or sing, you trace the contours of your inner landscape into audible form. Your voice is the vibrational signature of your soul - unique, embodied and sacred. To listen to it closely is to receive a living translation of what is unresolved, what is ripe, and what is ready to overflow into life.

The anatomy of disclosure

Physically, your vocal cords are delicate bands of muscle and mucosa stretched across the larynx. They vibrate when air flows from the lungs, shaped by the tongue, the soft palate, the jaw and the resonant chambers of your chest and face. Energetically, they sit at a crossroad where breath, intention and social story collide. The mouth and throat are the visible threshold between internal knowing and external reality. This threshold is where you learn whether speaking will be met with nourishment, indifference, correction or punishment. Over time these early responses become braided into the tissue of your voice, influencing tone, volume, timbre and the very capacity to make sound without fear.

Voice as holographic messenger

When I say your voice is a holographic messenger, I mean that the state of your throat reflects patterns present throughout your entire system. The voice holds echoes of the nervous system, the heart, the lungs, the gut and your earliest relational maps. As in the teachings that guide my work, the body does not punish - it communicates. A sore throat, chronic hoarseness, nodules, a tendency to clear your throat repeatedly, a habitual quietness in company - each of these is an invitation to inquire into how you have learned to meet the world with your sound. Symptoms become a code. They are not the enemy to be eradicated at all costs but the teacher asking for your attention and compassion.

When you were small you had to learn quickly the rules of safety. If speaking up resulted in shame, silence or worse, punishment, your nervous system would make the fastest possible association: sound equals danger. This association is not irrational when you were five, eight or twelve years old. For a young, dependent creature the adult world is the determining environment of survival. The system learns to constrict the throat, to shorten the breath, to lower the volume, or to push sounds into the body as swallowed anger. Later, as an adult, the pattern persists. Speaking truth becomes a risk to safety, and your throat becomes the battleground where your longing for authenticity and your learned need for safety both claim territory.

Early wounds and the wiring of silence

Think back gently to formative times when speaking up produced consequences. Perhaps you were told to be quiet at the dinner table, punished for contradicting an elder, or ridiculed when you showed emotion. Perhaps truth-telling led to being abandoned, to being labeled dramatic, to being dismissed as a troublemaker. These were not small transactions. They were neural inscriptions. The sympathetic nervous system learned quickly that the vibration of your voice might trigger an escalation: the parent who shushed you, the teacher who humiliated you in front of classmates, the sibling who mocked your attempt to name a feeling. Your body remembered the spatial and muscular patterns that accompanied survival. The throat closed down. The breath shortened. Words compressed into half-uttered sentences or into tight, apologetic murmurs.

Later you may have noticed familiar strategies: you become the agreeable one who nods and smiles even while your chest tightens, you speak softly to avoid attention, you interrupt yourself before the discomfort arrives, or you trade directness for sarcasm and passive aggression. Some people say little and pretend not to hear what hurts. Others speak loudly in rooms full of people yet cannot say what matters when it matters most. Each of these styles is coherent with an early survival calculus that kept you alive but at a cost: your authentic voice remains compromised.

Symptoms as sacred invitations

Vocal nodules and polyps often form on the cords where repeated strain or suppression meets exertion. Laryngitis can be a literal inflammation that follows a period of forced silencing when you cannot allow yourself to speak the truth and the body insists on shutting down until it is safe to speak again. Chronic throat clearing is a habit that physically manifests the tension of trying to dislodge words that have been held in too long. Stuttering frequently carries a history of emotional dysregulation around speaking moments when the stakes felt high. Loss of voice at critical times can feel like a cruel joke of fate, yet within it lives a precise message: your system is requesting a softening, a reconfiguration of safety before further outward projection.

When you treat these conditions only at the physical level without asking what the throat is trying to tell you, the symptom often migrates or reappears in another form. In the holographic model, addressing the voice without addressing the pattern that created the voice is like trimming a vine and wondering why the root still seeks water. The work is not to condemn symptoms but to converse with them. Where in your life have you been withholding your truth? To whom do you volunteer silence? What price did you unconsciously pay for the illusion of safety? These questions are not moralistic; they are practical. They invite you back into a relationship with your voice that is curious and tender rather than shame-based and reactive.

The Tao of speaking and listening

The Tao Te Ching teaches that "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao." This paradox sits at the heart of vocal practice. There are truths that cannot be neatly packaged into words, and yet the impulse to approximate them through language is a sacred part of being human. You do not need to force every ineffable knowing into declarative speech. Yet avoiding all speech is not the answer either. The wisdom is in discerning the right balance - in honoring the boundary between silence that preserves mystery and silence that protects old wounds. The Tao invites you to a fluid listening - to the soft place where breath and word meet without struggle. The voice that comes from there will be both humble and potent.

Rewiring the nervous system for safe expression

Healing the voice requires more than technique. It requires a renegotiation of nervous system safety. You can practice resonance and breath-work until the cows come home, yet if the sympathetic alarm still rings at the thought of speaking truth to the people who matter, your larynx will remember its old allegiance. This is where somatic re-patterning and gradual exposure hold such power. Begin with the body. Soften the jaw. Allow the nostrils to breathe freely. Find the natural length of your exhale and let it be your scaffold for sound. Practice making low, sustained hums in a place where you feel safe until the vibration moves from your head into your chest and then into your face. These vibrations, repeated with kindness and without performance anxiety, teach the tissues that sound does not have to be followed by threat. The nervous system learns new associations when you repeat a pattern of safety often enough that it becomes more familiar than the old alarmed response.

Start small. Speak a line of truth first into a pillow or into a soft fabric, then to a plant, then to a trusted friend, then in a room with a mirror. Each step is a recalibration. Each small truth that is safely witnessed becomes a new memory your body can rely on. Over time your voice will carry a different resonance - one of integrity that does not need to be loud to be real. The practice is not a theatrical performance but a slow and reverent reintroduction of you to your own frequency.

Practical and spiritual practices to free your sound

There are embodied tools that help move energy out of stagnation and into resonance. Breath is the first and most faithful ally. Explore long, supported exhalations with the softening of the belly as you let out a gentle "ah" or "mmm." Toning into vowels loosens the laryngeal muscles and changes the muscular memory of restriction. Sirens or gentle glissandos across your comfortable range align the cords without forcing them. Yawns are surprisingly powerful - they open the soft palate and relax the throat in a way that speaks better than instructions ever can.

Chanting and sacred sound can also be transformational. When you use sound in a group or in nature the voice becomes a shared field where old individual shame can be diluted by communal acceptance. The sustained repetition of a simple mantra or a single tone creates a container in which the nervous system learns to relax while sound continues. In Taoist practice there is emphasis on internal alchemy - transforming inner residue into refined vibration. You can apply this by turning resentment or fear into the fuel for a tone that expresses a boundary, a longing, or a grieving breath. Let the sound be both a release and a declaration.

Words matter, yes, but the way you say a thing matters more. Practice "I" statements that anchor your experience without projecting blame. Instead of stating a truth as a weapon or an accusation, lean into intention: "I feel," "I need," "I will." When you combine vulnerability with clear boundary your voice becomes a crucible of integrity. This is not weakness. It is a profound form of courage because it contains the willingness to be seen and heard as you are.

Reclaiming your story

There is ritual in reclaiming lost or diminished parts of yourself. You might write a letter in which you speak all the truths you were never allowed to say, then read it aloud in a safe setting, allowing the tone and feel of those words to settle into the body. You might create a small altar where you speak intentions into water and then offer that water to the earth. You might rehearse difficult conversations with a trusted witness who mirrors back not only what you said but how it landed, thereby allowing you to adjust tone, pace and intention until your outer speech matches your inner reality.

Forgiveness plays a subtle role here. Forgiveness does not mean erasing what happened or pretending that harm never occurred. It simply loosens the grip that past moments have on your present physiology. When you can, in moments of private tenderness, speak to the child within you who was shushed or scolded and tell them that you will not leave them alone anymore, something in the throat relaxes. You begin to take the child by the hand, teaching them how to breathe and how to make sound that is safe and true.

Allowing highest truth to flow resonantly

Ultimately the work is not about achieving a perfect voice. It is about inviting the highest expression of your truth to flow through whatever instrument you were given. This requires humility and a willingness to keep revising what truth looks like. The Tao speaks to this humility in its opening paradox: language cannot fully contain the source yet it is through language that you participate in the world. Your vocal cords are your participation. When you align breath, nervous system, emotional clarity and intention, your voice becomes both testimony and prayer. It carries not just what you think but what you are learning to be.

There will be moments of silence that are holy. There will be moments of furious truth-telling that change the course of a relationship or an inner habit. Both are necessary. The goal is not to be always speaking but to be available to speak from an integrity so deep that even your silence is honest. In this way your voice becomes a living bridge between inner mystery and outer life - a bridge that vibrates with the frequency of your ongoing reconciliation with yourself.

Approach this work with reverence and patience. The voice remembers a thousand survival strategies. The healing is incremental and luminous. Each time you choose to make sound with presence rather than to swallow it in fear you shift the field for yourself and for those who will hear you. When you honor your throat as a sacred threshold you restore not only the physical ease of your vocal cords but the very alignment of your life with your soul's vibration.

May you learn to let your true tone arise - not as an act of aggression or appeasement but as a clear, compassionate transmission of who you are. May you remember that silence and sound are both teachers and allies. And may the way you speak be a small, steady offering to the vast, ineffable Tao that both holds and moves through you.

Persistent or painful vocal symptoms should be evaluated by a medical/voice specialist; somatic practice complements but does not replace professional medical advice or treatment.

teachings.sourceTitle: From Poison to Power: Transcending Liver-Gallbladder Patterns
teachings.title: From Poison to Power: Transcending Liver-Gallbladder Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan explores how the liver and gallbladder can be understood as organs that metabolize not only physical substances but also emotional energies such as anger and bitterness. She invites readers to reframe anger as a life force to be listened to and processed rather than suppressed, offers a somatic practice to begin sensing and tending that inner fire, and points toward clearer discernment and boundary-setting as part of ongoing alchemy.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember a time, years ago, standing in my kitchen, a ceramic mug held tight in my hand. It was a beautiful mug, a deep cobalt blue, a gift from a dear friend. But in that moment, all I could feel was the searing heat of my own rage. A conversation with a loved one had left me feeling profoundly unseen, my words twisted, my intentions misunderstood. The anger was a hot, physical presence—a flood of energy that started in my solar plexus and shot up into my throat, my jaw, my temples. My first instinct was to either hurl the mug against the wall, to see it shatter into a thousand pieces, or to swallow the feeling down, to pretend it wasn’t there, to be the “good” and “spiritual” person I thought I was supposed to be. For a long moment, I stood vibrating with the force of it, caught between the explosive power of expression and the crushing weight of suppression.

What do you do with a feeling like that? A surge of raw, primal anger that feels like it could burn you from the inside out? It’s a tricky business, being human. We are taught so many things about anger — that it’s impolite, that it’s destructive, that it’s a “low vibration” emotion that enlightened people don’t feel. We are taught to be nice, to be accommodating, to keep the peace at all costs. But our bodies, in their infinite and uncompromising wisdom, know a different truth.

In the profound intelligence of our own biology, the liver and its faithful partner, the gallbladder, are the masters of metabolism and detoxification. The liver, a magnificent, resilient organ weighing about three pounds, is our primary filter, performing over 500 known functions. It is a tireless alchemist, working 24/7 to sort, process, and neutralize everything we take in — not just the food we eat and the air we breathe, but the experiences we have, the emotions we feel, the energies we encounter. It is the great metabolic engine of the body, tasked with the monumental job of discerning what is nourishing from what is toxic.

When we ingest a physical poison, the liver heroically does its best to break it down and escort it out of the system. It has a remarkable capacity to regenerate, to heal itself from damage. This physical resilience is a mirror for our spiritual and emotional potential. But what about the poisons that are not so tangible? What about the sharp sting of injustice, the slow-burn of resentment, the bitter taste of betrayal, the constant drip of self-criticism? These, too, must be metabolized. And this is where the liver-gallbladder system reveals its deeper, energetic purpose.

## The Sacred Fire of Anger

Anger, in its purest form, is simply life force. It’s a current of energy that rises up to say: *“No.” “This is not right.” “A boundary has been crossed.”* It is a sacred fire, meant to protect, to clarify, and to propel us into necessary action. It is not inherently destructive. The destruction comes when this powerful energy is either repressed and turned inward, or when it is expressed unconsciously and without skill.

When we feel that flash of anger, our nervous system is doing exactly what it was designed to do. The amygdala, the brain’s ancient smoke detector, signals a potential threat, and a cascade of hormones like adrenaline and cortisol are released, preparing us for fight or flight. This is a brilliant survival mechanism. The problem is not the initial surge; the problem is what we have been conditioned to do next. When we consistently swallow our anger, when we tell ourselves we have no right to feel it, that powerful, fiery energy doesn’t just disappear. It has to go somewhere. And often, it gets stored in the liver.

Think of the liver as a library of every experience you’ve ever had. When an experience is processed and integrated, the book is shelved neatly. But when an emotion like anger is denied, it’s like shoving the book into a corner, where it gathers dust and takes up space. Over time, this repressed energy can stagnate, creating a state of chronic internal inflammation. The liver, overwhelmed with the task of processing not just physical toxins but dense, undigested emotional energy, becomes congested. We might feel sluggish, irritable, or stuck. We might develop a kind of low-grade, simmering rage that colors all our interactions. The body is speaking to us, telling us that something is out of balance, that a powerful truth is being denied.

> The liver’s job is to metabolize our experiences, particularly those that feel unjust. When we don’t allow the energy of anger to move through us and be heard, it can become a poison that we hold within.

## From Bitterness to Alchemy

If the liver is the alchemist, the gallbladder is its storage vessel. It holds the bile produced by the liver, a substance essential for digesting fats. Energetically, the gallbladder is connected to the emotion of bitterness. When anger is held for a long time, when it is chewed on and re-lived and justified until it becomes a hard, crystallized story, it transforms into bitterness. The gallbladder, in its wisdom, can literally form gallstones from this crystallized bitterness, these hard little nuggets of old resentment.

I once worked with a woman, let’s call her Frances, who came to me with chronic digestive issues and a deep-seated feeling of resentment towards her family. She felt she had sacrificed her dreams for them and had never been appreciated. She was, in a word, bitter. During our work together, she revealed she also suffered from painful gallstones. As we gently began to unpack the layers of her story, we found decades of unspoken anger. Anger at her parents for not supporting her artistic talents, anger at her husband for not seeing her exhaustion, anger at herself for not speaking up. Each unspoken truth was a stone in the wall around her heart, and a stone in her gallbladder. The healing process for her was not about blaming her family, but about learning to voice her own needs, to grieve the lost dreams, and to finally, finally give herself the permission to be angry. It was a long journey, but as she began to reclaim her voice, her digestive issues eased, and she felt a lightness she hadn’t experienced in years. She was metabolizing the poison of bitterness and turning it into the power of self-advocacy.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

This is the beginning of conscious alchemy. It’s the process of turning the lead of our unprocessed pain into the gold of wisdom and empowerment. It requires courage, yes. It requires a willingness to feel what feels uncomfortable. But the alternative is to live in a state of perpetual, low-grade war with ourselves and the world.

## A Practice: Tending Your Inner Fire

How, then, do we begin to work with this potent energy? We can’t just decide to “let go” of anger. We must first learn to be with it, to understand its language. Here is a gentle practice you can try. Find a quiet space where you won’t be disturbed.

1.  **Connect with Your Body:** Sit or lie down comfortably. Close your eyes and take a few deep, grounding breaths. Bring your awareness to your body, just noticing the sensations present without judgment. Feel the weight of your body on the chair or floor.

2.  **Locate the Liver:** Place your right hand over the right side of your ribcage. This is the home of your liver. Just rest your hand there, offering a gentle, warming presence. Breathe into this space.

3.  **Invite the Feeling:** Gently call to mind a situation that brings up a feeling of anger or resentment. Choose something with a mild charge, not a full-blown rage. As you think of the situation, notice what happens in your body. Does your jaw tighten? Does your stomach clench? Does heat rise in your chest? Just observe.

4.  **Listen with Compassion:** As you feel the energy of anger, silently ask it: *“What do you have to tell me? What is your truth?”* Don’t look for a big, dramatic answer. It might be a single word, like “Unfair,” or “Stop.” It might be an image or a memory. Simply be open to receiving the message, without judgment. You are not the anger; you are the loving awareness holding the anger.

5.  **Breathe and Release:** Imagine that with every inhale, you are breathing in compassion and understanding for yourself. With every exhale, imagine you are releasing the intensity of the emotion, not pushing it away, but allowing it to soften and flow. Stay with this for a few minutes, just breathing and feeling.

This practice is not a one-time fix. It is a way of building a new relationship with a powerful part of yourself. It’s a way of creating new neural pathways in the brain, pathways that say, “It is safe to feel. I can handle this energy. I am capable of listening to my own wisdom.”

## The Power of Impeccable Discernment

The ultimate gift of a healthy, flowing liver-gallbladder system is the power of impeccable discernment. When we have cleared the backlog of old, stagnant anger and bitterness, we create space. We become clear channels. From this place of clarity, we can begin to make conscious choices about what we allow into our system in the first place.

This isn’t about building walls or living in a state of fearful protection. It’s about cultivating a refined sensitivity, like a connoisseur of fine wine developing a palate. You learn to taste the energetic notes of a situation. Does this conversation feel expansive or constricting? Does this food feel vital or heavy? Does this relationship feel respectful or diminishing? Your body knows. The wisdom is right there, in your gut, in the subtle signals of your nervous system, in the quiet knowing of your heart.

Transcending the liver-gallbladder pattern is about developing the power to fully metabolize all that you have ingested — physically, emotionally, and spiritually. It is about developing the capacity to process anger without storing it as bitterness. It is about becoming so impeccably discerning about what you take in that you no longer have to spend so much energy detoxifying.

Imagine what that would be like. To move through the world with an open heart, but also with a clear and loving “no.” To feel a surge of anger and to know how to honor its message without causing harm. To be able to digest life’s challenges and transform them into fuel for your journey. This is not a fantasy. This is your birthright. This is the power that resides within you, in the magnificent intelligence of your body, waiting to be reclaimed.

It begins with a single, conscious breath. It begins with the willingness to turn towards yourself with the deepest compassion. It begins with the choice to listen to the sacred messenger of your own body, and to trust the wisdom you find there.

teachings.sourceTitle: Your Heart: The First Declaration of Your Existence
teachings.title: Your Heart: The First Declaration of Your Existence
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to remember the heart as the first, pre-verbal declaration of our existence—a steady, life-affirming pulse that precedes thought and identity. She weaves biology, lived observation, and contemplative practice to suggest that coming home to the heart—through simple embodied attention—re-patterns nervous system reactivity and restores the balance of giving and receiving. The piece also holds space for the heart’s capacity to contain grief as well as joy, and offers a gentle, practical starting point for reconnecting with your felt sense of worth.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I want to tell you about the moment I stopped being afraid of the dark — not the literal dark, but the metaphorical one.

We arrive, and from the very first moment, we are asked to navigate a world of profound complexity, of immense beauty and sometimes, shattering pain. We search for our purpose, for our place, for the through-line that makes sense of it all. We look to our minds, our careers, our relationships, our achievements. But what if the first, and most profound, declaration of our purpose was made long before we could think, or strive, or even take our first breath?

I remember sitting with a young woman, a client, whose life was a testament to her incredible capability. She had built a successful business, curated a beautiful home, and was a pillar of strength for her friends and family. Yet, she sat across from me, her hands clenched in her lap, and confessed a feeling of deep, gnawing emptiness. “I feel like I have to keep doing, keep achieving,” she whispered, “to prove I have a right to be here.”

Her words landed with such resonance, a feeling I have come to know so intimately in my work and in my own journey. This deep-seated belief that our existence is conditional, that our worth must be earned through relentless effort. It’s a pattern of the wounded heart, a heart that learned somewhere along the way that it must sacrifice itself, must over-give, to justify its own beat.

But the heart’s truth is so much more fundamental, so much more unconditional than that. Let’s go back. Back to the very beginning, to that dark, watery sanctuary of the womb. Before the intricate latticework of the brain began to form, before the delicate buds of limbs emerged, there was a flicker. A pulse. A rhythmic, insistent beat.

It was the heart. The very first distinct organ to manifest.

Before thought, before identity, before any external validation, your heart declared, *I am here. I choose this journey. Let life begin.*

This is not just poetry; it is biological fact. That first heartbeat was the primary act of creation, the initial signature of your unique consciousness entering into matter. It was a declaration of purpose in its purest form. It wasn’t a question. It was a statement. A profound, unwavering assertion of your right to exist. You are here because your heart chose to beat.

## The Sun of Your Inner Solar System

Think of your heart as the central sun of your own inner solar system. Just as the sun radiates light and warmth, holding all the planets in its gravitational embrace, your heart circulates the very essence of life through your entire being. We learn in school that it pumps blood, delivering oxygen and nutrients. And this is true, a miracle of biological engineering. But the body’s wisdom teaches us that it circulates so much more.

It circulates energy. Life force. *Prana*. *Chi*. It is the engine of your vitality, the center of a vast, intelligent network. When the heart is open and coherent, this life-giving energy flows unimpeded, nourishing every cell, every organ, every system. We feel radiant, alive, connected. When the heart is constricted by fear, grief, or the old story that we are not enough, that flow is diminished. We feel depleted, isolated, and tired. The planets of our inner system grow cold and dim.

Modern neuroscience is now beginning to catch up with this ancient wisdom. Scientists have discovered that the heart has its own complex nervous system, a “heart-brain” of around 40,000 neurons. It can sense, feel, learn, and remember independently of the brain in your head. The heart sends far more information to the brain than the brain sends to the heart.

Even more astonishing is the heart’s electromagnetic field. It is, by far, the most powerful rhythmic bioelectric signal produced by the body. The heart
s field is about 60 times greater in amplitude than the electrical activity generated by the brain, and it can be detected several feet away from the body in all directions.

Think about that for a moment. Your heart is broadcasting a powerful, energetic signature into the world around you. When you walk into a room, your heart’s field interacts with the fields of others before you even speak a word. This is not woo-woo thinking; it is measurable physics. It is the science behind the feeling you get from some people—that sense of calm, of safety, of warmth. You are literally feeling the coherence of their heart’s field.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Coming Home to the Heart

I have a deep, abiding reverence for the heart. In my three decades of work as a healer, I have witnessed again and again that the longest and most arduous journey we can make is the eighteen inches from our head to our heart. We get so lost in the labyrinth of our thoughts, in the relentless analysis and problem-solving of the mind. The mind is a magnificent tool, but it is not the source of our wisdom. The heart is.

When we are disconnected from our heart, we live in a state of perpetual negotiation with life. We try to control outcomes, manage perceptions, and strategize our way to safety and love. It is exhausting. It is the source of the clenched jaw, the tight shoulders, the shallow breath. It is the signature of a nervous system caught in a chronic state of fight-or-flight. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is simply responding to the heart’s perceived state of exile.

Coming home to the heart is a practice. It is a gentle, moment-by-moment turning of our attention inward. It is learning to listen to its quieter, more subtle language—the language of feeling, of intuition, of a deep, inner knowing that transcends logic. It is the practice of asking, not “What do I think?” but “What do I feel?” Not “What should I do?” but “What does my heart know?”

One of the most powerful ways to begin this journey is simply to place a hand on your heart. Feel the warmth of your own touch. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest with each breath. And then, begin to breathe a little more deeply, a little more slowly. Imagine with each in-breath that you are drawing in pure, unconditional love and acceptance. Imagine with each out-breath that you are releasing the old stories, the self-judgment, the fear.

This simple act is a profound form of neural repatterning. You are signaling to your nervous system that you are safe. You are creating a state of heart coherence, where the rhythms of your heart, brain, and breath align. In this state, the body’s innate capacity for healing is activated. The mind becomes clear and calm. And you begin to remember the truth of who you are—not a being who must earn love, but a being who *is* love.

## The Courage to Receive

In the source material for the Body Cards, the heart’s core teaching is about the balance of giving and receiving. Its two-way pumping mechanism is a perfect metaphor for this sacred dynamic. Yet, so many of us have learned that it is better—safer, more noble—to give than to receive. A heart that only gives, that pumps its life force outward without allowing itself to be replenished, will eventually run dry. This is the anatomy of burnout, of compassion fatigue, of the heart attack that is the heart’s desperate, final cry for attention.

To receive is an act of profound courage. It requires a fundamental sense of self-worth, the deep inner knowing that you are worthy of being filled, of being nourished, of being loved. It is a radical act in a world that so often teaches us the opposite. But it is the key to a heart that can extend love without depletion, a heart that becomes a source-fed river rather than a stagnant pond.

Your heart’s first declaration was not one of service or sacrifice. It was a declaration of *being*. Your purpose is not to exhaust yourself in the giving. Your purpose is to embody the love that you are, and to let that love radiate outward naturally, as effortlessly as the sun shines. It is to be so full of your own life force that your very presence becomes a gift.

So, I invite you today to pause. To place a hand on your chest and feel that steady, faithful rhythm that has been with you from the very beginning. It is the rhythm of your own belonging. It is the sound of your own unwavering worth. Let it be the anchor that brings you home to yourself, again and again.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [When You Cannot Breathe: Suffocation, Grief, and Your Lungs](/blog/lungs-cannot-breathe-grief)
- [The Sacred Symbol of Nurture: What Your Breasts Are Telling You](/blog/breasts-sacred-symbol-nurture)

**More on Heart:**

- [Heart Attacks of the Soul: When Your Heart Demands Attention](/blog/heart-attacks-of-soul)
- [Dis-heartened: When Giving Depletes and Receiving Feels Impossible](/blog/heart-disheartened)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you remember the profound truth of your own heart’s first declaration. May you trust its wisdom, honor its rhythm, and have the courage to receive the infinite love that is your birthright.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


## The Heart as a Vessel for Grief and Joy

It is also essential to understand that the heart, in its immense capacity, is designed to hold the full spectrum of human emotion. It is a vessel not just for love and connection, but also for grief, for sorrow, for the pain of loss. We often try to shield our hearts from these experiences, believing them to be negative or damaging. We build walls, we numb ourselves, we distract ourselves, all in an effort to avoid the ache of a broken heart.

But a heart that has never been broken is a heart that has never truly loved. Grief is the natural, necessary counterpart to love. It is the measure of our connection, the testament to what mattered. To deny grief is to deny the love that preceded it. The heart knows how to hold this pain. It knows how to metabolize sorrow, transforming it into a deeper capacity for compassion, for empathy, for a more profound appreciation of the fleeting beauty of life.

When we allow ourselves to feel our grief fully, without judgment or resistance, we are not shattering our hearts. We are expanding them. We are creating more space within ourselves to hold both the sorrow and the joy, the darkness and the light. The heart that can weep is also the heart that can experience the most exquisite joy. The two are inextricably linked. A heart that is closed to one is closed to the other.

So, let your heart be a sanctuary for all of your feelings. Trust its resilience. Trust its alchemical power to transform pain into wisdom. Your heart is not a fragile thing to be protected from life. It is a powerful, dynamic, and ever-expanding center of your being, capable of holding the totality of your human experience with grace and courage. It is the source of your deepest strength and your most profound connection to the sacredness of all that is.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Web of Your Being: The Unified Field of Consciousness
teachings.title: The Web of Your Being: The Unified Field of Consciousness
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to sense the self as a unified "Web of Being": an energetic, informational field that links body, mind, emotion, and purpose. She frames coherence and integration — supported by contemporary neuroscience and somatic awareness — as the foundation for healing and for living purpose as a felt resonance rather than a distant goal. A brief, gentle breath-and-body scanning practice is offered to begin reconnecting fragmented parts and cultivating inner harmony.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Consider a time when you have felt utterly… scattered. Perhaps your mind was racing with a to-do list, while your heart was heavy with a personal concern, and your body was signaling its own needs through aches or fatigue. It is a common human experience to feel like a collection of disconnected parts, each one clamoring for attention, each one feeling isolated and overwhelmed. Have you ever felt that way? It can be like a symphony orchestra where every musician is playing a different song, at a different tempo. The result is just noise, a stressful cacophony that leaves you feeling exhausted and fragmented.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We learn to compartmentalize. We learn to isolate a physical pain from an emotional wound, to separate our spiritual longing from our intellectual reasoning. We are taught to see the body as a machine, a collection of systems that can be fixed part by part, like a car. Your lungs are for breathing, your stomach for digesting, your brain for thinking. But what if that’s not the whole story? What if the most profound truth of our embodiment isn’t in the individual parts, but in the miraculous, invisible web that holds them all together?

This is what I call the Web of Your Being. It isn’t a single organ or system you can point to in a medical textbook. It is the unified field of consciousness that permeates and connects every cell, every thought, every emotion, every impulse. It is the conductor of your inner symphony, the silent, intelligent presence that ensures the heart’s rhythm speaks to the brain’s electrical hum, and the gut’s intuition informs the soul’s deepest knowing. It is the ultimate Body Card, because it is the container for all the others. When this web is coherent and strong, information flows freely. Healing happens not just locally, but globally, across the entire system. But when it’s tangled or torn, we experience that sense of fragmentation, of being at war with ourselves.

## The Neuroscience of Coherence

Modern neuroscience is beginning to catch up to this ancient wisdom. Scientists now speak of “integration” as the hallmark of a healthy, resilient nervous system. Dr. Dan Siegel, a pioneer in interpersonal neurobiology, describes integration as the linking of differentiated parts. Think of it like a choir. You have the high sopranos, the deep basses, the rich altos and tenors. Each section is distinct, differentiated. But when they sing together, linked in harmony, they create a sound far more beautiful and complex than any single section could produce on its own. That is integration. It’s the synergy of the whole being greater than the sum of its parts.

When our being is integrated, there is a coherence to our internal state. The electrical signals from the heart, which have their own powerful electromagnetic field that can be measured several feet away from the body, become synchronized with our brain waves. Our breath deepens and slows, signaling to the ancient, reptilian part of our brain that we are safe. This state of coherence isn’t just a feeling of calm; it’s a biological reality that supports healing, clarity, and a profound sense of wholeness. The Web of Your Being is the very fabric of this coherence. It’s the energetic and informational matrix through which every part of you communicates with every other part. It’s a shimmering, dynamic network of light and information, constantly adapting and responding.

When we feel fragmented, it’s a sign that the web is being strained. A trauma, a loss, a chronic stress, a limiting belief… these experiences can create snags or even tears in the fabric. They create energetic knots of contraction. We start to feel like a collection of symptoms rather than a whole person. The pain in your shoulder is not just a shoulder problem; it’s a signal from the web, a communication that something in your field is out of balance. The anxiety in your chest is not just a nervous system issue; it’s a vibration that affects the entire field, from your hormonal balance to your thought patterns. The body is a hologram—the whole is contained in every part. You can touch one part of the web and feel the resonance across the entire structure.

## The Web and Your Sacred Purpose

So why does this matter? Because living from the awareness of your own unified field is the key to embodying your sacred purpose. When we are fragmented, we are easily pulled off-center. We are driven by the loudest, most painful part—the fearful thought, the aching joint, the wounded emotion. We spend our lives reacting, managing, and coping. We believe our purpose is something “out there” that we must find or achieve, a destination we must struggle toward. We chase after it, thinking if we just get that promotion, or find that partner, or finish that project, *then* we will feel whole and fulfilled.

But what if your purpose is not a destination, but a resonance? A frequency that you are meant to hold and express in the world? When you begin to tend to the Web of Your Being, you are no longer just “fixing” problems. You are tuning your instrument. You are cultivating the inner coherence that allows the unique music of your soul to play through you, unimpeded. It’s like tuning a guitar; you tighten one string, and it changes the sound of all the others. By bringing conscious, loving attention to the disconnected parts of yourself, you are tuning your entire being to the frequency of your own unique essence.

From this place of integration, your purpose reveals itself not as a job title or a grand accomplishment, but as a way of being. It’s the quality of presence you bring to your relationships. It’s the compassion that flows from your integrated heart. It’s the wisdom that arises from your coherent mind. It’s the unique flavor of love that only you can offer the world. When the web is whole, you don’t have to *find* your purpose; you simply *are* your purpose. You are a unified field of consciousness experiencing itself through the magnificent instrument of your embodied being, and your very existence becomes an offering. Your life itself becomes a prayer, a song, a dance of wholeness.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Tending to Your Inner Fabric: A Simple Practice

How, then, do we begin to repair and nurture this sacred web? It begins with listening. It begins with turning your awareness inward, not with the goal of fixing, but with the gentle intention of making contact. It’s a practice of radical inclusion, of allowing every part of your experience to have a voice. Here is a simple practice you can try right now.

Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down, where you won’t be disturbed for a few minutes. Close your eyes if that feels comfortable. Take a few slow, deep breaths, allowing your belly to soften and expand with each inhale, and release with each exhale.

Now, bring your awareness to your body. Just notice it. Scan your attention from your feet up to the crown of your head. Where in your body do you feel the most sensation? It might be a tingle, a warmth, an ache, a pressure. Don’t label it as “good” or “bad.” Just notice. And where in your body do you feel the least? Where is there a sense of numbness, or emptiness, or quiet?

Can you breathe into both places with equal tenderness? Imagine your breath is a current of warm, golden light. On your inhale, direct this light to the place of sensation. On your exhale, direct it to the place of numbness. You are not trying to change anything. You are simply bringing the light of your awareness to the disconnected places, letting them know they are seen. You are building a bridge of light between the parts of you that have been separated.

As you continue to breathe, you might begin to notice the conversations happening within you. You notice how a critical thought tightens your jaw. You notice how a memory of kindness softens your belly. You are witnessing the web in action. You are becoming conscious of the connections that were always there, just waiting for your attention. Stay with this for as long as you like. When you’re ready, gently bring your awareness back to the room, and open your eyes.

This is not a quick fix or a one-time event. It is a lifelong journey of coming home to yourself. It is the sacred work of becoming the loving conductor of your own symphony, of learning to listen for the harmony beneath the noise. It is the most important journey you will ever take.

Your body is not a collection of parts. It is a sacred, intelligent, unified field of light and information. It is the web of your being, and it is holding you, always. Can you feel it? Even now, can you sense the subtle hum of your own whololeness, the quiet song of your own soul? It’s there. It has always been there. Waiting for you to listen.

teachings.sourceTitle: Flowing with Life: Transcending Kidney Patterns
teachings.title: Flowing with Life: Transcending Kidney Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan uses the metaphor of a powerful river to illuminate how resisting life's currents—fear, grief, resentment—can crystallize in the body, often showing up in and around the kidneys. She invites readers to develop emotional literacy: to notice, breathe into, and be present with feelings so they can flow instead of becoming stuck. The piece offers a brief, gentle somatic practice and encouragement to trade victim consciousness for embodied trust and compassionate self-care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Consider the power of a river. Not a gentle, meandering stream, but a powerful, determined force that carves its way through the landscape. In the spring, swelled with snowmelt from the high mountains, it becomes a torrent of churning, silver-brown water. It can effortlessly carry entire trees downstream—roots, branches, and all. There is no arguing with it. One cannot reason with it, bargain with it, or ask it to please slow down. One can only respect its immense power and allow it to move as it needs to move.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We so often try to be the dam. We see the powerful currents of life—grief, love, fear, change—and our first instinct is to build a wall. We brace. We control, we manage, we contain what feels overwhelming. We believe, on some deep, often unconscious level, that if we can just hold it all back, we will be safe. But the river always, eventually, wins. And the strain of trying to hold it back, beloved one, is immense.

This is the story our kidneys tell. These two small, bean-shaped organs, nestled in our lower back against the strong muscles there, are the master alchemists of our internal ocean. Day in and day out, they perform a quiet miracle, filtering nearly 200 quarts of fluid. They are not simple strainers; they are profoundly intelligent. They meticulously sift through our blood, deciding with an ancient wisdom what to keep and what to release, maintaining the exquisitely delicate balance of our entire system. They are the guardians of our inner flow, the silent regulators of our life-sustaining sea.

When we are in harmony with the river of life, our kidneys function with quiet efficiency. But when we fight the current—when we try to dam our emotions, when we feel victimized by the circumstances of our lives, when we are gripped by fear—our kidneys bear the burden. They become the site of our resistance, the place where the battle against our own life force is waged.

## The Weight of the Unfelt

In spiritual work, we often see my dear ones whose bodies are speaking through the language of their kidneys. The patterns are often startlingly clear. There’s a sense of being overwhelmed by the tides of life, a feeling of being a small boat tossed on a merciless sea. This is the heart of victim consciousness—the belief that we are powerless against external forces, that life is happening *to* us, rather than *through* us.

When we inhabit this state, we often don’t allow ourselves to fully feel our emotions. Fear, in particular, has a chilling effect on the kidneys, according to ancient wisdom traditions like Chinese medicine. It’s a cold, contracting energy that constricts the very flow the kidneys are designed to manage. We might also be swimming in a murky soup of resentment, disappointment, or criticism, but we hold it all in, believing it’s unsafe or un-spiritual to express it. We try to be “good,” to keep the peace, to not make waves, to be the calm one, the strong one.

But the body, in its infinite wisdom, must do something with all that unexpressed energy. It cannot simply vanish. And so, it crystallizes. It is common for people to experience this in a very physical way, through recurring and agonizing issues like kidney stones. This can happen when someone, for example, swallows their own needs, frustration, and quiet anger for years in order to care for another. They may feel trapped, resentful, and deeply, secretly afraid of what would happen if they ever said “no.” The resulting kidney stones, those excruciatingly painful formations, can be seen as the physical manifestation of crystallized resentment and fear—hardened nuggets of unspoken truth that were never processed and released. They are the debris from the dam that was so dutifully built.

This isn’t about blame. It’s never about blame. Every pattern we develop, no matter how painful, once served a purpose. The pattern of emotional containment and the narrative of victimhood are often learned in childhood, wired into our tender nervous systems when we truly *were* powerless. If we grew up in an environment where expressing our big feelings was met with anger, dismissal, or punishment, we created a brilliant strategy: we learned to hold it in. We learned that our survival depended on being small, quiet, and agreeable. We created neural pathways for suppression, and our brain became incredibly efficient at it. It was a strategy for survival, and we must honor it for getting us through.

But now, as adults, that old survival strategy is costing us our vitality. It’s asking us to live in a state of constant, low-grade resistance to the very life force that wants to move through us. It’s exhausting. It’s like trying to hold a beach ball underwater—it takes constant effort and vigilance, and the moment you lose focus, it bursts to the surface, often with chaotic force.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Practice of Emotional Literacy

So what do we do? How do we learn to flow with the river instead of trying to dam it? The journey begins with developing what I call emotional literacy—the ability to feel, process, and release our emotions in real time, with compassion and without judgment.

This is not about being endlessly swept away by our feelings. It is the opposite. It is about becoming a conscious and loving container for our own experience. It’s the difference between being drowned by a wave and learning to surf it. Emotional literacy means we can say, “Ah, here is fear. I feel its cold grip in my belly, the tension in my shoulders, the shallow catch in my breath.” We meet it. We breathe with it. We don’t have to become it, and we certainly don’t have to act from it. We simply acknowledge its presence as a sensation in the body.

> To feel is to heal. To resist is to persist.

When we allow a feeling to be present, without judgment and without a story, it naturally begins to move. It flows. It’s the *resistance* to the feeling that keeps it stuck. The moment we stop fighting it, we are no longer a victim of it. We are in relationship with it. This is a profound shift. It’s the beginning of taking our power back—not power *over* life, but the power to be present *with* life, in all its messy, beautiful, and unpredictable glory.

Let’s try a small practice right now. Find a comfortable seat, close your eyes if that feels good, and take a gentle breath. Now, bring to mind a situation that causes a small amount of emotional charge for you—not a major trauma, but a minor annoyance or worry. As you hold it in your mind, scan your body. Where does the feeling live? Is it a tightness in your chest? A knot in your stomach? A buzz of energy in your hands? Don’t name it. Just feel it. Bring your breath to that place in your body. Imagine your breath is a warm, compassionate light, surrounding the sensation. You don’t need to change it or fix it. Your only job is to be with it. To let it know it is seen. Stay with it for five more breaths. Notice what happens. Does it shift? Does it soften? Does it move? This simple act of presence is the foundation of emotional literacy.

This practice rewires the brain. Each time you choose to meet a feeling with presence instead of suppression, you are carving a new neural pathway. You are teaching your nervous system, cell by cell, that it is safe to feel. You are moving from a state of sympathetic dominance—the “fight or flight” response that is so taxing on the kidneys—to a state of parasympathetic restoration, where the body can rest, digest, and heal.

This is how we begin to dismantle victim consciousness from the inside out. We stop looking outside of ourselves for someone to blame for our discomfort and start tending to our own inner world. We realize that while we may not be able to control the river, we can become masterful navigators. We can learn to read the currents, to trust our vessel—this sacred body—and to know that even the rapids are leading us somewhere essential.

Trust is the antidote to fear. Can you allow yourself to trust, just for a moment, that your body has an innate capacity to maintain perfect balance when you stop fighting the current? Can you trust that the river of your own life is carrying you toward a greater wholeness, even when you can’t see around the next bend? This isn’t a blind trust. It is a felt sense, a deep knowing that arises when we finally stop struggling and allow ourselves to be held by the water.
