teachings.sourceTitle: The Gift of Difficult Emotions
teachings.title: The Gift of Difficult Emotions
teachings.summary: Susan reframes difficult emotions — grief, anger, shame — not as enemies to be eradicated but as embodied messengers offering wisdom and healing. She outlines how the nervous system and neuroplasticity underlie emotional life and offers a gentle somatic practice of naming, locating, and breathing into sensations to allow feelings to complete their cycle. The emphasis is on curiosity, compassion, and steady practice rather than quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A dear friend once told me that the body is the unconscious mind made visible. I have never forgotten those words.

And one of the most profound aspects, I’ve found, is learning what to do with the emotions that feel… well, impossible. The grief that hollows you out. The anger that burns so hot you’re afraid you’ll incinerate everything in your path. The shame that makes you want to curl up and disappear. For years, my own relationship with these feelings was one of warfare. I saw them as enemies to be vanquished, problems to be solved, intruders to be evicted from the house of my being.

I remember one particular season of my life, a time thick with loss, when grief was a constant, unwelcome companion. It would arrive unannounced, a sudden wave crashing over me in the middle of the grocery store, my hand hovering over a carton of eggs. My strategy was simple: suppress, distract, and pretend. I would clench my jaw, push the feeling down into some dark basement of my soul, and focus with laser-like intensity on the task at hand. *I am fine*, I would tell myself, a mantra of denial. But I wasn’t fine. The suppressed grief began to speak through my body. A deep, rattling cough took hold, a constant tightness in my lungs, as if the unshed tears had pooled there, heavy and stagnant. My body was trying to tell me what my mind refused to acknowledge: you cannot outrun your own heart.

What if these difficult emotions are not problems to be solved? What if, instead, they are gifts to be received? Not the kind of gift you asked for, perhaps—more like a mysterious, unmarked package left on your doorstep. You don’t know what’s inside, and you’re a little afraid to open it. But your soul, in its infinite wisdom, has sent it for a reason.

## The Neuroscience of Emotion

Here’s a very good thing to know: your body is wired for wisdom, not for war. When a strong emotion arises, it’s not a malfunction. It’s a sophisticated, lightning-fast communication from your nervous system. The amygdala, a small almond-shaped region deep in your brain, acts as an emotional smoke detector. It scans your experience for anything that might be a threat—or anything that reminds it of a past threat—and sounds the alarm. This triggers a cascade of biochemical responses: adrenaline, cortisol, a racing heart, shallow breathing. This is the body’s ancient, intelligent way of preparing you to survive, the well-known “fight or flight” response of the sympathetic nervous system.

But here is the crucial part. When we suppress the emotion—when we tell ourselves, *I shouldn’t feel this way*, or *This is too much*—we interrupt the natural cycle of processing. The electrical and chemical energy of that emotion doesn’t just vanish. It has to go somewhere. And so, it gets stored in the body’s tissues. The unexpressed anger lodges in the liver, creating heat and bitterness. The unwept grief settles in the lungs, creating a sense of suffocation and melancholy. The unprocessed fear takes up residence in the kidneys, leading to a state of chronic exhaustion and overwhelm. The body, in its profound honesty, begins to manifest the very feelings we have refused to feel. It creates symptoms not to punish us, but to get our attention. It is a sacred messenger, knocking ever more loudly on the door of our awareness.

> “The symptom is the body’s way of telling a story that the mind has not yet been able to hear.”

This is not a life sentence. The beautiful truth of our being is something called neuroplasticity. Our brains are not fixed, static things. We can, and do, create new neural pathways throughout our lives. By consciously choosing to turn towards our difficult emotions with curiosity and compassion, we begin to wire the brain for a new response. We can learn to activate the other branch of our autonomic nervous system, the parasympathetic nervous system, often called the “rest and digest” system. This is the state where healing occurs. Instead of the well-worn path of suppression leading to physical distress, we can blaze a new trail—one of presence, allowance, and integration. We can teach our nervous system, cell by cell, that it is safe to feel.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Welcoming the Unwelcome Guests

So how do we do this? How do we learn to be with these powerful energies without being consumed by them? It begins with a shift in intention. Instead of trying to get *rid* of the feeling, we set an intention to get *curious* about it. We become the host, and the emotion is our guest. A difficult guest, to be sure, but one who has come bearing a gift.

My own journey with this was not a straight line. It was a spiral, a dance of two steps forward, one step back. I learned, slowly, to stop fighting the grief that lived in my lungs. When the wave would rise, instead of bracing against it, I would find a quiet place to sit. I would place a hand on my heart, a hand on my belly, and I would breathe. I wouldn’t try to change the feeling. I would simply acknowledge it. *Ah, grief, you are here. Welcome.*

I had a similar reckoning with anger. For most of my life, I believed anger was a “bad” emotion. I was a “good girl,” and good girls didn’t get angry. So I swallowed it. I remember a time when I felt deeply betrayed by a friend. The anger was a roaring fire in my gut, but I smiled and said it was okay. The next day, I woke up with a blinding migraine, a classic example of the body screaming what the voice will not. It took me years to understand that the anger itself wasn’t the problem; the problem was my judgment of it. The anger was simply energy, a powerful life force telling me that a boundary had been violated. It was a gift, asking me to stand up for myself, to honor my own truth. By welcoming the anger, by letting myself feel its heat without judgment, I was able to access its wisdom. The migraine subsided, and in its place was a newfound clarity and strength.

I began to ask these emotions questions, not with my analytical mind, but with the open curiosity of my heart. *What do you need me to know? What part of me are you trying to heal?* And in the quiet space of allowing, answers would surface. Not always in words, but in images, in memories, in a deep, somatic sense of understanding. I saw that the grief was not just for my own losses, but for the losses of my mother, and her mother before her. It was an ancient, collective river of sorrow, and my willingness to feel it was a gift not just to myself, but to my entire lineage.

This is the wisdom of the body. It doesn’t speak in spreadsheets and bullet points. It speaks in the language of sensation, of energy, of deep, intuitive knowing. The tightness in your shoulders is not just a muscle spasm; it’s the weight of responsibilities you were never meant to carry alone. The fire in your belly is not just indigestion; it’s the righteous anger of a boundary that has been crossed. The lump in your throat is not just a physical constriction; it’s the unexpressed truth your soul is longing to speak.

## How to Be With the Gift

Being with difficult emotions is a practice. It is not a one-time fix. It is a relationship you cultivate with yourself over a lifetime. It requires courage, gentleness, and a willingness to be present with what is true, right now. As it says in the Tao Te Ching, “The way to do is to be.” We do not need to *do* anything to the emotion; we simply need to *be* with it.

Here is a simple way to begin. The next time a difficult emotion arises, see if you can resist the urge to immediately distract yourself or push it away. Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down. Close your eyes, if that feels safe.

1.  **Acknowledge It:** Simply name what you are feeling. “This is anger.” “This is fear.” “This is shame.” Naming it creates a little bit of space between you and the emotion. You are the one who is aware of the anger; you are not the anger itself.

2.  **Locate It in Your Body:** Where does this emotion live in you? Is it a tightness in your chest? A knot in your stomach? A buzzing in your hands? Let your attention rest gently on that physical sensation. No judgment, no story. Just the pure sensation of it.

3.  **Breathe Into It:** Imagine you could direct your breath into that area of your body. With each inhale, imagine creating a little more space around the sensation. With each exhale, imagine a gentle softening, a letting go. You are not trying to force it to leave. You are simply bringing it your compassionate presence.

4.  **Listen for the Message:** Ask the sensation, *What is your gift for me?* Then, just listen. Be open to whatever arises. It might be a word, an image, a memory, or simply a shift in the sensation itself. Trust the wisdom that emerges from within.

This is not about wallowing in the emotion. It is about honoring it. It is about allowing its energy to move through you and complete its natural cycle, so that it does not become trapped in your tissues. It is a profound act of self-love, of coming home to the wholeness of your being.

These emotions are not a sign that you are broken. They are a sign that you are alive, that you are connected, that you have a heart capable of feeling the vast, complex, and sometimes painful beauty of this human experience. They are the gateways to your deepest healing, your most profound wisdom, and your most radiant love.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.title: The Thyroid - The Butterfly of Transformation and Metabolic Balance
teachings.summary: This piece presents the thyroid as a ‘butterfly’—a small gland that coordinates metabolism, timing, and the embodied expression of purpose—and invites readers to listen to how physiology and personal narrative intertwine. It describes hypothyroid and hyperthyroid patterns as meaningful protective strategies rooted in early experience, outlines lifestyle and somatic practices to support balance, and emphasizes patient, compassionate inquiry alongside conventional care. The tone is invitational and practice-oriented, encouraging small experiments and long-term re-patterning rather than quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The Thyroid - The Butterfly of Transformation and Metabolic Balance

You carry a tiny butterfly at the throat - two lobes of delicate tissue shaped like a winged messenger, settled over the windpipe. It is modest in size yet profound in influence. It secretes hormones that set the cadence of your metabolism, the tempo of cellular life, the speed at which thought and feeling are translated into action. When it sings in harmony, everything moves with appropriate ease. When it falters, the harmony becomes a story you feel in every cell. The thyroid is not merely an endocrine organ. It is a sacred translator between your intention and your embodiment, between your inner purpose and how that purpose is lived out through breath, voice, and movement.

The Physiology of a Metabolic Conductor

Physiologically, the thyroid responds to a conversation that begins in the brain. The hypothalamus and pituitary whisper instructions through releasing factors and thyroid stimulating hormone, and in turn the thyroid releases T4 and T3 - signals that tell every cell whether to accelerate, slow, store energy, burn fuel, or conserve. These hormones touch your heart rate, your digestion, your body temperature, your sleep architecture, your mood. The axis that connects brain and thyroid is exquisitely sensitive to stress, to the rhythms of light and dark, to nourishment and to the quiet architecture of your inner life. Think of it as the metronome of your living tempo. When the metronome is true you find a rhythm that fits both the outer world and the inner call. When it is discordant you may be pushed into frantic motion or heavy dampening.

The Thyroid as Messenger - Voice, Purpose, and Boundary

In the holographic language of the body, the throat region is about more than swallowing and breathing. It is the place where voice and truth meet gravity. The thyroid sits close to your vocal cords and your larynx - the tools through which you project who you are. When your thyroid is in balance you find an authentic rhythm for expression: you know when to speak, when to hold, when to sing, when to be silent. When it becomes unbalanced, your body speaks in ways that unfurl meaning if you are willing to listen. Hypothyroidism often feels like a damping down - a heaviness that sedates enthusiasm and clamps the voice. Hyperthyroidism feels like a speeding up - a flurry of words, a nervousness that runs ahead of your inner steadiness. Both are invitations to inquire into the relationship between purpose and fear, between authentic timing and strategies of survival.

In the Tao Te Ching there is a delicate counsel that steadies this inquiry: "Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished." Allow this to sit on your tongue as you consider your thyroid. The gland asks you to learn the art of timing, to discover your unique tempo that neither rushes nor stalls, that neither floods nor withholds. The butterfly that perches at your throat wants you to learn to move with nature rather than against it.

Hypothyroidism - The Quieting of Purpose

When your thyroid is underactive there can be a profound sense of slowing. Energy becomes reserved as if held for a distant future. You may notice fatigue, coldness, constipation, a slowing of thought, a softness to the edges of desire. The deeper narrative that often accompanies this physiology is one of fear that silences you. You learned early that certain expressions might be met with disapproval, that ambition or clear voice could bring rejection, that to be seen fully would be to risk abandonment. In response, you internalized a posture of conservation. It is a wise protective strategy for a child who needed safety. Later, when you are an adult with different resources, that same protective posture can keep your purpose dimmed.

Hypothyroidism is not moral failure. It is a protective architecture that once held you together. Your body has been saying, with every quieted cell, that it could not risk being too visible because visibility seemed dangerous. The invitation here is to translate that message into compassionate inquiry. What did you learn about being small? Where in your life are you still keeping your flame tucked away because of a remembered coldness? How has "safety" been negotiated through silence? These questions are not about blame. They are gateways to reclaiming a steadier, more heart-aligned rhythm in which you can let warmth return to your metabolism without hurrying or forcing it.

Hyperthyroidism - Speed as Insecurity

On the other wing of the butterfly is hyperthyroidism - a state when the system runs fast, sometimes chaotically. Your heart races, sleep dissolves, thoughts scatter, digestion becomes impatient. You might feel driven to act, to perform, to be pre-emptively generous with energy as if motion itself will keep disaster at bay. Beneath this speed often lives insecurity - the underlying belief that stillness will reveal unworthiness, that if you pause you will be found lacking, or that the next achievement is the proof of your right to exist and be loved.

When you operate from that validation-seeking place, your thyroid may fuel a nervous alacrity that looks like competence on the surface but feels hollow beneath. You hasten through life as if outrunning a shadow. The body, however, cannot maintain that tempo without cost. Anxiety, tremors, immune dysregulation, and eventual exhaustion are the natural consequences of chronic motion without anchoring. The work here is not merely to slow down. It is to discover a depth of presence that allows you to stand in your worth without performance, to hear your inner authority so that your outward speed aligns with genuine calling rather than urgency born of fear.

When the Immune and Thyroid Dance - Hashimoto and Graves

Autoimmune thyroid conditions such as Hashimoto or Graves amplify the story. When the immune system confuses self with other, when boundaries are injured, the thyroid may become embroiled in a civil war. Hashimoto often presents with a pattern of excessive protection that flips into internal attack - a metaphor of self-rejection or internalized criticism. Graves can present with an outward projection - a hypervigilant assertion of self that becomes defensive in its intensity. In the cards of the body these writings are not punitive. They are invitations to examine how you have defended your being, the costs of those defenses, and what new form of boundary might integrate strength and tenderness together.

Listening Somatically - Practices to Find Your Rhythm

The pathway back to balance always begins with listening. The body is a sacred messenger and the throat is its herald. Begin with the simple, slow practice of attending to the breath. Sit quietly and notice how the breath moves through the throat. Allow the exhale to lengthen gently until your nervous system feels soothed. Practice this daily and notice how the tempo of your days shifts when you are in habitual relationship with this softer rhythm.

Vocal practices are particularly powerful. Your voice is the direct line from thought and heart to expression. Try a practice of toning - a low, sustained vowel hum while placing your hand gently on the thyroid region. Notice the warmth, the vibration, the way sound can generate circulation and a sense of permission to make noise in the world. If movement feels supportive, gently roll your neck with breath, never forcing, always creating space around the throat. Allow micro-pauses in conversation - a cultivated stillness before your next sentence - to practice being present instead of reflexively proving yourself through speech.

Rooting into circadian wisdom is crucial. The thyroid listens to the rhythms of light and dark. Regular patterns of sleep, of exposure to natural light in the morning, and of easing toward rest in the evening help orient the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid conversation. In the physical realm this means tending to sleep hygiene, but in the symbolic realm it means choosing days and rhythms that reflect your internal truth rather than external expectation. Slow rituals before sleep, gentle sinks into warmth, avoiding overstimulation in the evenings will support the resourcing your gland needs to find equilibrium.

Food, Nourishment, and Gentle Biochemistry

The thyroid asks you to honor the earth medicines that nourish it - iodine, selenium, zinc, adequate protein, and a balanced energy intake framed within a life that is not chronically stressed. I offer this as invitation not prescription. If you are working with an endocrine condition please collaborate with clinicians you trust. The broader teaching is that your relationship to food mirrors your relationship to energy and safety. When you hoard calories, when you fast from nourishment because you are distrustful of abundance, your metabolism will reflect that strategy. When you overconsume as a way to soothe insecurity, your endocrine rhythms will again echo that reactivity. Learn to nourish in ways that affirm your right to be here and to be sustained.

Working with the Three-Card Process - Purpose, Inquiry, Transcendence

Take the threefold lens that has served so many on this journey and turn it toward the thyroid. Begin with Purpose. Quiet yourself and place your attention on the anatomical truth: this gland balances metabolism, energy, and timing. Thank it for its service. Notice physical sensations in the throat area and allow gratitude to soften the tissue's habitual tension. Let your sense of longing for clear purpose be anchored in physical appreciation.

Move into Inquiry. Ask with curiosity and compassion: Where have you dampened your voice out of fear? When did you learn that slowness or quietness would be safer than being visible? Where are you still running faster than your heart actually feels called to move, believing speed will protect you? Allow images and memories to rise without judgment. Journal whatever arises, even small details. The body remembers so much of what your mind would like to forget. Sit with those memories, breathe into them, and let the throat soften around these recollections. Notice ways your thyroid's story connects with childhood patterns about being seen, being heard, being approved.

Finally, embrace Transcendence. Imagine a new template for your relationship to voice and purpose. Speak aloud a short declaration: "I move in my true rhythm. My voice arrives at the right time. My energy is a steady stream." Repeat this slowly and with reverence, allowing the cells around the throat to listen. Visualize the butterfly wings opening wide but not beating frantically - steady, beautiful, aligned with wind and sky. Allow this embodiment to seep into small choices: one less urgent email, one longer pause before a reply, one moment of presence required to speak the next true thing.

Practical Steps Without Coercion

It is important to offer practices that respect the slow intelligence of the body. Begin with tiny experiments. Shift one small habit for a week and observe. Let morning light in before coffee. Allow five minutes of toning before a meeting. Choose food that feels nourishing rather than restrictive. Practice a nightly ritual that signals to the nervous system that it is safe to repair. Reach for healthcare partners who honor both conventional assessment and your embodied experience. When medication or intervention is helpful, it can be integrated with your psychospiritual work. There is no right or wrong path, only a steady alignment toward what allows your life and your cells to breathe in peace.

Re-patterning Paradigms - The Work of Lifetime

Your thyroid will not heal from a single practice. This gland hums in relation to long-lived paradigms that shaped your response to being alive. As the Elevate Your Body To Love teaching so tenderly shows, the body is holographic. When you shift one pattern - the way you speak your truth, the way you hold or release fear - you will ripple change into many other systems. The cards invite you to see symptoms not as punishment but as messages. When you treat your thyroid with reverence and curiosity rather than with shame or fear, you create a field in which transformation can occur.

Remember too the Taoist counsel: the way is often through non-struggle. When you stop trying to force an accelerated healing and instead cultivate a patient attentiveness, the systems that support the thyroid - sleep, nervous system regulation, immune integration, nourishment and voice - naturally begin to coordinate themselves. Non-striving does not mean passivity. It means wise action that follows the intelligence of the moment rather than the panic of habit. You learn to move like nature - not hurried but ordained, not frantic but fully alive.

An Offering of Presence

Be gentle with yourself. Whether your thyroid leans toward quiet or haste, whether you live with an autoimmune pattern or an intermittent imbalance, know that your body has always been trying to keep you whole in the best way it could with the resources available. Your work is not to force perfection, but to listen, understand, and lovingly reorient. Bring compassion to the child who first chose silence or speed. Hold that child in your arms now and tell them what they needed to hear then: You are safe. You are allowed to take up space. You do not have to move faster to be loved. You do not have to reduce your light to be accepted. You may choose your pace.

Allow the butterfly of your throat to teach you agility without franticness, expression without aggression, and devotion to a measured rhythm that honors earth and sky. Let the Tao be your teacher: in patient alignment with the natural way you will discover a metabolic balance that supports your authentic purpose. When your purpose aligns with your physiology, life moves with a kind of grace that feels inevitable and free. I am with you in this learning. Breathe, tone, listen, and step into your authentic timing. The butterfly is patient. You can be too.

teachings.sourceTitle: Gallstones of Bitterness: When Resentment Crystallizes
teachings.title: Gallstones of Bitterness: When Resentment Crystallizes
teachings.summary: Susan frames the body as a sacred messenger, exploring how long-held anger and resentment show up in the liver–gallbladder landscape and in habitual numbing behaviours. She invites a compassionate somatic inquiry—simple breath, a hand on the belly, and curious questions—as a way to notice and begin to metabolize bitterness without judgment. The piece emphasizes curiosity over forcing forgiveness and holds a compassionate stance toward survival strategies that once served us.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Something extraordinary happens when we stop running.

We love, we lose, we get our hearts bruised, and sometimes, we get angry. Not just a flash of irritation that comes and goes like a summer storm, but a deep, simmering anger that settles in our bones. A resentment that we chew on, over and over, until it becomes a part of us. What do we do with that?

I remember a woman I worked with years ago, a lovely, gentle soul who came to me with a host of digestive issues. She’d been to every specialist, tried every diet, but nothing seemed to touch the constant, gnawing discomfort in her upper abdomen. As we began to work together, a story emerged. A story of a long and bitter divorce, a betrayal that had left her feeling powerless and deeply, chronically angry. She spoke of her ex-husband with a quiet, tight-lipped fury that was startling in its intensity. “I’ll never forgive him,” she told me, her hands clenched in her lap. “Never.”

During one of our sessions, as my hands rested gently on her abdomen, I felt it. A cluster of hard, sharp little stones, tucked away beneath her liver. Gallstones. And in that moment, I knew. These were not just calcified bile. These were her unforgiven tears. Her crystallized bitterness. It was a profound moment of seeing—a direct transmission from her body, revealing the deep, energetic truth of her physical condition. Her body had taken the unprocessed emotional energy of her resentment and, in its incredible wisdom, had given it a physical form. It was a message, a desperate plea for attention and release.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

Our bodies are sacred messengers. They are constantly speaking to us, communicating their wisdom in a language of sensation, symptom, and symbol. And when it comes to the liver and gallbladder, the message is often about anger. The liver, our largest internal organ, is a metabolic powerhouse, performing over 500 functions. It is our master alchemist, our great processor, responsible for filtering toxins, aiding digestion, and so much more. On an energetic level, it is also responsible for processing our experiences—especially the ones that feel unjust, unfair, or infuriating.

When we are unable to process anger, when we swallow it down, suppress it, or let it curdle into resentment, the liver bears the burden. It becomes congested, stagnant, overwhelmed. The gallbladder, its close companion, stores the bile that the liver produces. Think of bile as the liquid expression of our ability to discern, to break things down, to digest our lives. When we are marinating in bitterness, that bile can thicken, harden, and crystallize into stones. Gallstones of bitterness. Resentment made manifest.

I have seen this pattern so many times in my three decades of practice. The client with chronic liver disease who has a long history of self-destructive patterns, using alcohol to numb a lifetime of unprocessed rage. The woman with the “hot” temper and the inflamed gallbladder. The man who feels perpetually victimized by life, his liver sluggish and overburdened. The body doesn’t lie. It simply reflects back to us the state of our consciousness. It is the ultimate truth-teller, the keeper of the score. And when we learn to listen to its language, we unlock a profound capacity for healing. We begin to see that our symptoms are not random afflictions but intelligent communications, guiding us back to wholeness.

## The Poison of Unprocessed Anger

Anger is not the problem. Anger is a healthy, natural life force. It is the energy that says, “No. This is not okay.” It is the fire that fuels healthy boundaries and protects our sacred yes. The problem arises when we don’t know how to metabolize it. When we are taught, as so many of us are, that anger is “bad” or “unspiritual.” So we push it down, we deny it, we pretend it isn’t there. But it is. And it begins to poison us from the inside out.

This unprocessed anger can morph into depression, a heavy, stagnant energy that dampens our life force. Or it can become a free-floating anxiety, a sense of constant, low-grade threat. And very often, it leads to self-destructive behaviors. The overeating, the drinking, the compulsive shopping, the endless scrolling—all attempts to numb the discomfort of that simmering rage. We are trying to soothe the savage beast within, but we are using poisons to do it. It’s a tragic misunderstanding, a desperate attempt to find peace in a way that only creates more suffering.

Here’s a very good thing to know: every pattern has served you. These self-destructive behaviors are not a sign of weakness or failure. They are a sign of a system that is trying, in its own way, to cope. They are a misguided attempt to manage an overwhelming internal state. The key is to meet these patterns not with judgment, but with a gentle, compassionate curiosity. To ask, “What is the pain you are trying to numb, beloved one? What is the anger you are so afraid to feel?”

## The Anesthesia of Modern Life

It’s worth pausing here to look at the myriad ways we attempt to numb ourselves. It’s not always as dramatic as a bottle of whiskey. Sometimes, it’s a pint of ice cream. Sometimes it’s the endless scroll through social media, a digital anesthetic that keeps us from feeling the sharp edges of our own lives. It can be compulsive work, obsessive exercise, or a relentless pursuit of external validation. These are all, in their own way, attempts to manage the unmanageable, to quiet the storm within.

I once worked with a man, a high-powered executive, who came to me for chronic fatigue. He was successful, respected, and deeply, profoundly tired. He ate a pristine diet, exercised daily, and did everything “right.” But as we talked, a different picture emerged. A picture of a man driven by a relentless, unspoken anger at a father who had never seen or valued him. He had channeled all of that fiery energy into his career, building an empire on a foundation of rage. His success was a monument to his unprocessed pain. And his body, in its infinite wisdom, was finally saying, “Enough.” The fatigue was not a weakness; it was a mercy. It was the body’s way of forcing him to stop, to rest, to finally turn and face the ghosts of his past.

This is the compassionate lens through which we must view our own patterns. Not as character flaws, but as survival strategies. The nervous system, when faced with overwhelming emotional intensity, will do whatever it takes to protect itself. It will numb, it will dissociate, it will create distractions. It is a brilliant, adaptive mechanism. But it is not a long-term solution. The energy of the unprocessed emotion remains trapped in the body, wreaking havoc on our tissues, our organs, our very life force. The only way out is through.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Path of Inquiry

So what do we do? How do we begin to unwind these ancient patterns and create new neural pathways of peace and self-compassion? We don’t do it by forcing forgiveness. We don’t do it by pretending we’re not angry. We do it by turning towards the anger, gently, slowly, and with great kindness. We do it through the path of inquiry.

Find a quiet moment to sit with yourself. Place a hand on your belly, over your liver and gallbladder. Take a few deep, slow breaths. And then, begin to ask.

> What am I bitter about?
>
> Who have I not forgiven?
>
> What injustice am I still holding onto?

Don’t search for the answers with your mind. Just ask the questions, and then listen. Listen with your whole body. You might feel a clenching in your jaw. A heat in your chest. A knot in your stomach. These are the whispers of your body’s wisdom. This is the anger, the resentment, the bitterness, speaking to you directly.

Your only job is to listen. To be present with the sensations, without judgment, without needing to fix or change anything. Can you just be with the heat? Can you just be with the clenching? Can you breathe into it, with a sense of gentle curiosity?

This is the beginning of transformation. Not by fighting the darkness, but by meeting it with the light of your own awareness. This is the practice of somatic mindfulness, of bringing a curious and compassionate attention to the felt sense of the body. It is a way of creating new neural pathways, of rewiring the brain’s response to old triggers. As you continue this practice, you may find that the anger begins to soften. The hardness begins to melt. You may have moments of insight, of understanding, of compassion for yourself and for the one who hurt you. This is not a linear process. It is a spiral, a dance. But with each step, you are rewriting the story. You are teaching your body, on a cellular level, that it is safe to let go. You are dissolving the gallstones of bitterness with the warmth of your own loving presence. You are, in essence, becoming your own healer.

This is the alchemy of the heart. The power to metabolize even the most painful experiences and transform them into wisdom, compassion, and a deeper connection to your own sacred self. It is the journey from resentment to release, from bitterness to blessing. It is the profound and holy work of being human. It is a testament to the resilience of the human spirit, and to the boundless capacity of the body to heal, when we finally learn to listen to its wisdom and honor its sacred messages.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Shame, Sexuality, and the Silencing of Creative Power
teachings.title: Shame, Sexuality, and the Silencing of Creative Power
teachings.summary: Susan explores how cultural messages about sexuality and the reproductive body can become encoded as shame, constricting both physical wellbeing and creative expression. She invites a somatic inquiry — gentle listening to the lower belly — as an entry point for reclaiming creative power and reweaving inherited narratives with compassion. The piece connects intergenerational conditioning, embodied symptoms, and the possibility of gradual, steady healing through presence.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman I worked with years ago—let’s call her Sylvia—came to me with a deep, unshakeable sense of creative blockage. She was a painter, a brilliant one, but her canvases had been sitting empty for months. As we talked, a story from her childhood surfaced. She was about seven, drawing with a set of new crayons, utterly absorbed in creating a vibrant, swirling world on paper. Her grandmother, a stern and devout woman, walked in. Seeing the drawing—a raw, uninhibited explosion of color and form—she snatched it away. “Nice girls don’t make such a mess,” she’d said, her voice tight with a disapproval that Sylvia felt in her bones.

It’s a seemingly small moment. A minor childhood wound. But as Sylvia spoke, the shame of it was still alive in her, a cold knot in her belly. That single sentence had fused three distinct concepts in her developing mind: her creative impulse, the act of making a “mess,” and the core idea of being a “nice girl.” To be good, she learned, was to be clean, contained, and certainly not to let her wild, colorful insides spill out onto the page. Her creative power had been sent into exile.

It’s a tricky business, being human. And it is an especially tricky business to be a human in a body that holds the sacred portal of creation.

For centuries, the reproductive center—the womb, the ovaries, the entire pelvic bowl—has been a place of profound contradiction. It has been revered as the source of all life, the ultimate symbol of feminine power. And it has been reviled, feared, and controlled. This is the great paradox we have inherited. Our culture has, for generations, whispered a dangerous and confusing story about sexuality and creation. It has taught us that this part of our body is simultaneously a source of life and a source of sin. A gateway to the divine, and a gateway to shame.

These are not just abstract historical ideas. These are messages that have been encoded into our collective consciousness, passed down through our grandmothers and their grandmothers before them. They form the very bedrock of our neural pathways, shaping our unconscious beliefs about our bodies, our pleasure, and our power long before we have the language to question them.

## The Echoes in the Tissues

The body is a sacred messenger, and it never lies. When we carry deep wounds around our sexuality, our creativity, and our worth, the body will find a way to speak of them. In my three decades of healing work, I have sat with countless individuals whose reproductive issues were the physical manifestation of these ancient, inherited conflicts.

Endometriosis, fibroids, painful cycles, infertility… these conditions are not punishments. They are not failures. They are communications. They are the body’s desperate attempt to get our attention, to show us where the energy is stuck. The body is simply reflecting a story that has been playing out for generations—a story that often involves the silencing of creative power and the demonization of sexual energy.

Think of the language we use. We speak of a “barren” womb. A “hysterical” woman—a word that comes from *hystera*, the Greek word for uterus. These are not neutral terms. They are laden with judgment, with the subtle but pervasive cultural belief that a woman’s worth is tied to her reproductive capacity, and that her emotions are untrustworthy and chaotic, originating from that same mysterious, powerful place.

When we experience a reproductive challenge, it can feel like a deeply personal failing. But what if it isn’t personal at all? What if you are simply the one in your lineage who is finally feeling the full weight of this collective wound? What if your body, in its infinite wisdom, is inviting you to be the one who finally turns to face it, with compassion and curiosity?

This is the inquiry. It is not about blaming our ancestors or our culture. It is about seeing the pattern with clear eyes. It is about gently asking: Where did I learn that my creative fire was dangerous? Where did I learn that my sexuality was something to be controlled, hidden, or ashamed of? Who taught me that my body was not a safe and sacred home?

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming the Sacred Portal

For so many, the journey of healing this wound begins with a simple, radical act: listening. It begins with placing a hand on your lower belly and breathing into that space. Not to fix it, not to change it, but simply to be with it. To offer it your presence.

What do you feel there? Is there warmth? Coldness? A sense of emptiness or a feeling of fullness? Is there a knot of tension, or a gentle hum of energy? There is no right or wrong answer. The point is simply to make contact. To let this part of your body know that you are here. You are listening.

This is how we begin to rewire those ancient neural pathways of shame and fear. We create a new experience in the present moment—an experience of safety, acceptance, and loving attention. We introduce a new frequency. The frequency of compassion.

From this place of gentle presence, we can begin to untangle the threads. We can see the connection between the shame we feel about our bodies and the fear we have of our own creative power. We can recognize that the impulse to create—whether it’s a child, a work of art, a business, or a garden—comes from the very same energetic center as our sexual life force. They are not separate. To shut down one is to diminish the other.

What would it be like to reclaim this entire territory as sacred? To honor your sexuality as a divine gift, a source of pleasure, connection, and vitality that is your birthright? What would it be like to trust your innate capacity to generate, to bring forth new life and new ideas into the world, without apology or permission?

This is not about becoming a “goddess” or forcing some kind of performative self-love. It is a much quieter, more profound transformation. It is the simple, steady act of returning home to yourself. It is the realization that you are, and have always been, a creator. Your body is a vessel for this incredible life force, this creative fire. It was never shameful. It was never a mess. It was, and is, a miracle.

## The Creative Womb

It is essential to understand that this sacred center is not solely for the creation of children. It is the energetic furnace for *all* creation. The same life force, the same potent energy that can grow a human being, is the energy you draw upon to write a poem, to solve a complex problem at work, to launch a community project, or to birth a new version of yourself. When we talk about the womb, we are talking about a creative engine.

Think of the artist Sylvia. The shame that landed in her seven-year-old body didn’t just block her ability to draw; it severed her connection to her innate creative wellspring. The message she received was that her raw, instinctual, generative power was “too much.” And so, the energy that was meant to flow outwards onto the canvas turned inward, becoming a source of stagnation and self-doubt. Her creative power, silenced, became a source of pain.

This is a pattern I see over and over. The woman who longs to start her own business but is plagued by mysterious pelvic pain. The writer who feels a deep calling to share her story but struggles with chronic infections. The body is reflecting the core conflict: a deep, soul-level desire to create, warring with a lifetime of conditioning that says it is not safe, not right, or not possible. Healing the reproductive system is therefore intrinsically linked to unlocking your creative potential. As you bring loving awareness back to this part of your body, you are not just healing a physical symptom; you are tending to the very soil from which your life’s work, your joy, and your most authentic expressions are meant to bloom.

This is the work of a lifetime. It is slow, patient, and deeply personal. There is no destination, only a continual unfolding. A gradual remembering of the truth that has been held in your cells all along: that you are whole, you are holy, and you are free. It is the journey of healing not just for ourselves, but for the generations that came before us and the ones that will follow. Every time you choose to honor your body’s wisdom, every time you allow your creative energy to flow without judgment, you are sending a ripple of healing out into the world.

teachings.sourceTitle: Ulcers, Acid, and the Corrosion of Bitterness
teachings.title: Ulcers, Acid, and the Corrosion of Bitterness
teachings.summary: Susan reads stomach pain—ulcers and acid reflux—as the body’s language for carried bitterness and unprocessed grievance, showing how emotional patterns can shape physiology. She connects this to the gut–brain axis and neural habit, then offers a gentle somatic practice (hand on belly, compassionate breath, inquiry) to begin releasing corrosive energy and reclaiming personal power. The emphasis is on presence and paced transformation rather than forcing outcomes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The old farmhouse kitchen smelled of yeast and damp earth, a scent that usually meant comfort. But that day, a knot was tightening in my belly, a physical clenching that had nothing to do with hunger. My aunt, a woman whose hands were perpetually dusted with flour, was recounting a story from decades past—a story of betrayal, a friendship fractured over a misunderstanding that had been left to fester. As she spoke, her voice thin and tight, I watched her unconsciously press a hand to her stomach, right below her ribs. “It just burns me up, even now,” she whispered. And in that moment, I saw it. The story wasn’t just a memory; it was a meal she’d been unable to digest for thirty years, a corrosive acid of bitterness she kept swallowing down, only to have it rise up again and again.

This is the language of the body, beloved. It doesn’t speak in hypotheticals; it speaks in the raw, physical truth of sensation. Your stomach, in its profound wisdom, is not just a digestive organ. It is a vessel for experience. It is the seat of your personal power, the alchemical cauldron where you transmute the world you take in—the food, the emotions, the energies, the stories. And when something is indigestible, when an experience is too sharp, too painful, too steeped in injustice to be processed, the stomach will tell you. It will churn. It will burn. It will ache. It is saying, with no uncertainty, *this is making me sick.*

Think of the searing pain of an ulcer. It’s a wound, an erosion of the protective lining of your being. On a physical level, we might blame bacteria or medication, but let’s go deeper, into the energetic truth of the matter. What is the emotional equivalent of a corrosive substance that eats away at you from the inside? It is bitterness. It is resentment. It is the replaying of old wounds, the constant chewing on a grievance that should have been released long ago. It’s the story of “what they did to me,” a narrative that keeps you tethered to a past that is poisoning your present. Each time you run that story, you are swallowing the same poison. The body, in its unwavering honesty, simply reflects this inner state, creating a physical wound to mirror the spiritual one.

And what of acid reflux? That fiery sensation in the chest, the sour taste in the back of the throat. This is the body’s desperate attempt to reject what it has been forced to swallow. It is the physical manifestation of words you couldn’t speak, of anger you weren’t “allowed” to feel, of a boundary that was crossed. It’s the energy of “I can’t stomach this anymore” made literal. The pressure builds, the valve that is meant to keep things down gives way, and the undigested pain comes surging back up, demanding to be acknowledged. It’s not a malfunction; it’s a message. It’s the soul’s cry, echoing through the tissues of your esophagus: *Please, listen. This doesn’t belong here.*

From a neuroscience perspective, we see this connection in the intricate dance of the gut-brain axis. When you perceive a threat—and replaying a bitter memory is perceived by the nervous system as a very real threat—your brain floods your system with stress hormones like cortisol. This isn’t just a mental event. It has a direct, physical impact, altering your gut microbiome, increasing inflammation, and ramping up acid production. You are creating the very physiological conditions for corrosion. Your neural pathways, grooved by the habit of resentment, become a superhighway for signals of distress, telling your stomach to stay in a state of high alert, perpetually prepared for an attack that is coming from within.

Quantum physics invites us to see this from the perspective of frequency. Every emotion carries a specific energetic signature. Joy, compassion, and peace vibrate at high, harmonious frequencies that promote coherence and ease in the body. Bitterness, resentment, and anger vibrate at low, dissonant frequencies. When you hold onto these emotions, you are holding your entire being in a state of energetic dissonance. This isn’t just a metaphor. This low-frequency energy disrupts the cellular communication in your body, creating static in the system. The cells of your stomach lining, bathed in this frequency of corrosion, begin to break down. They are responding to the environment you have created with your consciousness.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

So what do we do? How do we begin to heal these deep, burning wounds? The answer is not to fight, to force, or to “get over it.” That is the energy of struggle, the very thing that created the tension in the first place. The path to healing is through compassion. It is through turning towards the pain with a gentle, loving awareness. It begins with placing a hand on your own belly, just as my aunt did, but this time, with a different intention. Not to suppress the burn, but to feel it. To acknowledge it. To offer it your presence.

Perhaps you might ask the sensation, “What is it you are holding for me? What is the story you need me to hear?” You are not asking for an intellectual answer. You are creating a space for the stored energy to be felt, without judgment. What would it be like to simply allow the heat, the ache, the churning, to be there? To breathe into it, not to push it away, but to infuse it with the spaciousness of your awareness. This is how the energy begins to move. It’s not about forgiving the other person for their sake; it’s about liberating yourself from the prison of the past.

Ancient wisdom traditions have always understood this. In the yogic system, the stomach is the home of the Manipura chakra, the solar plexus, which governs our sense of self, our will, our power. When we give our power away to a past grievance, this energy center becomes blocked, stagnant. The fire of digestion becomes a fire of destruction. Practices like gentle breathwork—imagining you can breathe all the way down into your belly, filling it with soft, healing light—can begin to soothe this inner fire and restore your sense of sovereignty. You are no longer a victim of your past; you are the compassionate witness of your own healing journey.

Every pattern has served you. The bitterness was a shield, a way your system tried to protect you from being hurt again. The acid was a warrior, trying to fight a battle you couldn’t voice. Thank these parts of you. They have worked so hard. And now, perhaps, you can let them know that you are safe. That you are here. That you are ready to digest this experience in a new way—not as poison, but as a story that is finally ready to be released. What would it be like to let it go, to feel the spaciousness that comes when you are no longer corroding from within? To allow the fire in your belly to become the fire of transformation, of warmth, of life itself.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Let’s make this even more tangible, beloved. Let’s create a small, sacred practice you can turn to whenever you feel that familiar burn of resentment or the churn of an indigestible emotion. Find a quiet moment, perhaps in the morning before the day begins or in the evening as you unwind.

**A Practice for Releasing Corrosive Energies:**

1.  **Settle into Your Body:** Sit or lie down comfortably. Close your eyes and take three deep, cleansing breaths. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing the frantic energy of the day, letting your shoulders drop, your jaw soften, your body grow heavy and supported by the earth beneath you.

2.  **Place Your Hands on Your Stomach:** Bring a gentle, warm awareness to your solar plexus, the area of your stomach. Your hands are vessels of healing, of love. Let that warmth penetrate your skin, a message of pure presence to this part of your body that has been holding so much.

3.  **Invite the Sensation to Speak:** Without needing to change or fix anything, simply notice the sensations in your stomach. Is it hot? Tight? Aching? Empty? Just observe. Now, you might silently ask, *“What is the story you are holding?”* or *“What is the bitterness made of?”* Don’t search for an answer with your mind. Be patient. An image might arise, a memory, a single word, a face. It might be something you haven’t thought of in years. It might be the very thing you were ruminating on this morning. Whatever comes, simply allow it to be seen.

4.  **The Alchemy of Breath:** Now, begin to breathe with a specific intention. As you inhale, imagine you are drawing in a beautiful, liquid-gold light of pure compassion. Imagine this light flowing all the way down into your stomach, surrounding the knot of pain, bathing the ulcerated wound, filling the entire space with its gentle, healing frequency. As you exhale, imagine a soft, grey smoke leaving your body—the smoke of the old story, the bitterness, the resentment. You don’t have to force it out; you are simply making space for it to leave. Inhale golden light; exhale grey smoke. Continue this for several minutes. You are not fighting the darkness; you are simply turning on the light.

5.  **A New Narrative:** Once you feel a shift, a sense of softening or release, offer a new message to your body. You might say, silently or aloud, *“I am willing to release this story. I am willing to digest this experience. I reclaim my power from this past moment. I choose peace in my body now.”* Feel the resonance of these words in your cells. Feel them as a new frequency, a new possibility.

This practice is not a one-time fix. It is a returning, a remembering, a way of tending to your inner landscape with the same care you would give to a precious garden. Each time you engage in this practice, you are carving new neural pathways in your brain. You are teaching your nervous system that it is safe to let go. You are reminding your cells that they can attune to the frequency of healing, not the frequency of corrosion.

It’s also powerful to bring this awareness into your daily life. When you feel the acid rise as you sit in traffic, or the clenching in your gut when a particular person’s name is mentioned, can you, just for a moment, place a hand on your belly and take one conscious, compassionate breath? Can you whisper to yourself, *“I am here with you. Let’s release this.”* This is how you transform a lifetime of unconscious reaction into a sacred practice of conscious healing. You are not just managing a symptom; you are healing the wound at its source. You are rewriting the story, not just in your mind, but in the very tissues of your body.

teachings.sourceTitle: When Holding On Hurts: The Emotional Patterns Behind Bladder Issues
teachings.title: When Holding On Hurts: The Emotional Patterns Behind Bladder Issues
teachings.summary: Susan connects chronic bladder symptoms with longstanding patterns of holding, control, and suppressed emotion, reframing the bladder as a messenger for what we haven’t allowed ourselves to release. She describes nervous-system mechanisms that embed suppression in the body, offers compassionate reframe and small behavioral experiments, and provides a brief guided awareness practice to begin softening habitual holding.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I want to begin by saying something that might surprise you: you already know the answer.

We learn so early to hold it all in. To be the good girl, the easy-going friend, the capable colleague. We learn to clench our jaws, swallow our words, and keep the peace. We become exquisite artists of control, believing on some deep, often unconscious level, that if we can just manage everything—our feelings, our words, the people around us—we will finally be safe, be loved, be rewarded.

And our bodies? Our beautiful, loyal bodies keep the score.

I’ve come to see the body as a sacred messenger, a living library of our experiences, beliefs, and deepest truths. And in this library, the bladder holds a particularly poignant story. It is the physical reservoir for the emotions we’ve deemed too messy, too inconvenient, or too dangerous to release. It’s where we store the energy of a lifetime of “holding it together.”

Physiologically, the bladder has a dual function: to hold and to release. It is a vessel of completion. Emotionally and energetically, it mirrors this exact function. It shows us our relationship with control and surrender. When this relationship is out of balance, when we are chronically holding on, the bladder will often be the first to send up a flare. It might whisper at first—a little urgency, a feeling of not-quite-empty. But if we don’t listen, it will begin to speak louder, sometimes even scream, through the language of pain, pressure, and chronic infection.

## The Good Girl's Reward

I remember a client, a lovely woman in her late forties, who came to me with a history of debilitating, recurrent bladder infections. She was, by all accounts, a pillar of her community. She ran a successful business, cared for her aging parents, and raised two impeccable children. She did everything *right*. And she was in constant, burning pain.

As we sat together, a story began to unfold. It was a story of a lifetime of being ‘good.’ Of anticipating everyone’s needs, of smoothing over conflict before it could erupt, of never, ever letting her own disappointment show. She had held in her frustration when her husband forgot their anniversary, held in her exhaustion when her parents demanded more, held in her own creative longings to make space for her children’s. She had been promised, in the silent contract so many of us make with life, that if she was good, she would be rewarded with love, ease, and happiness. But the reward never came. Instead, she got cystitis—a literal inflammation, a burning resentment that had nowhere else to go.

Her bladder, this soft, compliant organ, had become the container for all the unexpressed anger and grief. The burning she felt was the heat of her own life force, her own truth, demanding to be felt. It was the body’s way of saying, *“This is not okay. I cannot hold this anymore.”*

This isn't just a poetic idea; it's rooted in the way our nervous systems are designed. When we consistently suppress a natural impulse—the impulse to cry, to say no, to rest, to create—we are sending a powerful signal to our brain. We are, in essence, carving a neural pathway that says, “It is not safe to release. It is better to hold on.” Over time, this pathway becomes a superhighway. The body learns that control equals safety, and it begins to apply this logic everywhere, even to the natural, rhythmic functions of our own physiology. The simple, beautiful act of letting go becomes freighted with fear and shame.

## The Neuroscience of Suppression

Let’s look a little deeper at what’s happening in the brain. When you have an emotional response, your limbic system, the ancient, instinctual part of your brain, fires up. It’s preparing you for action—to fight, to flee, to connect. But then, your prefrontal cortex, the more modern, “thinking” part of your brain, steps in. It’s the part that holds the social rules, the family conditioning, the belief that “good people don’t get angry.” It acts like a dam, holding back the flood of emotional energy. This is an incredibly energy-intensive process. It requires a huge amount of internal resources to maintain that dam, day in and day out.

That suppressed energy doesn’t just vanish. It has to go somewhere. Energy is just that—energy. It can’t be destroyed; it can only be transformed. And so, it gets pushed down, deep into the tissues of the body. For many, especially women conditioned to be accommodating and pleasant, the pelvic bowl becomes a primary storage facility. The bladder, with its function of holding and releasing, becomes a natural energetic match for this pattern. The resentment, the unspoken “no,” the tears that were never shed—they crystallize, energetically, in this very soft and vulnerable part of our bodies. The result can be a feeling of constant pressure, of urgency, or the fiery pain of inflammation. It’s the body, in its infinite wisdom, trying to get our attention.

I worked with another client, a man this time, a successful lawyer who suffered from an overactive bladder. He was constantly scanning for the nearest restroom, his life circumscribed by a tight radius of anxiety. His story was different on the surface, but the underlying pattern was the same. He had grown up with a highly critical father and learned that the only way to be safe was to be perfect, to control every variable, to never give anyone a reason to find fault. He had built a life that looked successful from the outside, but inside, he was in a constant state of high alert. His bladder was simply mirroring his mental state: the constant, urgent need to control, and the terror of what might happen if he let go.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Guided Practice: Releasing the Flow

This is not about forcing or fixing. It is a gentle invitation to begin a new conversation with your body. Find a quiet moment where you won’t be disturbed. You can lie down or sit comfortably.

>1.  **Arrive in Your Body:** Close your eyes and take three soft, easy breaths. Don’t try to change your breath, just notice it. Feel the points of contact between your body and the surface beneath you. Let yourself be held.
>2.  **Connect with Your Bladder:** Bring your awareness to your lower belly, the home of your bladder. You might even place a warm hand there. Simply notice this space. Is there warmth? Coolness? Tension? Numbness? There is no right or wrong way to feel. Just be present with what is.
>3.  **Offer a Word of Kindness:** Silently, in your own heart, offer a word of kindness to this part of your body. It might be something like, “Thank you for working so hard for me.” Or, “I’m here with you now.” Or simply, “Peace.” Feel the resonance of this kindness in your body.
>4.  **Invite a Gentle Release:** As you continue to breathe, imagine with each exhale that you are creating a little more space in your pelvic bowl. You are not forcing anything out. You are simply inviting a gentle, energetic softening. Imagine a tightly clenched fist, and with each breath, one finger gently unfurls. Your exhale is the invitation to release what is ready to be released.
>5.  **Listen for Wisdom:** As you rest in this space of gentle awareness, you might ask your body, “What do you need me to know?” or “What is ready to be released?” Don’t search for an answer. Simply listen in the quiet. The answer may come as a word, an image, a feeling, or a memory. It may come later in your day. Trust the process.

Stay with this practice for 5-10 minutes. When you are ready, gently bring your awareness back to the room. Wiggle your fingers and toes. And as you move back into your day, carry this sense of gentle presence with you.

## The Courage to Flow

How do we begin to unwind a pattern that is so deeply embedded in our wiring, a pattern we may have inherited from generations of ancestors who also learned that their survival depended on staying small and quiet?

It begins with compassion. It begins with acknowledging the profound intelligence of the pattern. It served you. It kept you safe in a family or a culture where your full expression was not welcome. You learned to control your natural flow because you believed it would earn you love, and that is a profoundly intelligent, adaptive strategy.

But now… perhaps there is another way. What would it be like to allow for a different possibility? The possibility that your release is not shameful, but essential. That your needs are not an inconvenience, but a vital signal from your soul. That letting go is not a failure of control, but an act of profound trust.

We can start to create new neural pathways. Tiny ones, at first. We can practice releasing in small, safe ways. It might be as simple as allowing yourself a full, deep, audible sigh. Or taking five minutes to sit and do nothing when your inner taskmaster is screaming at you to be productive. It might be writing down the angry words you wish you could say, and then safely burning the paper, releasing the energy.

For the lawyer, the healing began when he started to consciously practice imperfection. He would deliberately leave a typo in an internal email. He would allow himself to be five minutes late for a non-essential meeting. These small acts of rebellion against his own inner tyrant began to create new neural pathways. They sent a new message to his nervous system: “You can let go a little, and you will still be safe.” Over time, his bladder began to relax. The urgency subsided. He found he could go for hours without thinking about a restroom.

This is the work of coming home to ourselves. It is the journey of reclaiming the parts of us we’ve suppressed and learning to trust the magnificent wisdom of our bodies. Your bladder isn’t the enemy. It is a sacred messenger, asking you to look at where you are holding on too tightly, where you are clinging to the hope of a reward that will never come from outside yourself. It is inviting you to find the courage to let go, to trust the flow, and to discover the incredible freedom that awaits on the other side of surrender.

It is inviting you to give yourself the love you were always waiting for.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Flowing with Life: Transcending Kidney Patterns](/blog/kidneys-flowing-with-life)
- [The Sacred Portal of Creation: Your Reproductive System Speaks](/blog/reproductive-sacred-portal)
- [From Hypervigilance to Peace: Transcending Nervous System Patterns](/blog/nervous-system-hypervigilance-peace)

**More on Bladder:**

- [The Flow of Completion: Transcending Bladder Patterns](/blog/bladder-flow-of-completion)
- [A Guided Practice for Bladder Healing and Release](/blog/bladder-guided-practice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.title: Developing a Conscious Loving Relationship with Yourself
teachings.summary: Susan offers a gentle, body-centered invitation to move from trying to fix ourselves into developing a conscious, loving relationship with all our parts. She links this shift to nervous-system regulation and neuroplasticity, describing how curiosity and compassionate presence change physiology and carve new neural pathways. Practical, accessible steps are offered—naming, curious inquiry, compassionate touch, and listening to bodily signals—as ongoing practices rather than one-time fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There's a word in Japanese — kintsukuroi — that means to repair with gold, making the broken thing more beautiful than before.

Isn’t it?

For years, a part of my body and I were at war. My shoulders, to be specific. They held a permanent, stony tension, a kind of braced-for-impact posture I carried into every room. I tried everything to fix them: massage, stretching, ergonomic chairs, sheer willpower. I’d command them to *relax*, my inner voice a frustrated drill sergeant. And for a moment, they might yield, only to creep back up towards my ears the moment my attention wavered. They were a problem to be solved, a flaw to be corrected. My relationship with them was one of exasperation and control.

It was only when I stopped trying to *fix* them and started to get curious that anything truly began to shift. What if this tension wasn’t a flaw, but a message? What if this part of me wasn’t disobedient, but devoted? Devoted to holding a story I hadn’t yet been able to hear. I began to wonder, with a softness that was entirely new to me: *Beloved shoulders, what is it you are carrying for me?*

This is the heart of what I’ve come to understand as true healing. It is not about eradicating the parts of ourselves we find inconvenient, messy, or broken. Healing is the courageous and tender act of developing a conscious, loving relationship with *all* of yourself. The stony shoulders, the anxious heart, the inner critic, the frightened child… all of it. It’s a radical shift from self-improvement to self-attunement.

## The Neuroscience of Internal Safety

This isn’t just a poetic idea; it’s rooted in the very architecture of our nervous systems. Our brains are, first and foremost, prediction and survival machines. When we treat a part of ourselves with judgment, frustration, or rejection, our brain interprets this as an internal threat. The inner critic’s voice, laced with cortisol-spiking urgency, sounds just like an external predator to our ancient neurology. This activates the sympathetic nervous system—the “fight, flight, or freeze” response. The body tenses, the breath shortens, inflammation rises. We are, quite literally, at war with ourselves, running on a constant, draining hum of high-beta brainwave activity.

Conversely, when we can turn towards these same parts with a gentle, curious attention—a practice central to modalities like Internal Family Systems (IFS)—we send a profoundly different signal. We are communicating safety. This is the language of the parasympathetic nervous system, the state of “rest, digest, and heal.” When we place a hand on our anxious chest and whisper, *I’m here with you*, we are not just offering a nice thought. We are changing our physiology. We are inviting our brainwaves to slow down into the coherent, healing rhythms of alpha and theta. We are bathing our cells in a different chemistry—one of connection, not conflict.

Through the stunning gift of neuroplasticity, this new response begins to carve new neural pathways. The well-worn groove of self-rejection, which may have been carved in early childhood, begins to soften. A new path, one of self-compassion and internal safety, becomes easier and easier to access. We are not just changing our minds; we are re-wiring our brains for love. We are becoming our own safe harbor.

## My Journey to a Truer Love

My own journey with this was not a straight line. It was a spiral, circling back again and again. For me, the deepest work was with a part of me that carried a profound sense of inadequacy, a feeling that I was somehow “too much” and “not enough” all at once. It was a feeling that lived deep in my gut, a familiar clenching I had known since childhood.

For decades, I tried to override it. I tried to prove it wrong through accomplishment and perfectionism. I tried to meditate it away. But it was a loyal companion, always ready to whisper its familiar, painful story. It was exhausting.

The shift came when I learned to see it not as *me*, but as a *part* of me. A young part, who had learned this feeling as a survival strategy in a world that felt overwhelming. Following the wisdom of IFS, I began to approach this part not with an agenda to banish it, but with a genuine desire to know it.

I would find a quiet moment, place my hands on my stomach, and breathe into the knot of sensation there. *Hello in there*, I’d say silently. *I know you’re scared. Thank you for trying so hard to keep me safe. But I’m the adult now. I can handle this. You can rest.*

At first, it felt absurd. The critic part would chime in, *“What are you doing? This is ridiculous.”* But I persisted, gently asking the critic to step aside and give me a little space. And slowly, miraculously, the clenching began to soften. The story began to lose its power. By offering this wounded part of myself the consistent, loving presence of my own adult consciousness—what IFS calls the Self—it no longer needed to scream for my attention. It could finally begin to trust that I was here, that *we* were safe. This, I’ve learned, is the essence of self-love in action. It’s not a feeling you wait for; it’s a commitment you practice, breath by breath.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Tao of Self-Compassion

There is a deep wisdom in the Tao Te Ching that speaks to this process. It says, “The softest thing in the universe overcomes the hardest thing in the universe.” We are so often taught to meet our inner demons with force, to battle our flaws into submission. But this only creates more internal violence.

The Tao invites us into the way of water—yielding, soft, persistent. Water doesn’t fight the rock; it flows around it, gently wearing it away over time. This is the nature of self-compassion. It is the softest thing. It doesn’t argue with the inner critic or try to wrestle anxiety to the ground. It simply creates a container of loving presence around the hardness, the fear, the pain. It holds it all. And in that holding, the hardness begins to dissolve. The sharp edges of our pain, held in the soft embrace of our own awareness, begin to lose their power to wound us.

> When you are content to be simply yourself and don’t compare or compete, everybody will respect you.

This is the promise of a loving inner relationship. When we stop competing with ourselves, when we lay down our arms in the internal battlefield, a profound sense of peace becomes possible. We are no longer trying to be a better version of ourselves. We are simply, fully, and lovingly present with the self that is here, right now.

## The Body’s Unfailing Wisdom

Your body is the sacred ground where this relationship plays out. It does not know how to lie. It is the most exquisitely sensitive instrument, constantly reflecting the quality of your inner world. When you are engaged in self-rejection, your body responds. It might be the tension in your shoulders, carrying burdens that are not yours to carry. It might be the acid in your stomach, trying to digest an experience that feels indigestible. It might be the fear held in your kidneys, or the bitterness crystallized in your gallbladder. These are not punishments. They are communications. They are the body’s wisdom, calling you back home.

When you begin to cultivate a genuine, compassionate relationship with yourself, the body also responds. The breath deepens, spontaneously. The shoulders drop, an inch at a time. The digestive system, no longer needing to process a constant stream of internal threat, can do its work with ease. This isn’t about forcing your body to relax. It’s about creating the conditions of internal safety where relaxation is the natural result. It’s the difference between demanding a flower bloom and tending to the soil, water, and light that allow it to unfold in its own perfect time.

## Practical Steps for a More Loving Relationship

This is not a one-time fix, but a lifelong practice of turning towards yourself with love, again and again. Here are a few gentle ways to begin:

> 1. **Pause and Name.** When you feel a wave of anxiety, a surge of self-criticism, or a familiar physical pain, simply pause. Acknowledge it without judgment. “Ah, there is the inner critic.” Or, “I feel that familiar tightness in my chest.” Naming it creates a small, sacred space between you and the experience. It shifts you from being consumed by the feeling to being the compassionate witness of it.

> 2. **Get Curious, Not Furious.** Instead of the usual, “Why am I like this?” try a gentler question. You might ask this part of you: *What are you afraid would happen if you weren’t here? What is it you are trying to protect me from?* Listen for the answer not just in words, but in feelings, images, and sensations. You may be surprised by the wisdom in the answer. Often, the parts we judge most harshly are trying to protect us in outdated, but well-intentioned, ways.

> 3. **Offer a Gesture of Kindness.** Place a hand on the part of your body where you feel the sensation most strongly. You don’t need to say anything. The simple act of warm, physical touch is a powerful signal of presence and care to your nervous system. It says, *I am here with you. You are not alone in this.* Feel the warmth of your hand, the gentle pressure. Let it be an anchor in the present moment.

> 4. **Speak a Different Truth.** Offer a few words of compassion to the part of you that is struggling. It could be as simple as, *I know this is hard. We’ll get through this together.* Or, *Thank you for working so hard. I’m here to help now.* Find the words that feel true and gentle for you. Let the vibration of these words be a balm.

> 5. **Listen to the Body’s Whisper.** Before the messages become screams, practice tuning into the subtle language of your body. At different points in the day, close your eyes and do a gentle scan. Where is there ease? Where is there tension? Where is there warmth or coolness? No need to change anything. Simply listen. This practice of deep listening is itself an act of profound love.

This is the journey. Not to a perfected self, but to a whole self. A self where every part is welcome, every story is honored, and every symptom is seen as a sacred messenger, calling you deeper into the boundless ocean of your own love.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
