teachings.sourceTitle: Speaking Your Highest Truth: Transcending Vocal Patterns
teachings.title: Speaking Your Highest Truth: Transcending Vocal Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan uses a personal memory of being silenced in a boardroom to illuminate how patterns of silence become embodied in the throat, shaping breath, vocal tone, and nervous-system responses. She brings together neuroscience, yogic throat-chakra imagery, and gentle practices—listening, breath, humming, and small acts of truthful speech—to invite a gradual repatterning toward safer, heart-centered expression.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The teacup rattled in its saucer, a tiny earthquake betraying the tremor in my hand. I was twenty-three, sitting in a sterile boardroom that smelled of stale coffee and quiet desperation. All around the polished mahogany table, men in identical grey suits nodded along to a presentation I knew was based on flawed data. A project I had poured months of my life into was about to be railroaded by a narrative that was convenient, but untrue.

My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic drumbeat against the silent scream lodged in my throat. *Speak up*, a small, fierce voice inside me urged. *This is wrong.* But the air was thick with unspoken rules, with the heavy expectation of deference. I was the youngest person in the room, the only woman, and a junior analyst. My vocal cords felt encased in ice. The words, my truth, were frozen solid somewhere between my heart and my mouth. I remember the physical sensation of it—a tightening in my chest, a lump of concrete in my larynx. I said nothing. I watched the decision be made, a silent accomplice to a lie.

That memory, for a long time, was a source of deep shame. It was a potent symbol of every time I had swallowed my words, every time I had allowed the fear of judgment or rejection to muzzle my own knowing. Perhaps you have a memory like that too? A moment where your truth felt too dangerous, too disruptive, to set free? A family dinner, a conversation with a partner, a meeting at work… a moment where silence felt like the only safe choice.

Every pattern, beloved, has served you. That silence, that hesitation, was a form of protection. For many of us, especially as sensitive, intuitive beings, we learned early on that speaking our full, unfiltered truth could lead to disharmony. It could lead to being misunderstood, ridiculed, or even punished. Our nervous systems, in their infinite wisdom, created a strategy: stay quiet, stay safe. The vocal cords, those delicate, powerful folds of tissue, learn to constrict not just from physical strain, but from the energetic weight of unspoken words and unexpressed emotions.

This isn’t just a poetic idea—it’s woven into our very biology. Neuroscience shows us how traumatic experiences, especially those that involve feeling unheard or silenced, create deep imprints in our neural pathways. The amygdala, our brain’s vigilant alarm system, flags the act of speaking up as a threat. In response, the body floods with cortisol, the larynx tightens, the breath becomes shallow. We are, in a very real sense, physically preparing for a battle that is long over. The body remembers the danger, even when the conscious mind has moved on. The echo of “don’t you dare” from a parent, the sting of a teacher’s criticism, the cold shoulder from a friend after a disagreement—it all lives in the cellular memory of our throats.

But here’s the beautiful truth that lies beneath that protective layer: your voice is so much more than a mechanism for communication. It is a carrier of frequency. It is the bridge between your inner world and the outer world. Ancient wisdom traditions have always understood this. In yogic philosophy, the fifth chakra, *Vishuddha*, located at the throat, is the center of truth, purification, and authentic expression. When this energy center is blocked, we experience frustration, a feeling of being stuck, and a disconnect from our own inner authority. When it is open and flowing, our creativity blossoms, our communication is clear and compassionate, and we speak from a place of profound alignment.

What would it be like to speak not just from the mind, with its carefully curated scripts and calculated risks, but from the unified field of your head *and* your heart? This is the essence of transcendence. It’s not about forcing yourself to speak when it feels terrifying. It’s not about pushing against the fear. It’s about gently, compassionately, creating a new inner environment. It’s about cultivating a sense of profound safety within your own being, so that the truth that resides in your heart feels not just safe, but *welcome* to emerge.

Speaking from this unified field is a sensory experience. It feels like warmth spreading from your chest up into your throat. The words have a different resonance, a different timbre. They land differently, both for you and for the listener. They are not sharp-edged weapons of righteousness, but resonant frequencies of love, harmony, and a deep, unwavering knowing. This is the voice that can say, “No, that doesn’t feel right to me,” with kindness and without apology. This is the voice that can say, “I love you,” with the full force of its meaning. This is the voice that can share a vulnerable story, not for validation, but as a gift of connection.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

So how do we begin to cultivate this unified field? How do we gently coax our frozen truths into the warmth of expression? It begins not with a grand declaration, but with a subtle inner shift. It begins with listening. Not to the cacophony of inner critics or the echoes of past wounds, but to the quiet, steady hum of your own soul’s frequency beneath it all. Can you feel it now? A gentle vibration in the center of your chest, a warmth that has nothing to prove.

This is where the wisdom of quantum physics offers us such a graceful perspective. The quantum field is a field of infinite possibility, a sea of pure potential. Our focused awareness is what collapses these possibilities into our experienced reality. When our awareness is habitually focused on the danger of speaking, on the potential for rejection, we are literally instructing the field to manifest experiences that validate this fear. Our vocal cords constrict, our words falter, and the world reflects our belief that it is not safe to be fully seen and heard.

But what if we were to consciously place our awareness elsewhere? What if, for just a few moments each day, you were to place your hand on your throat, close your eyes, and simply… listen? Not for words, but for sensation. Is there tightness? Coolness? A sense of blockage? Don’t try to change it. Simply bring the gentle, non-judgmental light of your awareness to it. Breathe into that space. Imagine your breath is a soft, luminous turquoise light, the color of the throat chakra, bathing the entire area in healing and acceptance. This simple act of presence begins to repattern the energy. You are sending a new signal to your nervous system: *I am here. I am listening. You are safe with me.*

From this place of inner safety, we can begin to play with sound. Humming is one of the most powerful and gentle ways to awaken the vocal cords. Feel the vibration in your lips, your throat, your chest. It’s a form of internal massage, breaking up the energetic stagnation of silence. Allow yourself to sigh, audibly and with release. These are not just sounds; they are frequencies. They are the beginning of reclaiming your voice, not for performance, but for your own liberation. You are reminding your body that it is safe to make noise, safe to take up sonic space.

This is the beautiful dance of neuroplasticity. We are not doomed to repeat the same patterns forever. By introducing new, gentle experiences, we are carving new neural pathways. The old, well-worn groove of “silence = safety” can be lovingly replaced with a new one: “authentic expression = connection and freedom.” It starts small. Perhaps it’s saying, “Actually, I’d prefer the window seat,” when you would normally just acquiesce. Perhaps it’s sharing a heartfelt compliment you might have otherwise kept to yourself. Each tiny act of truth-telling is a victory, a reinforcement of this new pathway. Think of it as sacred resistance against the tyranny of the old guard within. It’s choosing the slightly more expansive restaurant for dinner instead of the ‘usual’ one everyone else expects. It’s admitting, “I don’t know the answer to that,” instead of fumbling for a facade of competence. It’s sharing a piece of your art, a line of poetry, or an idea that feels vulnerable and alive. These small, consistent acts of courage are the threads from which a new reality is woven, a reality where your voice is not a liability, but a cherished and essential part of your wholeness.

Years after that boardroom experience, I found myself in another meeting. This time, I was a consultant, hired for my expertise. A senior executive, a man with a booming voice and an intimidating presence, dismissed a key finding in my report. The old pattern flared instantly—the heat in my face, the familiar clamp in my throat. The room fell silent. In that pause, which felt like an eternity, I had a choice. I could retreat into the familiar safety of silence, or I could honor the truth that was pulsing in my heart.

I took a slow breath. I placed my hand on my lap, a quiet anchor to my own body. And I spoke. My voice didn’t boom. It wasn’t aggressive. It was quiet, but it was clear. “I hear your concern,” I said, meeting his gaze. “And I see the data differently. From my perspective, this particular metric is the most crucial indicator of the problem we’re trying to solve. Let me walk you through my reasoning one more time.” I spoke from my knowing, from the unified field. I wasn’t trying to win or be right; I was simply offering my truth as a contribution. The energy in the room shifted. The executive leaned forward, his expression softening from dismissive to curious. He listened. In that moment, the old wound didn’t just heal; it transformed into a source of power.

This is the invitation for you, beloved. To see your voice not as a source of potential conflict, but as your unique contribution to the symphony of life. Your truth, spoken with love, is a frequency that the world desperately needs. It has the power to heal, to connect, to inspire. When you allow your highest truth to flow, you give others permission to do the same. You become a beacon, a resonant field of authenticity that creates ripples you may never even see.

This is a journey, not a destination. There will be days when the old patterns feel strong, when silence feels like the only option. On those days, be extra gentle with yourself. Place a hand on your heart, another on your throat, and whisper, “I am with you.” Remember that every pattern has served you, and you can now choose a new way. You can choose to allow the frequencies of goodness, harmony, and love to flow through you, carried on the sacred vessel of your own voice.


---

teachings.sourceTitle: Transcending the Breast: Becoming the Source That Never Runs Dry
teachings.title: Transcending the Breast: Becoming the Source That Never Runs Dry
teachings.summary: Susan explores how cultural expectations to give and mother others can create chronic depletion that shows up in the body—often in the breasts—as pain, density, or grief. She frames these signals as sacred messengers urging self-care, and offers a short, heart-centered practice alongside an invitation to develop boundaries and daily self-mothering. The piece emphasizes neuroplasticity and lineage healing: habits can change, and tending your own wellspring benefits both you and future generations.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was reading the Tao te Ching the other evening — as I often do when the world feels particularly noisy.

Especially for women. We are taught, almost from birth, that our value lies in our capacity to nurture, to give, to be an endless wellspring for others. And our breasts, more than any other part of our bodies, become the symbol of this sacred, and often depleting, offering.

I remember a client, years ago, a woman with a heart so big you could feel its warmth from across the room. She came to me with a deep, aching pain in her left breast. It had been there for months, a persistent, nagging throb that doctors couldn’t explain. She was a mother of three, a devoted wife, the go-to person for everyone in her life. She poured and she poured, and she never, ever, asked for anything in return. Her well was running dry. And her body, in its profound wisdom, was sending up a flare. The pain wasn’t an enemy; it was a sacred messenger, a desperate plea for her own attention, her own care.

Her story is not unique. In my thirty years of practice, I have sat with so many women carrying this same pattern of depletion, this silent grief held in the soft tissue of their chests. We see it manifest as pain, as cysts, as a deep-seated fear of illness. These are not just physical symptoms; they are messages from a body that is crying out to be mothered, to be held, to be replenished.

Our bodies are sacred messengers, and the breasts speak a language of profound emotional and spiritual truth. They are the seat of the mother archetype, the physical embodiment of our ability to nourish. But here is a very good thing to know: you cannot give what you do not allow yourself to receive. When we over-invest in mothering others without first mothering ourselves, we create an internal drought. The river of our own life force begins to shrink, and the body, in its infinite wisdom, sends a signal. A pain. A lump. A fear. It’s a call to return home to yourself. It is an invitation to finally, deeply, truly mother yourself.

## The Depletion Pattern: Recognizing the Signs

How do you know if you’re caught in a depletion pattern? It often begins subtly. A feeling of being constantly tired, even after a full night’s sleep. A sense of resentment that simmers just below the surface. A feeling of being unseen, unappreciated. You might find yourself saying “yes” when you desperately want to say “no.” You might feel a pang of guilt when you even consider taking time for yourself.

These are not character flaws. They are deeply ingrained neural pathways, often laid down in childhood. We learn that our goodness is conditional, that our worth is tied to our usefulness. We learn to override our own needs to keep the peace, to earn love, to feel secure. The brain, in its incredible efficiency, automates this pattern. It becomes our default setting. But the body… the body keeps the score. It holds the ungrieved losses, the unexpressed boundaries, the deep thirst for our own loving attention. Think of it like this: every time you override a need, a small energetic charge gets stored in your tissues. Over years, these charges accumulate, creating density, tension, and eventually, symptoms. Your body is literally holding the weight of a thousand tiny 'no's' that you couldn't say.

When these patterns are held for too long, they can crystallize. In the body, this can manifest as physical hardness—lumps, cysts, dense tissue. It is the physical manifestation of crystallized grief, of resentments that have been swallowed, of a heart that has been armored against its own needs. The body is simply trying to contain what the mind has refused to process.

But here is the beautiful truth: these patterns are not life sentences. Neuroplasticity, the brain’s amazing ability to rewire itself, shows us that we can create new pathways. We can learn to mother ourselves. We can learn to set boundaries not as acts of selfishness, but as acts of profound self-love and preservation. We can become the source that never runs dry. And in doing so, we don't just heal ourselves; we send a ripple of healing backward and forward through our lineage.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Guided Practice for Breast Healing and Self-Nurturing

This is not about fixing yourself. You are not broken. You have never been broken. This is about developing a conscious, loving relationship with yourself. It is about learning to listen to the whispers of your body before they become screams. This practice is a starting point, a gentle invitation to come home to yourself.

Find a quiet, comfortable space where you will not be disturbed. You can sit or lie down. Close your eyes and take three deep, cleansing breaths. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing the tensions of the day.

**Step 1: The Hand of Compassion**

Bring your right hand to your heart, and your left hand to your lower belly. Just rest them there. Feel the warmth of your own touch. For a few moments, simply notice your breath. Notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest and belly beneath your hands. You don’t need to change anything. Just be present with the simple, miraculous fact of your own breath.

**Step 2: Acknowledging the Pattern**

Now, gently bring your awareness to your breasts. You can keep your hands where they are, or you can gently cup your breasts with your hands. Whatever feels most supportive. Silently, or out loud, acknowledge the pattern of over-giving. You might say something like:

> “I see how I have poured myself out for others. I see how I have neglected my own well. I acknowledge the exhaustion, the resentment, the grief that I have been carrying.”

Stay with this for a few moments. There is no need to judge or to fix. Simply acknowledge. This is the sacred act of witnessing your own experience.

**Step 3: The Heart-Centered Meditation**

Now, imagine a beautiful, warm light in the center of your chest. It can be any color that feels nurturing to you—a soft pink, a warm gold, a gentle green. This is the light of your own heart, your own infinite source of love.

With each inhale, imagine you are drawing this light up into your breasts. Imagine it filling every cell, every space, with warmth, with compassion, with love. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing the old stories, the old griefs, the old patterns of depletion. Inhale love. Exhale what is no longer yours to carry.

Continue this for several minutes. If your mind wanders, gently guide it back to the breath and the light. This is a practice of deep receiving. You are allowing yourself to be filled from your own inner wellspring.

**Step 4: Setting a Loving Boundary**

Now, bring to mind one small, gentle boundary you can set in your life this week. It does not have to be a grand gesture. Perhaps it is saying “no” to a small request. Perhaps it is taking fifteen minutes to sit in silence. Perhaps it is asking for help.

Visualize yourself setting this boundary with grace and with love. See it not as a rejection of another, but as an embrace of yourself. Feel the sense of spaciousness that this boundary creates within you. Know that this is an act of profound self-nurturing.

**Step 5: The Blessing**

To close, bring your hands back to your heart. Offer yourself a blessing. It might be something like:

> “May I be filled with loving-kindness. May I be well. May I be peaceful and at ease. May I be happy.”

Take one more deep breath, and when you are ready, gently open your eyes.

## Becoming the Source

This practice is a beginning, a single step on the path back to yourself. Mothering yourself is a daily devotion, a moment-by-moment choice to turn towards yourself with the same love and tenderness you so freely offer to others. It is the radical and necessary practice of filling your own cup first, so that you may give from the glorious, abundant overflow, not from the depleted dregs.

When you learn to nurture yourself, you become a source-fed river that never runs dry. Your giving becomes a joyous offering, not a depleting sacrifice. You teach others, by your example, that receiving is as sacred as giving. You heal not only yourself, but the generations of women who came before you, who did not know they had a choice.

It’s a tricky business, being human. But you are not alone in it. Your body is your wisest teacher, your most faithful friend. Listen to its messages. Honor its needs. And know that you are worthy of all the love, all the care, all the tenderness you so generously pour into the world.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Heart Attacks of the Soul: When Your Heart Demands Attention
teachings.title: Heart Attacks of the Soul: When Your Heart Demands Attention
teachings.summary: Susan names a gradual emotional depletion she calls a “heart attack of the soul”—a slow dimming of the heart’s vitality caused by chronic self-abandonment, over-giving, and disconnection. She describes how the heart communicates this suffering through emotions and somatic signals, and offers a gentle, embodied practice of hand-on-heart breathing as a way to listen, re-member, and begin to re-source oneself with self-compassion. The piece invites ongoing, attentive care rather than quick fixes, and honors the heart as a primary, wise source of guidance.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was holding a newborn baby last week — my friend's granddaughter — and I was struck, as I always am, by the perfection of it.

We arrive in this world as bundles of pure, unfiltered love, our hearts beating in perfect resonance with the life force that animates us. We reach out with open arms, expecting that the world will meet us with the same unconditional love that we embody. And for a time, perhaps it does. But then, life happens. We experience the sting of rejection, the ache of loss, the subtle and not-so-subtle messages that our love is too much, or not enough.

I remember a client, a woman in her late fifties whom I’ll call Claire. She came to me presenting a life that looked, from the outside, like a masterpiece. A long, successful career as a landscape architect, a marriage of thirty years, two grown children who adored her. She had, by all accounts, “made it.” But her eyes told a different story. They were tired, listless, and held a profound, unnamed sorrow. “It’s as if my heart has gone silent,” she told me, her voice a fragile whisper. “I go through the motions. I smile at my husband, I listen to my children’s stories, I sign the checks for the charities I’m supposed to care about. But I don’t *feel* anything. It’s a hollowness, a quiet, persistent ache right here,” she said, placing a hand over her sternum. “It’s like the pilot light has gone out.”

Claire’s words resonated with a truth I have come to see again and again in my work. It’s a phenomenon I call the “heart attack of the soul.” This isn’t a sudden, dramatic medical event that sends you to the emergency room. It’s a slow, creeping erosion of the heart’s vitality, a gradual withdrawal of its energy in the face of chronic emotional pain, neglect, and disconnection. It’s the soul’s desperate, last-ditch effort to get our attention, to scream, *I can no longer bear this separation from my own essence. I need you. Now.*

## The Heart’s First Declaration

Here is a very good thing to know: before you had a brain, before you had limbs, before you had any conscious thought, you had a heart. In the sacred, silent darkness of the womb, the heart is the first distinct organ to manifest. It is the first declaration of your unique existence, the central sun around which your entire being constellates. Its rhythmic pulse is the drumbeat of your life, a constant, unwavering reminder of your aliveness, a cellular memory of your origin in love.

The heart’s wisdom is primal, intuitive, and deeply connected to the universal flow of love. It operates on a simple, elegant principle: the two-way pump. It receives, and it gives. It draws in the oxygen-rich blood of life, and it extends it out to every cell in the body. This is the fundamental rhythm of life, the sacred exchange that sustains us. But what happens when that exchange becomes imbalanced? What happens when we are taught, subtly or overtly, that our worth is contingent on our giving, that to receive is selfish or indulgent?

This is where the heart begins to suffer. So many of us, especially women, are conditioned to be the primary caregivers, the emotional pillars of our families and communities. We learn to sacrifice our own needs, our own desires, to justify our existence. We become so adept at tending to the hearts of others that we forget that our own heart is a living, breathing entity with its own needs, its own longings. And slowly, imperceptibly, our own hearts begin to starve. We keep pumping out love, support, and energy, but the reservoir isn’t being replenished. The well begins to run dry.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Language of a Grieving Heart

When the heart is starved, it doesn’t just go silent. It begins to speak in a different language—the language of symptoms. It might manifest as a persistent anxiety, a low-grade depression, a chronic fatigue that no amount of sleep can cure. It can show up as palpitations, a racing pulse, or a feeling of constriction in the chest. These are not random malfunctions. These are communications. The heart, in its profound wisdom, is sending out an SOS.

From a physiological perspective, the heart has its own intricate nervous system, often called the “heart-brain.” This network of neurons allows the heart to learn, remember, and make decisions independently of the cranial brain. It sends far more information to the brain than the brain sends to the heart. When we experience chronic emotional distress—the grief of an unmet need, the anger of a boundary crossed, the fear of abandonment—the heart-brain registers this as a threat. It sends signals up the vagus nerve to the brain, triggering the release of stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline.

This is the body’s ancient, intelligent survival mechanism at play. It’s designed to protect us from immediate danger. But when the “danger” is a persistent lack of self-love, a chronic pattern of self-abandonment, the system goes into overdrive. The body becomes a war zone. The nervous system gets locked in a sympathetic “fight-or-flight” response, and the heart bears the brunt of the battle. This is the neurobiology of a broken heart. It’s not just a feeling; it’s a physiological reality.

## Transcending the Wounded Heart: A Practice

So how do we begin to answer the heart’s call? How do we heal the heart that has learned to protect itself by shutting down? The journey back to the heart is not one of fixing or forcing, but of listening. It begins with the radical act of turning your attention inward and offering yourself the one thing you’ve been seeking all along: your own unconditional love and presence.

I invite you to try a simple practice. Find a quiet space where you won’t be disturbed. Sit or lie down comfortably, and gently close your eyes.

1.  **Arrive in Your Body:** Take a few slow, deep breaths. With each inhale, feel your belly and chest expand. With each exhale, release any tension you might be holding in your jaw, your shoulders, your hands. Simply arrive in the physical container of your being.

2.  **Hand on Heart:** Gently place one or both hands over the center of your chest. Don’t press or probe, just let the warmth of your hands rest on your heart space. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest with each breath. You might even feel the subtle beat of your heart beneath your palm.

3.  **Acknowledge Your Heart:** Silently, or out loud, speak to your heart as you would a beloved friend. You might say, “Heart, I am here with you now.” Or, “I am listening.” Or simply, “I love you.” There’s no need for fancy words. Just a simple, sincere acknowledgment.

4.  **Breathe with Your Heart:** Now, imagine that you can breathe directly into your heart. With each inhale, visualize a stream of warm, golden light pouring into your heart space, filling it with compassion, tenderness, and grace. With each exhale, imagine you are breathing out any pain, any constriction, any old story of unworthiness. Continue this for several minutes, allowing your heart to be bathed in the light of your own loving awareness.

5.  **Listen for the Whisper:** As you continue to breathe with your heart, simply listen. Don’t strive for a particular outcome or a profound revelation. Just remain open and receptive. Your heart may speak in images, in feelings, in memories, or in a quiet, inner knowing. It may simply be a feeling of warmth, of softening, of peace. Trust whatever comes.

This practice is not a one-time fix. It is a way of life. It is the sacred act of turning toward yourself, of choosing to mother your own heart, to be the source of your own love. The heart that loves itself first, that appreciates its own journey, that fills its own cup—this is the heart that naturally, effortlessly, extends love to others without depletion. It becomes a radiant sun, warming everything in its orbit.

You are a divinely-inspired human on a sacred journey. You are not here to earn your worth through endless doing and giving. You are here to be a vessel of love, and that love must begin with you. Whole-heartedly, courageously, and tenderly validate your own existence. Your heart is waiting.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Inspiration and Expiration: The Spiritual Dimensions of Breath](/blog/lungs-inspiration-expiration)
- [Self-Mothering: The Deepest Healing Your Breasts Can Offer](/blog/breasts-self-mothering)

**More on Heart:**

- [Dis-heartened: When Giving Depletes and Receiving Feels Impossible](/blog/heart-disheartened)
- [Your Heart: The First Declaration of Your Existence](/blog/heart-first-declaration)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Stomach - The Alchemical Cauldron of Experience
teachings.title: The Stomach - The Alchemical Cauldron of Experience
teachings.summary: Susan frames the stomach as an "alchemical cauldron" where physiological digestion mirrors the inner work of metabolizing experience. She explores the balance of corrosive truth (acid) and protective safety (mucous), reads ulcers as meaningful boundary-signals, and offers somatic practices—breath, slow eating, small dosages, and embodied listening—to increase capacity and transform pain into wisdom. The piece invites practical attention to bodily signals while urging medical care when needed and compassionate inquiry into the life patterns that produce distress.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You carry within you an alchemical cauldron. It sits beneath your ribs, a muscular chamber lined in rose-gold mucosa, a place where the world you swallow meets the raw chemistry of life. You call it the stomach, and yet it is far more than an organ. It is the first great translator of what you take in - the place where food becomes experience, where taste becomes tissue, where the outer world is rendered into inner substance. In this cauldron the acidic crucible of hydrochloric acid and digestive enzymes does something sacred. It dissolves, burns away, renders edible what had been foreign, and offers you, molecule by molecule, the nutrients of living. This physiology is a mirror for your psyche. The same alchemy is demanded of you emotionally and spiritually - to metabolize what happens to you so it nourishes rather than corrodes.

In the Tao Te Ching you find a whisper that guides this work: "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao." That line invites you into humility about every translation - including the body’s. Your stomach speaks a language older and truer than words. It tells you when something you ingest is life-giving, and when something, even if wrapped in the garb of familiarity or necessity, is slowly making you ill. The voice of the stomach is not dramatic. It is steady, patient, persistent. It will whisper through sensations of fullness, burning, gnawing, nausea, bloating, or the slow collapse of appetite. When you learn to listen, you will discover it offers you a strict, compassionate feedback system so you can become a masterful alchemist of your life.

The Alchemy of Acid and Meaning

Think for a moment about the chemistry that takes place in that chamber. Acid is a fierce presence. Hydrochloric acid lowers the pH to a place where proteins unfurl and enzymes can work. The stomach is intentionally corrosive in order to reveal the nourishing elements hidden within the harshness of raw material. Without that corrosive force you would not extract the life-sustaining components of what you eat. And yet your stomach is not a reckless furnace. It is guarded by a mucosal lining, a careful mucous shield that protects the living tissues from the very acidity that makes life possible.

Psychologically this is identical. To metabolize experience you must allow a certain kind of interior "corrosion" - a willingness to let challenging truths and bitter feelings unfold, to pull apart old narratives so their nutritive core can be released. This is not the same as cruelty to yourself. The mucosal lining is the intimate sense of safety, the inner yes that says you can enfold the fire without being consumed. When you face grief, anger, betrayal, or humiliation and you have cultivated an inner protective tenderness, the corrosive power of truth works to reveal wisdom rather than to erode you into cynicism.

When you cannot metabolize, the corrosive forces of life find no balanced container. They begin to erode. In the stomach this becomes ulcers - localized wear through the mucosal shield into the living tissue beneath. Ulcers are the body saying plainly: this is making me sick. The same phenomenon happens in the psyche. Unprocessed shame, shame that has been swallowed again and again because you needed to survive, begins to gnaw at your capacity to hold life in a nourishing way. You begin to experience that familiar burning - not localized only in the belly, but as an undercurrent of irritation in your thinking, a vigilance in your nervous system, a hardness in your heart.

Ulcer as Message

Ulcers are not merely medical facts. They are letters written in acid upon living flesh. They tell a story about the relationship between the world you take in and the safety you maintain around that process. Sometimes ulcers appear in those who have been obliged to swallow things that felt intolerable - constant criticism, moral compromise, a work culture that asks you to betray your values, a relationship where truth is punished. Sometimes they arise when you have habitually swallowed your anger, preferring the fragile security of being agreeable to the terrifying freedom of saying no. Ulcers then become the body’s blunt wisdom: you cannot keep ingesting poison and pretend nothing will change inside.

There is a tenderness, though, in this message. The ulcer is not only a condemnation. It is a boundary-maker. It imposes limits so that the body will be noticed again. When you are vibrating with chronic busyness, numbed by stimulants or sedated by overwork, the stomach may quietly wear thin until something forces you to stop. In that forced stillness is the possibility of redirection - the chance to become the kind of alchemist who turns corrosive pain into refining fire, and refining fire into clarity and nourishment.

Capacity to Metabolize Experience

Ask yourself how much you can really digest. Not in terms of willpower, but in terms of developmental capacity. Some people are built by upbringing and culture to handle large amounts of emotional and situational content. Others are given only fragments of safety and thus operate with a delicate capacity. The stomach teaches you this in a visceral way. There is a limit to how much raw emotional protein any one human can have broken down at a time. When you exceed your capacity you will sense it first as a tightening, as indigestion, as an inability to "swallow" what you are being asked to accept.

Your inner digestive capacity can be expanded, and this is the work of spiritual and somatic development. It does not mean forcing more down at once. It means cultivating both the acid that allows digestion to occur and the mucous that protects you. Acid without mucous is destruction. Mucous without acid is stagnation. You must train both the courage to face truth and the tenderness to hold yourself through its corrosive effect. This requires practices that are physiological as well as contemplative - regulated breath, slow mindful eating, the softening of the diaphragm, practices that increase vagal tone so your nervous system knows you are safe enough to let digestion proceed.

When you do this work you metabolize grief rather than hoarding it. You understand anger as an energetic signal that something needs boundary and direction. You digest disappointment until it becomes knowledge instead of becoming the acid that corrodes your trust in life. The stomach, when honored, becomes a wise teacher. It trains you in timing - what to ingest, when to rest, when to purge - and in discrimination - what is nourishment and what is toxin for you now.

Transforming Difficulty into Wisdom

To become an alchemist of experience you must learn the labors of transmutation. The first step is radical listening. Place your hand upon your belly and feel the textures of your attention. When you are willing to receive the information your stomach provides, the practice of translation begins. Ask it simple questions. Where is the tension most dense? Is the sensation located under the sternum - a raw center of vulnerability and exposure - or lower, a thick knot of kept anger? Does your body constrict when you consider saying no? Does it open when you imagine boundaries articulated with kindness?

Next, map what you ingest. Not only the food but the cultural messages, the habitual agreements, the narratives of obligation you consume because they were on offer. Often the stomach is the first to sense that something from the external field does not belong. It will say no even if your mind rationalizes acceptance. Trust that wisdom. Learn the difference between temporary discomfort that signals growth, and chronic corrosive ingestion that signals the need for change. A life of continuous acid without protective mucous is not growth. It is erosion.

Then practice the art of discharge. The body must expel what it cannot incorporate. This takes many forms - tears, bitter words spoken in timely defense, a ceremonial release of a beloved possession, a change in diet that cuts off a habitual partner in toxicity, or a structural boundary set with someone whose presence consistently erodes you. Discharge is not revenge. It is the body's necessary excretion to restore balance. The Taoist path teaches you this elegantly. In chapter 48 of the Tao Te Ching you find a guidance close to this work: "In the pursuit of learning you get every day something to increase. In the pursuit of Tao you get every day something to diminish. Less and less do you do until you arrive at non-action." The point is not to accumulate more capacity by force, but to simplify what you take in until your system finds right proportion and wisdom emerges naturally.

Rituals of Refinement

To steward your gastric wisdom create rituals that respect the stomach as a teacher. Before you eat, take three full, slow breaths and settle the nervous system. Chew slowly. Taste deliberately. Let each mouthful be a conversation rather than a hurried transaction. When you confront an uncomfortable conversation or decision, breathe into the belly first. Give your diaphragm permission to move, your pelvic floor to release, your heart to slow. This somatic pause strengthens the mucous - your felt sense of safety - so that the acid of truth can do its work without doing violence.

Furthermore, cultivate the art of small dosages. The alchemist never pours a river of raw material into the retort all at once. Instead the process takes measure. Break difficult conversations into smaller bites. Offer and receive feedback in manageable increments. Test the water of a relationship with a gentle boundary before you announce a full rearrangement. This is not cowardice. It is wise physiology in action. The stomach, in this metaphor, is always teaching you how to feed your soul sustainably.

And when an ulcer appears, respond with reverence not shame. Seek medical care with humility and curiosity. At the same time, inquire into the life that produced it. Where has your interior mucous thinned? What have you been swallowing that you could stop? What honest word have you withheld because you feared the fallout? Sometimes the most loving act is leaving a situation that repeatedly erodes you. Other times healing requires the fierce gentleness of forgiveness, a clearing of victim storylines, a reorganizing of rituals around self-protection.

The Holographic Stomach

Remember that the stomach is holographic. Its condition will reverberate through your entire being. When you reclaim your capacity to metabolize, your breathing deepens, your nervous system relaxes, your head quiets, your face softens, your hands unclench. The stomach is both local and systemic. It is a nexus through which your relational life, your cultural inheritance, your personal story, and your moment-to-moment choices all pass and are evaluated. This is why working with the stomach ripples into larger transformation. Attend to this chamber and you are attending to the way you process life itself.

In practical terms this means building practices that are integrated - dietary attention, yes, but also attention to emotional diet. It means the courage to turn away from relationships that insist you swallow falsehoods. It means learning to speak your hunger - not only for food but for respect, for presence, for clarity - and to advocate for what rightly nourishes you. The art of alchemy requires precise language. Learn to tell the truth about what you need in a way that preserves dignity for both you and the other.

Becoming the Masterful Alchemist

There is a discipline to becoming a masterful alchemist. It is not a heroic sprint but a steady cultivation of contact and care. Begin with small actions that respect your stomach as teacher. Slow your inhalation. Slow your ingestion. Say no when you mean no. Let tears have a road to exit. Make friends with your anger so it becomes a tool for boundary-setting rather than a toxin you swallow. Invite the body to speak to you through simple inquiries. Place your hand on your belly and ask, "What am I carrying that I can release?" Wait in the posture of listening. Respond with kindness. Repeat this daily until your body teaches you the language of your next right step.

You will fail sometimes. You will swallow when you mean to refuse. The work is not to be perfect. It is to return, again and again, with curiosity and tenderness. In the quiet of this practice you will witness your capacity expand. The mucous will thicken with safety. Your digestive acids will be allowed to do their refining rather than their destruction. What once burned will be transformed into fuel. What once gnawed will be integrated into your story as a source of compassion for yourself and others.

And so your stomach becomes not only an organ of digestion but a laboratory of soulwork. You learn to metabolize experiences into wisdom, to convert the bitter into a clear medicine, to make from your wounds a recipe for compassion. The true alchemist does not seek to avoid hardship. Rather, they learn to receive hardship into a vessel that can contain and refine it. As Lao Tzu might remind you with his quiet paradox, it is often in the soft, receptive places of your being that the greatest transformation occurs. When you become an alchemist of your own life you realize you are not merely surviving what comes to you. You are, with intention and tenderness, making it into something that sustains you.

Listen to your stomach. Learn its letters and its grammar. Honor the acids and honor the mucous. Let the cauldron do what it was designed to do - transform, not destroy. In the patient company of that inner alchemy your life will be slowly, surely refined into wisdom. You will not only eat the world. You will be fed by it.

teachings.sourceTitle: What Would It Be Like to Elevate Everything to Love?
teachings.title: What Would It Be Like to Elevate Everything to Love?
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to notice moments of reactivity and asks a single transforming question: "What would it be like to elevate this to love?" The piece explores love as a state or frequency that can shift body and mind—invoking heart coherence, the vagus nerve, and neuroplasticity—while emphasizing compassionate presence, honest holding of pain, and small daily practices rather than spiritual bypassing. Throughout she offers grounded examples and an encouragement to turn toward difficult feelings with curiosity and gentle care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Before we begin, I want to acknowledge something: you are here. That matters more than you might realize.

Just the other day, I was standing in my kitchen, the scent of damp earth rising from the garden after an early spring rain. I was watching a single drop of water tremble on the tip of a rose leaf, and I felt a familiar tightness in my chest, a cold knot just below my sternum. A conversation from the day before, one that left me feeling unseen and profoundly misunderstood, was replaying itself in my mind for the tenth…or perhaps the twentieth…time.

My body, in its infinite wisdom and memory, was reacting as if the conversation were happening all over again. The subtle clenching in my jaw, the almost imperceptible shallowing of my breath, the old, familiar story of injustice and not-enoughness churning inside me. It’s a powerful current, that river of righteousness. It feels so justified, so *real*.

In that moment, I had a choice. I could let that story run its course, deepening its well-worn neural grooves, allowing the corrosive chemistry of stress to flood my system. I could spend the rest of the afternoon caught in its grip, my energy draining away into a pointless mental battle. Or I could ask the question that has become the central anchor of my life and my work, the question that has saved me time and time again.

*What would it be like to elevate this to love?*

Not to ignore it. Not to pretend it didn’t hurt. Not to slap a coat of spiritual paint over a genuinely painful human emotion. But to elevate it. To hold the entire messy, uncomfortable, painful experience in a new and higher consciousness. To lift it out of the cramped basement of reactivity and into the spacious cathedral of the heart. What would that even mean?

## Love as a State of Being, Not Just an Emotion

We tend to think of love as an emotion we feel *for* someone or something. A romantic partner, a newborn baby, a breathtaking sunset. And it is that, of course. That feeling is a beautiful, vital part of our human experience. But it is only one expression of love’s true nature. In the quiet depths of our being, love is not just an emotion—it is a frequency. A state of consciousness. It is the fundamental resonance of the universe, the creative force from which all things arise.

Modern neuroscience is beginning to map what the ancient wisdom traditions have always known. When we experience emotions like compassion, gratitude, or what we can simply call love, our entire biology shifts. Our heart rhythms, when measured, become more coherent, creating a smooth, harmonious wave pattern. This isn't just a poetic idea; it's a measurable physiological reality. This state of “heart coherence” doesn't just stay in the heart. The heart, it turns out, sends far more information to the brain than the brain sends to the heart. This coherent signal travels up the vagus nerve, the superhighway of the body's nervous system, and has a profound effect on our mental and emotional state. It quiets the amygdala, the brain's fear center, enhances our cognitive function, and bathes our entire system in restorative chemistry like oxytocin, often called the
'love hormone.'

To elevate something to love is to consciously choose to shift our own frequency. It is to decide that we will no longer resonate with the frequency of anger, of victimhood, of fear. It is to choose to attune ourselves, right in the midst of the storm, to the frequency of love. It is an act of profound and gentle power, a declaration that you are the master of your own inner state.

## The Alchemy of Genuine Transformation

Let’s be very clear. This is not spiritual bypassing. It is not pasting a smiley face over our pain or pretending that we are not affected by the challenges of life. That would be a denial of our humanity, and our humanity is sacred. The invitation is not to deny the pain, but to hold it. To bring it so close that it can be touched by the warmth of our own compassionate presence. This is the difference between suppression and transformation.

To elevate a difficult experience to love is a form of sacred alchemy. It is the process of transforming the lead of our suffering into the gold of wisdom. It means looking at the person who angered you and asking, with genuine curiosity, “What wound in them is speaking? What part of me is triggered by this, and what is it here to teach me?” It means feeling the profound ache of grief and allowing it to carve you into a more spacious and compassionate vessel, capable of holding more of life’s beauty and sorrow.

I remember a time years ago when a professional collaboration ended in a way that felt like a deep betrayal. For months, I was consumed by feelings of anger and injustice. I rehearsed the story endlessly, each retelling tightening the knot of resentment in my gut. I was exhausted, depleted, and my body was starting to protest with migraines and digestive issues. One day, in the depths of my meditation, the question floated into my awareness: *What would it be like to elevate this to love?* My first reaction was resistance. *Never! They don’t deserve it!* But the question persisted, gently.

Slowly, tentatively, I began to hold the entire situation in a field of love. I pictured the other person not as a villain, but as a soul struggling with their own fears and insecurities. I pictured myself, not as a victim, but as a resilient being capable of healing. I didn’t have to forgive them in that moment. I just had to be willing to hold the pain in a different way. This is the wisdom echoed in the Tao te Ching:

> “The softest thing in the universe
> Overcomes the hardest thing in the universe.”

Love is that softest thing. It does not fight. It does not argue. It does not resist. It simply surrounds, permeates, and transforms whatever it touches. When I stood in my kitchen, feeling the tightness in my chest, elevating it to love meant placing my hand on my heart. It meant breathing into the tightness, not trying to force it away, but infusing it with a gentle, accepting warmth. It meant acknowledging the part of me that felt hurt and whispering to her, “I am here with you. I see you. This is a painful feeling, and we will hold it together in love.”

Slowly, something shifts. The grip of the story loosens. The body begins to soften. A new possibility emerges—one that is not available when we are locked in the tight, narrow frequency of reactivity.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Rewiring Your Reality, One Thought at a Time

This practice, this gentle and consistent turning toward love, is not just a momentary relief. It is the work of rewiring your own brain. Every time you choose to interrupt a reactive pattern—a thought of resentment, a spiral of anxiety, a jab of self-criticism—and introduce the frequency of love, you are weakening old neural pathways and building new ones. This is neuroplasticity in action. You are, quite literally, sculpting your brain for peace.

You are teaching your system, at the most fundamental level, that it is possible to feel safe and whole even when faced with external dissonance. You are moving from a state of being at the mercy of the world to a state of being anchored in your own unshakable core of love. This is the foundation of true resilience. It’s not about having a thick skin; it’s about having a soft, open, and coherent heart.

It begins with the small things, the tiny moments that make up a life. The driver who cuts you off in traffic. The critical comment from a family member. The wave of exhaustion at the end of a long day. The flicker of comparison when you scroll through social media. In each instance, the question arises: *What would it be like to elevate this to love?*

Perhaps it means sending a thought of peace to the other driver, imagining they are rushing to a sick child, and feeling the immediate release in your own shoulders. Perhaps it means seeing the fear behind the criticism and meeting it with compassion for both the other person and yourself, refusing to internalize the barb. Perhaps it means wrapping yourself in a blanket of radical self-acceptance and allowing yourself to simply be tired, without the added layer of judgment.

This is how we transform the world. Not by changing everyone else, but by changing our own inner state. Love is a frequency that ripples outward, touching everything and everyone in its field. By choosing to embody it, you become a source of that healing frequency for the entire planet. You become a point of coherence in a chaotic world. You become a quiet, powerful force for peace.

It is the most important work we can do.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

So I ask you, beloved one, what in your life is calling to be elevated? What experience, what relationship, what old story is waiting to be held in the arms of your own vast and unconditional love? What would it be like to trust that you have the capacity to transform it all?

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

reflectionPrompts: Name a recent moment when you felt a familiar reactive pattern (anger, resentment, shame, etc.). What sensations arose in your body, and what would it look like to hold that moment with curious, compassionate attention instead of reopening the story?

Where in your life do you most often replay old narratives (work, family, relationships, social media)? What is one tiny interruption you could introduce—right in the middle of that pattern—to begin shifting the neural groove toward a more loving resonance?

Reflect on a time when attempting to ‘stay positive’ felt like bypassing pain. How might you practice holding that pain alongside love—without rushing forgiveness—and what support or boundaries might help you do that safely?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Place one hand gently over your heart, soften your jaw, and take six slow, mindful breaths (inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6). As you breathe, invite a simple phrase such as “I am here with you” or “This is felt and held,” letting the words land where you feel tightness. Notice any micro-shift in the body; if sensations become intense, slow your breathing, rest, and reach out to a trusted person or professional as needed.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article includes descriptions of grief, betrayal, intense emotional pain, and physical stress reactions; if reading it brings up strong feelings, please pause and ground yourself before continuing.

The suggested inner practices are gentle supports, not substitutes for professional mental health care; if you are processing trauma, persistent distress, or find practices triggering, consider working with a qualified therapist or support person.

If physical symptoms (chest tightness, migraines, digestive issues, or other bodily distress) are new, severe, or ongoing, consult a qualified healthcare provider; the contemplative practices here are complementary and should not replace medical evaluation or treatment.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Still Point: Where Deep Healing Begins
teachings.title: The Still Point: Where Deep Healing Begins
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers into the experience of the "still point"—a somatic pause encountered in cranial sacral work and in everyday moments of quiet—as a fertile, intelligent space where the nervous system can downshift and restorative processes can begin. She links this lived experience to nervous-system physiology and offers simple, accessible ways to notice and cultivate moments of stillness as an act of self-compassion.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are pulled in a thousand directions at once, our nervous systems humming with the constant thrum of information, expectation, and the relentless pace of modern life. We crave connection, yet we feel isolated. We long for peace, yet our minds are a whirlwind of activity. It’s a paradox, this beautiful, messy existence. But what if I told you there is a place within you—a sanctuary of profound stillness—where the noise of the world fades away and the deepest healing can begin? It’s a place I’ve come to know intimately, both in my own journey and in the sacred space I hold for my clients. It is the still point. ## The Ocean Within In the world of cranial sacral therapy, the still point is a known phenomenon. It’s a moment, brief or extended, when the rhythmic tide of cerebrospinal fluid—that gentle, oceanic pulse that flows within the dural membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord—seems to pause. The entire system comes to a profound state of rest. It’s not an absence of life; it’s a suspension. A moment of pure potential. Imagine a snow globe. When you shake it, the glitter—the thoughts, the worries, the to-do lists—swirls in a chaotic flurry. You can’t see the landscape inside. But when you set it down and allow the glitter to settle, the scene becomes clear. The still point is that moment of settling. The system isn’t stopping; it’s reorganizing. It’s in this quiet, intelligent pause that the body’s innate wisdom takes over, recalibrating and finding its way back to equilibrium. I remember a client, a woman in her late forties who came to me feeling utterly depleted. She was a caregiver to her aging parents, a mother to two teenagers, and a partner in a demanding business. Her shoulders were permanently hunched, her breath was shallow, and her energy was frayed. As she lay on the table, I could feel the frenetic buzz in her system. My hands, gently cradling her head, listened to the story her body was telling—a story of overwhelm and exhaustion. Midway through the session, it happened. The subtle rhythm I was tracking simply…ceased. The tide went out, and there was only a vast, silent expanse. Her whole body softened. Her breath deepened, spontaneously. In that stillness, her nervous system, which had been locked in a state of high alert for years, finally received the message that it was safe to let go. It was a sacred moment, a glimpse into the profound intelligence of the body to heal itself when given the chance. ## The Neuroscience of Stillness This isn’t just esoteric theory; it’s grounded in the elegant workings of our own biology. When we enter these states of deep rest, we shift from the sympathetic nervous system—our “fight or flight” mode—to the parasympathetic nervous system, often called the “rest and digest” or “tend and befriend” state. This is the domain of the vagus nerve, a wandering cranial nerve that connects the brain to the heart, lungs, and gut. When the parasympathetic system is dominant, our heart rate slows, our blood pressure drops, and our bodies can finally get to the essential work of repair and regeneration. This is when cellular cleanup happens, when inflammation is reduced, and when the brain can consolidate memories and process emotional experiences. Stillness isn’t empty; it’s a hive of restorative activity. It’s the prerequisite for true healing. Think of it like a garden. You can’t force a seed to grow by pulling on it. You must provide the right conditions—good soil, water, sunlight—and then you must wait. You must trust the process. The still point is the fertile soil. It’s the space where we allow the seeds of healing to germinate, tended by an intelligence far older and wiser than our conscious minds. ## Finding Your Own Still Point While a cranial sacral session can be a powerful gateway to this experience, the beautiful truth is that you can cultivate these moments of stillness in your own life. It doesn’t require a special room or a guru on a mountaintop. It requires only your intention and a willingness to turn inward. It might be found in the simple act of pausing to feel the warmth of a mug of tea in your hands, noticing the steam curl into the air. It might be in the space between breaths during a quiet meditation. It could be the feeling of your feet planted firmly on the earth, a moment of grounding in the midst of a chaotic day. I often find my still point in my garden. Just this morning, I was sitting on the damp earth, the scent of rain-soaked soil rising around me. I watched a single drop of water tremble on the edge of a hosta leaf, a perfect, shimmering jewel. In that moment, there was no past, no future. There was only the leaf, the water, the cool air on my skin. My mind, which had been racing with the day’s agenda, grew quiet. And in that quiet, I felt a profound sense of peace. A homecoming. This is the wisdom the ancient Taoists spoke of—the power of *wu wei*, of effortless action, of being rather than doing. The Tao Te Ching tells us: > "Empty yourself of everything. > Let the mind rest at peace. > The ten thousand things rise and fall while the Self watches their return. > They grow and flourish and then return to the source. > Returning to the source is stillness, which is the way of nature." This returning to the source…this is the still point. It is our nature. It is the wellspring from which all true healing flows. It is always there, beneath the surface of our busy lives, waiting for us to come home. So I invite you, my dear one, to seek out your own moments of stillness. Don’t see it as another task to add to your list. See it as an act of radical self-compassion. A gift to your weary nervous system. Let the snow globe of your mind settle. Allow the tide of your inner ocean to pause. And in that sacred quiet, feel the gentle, powerful work of healing begin.

teachings.sourceTitle: Love as a Practice, Not a Feeling: The Daily Discipline of the Heart
teachings.title: Love as a Practice, Not a Feeling: The Daily Discipline of the Heart
teachings.summary: Susan reframes love as an active, daily practice rather than a passive feeling, inviting readers to cultivate connection through small, intentional choices: presence, vulnerability, repair, and gratitude. She links the neurochemistry of early romantic intensity to its unsustainability and offers a somatic compass—noticing bodily signals—as a guide for heart-centered practice. The piece emphasizes steady, patient tending (wu wei) as the path to lasting intimacy.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human heart. We are taught so little about its true nature, yet we are expected to navigate its vast and wild terrain for our entire lives. We are handed a compass that spins wildly, a map with entire continents missing, and told to find our way to the promised land of love. We have been taught that love is something that happens *to* us—a feeling that arrives unbidden, a lightning strike, a fever that takes hold. It’s a story told in our songs, our movies, our most cherished cultural myths. It’s the stuff of fairy tales: a passive state of blissful reception. And so we wait. We wait to be found, to be struck, to be filled up by a feeling so grand it will solve the ache of being alone. But what if that’s the wrong map entirely? What if love isn’t a feeling at all? Or, not *just* a feeling. What if, beloved one, love is actually a practice? A daily, conscious, sometimes-messy discipline of the heart that we can cultivate, strengthen, and deepen through our own intention. ## The Grand Myth of the Uncontrollable Heart The initial rush of falling in love is a potent cocktail, and our brains are wired to drink it in. Neuroscience tells us that the early stages of romantic love are flooded with dopamine, the neurotransmitter of reward and craving, and norepinephrine, which gives us that giddy, can’t-eat, can’t-sleep focus. It’s a state of beautiful, temporary insanity. It feels fantastic. It feels like *everything*. But it is, by its very nature, unsustainable. No nervous system can exist in a perpetual state of high-alert activation. This is where the story often breaks down. When the initial dopamine-fueled intensity inevitably wanes, we panic. We think the love is gone. We think we’ve failed, or that our partner has failed us. We mourn the loss of the *feeling*, because we were taught the feeling was the entire point. This is where the real journey begins. This is the threshold between love as a fleeting state and love as a devoted practice. It’s the choice point where we decide to consciously cultivate the neurochemistry of lasting connection—the bonding hormones of oxytocin and vasopressin, which are released not through novelty and craving, but through consistent, attuned presence, touch, and shared vulnerability. ## Lessons from the Garden I remember the first year I tried to grow a real garden on my little balcony. I was full of romantic notions. I bought beautiful terracotta pots and packets of seeds with glorious pictures of lush tomatoes and fragrant basil. I planted them with great ceremony, watered them once, and then… I got busy. I expected the magic to happen on its own. A week later, all I had was dry, cracked earth. My neighbor, a woman with a garden so vibrant it seemed to hum with life, saw my sad little pots. She didn’t lecture me. She just smiled and said, “They ask for a little something every day.” So I began the practice. I learned to stick my finger in the soil to feel its thirst. I learned which plants needed the morning sun and which preferred the afternoon shade. I learned to gently pinch back the dead leaves to make way for new growth. It wasn’t always glamorous. Some days it was a chore. But I showed up. And slowly, miraculously, life began to unfurl. The daily, mundane acts of tending—of showing up, of paying attention, of offering what was needed—were the very things that created the conditions for beauty to flourish. It wasn’t magic. It was practice. Our hearts are no different. They ask for a little something every day. ## The Practice of Turning Towards So what does this practice of love look like, day to day? It’s less about grand gestures and more about a thousand small, intentional choices. It is the practice of turning *towards* instead of away. It’s turning towards your partner to truly listen when they speak of their day, even when you are tired and the television is calling. It’s putting your phone down, making eye contact, and offering the gift of your full, undivided presence. This is the practice of *attunement*. It’s turning towards the messy, uncomfortable conversations. When there is a rupture—and in any real relationship, there will always be ruptures—the practice is not to retreat into silence or armor up with blame. The practice is to say, “That didn’t feel good. Can we talk about it?” It’s the courageous act of repair, of tending to the space between you. This is the practice of *vulnerability*. It’s turning towards the good. Our brains have a negativity bias, a primal survival mechanism that keeps us scanning for threats. The practice of love involves consciously overriding this default setting. It’s actively looking for what you appreciate in another, and *saying it out loud*. It’s celebrating the small wins, the shared laughter, the quiet moment of connection over a cup of tea. This is the practice of *gratitude*. This is the wisdom echoed in the Tao Te Ching, which speaks of action that arises from a place of deep alignment, not frantic effort. The practice of love isn’t a grind. It is a form of *wu wei*, or effortless action—not because it requires no effort, but because the effort is so aligned with our deepest nature that it becomes a flow. It is the steady, patient, powerful action of water carving stone. It is showing up, again and again, as the most open, compassionate version of yourself that you can be in that moment. ## The Body as a Compass How do you know if you are on the right path, my friend? Check in with your body. The body never lies. Think of a time you felt truly, safely loved. Where did you feel it? Perhaps a warmth spreading through your chest. A softening in your jaw. A deep, settled breath that seemed to reach all the way down to your feet. That is the somatic signature of connection. That is your body saying *yes*. Now, think of a time you felt disconnected, unseen, or in conflict. What happens in your body? A tightening in the throat. A clenching in the stomach. A shallow breath held high in the chest. That is the body’s wisdom, too. It is a sacred signal, asking you to pay attention. The practice of love is also a practice of listening to these signals. It’s noticing the clench and consciously choosing to soften. It’s feeling the tightness and choosing to breathe into it. It is the moment-to-moment choice to bring your body back to a state of safety and openness, from which true connection is possible. Love is not a prize to be won. It is a sanctuary to be built, brick by brick, choice by choice, day by day. It is the discipline of the heart, and its reward is not a fleeting feeling, but a deep and abiding home for your soul.

If alone: close your eyes, do a 60-second body scan noticing places of tightness or ease, breathe into one area for two minutes, then decide one small, tangible act of care you can offer yourself or another today.
