teachings.sourceTitle: The Shoulders - The Cradle of Responsibility and the Gateway of Extension
teachings.title: The Shoulders - The Cradle of Responsibility and the Gateway of Extension
teachings.summary: Susan invites you to listen to your shoulders as a living map of responsibility, offering both physiological insight and poetic inquiry. The piece weaves anatomy, Taoist principles, and somatic practice to help you discern what you were made to carry and what can be compassionately released. Through simple embodied experiments — breath, mindful touch, and imaginative delegation — you are guided toward a lighter, more responsive posture in life and relationship.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The Shoulders - The Cradle of Responsibility and the Gateway of Extension

You carry your world on a scaffolding that is both miraculous and vulnerable. The shoulders, those complex ball-and-socket marvels, are the most flexible joints in your body. They allow you to reach, to embrace, to push away, to lift, to rest your hands upon the earth or the breast of another. In their architecture you find capacity - for movement, for contact, for the literal and symbolic extension of yourself into the world. And because they are so capable, they are also the place where the weight of your interior life often first translates into physical sensation. The shoulders become the cradle of responsibility and the gateway of extension, and in their ache and release lie teachings about what you are willing to carry and what you are being asked to set down.

When you learn to listen to the shoulders as a sacred messenger, you will discover patterns that have been intimate companions for years, perhaps decades. The body is never random. A stubborn stiffness across the top of the shoulders, a persistent knot between the shoulder blades, a chronic right-sided pressure, or an old left-sided injury - each of these is a line in the story of your life. They are not punishments. They are languages of the deeper self asking to be heard. This is the holographic truth: the same themes that bind your relationships, your work, your identity, also live in the tissues of your shoulders. Addressing one ripple will transform the whole pond.

The Physiology of Bearing

Consider the shoulder as a masterful compromise between mobility and stability. The humerus sits deep in the glenoid fossa, cushioned by delicate labral tissue, orchestrated by rotator cuff muscles and an elaborate web of ligaments, tendons, fascia and neural communication. This system prizes freedom - to arc, to circle, to reach beyond the known. Yet that freedom is conditional. It depends on balance. When you habitually lean into one kind of movement - always reaching outward to give, or always pulling inward to protect - the shoulder remodels itself. Muscles shorten, fascia densifies, breathing patterns change. The nervous system holds the memory of threat and obligation as if it were an ever-present load.

In Taoist teaching the body is not separate from the river of life. The Tao Te Ching begins with the paradox of naming and not naming. You might say: the shoulder that can be named is not the whole shoulder. Still, there is a way to speak of it that honors both its physiology and its poetry. The Tao reminds you that the soft and yielding overcome the hard and rigid. In the shoulders this is literal. When you learn to soften, to yield intelligently, tension dissipates. When you clench in righteous bearing, pain hardens into chronic story.

Responsibility as Load and as Blessing

Responsibility is a strangely double-headed creature. On one wing it is the faculty that allows you to care, to answer the call of life, to be reliable. On the other wing it can become a tyranny - a belief that you must be the singular bearer of outcomes, the solver, the protector at any cost. Your shoulders often reveal how you relate to those wings. When you feel a heavy, habitual constriction across the top of the shoulders you are likely carrying more than is yours to bear. The body archives the electrochemical signature of vows, promises, and cultural demands. Children taught early to be caretakers of adults, people raised in families where someone had to be the stabilizer, adults who took on responsibility to be loved - these stories often lodge themselves in the trapezius and levator scapulae like quiet tenants that never pack up.

Your left shoulder tends to be the repository of emotional burdens. It is the place where the weight of grief, of unresolved longing, of empathic absorption sits and waits. Because the left side is more intimately linked with affective processing in many bodies, it becomes the place where relational sorrow, the sticky residue of others' disappointments, and the ghosts of unmet childhood needs find purchase. You may notice a dull, persistent heaviness on the left when you have been carrying someone else’s pain as if it were your own. You may wake with a left shoulder that protests after a night of worrying about someone you love. This is not moralizing. It is simply anatomical truth made tender.

Your right shoulder most commonly bears duty - the pragmatic, disciplined, public-sphere responsibilities. It is the shoulder of the workday, of contractual obligations, of the quiet determination to make systems function. When your right shoulder tightens, you may be living under the belief that to be valuable you must demonstrate competence and reliability, that failure to perform will lead to loss. That tightness is honorable, but it is only one expression of existence. Over time the right shoulder can harden into a fortress, preventing you from receiving as much as you give. It can become a statue of duty that cannot move when life asks for gentleness.

Distinguishing the True Load

Discernment about what is yours to carry is the central practical art here. The shoulders will not do this for you. They will merely reflect your current choices. You must learn to ask subtle questions and to listen with the body as much as with the mind. Does this burden belong to your contract with life, or is it an old script you have rehearsed so often that you cannot tell it from your identity? Is the weight in your shoulders actually a loyalty to a wounded story that no longer protects you? Are you carrying an unspoken agreement to make someone else safe, at the cost of your own ease? These questions are not meant to shame. They are invitations to reclaim freedom.

Discernment requires both tenderness and boundary. Taoism offers you a guide here: cultivate wu wei, the art of non-doing that is not passivity but intelligent response. When you practice wu wei you do not reflexively shoulder every demand. You do not perform heroics out of hunger for validation. You allow the momentum of life to show you where your energy is most potent and where it would be wasted. When you practice this art, your shoulders literally align differently. The muscles that had been overburdened relax because you are no longer doing undue work. The fascia that had hardened can rehydrate. The shoulder becomes a gateway of extension rather than an archive of sacrifice.

There are practical somatic clues to know whether a load is truly yours. When you imagine saying yes or no to a request, notice the visceral reaction in your shoulders. If the chest opens and the shoulders broaden, you are likely aligned with your authentic capacity. If the chest tightens and the left shoulder immediately drops, or the right bunches, there is a mismatch. Watch where your breath changes as you consider responsibilities. Your breath is the barometer. Slower, deeper breath with an open collarbone says yes from an embodied ground. Rapid, shallow breath with a neck-hunched response signals a conditioned obligation.

Mapping the Inner Geography

Turn your attention to the space between your shoulder blades. This region is called the dorsal midline, the spine’s soft partner in bearing both literal and figurative loads. When this region is constricted you cannot easily receive support. You may think you are unsupported because you have habitually refused support to avoid vulnerability. The shoulder blades remember that refusal. They harden into shields. The Tao teaches that the valley is the place of receptivity. "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao," and also, the low and yielding place holds the water. Allow your shoulder blades to descend into the valley of receiving. Let them become broad plates that both stabilize and invite contact. This is not a weakness. It is a wisdom practice in which you learn to let down arms without losing integrity.

Now consider your collarbones. They are the bridge between sternum and shoulder, the architecture of your openness. When collarbones are depressed, so is your invitation to life. When they are lifted with ease, you carry your heart forward with dignity rather than with braced exertion. This structural language is subtle, but it reverberates through every interaction you have. In intimacy, in work, in parenting, the way you hold your collarbones sends a signal of whether you are carrying burdens as armor or as an honest part of care.

A Practice of Discerning Release

Your practice does not have to be elaborate to be potent. It needs only to be steady and embodied. Start with a moment of inquiry in the morning or before sleep. Sit or stand with both feet grounded. Invite your hands to rest lightly on the tops of your shoulders. Feel the temperature of your skin. Name silently the weights you suspect you are carrying - not as an exercise in worry, but as an act of recognition: this is the fear I have been carrying, this is the promise I have been sustaining, this is an old grief I keep holding. Notice where in the shoulder this naming lands. Does the left deepen? Does the right contract? Breathe into that place for three long, soft breaths. Each exhale is an opportunity to let go of story that is not required for the task at hand.

Then practice the art of strategic lowering. Lower does not mean dropping responsibility recklessly. It means releasing the unnecessary. Imagine a ledger in which you note all the tasks you perform because you believe you must. Now imagine that some of those tasks are assigned to a colleague, a family member, a system, or to life itself. Feel the surprising space as you imagine delegating a single item. Let your body sense the opening across the trapezius and the gentle descent of the shoulders. Do this repeatedly. It is a somatic retraining. Over time your nervous system will learn that releasing is not betrayal. It is clarity.

Another practice is the ritual of offering. When a burden arrives, physically place your hand on your shoulder, and say aloud, "I acknowledge this weight. I will hold what is mine with courage. I will offer back what is not mine with compassion." Say it like a vow of tenderness. Let the words seep into the tissue memory. Then imagine sending the surplus weight into the earth or into the hands of those who created it. This symbolic action trains the muscular and nervous systems to differentiate. You are not abandoning. You are aligning.

When the Shoulder Speaks Through Pain

There will be times when the body insists with unrelenting pain that you cannot ignore. A frozen shoulder, a tendonitis flare, a sudden sharpness when you reach across a table - these are urgent teachers. Slow down. Respect the language. Pain is not a proof of failure. It is an invitation to re-evaluate. Begin with medical discernment. Pain can be structural and require intervention. But also, take the pain as a question: what responsibility have I agreed to that is draining my life force? What old loyalty is anatomically fixed in my shoulder blades? Instead of asking only what to fix, ask what to forgive. Forgiveness of yourself and others is often the solvent that allows tissue to release.

In my work I have watched people reclaim enormous freedom when they learn to distinguish their obligations from others' expectations. One woman carried the relentless shoulder tension of her family’s shame for decades. She believed that to lighten her family’s burden she must carry it like a path to redemption. When she began to reassign certain responsibilities to her siblings and to stand in her own needs, the shoulder tension shifted along with her relationships. The transformation was not only physical. Choices that were previously impossible now felt doable. Shoulders that had been locked finally remembered how to reach and to receive.

The Gateway of Extension

When you stop overloading your shoulders, they become what they were designed to be - gateways, not prisons. Extension is not merely about reaching outward. It is about offering your presence into the world with integrity. You extend when you allow your hands to hold another without collapsing. You extend when you take a stand that is wise and measured rather than desperate and heavy. You extend when you receive a gift without encrusting gratitude with guilt. The shoulders teach you how to be a conduit rather than a barrier.

Here the Taoist line about softness and yielding returns. You are asked to cultivate a flexible strength - a pliability that is not weakness but exquisite responsiveness. When you are supple in your shoulders, you do not flail. You respond. You discern. You choose. The larger lesson is cosmic and tender: not everything that asks for carrying must be carried by you. This is the way of efficiency and grace. Let your shoulders remember movement as a sacred economy: what you lift you lift with intention; what you release you release with blessing.

Finally, remember that this is a practice that requires patience. The body does not change overnight. The nervous system needs repetition and evidence that safety is real. Give yourself the kindness of small, consistent acts of redistribution. Ask for help early and often. Learn to receive. Notice how the left shoulder loosens when you allow someone to hold you emotionally. Notice how the right shoulder softens when you permit tasks to be shared. These are the daily miracles, subtle and profound, that teach you how to live lightly within your responsibilities while remaining wholly available to love.

You are not merely a bearer of burdens. You are an instrument of clarity and a field of transformation. In tending your shoulders with curiosity, with Taoist wisdom of yielding and strength, with somatic practices of discernment and release, you will come to know a new posture - one that holds the world with a heart that is steady and hands that are free. In this posture you will find your true gateway of extension.

teachings.sourceTitle: Cold Hands, Warm Heart? The Emotional Truth in Your Fingers
teachings.title: Cold Hands, Warm Heart? The Emotional Truth in Your Fingers
teachings.summary: Susan explores how the hands act as embodied messengers of the heart, translating long-standing emotional patterns into sensations and symptoms. Through client stories and neurobiological framing she invites a compassionate listening to the body, offering a simple, grounding self-touch practice to begin a gentle dialogue with your hands. The piece emphasizes curiosity, nonjudgmental attention, and the idea that symptoms are communications rather than enemies. Healing is framed as an inner conversation that may unfold alongside other forms of care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I want to talk about the spaces between things — the pauses, the silences, the gaps where something new can emerge.

We navigate this world with the tools we are given, and perhaps none are more intimate to our experience than our hands. They are the first to reach, the first to feel, the first to build and to soothe. But what happens when the very instruments we use to engage with life begin to betray us?

A woman I’ll call Vivienne came to see me years ago, her hands wrapped in soft white cotton gloves. She was a potter, a creator whose greatest joy—and her livelihood—was the feeling of cool, wet clay spinning into form under her palms. But her hands had become her tormentors. When she slowly, painfully, peeled off the gloves, I saw the source of her despair: a raw, weeping eczema that covered her fingers and palms, angry and inflamed. The skin was broken, the landscape of her hands utterly changed. The slightest touch was an agony. She’d tried every cream, every diet, every specialist, from dermatologists to allergists. Nothing had touched it.

“I can’t handle it anymore, Susan,” she wept in our first session, and the double meaning of her words hung in the air between us. She couldn’t handle the relentless physical pain, the itching, the bleeding. But on a much deeper level, she was confessing a soul-level exhaustion. She felt she could no longer handle her life. A difficult marriage, a child struggling in school, the quiet desperation of a dream that felt like it was slipping away—it was all there, in her hands.

Her hands, those beautiful, creative instruments, were simply telling the truth of a heart that felt overwhelmed, raw, and unsafe. They had become the physical manifestation of a spirit that was itching to do something different, yet felt trapped.

## The Heart’s Emissaries

Have you ever stopped to truly consider your hands? Not just as tools, but as sacred extensions of your very core. In the energetic anatomy of the body, the hands are direct emissaries of the heart. They extend from the heart’s center, tasked with carrying its energy, its intentions, its love, out into the world through the power of touch, of gesture, of creation. They are how we give and how we receive. How we hold on, and how we let go.

When the flow of energy from the heart is open and trusting, our hands are soft, capable, and warm. But when the heart feels constricted, unsafe, or burdened, that energy is disrupted. The hands become the body’s sacred messengers, speaking a language of symptoms. Cold hands may signal a heart that has pulled its energy inward, a feeling of being “out of touch” with life or with love. Clenched fists can reflect a spirit bracing against a perceived threat. And conditions like Vivienne’s… they often speak of a profound conflict, an irritation with the circumstances we find ourselves in, a desperate, itching need for change that we feel powerless to enact.

This isn’t a judgment. It’s a beautiful, biological truth. Your body is always, *always* communicating with you, and it does so with the most profound love. It is a sacred messenger, and its symptoms are not enemies to be vanquished, but loving communications to be decoded. It is simply asking you to listen.

## The Neural Duet of Hand and Heart

This connection is not just poetry; it’s woven into our very neurobiology. The human brain devotes a stunning amount of real estate to the hands. If you were to look at a sensory map of the brain—what scientists call the homunculus—you would see a creature with enormous hands, lips, and tongue, because these areas are rich with nerve endings, constantly sending a flood of information back to the brain’s processing centers.

These neural pathways are not one-way streets. They are a constant, humming duet between sensation, action, and emotion. When you touch something, the sensation travels up your arm to your brain, which then cross-references this input with your emotional memory. Is this touch safe? Is it pleasurable? Is it threatening? The brain then sends a signal back down, instructing the hand on how to respond—to recoil, to soften, to grasp.

When we live in a state of chronic stress, anxiety, or emotional overwhelm—when we feel, like Vivienne, that we just can’t *handle* it—our nervous system gets locked in a state of high alert. This is the sympathetic “fight-or-flight” response, a brilliant survival mechanism designed for short-term threats. But when the “threat” is not a saber-toothed tiger but a constant, low-grade fear about finances, a difficult relationship, or a deep-seated feeling of inadequacy, the system never gets to switch off. The body is flooded with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline. Blood is shunted away from the extremities—the hands and feet—and redirected to the major muscle groups and vital organs, preparing the body for a danger that is perceived but not physically present. The result? Cold hands. A heart that feels unsafe literally pulls its warmth and energy back from the front lines of engagement with the world, conserving resources for a battle that is being waged internally.

Over time, these neural pathways become deeply grooved. The body *learns* that the world is a place that requires bracing, that touch is dangerous, that it’s not safe to reach out. The hands, in their infinite wisdom, simply reflect this learned state of being. They become the physical evidence of a heart pattern that has been running, often unconsciously, for a very long time.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Heavy Hand, A Closed Fist

I remember another client, a successful businessman named Robert, who came to me with debilitating arthritis in his hands. His fingers were gnarled, his joints swollen and painful. He spoke of his life with a kind of rigid pride. He had built his company from the ground up, priding himself on being a “strong hand” at the helm. He managed every detail, controlled every outcome. He was, in his own words, often “heavy-handed” with his employees and even his family.

As we worked together, a deeper story emerged, one that had been locked away even from himself. He told me of a childhood where life felt utterly chaotic and out of control. An alcoholic father, a mother lost in her own depression. He learned, in the way a child does, that the only way to feel a sliver of safety was to grip tightly to everything and everyone around him. To control the outcome. To manage the chaos. His hands, now locked into a painful, rigid clench, were a perfect mirror of the emotional and mental patterns he had used to survive. He was so afraid of life slipping through his fingers that he had created a closed fist, a posture of perpetual defense. And that clenching, that constant, unconscious tension held for decades, had finally crystallized into his very bones.

His body wasn’t punishing him. It was sending him a desperate, loving message. *Let go. It is safe to open now. You don’t have to handle everything alone. You don’t have to hold so tightly.*

The journey of healing for Robert, as for Vivienne, was not about finding a magic cream or a pill. It was about learning to listen to the story their hands were telling. It was about gently, compassionately turning toward the fear, the grief, and the old beliefs that had been running the show. It was about cultivating a new relationship with themselves, one based not on control, but on trust.

## An Invitation to Open

What would it be like, just for a moment, to befriend your own hands? To see them not as failing you, but as speaking to you?

Perhaps you might try this. It is a simple practice, but a profound one.

Find a quiet moment where you will not be disturbed. Sit comfortably in a chair, with your feet flat on the floor. Allow your spine to be long and graceful. Place one hand over the center of your chest, your heart space, and the other hand over your low belly. Close your eyes, or let your gaze soften.

For a few moments, just feel the gentle weight of your own hands on your body. Feel the warmth of your own touch. This is a powerful act of self-soothing, a signal to your nervous system that in this moment, you are safe. Breathe into that connection, a slow, deep inhale, and a long, soft exhale.

Now, bring your full, compassionate awareness to your hands. All of it. Any coolness, any warmth, any tingling, any stiffness, any pain. Don’t try to change a thing. Don’t judge it as ‘good’ or ‘bad’. Simply be with the reality of the sensation, as if you were a curious, loving scientist observing a fascinating phenomenon. Offer it your gentle, undivided attention.

As you continue to breathe, you might whisper to them, silently or out loud: *Thank you. Thank you for all that you do. Thank you for how you carry me through this world. Thank you for your messages. I am listening now.*

Stay with this for a few minutes. Notice what happens in your body. A softening, perhaps. A flicker of warmth spreading through your fingers. An emotion—grief, maybe, or anger, or a deep sadness—rising to the surface. If emotions come, just allow them. They are simply energy moving, old stories releasing. This is the beginning of a conversation. A conversation with the deep wisdom of your body, a wisdom that has been waiting for you to turn toward it with love.

Handling life beautifully isn’t about developing a stronger grip. It’s about cultivating a sensitive, responsive touch. It’s about learning to hold life with open palms, trusting that you can be with the full spectrum of experience—the joy, the sorrow, the beauty, the pain—without needing to clench against it. When we can do this, our hands cease to be instruments of fear and control. They become what they were always meant to be: instruments of grace, extending the infinite love of our own hearts into a world that so desperately needs that touch.

Your hands are not your enemy. They are the keepers of a deep truth, waiting patiently to be heard. Listen. They are showing you the way home to yourself.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


---

teachings.sourceTitle: Stuck, Uncertain, Afraid to Step Forward: What Your Feet Know
teachings.title: Stuck, Uncertain, Afraid to Step Forward: What Your Feet Know
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to recognize their feet as somatic messengers that can reflect emotional 'stuckness'—linking childhood patterns, nervous-system states, and life choices to sensations in the feet. She offers a gentle practice of listening and compassionate inquiry, and names neuroplasticity and building an internal secure base as pathways for change. The emphasis is on tending fear with curiosity rather than forcing movement.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
What would it be like to live one entire day without apology?

And sometimes, the most profound parts show up in the most ordinary places. Like our feet.

I remember a client from years ago, a brilliant woman, a CEO of a company she’d built from the ground up. She came to me complaining of a deep, searing pain in the arch of her left foot. Plantar fasciitis, the doctors had said. They’d given her orthotics, exercises, told her to rest. But the pain persisted, a sharp, insistent ache that made her first steps out of bed in the morning a study in agony.

As she spoke, I watched her feet, tucked neatly beside each other on the floor. They were beautiful feet, strong and elegant, but they were also incredibly still. Held. As if they were bracing for something. I asked her, “If your feet could speak, what would they say about your next step?”

She looked at me, her composure cracking just a little. Tears welled. “They’d say they’re terrified,” she whispered. “They’d say, ‘Don’t make us move. We don’t know where we’re going.’”

This is the secret language of our feet. They are our interface with the earth, our foundation, the very ground of our being. With 26 bones and a complex network of muscles, ligaments, and nerves, they are masterpieces of engineering designed for sensitivity and strength, flexibility and power. They are meant to carry us forward on our journey, to adapt to new terrain, to support us as we dance through the beautiful, messy, unpredictable choreography of life. But what happens when we’re afraid to take the next step?

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

Your body is a sacred messenger, and your feet are some of its most profound truth-tellers. When we feel stuck in a life situation—a relationship that no longer nourishes us, a job that feels like a dead end, a creative project that has stalled—that feeling of being “stuck” isn’t just a metaphor. It’s an energetic reality that can manifest physically, right down to the soles of our feet.

Think about the language we use. We get “cold feet.” We feel “lead-footed” when a task feels daunting. We worry about the ground crumbling “beneath our feet” when our sense of security is threatened. This isn’t a coincidence. Our bodies and our consciousness are inextricably woven together. The patterns in our lives are the patterns in our tissues. Our biography becomes our biology.

Foot pain, injuries, chronic tension… these are often the body’s way of communicating a deep internal conflict about our direction. There’s a part of us that knows it’s time to move, to step into the unknown, to leave the familiar shore. And there’s another part, often a much younger part, that is terrified. This part digs its heels in. It wants to stay put, where it’s safe. The resulting pain is the friction between these two opposing forces. It’s the physical manifestation of your inner war.

I see this so often in my practice. The ankle that twists right before a big move. The bunion that aches when family conflict arises. The neuropathy that numbs the feet, disconnecting a person from their very foundation, when life feels too overwhelming to feel. I worked with a young man once whose feet were so cold, they were almost blue, even in the summer. He was a gifted artist, but he was frozen, unable to take the steps to put his work out into the world. His feet were literally embodying his fear of stepping into the spotlight, of being seen. The energy, the life force, had simply stopped flowing to his foundation.

## The Neural Pathways of ‘Stuckness’

From a neuroscience perspective, this makes perfect sense. Our brains are wired for survival. When we have experiences, especially in childhood, that teach us that moving forward is dangerous or that we won’t be supported if we take a risk, we create deep neural pathways. These pathways, coated in a fatty substance called myelin, become our brain’s superhighways. They become our default setting. The brain learns: *new direction = danger; staying put = safety.*

This isn’t just a mental state; it’s a physiological one. These early experiences tune our autonomic nervous system. The sympathetic nervous system—our “fight or flight” response—becomes chronically activated. The body is constantly on high alert, ready for a threat that may no longer exist. The muscles in our legs and feet remain subtly tensed, ready to flee or freeze. The energy of the body is directed away from restorative functions and toward hypervigilance. This is exhausting. And it makes the idea of taking a deliberate, relaxed step forward feel almost impossible.

This is particularly true for those of us who didn’t feel a secure sense of support in our early lives. A child who grows up in an environment of instability or criticism, who doesn’t have a safe base to return to, often develops issues with their feet. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is trying to create the stability that is missing externally. The feet might turn inward, the arches might collapse, the toes might grip for dear life. The body is trying to anchor itself to the ground because the relational ground feels so shaky.

These patterns, laid down in childhood, don’t just disappear. They become the unconscious blueprint for how we move through life. As adults, we might find ourselves hesitating on the brink of a great opportunity, sabotaging a new relationship, or simply feeling a pervasive sense of being mired in mud, unable to move forward. We are, in a very real sense, still that child, with feet that learned it wasn’t safe to take the next step.

But here is the beautiful, hopeful truth: you are not broken. You have never been broken. And those neural pathways? They are not set in stone. Through the miracle of neuroplasticity, we can create new ones. By bringing gentle, consistent, loving awareness to our bodies, we can begin to signal to our nervous system that we are safe *now*. We can activate the parasympathetic nervous system—our “rest and digest” state—and teach our bodies, and our brains, a new story.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## What Your Feet Know

So, what would it be like to befriend your feet? To listen to their story not with judgment, but with a deep and gentle curiosity? Our feet have carried us through our entire lives. They have walked on holy ground and hard pavement. They have danced and stumbled. They deserve our reverence.

I invite you to try a little experiment. Find a quiet moment to sit down and simply be with your feet. If you can, take off your shoes and socks. Place your hands on them. Feel their temperature, their texture. Are they warm or cold? Tense or relaxed? Simply notice, without needing to change a thing. Acknowledge them. Thank them for the journey they have carried you on so far.

Now, bring your awareness to any places of discomfort or pain. Instead of recoiling from the sensation, see if you can breathe into it. Imagine you are sending your breath, like a wave of warm, loving attention, directly to that spot. And then, ask it a question. You might ask:

> *What are you trying to tell me?*
> *What are you afraid of?*
> *What do you need to feel safe enough to move forward?*
> *Whose path are you trying to walk? And what is your own?*

Don’t search for an answer with your mind. Just listen. Listen with your whole being. The answer might come as a word, an image, a memory, or just a subtle shift in sensation. It might not come right away, and that’s okay. The practice is in the listening. It’s in the turning *towards* your body’s wisdom, rather than away from it. It’s a practice of profound respect for the intelligence that lives in your very cells.

This is the beginning of a new relationship with yourself. A relationship grounded in compassion and presence. When we stop treating our body’s messages as problems to be fixed and start hearing them as sacred communications from our soul, everything begins to shift. The pain in your foot is not an enemy. It is a beloved messenger, pointing you back to a part of yourself that is longing for your attention, your love, your support.

It’s showing you where the foundation needs to be rebuilt, not from the outside in, but from the inside out. It’s inviting you to become your own secure base. To learn to whisper to that frightened inner child, “I’ve got you. We can do this together. One small, uncertain, beautiful step at a time.”

My client, the CEO with the aching foot? She began to listen. She realized her terror wasn’t about her business, which was thriving. It was about her personal life. She had been wanting to leave her marriage for years but was terrified of stepping out on her own, of the ground crumbling beneath her feet. Her foot pain was the voice of that fear. As she began to gently acknowledge it, to get support, to build a foundation of self-compassion, the pain began to subside. She eventually took that step, not with a sudden leap, but with a quiet, grounded certainty. Her feet, finally feeling supported from within, were ready to carry her.

This is how we transform. Not by forcing ourselves forward, but by tending to the parts of us that are afraid to move. By grounding ourselves in the unwavering support of the earth beneath us and the unwavering love of the consciousness within us. We learn to be both lead-footed and fleet-footed—grounded and free. We learn to trust that the next step will always be revealed, right when we need it.


---

May you walk in grace, may you trust your footing, and may you feel the solid ground of your own being rising up to meet you with every step.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Alchemical Cauldron: What Your Stomach Is Digesting
teachings.title: The Alchemical Cauldron: What Your Stomach Is Digesting
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard the stomach as an alchemical cauldron where not only food but emotions and experiences are metabolized. She traces the gut–brain dialogue, describes how chronic stress and unspoken feeling can create physical symptoms, and offers compassionate, embodied practices—presence, breath, movement, sound, and journaling—to begin gently transmuting undigested experiences into wisdom. The piece emphasizes patience, self-compassion, and the development of new neural pathways of safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The old farmhouse table was laden with my grandmother’s Sunday roast—potatoes glistening with butter, carrots sweetened by the long, slow heat, and a chicken so tender it surrendered at the mere suggestion of a fork. But what I remember most vividly from those dinners is the silence. It was a heavy, thick silence, a presence of its own at the table. It was the silence of unspoken resentments, of worries swallowed down with mouthfuls of gravy, of griefs tucked away so neatly they were nearly invisible. My grandfather would clear his throat, a sound like grinding stones, and my stomach, a child’s stomach, would clench in response. I learned early that some things are not meant for the dinner table, and that some things, once swallowed, sit like stones in the belly for a lifetime.

What if I told you that your stomach is far more than a simple digestive organ? That it is, in fact, a powerful alchemical cauldron, a sacred space where the world outside of you is transformed into the very substance of you. It’s a crucible, working with potent acids and enzymes to break down, to transmute, to turn the external into life-giving energy. This is a process of profound surrender and trust. We take in something from the world, and we trust our body to know what to do with it—to separate nutrient from waste, to build us up, cell by precious cell.

And yet, we only seem to apply this understanding to food. We rarely consider that our psychological and emotional experiences require the very same process of digestion. Every conversation, every news headline, every interaction, every memory—it all enters our system. It, too, must be metabolized. And the stomach, with its deep intelligence and its intimate connection to our emotional brain, is often where this secondary digestion takes place. Have you ever felt that pit in your stomach before a difficult conversation? Or the queasy, sour feeling that accompanies a betrayal? That is your body, speaking its truth. That is the alchemical cauldron, bubbling with an experience it is struggling to process.

The language we use is so revealing, isn’t it? “I can’t stomach that,” we say. “That news just made me sick.” “I’m having trouble digesting this information.” This isn’t mere metaphor, beloved. This is your body’s deep wisdom, communicating through the felt sense. The gut-brain axis is a stunningly real and intricate superhighway of information, with the vagus nerve acting as a primary channel. Your thoughts and emotions are constantly sending signals southward, and the state of your gut is sending equally potent signals northward. When we are in a state of chronic stress, fear, or anxiety, the brain floods our system with cortisol. This isn’t just a mental experience; it’s a full-body event. That cortisol can inhibit the production of stomach acid, slow the emptying of the stomach, and even alter the delicate microbiome that is essential for not just physical health, but for mental and emotional balance. An ulcer, the searing pain of indigestion, the chronic bloat—these are not random malfunctions. They are often a desperate plea from a body that is being asked to digest the indigestible. This enteric nervous system, often called our “second brain,” is lined with millions of neurons that are in constant dialogue with the brain in our head. It’s a profoundly intelligent system, capable of learning, remembering, and producing feelings. When we experience trauma or chronic stress, the neural pathways in our gut can become deeply grooved, just like in the brain. The stomach learns to clench at the first sign of emotional threat. It learns to overproduce acid in anticipation of conflict. It learns to shut down when the world feels too overwhelming. We are not just thinking our stress; we are embodying it, and the stomach is often on the front lines, a faithful soldier bearing the brunt of our inner wars. Healing, then, is not about punishing the body or forcing it into submission. It is about creating new neural pathways of safety and peace, both in our minds and in the very real, very intelligent brain in our gut.

Think of the experiences you’ve swallowed whole. The anger you choked down in the face of injustice to keep the peace. The grief that felt too vast to express, so you packed it away, deep in your tissues. The fear that you were told was irrational, so you pretended it wasn’t there. These experiences do not simply vanish. They remain within us as energetic density, as undigested fragments of life. They churn in that sacred cauldron, creating a low-grade internal fermentation. This is the ‘sickness’ we feel. It’s the body saying, “I cannot transmute this. I cannot turn this into life force. It is sitting here, like a stone.” Every pattern, even this one, has served you. Swallowing your truth may have kept you safe in a childhood home where emotional expression was dangerous. It may have been a necessary strategy for survival. But now, perhaps, it is time to ask if that pattern is still serving your highest evolution.

I remember a time, years ago, when I was navigating a particularly painful ending to a friendship. The sense of betrayal felt enormous, a jagged pill I couldn’t seem to swallow. For weeks, I had a persistent, low-grade nausea. Food was unappealing. My whole digestive system felt sluggish and heavy. I was, quite literally, sick with grief and anger. One afternoon, sitting in meditation, I brought my awareness to the discomfort, to that constant, sour churning. And what arose was not a thought, but an image: a tangled knot of thick, black rope in the center of my stomach. Instead of recoiling, I simply stayed with it. I breathed into it. And slowly, over many days of returning to this practice, I began to see that the knot was woven from my own unspoken words, my unexpressed boundaries, my uncried tears. The nausea was the physical manifestation of all the energy I was using to keep that knot bound tight. Gently, compassionately, I began to allow the threads to loosen. It wasn’t a dramatic unraveling, but a slow, tender process of allowing the feelings to be felt, the tears to be shed, the anger to be acknowledged in the safety of my own presence. And as the emotional energy began to move, the physical symptoms, in their own time, began to recede.

What would it be like to approach these stored experiences not as poison, but as medicine? To trust that even the most challenging, bitter, and painful moments of our lives contain nutrients for our soul’s evolution? This is the work of the alchemist. The alchemist does not shy away from the lead; they see it as the very substance of gold. They understand that transformation requires a crucible, that it requires heat, and that it requires a willingness to be with what is, in all its intensity. The lead of shame, for instance, when met with the heat of radical self-compassion, can be transformed into the gold of humility and self-acceptance. The lead of deep-seated fear, when held in the crucible of presence, can become the gold of wisdom and inner strength. Your stomach is the vessel for this profound work. It holds the raw materials. Your awareness is the flame. It is a sacred and powerful process, turning the heaviest parts of your story into the most luminous aspects of your being.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

Beginning this alchemical process is a gentle act. It begins with awareness, with bringing a soft, compassionate presence to the sensations in your body. When you feel that familiar clenching in your solar plexus, what if, instead of ignoring it or wishing it away, you simply paused? You might place a warm hand on your belly. You might breathe into the sensation, not to force it to change, but simply to acknowledge it. “I feel you. I know you are there.” This simple act of loving presence is a powerful balm. It’s like adding a soothing liquid to a boiling pot, allowing the contents to settle.

From this place of presence, you can begin to gently inquire. You might ask your stomach, “Beloved, what are you holding for me right now? What experience is asking to be seen?” The answer may not come in words. It may come as an image, a memory, a feeling. A flash of a face. The echo of a long-forgotten phrase. The key is to not judge what arises. Your only task is to witness. To allow. This is how we begin to metabolize our lives on an emotional level. We offer the undigested morsels the one thing they never received: our compassionate, non-judgmental attention. Perhaps you might try journaling, letting the words flow without censorship, giving voice to the parts of you that were silenced. What does the anger want to say? What does the grief need to express? Another beautiful practice is movement. Put on a piece of music that resonates with the feeling in your belly and allow your body to move. Let it shake, sway, stretch, or curl. The body holds the score, and it knows how to release it if we give it permission and a safe container. Sound can also be a powerful tool for transmutation. You don’t need to be a singer; simply allowing a hum to vibrate in your chest and belly, or even a sigh, a groan, or a shout into a pillow can begin to break up the energetic density. These are not about ‘getting rid of’ the feeling, but about allowing the trapped energy to finally complete its circuit and flow.

Consider, too, the concept of developing a palate for the full spectrum of life. We’ve been conditioned to crave only the sweet: happiness, joy, ease, success. We are taught to fear and reject the bitter, the sour, the salty: grief, anger, failure, disappointment. But a mature palate, like a mature soul, understands that wholeness requires all the flavors. Bitterness can cleanse. Sourness can awaken. Saltiness can preserve. When we consciously allow ourselves to taste the bitterness of our sorrow, without letting it consume us, we are cleansing our emotional body. When we permit the sour tang of our righteous anger to move through us, we are awakening to our boundaries and our truth. We are developing the capacity to digest the entirety of our human experience, trusting that every last bit of it can be transformed into wisdom and compassion.

This is a journey, not a destination. It is the practice of a lifetime. It is learning to trust the incredible intelligence of your body. It is choosing to believe that you are not broken, but are, in fact, a masterful alchemist in training. The stomach, this cauldron of transformation, is your partner in this sacred work. It is constantly speaking to you, guiding you, inviting you to look deeper at what you are taking in—not just at your dinner table, but in your life. It invites you to ask: What am I feeding myself? What am I refusing to digest? And what would it be like to finally, lovingly, metabolize it all?

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Gut–brain axis and the enteric nervous system
