teachings.sourceTitle: Unwinding the Body's Story: How Fascia Holds Our History
teachings.title: Unwinding the Body's Story: How Fascia Holds Our History
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard fascia not as inert tissue but as a living, three‑dimensional matrix that stores the imprints of our physical and emotional history. Through gentle, present-centered craniosacral work and mindful self-practices, the body can be supported to ‘unwind’ held tension, shift nervous-system state, and recover ease. The piece offers practical ways to begin listening — body-scanning, gentle movement, and mindful touch — while emphasizing safety, presence, and non‑forcing as the conditions for release.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this body of ours. We inhabit it, we move through the world with it, it is the only true home we will ever know—and yet, for the most part, we remain strangers to its deepest conversations. We feel an ache here, a tension there, a sudden wave of fatigue that washes over us, and we might reach for a painkiller, or another cup of coffee, pushing the body’s whispers to the background so we can get on with the business of living. But what if those whispers are not interruptions? What if they are invitations? What if they are the opening lines of a story only you can tell? For years, in my practice as a craniosacral therapist and in my own journey of healing, I have been in a deep and reverent dialogue with the body’s most intimate storytelling medium: the fascia. It is a word that might be new to you, or perhaps you’ve heard it in a yoga class or a physical therapist’s office. But I invite you to know it in a new way. Not as a clinical term, but as a living, breathing part of your own sacred text. ## The Living Library Within Imagine a substance so pervasive that it touches every other part of you. A silvery-white, crystalline web that wraps and weaves through every muscle, every bone, every organ, every nerve, every blood vessel, right down to the cellular level. This is fascia. It is not a collection of separate sheaths, but one single, uninterrupted, three-dimensional matrix that holds your shape and allows you to move. The anatomists of old used to dismiss it, cutting it away to get to what they considered the “important” structures. But we are now beginning to understand, through the lens of modern neuroscience and quantum physics, what the ancient wisdom traditions have always known: this connective tissue is, in fact, a primary organ of communication. > Your fascia is a liquid-crystalline matrix, capable of receiving, storing, and transmitting information at the speed of light. It is, in essence, a living record of your history, holding the imprints of every fall, every fright, every moment of bracing against life. Think of it. The time you fell off your bike as a child, the shock of the impact reverberating through your small frame. The way you held your breath during a difficult conversation, your shoulders tightening, your jaw clenching. The slow, creeping tension of sitting at a desk day after day, your body subtly adapting to the posture of stress. These are not just memories stored in your brain. They are experiences stored in your fascia. The tissue, in its intelligence, tightens and thickens around these points of impact—physical or emotional—to protect you. It forms a kind of internal armor. And while this armor is brilliant in the short term, over time it can create patterns of restriction, pain, and disconnection. ## A Personal Encounter I remember a client I worked with years ago, a woman in her late forties who came to me with chronic, debilitating neck pain. She had tried everything—massage, chiropractic, physiotherapy—with only temporary relief. As I gently placed my hands on her head and neck, tuning into the subtle rhythms of her system, I felt an immense density, a profound lack of movement in the tissues at the base of her skull. It felt… ancient. And sad. I didn’t push or force. I simply listened with my hands, offering a sense of safety and presence. And slowly, a story began to emerge. Not in words, but in sensation. A memory surfaced for her, one she hadn’t thought of in decades. She was five years old, in the hospital for a tonsillectomy, and she was terrified. She remembered the feeling of being held down as the anesthesia mask was placed over her face, the sense of utter powerlessness, the desperate fight in her small body. As she shared this, I could feel the tissue under my hands begin to soften, to release, to *unwind*. It was as if this 40-year-old story, held in the frozen landscape of her fascia, was finally being heard. By the end of our session, the pain was gone. More importantly, she felt a sense of coming home to herself she hadn’t realized was missing. This is the power of working with the body’s story. It is not about “fixing” a problem. It is about creating the conditions of safety and presence required for the body to release what it has been holding. It is about honoring the incredible intelligence that has been protecting you all these years. ## The Science of Unwinding What is happening in these moments of release? From a neuroscience perspective, we are shifting the nervous system out of a sympathetic “fight-or-flight” state and into a parasympathetic “rest-and-digest” state. When we are stressed or traumatized, the amygdala—the brain’s smoke detector—is on high alert, signaling the fascia to tighten and the body to brace. Gentle, sustained, mindful touch communicates safety to the nervous system. It says, *“You are safe now. You can let go.”* This sense of safety allows the ground substance of the fascia—a gel-like substance that is normally fluid—to soften and become more liquid. This is the “unwinding” we feel. It’s a literal change of state, a melting of the frozen patterns. As the tissue releases, it frees up nerves that were compressed, improves blood flow and lymphatic drainage, and restores a sense of ease and fluidity to the entire system. It’s a profound act of self-regulation, guided by the body’s own innate wisdom. This reminds me of the wisdom of the Tao Te Ching, which often speaks of the power of water, of softness, of yielding. It says, “The supreme good is like water, which nourishes all things without trying to.” In the same way, healing the fascia is not about forcing change, but about creating the space for the body’s own intelligence to flow, to soften what is rigid, and to find its way back to wholeness. ## Your Invitation to Listen So how can you begin to listen to the story your own fascia is telling, beloved one? It begins with presence. With turning your attention inward, not with an agenda to fix, but with a gentle curiosity. * **Body Scan:** Lie down comfortably and bring your awareness to your body. Notice where you feel tension, tightness, or holding. Don’t judge it. Just notice. Breathe into those spaces with kindness. * **Gentle Movement:** Explore slow, mindful movements. Stretching, yoga, or simply rocking gently. Notice the feeling of the tissues gliding over one another. Where is there ease? Where is there restriction? Move with the intention of exploration, not accomplishment. * **Mindful Touch:** Place your own hands on an area of your body that feels tense or sore. Don’t press or knead. Just rest your hands there, offering warmth and presence. Imagine your breath flowing into that area, bringing with it a sense of spaciousness and care. This is not a quick fix. It is a practice. A lifelong conversation with my friend that is your body. It is the slow, sacred work of unwinding the stories held within, not to erase them, but to integrate them, to transform them from sources of pain into sources of wisdom and strength. Your body has been waiting for you. It has been whispering its stories in the language of sensation. Are you ready to listen?

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan
keyThemes: Fascia as a continuous, information-bearing matrix that holds physical and emotional memory
The body as storyteller: sensations as invitations rather than problems to be fixed
Unwinding through safety and presence — shifting from sympathetic to parasympathetic states
Craniosacral/mindful touch as a non‑coercive doorway to release and integration
Practice over time: curiosity, self‑compassion, and slow exploration
reflectionPrompts: Recall a moment when your body braced or went still (big or small). What sensations arise now when you bring that memory to mind, and where in the body do you notice them?
Where in your daily posture or habitual movement do you notice restriction or ‘armor’? What has that pattern protected you from, and what might it be inviting you to learn?
When you place one hand on a place of tension, what emotions, images, or subtle shifts come forward? How does offering presence (rather than trying to fix) change your experience?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a comfortable, supported position lying on your back or seated with good back support. Take three slow, soft breaths to arrive. Place one or both hands gently over an area that feels tight or held (no pressure). For 3–5 minutes, breathe kindly into that place and rest your attention there; notice sensations, warmth, subtle shifts, or nothing at all. If you feel increased pain, dizziness, or distress, stop and consult your healthcare provider. This simple, gentle presence is a supportive complement to — not a replacement for — medical or therapeutic care.
sensitiveContentNotes: The article includes themes of medical/childhood fear, powerlessness, and bodily-held trauma; these can evoke strong feelings or memories.

You have full permission to pause the practice at any time, step away, or shorten the invitation. If memories or sensations feel overwhelming, consider reaching out to a trusted therapist, bodyworker, or medical professional for support.
If you are in acute pain, have recent injury, or ongoing medical concerns, seek guidance from qualified healthcare providers before attempting bodywork or self-touch practices.

teachings.sourceTitle: Why We Hold On: Understanding the Wisdom of Our Defenses
teachings.title: Why We Hold On: Understanding the Wisdom of Our Defenses
teachings.summary: Susan reframes habitual defenses—not as flaws to banish but as intelligent survival strategies forged by a younger nervous system. She invites a compassionate practice of noticing, acknowledging, and appreciating these protective parts so the body can gradually soften and new neural pathways of safety and self-compassion can form. The piece links nervous-system patterning to lived bodily sensations and offers an embodied path of re-parenting rather than forceful eradication of responses.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I once watched a butterfly emerge from its chrysalis, and it took nearly an hour.

For years, I had a peculiar habit. Whenever I felt overwhelmed or anxious, I would find myself meticulously organizing my bookshelves. Not just tidying, but a full-scale excavation. Books off the shelves, dusted, sorted by genre, then author, then—if the anxiety was particularly potent—by color. My partner would find me there, hours later, surrounded by stacks of paper and ink, the scent of old pages in the air. I’d be lost in a task that was both utterly pointless and, in some mysterious way, deeply soothing. My mind, which moments before had been a storm of worry, would be quiet, focused only on the crisp edges of a hardcover or the smooth spine of a paperback. For a long time, I saw it as a flaw. A silly, time-wasting tic. Another way I was failing to be productive or “properly” manage my stress. It was a secret shame, this compulsion to order the inanimate when my inner world was in disarray.

And then, one day, a new question arose, soft as a whisper. Not, *Why do I do this strange thing?* but, *What is the wisdom in this? What is this trying to do for me?*

The answer, when it came, was a revelation. In a moment of chaos, my system had found a way to create order. In a world that felt too big and too fast, it had found a small, manageable corner and made it coherent. It was a defense. And it was, in its own way, brilliant.

We all have them, don’t we? These patterns, these habits, these ways of being that we’ve carried for so long we can’t remember a time without them. The reflexive apology. The clenching of the jaw in a difficult conversation. The need to be the “good one,” the helper, the one who never needs a thing. The tendency to retreat into stony silence when hurt, building a fortress brick by silent brick.

We often treat these parts of ourselves as enemies. We declare war on our procrastination, our anxiety, our people-pleasing. We try to excise them, to discipline them into submission, to hustle and grind our way to a more “evolved” version of ourselves. We believe that if we could just get *rid* of these tendencies, we would finally be free.

But what if I told you that every single one of those defenses was created, with exquisite intelligence, to protect you? What if every pattern you now judge as a weakness was once your most ingenious strategy for survival?

## The Well-Worn Path

Here’s a very good thing to know. Our brain is a marvel of efficiency. It is designed to conserve energy, and one of the primary ways it does this is by creating and reinforcing neural pathways. Think of it like a path through a forest. The first time you walk it, you have to push through branches and high grass. It’s slow, and it takes a lot of energy. But if you walk that same path every day, the grass gets trampled down, the branches are pushed aside, and soon, a clear, easy trail emerges. Your brain loves this. It loves the well-worn path.

When we are young, our brains are extraordinarily plastic, rapidly forming these pathways based on our experiences. This is the essence of neuroplasticity—the brain’s ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections. If, as a child, crying out for help led to punishment, dismissal, or simply being ignored, the brain, in its incredible wisdom, forges a pathway: *It is not safe to show vulnerability. To be safe, I must be silent and self-reliant.* This isn't a thought; it's a somatic, cellular-level conclusion. If being perfect and achieving was the only way to receive the warmth of love and approval, a super-highway gets paved in the neural landscape: *My worth is conditional. I must perform to be loved.* Every 'A' on a report card, every compliment for being 'the good girl,' deepens that groove.

These are not conscious decisions. They are brilliant, lightning-fast adaptations made by a young nervous system trying to navigate its world and secure its connection to its caregivers—a connection that, for a child, is synonymous with life itself. The patterns that result—the hyper-independence, the perfectionism, the fear of taking up space—are not character flaws. They are artifacts of love. They are the legacy of a younger self who did everything in its power to stay safe and loved in the world it knew.

And so, years later, even when the original danger has long passed, the brain, by default, continues to send its electrical signals down that familiar, energy-efficient path. The adult who is now in a safe, loving partnership still finds it almost impossible to ask for help, because the neural pathway for hyper-independence is a six-lane expressway, while the path for receiving support is an overgrown trail in the woods. The well-worn trail of “I’m fine, I don’t need anything” is so much quicker and requires so much less metabolic energy for the brain than bushwhacking a new path of “This is hard, and I need support.” The old defense, created to protect, becomes a cage—a comfortable, familiar cage, but a cage nonetheless.

## The Body as a Living Archive

And these patterns don’t just live in our thoughts. They are held, archived, and expressed in the very tissues of our bodies. The body keeps the score, always. It is the living library of our every experience.

That feeling of “carrying the weight of the world” might manifest as the chronically tight, burdened shoulders that ache with a responsibility that was never truly yours to carry. The unspoken words, the truths you swallowed for fear of conflict, can become a tightness in the throat, a clenching in the jaw, a feeling that you don’t have a voice.

> In my work with The Elevated Body cards, we see this beautiful, heartbreaking wisdom written into the body’s tissues. The hips and legs, our foundation for moving through the world, can become rigid and painful when we are inflexible in our approach to life, when we feel we don’t have a “leg to stand on.” The stomach, that alchemical cauldron designed to transform what we take in, can burn with indigestion or ulcers when we are forced to stomach experiences that feel fundamentally unjust or untrue. Even the immune system, our guardian of identity, can become confused in this inner conflict, sometimes turning on the self in an autoimmune response—the ultimate crisis of identity, where the body can no longer distinguish between 'self' and 'other' because we have spent a lifetime contorting our 'self' to please an 'other'.

Your body is not betraying you with these symptoms. It is speaking to you. It is pointing, with loving precision, to the places where these old, protective patterns are stored. The pain in your back is not the enemy; it is a messenger from a younger you who learned to brace against impact. The anxiety in your chest is not a malfunction; it is the echo of a time when hyper-vigilance was necessary for survival.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## From Judgment to Reverence

So, what do we do? If we cannot fight these patterns into submission, how do we find freedom?

We begin by shifting our stance from judgment to reverence. We lay down our weapons and approach these wounded, protective parts of ourselves with a gentle curiosity. We learn to honor them.

This is not a passive surrender. It is a deeply conscious and courageous act of spiritual maturity. It is the practice of turning toward the defense, instead of away from it. It’s a process that unfolds in layers, with infinite patience.

First, there is the **Notice**. You simply begin to notice, without judgment, when a defense is activated. The urge to apologize for your existence. The immediate “yes” when your body is screaming “no.” The tightening in your solar plexus when your boss speaks to you in a certain tone. You just watch. *Ah, there it is. The clenching in my jaw.*

Second, there is the **Acknowledge**. You name it, gently. *This is my protector part. This is the part that learned it needs to be small to be safe.* You are not the pattern; you are the awareness that is noticing the pattern. This distinction is everything.

Third, there is the **Appreciate**. This is where the reverence comes in. You actively thank this part of you. You might place a hand on your heart, or wherever you feel the sensation in your body, and send it a wave of gratitude. *Thank you for working so hard to keep me safe for so long. I see how exhausted you are. I appreciate your vigilance.*

Instead of chastising yourself, you can pause. Take a breath. And ask, with genuine warmth:

*Hello, old friend. I see you.*
*I know you are here to protect me. What are you afraid would happen if you didn’t do your job right now?*
*Thank you for working so hard to keep me safe for so long.*

When you meet a defense with this kind of consistent, embodied compassion, something miraculous happens. It begins to soften. The energy that was locked up in maintaining that rigid posture begins to release. The clenched fist of a terrified child cannot be pried open by force. But it may, in the presence of unwavering love and safety, choose to unfurl on its own, finger by finger. This is not a one-time event. It is a relationship you build with yourself, moment by moment, breath by breath.

This is the work of creating internal safety. It is letting the younger parts of you know, through your consistent, loving presence, that the war is over. You are grown now. You have resources you didn’t have then. You can protect yourself in new ways. You can handle rejection. You can survive disapproval. You can learn to give and receive support.

You are, in essence, re-parenting yourself. You are building a new neural pathway—a pathway of self-compassion and trust. And every time you choose this new path, you make it a little clearer, a little easier to walk next time.

This is the gentle art of transformation. Not through force, but through love. Not by getting rid of parts of yourself, but by integrating them into a more spacious and compassionate whole. It is understanding that the very things you thought were your greatest flaws were, in fact, your most sacred wisdom in disguise.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you learn to honor the brilliant strategies that have brought you this far. And may you, with infinite gentleness, lay down the old burdens and walk forward into the fullness of who you are now.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
keyThemes: Defenses as adaptive wisdom rather than personal failure
Neuroplasticity and the energy-efficiency of habitual neural paths
The body as an archive that holds emotional history
Gentle, relational approaches to inner parts (notice → acknowledge → appreciate)
Re-parenting the self and building internal safety
Integration over eradication — transformation through compassion
reflectionPrompts: Name a habitual response you have (e.g., people-pleasing, silence, perfectionism). What survival purpose might that response have served in your younger life?
When that pattern shows up now, where do you feel it in your body? Describe the physical sensations, any images or memories that arise, and how your breath shifts.
If you could speak directly to the part of you that developed that defense, what might you say first to acknowledge its service and offer it one small reassurance?
teachings.practiceInvitation: For 3–5 minutes, find a quiet seat and place one hand where you feel the sensation most strongly (heart, throat, belly, shoulders). Breathe slowly and simply notice the sensation without trying to change it. Silently name the impulse you observe (e.g., “protecting,” “small to be safe”), then place your other hand over the first and offer a brief sentence of gratitude—“Thank you for keeping me safe.” Finish by imagining one small message of reassurance you can offer this part (e.g., “You are seen; I am here”) and take one calming exhale. If you become overwhelmed or notice worrying physical symptoms, pause and contact a trusted mental-health or medical professional—this practice is complementary and not a substitute for professional care.
sensitiveContentNotes: The article discusses childhood survival strategies, patterns born of past hurt, and may evoke memories of neglect, abandonment, or emotional pain.
You have full permission to pause any reflection or practice if it feels too intense; grounding or reaching out to a trusted person can be helpful.
If reflection or bodily sensations bring up significant distress, flashbacks, or physical symptoms, consider connecting with a qualified therapist, counselor, or medical provider for support.

teachings.sourceTitle: Healing the Mother Wound Through Your Body's Wisdom
teachings.title: Healing the Mother Wound Through Your Body's Wisdom
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to trace how unmet maternal nourishment can lodge in the body—particularly in the breasts—and to recognize those sensations as communicating a need rather than a fault. The piece offers a compassionate, body-based practice for 'mothering' oneself, encourages reclaiming creativity as a form of nourishment, and frames healing as rewiring the nervous system through repeated self-compassionate responses.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Something beautiful happens when we finally stop fighting ourselves.

And it’s perhaps an even more revealing business being a daughter.

Many of us have experienced moments that suddenly connect us to our past in a powerful way. A quiet moment after a family interaction, a particular quality of silence, or an unexpected wave of emotion can bring to the surface feelings that are old and familiar. These feelings often point to a deeper pattern, a hollow ache in the center of the chest, a sense of reaching for something that simply isn't there. This can be the echo of our own upbringing, the legacy of our relationship with our own mothers.

This is the landscape of what many now call the “mother wound.” It’s a complex terrain of love and loss, of longing and resentment. It’s the grief for the mothering we didn’t receive, whether our mothers were physically absent, emotionally distant, or simply human beings struggling with their own unhealed wounds. And so often, this wound makes its home in our bodies. It’s not just a story we tell ourselves; it’s a biological reality. Our cells hold the memory of that early-life lack. And specifically, it can settle in the soft, sacred tissue of our breasts.

Our breasts, in the language of the body, are the archetypal symbol of nurture. They are designed to feed, to comfort, to sustain life. They are the biological extension of the mothering principle. When our experience of being mothered has left us feeling unnourished, unseen, or unsafe, our breasts can reflect that depletion. They can become tender, cystic, or even develop more serious conditions. These are not punishments. They are communications. Your body, in its infinite wisdom, is sending you a message, asking you to come home to yourself. It’s a sacred invitation to finally give yourself the nourishment you’ve always craved.

## The River and the Source

It is a common pattern for so many people, especially women, to believe that their value lies in being a boundless river of giving. The role of mother, partner, or caregiver can come with an unspoken expectation to pour oneself out for others. This is often mistaken for love. But giving from a place of depletion means running on a finite source, and the body keeps the score. This can lead to a persistent, low-grade exhaustion, a subtle resentment simmering just beneath the surface, and physical manifestations of the ache in the heart, such as breast tenderness.

What is essential to understand, for our own healing and in supporting others, is that we are not meant to be self-contained reservoirs of love. We are meant to be channels. A healthy river doesn’t try to generate its own water; it is fed by a vast, inexhaustible source. For us, that source is the universal wellspring of love, of life force, of consciousness itself. Our primary responsibility is not to give to others, but to keep our own channel to that source clear and open.

When we try to nurture others from an empty cup, we inevitably create what I call “energetic scar tissue.” Hard lumps of crystallized grief for the love we didn’t get. Pockets of resentment for the sacrifices we made. A deep, often unconscious, belief that we must over-give to be worthy of love. This is the mother wound playing out in our biology. The neural pathways laid down in childhood—the ones that learned “I must take care of others to be safe” or “My needs don’t matter”—continue to fire, keeping our nervous systems in a state of low-grade threat and our bodies in a state of depletion. This isn't a metaphor. This is neuroscience. The repeated firing of these stress-related pathways strengthens them, creating a default state of anxiety and burnout. Your body is literally stuck in a pattern of survival, even when the original threat is long gone.

Healing this wound is not about blaming our mothers. They, too, were daughters, inheriting their own legacy of lack. It is about taking radical responsibility for our own nourishment. It is about learning to mother ourselves with the tenderness and fierce compassion we always longed for.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Nurturing Your Creative Selfhood

An essential part of this self-mothering is the nurturing of our own creativity. So often, the mother wound is passed down through generations of women who were disconnected from their own creative fire. They poured all their life force into their children, their homes, their partners, leaving nothing for their own art, their own music, their own unexpressed dreams. And so we learn, by osmosis, that a woman’s creativity is a luxury, something to be indulged in only after everyone else’s needs are met.

This is a profound loss. Your creativity is not a luxury. It is a vital, non-negotiable part of your being. It is the voice of your soul. When you deny it, you deny a fundamental aspect of yourself. The energy of that unexpressed creativity doesn’t just disappear. It can stagnate, turning into frustration, depression, or even physical illness. It can become another layer of resentment, another hard lump in the soft tissue of your breasts.

To heal the mother wound is to reclaim your right to your own creative life. It is to give yourself permission to paint, to write, to dance, to sing, to garden, to do whatever it is that makes your soul feel alive. It doesn’t have to be a masterpiece. It doesn’t have to be for anyone else. It is for you. It is the act of filling your own cup, of connecting with that inexhaustible source of life force. When you are engaged in a creative act that you love, you are in a state of flow. You are channeling something larger than yourself. You are, in that moment, a Source-fed river.

## Becoming Your Own Mother: A Practice

So what does it mean, to mother yourself? It is a practice, a moment-by-moment turning towards yourself with kindness. It is a conscious choice to reparent the parts of you that feel small, lost, or unworthy. It is the sacred work of rewiring your own nervous system for love.

Let’s try something right now. Find a quiet place where you can be undisturbed for a few minutes. Sit or lie down comfortably.

> **Step 1: Arrive in Your Body**
> Close your eyes gently. Take a few slow, deep breaths. Feel the points of contact between your body and the surface beneath you. Feel the weight of your own being, here and now. Let go of the day. Let go of the to-do lists. Simply arrive in this moment, in this body.

> **Step 2: Place Your Hands on Your Heart and Breasts**
> Gently place one hand over the center of your chest, your heart space. Place the other hand on the soft tissue of one of your breasts. If this feels uncomfortable, you can place it on your belly or your arm. The intention is simply to make contact with yourself. Feel the warmth of your own hands. This simple act of touch sends a powerful signal of safety to your nervous system.

> **Step 3: Breathe and Listen**
> Now, just breathe. Breathe into the space beneath your hands. You don’t need to force anything. Just allow your breath to be a gentle wave of presence. As you breathe, begin to listen. Ask inwardly, “Beloved one, what do you need from me right now?” The ‘beloved one’ is the part of you that is hurting, the part that feels the ache of the mother wound. Don’t search for an answer. Let it arise. It might be a word, like *rest*, or *peace*, or *to be held*. It might be an image, a memory, a sensation. Whatever comes, receive it without judgment.

> **Step 4: Offer a Message of Love**
> Whatever you heard, whatever you felt, offer a simple message of love and acceptance. You might say to yourself, silently, “I am here with you.” “You are allowed to feel this.” “You are worthy of love and care.” “I will not abandon you.” Feel the resonance of these words in your body. This is not about fixing anything. It is about being with yourself in a new way.

This is how we begin to create new neural pathways. Every time you respond to your body’s signals with care instead of criticism, you are rewiring your brain for self-compassion. You are teaching your nervous system, through direct experience, that you are safe, that you are worthy of care. This is the work of neuroplasticity in action. We are not doomed to repeat the patterns of the past. We have the power, in this very moment, to create a new one.

Finally, becoming your own mother means joyfully giving from a place of overflow, not obligation. When you are deeply nourished, when your own cup is full, your giving becomes a spontaneous expression of your being. It is no longer a transaction, a way to earn love or prove your worth. It is a gift, freely given, with no expectation of return. You learn discernment. You learn to say “no” not from a place of anger, but from a place of deep self-respect. You trust in the inherent wellbeing of others, knowing that it is not your job to save them or fix them. You simply love them.

You become the Source-fed river that never runs dry, your life a testament to the truth that the more you give to yourself, the more you have to offer the world.

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reclaim the reproductive system as a broader sacred portal of creative energy—not only for childbearing but for art, work, relationships, and life purpose. She traces how cultural shame and personal wounding can lead to disconnection and embodied symptoms, and offers a compassionate, somatic approach of gentle listening, breath, and hand placement to begin restoring safety and creative flow. Healing is framed as gradual, non‑judgmental rewiring of neural pathways and a return to embodied creativity.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was with a client recently, a woman of incredible talent and vision, who came to me feeling utterly stuck. She was a writer, a poet whose words usually flowed like a clear river, but for months, she’d felt a sense of profound creative drought. “It’s like the well is dry, Susan,” she told me, her hands resting on her lower belly. “But it’s more than that. It feels… barren. Empty. Not just in my mind, but *here*.”

Her gesture was one I have come to know so intimately, both in my clients and in myself. It’s the gesture that points to the sacred center of our being, the vessel of creation itself—the reproductive system. We have been taught to think of this part of our body in such limited terms. For reproduction. For pleasure, if we’re lucky. For the monthly cycles of hormonal shifts that are often treated as a problem to be managed. But what if it is so much more?

What if this sacred portal, this womb space—whether you have a physical womb or not, for the energy of it exists in all of us—is the very epicenter of our creative power in the world? Not just for creating children, but for creating art, for birthing new ideas, for cultivating businesses, for generating love, for composing the life that is uniquely ours to live. This, beloved, is one of the deepest truths the body has to share.

## The Vessel of All Creation

It’s a very good thing to know that your body is a sacred messenger, and every part of it has a story to tell. The reproductive system speaks of our innate, divine capacity to generate. It is the literal and symbolic space where life force is concentrated, gestated, and brought forth into the world. Before an idea becomes a plan, before a project has a structure, it is a seed, a spark of potential held in the energetic warmth of this creative cauldron.

Think of the sheer power held here. The potential to create a human being is, in itself, a miracle that defies comprehension. But that same generative, life-creating energy is the fuel for *all* our creative endeavors. When we feel a passionate urge to paint, to write a book, to start a community garden, to solve a complex problem at work—that is the same creative life force, the same shakti, stirring within our sacred center.

For centuries, however, this center has been a place of immense cultural and personal wounding. It has been revered and reviled, worshipped and desecrated. The natural, cyclical rhythms of the body have been medicalized. The raw, potent, and beautiful power of our sexuality has been shamed, controlled, and distorted. We have inherited neural pathways, passed down through generations, that teach us this part of ourselves is dangerous, unclean, or something to be kept hidden. And so, we disconnect. We numb. We armor ourselves against our own creative fire.

> We build walls around the very source of our power, and then we wonder why we feel so powerless.

This disconnection is where so much of our suffering begins. When we are cut off from our creative center, we feel adrift, purposeless, and yes—barren. The river of our creative expression slows to a trickle, and we feel a deep, aching sense that something essential is missing. It’s a feeling that can permeate everything. Work feels draining, relationships feel flat, and a persistent, low-grade sense of ‘is this all there is?’ can settle over our lives. We might try to fix it from the outside—change jobs, move cities, find a new partner—but the feeling persists, because the source of the disconnection is internal. It is a spiritual and energetic starvation, a cutting off from the very wellspring of our life force.

## When the River Runs Dry

Your body, in its infinite wisdom, will always try to communicate with you. And when there is a deep wound or disconnection in your relationship with your own creative and sexual nature, your reproductive system will often be the messenger. It’s a tricky business, being human, and these symptoms are not a punishment. They are a profound invitation to come home to yourself.

Issues that we label as “women’s problems”—painful periods, endometriosis, cysts, infertility, low libido—are so often the body’s way of speaking a truth we have not been able to consciously acknowledge. These are not just mechanical failures or hormonal imbalances; they are the physical manifestations of deep wounds around our creativity, our sexuality, and our worth.

*   A history of feeling shamed for your body or your desires can crystallize into physical pain, a literal guarding of this sacred space.
*   A lifetime of putting everyone else’s needs first, of believing your creative impulses are selfish or frivolous, can lead to a sense of energetic depletion in the womb space.
*   Unexpressed grief or rage, particularly related to violations of your boundaries, can become stored in the tissues, leading to inflammation and dysfunction.

These patterns are not your fault. You are not broken. You have never been broken. Every pattern has served you. The armoring around your creative center likely helped you survive in environments where your full, radiant power was not safe to express. Perhaps as a child, your spontaneous bursts of creative joy were met with criticism or dismissal. Perhaps your burgeoning sexuality was shamed, either directly or through the silent, pervasive messages of a culture that fears the untamed feminine. Your intelligent system, in its profound desire to protect you, learned to dampen the fire, to wall off the sacred portal, to keep you safe. But now, beloved, that old armor may be constricting your very life force. The very pain that brings you to your knees is the gateway to a new level of healing, a reclamation of a part of you that has been waiting patiently in the shadows. It is an invitation to lay down the old weapons of self-protection and to learn a new way of being: one of radical self-trust and courageous vulnerability.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming Your Sacred Center

So how do we begin to heal this profound disconnection? How do we reclaim our body as a sacred vessel and honor our sexuality and creativity as the divine gifts they are? It begins not with force, but with gentle, loving attention. It begins with listening.

Healing this space is a journey of rewiring those ancient neural pathways of shame and fear. It’s about creating new pathways of safety, pleasure, and radical self-acceptance. It starts with the simple, revolutionary act of placing your hands on your lower belly and breathing. Sending warmth, and breath, and curiosity into this space. Not demanding anything from it, but simply saying, *I am here. I am listening. What do you have to tell me?*

Perhaps you feel nothing at first. Perhaps you feel a flood of grief. Perhaps you feel a flicker of warmth. All of it is welcome. You are simply creating a conscious, loving relationship with a part of yourself that may have been ignored for a very long time. You are letting your body know that you are ready to trust its wisdom.

From this place of gentle presence, you can begin to explore. You might ask, what creative impulses have I ignored? Where in my life have I silenced my own generative power? What would it feel like to see my sexuality not as a source of shame or performance, but as a sacred, vital part of my life force?

This is the work of the sacred feminine, an energy that exists within every human being, regardless of gender. It is the work of returning to the body, of honoring its cycles, of trusting its innate capacity to generate, heal, and transform. It is the understanding that you are a creator, not by what you *do*, but by who you *are*. Your very existence is a creative act. It is a courageous turning-towards, a willingness to feel what has been unfelt, to hear what has been unspoken. It is the deep, embodied knowing that your pleasure is not a luxury, but a vital nutrient for your soul. It is the reclamation of your right to create, to express, to be fully, gloriously alive in a body you love and trust.

As you begin to tend to this sacred fire within, you may be astonished at what happens. The writer’s block that felt like a concrete wall begins to crumble. The passion for a long-lost hobby—painting, dancing, singing—returns with a surprising intensity. A new sense of purpose and vitality infuses your days, not as a frantic ‘doing,’ but as a quiet, grounded sense of alignment. Your relationships become more authentic, more intimate, because you are no longer hiding essential parts of yourself. By healing the root, you nourish every single branch of your life. The way you speak, the way you walk, the way you work, the way you love—all of it becomes infused with the radiant energy of your reclaimed creative center.


---

teachings.title: A Grounding Practice for Feet and Foundation
teachings.summary: Susan invites a slow, sensory reconnection with the feet as both physical foundation and energetic interface with the earth. The article offers a short, accessible practice—barefoot grounding, slow walking, self-massage, and a root visualization—framed as a gentle path to greater nervous-system regulation and somatic awareness. teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember walking across the cool, damp grass of my grandmother’s garden as a child. My small feet, bare against the earth, could feel everything—the tickle of clover, the slight give of the soil after a morning rain, the occasional sharp surprise of a twig. There was a conversation happening in that simple contact. A sense of belonging. My feet knew the ground, and the ground, it seemed, knew me.

When did we forget that language? When did we trade that intimate, sensory connection for stiff shoes and a life lived mostly indoors, our feet insulated from the very ground that supports our entire existence? It’s a tricky business, being human. We build our lives in the sky, in our minds, in the cloud… and we forget our roots. So often, we are a walking head, completely disconnected from the body below.

Our feet are our foundation. Not just physically, but energetically. They are the interface between our individual being and the vast, steadying presence of the Earth. With 26 bones, 33 joints, and over 100 muscles, tendons, and ligaments in each foot, they are marvels of biological engineering—designed for sensitivity, flexibility, and strength. They are meant to read the terrain, to send a constant stream of information up through our legs and spine, informing our posture, our balance, our very way of moving through the world. When we lose connection with our feet, we lose our grounding. We become like trees with shallow roots in a storm, easily swayed by the winds of anxiety, overwhelm, and uncertainty.

In my years of practice, I have seen time and again how issues with the feet reveal our deepest conflicts about our journey. Pain, stiffness, or injury in the feet often points to a feeling of being stuck, a fear of taking the next step, or a profound uncertainty about our direction in life. This isn’t just a metaphor; it’s the body’s wisdom speaking to us directly. The body is a sacred messenger, and its symptoms are communications, not enemies to be silenced.

Many of us who felt unsupported in childhood—emotionally or physically—develop patterns of tension in our feet. We learn to hold ourselves rigidly, to brace against a world that feels unstable. Our feet, which should be our connection to a supportive earth, become armored and numb. This sends a signal of constant, low-grade threat to our nervous system, keeping it in a state of hypervigilance. We lose the ability to receive the grounding energy that is our birthright. But here is a very good thing to know: you can change this. You can re-establish that sacred conversation. By bringing conscious, loving attention back to your feet, you can literally rewire the neural pathways of disconnection. You can signal to your nervous system that you are safe, that you are supported, and that it’s okay to rest. You can cultivate a profound sense of being held, right here, right now.

## A Guided Practice: Reconnecting with Your Feet

This isn’t about adding another complicated task to your to-do list. It’s an invitation to come home to yourself, one step at a time. Find a quiet space where you can be undisturbed for ten to fifteen minutes. You can do this indoors or, even better, outdoors on a patch of grass, sand, or earth. The direct contact with the natural world offers a unique level of energetic exchange.

**Step 1: The Barefoot Welcome**

Begin by taking off your shoes and socks. If you’re indoors, simply stand on the floor. If you’re outside, feel the texture of the ground beneath you. Just stand for a moment. Close your eyes if that feels comfortable. Bring all of your awareness, all of your gentle, curious attention, into the soles of your feet. Let your attention drop down from your busy mind like a feather floating gently downward, landing softly in your feet.

Notice the points of contact. Can you feel the ball of your foot? The outer edge? Your heel? Your toes? Don’t judge what you feel, just notice. Is there pressure? Tingling? Numbness? Warmth? Coolness? Is the floor hard and unyielding, or is the earth soft and receptive? Simply receive the information without needing to change it. You are just listening to a long-forgotten language. You are remembering.

**Step 2: The Walking Meditation**

Now, begin to walk. Slowly. More slowly than you think you need to. This slowness is a radical act in our fast-paced world. As you lift one foot, feel the sensation of release, the air on your skin. As you place it down, feel the full, exquisite sequence of contact: the heel landing first, then the roll through the outer edge of the foot to the mid-foot, the press of the ball, the final, supportive push-off from the toes. It’s a dance. A prayer in motion.

Pay attention to the subtle shifts in weight and balance. Feel the muscles in your feet and lower legs engaging to keep you stable. These are ancient movements, ancient pathways of knowing. Imagine with every step that you are pressing a kiss onto the earth. And with every step, the earth is kissing you back, sending a little pulse of calming, grounding energy, of support, up into your body. This isn’t just imagination; on an energetic level, this exchange is real. You are plugging into a vast, planetary circuit of support, letting your nervous system know it can stand down from high alert.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

**Step 3: The Self-Massage of Gratitude**

After your slow walk, find a comfortable place to sit. Take one foot into your hands. Look at it as if for the first time. This foot has carried you through your entire life. It has stood on countless surfaces, walked countless miles, borne your weight through joy and sorrow. It has been squeezed into shoes, ignored, and taken for granted. It deserves your gratitude.

Using your thumbs, begin to press gently into the sole of your foot. Explore the dense tissue of the arch, the firmness of the heel, the pad beneath the toes. If you find a tender spot, don’t force it. Pause. Breathe into it. Imagine your breath as a warm, healing light, softening and releasing the stored tension. Use your fingers to gently pull and rotate each toe, creating space in the joints. Rub the top of your foot, the ankle. Make small circles around the ankle bones. You are not trying to “fix” anything. You are simply offering loving attention. You are saying, with your hands and your heart, *I see you. I feel you. Thank you.*

Repeat with the other foot, offering it the same quality of unhurried presence and gratitude.

**Step 4: The Earth Connection Visualization**

Now, with both feet back on the ground, sit or stand with a straight but soft spine. Close your eyes once more. Imagine roots growing from the soles of your feet. See them, feel them, extending deep, deep into the earth. Past the topsoil, through layers of clay and rock, down, down, down into the warm, glowing, crystalline heart of the planet.

Feel the strength and stability of these roots. They are your connection to an unwavering source of support. Feel them drawing up a powerful, calming, nourishing energy from the earth’s core. This energy is patient, steady, and unconditional. It flows up your roots and into the soles of your feet, bathing them in a gentle, golden light. Feel this energy flowing up into your ankles, your calves, your knees… filling your entire body with a sense of profound safety and peace. You are anchored. You are held. You are home.

Rest in this feeling for as long as you like. Know that you can return to this practice, and this feeling, anytime you feel adrift or caught in the storms of your mind.

## Your Daily Grounding

This practice is a beautiful, restorative ritual. But grounding is not a one-time event. It’s a way of life. It’s the conscious choice to inhabit your body, to connect with the earth, to be present in your own life.

You can find moments to ground throughout your day. Wiggle your toes while you’re sitting at your desk. Feel the solidness of your feet on the floor while you wait in line at the grocery store. When you feel anxiety rising, bring your attention down to your feet. Take a few moments to walk barefoot in your home or garden. Every small act of connection reinforces the neural pathways of safety and belonging, making it easier and more natural to access this state of grounded presence.

It is from this place of groundedness that we can truly begin to heal and transform. When we are rooted, we are not so easily shaken. We can face the challenges of life with more grace, more resilience, and a deeper trust in our own journey. We can finally feel safe enough to let our own unique, beautiful energy flow, to take the next step, and the next, with confidence and peace.


---

## Explore Related Systems

**More on Feet:**

May you walk in beauty and in trust, feeling the unwavering support of the earth with every step.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a word I keep coming back to, again and again, in my work and in my life: spaciousness.

We arrive as cosmic, energetic beings, taking up residence in these beautiful, gravity-bound bodies. And perhaps no part of us tells this story more profoundly than our hips and legs. They are our ultimate grounding rods, the twin pillars that connect our infinite, starry origins to the solid, trustworthy earth beneath our feet. They are designed for both incredible stability and remarkable mobility, a paradox that holds the very essence of our journey here.

I remember standing at the edge of the Pacific, my feet sinking into the wet sand, the cold water rushing over my ankles. I’d been feeling… untethered. A project I had poured my heart into had dissolved, a relationship had shifted, and I felt a familiar, shaky uncertainty. My mind was racing, a frantic hamster on a wheel, trying to figure it all out, to find a solid place to stand when the ground beneath me felt like it was giving way. But as the waves pulled the sand from under my feet, a different kind of knowing arose. It came not from my head, but from my legs. I could feel the vast, intricate network of muscles, bones, and nerves firing and adjusting, holding me upright in the face of the ocean’s relentless push and pull. My hips, my powerful pelvis, acted as a sacred basin, a center of gravity keeping me rooted. In that moment, they weren’t just limbs; they were my connection to the planet, my anchors in the storm. It was a profound moment of embodiment, a visceral reminder that our bodies are not separate from our experience, but are the very vessel through which we navigate the currents of our lives. I stayed for a long time, just feeling that subtle, constant dance of adjustment, my body’s wisdom far outstripping my mind’s panic. It was a homecoming.

This is the magic of our hips and legs. They are our dance partners in this grand, unpredictable choreography of life.

## The Body's Brilliant Design

Think of the sheer brilliance of their design. The hip joint, a perfect ball-and-socket, is engineered for movement in every direction—forward, backward, side to side, and in full, glorious rotation. This isn’t an accident. It’s an invitation to move through life with fluidity and grace, to be able to shift your stance, change direction, and bow to what is. Rigidity, that feeling of being “stuck,” often manifests here first, in hips that feel tight and unyielding. It’s the body’s way of saying, *Perhaps there is a new direction waiting for you, if you’re willing to soften and allow it.*

And then there is the wonder of proprioception—our body’s innate ability to know where it is in space without looking. It’s a constant, subconscious conversation happening between the nerve endings in our muscles and joints and the processing centers in our brain. This neural symphony is what allows you to walk through a dark room without bumping into furniture, to feel the subtle shift in terrain under your feet, to dance with your eyes closed. It is your body’s deep, cellular intelligence at work. Information from specialized receptors in your muscles (spindles) and tendons (Golgi tendon organs) travels up the spinal cord along specific neural pathways, informing the cerebellum and cortex of your every move, your every shift in balance. It’s a feedback loop of breathtaking speed and complexity. When we feel disconnected or “in our heads,” we are often cut off from this rich source of information. The path back to presence is often as simple as bringing your awareness down, down, down into your legs and feet. Feel them on the floor. Sense their strength. You are here. You are held. This is not just a mental exercise; it is a physiological one. When you bring your conscious awareness to a part of your body, you are literally changing the neural pathways, inviting a new level of communication and connection. You are reminding your nervous system that it is safe to be present, to be here, in this moment.

So often, issues in the hips and legs—the sciatica, the knee pain, the feeling of having “no leg to stand on”—are echoes of a deeper inflexibility. They speak of a place where we are holding on too tightly to a particular outcome, a specific belief, or an old story. We are designed to be both stable *and* mobile, rooted *and* free. Flexibility isn’t weakness, and stability doesn’t require rigidity. It’s a dance, a beautiful, dynamic tension that our bodies understand completely. Our bodies are constantly seeking this balance, this homeostasis. When we ignore the whispers of our bodies, they will begin to shout. The pain in our hips may be a cry for us to examine where we are being inflexible in our lives, where we are refusing to bend or yield. The weakness in our knees may be a sign that we are not allowing ourselves to be vulnerable, to soften into the support that is all around us.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Purpose in Your Stance

Our hips and legs are not just for getting from one place to another. They are about purpose. They are what allow us to take a stand for what we believe in, to walk our path with integrity, and to ground our dreams in the soil of reality. When we feel unsupported in our lives, or uncertain of our direction, it is often our legs and hips that will cry out for our attention.

I worked with a dear one once, a man who had chronic hip pain that no amount of stretching or therapy could seem to touch. As we sat together, it emerged that he felt deeply conflicted about his life’s work. He was in a career that provided financial stability but starved his soul. He felt he had no “leg to stand on” if he were to leave it. His body, in its infinite wisdom, was simply mirroring this internal conflict. The pain was not an enemy to be vanquished; it was a sacred messenger, asking him to look at the place where his life was out of alignment with his heart’s true purpose. The pain was a conversation starter.

The healing came not from forcing the hip to release, but from gently, compassionately acknowledging the fear. It came from exploring, in the safety of our sessions, what it might feel like to take one small, tentative step in a new direction. We didn’t try to solve the whole career dilemma at once. Instead, we brought awareness to the legs. We did simple, grounding exercises. Standing, he would feel his feet on the floor, then slowly shift his weight from one foot to the other, noticing the subtle adjustments in his hips and legs. He began to feel, in his body, that he *could* be supported, even in the midst of uncertainty. The body doesn’t need you to have all the answers. It just needs to know you’re listening. When you begin to align your steps with your soul’s calling, you will be amazed at the support that rises to meet you, both from within and without. This is the power of embodiment. When we inhabit our bodies fully, we are no longer at the mercy of our circumstances. We become active participants in our own healing, our own becoming.

Your legs are your connection to the earth, to your ancestors, to the long line of beings who have walked this planet. They carry the stories of your lineage, the resilience of your past, and the potential of your future. They are your foundation, the firm ground from which you can reach for the stars. Every step you take is a declaration of your existence, a claiming of your right to be here, in this body, on this earth. Every time you stand tall, you are honoring the journey that has brought you to this moment.

So, I invite you to pause for a moment. Find a comfortable place to stand. Take your shoes off, if you can. Feel your feet on the floor. Rock gently forward and back, side to side. Notice the tiny, brilliant adjustments your legs and hips are making to keep you balanced. Place your hands on your hips. Feel the strength and stability in your pelvis, this bony cradle of your creative energy. Send your awareness down through your powerful legs, all the way to the soles of your feet. Feel your connection to the earth. You are a bridge between heaven and earth, a being of both spirit and form. And your hips and legs? They are the foundation of your glorious, sacred dance through life. Allow yourself to feel the support that is always there for you, the unwavering strength of your own two feet on the ground. From this place of groundedness, you can move with grace and courage, ready to meet whatever comes your way.


---

teachings.sourceTitle: Like Cures Like: The Elegant Wisdom of Homeopathic Healing
teachings.title: Like Cures Like: The Elegant Wisdom of Homeopathic Healing
teachings.summary: Susan presents homeopathy’s central idea—‘like cures like’—as an invitation to engage with healing as a subtle, respectful conversation with the body’s innate intelligence. Through explanation of potentiation and a patient anecdote, she encourages listening for the unique, often paradoxical qualities of symptoms and honoring whole-person, individualized approaches to wellbeing.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are wired for survival, for healing, for wholeness. Our bodies are exquisite feedback systems, constantly whispering—and sometimes shouting—what they need to find their way back to balance. Yet, we so often find ourselves at odds with this innate intelligence, trying to force, to fix, to control the very processes that are designed to save us. What if the path to healing wasn’t a battle? What if it was more like a dance, a gentle persuasion, a subtle conversation with the deepest wisdom of our being? This is the elegant and often misunderstood world of homeopathy, a system of medicine built on a principle that feels both radical and deeply resonant: *similia similibus curentur*, or “like cures like.” ## The Elegant Wisdom of Similars The principle of like cures like is one of the most beautiful and counterintuitive ideas in all of healing. It suggests that a substance that can produce a certain set of symptoms in a healthy person can, in a very small, potentized dose, cure those same symptoms in a person who is unwell. It’s a paradox that holds a profound truth about the nature of the body and the nature of healing itself. Think of it this way. Imagine you have a fever. Your body is generating heat, a sign that your immune system is actively fighting something off. The conventional approach might be to take a medication that suppresses the fever, that forces the temperature down. This can provide temporary relief, but it also works *against* the body’s own healing efforts. It’s like telling a crying child to be quiet without asking why they are upset. Homeopathy takes a different approach. A homeopathic practitioner might give you a remedy made from a substance that, in a larger dose, would actually *cause* a fever. The remedy doesn’t suppress the symptom; it mirrors it. It speaks the body’s own language. It’s a gentle nudge, a whisper of recognition that says, “I see what you are trying to do. Let me help you do it more efficiently.” The infinitesimal dose stimulates the very healing response the body has been trying to mount, allowing it to complete the process and return to a state of ease. I remember a client who came to me years ago, a woman we’ll call Sarah. She was plagued by a persistent, dry, hacking cough that had lingered for weeks after a cold. It was worse at night, keeping her and her husband awake. She had tried everything—syrups, lozenges, inhalers—but nothing touched it. The cough was relentless, a constant irritation in her throat and a source of deep exhaustion. As we talked, I learned more about the specific quality of her cough. It was tickling, incessant, and accompanied by a feeling of restlessness. She felt she had to constantly move. Listening to her, I was reminded of the homeopathic remedy *Ignatia amara*, which is often indicated for conditions that have a paradoxical or hysterical quality, much like her unending cough that served no purpose. *Ignatia* in its raw form can produce a similar irritating cough. I gave her a single dose of the remedy in a high potency. The next day, she called me, her voice filled with a quiet awe. The cough, she said, had simply…stopped. It was as if her body, having finally been understood, could let go of the struggle. ## The Science of Subtlety To the modern mind, accustomed to the brute force of pharmaceuticals, the idea of an infinitesimal dose having any effect at all can seem preposterous. Homeopathic remedies are prepared through a process of serial dilution and succussion (vigorous shaking), which potentizes the substance. In many high-potency remedies, there may be no original molecules of the substance left. And this, of course, is where homeopathy and conventional science part ways. But what if we are looking at it through the wrong lens? What if the healing power of a homeopathic remedy isn’t chemical, but energetic? Quantum physics teaches us that on a subatomic level, everything is energy and information. The water used in the dilution process may be acting as a carrier for the energetic blueprint of the original substance. The succussion may be amplifying that signature, creating a remedy that communicates with the body on a vibrational level. This resonates with the ancient wisdom of the Tao te Ching, which speaks of the power of the soft and the subtle: > “The supreme good is like water, > which nourishes all things without trying to. > It is content with the low places that people disdain. > Thus it is like the Tao.” Homeopathy is like water. It doesn’t force, it doesn’t fight. It gently, persistently, and intelligently works with the body’s own flow, with the innate healing intelligence that is our birthright. It trusts the wisdom of the organism, a wisdom that is far older and deeper than our conscious minds can comprehend. ## A Sacred Conversation Working with homeopathy is a process of deep listening. It’s about paying attention to the unique and peculiar ways that imbalance expresses itself in each individual. It’s not about diagnosing a disease and applying a one-size-fits-all label. It’s about seeing the whole person—their physical symptoms, their emotional state, their energetic patterns—and finding a remedy that resonates with that totality. This is a sacred act, beloved one. It is a way of honoring the incredible intelligence of your body and your soul. It is a way of remembering that you are not a machine to be fixed, but a living, breathing, dynamic being on a journey of healing and self-discovery. Your body is always talking to you. It is always guiding you toward wholeness. The question is, are you willing to listen? Are you willing to trust the subtle whispers of your own being? Are you willing to entertain the elegant, paradoxical, and profoundly healing wisdom of “like cures like”?

Discover what your body is telling you

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.
