teachings.sourceTitle: Beyond Attack and Defend: The Transcendence of Your Immune System
teachings.title: Beyond Attack and Defend: The Transcendence of Your Immune System
teachings.summary: Susan invites a shift from the popular war-metaphor of the immune system toward seeing it as a discerning, integrative intelligence that is deeply linked to the nervous system and our sense of self. She explores how chronic stress and unresolved trauma can lock the body into a state of constant defense, sometimes producing autoimmune patterns, and offers a short somatic practice to ‘befriend’ symptoms as messengers rather than enemies. The piece calls for radical self-compassion, inner listening, and a move from separation to embodied belonging.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is something I want to share with you today, something that has been quietly unfolding in my awareness for some time now.

I remember a summer, years ago, when my body went to war with a field of wildflowers. One moment, I was walking through a meadow near my home in Vancouver, the air thick with the sweet, heavy scent of pollen and the buzz of happy bees. The next, my eyes were streaming, my throat was closing, and my skin was erupting in angry, red welts. My body, in its infinite wisdom, had identified the pollen as a dangerous invader and launched a full-scale attack. For weeks, I was miserable, caught in the crossfire of a battle I didn’t understand, a prisoner in my own home while the world outside was bursting with life.

We talk about our bodies in such violent terms, don’t we? We “fight off” a cold. We “battle” disease. Our immune system is our personal army, our first line of “defense” against a hostile world. We envision it as a vigilant soldier, endlessly patrolling the borders of our being, ready to attack and destroy anything that doesn’t belong. It’s a story of separation, of us against them, of a fragile self holding out against a dangerous world.

But what if that’s not the whole story? What if that very metaphor, that story of war, is the source of so much of our suffering? What if the constant state of high alert, of attack and defend, is actually a profound misunderstanding of a much deeper, more sacred process? What if the deepest wisdom of our immune system isn’t about fighting a war, but about learning to dance?

## The Master of Discernment

The immune system is, at its core, a master of discernment. Its primary job is not to attack, but to distinguish between “self” and “other.” It’s a process of exquisite sensitivity, a constant, flowing conversation between your body and the world. It’s not a blunt instrument of war, but a highly intelligent system of information gathering and response. It is the very edge of our identity, the place where we meet the world.

Think about it: every moment of every day, you are taking in the world. You are breathing in air, drinking water, eating food. You are constantly being penetrated by a universe of influences — bacteria, viruses, pollen, but also thoughts, emotions, energies from the people and places around you. Your immune system is the gatekeeper, the one who decides what to welcome in, what to integrate as nourishment, and what to gently, lovingly release.

This process of discernment is deeply connected to your nervous system. When your brain perceives a threat — whether it’s a real physical danger like a speeding car, or a perceived emotional one like a critical comment from your boss — it sends a signal to your body to go on high alert. Your heart rate increases, your muscles tense, and your immune system ramps up its defenses. This is the classic “fight or flight” response, a survival mechanism that has kept us alive for millennia. It’s a beautiful, powerful system.

But what happens when we get stuck in that state of high alert? What happens when our nervous system, often because of unresolved trauma or chronic stress, is constantly telling our immune system that we are under attack? The result is chronic inflammation, a low-grade, persistent state of immune activation that has been linked to a host of modern ailments, from heart disease and arthritis to depression and anxiety. The "soldier" never gets to rest. The war footing becomes the default state of being. And a body at war with the world is an exhausted body.

## The Crisis of Identity

When the immune system’s discerning dance becomes a frantic, confused battle, it can lead to what I call a crisis of identity. In autoimmune conditions, the body literally starts attacking its own tissues. The line between “self” and “other” becomes so blurred that the system can no longer recognize its own home. It’s the ultimate form of self-rejection, a fundamental alienation from the very fabric of your being. The body, in its desperate attempt to protect you, turns on itself.

But you don’t have to have a diagnosed autoimmune condition to experience this crisis of identity. So many of us are at war with ourselves in more subtle ways. We reject the parts of ourselves that we deem unacceptable — our anger, our sadness, our vulnerability, our deep needs. We try to wall ourselves off from the world, to create a fortress of self-protection. We build emotional walls, create rigid beliefs, and hold our breath, hoping to keep the "bad" stuff out. But in doing so, we also cut ourselves off from the very source of our vitality, from the nourishment and connection that we so deeply crave.

This internal battle is exhausting. It consumes vast amounts of life force. It’s the feeling of being perpetually on guard, of scanning every interaction for potential threats, of holding your own emotions at bay for fear they will overwhelm you. It is a lonely, painful way to live.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

What if we could begin to see all of these influences — even the ones that seem harmful — as doorways into our highest growth? What if the pollen that sent my body into a tailspin wasn’t an enemy to be vanquished, but a messenger trying to get my attention? What if the parts of ourselves that we reject are the very parts that hold the key to our wholeness? What if the symptom is not the problem, but the *solution* trying to emerge?

## The Shift to Integration

This is the shift from a mindset of attack and defend to one of discernment and integration. It’s a move from seeing the world as a battlefield to seeing it as a dance. It’s a recognition that we are not separate from the world, but intimately and inextricably connected to it. It’s a journey from alienation to intimacy, first with ourselves, and then with all of life.

This shift requires a deep listening, a turning inward to the wisdom of your own body. It requires a willingness to sit with the discomfort, to feel the feelings you’ve been trying to avoid. It requires a radical act of self-compassion, of welcoming home all the exiled parts of yourself. It means treating your body not as a machine that is broken, but as a sacred, living intelligence that is always, *always* communicating with you.

It’s not about being passive or letting yourself be a doormat. It’s about developing a new kind of strength, a flexible resilience that allows you to bend without breaking. It’s about learning to trust the intelligence of your body, to know that it is always, always working for your highest good, even when its methods are mysterious and uncomfortable. It’s about cultivating the capacity to be with what *is*, without needing to immediately fix it, fight it, or flee from it.

## A Practice: Befriending the Messenger

I invite you to try a small practice. The next time you feel a symptom in your body — a headache, a pang of indigestion, an allergic itch, a wave of fatigue — try this:

1.  **Pause.** Instead of immediately reaching for a pill or a distraction, simply stop. Find a quiet place to sit or lie down for just a few minutes.
2.  **Breathe.** Take three slow, deep breaths. With each exhale, consciously soften the area of your body that is calling for your attention. Soften your jaw, your shoulders, your belly.
3.  **Acknowledge.** Place a gentle hand on the part of your body that is speaking to you. Silently, or out loud, say, “I see you. I feel you. I am listening.” You are not endorsing the pain; you are simply acknowledging its presence with respect.
4.  **Ask.** With genuine curiosity, ask the sensation: “What message do you have for me? What do you need me to know?” Don’t try to figure it out with your mind. Just ask, and then listen in the quiet. The answer may not come in words. It might be an image, a memory, a feeling. It might be a simple sense of “slow down,” or “let go,” or “speak up.”
5.  **Offer Gratitude.** Thank your body for its communication. Thank this part of you for working so hard to keep you safe and to bring you back into balance. Send it a wave of love and appreciation.

This is not a magic cure. It is a practice of relationship. It is the beginning of a conversation. It is how we begin to transform the inner war into a dance of co-creation.

## The Ultimate Transcendence

And here is the deepest truth, the one that can feel both terrifying and liberating: at the most fundamental level, there are no borders. The idea of a separate self, a fortress to be defended, is an illusion created by the mind. You are not a lonely outpost in a hostile universe. You are a wave in the ocean of existence, a unique and precious expression of the one life that flows through all things.

When you can truly grasp this, when you can feel it in your bones, the need to attack and defend simply falls away. There is nothing to fight against, because you are not separate from anything. There is nothing to protect, because your true nature is indestructible. All of life is your own self, expressing in a billion different forms.

This is the transcendence of the immune system. It’s a move beyond the dualistic thinking of good and bad, self and other, to a place of radical acceptance and unconditional love. It’s a recognition that you are not just *in* the universe, you *are* the universe. And the universe is not at war with itself.

So the next time you feel your body going into attack mode, I invite you to pause. To take a breath. To place a hand on your heart and whisper to yourself: *You are safe. You are whole. You are loved. All is well.*

And then, listen. Listen to the wisdom of your body. It has a story to tell you, a story of healing, of wholeness, and of the infinite, boundless love that you are.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


---

teachings.sourceTitle: Embodied Healing: Beyond the Mind's Understanding
teachings.title: Embodied Healing: Beyond the Mind's Understanding
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to close the gap between intellectual understanding and lived, bodily knowing, arguing that lasting healing happens when we listen to the body’s sensations rather than only the mind’s stories. She describes how experiences—especially early survival responses—are encoded somatically and offers accessible somatic practices (three-breath pause, befriending sensations, intuitive movement) to begin returning attention to the body. The article frames this work as gentle, curiosity-led, and complementary to therapeutic or medical care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a particular kind of bravery that the world rarely celebrates — the bravery of being vulnerable.

I remember sitting in my therapist's office years ago, long before I began my own practice. I was talking, as I often did, about a painful pattern in my life. I had turned it over and over in my mind, analyzed its origins, traced its roots back to childhood with what I thought was stunning clarity. I had read all the books, I understood the psychology, I could have drawn you a detailed diagram of my own dysfunction.

“I *understand* it,” I said, the frustration thick in my throat. “I see exactly where it comes from, why I do it… so why can’t I stop?”

My therapist, a wise woman with kind eyes, listened patiently. When I finally ran out of steam, she said something that would change the entire course of my life and my work. “Susan,” she said gently, “you’ve built a beautiful map of the territory. But you haven’t yet set foot in the land.”

A map of the territory. It was the perfect metaphor. My mind had done its job brilliantly. It had gathered information, created a narrative, and identified the problem from a safe, intellectual distance. But the healing… the healing wasn’t in the map. It was in the land. And the land was my body.

This experience was a profound turning point. It was the moment I realized that all my intellectual understanding was like standing on the shore, looking at a picture of the ocean. I could describe the water, talk about its properties, even understand the physics of the tides. But I hadn’t yet felt the shock of the cold, the pull of the current, the sublime surrender of floating in its vastness. The healing, I was beginning to see, was in the swimming.

## The Great Divide: Head vs. Body

This is a chasm so many of us live with—the gap between what we *know* in our heads and what we *feel* in our bones. It’s the experience of knowing you are safe, but your heart still pounds with anxiety. It’s knowing you deserve love, but still flinching at a kind touch. It’s understanding a pattern of self-sabotage, yet continuing to enact it with a sense of helpless horror.

Our culture has taught us to privilege the mind. We are praised for our intellect, our rationality, our ability to “figure things out.” The mind is the CEO, the project manager, the one in charge. The body? It’s often treated as a vehicle to be managed, disciplined, and occasionally indulged—a machine to carry the all-important brain around. We are taught to push through its pain, ignore its whispers, and override its needs in the service of productivity or external goals.

But this is a profound misunderstanding of who we are. We are not just minds. We are whole beings, an integrated system of consciousness, energy, and matter. And true, lasting healing cannot happen if we only engage the thinking part of ourselves. It’s like trying to nourish a plant by only watering one leaf.

Why is this? The neuroscience is fascinating here, and it affirms what ancient wisdom traditions have always known. Our experiences, especially the ones from early in life when our brains are most malleable, are not stored as neat, cognitive memories filed away in a mental cabinet. They are encoded in the body—in the intricate web of our nervous system, the fascia that wraps our muscles, our very cells. The brain’s limbic system, the seat of our emotions and survival responses, records experience on a purely somatic level. It doesn’t speak in language; it speaks in sensation. Tightness in the chest. A knot in the stomach. A flush of heat. A sudden wave of exhaustion. These are the words of the body’s native tongue.

When we try to heal only with the neocortex—the “thinking brain”—we are speaking the wrong language. We are sending a memo to a part of ourselves that only understands poetry. The mind can create a story about the past, but the body *is* the past, living in the present. It holds the energetic imprint of every joy, every sorrow, every moment of terror or overwhelm. Until we address it on its own terms, we remain divided.

## The Body’s Sacred Language

The body doesn’t heal in a straight line. It doesn’t respond to logic or debate. Its wisdom is ancient, primal, and deeply intuitive. It doesn’t want to be “fixed” or “overcome.” It wants to be heard. As the Tao Te Ching reminds us, “The way to do is to be.” The body invites us into a state of being, not just doing.

Think of the last time you had a headache. Was it just a random pain? Or was your body communicating something? As I explore in my work with The Body Cards, the head is the throne of our identity. A headache is often the feeling of our consciousness pressing against the constraints of our own limited beliefs. It’s the tension of trying to figure everything out, of relentless mental gymnastics. The mind is a magnificent tool, but it is not the sole authority on your life. The pain is a messenger, asking you to soften, to let go of the need for control, to allow for a wisdom beyond thought.

Healing happens when we learn to listen to this other language. When we bypass the chattering mind and drop our awareness down into the feeling, sensing, living reality of the body. This is not about wallowing in pain. It’s about bringing a compassionate, curious presence to what is actually there.

It’s the beginning of a sacred conversation.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

When we do this, something miraculous begins to happen. The frozen, stuck places within us—the crystallized grief in our lungs, the bitterness stored in our liver, the fear held in our kidneys—begin to thaw under the warmth of our own attention. This isn’t a mental process. It’s a physiological one. The nervous system, which has been locked in a state of high-alert, sympathetic dominance (“fight or flight”), begins to shift into a state of restorative, parasympathetic calm (“rest and digest”).

This is the essence of somatic processing. We are giving the body a chance to complete the survival responses that it never got to finish. When we were overwhelmed as children, we couldn’t fight or flee, so we froze. That freeze response traps an immense amount of energy in the nervous system. Embodied healing allows that energy to finally move and release, not by re-living the trauma, but by feeling the sensations in a safe and present container. It’s a gentle, titrated process of letting the body tell its story and finally come to a state of completion.

New neural pathways can be formed. Neuroplasticity, the brain’s amazing ability to reorganize itself, is not just a mental phenomenon. It is a whole-body experience. When we introduce new somatic experiences—of safety, of calm, of gentle movement, of pleasure—we are, quite literally, rewiring the ancient pathways of fear and threat. We are teaching our bodies, on a cellular level, that we are safe *now*. That we are no longer that powerless child. That we can handle the beautiful, messy, unpredictable flow of life.

## From Map to Land: Practical Approaches to Embodied Healing

So how do we step out of the map and into the land? It is a practice. It is a returning, over and over again, to the body as a source of wisdom and a vessel of healing. It is not another thing to perfect or achieve. It is a gentle turning inward, a gesture of profound kindness to ourselves.

You might begin simply. It doesn’t require a special cushion or a silent retreat. It can happen right here, right now.

1.  **The Three-Breath Pause:** Wherever you are, whatever you are doing, take a moment to pause. Take one breath and notice the air coming in and out of your body. On the second breath, bring your awareness to the feeling of your feet on the floor, the solid ground beneath you. On the third breath, ask yourself, “What am I sensing in my body right now?” No judgment. No story. Just sensation. A tingling in the hands? A tightness in the jaw? A warmth in the belly? Just notice. This is the first step in rebuilding the mind-body connection.

2.  **Befriend a Sensation:** The next time you feel a strong emotion—anxiety, anger, sadness—resist the urge to immediately analyze it or push it away. Instead, get curious. Where does that emotion live in your body as a pure sensation? Is the anxiety a vibration in your chest? Is the anger a heat in your neck? Can you bring a gentle, allowing attention to that spot? Breathe into it. You might even place a hand there, a gesture of comfort and presence. You are not trying to make it go away. You are simply saying, “I feel you. I am here with you.”

3.  **Move with Intuition:** Put on a piece of music and allow your body to move in whatever way it wants to. Not exercise. Not performance. Just movement. Let your arms sway, your hips circle, your shoulders release. Let your body lead. This can be a powerful way to unlock stuck energy and emotion without ever needing to put it into words. Your body has a wisdom that your mind can’t access. Let it speak through movement.

This is the beginning of embodied healing. It is the shift from understanding to *knowing*. It is the difference between reading a book about love and feeling love’s warmth spread through your entire being. It is the difference between a black-and-white map and the full-color, sensory richness of the land itself.

Your body is not a problem to be solved. It is a sacred messenger, a wise companion, and the ultimate ground of your being. It has been waiting, with infinite patience, for you to come home.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.title: Fragmentation and Wholeness: When Your Inner Orchestra Plays Off-Key
teachings.summary: Susan explores how we fragment—splitting into parts to survive overwhelm—and names that splitting as an adaptive but costly response that shows up in body, mind, and nervous system. She reframes healing as a compassionate, patient practice of listening to exiled parts and re-weaving the "Web of Your Being," offering an accessible somatic invitation to begin that reconnection. The emphasis is on witnessing rather than fixing, and on small acts of presence that strengthen internal communication.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
We are, all of us, walking contradictions. And that, beloved, is not a flaw.

And one of the most profound aspects, I’ve found, is holding ourselves together when life seems determined to pull us apart.

I remember a particular afternoon years ago, when my children were small. The phone was ringing, the kettle was screaming, my youngest was tugging at my jeans with jam-sticky hands, and my oldest needed help with a school project *right now*. In that moment, I felt myself… split. A part of me was the competent mother, trying to triage the chaos. Another part was a resentful, exhausted woman who just wanted to sit in a quiet room. A third part, a much younger part, was simply terrified by the overwhelming noise and demand. I felt like a committee of strangers, all shouting at once, with no one in charge. I went numb. I moved through the motions, made the snack, answered the phone, but *I* wasn’t really there. I had, in a very real sense, left the building. My body was on autopilot, but my consciousness had retreated to a distant, quiet room somewhere in the back of my mind, watching the scene unfold on a grainy television screen. It was a profound and unsettling moment of self-abandonment, a quiet tearing in the fabric of my own being.

Have you ever felt that way? That sense of being disconnected from yourself, of watching your life from a distance? As if you’re a collection of disparate parts rather than a cohesive whole? This experience of fragmentation is a profound and often painful aspect of the human journey. It’s a state where our inner orchestra, the beautiful symphony of our being, is playing wildly off-key, with some instruments screeching and others gone silent altogether.

## The Web of Your Being

In the language of the Body Cards, we call this symphony the *Web of Your Being*. It isn’t a single organ or system, but the miraculous, invisible field of consciousness that holds every part of you—your cells, your thoughts, your emotions, your history, your spirit—in a unified whole. It is the energetic matrix, the very fabric of your embodied existence. When this web is strong and vibrant, we feel integrated, present, and alive. We feel like *ourselves*.

But when the web is strained, torn, or tangled, we experience what modern psychology calls dissociation or what I simply call fragmentation. It’s a brilliant, adaptive survival strategy, by the way. When an experience is too overwhelming, too painful, or too terrifying for our nervous system to handle, a part of us checks out. The brain, in its infinite wisdom, creates a kind of internal partition. It’s a neurological circuit breaker that flips to prevent a total system overload. A child in a chaotic home learns to numb their feelings to survive. An adult in a high-stress job learns to disconnect from their body’s exhaustion to keep performing. We learn to silence the parts of ourselves that are inconvenient, wounded, or deemed unacceptable.

This isn’t a character flaw; it’s a testament to our resilience. But it comes at a cost. When we continually numb ourselves, we lose touch with our own wholeness. We start to believe we *are* only the competent, achieving part, while the vulnerable, feeling parts are exiled to the basement of our consciousness. We build an identity around being 'strong,' 'capable,' or 'low-maintenance,' not realizing that this identity is a fortress built to keep our own tender, wounded aspects locked away. This is the great illusion of fragmentation: we mistake a part of ourselves for the whole, and in doing so, we lose access to the immense wisdom, creativity, and vitality that resides in the parts we have disowned. We might live entirely in our heads, brilliant at analyzing and thinking, but completely cut off from the wisdom of our heart and the messages of our body. Or we might be so swamped by emotion that we lose our grounding, unable to access the part of us that is stable and clear. The orchestra is no longer a symphony; it’s a cacophony.

## The Neuroscience of Coming Home

What’s so fascinating is that neuroscience is now showing us the physical reality of this fragmentation. We can see how chronic stress and trauma can strengthen the neural pathways leading to the brain’s fear center, the amygdala, while weakening the connections to the prefrontal cortex, the seat of our rational thought and self-awareness. The communication breaks down. The body might be screaming in pain or exhaustion, but the signal never reaches the head office. This is the biology of dissociation—a literal disconnection in the wiring of our internal communication network.

Over my years of working with clients, I’ve seen these patterns of fragmentation show up in countless ways. I see it in the woman with chronic shoulder pain who has carried the emotional burdens of her family for so long that she no longer recognizes them as separate from her own body. I see it in the man with digestive issues who has never been able to “stomach” the injustices he’s experienced. The body, in its profound wisdom, always tells the truth. It is the ultimate truth-teller, the keeper of the stories that our conscious mind has deemed too painful or inconvenient to hold. The whispers of the silenced instruments in our inner orchestra—the grief we never allowed ourselves to feel, the anger we were taught was 'unladylike,' the terror that was too overwhelming to process—don't simply disappear. They crystallize in our tissues. They become the tension in our shoulders, the ache in our lower back, the knot in our stomach. The body becomes a battlefield for a war we don't even know we are fighting. The roar of physical symptoms is often the desperate cry of a part of ourselves that has been ignored for far too long.

The journey back to wholeness, then, is not about forcing the orchestra to play the “right” music. It’s not about getting rid of the “bad” parts of ourselves. It is a journey of listening. It is the practice of becoming a compassionate conductor for your own magnificent, messy, and miraculous being.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

Integration is the opposite of fragmentation. It’s the process of weaving those disconnected neural pathways back together. It’s about gently, safely, and lovingly turning toward the parts of ourselves we’ve exiled. It’s extending an invitation to the numb places, the angry places, the terrified places, and letting them know it’s finally safe to come home. This is the heart of healing. It’s the slow, patient work of re-establishing trust with yourself.

## An Invitation to Listen

So, how do we begin? It starts with a simple, radical act: the willingness to listen. To pause the endless doing and simply be. I invite you to try this, perhaps right now. Find a quiet space, close your eyes, and take a few gentle breaths.

> Bring your awareness into your body. Don’t try to change anything. Just notice. Where in your body do you feel the most sensation? Where do you feel the least? Can you get curious about the quiet places, the numb places? What would it be like to send a little breath, a little warmth, into one of those areas? No agenda. Just a gentle hello.

Now, ask your inner world a question: *Who is here right now?* Listen for the answers. Perhaps the Achiever is here, worrying about your to-do list. Perhaps the Inner Critic is here, judging this whole process. Perhaps a tired, small child is here, just wanting a rest. You don’t have to do anything with what you find. The goal is not to fix, but to witness. To allow all the members of your orchestra to be seen and heard, without judgment.

This is the practice of building your inner web. Each time you pause to listen, you are spinning a thread of connection. Each time you offer a moment of compassion to a difficult feeling, you are mending a tear. You are reminding yourself that you are a unified field of consciousness, vast enough to hold every note, every dissonance, every silence. You are the conductor, yes, but you are also the music itself. Your only real job is not to force a perfect performance, but to love the entire orchestra into a state of resonant harmony. It is about creating a space of such profound safety and acceptance within yourself that even the most timid or discordant instrument feels safe enough to sound its true note, knowing it will be held in the loving embrace of the whole.

It is not a journey to perfection, but a journey to wholeness. It is the sacred, lifelong work of coming home to the magnificent instrument of your embodied being. It is the journey of a thousand small steps, each one a choice to listen, to feel, to connect. And as you do, you will find that the cacophony begins to soften. The screeching violins find their melody, the silent cellos begin to hum, and a deep, resonant harmony begins to emerge. This is the sound of your own wholeness. This is the sound of you, finally allowing your true and beautiful song to be sung.

teachings.sourceTitle: Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision
teachings.title: Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision
teachings.summary: Susan reflects on how physical sight often mirrors our inner landscape, using nearsightedness and farsightedness as metaphors for trust in the future and avoidance of the present. She weaves somatic insight and neuroscience to invite compassionate, curiosity-led practices that help re-pattern perception while honoring conventional eye care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a moment, just before sleep, when the body softens and the mind releases its grip.

And one of the most profound aspects is how we see—or don’t see—the world around us and the path before us.

I remember a client from years ago, a brilliant architect in her late forties, who came to me for chronic neck pain. But as we worked together, a different story began to emerge. She spoke of a recurring dream where she was trying to read a blueprint, but the lines kept blurring, shifting, refusing to come into focus. In her waking life, her eyesight was getting progressively worse. She was severely nearsighted, and her optometrist had just prescribed, yet again, a stronger prescription.

“It feels like the future is a fog,” she confessed one day, her voice barely a whisper. “I can see the task right in front of me, the line on the page, the brick being laid. But when I look up… when I try to imagine the finished building, or my life in five years… it’s just a blur. A terrifying, indistinct blur.”

Her words struck me with such force. Here was the poetry of the body, speaking its truth so plainly. Her eyes, her physical eyes, were reflecting the exact state of her inner vision. The far future felt unsafe to trust, so her body had decided not to even try to see it clearly.

This is a conversation I’ve had in a thousand different forms in my three decades of healing work. Our vision is not just a mechanical process of light hitting the retina. It is a profound act of interpretation, deeply entwined with our beliefs, our fears, and our history. The statement, “I see,” means both to perceive with the eyes and to understand with the mind. The two are inseparable.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

Your body is a sacred messenger, and your eyes are its eloquent scribes. They are constantly writing the story of your inner world onto the canvas of your physical perception. When there is a conflict about what you are willing to look at—whether in your past, your present, or your future—your eyes will often be the first to let you know.

Think about the language we use. We speak of a “blinding truth,” of “turning a blind eye,” of being “blind-sided.” We have “blindsight” and “hindsight.” We get “stars in our eyes” or have our vision “clouded by tears.” This isn’t just metaphor; it’s a reflection of a deep, embodied wisdom that knows our physical and inner vision are intimately connected.

The light that enters your pupils is processed by the visual cortex in your brain, yes. But it is *interpreted* by the vast, intricate web of your consciousness, which is shaped by every experience you’ve ever had. Your beliefs act as a filter, determining what you focus on, what you magnify, and what you blur out.

For my architect client, a childhood marked by sudden, destabilizing changes had taught her a core belief: the future is not to be trusted. Her nervous system had learned that looking too far ahead was a recipe for disappointment and pain. So, her eyes complied. They focused beautifully on the present, the immediate, the controllable. But the horizon? That was off-limits.

Conversely, I’ve worked with many people who are farsighted. They can see the grand vision, the ten-year plan, the ultimate destination, with stunning clarity. But the present moment? The details of their current circumstances? It’s a painful, uncomfortable blur. For them, the present often feels too difficult to bear. Looking far into the distance becomes a survival strategy, a way to dissociate from the pain of *right now*. Their eyes, ever loyal, adjust accordingly.

## The Neuroscience of Sight and Belief

This isn't just a beautiful spiritual idea; it has roots in the very wiring of our brains. Neuroscientists have shown that our brains are predictive machines. They are constantly making guesses about the world based on past experiences. These predictions then influence what we actually perceive. You don't just see with your eyes; you see with your brain, and your brain sees with your history.

When a core belief like "the future is unsafe" is established, especially in childhood when the brain is so malleable, it creates deep neural pathways. The brain then works to confirm this belief. It will literally filter and interpret incoming data from the eyes to match the prediction. It’s a form of confirmation bias, but it’s happening at the physiological level of perception. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy written in neural code.

The muscles in and around your eyes, which are responsible for focusing, can also become chronically tensed in response to these beliefs. If you’re constantly bracing for a painful future, a subtle, chronic tension can take hold, physically altering the way your eyes focus light. The body is always listening to the mind, and it responds with unwavering loyalty.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Seeing with New Eyes

So what do we do with this? If you wear glasses or contacts, are you doomed to a life of emotional seeing-eye dogs? Of course not. This isn’t about blame or shame. It’s about compassion, curiosity, and the profound potential for transformation. It’s about understanding that your prescription, whether for nearsightedness or farsightedness, is not a life sentence. It is a message. A starting point for a deeper conversation with yourself.

Here’s a very good thing to know: your body, in its infinite wisdom, is always seeking wholeness. Your symptoms are not your enemy; they are communications from your soul, pointing you back toward alignment. The blurring in your vision is simply a request to look at what you’ve been avoiding.

If you are nearsighted, the invitation is to gently, tenderly, begin to build trust in the future. Not through force or Pollyanna-ish affirmations, but through the body. Through the felt sense of safety in the present moment. You might practice feeling your feet on the ground, the solid support of the earth beneath you, and whispering to your nervous system, “Right here, right now, I am safe.” As the present becomes a sanctuary, the future becomes less of a threat. The horizon can begin to come into focus, not as a source of anxiety, but as a field of possibility. You can also try a practice of "energetic seeing." Close your eyes, and imagine a future event that feels even a little bit safe and welcoming. A cup of tea tomorrow morning. A walk in the park next week. Feel the *feeling* of that safety in your body. Let your eyes, even behind their lids, soften and relax into that feeling. You are gently re-patterning your brain to associate the future with safety, one moment at a time.

If you are farsighted, the invitation is to come home to the present. To allow your gaze to soften and land on the details of your immediate life, even the uncomfortable ones. It’s a practice of presence, of meeting the moment without judgment. What if the pain you’re avoiding has medicine in it? What if the messiness of your current reality holds the very nutrients your soul needs to grow? By allowing your eyes to rest on what is, you signal to your body that it’s safe to be here, now. That you don’t need to escape into a distant future to survive. A beautiful practice for this is to find one small, simple thing in your immediate environment and truly *see* it for a full minute. A flower petal. The texture of the wood on your table. The way the light catches a dust mote in the air. Let your eyes drink in the detail, the color, the form. This simple act of focused, present-moment seeing can be a powerful anchor for a nervous system that’s used to fleeing.

## The Light of Understanding

Ultimately, the journey of healing our vision is about learning to see with new eyes—eyes illuminated by a higher consciousness, by the light of love itself. It’s about releasing the need to “keep an eye on” everything, to control and manage and predict. It’s about surrendering to a wisdom that is deeper than sight, a knowing that resides in the heart.

When you begin to heal the underlying emotional patterns, the beliefs that have been shaping your perception, something miraculous happens. The world doesn’t change, but your *experience* of it does. You begin to see through the filter of love, rather than the filter of fear. You see the inherent goodness in yourself and others. You see the sacredness in the mundane. You see the path forward not as a tightrope to be walked in terror, but as a dance to be joined with grace.

This is the transcendence of the eyes. To move from mere perception to true understanding. To see yourself and your life not as a problem to be fixed, but as a mystery to be lived. To know, in your very bones, that you are held in a love so vast it sees you, all of you, and calls you beloved.

teachings.sourceTitle: Reclaiming Your Creative Fire: Healing Reproductive Patterns
teachings.title: Reclaiming Your Creative Fire: Healing Reproductive Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe the reproductive system as the sacred center of creative power, where physical symptoms can be read as meaningful messages rather than enemies. Using Genevieve’s story, she shows how integrating medical care with inner work—listening, visualization, movement, and boundary-setting—can help reclaim creative and sexual agency. The piece emphasizes ancestral patterns, nervous-system conditioning, and the practical possibility of building new neural pathways through sustained, embodied practices.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I've been thinking about courage lately — not the dramatic, sword-wielding kind, but the quiet, trembling kind.

And it is perhaps never more revealing than when we venture into the territory of our reproductive system—the sacred, and so often silent, center of our creative power.

A woman I’ll call Genevieve came to see me years ago. She was in her late forties, a successful graphic designer with a sharp wit and a deep sadness in her eyes. She was suffering from debilitating fibroids, and her doctors were recommending a hysterectomy. On paper, it was a straightforward medical decision. But for Genevieve, it felt like a profound and devastating failure. She sat in my office, twisting a tissue in her hands, her body language a portrait of constriction.

“It’s not just an organ, Susan,” she told me, her voice thick with unshed tears. “It feels like they’re taking away… my womanhood. My creativity. The possibility of… something. Even though I never had children, and I don’t want them now. It’s deeper than that.”

It is always deeper than that.

The reproductive system is not just a collection of parts for procreation. It is the sacred portal of creation itself. Not just the creation of children, but the creation of art, of ideas, of new neural pathways, of a new life for yourself. It is the seat of our raw, untamed life force, the primal, creative pulse of the universe expressing itself through us. And for this very reason, it has been a place of immense cultural and personal wounding.

For centuries, this part of the body has been a battleground. It has been revered and reviled, worshipped and controlled, celebrated and shamed. The energy of our lineage—the unspoken stories of our mothers, grandmothers, and the women who came before them—is held in the very tissues of our wombs, our ovaries, our pelvic bowls. Their fears, their resilience, their silenced creative impulses, their sexual shame… it all lives within us. Not as a curse, but as a current. An energetic inheritance we are invited to heal. This isn't just a poetic idea; it's a concept that emerging science around epigenetics is beginning to validate. The experiences of our ancestors can influence our gene expression, meaning we can inherit predispositions to certain emotional and physical patterns. The trauma of a grandmother who was shamed for her desires can literally be written into the code that gets passed down, leaving us with a sense of unease in our own bodies that we can't logically explain.

## The Body as a Sacred Messenger

When the reproductive system begins to cry out—through pain, through cysts, through infertility, through hormonal chaos—it is not a betrayal. It is a message. A sacred, urgent communication from the deepest part of your being. The body is asking you to listen. To turn your loving attention toward a place you may have learned to ignore, to fear, or to objectify.

Think about the language we use. We have “problematic” periods, “raging” hormones, “hostile” uterine environments. We declare war on our own bodies. But what if we could see these symptoms not as enemies, but as messengers from a wise, wild, and wounded part of ourselves? What if the fibroid, like Genevieve’s, was not a monster to be excised, but a dense, concentrated ball of unexpressed creative energy? A lifetime of brilliant ideas, unpainted canvases, and unsung songs, literally taking up residence in her womb.

This is not to say that medical intervention is wrong. It is a vital and often life-saving tool. But it is incomplete if it does not also address the deeper energetic and emotional patterns at play. Healing is not about choosing between a medical approach and a holistic one. It is about integration. It is about creating a conversation between the head and the body, between science and the soul. It’s about understanding that our physical structures are inseparable from the consciousness that inhabits them. A surgeon can remove a fibroid, but they cannot remove the energetic pattern that created it. That is our sacred work to do.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Patterns We Inherit

So many of the women I work with carry a profound, often unconscious, fear of their own power. This is a direct inheritance. For generations, a woman’s power—her sexual power, her creative power, her intuitive power—was dangerous. It could get her ostracized, institutionalized, or killed. So, we learned to suppress it. To dampen our own creative fire. We became very, very good at being small.

The neural pathways for this suppression are deep. They are ancient superhighways in our nervous systems, carved by generations of conditioning. We learn to disconnect from our pelvic bowl, to hold our breath, to clench our jaws. We dissociate from our desire. We channel all that magnificent creative energy into safe, acceptable outlets: taking care of everyone else, perfecting our homes, being the “good girl,” achieving in our careers in ways that don't threaten the status quo.

And the body, in its infinite wisdom, keeps the score. The energy that is not expressed, not allowed to flow, must go somewhere. It can crystallize into pain. It can manifest as endometriosis, where the tissue that belongs inside the womb—the creative lining—migrates to places it doesn’t belong, a poignant metaphor for creative energy that feels it has no proper home. It can show up as PCOS, a complex metabolic and hormonal condition that often involves a deep confusion around feminine identity and expression. The body is not failing; it is adapting to a set of instructions, often unconscious, that tell it to shut down its own power.

Sexual shame is another huge piece of this puzzle. We live in a culture that is saturated with sexualized images, yet deeply terrified of authentic, embodied sexuality. We are taught that our desire is too much, or not enough. That our bodies are for the pleasure of others. That our sacred centers are transactional. This creates a profound split. We numb ourselves to both the pleasure and the pain. Healing the reproductive system is impossible without gently, compassionately, and courageously reclaiming our sexuality as a sacred and vital part of our life force. It’s about moving from a place of shame or objectification to a place of reverence for this incredible capacity for pleasure, connection, and creation.

## Reclaiming Your Creative Fire

For Genevieve, the journey began with a simple, radical act: she started listening to her body. Instead of seeing the fibroids as a hostile invasion, we began to approach them with curiosity. We used meditation and visualization to bring a soft, loving awareness to her womb. I asked her, “If this energy could speak, what would it say? If it could create, what would it create?”

At first, there was only silence. And then, a torrent of grief. Grief for the artist she had never allowed herself to be. Grief for the passion she had tamed into a tidy, respectable career. Then came the anger—a clean, hot anger at a world that had taught her to be afraid of her own brilliance. And under the anger, a wellspring of pure, unadulterated creative power.

Genevieve started painting. Huge, messy, abstract canvases that filled her small apartment. She used colors she had never dared to use in her design work—fiery oranges, deep indigos, shocking pinks. She danced in her living room to loud music, letting her hips move in ways they hadn’t in decades. She wrote poetry that didn’t rhyme and didn’t make sense, but felt profoundly true. She started to say “no” at work. She started to claim space. She began to have a relationship with her own desire, separate from any partner. She was, in essence, re-mothering herself. She was tending to the creative fire she had banked for decades.

Her journey was not linear. There was fear. There was backlash from those who were comfortable with the old, smaller version of her. But she was building new neural pathways. Through her consistent new actions and choices, she was literally rewiring her brain, proving to her nervous system, cell by cell, that it was safe to be powerful. That her creativity was not a threat, but a gift. That her body was not a problem to be solved, but a sacred vessel to be honored.

In the end, Genevieve did have a medical procedure, but it was a less invasive one than the hysterectomy. And she approached it not with a sense of failure, but with a sense of reverence. It was a conscious choice, a clearing of the old to make way for the new. She was not losing her womanhood; she was reclaiming it on her own terms. Her healing wasn't about getting rid of a symptom; it was about integrating the message the symptom was carrying.

Your body is not a battlefield. It is a garden. It may have been untended for a long time. There may be weeds. The soil may be dry. But the seeds of your creative fire are still there, dormant, waiting. They are waiting for your loving attention. They are waiting for your permission to grow.

What would it be like to place a hand on your lower belly and simply breathe? To send a current of warmth and acceptance into that sacred space, without needing to fix or change anything? To whisper to your body, “Thank you. I am listening.” This is where the healing begins. It begins in the quiet moments of presence, in the courageous act of turning toward yourself with love. It begins with the radical and beautiful recognition that you are, and have always been, a creator.


---

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe breasts as sacred symbols of nurture and as embodied messengers revealing the balance between giving and receiving. Drawing on clinical stories and compassionate insight, she links breast symptoms and pain to patterns of depletion, the mother wound, and the need for self-nurture, and offers presence-based practices to begin reclaiming bodily and emotional wholeness. The piece emphasizes gentle curiosity, small consistent acts of self-care, and the possibility of creating new neural pathways of self-reception.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember sitting in a circle of women, many years ago, during a healing workshop I was leading. The room was dimly lit, smelling of sage and rain-soaked cedar from the Vancouver outside. We were exploring the body’s landscape, a journey I’ve guided hundreds of souls through, and the conversation turned, as it often does, to our breasts. One woman, a lawyer in her fifties with a fierce intellect and a guarded heart, confessed with a tremor in her voice that she’d always hated her small breasts. She saw them as a sign of her inadequacy, a cosmic joke on a woman who had to fight to be seen in a man’s world. Another, a painter with vibrant canvases and a haunted look in her eyes, spoke of the raw shame she felt after her mastectomy. It wasn’t just the loss of a breast; it was as if a core part of her identity, her very essence as a woman, had been stolen, leaving a phantom limb of grief.

A third, a young mother with exhaustion etched into the lines around her eyes, spoke of the immense pressure she felt to breastfeed, the endless chorus of “breast is best.” When her body wouldn’t cooperate, the guilt consumed her. She felt like a failure at the most primal level of motherhood. Each story was unique, a tapestry woven with personal history and pain, yet a common thread of judgment, of *not-enoughness*, of a deep and aching disconnect, wove through them all.

It’s a tricky business, being human… and perhaps even trickier, being a woman in a world that has so many opinions about our bodies.

Our breasts. Have we ever considered them outside the context of size, or sexualization, or even disease? Have we ever truly sat with them as the sacred symbols they are? They are the most visible, undeniable emblem of our femaleness, the physical manifestation of the mother archetype. They are, by their very design, meant to nourish. From the moment we are born, we seek the breast. It is our first source of comfort, of sustenance, of life itself. It is the physical embodiment of unconditional love.

But the question that echoes through the lives of so many women is this… who are we nourishing? And are we, ourselves, being nourished in return? The answer to this question, I have found, is one of the most profound indicators of our overall well-being, a barometer of our connection to our own sacred feminine nature.

## The River of Nurture

In my decades of work as a healer, sitting with the sacred stories of countless women, I have seen the body speak its truth through the breasts. Through tenderness, through pain, through cysts, through the terrifying diagnosis of cancer. And so often, the story underneath is one of depletion. A story of giving, and giving, and giving… until the well runs dry.

Our bodies are such profound communicators. They are not our enemies. They don’t create symptoms to punish us. They create them to get our attention, to signal an imbalance, to call us home to ourselves. When it comes to our breasts, the message is often about the delicate, crucial balance between nurturing others and nurturing ourselves. Think of it as a sacred accounting. Are you pouring out more than you are taking in? Are your energetic accounts overdrawn?

Many of us have learned that to be a “good” woman—a good mother, partner, daughter, friend—is to be endlessly giving. We pour our love, our energy, our time, our very life force into others, believing this is the path to worthiness. We become the emotional bedrock for our families, the tireless engine in our careers, the ever-available friend. Yet, when we do this without first filling our own cup, we are giving from a place of lack. The river of nurture becomes a shallow, stagnant pool. This is where resentment can take root. I see it so often in my practice: a hardness, a crystallized grief or anger that manifests physically in the tender tissues of the breast. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is creating a physical boundary, a wall of protection, saying, *No more. What about me?*

This isn’t selfishness. It’s a fundamental law of energy, as real as gravity. You simply cannot give what you do not have. A river that is not fed by a source will eventually cease to flow. Your capacity to truly nourish another—your child, your partner, your community, your creative work—is directly proportional to your capacity to nourish yourself. It is the difference between offering a sip of water from a nearly empty cup, and allowing others to drink from the overflow of a gushing spring. One is an act of survival; the other is an act of grace.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Echo of the Mother

Our relationship with our breasts is often a mirror of our relationship with our own mothers, and with the concept of mothering itself. If we felt unnurtured as children, if our mother was absent emotionally or physically, if her love felt conditional or scarce, we may carry a deep, unconscious grief. This can manifest as a discomfort with our own feminine nature, a feeling of not-enoughness that gets projected onto our bodies. How we feel about the size and shape of our breasts often reflects our ease—or dis-ease—with our own innate femininity and our capacity to receive.

This isn’t about blame. It is so important to hold this with compassion. Every mother does the best she can with the tools and consciousness she has, often passing down the very patterns she inherited. But it *is* about awareness. It’s about recognizing the patterns that live within us, the neural pathways carved in our earliest years that tell us how to receive love and whether we are worthy of it. The beautiful thing about our brains—a concept neuroscience calls neuroplasticity—is that these pathways are not fixed. We are not doomed to repeat the past. We can create new ones. We can learn to mother ourselves.

What would it be like to offer yourself the tenderness you longed for? To hold yourself with the compassion you deserved? This is not just a psychological exercise; it is a profound act of physical healing. When we begin to truly nourish ourselves, to fill our own inner well, we release the grief and resentment that may have taken up residence in our bodies. We soften the hard places. We allow the energy to flow again. I once worked with a woman who had a recurring dream of a stone fountain in a barren courtyard. She was always thirsty, but the fountain was dry. As we worked together, she began to practice small, consistent acts of self-nurture: taking a bath with Epsom salts, buying herself a single, perfect rose each week, speaking to herself in the mirror with words of kindness. It felt awkward at first, even foolish. But she persisted. One day, she came to our session with a radiant smile that seemed to light up the room. “The fountain,” she said, her voice filled with wonder, “it’s flowing.” Her life began to transform. Her relationships deepened. And the chronic pain in her breast, which had plagued her for years, began to subside, replaced by a gentle warmth.

## The Sacred Feminine Embodied

To heal our relationship with our breasts is to heal our relationship with the sacred feminine itself. It is to reclaim our bodies from cultural judgment and to see them as they are: miraculous, intelligent, and holy.

Your body is a sacred messenger. Every sensation, every symptom, is a love letter from your soul. Your breasts, in their softness and their strength, are calling you back to yourself. They are asking you to honor the cycles of giving and receiving. They are inviting you to become a source-fed river, one that can nourish the world from a place of wholeness, not depletion.

This journey begins with presence. It begins with placing a hand over your heart, over your breast, and simply breathing. Feeling. Listening. Not with judgment, but with a gentle curiosity. What is the sensation there? What is the emotion living beneath the surface? What does it need to feel safe, to feel loved, to feel whole?

You don’t need to have all the answers. The simple act of turning your attention inward, with love, is a powerful act of transformation. You are rewriting the story. You are creating new neural pathways of self-love and acceptance. You are remembering that you are not broken. You have never been broken.

Take a moment, right now, to do this. Find a quiet space. Place your hand on your heart. Close your eyes. Take a deep, slow breath in, filling your belly, your ribs, your chest. And as you exhale, let go of any judgment you might be holding about your body. Let go of the stories, the comparisons, the fears. Simply be with yourself, in this moment. Feel the warmth of your hand. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest. This is the beginning of coming home to yourself. This is the path to embodying the sacred feminine in all its fullness, all its power, all its love.

You are a vessel of infinite love, and it is your birthright to be filled.


---

teachings.sourceTitle: The Womb as Sacred Vessel: Transcending Reproductive Wounds
teachings.title: The Womb as Sacred Vessel: Transcending Reproductive Wounds
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reclaim the womb as a sacred vessel and to understand reproductive symptoms as meaningful messages from the body rather than random afflictions. She names how cultural shame, trauma, and ancestral echoes can block creative and sexual energy, and offers gentle, embodied practices—breath, touch, movement, and voice—as pathways to safety, presence, and renewal. The piece emphasizes tenderness, nervous‑system regulation, and lineage healing while affirming that creativity and sexuality are intrinsic birthrights.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman came to see me last year carrying something invisible but immensely heavy.

And it is perhaps nowhere more revealing than in the landscape of our reproductive system… a place of such profound creative power, and for so many, a place of profound wounding.

I remember a woman I worked with years ago, a beautiful artist with paint-splattered hands and a sadness in her eyes that she couldn’t quite name. She came to me for chronic pelvic pain, a dull, persistent ache that doctors couldn’t diagnose. As we began to gently explore the energy of this space in her body, a torrent of grief poured out. Stories of shame, of sexuality used as a weapon against her, of a deep, unspoken belief that her body was not her own. Her womb, the very center of her creative power, had become a vessel for sorrow.

This is not an uncommon story. For centuries, the womb has been a battleground. A sacred portal revered for its life-giving magic… and a site of control, fear, and shame. Our culture has sent us so many conflicting messages: that our sexuality is a commodity, a sin, a duty, a performance. Rarely is it spoken of as a divine gift. A sacred current of life force that flows through us.

And so, we learn to disconnect. We armor ourselves against our own bodies. We carry the wounds of our mothers and grandmothers… the echoes of a lineage that was taught to fear its own power. The pain we feel—whether it’s physical, like my client’s, or the more nebulous ache of creative unfulfillment—is a messenger. It is the voice of the body, whispering… and sometimes screaming… for our loving attention.

## The Body as a Sacred Messenger

Here’s a very good thing to know: your body is always, *always* on your side. It is a sacred messenger, and its symptoms are not random afflictions. They are communications, pointing you toward the places that are calling for healing, for integration, for love.

When we experience issues in the reproductive system—be it infertility, painful periods, cysts, or a general sense of disconnection from our creative fire—it is an invitation to look deeper. To ask, with infinite compassion: *What is the story my body is telling?*

Our bodies are not just biological machines. They are fields of consciousness, holding our memories, our beliefs, and the energetic imprints of our experiences. The reproductive system, in particular, is a potent center of this energetic information. It is the seat of our innate capacity to generate, to create, and to bring forth new life in all its forms—not just babies, but art, ideas, businesses, and new ways of being.

When this center is wounded, when it is burdened by shame, fear, or trauma, that creative life force becomes blocked. It can manifest as physical illness, or as a feeling of being stuck, stagnant, and unable to move forward in our lives. We may feel a deep longing to create, but find ourselves paralyzed by self-doubt and a sense of unworthiness.

But here is the beautiful, miraculous truth: you are not broken. You have never been broken. Those wounds, those blockages, are not a life sentence. They are simply places where the energy of love has been forgotten. And what has been forgotten… can be remembered.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming Your Sacred Vessel

Transcending these reproductive wounds is not about “fixing” yourself. It is about reclaiming your body as a sacred vessel. It is about remembering the truth of who you are: a creator, whose birthright it is to generate and express the unique life force that flows through you.

This is a journey of profound tenderness. It requires us to turn toward the parts of ourselves we have been taught to reject, to listen to the stories held in our tissues, and to offer them the one thing they have been longing for. Our unconditional love.

One of the most powerful ways to begin this journey is to cultivate a conscious relationship with your womb. To begin to see it not as a source of pain or shame, but as a sacred portal of creation. You might place your hands on your lower belly and simply breathe. Feel the warmth of your own touch. You might whisper to your womb, “I am here. I am listening. Thank you.”

This is not just a sweet sentiment. It is a powerful act of neural rewiring. When you bring your loving, conscious attention to a part of your body, you are literally creating new neural pathways. You are teaching your nervous system that it is safe to feel, to connect, to be present in this sacred space. Wow.

As you continue this practice, you may find that memories or emotions arise. Grief, anger, shame. This is a natural part of the healing process. Your body is finally feeling safe enough to release what it has been holding. Your task is not to judge or analyze, but simply to witness. To be the compassionate, loving presence that these wounded parts of you have always needed.

> “You are a creator — this is your birthright.”

Trust your innate capacity to generate, create, and bring forth new life in all its forms. This is not something you have to earn or strive for. It is the very essence of who you are. Your sexuality is a divine gift, a current of creative energy that is meant to flow through you with joy and vitality.

As you begin to heal these reproductive wounds, you will find that your creative energy begins to flow more freely. You may feel a renewed sense of purpose, a desire to express yourself in new ways. You may find that your relationships become more intimate and authentic. You may even find that your physical symptoms begin to ease, as the energy in your body comes into a state of greater harmony and flow.

This is the journey of transcendence. It is not about escaping the body, but about embodying our divinity more and more fully. It is about remembering that we are not separate from the creative power of the universe… but a unique and beautiful expression of it.

Your womb is a sacred vessel. Your body is a temple. And you, beloved one, are a creator. What a thing to know.


---

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


## The Echoes in Our Cells

It’s fascinating, isn’t it? How a single experience can ripple through a lifetime. Neuroscience now shows us how trauma—big or small—can become physically wired into our nervous system. An experience of violation or shame, especially in our formative years, creates a powerful neural pathway. The brain, in its brilliant attempt to keep us safe, essentially learns: *this part of my body is a source of danger*. And so, it creates a pattern of dissociation, a subtle (or not-so-subtle) numbing. We learn to live slightly outside of ourselves, our life force rerouted around this perceived danger zone.

I see this so often with clients. A woman who feels a complete disconnect from her desire, who goes through the motions of intimacy but feels nothing. Another who desperately wants to launch her creative project but finds herself utterly frozen, unable to take the first step. When we trace these patterns back, we almost always find a moment, or a series of moments, where their creative, sexual essence was shamed, dismissed, or violated. The body, in its infinite wisdom, decided it was safer to shut down the power plant than to risk another explosion.

And it’s not just our own stories we carry. The science of epigenetics is beginning to confirm what ancient wisdom has always known: that we inherit the emotional and energetic imprints of our ancestors. The unspoken grief of a grandmother who lost a child, the shame of a great-grandmother who was forced into a loveless marriage—these echoes can live on in our cells, shaping our beliefs and our biology in ways we may not even realize. Your struggle may not have started with you, but the healing can. When you do this work, you are not just reclaiming your own life force; you are sending a ripple of healing backward and forward through your lineage.

## The Practice of Coming Home

So how do we begin to dismantle these ancient walls and come home to ourselves? It is a practice, a gentle and devoted returning, moment by moment.

It begins with the breath. Your breath is the most powerful tool you have for anchoring yourself in the present moment and soothing a dysregulated nervous system. When you feel that familiar clench of fear or shame, can you pause, and take one conscious breath? Inhale deeply into your lower belly, imagining you are sending a wave of warm, loving energy into your womb space. As you exhale, release the tension, the story, the fear. This simple act, repeated over time, is a profound declaration to your body: *I am here with you. You are safe.*

From there, you might explore gentle movement. Put on a piece of music that moves you and allow your hips to sway. Not a performance, not for anyone else’s gaze, but a simple, sensual exploration of your own body. Feel the way your pelvis can rock and circle, the way your spine can undulate. You are reawakening a dormant language, the native tongue of your body’s wisdom. There is no right or wrong way to do this. There is only your way.

And finally, there is the power of your own voice. Find a quiet moment and speak your truth, even if only to yourself. You might write it in a journal, or speak it aloud to the empty room. “I am ready to reclaim my creative power.” “I release the shame that was never mine to carry.” “My sexuality is sacred and holy.” Feel the vibration of these words in your body. You are not just saying them; you are *becoming* them. You are calling your power home.

This is the sacred work of our time. To heal the divide between body and soul, to reclaim the parts of ourselves that have been cast into shadow, and to remember the magnificent, creative beings we were born to be. It is a journey of a thousand small steps, each one a prayer, each one a homecoming.

On the fourth breath, whisper or think a short, kind phrase to your womb (for example, “I am here,” “You are safe,” or “Thank you”). teachings.sourceTitle: When Flexibility Becomes Rigidity: What Your Hips Are Holding
teachings.title: When Flexibility Becomes Rigidity: What Your Hips Are Holding
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider chronic hip and leg tension as embodied expressions of psychological rigidity—patterns of control, protection, and early survival strategies that the nervous system learned to keep us safe. Rather than forcing physical fixes, she offers a compassionate, listening-based somatic practice to cultivate interoception, safety, and gradual neuroplastic change, reframing flexibility as strength.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A few years ago, I was working with a client—a brilliant woman, a CEO who had built an empire from the ground up. She walked into my office with a sense of purpose that seemed to precede her, her movements precise and contained. She came to me for persistent, debilitating pain in her right hip. She’d seen every specialist, tried every therapy, but the pain remained, a stubborn anchor in her otherwise meticulously controlled life. “I don’t understand it,” she told me, her voice tight with a frustration that felt like a well-worn coat. “I’m disciplined. I’m strong. I do yoga every single day. I *should* be flexible.”

And there it was. The word that was both the key and the lock: *should*.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We learn to equate strength with rigidity, stability with control. We build our lives on foundations of belief that we think are solid, only to find that they are brittle. And nowhere does this show up more clearly, more insistently, than in our hips and legs. Our hips and legs are our ultimate grounding rods. They are the foundation of our dance through life, the very structures that grant us both stability and mobility. The magnificent ball-and-socket joint of the hip is designed to move in every direction—to swing, to circle, to yield, to press forward. Yet, so often, we hold it captive, frozen by stories we’ve long forgotten we’re telling ourselves.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

When we experience chronic pain, tightness, or injury in our hips and legs, it is a profound communication from the body. It’s a message, not a malfunction. The body is whispering—or sometimes, screaming—that our approach to life has become inflexible. We may feel we don’t have a “leg to stand on,” either in an argument or in our own life’s purpose. We might be terrified of being made to “bend at the knees,” to surrender to something or someone, because we’ve learned that surrender is weakness, that to yield is to lose.

I see this pattern so often. The belief that to be stable, we must be rigid. To be safe, we must be unbending. These are not just ideas; they are neural pathways carved deep into our brains, often from very early experiences. When a child doesn’t feel safe or supported, their very way of standing, of walking, of holding themselves in the world, can become a pattern of defense. The legs, which should feel firmly planted on a supportive earth, instead learn to brace. The hips, which should be fluid, learn to lock.

This isn’t a conscious choice. It’s a brilliant, adaptive strategy of the nervous system to keep us safe in a world that felt unsafe. The brain’s primary job, after all, is survival. It creates these patterns of holding and tension as a way to protect the vulnerable core of our being. But as we grow, that once-protective pattern becomes a cage. The rigidity that once served us now limits us. We become so weighted down by the armoring, by the negative beliefs we carry about ourselves and the world, that our legs feel as if they might just give out.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Illusion of Control

My client, the CEO, had built her life on a foundation of control. Every variable was managed, every outcome predicted. Her yoga practice, which she believed was about flexibility, had become another form of control—a way to force her body into submission, to achieve a perfect pose. Her hip was not failing; it was rebelling. It was refusing to be forced.

As we worked together, we didn’t focus on stretching the hip. We focused on listening to it. What was the story it was holding? What was the fear that kept it so locked down? Gently, slowly, we began to explore the underlying belief that if she wasn’t in absolute control, everything would fall apart. That if she were to truly be flexible—in her body, in her business, in her relationships—she would be weak and vulnerable.

This is the great misunderstanding. True flexibility is not weakness. It is a form of profound strength. Think of a great tree in a storm. The rigid, brittle branches are the first to snap. The trunk and limbs that can sway, that can yield to the force of the wind, are the ones that remain standing. They are both stable *and* flexible.

Our bodies are built for this kind of flexible stability. Our hips are designed to allow us to stay in step with the changing rhythms of life, no matter the music, no matter the dance partner. But when we cling to old fears, old hurts, old beliefs about what is and is not safe, we freeze the dance. We turn the fluid grace of the body into a rigid statue.

## A Practice for Listening

This is not about forcing or fixing. This is a practice of deep listening, of creating a new relationship with your body based on trust and compassion. Find a quiet space where you can lie down comfortably.

> Lie on your back, with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. Place your hands gently on your lower belly or on your hip joints. Close your eyes.

> For a few moments, simply arrive. Feel the weight of your body on the floor. Notice the rhythm of your breath, without changing it. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your hands.

> Now, bring your awareness to your hips. Don’t try to change anything. Just notice. Is there a sensation of tightness? Of gripping? Of ease? Is one side different from the other? Be a gentle, curious observer.

> If you notice a place of tension, imagine you could breathe directly into that space. Not to force it to release, but to bring it a quality of warmth, of presence. A simple message: *I feel you. I am here with you.*

> You might ask, in the quiet of your own heart, “What are you holding for me?” or “What do you need me to know?” Don’t search for an answer. Simply create the space for a response to arise. It may come as a word, an image, a feeling, a memory. It may not come at all, and that is perfectly okay. The practice is the listening itself.

> Stay here for five to ten minutes, just breathing and being with your body. When you are ready, gently begin to wiggle your fingers and toes. Slowly, roll to one side and rest for a moment before pressing yourself up to a seated position.

This practice, done regularly, begins to rewire the brain. It communicates to the nervous system on a profound level that you are safe. It creates new neural pathways of self-compassion and interoception—the felt sense of the internal state of the body. This is the foundation of neuroplasticity in action. We are not just stretching muscles; we are transforming our consciousness.

## A New Way of Being

What would it be like to allow your hips to be soft? To trust that you can be stable without being rigid? This isn’t about forcing a stretch or pushing through pain. It’s about creating safety from the inside out. It’s about letting your nervous system know that you are no longer that child who had to brace against the world. You are an adult, with resources, with wisdom, with the capacity to choose a new way.

It begins with this gentle inquiry. Placing a hand on your hip and simply breathing. Noticing the sensation without judgment. Is there tightness? Is there holding? Just notice. You might ask it, softly, “What are you holding for me?” You may not get an answer in words. It might be a feeling, an image, a memory. The key is to stay present, to listen with compassionate curiosity.

This is the work of transformation. It is the work of rewiring those ancient neural pathways, of showing your body, cell by cell, that it is safe to let go. It is safe to be fluid. It is safe to trust in the support of the earth beneath you and the wisdom of the body that carries you.

Your hips are not the enemy. The pain is not a punishment. It is an invitation. An invitation to step beyond the old fears, to release the illusion of control, and to rediscover the fluid, graceful, powerful dance of your own being.


---
