teachings.sourceTitle: Your Body as Oracle: How to Read the Messages in Your Symptoms
teachings.title: Your Body as Oracle: How to Read the Messages in Your Symptoms
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to shift from treating the body as a machine to listening to it as an oracle, where symptoms are meaningful messages rather than mere malfunctions. She situates this practice in somatic neuroscience (Polyvagal theory) and Taoist imagery of flow, and offers a gentle, curiosity-based inquiry to begin decoding what sensations are asking you to notice and change.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are gifted these incredible bodies—these vessels of flesh and bone, nerve and sinew—and yet, so often, we treat them like machines. We expect them to perform, to comply, to keep running smoothly until a part breaks down. And when it does, when a symptom arises, our first instinct is to silence it, to fix it, to make the noise stop so we can get back to our regularly scheduled lives. But what if that’s the wrong approach entirely? What if you approached your body not as a machine that breaks down, but as an oracle that speaks? What if every symptom, every ache, every persistent pattern was not a sign of failure, but a message? A sacred invitation to understand what has been hidden in plain sight, right there within your own skin. This is the great work, beloved one. To learn the language of your own body. To understand that it is constantly communicating with you, offering you wisdom, guidance, and a direct line to the deepest truths of your soul. Your body is not a traitor. It is your most loyal and devoted ally, and it is holding the keys to your healing. ## The Body as a Living Oracle We tend to think of oracles as something external—a wise woman in a cave, a deck of cards, the alignment of the stars. We seek answers outside of ourselves, hoping for a sign, a map, a clear path forward. But the most profound, most intimate, and most accurate oracle you will ever have is the one you inhabit every single moment of every single day. It is your body. I remember a client I worked with years ago, a brilliant woman who was a force in her industry. She came to me with debilitating migraines. She had seen every specialist, tried every medication, and was at her wit’s end. The pain was a thief, stealing days from her life, and she just wanted it to stop. As we began our work together, I didn’t ask her about the pain’s intensity or frequency. I asked her, “If the pain had a voice, what would it be trying to tell you?” She was taken aback. No one had ever asked her that before. We sat in the quiet of my office, the soft afternoon light filtering through the windows, and she closed her eyes. After a few moments, tears began to stream down her face. “It would say,” she whispered, “that I need to stop. That I can’t keep pushing this hard. That I’m carrying the weight of everyone else’s expectations, and it’s crushing me.” That was the beginning of her healing. Not a new pill or a new therapy, but a new conversation. A conversation with her own body. The migraines were not a random malfunction; they were a desperate plea from her soul, transmitted through the language of her nervous system. They were the only way her body could get her attention, the only way to make her stop and listen. This is the essence of the body as an oracle. It speaks in the language of sensation: tightness in the chest, a knot in the stomach, a recurring ache in the left shoulder, the exhaustion that settles deep in your bones. These are not random occurrences. They are symbols. They are metaphors. They are the voice of your inner wisdom, bubbling up to the surface, asking to be heard. ## The Neuroscience of Somatic Wisdom This isn’t just poetry or mysticism; it’s grounded in the very real science of our nervous system. Our bodies are intricate networks of information, constantly processing our experiences, both conscious and unconscious. Dr. Stephen Porges’ Polyvagal Theory gives us a beautiful map for understanding this. It teaches us that our autonomic nervous system is constantly scanning our environment for cues of safety and danger, a process called *neuroception*. When we experience something that our nervous system perceives as a threat—whether it’s a real physical danger or an emotional one, like a harsh word from a loved one or the pressure of a deadline—our body shifts into a state of protection. It might go into a fight-or-flight response, flooding our system with adrenaline and cortisol, creating that feeling of anxiety, tension, and hyper-vigilance. Or, if the threat feels too overwhelming, it might go into a freeze or shutdown response, leading to feelings of numbness, disconnection, and fatigue. These are not just fleeting feelings. When we experience these states repeatedly, especially in our early lives, they can become patterned into our nervous system. They become our default setting. The unresolved energy of those protective responses gets stored in our tissues, in our fascia, in our cellular memory. And over time, that stored energy can manifest as chronic symptoms. That persistent tightness in your jaw? It might be the stored energy of all the words you’ve swallowed, the anger you never expressed. That chronic back pain? It could be the physical manifestation of feeling unsupported or carrying too much responsibility. That digestive distress? It might be your body’s way of saying it can’t stomach a situation you’re in. Your body is keeping the score, as Dr. Bessel van der Kolk so aptly put it. It is a living archive of your entire life’s experience. And the symptoms are simply the librarians, pointing you to the sections that need your attention. ## Learning to Read the Signs So, how do we begin to learn this language? How do we shift from trying to silence our symptoms to learning to listen to them? It begins with a simple, yet profound, shift in orientation. It begins with curiosity. The next time a symptom arises, I invite you to try this. Instead of immediately reaching for a remedy, take a moment. Find a quiet space where you can be with yourself. Close your eyes. Take a few gentle breaths, and then bring your awareness to the sensation in your body. Don’t judge it. Don’t try to change it. Just be with it. Notice its qualities. Is it sharp or dull? Hot or cold? Is it vibrating or still? Where exactly is it located? Does it have a color? A shape? A texture? And then, with a sense of gentle inquiry, you can ask it a question. You might ask: * “What is the message you have for me?” * “What do you need me to know?” * “When did you first arrive?” * “What were you trying to protect me from?” Don’t strain for an answer. The mind will want to jump in and analyze, to figure it out. See if you can let that go and just listen with your whole being. The answer may not come in words. It might come as an image, a memory, a sudden feeling, or just a subtle shift in the sensation itself. Trust whatever arises. This is a practice. It’s like learning any new language. At first, it might feel awkward and unfamiliar. You might not understand everything. But the more you practice, the more you show up with consistent, compassionate attention, the more fluent you will become. Your body will learn that it is finally safe to speak, and you will learn how to listen. ## The Wisdom of the Tao The Tao Te Ching teaches us about the power of water. It flows, it yields, it nourishes, and yet it has the power to overcome all obstacles. It doesn’t force; it finds the path of least resistance. Our bodies hold this same wisdom. > “The supreme good is like water, > Which nourishes all things without trying to. > It is content with the low places that people disdain.” When we are in alignment with our own inner nature, with our Tao, there is a sense of flow and ease in our bodies. When we are out of alignment—when we are pushing, striving, forcing, or ignoring our own needs—our bodies will let us know. The flow becomes blocked. The energy stagnates. And this stagnation is often the root of physical discomfort. Your symptoms are a call to return to your own natural flow. They are asking you to look at where you are being rigid, where you are resisting your own truth, where you are living in a way that is out of integrity with your soul. Are you in a job that drains your life force? A relationship that constricts your heart? Are you holding onto old griefs or resentments that are weighing you down? Your body knows. It is the ultimate truth-teller. It has no agenda other than your wholeness and your well-being. When you learn to listen to its whispers, you won’t have to wait for it to scream.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
This journey of learning to listen to your body is one of the most profound acts of self-love you can undertake. It is a returning home to yourself. It is a reclamation of your own innate wisdom and power. You don’t need to look outside for the answers, my dear one. They are already living inside of you, waiting patiently to be heard. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Headaches, Migraines, and the Prison of Overthinking
teachings.title: Headaches, Migraines, and the Prison of Overthinking
teachings.summary: Susan links chronic headaches and migraines to the habitual prison of overthinking, suggesting that pain often signals a disconnect between the thinking mind and the body’s deeper wisdom. She offers a gentle somatic inquiry—acknowledging sensations, noticing thought patterns, and dropping into the body—to interrupt habitual tension and invite a kinder relationship between head, heart, and body. The piece frames pain as a messenger and encourages sustained, compassionate practice rather than quick fixes.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was making soup the other day — a simple thing, really — when I was struck by how much healing resembles cooking.

And part of that business, for so many of us, involves the head. That three-pound universe, as the neuroscientists call it, perched atop our shoulders, constantly trying to run the show.

I remember a time, years ago, when I was navigating a particularly complex family situation. It felt like a knot of impossible threads, a tangle of old wounds and unspoken expectations. Every night, I would lie awake, the darkness of my bedroom feeling not restful, but charged with a frantic energy. My mind was a relentless engine, turning the problem over and over like a stone in a tumbler. I was *thinking* so hard, convinced that if I just analyzed it from one more angle, rehearsed one more imaginary conversation, or planned for one more potential outcome, I could find the ‘right’ answer—the one that would fix everything and make everyone happy.

I was trying to be the hero, the fixer, the one who could hold it all together. And every morning, I would wake up with a crushing headache. It wasn’t the searing, electric pain of a migraine, not yet. It was a dull, persistent pressure, a physical sensation of being trapped. It felt like a metal band was being slowly, inexorably tightened around my skull. My body was speaking to me, of course. It was sending a clear, unambiguous signal that my approach was not only failing, but causing harm. But I wasn’t listening. I was too busy… thinking.

This is a story I hear in countless variations in my practice. The woman who gets a migraine every Sunday night as she mentally prepares for a week at a job that drains her soul. The man who feels a tension headache building every time he has to speak with his demanding father. We have been taught to revere the intellect, to believe that our thinking mind is our greatest asset. And it is a magnificent tool, no doubt. But when it becomes the sole authority, when we try to use it to solve the mysteries of the heart and the soul, it can become a prison. The pain we feel in our heads is often the sound of our own consciousness, our own life force, pressing against the rigid bars of our limited belief systems.

## The Tyranny of the Thinking Mind

Our brains are wired for efficiency. They create neural pathways that function like well-worn grooves in a record. When we think the same thoughts over and over—*I have to get this right, I can’t make a mistake, I need to control this outcome, It’s all up to me*—we deepen those grooves. We are, in a very real sense, programming our own nervous system to exist in a state of high alert. This creates a feedback loop of mental pressure that eventually has to go somewhere. For many, it manifests as physical pain.

Headaches and migraines are so often the body’s cry for a ceasefire in the war of the mind. They are the physical expression of overthinking, of trying to figure everything out, of placing far too much pressure on ourselves to perform, to know, to be certain in a world that is inherently uncertain. The conflict is not just in our heads; it’s a fundamental schism between our head’s knowledge and our heart’s deep, intuitive wisdom. The head wants a spreadsheet, a five-point plan. The heart speaks in the quiet language of feeling, image, and sensation. The head says, “This is logical.” The heart whispers, *“This feels true.”*

Think about the quality of that pain. A tension headache feels like a vise grip, a relentless constriction. A migraine can feel like a lightning storm, a sensory explosion that makes light, sound, and even touch feel like an assault. This isn’t just random biological noise. This is a message, written in the language of the body.

The constriction is the feeling of your own beautiful, expansive consciousness being squeezed into the narrow confines of a belief that you *must* figure it all out alone. It’s the energy of your being, which wants to flow and expand, hitting the wall of a rigid mental pattern. The storm of a migraine is the raw energy of your spirit, rebelling against the cage. It’s a desperate attempt by your system to break through the dam of control and release the pent-up energy.

What if the pain is not an enemy to be defeated, but a messenger to be welcomed? A sacred signal from your body that it is time to lay down the weapons of the mind and listen on a deeper level?

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Gentle Inquiry

Before we can shift this pattern, we must first become aware of it. This is not another task for the thinking mind to *do*. It is an invitation to simply notice. The next time you feel the familiar stirrings of a headache, or even just the sensation of mental tension, try this gentle practice.

Find a quiet place where you can sit for a few moments without interruption. Close your eyes if that feels comfortable. Instead of immediately reaching for a pill or trying to push the pain away, simply allow your awareness to turn inward.

1.  **Acknowledge the Sensation:** Without judgment, simply notice the feeling in your head. Is it sharp or dull? Is it pulsing or constant? Is it in one specific spot or all over? Don’t try to change it. Just… be with it. Greet it with a sense of neutral curiosity, as if you were a scientist observing a new phenomenon.

2.  **Listen for the Thoughts:** Now, gently tune your awareness to the thoughts that are present. What are the stories your mind is telling you? Are you rehearsing a future conversation? Are you replaying a past event? Are you worrying about what someone else is thinking? Again, no judgment. Simply notice the content and the *feeling* of the thoughts. Let them be there.

3.  **Drop into the Body:** Now, gently guide your awareness downward, out of your head. Feel the weight of your body on the chair. Feel your feet on the floor. Place one hand on your heart and one hand on your belly. Feel the warmth of your hands. Take a slow, gentle breath, and feel the slight rise and fall of your abdomen. Stay here for a few breaths, simply feeling the sensations in your body.

This simple process is not about fixing the headache. It is about interrupting the pattern. It is a radical act of shifting your attention from the tyranny of the mind to the quiet wisdom of the body. It is the beginning of a new conversation.

## From Conflict to Coherence

Healing this deep divide doesn’t mean abandoning our intellect. It means inviting it into a new relationship, a dance with the other ways of knowing that reside within us. It’s about cultivating coherence between the head, the heart, and the body’s innate wisdom. The brain is a magnificent tool, but it is not the totality of your intelligence.

I learned, slowly, to listen to my headaches. When I felt that familiar pressure begin to build, I would stop my frantic doing and begin this practice of gentle inquiry. I wouldn’t try to *stop* the thinking, which only creates more tension. Instead, I would simply notice it with a surprising amount of tenderness. *Ah, there’s the thinking mind, trying so hard to keep me safe. Thank you for your diligence. I see how hard you are working.*

By acknowledging the mind’s efforts with compassion instead of frustration, something remarkable happens. It begins to soften. The grip loosens. By dropping our awareness down, out of the head and into the body, we change the channel. We shift from the frantic, high-frequency buzz of mental control to the slower, deeper rhythm of somatic wisdom. We begin to access the heart’s intelligence, which doesn’t operate on linear logic but on resonance, feeling, and a profound sense of connection to a larger whole.

This is not a one-time fix, but a lifelong practice. It is the practice of noticing when you are caught in the prison of overthinking and gently, kindly, guiding yourself back home to the vast, open landscape of your embodied presence. It is the courage to say, “I don’t know the answer right now,” and to trust that clarity will arise not from more thinking, but from a place of deep, quiet listening. It is the willingness to be in the messy uncertainty of the present moment, without needing to immediately control it.

The next time you feel the stirrings of a headache, see if you can meet it with this new quality of attention. Ask it, gently, “What are you trying to tell me? Where am I putting pressure on myself? What rigid belief is my consciousness pressing against?” You may be surprised by the wisdom that echoes back in the quiet space you create.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Windows of Perception: What Your Eyes Reveal About Your Inner World](/blog/eyes-windows-of-perception)
- [Standing Tall in Your Truth: Transcending Spinal Patterns](/blog/spine-standing-tall)
- [A Somatic Practice for Calming Your Nervous System](/blog/nervous-system-somatic-practice)

**More on Head:**

- [The Crown of Consciousness: What Your Head Is Really Telling You](/blog/head-crown-of-consciousness)
- [A Practice for Quieting the Mind and Trusting Deeper Wisdom](/blog/head-quieting-mind-practice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you have the courage to release the need to figure it all out, and the grace to open to the profound wisdom that flows when you are simply present to the miracle of your own being. May your mind become a trusted friend, and your body a sacred guide.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Losing Your Voice: When Authentic Expression Feels Dangerous
teachings.title: Losing Your Voice: When Authentic Expression Feels Dangerous
teachings.summary: Susan uses a personal story of losing her voice to explore how withheld speech becomes embodied as physical symptoms and nervous-system protection. She frames the throat as the bridge between heart and mind and offers gentle practices—journaling, diaphragmatic breath, humming—to create new, safety-based neural associations for authentic expression. The piece leans into radical compassion for survival patterns while inviting steady, embodied steps toward reclaiming one’s voice.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The teacup rattled in its saucer, a tiny earthquake in my hands. I was twenty-three, sitting across from my mother in a cafe that smelled of burnt coffee and old regrets. She was telling a story about my childhood, a story I’d heard a hundred times, but this time, the details were sharper, the edges more jagged. And wrong. My memory, a vivid, Technicolor movie, played a completely different version. I opened my mouth to correct her, to say, *“No, that’s not how it was. You’re forgetting the part where…”* But the words caught in my throat, a tangled knot of old fear and a desperate need to keep the peace. A familiar tightness seized my larynx. I swallowed. And said nothing.

For the next three days, I could barely speak above a whisper. Laryngitis, the doctor said. Rest your voice. But I knew, with a certainty that resonated deeper than bone, that it wasn’t a virus I was fighting. It was a lifetime of swallowed words, a chorus of unspoken truths that had finally decided to stage a protest, right there in the delicate tissues of my vocal cords.

This is a tricky business, this human experience of voice. Not just the sounds we make, but the truth we carry. Your voice, beloved, is so much more than a biological function. It is the vibrational signature of your soul, the primary way you translate the exquisite, non-physical energy of your inner being into the physical world. It’s where your consciousness takes flight, where your inner truth finds its frequency and ripples out into the universe. The throat, in the great map of our energy systems, is the bridge. It’s the sacred space where the wisdom of the heart meets the logic of the mind, where raw feeling is alchemized into expression.

So what happens when that bridge is blocked? What happens when speaking our truth feels not just uncomfortable, but dangerous?

The body, in its infinite wisdom, always tells the story. Issues with the voice—chronic hoarseness, nodes on the vocal cords, a recurring pattern of “losing” your voice—are rarely just physical. They are profound communications from a deeper part of you. They are the echoes of a conflict, a dissonance between what you know to be true in your heart and what you feel safe to express in the world. When you consistently speak what you think others want to hear, when you silence the quiet (or roaring) call of your own soul to please, to placate, to survive… the body pays the price. The very instrument of your truth begins to shut down.

Perhaps you can feel it now, a subtle tightness in your own throat as you read these words. A ghost of a memory. A sensation of being small, of being silenced. For so many of us, the wounding begins in childhood. We are told we are “too much,” “too loud,” “too sensitive.” We learn, through a glance, a sharp word, or the withdrawal of love, that our authentic expression is not welcome. That our truth makes others uncomfortable. And so, we learn to modulate. To edit. To swallow. We become exquisite editors of our own souls, cutting and pasting our truth until it’s a pale, polite, and acceptable version of the original masterpiece.

These experiences aren’t just psychological memories; they are imprinted in our very neurology. When speaking up is met with punishment or rejection, our nervous system creates a powerful association: Authentic Expression = Danger. The amygdala, the brain’s little smoke detector, tags the act of speaking our truth as a threat to our survival. From that moment on, every time a similar situation arises, the alarm bells go off. The body floods with cortisol and adrenaline. The vagus nerve, which wanders from the brainstem all the way down to the gut and is intimately connected to our vocal cords, can go into a state of freeze. The muscles in the throat constrict. The breath becomes shallow. And the words… the words die before they are ever born. We are, quite literally, silenced by our own biology, a biology programmed by past pain.

This isn’t a flaw. It’s a survival mechanism. Every pattern has served you. The pattern of silence once kept you safe. It helped you belong. It ensured your connection to those you depended on. So the first step is not to judge this part of you, but to meet it with radical compassion. To place a hand on your throat and whisper, *“Thank you. Thank you for trying so hard to protect me. I understand why you did this. And now, we can learn a new way.”*

Let’s be clear: this is not about blaming those who may have silenced you. They were often acting from their own unhealed wounds, their own programmed fears. This is about reclaiming your own power, your own sovereignty over your expression. It’s about understanding the elegant, if painful, logic of your own system. The body is never against you. It is always, always, working for you, based on the information it has. Our work is to give it new, more empowering information. To consciously create experiences of safety and reward around speaking our truth, however small, so the nervous system can begin to relax its guard and write a new story, a new neural pathway where your voice is not a source of danger, but a source of connection and authentic power.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

The cost of this silence is immense. When we swallow our words, we are also swallowing our life force. The energy of that unspoken truth doesn’t just vanish. It gets stored in the body. It can manifest as chronic tension in the neck and shoulders, as thyroid issues, as a persistent lump in the throat. It creates a dam in our energetic system, and the pressure builds. This is the weight of the unspoken, the burden of the inauthentic. It’s exhausting, isn’t it? To live a life of constant performance, of holding back the river of your own being.

What would it be like, just for a moment, to let that river flow? To feel the energy of your truth, not as a threat, but as the purest expression of your own divine nature?

The journey back to your authentic voice is not about becoming louder or more aggressive. It’s a journey inward. It’s about creating a profound sense of safety within your own being, a sanctuary where your truth is allowed to exist, first and foremost, for *you*. It begins with listening. Listening to the whispers beneath the silence. What are the words you’ve been swallowing? What is the truth that is aching to be spoken?

Perhaps you might start with a journal, a sacred space where no one else’s opinion matters. Let the words flow, uncensored. The angry words. The sad words. The beautiful, wild, inconvenient words. Let them out. Give them form. See them on the page. This is a powerful act of validation. You are telling your soul, “I hear you. You matter.”

From there, we can begin to gently re-inhabit the physical space of the voice. Sound is vibration. And vibration can shift energy. It’s quantum physics in its most personal form. You can change your frequency. Try humming. Yes, humming. Feel the vibration in your chest, your throat, your lips. It’s a gentle massage for the vocal cords and the vagus nerve, a signal of safety and calm. Put on a piece of music you love and sing along in the car, with no one listening. Feel the pure, uninhibited joy of your own sound filling the space. These small acts begin to rewire those old neural pathways. They create new associations: Voice = Safety. Voice = Joy. Voice = Me.

And then, there is the breath. The voice is nothing but breath given shape and sound. When we are afraid, our breath is shallow, held high in the chest. This is the breath of the flight-or-fight response. To reclaim the voice, we must first reclaim the breath. Practice deep, diaphragmatic breathing. Lie on the floor, place a hand on your belly, and as you inhale, feel your hand rise. As you exhale, feel it fall. This simple act sends a powerful message of safety to the nervous system. It activates the parasympathetic state, the 'rest and digest' mode, where healing and restoration happen. When you speak from a place of deep, grounded breath, your voice has more resonance, more power, and more truth. It is literally sourced from a deeper, calmer place within you. This is not about performance; it is about presence. It is about anchoring your expression in the solid foundation of your own life-giving breath.

I remember, after that cafe incident with my mother, spending weeks in a kind of vocal wilderness. My whisper was a constant reminder of all the things I hadn’t said. One afternoon, sitting in my car, I felt a wave of grief wash over me—for the little girl who learned to be quiet, for the young woman who was still so afraid. And I just started to make a sound. A low, mournful hum. It grew into a tone, then a wail, then a song with no words. I wasn’t performing. I wasn’t even trying to sing well. I was just letting the sound of my own pain, my own truth, finally have its moment. And as the sound poured out, something inside me broke free. The tightness in my throat dissolved, replaced by a warm, spacious ache. The next morning, my voice was back. Hoarse, but there. It was a beginning.

Reclaiming your voice is not a one-time event. It’s a practice. A daily, moment-by-moment choice to honor the truth that lives within you. It’s the courage to say, “That doesn’t work for me.” The grace to whisper, “I need your help.” The power to declare, “This is who I am.” Each time you speak your truth, with compassion and clarity, you strengthen the bridge between your heart and the world. You reclaim a piece of your own sacred energy.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Inspiration and Expiration: The Spiritual Dimensions of Breath](/blog/lungs-inspiration-expiration)
- [The Instruments of Love's Expression: What Your Hands Reveal](/blog/hands-instruments-of-love)

**More on Vocal Cords:**

- [A Practice for Freeing Your Voice and Speaking with Love](/blog/vocal-cords-freeing-voice-practice)
- [The Silver Tongue and the Silent Scream: Two Sides of Vocal Wounding](/blog/vocal-cords-silver-tongue)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

Your voice is a gift. Not just to yourself, but to the world. There is a frequency that only you can emit, a note in the grand symphony of the universe that only you can sing. Your story, your wisdom, your unique perspective—it is all encoded in the vibration of your voice. To withhold it is to rob the world of your medicine. To express it, authentically and lovingly, is to contribute to the healing of us all. It is the ultimate act of love.

So take a breath, beloved. Place a hand on your heart, and another on your throat. Feel the connection. Feel the river of your own truth, waiting. You don’t have to force it. You don’t have to shout. Just open the gate, even a tiny crack. And let your soul begin to sing.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Releasing the Ego's Throne: Your Head as Servant, Not Master
teachings.title: Releasing the Ego's Throne: Your Head as Servant, Not Master
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to gently dethrone the ego and reframe the brain as a magnificent servant rather than the sole authority. She explores how relentless thinking shows up as physical tension and proposes cultivating a dialogue between head, heart, and body to access deeper, integrated wisdom and build new neural pathways toward ease.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Consider the objects in our environment—a smooth stone, a piece of art, a simple houseplant. Each holds a quiet presence, a silent testament to the world beyond our own busy minds.

We arrive with this magnificent three-pound universe nestled in our skulls, a biological supercomputer capable of composing symphonies, designing cities, and contemplating the very nature of existence. And for many of us, this incredible tool, the brain, becomes the undisputed ruler of our inner kingdom. It becomes the throne from which the ego directs our lives.

Many of us have experienced periods where the mind takes complete control. It's a common pattern to believe that if we can just *think* our way through our challenges, we can solve them. This can lead to sleepless nights, the mind racing like a hamster on a wheel, analyzing every conversation, every decision, every perceived misstep. We create intricate mental flowcharts of what to do if X happened, and contingency plans for when Y inevitably goes wrong. The head becomes a fortress, and we become its loyal, exhausted soldiers, constantly patrolling the ramparts of our own anxiety.

There are moments when we are completely lost in a spiral of worry. Shoulders inch up towards the ears, the jaw clenches, and a familiar tension begins to pulse behind the eyes. It's easy to become so consumed by the mental gymnastics of trying to “figure it all out” that we don’t notice the simple realities around us—a bird on a fence post, a cup of tea growing cold, the feeling of the air on our skin. In such a moment, a quiet question can arise from a deeper place within: *What if you didn’t have to figure it all out?*

What if, indeed? The thought is both terrifying and liberating. For so many people, the intellect has been their most trusted ally, their primary tool for navigating the world. The idea of releasing its grip can feel like stepping off a cliff. But the truth is, relentless thinking doesn’t actually solve anything. It just creates more tension, more fear, and a profound sense of separation from the simple, present reality of life—a life that includes birds on a fence post and cooling cups of tea.

## The Brain is a Tool, Not a Tyrant

Here’s a very good thing to know: your brain is a magnificent servant, but it makes a terrible master. It is designed to be an instrument, a processor of information, a loyal conduit for the wisdom that flows from a much deeper source. The issues arise when we mistake the tool for the user. We place the ego, with its fears and its endless need for control, upon the throne of our consciousness and tell the brain to protect its reign at all costs.

This is where we see the emergence of what many practitioners call “head issues.” The chronic headaches and migraines, the tight jaws, the relentless mental chatter—these are often symptoms of consciousness pressing against the rigid constraints of our own limited belief systems. The brain, in its effort to keep us “safe” based on old programming, creates neural pathways that become deep, familiar grooves. We think the same worried thoughts, run the same anxious scenarios, and our nervous system responds as if the perceived threat is real, flooding our bodies with stress hormones. We get stuck in a feedback loop where the head, in its attempt to control everything, creates the very suffering it’s trying to avoid.

Neuroscience shows us that these patterns are not fixed. Through the beautiful principle of neuroplasticity, we have the power to create new neural pathways. We can consciously choose to shift our attention away from the tyrannical voice of the ego-driven mind and cultivate a relationship with other, equally valid, forms of intelligence that reside within us. This isn’t about demonizing the intellect; it’s about restoring it to its rightful place as part of a larger, integrated system of wisdom.

> The brain is a magnificent tool, but it is not meant to be the sole authority. Its true purpose is to be the crown of consciousness through which divine intelligence can express itself.

When we allow the head to be the sole authority, we cut ourselves off from the profound wisdom of the body, the intuitive knowing of the heart, and the quiet guidance of our soul. We live in a state of perpetual negotiation with reality, trying to manage, predict, and control life, rather than participating in its mysterious and beautiful unfolding. This is not a life of freedom. It is a life of constriction, of living in a small, walled-off room when a vast, open landscape is waiting for you.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Befriending Your Inner Council

So how do we begin to gently guide the ego off its throne and invite the head to relax into its true purpose? It begins with cultivating a relationship with the other members of your inner council: your body, your heart, and your intuition.

The process of shifting from mind-based control to embodied awareness often begins with a simple choice. Instead of following frantic thoughts, one can bring awareness to the physical sensations in the body. One can notice the tension in the shoulders and consciously invite it to soften, feel the warmth of the sun on the skin, or the solid ground beneath the feet. It is possible to listen to the sound of the wind in the trees. The goal isn’t to stop the thoughts, but to stop making them the center of the universe. It is about expanding awareness to include the rich, sensory experience of the present moment.

This is the beginning of embodying wisdom. Your body is a sacred messenger, constantly communicating with you. It doesn’t speak in spreadsheets and analytical reports; it speaks in sensations, in whispers of tension and ease, in feelings of expansion and contraction. Learning to listen to this language is a radical act of self-trust. It is a declaration that you are more than your thoughts, that your wisdom is not confined to the space between your ears. It is a homecoming to the truth of your whole being.

Here is a simple practice you can try to begin this conversation with your inner council:

1.  **Find a quiet space** where you can sit or lie down comfortably for a few minutes without interruption. Let this be a dedicated time for you, a small sanctuary in your day.
2.  **Close your eyes** and take a few gentle, deep breaths. Don’t force anything; simply allow your breath to move in and out. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest and belly. This simple act of focusing on the breath is a powerful anchor to the present moment.
3.  **Bring your awareness to your head.** Notice any sensations present. Is there tension in your jaw, your forehead, your temples? Is your mind busy or quiet? Simply observe without judgment. You might even place a gentle hand on your forehead, offering a bit of comfort and presence. Imagine you are offering a silent, compassionate “hello” to your mind.
4.  **Now, gently shift your awareness down into your heart space,** in the center of your chest. What do you notice here? Is there a sense of openness, or tightness? Warmth, or coolness? Again, just be with what is, without needing to change it. You can place a hand over your heart, feeling the warmth of your own touch. This is the seat of your emotional wisdom, your capacity for love and connection.
5.  **Finally, bring your awareness down into your belly and your feet.** Feel your connection to the earth. Sense the solid, grounding presence of your physical body. Feel the weight of your body being held and supported. This is your center of gravity, your connection to the earth, your intuitive gut knowing.
6.  **Now, imagine these three centers—head, heart, and body—in gentle communication.** You might ask, from your heart, “What does my body know about this situation?” And then listen, not with your analytical mind, but with your whole being, for the subtle shifts in sensation that are the body’s reply. You might then ask, from your body, “What does my heart need to feel safe?” And listen again. Let the answers come not in words, but in feelings, images, and a simple, quiet knowing.

This isn’t about getting a definitive, logical answer. It’s about developing a felt sense of these different streams of intelligence. It’s about remembering that you are a whole being, and that true wisdom arises from the integration of all your parts. It’s about accepting yourself as enough, right now, without having to figure it all out first.

As you practice this, you begin to build new neural pathways. You teach your nervous system that it is safe to release the hyper-vigilance of the mind and to trust the wisdom that is always present in your body and heart. The head begins to relax. The mental gymnastics cease. And in that quiet space, a deeper intelligence can finally be heard.

The head, released from the burden of being the sole authority, can finally assume its true role: to be the crown of your being, a radiant antenna of consciousness through which the light of your own soul and the wisdom of the universe can express itself. It becomes a servant to love, not a master of fear.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision](/blog/eyes-emotional-roots-of-vision)
- [A Practice for Spinal Freedom and Authentic Uprightness](/blog/spine-freedom-practice)
- [Fight, Flight, Freeze: When Your Nervous System Runs the Show](/blog/nervous-system-fight-flight-freeze)

**More on Head:**

- [The Crown of Consciousness: What Your Head Is Really Telling You](/blog/head-crown-of-consciousness)
- [Headaches, Migraines, and the Prison of Overthinking](/blog/head-headaches-overthinking)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you have the courage to gently dethrone the ego and the grace to trust the magnificent, integrated wisdom that you are. May your mind become a clear and beautiful vessel for the expression of your deepest truth.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Imagine your head, heart, and belly as members of an inner council. What might each one say about a current worry or decision if you listened without arguing or fixing?

What small, practical reminder could you place in your day to return the brain to a servant role (for example, a two-minute pause, a hand on your heart, or a grounding breath)? How will you try it tomorrow?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Set aside 5 minutes in a quiet place. Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and follow your breath for a few gentle inhales and exhales. Bring attention to your head—notice any tightness or mental activity without judgment, and (if it feels safe) rest a gentle hand on your forehead. Slowly shift awareness to your heart—place a hand there if you wish and notice warmth, openness, or tension. Move your attention down into your belly and feet, feeling grounded and supported. Once you’ve felt each center, ask one simple question aloud or silently (for example, “What does my body need right now?”) and wait for a felt-sense response rather than words. Finish by thanking each center and taking a grounding breath. If you experience persistent pain, frequent headaches, or other medical concerns, please consult a qualified healthcare professional; this practice is a gentle support and not a substitute for medical care.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Lungs - The Sacred Exchange of Life Force
teachings.title: The Lungs - The Sacred Exchange of Life Force
teachings.summary: Susan presents the lungs as a sacred interface between inner and outer worlds, inviting readers to see breath as both physiology and spiritual practice. The piece links breathing patterns with emotional life—boundaries, grief, depression, and agency—and offers gentle, somatic invitations for listening, releasing, and reclaiming voice. It emphasizes discernment about what we inhale (literal and metaphorical) and cautions gentle, supported exploration when trauma or intense material arises.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You have lungs because life insists you participate in the exquisite conversation between inner world and outer world. Each breath is a sacred exchange - a tiny sacrament that happens tens of thousands of times across your life, silently knitting you to air, to other beings, to the blue of the sky and the traffic of the city. The lungs are not mere mechanics for oxygen. They are the intimate membrane where spirit meets circumstance, where what sustains you enters and what no longer serves you is expelled. To attend to your lungs is to attend to your capacity to receive, to let go, and to stand in a living, embodied reciprocity with the world. In that thin alveolar tissue your biography and your environment converge, and from there your life either expands or contracts.

The Lungs as Messenger

Your body is a messenger and the lungs are one of its most eloquent spokespeople. When you feel constricted, when joy seems distant and inspiration difficult to draw in, your lungs translate those interior truths into the language of breath. The booklet calls the respiratory system the intimate interface between inner and outer worlds, and that is literal and metaphoric at once. Lungs teach you about exchange. They teach you about boundaries. They reveal what you accept into your life and what you cannot yet release. When breath is full and effortless, you are in relationship with life. When breath is shallow, frightened, or clogged, you are living under an invisible pressure that has seeped into your tissues and become part of your posture.

From the earliest years you developed paradigms about what the world can offer and what it might take away. If you learned, even implicitly, that the air of life is scarce, that love must be earned through smallness, your nervous system will constrict the diaphragm and keep the chest high and guarded. That pattern is a faithful adaptation - it once did its work. But its continued presence in adult life often looks like fatigue, low mood, anxiety, or a chronic sense of suffocation. Your lungs will hold the imprint of being smothered, dismissed, or not allowed to make a sound. They also hold your first longing, your first grief, your first awe. The flesh remembers what the mind forgets.

Shallow Breath and the Quiet of Depression

Depression often shows itself in the narrowing of breath. The breath that once rose easily into the belly learns to skim the upper chest, short and polite, as if afraid to take up space. When you breathe shallowly, your body experiences a perpetual low-grade alarm: oxygenation is limited, parasympathetic tone is reduced, serotonin and dopamine can be hard to mobilize. But the physiology is only half the story. The breath and the feeling feed one another. The world seems heavy because your inhale is small. Your inhale is small because the world seems heavy. This is a holographic conversation where inner belief and outer biology mirror and reinforce each other.

In those seasons when you wake heavy and the day feels like moving through cotton, attend to the rhythm of your breathing before you attempt any other change. Even a small, compassionate invitation to let air travel into your body more fully can reroute neural patterns. When the diaphragm finds a little more room, the mind finds a little more possibility. You are not being naive if you acknowledge that depression has layers that may require therapy, medication, and community. Yet alongside those supports, breath is the simplest, most democratic medicine. It is both a doorway and a teacher. As the Tao Te Ching asks you to empty and simplify - "Empty yourself of everything; let the mind rest at peace" - your breath offers that literal emptying and filling where transformation begins.

Suffocation by Circumstance

There are life contexts that mimic physical suffocation. A job that erodes your creativity, a relationship that clamps your voice, cultural messages that insist you shrink - any of these can compress your chest with the sensation of running out of air. This is not dramatic metaphor for the sake of language. The nervous system cannot always tell the difference between oxygen deprivation and the slow erosion of dignity. Both activate fight, flight, freeze. Your breathing pattern will adapt to survive. But adaptation can calcify into resignation.

When you feel metaphorically suffocated, the lungs are asking two central questions: What are you still inhaling that is not yours to take, and what are you not yet willing to exhale? It is a practice of discernment as much as of breath mechanics. Consider the cultural narratives you breathe in - anxieties about scarcity, worn beliefs about who you must be to belong. Consider the grudges, the resentments, the unspoken words lodged in your ribs that no one has helped you release. Both the intake and the withholding are energetic acts. Each inhale that repeats past programming deepens it. Each withheld exhale preserves what has already served its purpose. The lungs sit between these poles and, if you are willing, they will show you how to change your relationship to both.

Breath as Agency - Moving from Victim to Participant

One of the great gifts of working with breath is that it asks less of your belief and more of your attention. Breath is automatic, yes, but it is also one of the rare autonomic functions you can consciously influence. That is a spiritual technology. The moment you notice your breath you have shifted from a passive recipient of sensation into an active steward. In that noticing you become a participant in your physiology. This is where choice lives. Even in small measures, you can teach yourself to breathe differently and thereby invite a different life experience.

Start by retrieving the simple question: What they are trying to tell you? This is not an interrogation of blame but a gentle curiosity. Where do you hold tension? What surfaces when you intentionally lengthen your exhale? Some practices are subtle and patient. You can place one hand on your belly, the other on your ribs, and simply invite the breath to travel downward into the belly, then allow a long, unforced exhale that feels like an opening. You can practice a sigh - an audible, loving release - and notice how much space that makes in your chest. The Tao reminds you that often less is more. "Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished." Your breath will teach you that the smallest, kindest adjustments often yield the deepest shifts.

Embodied Practices for the Lungs

There is no one right way to breathe. There are invitations to explore that will meet you exactly where you are. Begin with what I call the Return to the Belly. Sit or lie where you feel safe. Place your hands so you can feel the expansion of your lower ribs. Inhale through the nose and imagine drawing air into the farthest edges of your back and belly. Do not push. Then exhale with a soft, extended release as if you are willing the body to relax a little more with each soundless "ah." Repeat this for five to ten cycles. You will likely feel the difference not just in your chest but in the way your shoulders descend and your jaw softens.

When grief or heaviness sits like a stone in the chest, allow the breath to be a midwife for the sorrow. Expand the in-breath as a spacious invitation to gather the grief without resistance. On the out-breath, audibly sigh if that feels natural. The voice is a companion to the lungs; to make sound is to claim space. Sometimes the safe release of an audible breath, even a single long exhale through the mouth, is the sacramental act that loosens what has been lodged too long.

If panic or tightness rushes in, extend the exhale gently and lengthen it by a count of one or two compared to the inhale. This simple elongation taps into the vagal pathways that calm the nervous system. Place your attention on the back of your neck and the hollow at your collarbones. Let your exhales become the invitation to descend from hypervigilance into presence. I have seen time and again how a few conscious breaths can move someone out of freeze into a felt sense of agency. Breath gives you a place to stand inside the storm.

Working with the Inner-Outer Exchange

Because your lungs are the only internal organ in constant contact with the outside world, they are especially sensitive to what we might call atmospheric influences - physical toxins, yes, but also cultural, relational, and psychic atmospheres. You inhale not only oxygen but metaphors. You take in the anxious cadence of another person in close proximity, the political static of the news, the toxic air of a workplace. Learning to steward what you inhale is a spiritual practice. It is not about avoiding life but about choosing the atmosphere that nourishes you most of the time.

You can create small rituals that support this stewardship. Before entering a tense space, take three centering breaths and ask to be shielded from what is not yours. Imagine a gentle translucent membrane around the lungs that lets in what is nourishing and converts or neutralizes what is harmful. On the other side of that ritual is the practice of discernment: when you notice chronic constriction in response to a person or place, ask, with curiosity not accusation, whether you are being asked to change something externally or whether your own boundary needs reasserting. Sometimes the lungs will prompt you to leave the room, change the job, or stop a relationship. Other times they ask you to shift an inner story. Both responses are valid. The lungs will tell you which one feels like truth in the tissue.

Voice, Grief, and the Work of Exhaling

Many people carry their unspoken life in the lungs. Words left unwritten, confrontations avoided, apologies withheld - these accumulate in the interstitial spaces and weigh on your ability to take full breaths. The voice, supported by the breath, is the bridge from inner truth to outer life. When you begin to speak what you have kept small, the lungs become liberated. You cannot separate the practice of honest speech from the freedom of the breath. Both require safety, which is why it is essential to practice in environments where you are not punished for expanding.

Grief, especially, needs breath to move. It is not a problem to be fixed but a presence to be honored. Allow yourself to feel each inhale as a collection of tenderness and each exhale as a passage through which sorrow can travel out of bone and into the air. Over time grief softens and becomes a kind of companion rather than a fetter. The lungs know how to transmute fixed sorrow if you give them permission to do so.

Embodied Inquiry

Find a quiet hour and lay one hand over the heart and one hand on the belly. Breathe and notice what arises. Ask directly: What am I carrying that is not mine? What do I need to release now so my breath can be deeper? Be patient. Listen to the small sensations that ripple across your ribs. They are the beginning of language. Journal whatever images, memories, or words arrive. Often the lungs will first speak in sensation and only later in narrative. This is why somatic listening matters. You are listening to a body that has been holding, storing, and finally, longing to speak.

If you have the Elevate Your Body To Love cards, draw the three lung cards and sit with their Purpose, Inquiry, and Transcendence. Touch the images. Let the words wash across your ribs. The process is not an intellectual exercise. It is an embodied conversation where the cards act as a translator for what the lungs have been trying to say. If tears come, they are part of the airway working again.

When Breath Work Touches Trauma

Some bodies keep sorrow and fear in tight coils that can unravel quickly when the breath is invited to change. If you have a history of trauma, be gentle. Breath work can sometimes release powerful material that needs supportive container and skilled guidance. If, during practice, you feel disoriented, dissociative, or flooded, bring yourself back to small, local sensations - the weight of your feet, the texture of a chair, the presence of a hand on your belly. If you are in crisis or finding it overwhelming, seek the support of a therapist or somatic practitioner. The lungs will wait to be worked with gently and respectfully. Healing is not a race but a steady pilgrimage.

Living the Lungs' Teaching

What your lungs offer ultimately is a model for life. They remind you to be an honest exchange point: take in what sustains you and let go of what poisons you. They teach you to inhabit your edges, to allow expansion and contraction as the rhythm of living. The Tao invites a similar posture: practice simplicity, trust the natural unfolding, let go of unnecessary holdings, and in that surrender discover the capacity to move more deftly through life. "Empty yourself of everything; let the mind rest at peace." You can practice that emptiness with each exhale. You can practice presence with each inhale.

When you take responsibility for the breath you draw, you step out of victimhood. Victimhood is surrender to the sense that life happens to you. Conscious breath is the first gesture of reclaiming your sovereignty. It does not mean you will never be wounded. It does not mean the world will always be easy. It means you have a reliable ally in your lungs, one that can help you choose how you meet life moment by moment. The daily discipline of returning to breath teaches you to notice the moments of withholding, to respond with compassionate action, and to cultivate an inner atmosphere that attracts what you most need.

So when you feel the chest tight, when the world seems to press its thumb on your throat, remember: the lungs are calling you home to yourself. Attend with tenderness. Breathe long enough to remember what it feels like to be spacious. Speak the words lodged inside you if you can. Move your body in ways that open the ribs. Let the exhale be a ritual of release and the inhale a holy invitation. You are not merely a passenger of breath. You are a participant in an ongoing sacrament. As you learn to meet the air with greater clarity and choice, you also learn to meet life differently. That is the work of the lungs and of a soul learning to live incarnate, awake, and free.

May each breath be a small liturgy that returns you to your own fierce and gentle heart. May you inhale courage and exhale what no longer belongs to you. May the lungs teach you how to dance in the rhythm of receiving and releasing until you know with absolute certainty that you belong in this world.

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reclaim the lost skill of listening to the body, framing interoception as a central, trainable capacity that translates bodily signals into lived wisdom. She contrasts raw bodily sensation with the mind’s narrative, and offers gentle practices — a compassionate body scan, dialoguing with symptoms, and attending to the felt sense — to restore a kinder, more curious relationship with the body.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a kind of knowing that lives below thought, below language, below even feeling.

I remember a time, years ago, standing in my kitchen, a mug of tea growing cold in my hands. I was staring out the window at the Vancouver rain, but I wasn’t seeing it. My mind was a whirlwind, a frantic spinning of to-do lists and obligations and the heavy weight of a decision I had to make. My shoulders were clenched up by my ears, a familiar ache had started in my lower back, and my stomach was in a tight, anxious knot. For days, my body had been sending me these signals—whispers of exhaustion, pleas for rest. And for days, I had been ignoring them, pushing through, telling myself I didn’t have time to slow down.

I took a sip of tea and a wave of dizziness washed over me. It was so sudden, so potent, that I had to grip the counter to steady myself. And in that moment of forced stillness, a question, clear as a bell, landed in my awareness: *What if you just stopped?* It wasn’t my voice. It was deeper, quieter, and it came not from my head, but from the very center of my being. It was the voice of my body, no longer whispering, but shouting to be heard.

How often do we do this? We treat our bodies like vehicles we’re driving, sometimes recklessly, to get our minds where they need to go. We override their signals with caffeine, sugar, and sheer willpower, dismissing their wisdom as inconvenient, irrelevant, or worse, as a sign of weakness. We’ve become brilliant at living from the neck up, navigating our lives from the bustling command center of the analytical mind, while the vast, intelligent landscape of the body lies forgotten, its messages unheard.

But what if your body isn’t just a vehicle? What if it is the most sacred text you will ever read, a divine messenger offering you constant, unerring guidance on your path? Reclaiming the sacred art of listening to your body is not another wellness trend to perfect. It is a homecoming. It is a radical act of love that has the power to transform everything.

## The Science of Your Inner World

This deep listening is not just a poetic concept; it’s a neurological capacity. Scientists call it *interoception*—the nervous system’s ability to sense and interpret the internal signals of the body. Think of it as your eighth sense. While your other senses tell you about the outside world, interoception tells you about your inner world: your heartbeat, your breath, the feeling of hunger or fullness, the subtle clench of a muscle, the warmth that spreads through your chest in a moment of connection.

These signals travel along ancient neural pathways from your organs and tissues up to a special region in the brain called the insular cortex. This is where the raw data of sensation is translated into conscious feeling. A drop in blood sugar becomes the feeling of hunger. A tightening in the chest becomes the emotion of anxiety. The insula is the bridge between your body and your feelings, the place where biology becomes biography.

For our ancestors, sharp interoception was a matter of survival. It was the gut feeling that a predator was near, the internal cue that a water source was tainted. In our modern world, the threats have changed, but the wisdom of this system remains just as vital. It is the key to emotional regulation, to empathy, to intuition, and to making decisions that are in true alignment with our well-being. When we are disconnected from our interoceptive sense, we are navigating our lives with a faulty GPS, guided only by the loud, often unreliable, stories of the mind.

## The Body’s Signal vs. The Mind’s Story

Here is a very good thing to know: the body’s signal is always true. It is pure, present-moment information. A knot in the stomach is simply a knot in the stomach. A racing heart is simply a racing heart. It is a sensation, free of judgment or narrative.

The mind, in its brilliant and sometimes maddening effort to make sense of everything, immediately jumps in and weaves a story around the signal. This story is almost never new. It is a well-worn neural groove, a tale cobbled together from past hurts, future fears, and deeply ingrained beliefs about ourselves and the world.

The body says: *My chest is tight.*

The mind says: *Oh no, something is wrong. It’s anxiety. I’m going to have a panic attack. I can’t handle this. I’m failing. Remember that time I failed before? This is just like that. I’m not good enough.*

Do you feel the difference? The signal is a clean, simple fact. The story is a tangled, emotionally charged drama. The work of body listening is to learn to create a sacred pause between the signal and the story. To notice the sensation itself, to get curious about it, to breathe with it *before* we let the mind hijack the experience. When we can do this, we move from a state of unconscious reaction to one of conscious relationship. We stop being at the mercy of our old patterns and start to access the clear, compassionate wisdom that lies beneath them.

Most of us have lost this innate ability not because we are flawed, but because we have been so exquisitely conditioned to do so. From a young age, we are taught to override our bodies. To sit still when we need to move. To be quiet when we need to express. To finish our plate when we are full. We learn that belonging and safety often depend on ignoring our own internal cues in favor of external rules. Over time, the neural pathways of interoception become faint, and the loud voice of the inner critic and the anxious mind takes over. We forget the language of our own sacred text.

But the beautiful truth of neuroplasticity is that these pathways can be reawakened. The connection can be restored. You can learn to read your own body again. You can come home.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Practices for Deepening Your Listening

This is not about achieving a perfect state of bodily bliss. It’s about cultivating a relationship, one that is built on trust, curiosity, and infinite compassion. It is a practice, not a performance. Here are a few ways you might begin.

### 1. The Compassionate Body Scan

This is a simple yet profound way to check in. You can do this in five minutes. Find a quiet place to sit or lie down. Close your eyes and take a few gentle breaths.

Begin by bringing your awareness to your feet. Just notice what is there. Is there warmth? Coolness? Tingling? Pressure? You don’t need to change or fix anything. You are just listening. Offer a silent word of thanks to your feet for all the places they have carried you.

Slowly, move your awareness up through your body—your legs, your hips, your belly, your chest, your shoulders, your arms, your hands, your neck, your face, your head. With each part, you are simply asking, *“What is here?”* and listening with gentle, non-judgmental attention. If you meet a place of tension or pain, see if you can breathe into it, not to force it to release, but to let it know it is seen. To surround it with presence. This practice rewires the brain to pay attention to the body with kindness rather than criticism.

### 2. Symptom as Messenger

Our culture teaches us to see physical symptoms as an enemy—something to be silenced, medicated, or removed. But what if a symptom is not an adversary, but a messenger? A communication from a part of you that has been unable to get your attention in any other way.

Next time you feel a persistent ache, a knot of tension, or a wave of fatigue, try this. Find a quiet moment. Place a hand on the part of your body that is speaking to you. Close your eyes and breathe into the sensation.

Then, ask it a question. You can ask silently, in your mind, or whisper it aloud. Good questions are simple and open-ended:

*   *What do you need?*
*   *What are you trying to tell me?*
*   *If you had a voice, what would you say?*

Don’t strain for an answer. Just listen in the stillness. The answer may not come in words. It might be an image, a memory, a sudden emotion, or just a subtle shift in the sensation itself. Trust what comes. This practice shifts you from fighting your body to being in dialogue with it. It is a profound act of self-restoration.

### 3. Feeling the ‘Felt Sense’

Sometimes, the body’s wisdom isn’t a sharp, specific sensation, but a vague, all-over feeling—a ‘felt sense’ of a situation. It’s that murky feeling of ‘something’s not right here,’ or the quiet, inner hum of ‘yes, this is it.’

To tap into this, think of a situation in your life you’re holding a question about. Don’t think about the pros and cons in your head. Instead, bring the whole situation to mind and ask your body, *“How does this feel in here?”* Then, wait. Let a holistic sense of it form in your torso, in your chest and belly. It might be heavy, or fluttery, or tight, or spacious. Give it a name, even a strange one. ‘The tight-grey-wall feeling.’ ‘The jumpy-river feeling.’

Stay with that felt sense for a few moments. Breathe with it. What is the quality of it? What does *it* need? This practice bypasses the analytical mind and connects you to a deeper, more holistic intelligence that knows the way.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

Reclaiming this connection is the most loving thing you can do for yourself. It is the path to healing, to wholeness, and to a life guided not by fear and obligation, but by the deep, resonant truth of your own being. Your body has been waiting, with infinite patience, for you to turn your awareness inward and listen. It is ready to tell you everything you need to know.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Distinguishing raw bodily signals from the mind’s stories and judgments

reflectionPrompts: Notice a bodily sensation right now (tightness, warmth, fluttering). How does it feel when you describe it without adding a story or evaluation? What shifts when you simply name the sensation?
Recall a recent decision or stressor. Bring it into your awareness and ask, quietly, ‘How does this feel in my body?’ What images, words, or physical cues arise, and what might they be offering you?

Think of a persistent physical symptom or habitual tension. If you place a hand there and ask, ‘What do you need?’, what response—image, emotion, or small change in sensation—comes forward? What gentle next step could you offer that part of yourself?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Try a three-minute compassionate check-in: sit comfortably, close your eyes if that feels safe, place one hand over your belly or heart, and take five slow, gentle breaths. On the next in-breath, notice one physical sensation without labeling it; on the out-breath, offer a silent phrase of kindness (for example, “I see you”). End by pausing and noticing whether anything feels different; if the practice raises distressing sensations, stop and rest.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article invites within-body awareness that can bring up strong emotions or memories. You have permission to pause at any time, step away from the practice, and return when you feel ready.

If attending to bodily sensations evokes intense anxiety, panic, or traumatic memories, consider doing the practice with a trusted person present or seek support from a qualified therapist or clinician.
Listening to bodily signals is complementary to, not a replacement for, medical evaluation or treatment. For persistent or concerning physical symptoms, consult your healthcare provider.

teachings.sourceTitle: A Conversation with Your Body: The Practice of Deep Listening
teachings.title: A Conversation with Your Body: The Practice of Deep Listening
teachings.summary: Susan invites a gentle, nonjudgmental practice of deep listening to the body, framing sensation as language rather than problem to be fixed. She names how neuroscience (including the vagus nerve and mindsight) supports this approach, offers a clear step-by-step listening practice, and shares examples of how shifting relationship to symptoms can reveal unmet needs. The piece emphasizes curiosity, compassion, and building an ongoing dialogue with the living wisdom of the body.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are gifted this miraculous vessel, this body, a universe of sensation and wisdom, and yet we so often treat it like a stranger. Or worse, an adversary. When was the last time you truly listened to your body? Not to diagnose it, not to critique it, not to fix it… but simply to *hear* what it has to say? The practice of deep listening is one of the most transformative skills we can develop on our healing journey. It’s a conversation. A sacred dialogue. And it begins with the radical act of paying attention. ## The Language of the Body Your body is speaking to you, always. It speaks in the language of sensation — the flutter in your chest, the tightness in your jaw, the warmth that spreads across your skin. It communicates through whispers of fatigue, shouts of pain, and the quiet hum of contentment. For years, I ignored this language. I lived almost entirely in my head, a world of thoughts, plans, and anxieties. My body was just the vehicle that carried my brain from one task to the next. I remember one afternoon, years ago, sitting in my garden. The sun was warm on my face, a gentle breeze rustled the leaves of the birch tree, and a small, persistent ache was blooming in my lower back. I’d been feeling it for weeks, a dull throb that I’d been diligently ignoring. But on this day, for some reason, I decided to listen. Instead of immediately reaching for a painkiller or stretching it out, I simply closed my eyes and brought my awareness to the sensation. I didn’t try to change it. I just… listened. And in that listening, a memory surfaced, sharp and clear: a fall from my bike as a child, the fear and the impact, a moment of feeling utterly alone and unsupported. The ache in my back wasn't just physical; it was an echo of an old story, a pocket of unfelt emotion that had been patiently waiting for my attention. This is the work, beloved one. To turn towards these places within us with curiosity and compassion. ## Neuroscience and the Symphony of Self Modern neuroscience is beginning to map what the ancient wisdom traditions have known for millennia: our bodies and minds are inextricably linked. The field of interpersonal neurobiology, pioneered by Dr. Dan Siegel, speaks of the ‘triangle of well-being,’ composed of the brain, the mind, and our relationships. When we bring compassionate attention to our internal state — a process called ‘mindsight’ — we are literally rewiring our brains for greater integration and resilience. Think of your nervous system. The vagus nerve, the longest cranial nerve, wanders from the brainstem down through the heart and lungs and into the gut. It’s a superhighway of information, constantly sending signals in both directions. When you take a slow, deep breath and feel your shoulders drop, you are sending a message of safety up the vagus nerve to your brain, calming the entire system. This isn’t just a nice idea; it’s neurobiology in action. > “The body is the subconscious mind.” - Dr. Joe Dispenza This is why body-based practices are so powerful. They bypass the analytical, story-telling mind and speak directly to the deeper, older parts of our brain. When we engage in practices like mindful movement, breathwork, or simply paying attention to the sensations in our feet on the ground, we are building our capacity to be present with what is. We are learning to self-regulate not through force, but through gentle, consistent attention. ## The Practice of Deep Listening So how do we begin this conversation? It’s simpler than you might think. It doesn’t require a special cushion or a silent retreat — though those can be lovely. It can begin right here, right now. 1. **Find a quiet moment.** Just a few minutes to start. You can be sitting, standing, or lying down. 2. **Close your eyes, if that feels comfortable.** Take a few gentle breaths, not to change anything, but simply to arrive in this moment. 3. **Scan your body with your awareness.** Start at your feet and slowly travel up through your legs, your torso, your arms, your neck, your head. Just notice. Is there warmth? Tingling? Tightness? Numbness? No sensation is too small or insignificant. 4. **Greet whatever you find with curiosity.** If you find a place of tension, instead of the immediate impulse to make it go away, can you soften around it? Can you breathe into it? Can you ask it, gently, “What do you have to tell me?” 5. **Listen for the answer.** The answer may not come in words. It might be an image, a feeling, a memory, or just a subtle shift in the sensation itself. Trust whatever arises. There is no right or wrong way to do this. This is a practice of building relationship. A relationship with the deepest, wisest part of yourself. It’s a journey from seeing the body as an ‘it’ to knowing it as a ‘thou’ — a sacred partner on this path of being human. I remember a client I worked with who suffered from chronic migraines. For years, she had battled them, resented them, and done everything in her power to eradicate them. Through our work, she began to practice this deep listening. When she felt the first twinge of a migraine, instead of her usual panic, she would lie down, place a hand on her heart, and ask, “What do you need, dear one?” Over time, she began to understand that the migraines were a desperate cry from her system for rest, for boundaries, for a life that was less about doing and more about being. The migraines didn’t disappear overnight, but her relationship to them — and to herself — was utterly transformed.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
Your body has been with you through every moment of your life. It has held you, carried you, and fought for you. It holds the stories of your ancestors and the dreams of your future. It is a living library of wisdom, a faithful companion, a sacred temple. May you have the courage to listen to its whispers… before they become screams. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

Body as messenger and living storehouse of memory
Practical, brief practices for embodied awareness (body scan, breath)
Neuroscience supporting mind–body integration (vagus nerve, mindsight)
