teachings.sourceTitle: Sacred Wounds: The Gifts Hidden Inside Our Deepest Pain
teachings.title: Sacred Wounds: The Gifts Hidden Inside Our Deepest Pain
teachings.summary: Susan reframes personal wounds not as defects to be erased but as sacred openings—like kintsugi repairs—that can become sources of compassion, purpose, and service. She invites a gentle, body-centered practice of listening to sensations and tending the inner child so that pain can be metabolized and transformed rather than numbed or bypassed. The article offers practical guidance for approaching wounds with curiosity and tenderness, and points to the ways our deepest hurts can become our most precious medicine.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a strange and tender thing, this human experience. We arrive with open hearts, soft bodies, and a soul-level trust in the goodness of life. And then… life happens. We get bumped and bruised. We are failed by people we love. We fail ourselves. We experience loss, betrayal, and the thousand tiny heartbreaks that accumulate over a lifetime. We develop wounds. For most of my life, I saw my wounds as liabilities. Flaws to be fixed. Scars to be hidden. I spent years—and a small fortune—trying to erase them, to become a smooth, unbroken version of myself. I thought that was the goal of healing: to get back to a place of pristine wholeness, to a time *before* the cracks appeared. But what if that’s not the goal at all? What if the wound you have been trying so desperately to heal is actually the doorway to your greatest gift? What if our deepest pain contains the very medicine we—and the world—are longing for? This is the revolutionary truth of the sacred wound. ## The Alchemy of the Wound In the Japanese art of *kintsugi*, broken pottery is repaired with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. The philosophy behind it is one of embracing the flawed and the imperfect. The breakage and repair are treated as part of the object's history, rather than something to disguise. The result is a piece that is more beautiful, more resilient, and more precious than it was before it was broken. This is how I’ve come to see our wounds. They are not mistakes. They are not evidence of our brokenness. They are the sacred cracks through which our inner light can finally shine. They are the places where the gold gets in. We live in a culture that pathologizes pain. We are taught to numb it, to bypass it, to “think positive” and move on. But the soul doesn’t operate on that timeline. The soul knows that every wound has a voice, a story, a wisdom that it is trying to impart. When we refuse to listen—when we armor our hearts against the pain—we also cut ourselves off from the gift. The wound itself is a powerful teacher. It shows us where we are vulnerable, where we need more tenderness, where our old strategies and defenses are no longer serving us. It invites us into a deeper relationship with ourselves, one based not on perfection, but on profound self-acceptance. > To be human is to be broken and broken is to be open. > —Louise Penny ## A Story of a Sacred Wound I remember a client I worked with years ago, a woman I’ll call Sarah. She came to me carrying a deep wound of unworthiness. It stemmed from a childhood where her parents, struggling with their own demons, were often critical and emotionally unavailable. Sarah grew into a woman who was a chronic over-achiever, constantly seeking external validation to quiet the relentless inner voice that told her she wasn’t good enough. She had built a fortress around her heart. On the outside, she was successful, competent, and put-together. On the inside, she was crumbling. Our work together was not about “fixing” her feeling of unworthiness. It was about turning towards it with a radical curiosity and a tenderness she had never allowed herself. We didn't try to argue with the inner critic; we listened to it. We asked it what it was afraid of. We explored the landscape of that wound, not as a problem to be solved, but as a sacred site to be visited. I recall one session vividly. We were working with a deep ache she felt in her chest, a physical manifestation of this old pain. I invited her to simply be with the sensation, to breathe into it, to offer it her presence. Tears began to stream down her face. Not tears of despair, but of release. “It’s just a little girl,” she whispered. “She’s been in there all this time, just wanting to be seen.” In that moment, something shifted. By finally allowing herself to feel the full depth of her wound, she discovered its hidden gift. The wound of unworthiness, once a source of immense suffering, began to transform into a wellspring of profound empathy. Because she knew, in her own bones, what it felt like to feel unseen, she became exquisitely attuned to the emotional states of others. Her greatest pain became her greatest superpower. Sarah eventually left her corporate job and trained as a therapist, specializing in inner-child work. She now guides others through the very landscape she once found so terrifying. The gold that repaired her own brokenness became the light she now shares with the world. ## The Wisdom of the Emptiness This process of turning towards our pain is a central theme in many ancient wisdom traditions. The Tao Te Ching, a text that has been a dear companion on my own journey, speaks to this beautifully. In the eleventh chapter, Lao Tzu writes: > Thirty spokes share the wheel's hub; > It is the center hole that makes it useful. > Shape clay into a vessel; > It is the space within that makes it useful. > Cut doors and windows for a room; > It is the holes which make it useful. > Therefore profit comes from what is there; > Usefulness from what is not there. Our wounds are the “what is not there.” They are the empty spaces, the hollows, the breaks in our wholeness. And it is precisely this emptiness that creates our capacity. It is the wound of loss that carves out the space in our hearts to hold more compassion. It is the wound of betrayal that teaches us the true meaning of integrity and self-loyalty. It is the wound of not-belonging that fuels our quest for authentic connection and community. Your wound creates your usefulness. It is not a deficit. It is a crucible. It is the holy ground where your humanity is forged. ## Tending to Your Own Wounds So how do we begin to relate to our own wounds as sacred, beloved one? It is a practice. It is a gentle, moment-by-moment turning towards. It begins with the body. Our bodies are the living libraries of our experiences, holding the stories that our minds may have forgotten or suppressed. That tightness in your jaw, the knot in your stomach, the ache in your lower back… these are not random symptoms. They are communications from your soul, broadcast through the sensitive tissues of your body. Can you get curious about these sensations? Instead of immediately trying to make them go away, can you pause and listen? Place a hand on the part of your body that feels tense or painful. Breathe. Soften around the edges of the sensation. You might ask it, gently, “What do you have to tell me?” or “What do you need right now?” There is no need to force an answer. The simple act of offering your compassionate attention is a powerful balm. It sends a message to your nervous system, and to the deepest parts of your being, that you are safe, that you are whole, and that all parts of you are welcome here. This is not about navel-gazing or becoming stuck in the story of your pain. It is the opposite. It is about metabolizing the pain, integrating its wisdom, and liberating the life force that has been trapped within it. When we do this, the wound ceases to be a source of limitation and becomes a source of power, purpose, and profound connection to all of life. Your wound is not what’s wrong with you. It is what’s *right* with you. It is the signature of your unique soul, the mark of your journey, and the source of your most precious medicine.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
What if you were to lay down the burden of trying to be unbroken? What if, instead, you were to pick up the gold and begin to lovingly trace the lines of your own sacred wounds? What if you were to trust that you are more beautiful, not in spite of your cracks, but because of them? This is the path of true healing. It is the journey home to the magnificent, resilient, and perfectly imperfect soul you have always been. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

Kintsugi metaphor: beauty and resilience through repair
Body as living archive of emotional pain

Take three slow, gentle breaths, softening on the exhale. With curiosity and kindness, offer this simple question inwardly: “What do you need right now?” Wait without forcing an answer; notice images, words, shifts in sensation, or simply the presence of feeling. When you finish, place both hands over your heart, thank this part of you for speaking, and rest for a moment. If at any point you feel overwhelmed or notice alarming physical symptoms, stop and reach out to a trusted care provider or emergency services—this practice is a complement to, not a replacement for, medical or mental-health care.
sensitiveContentNotes: This piece explores childhood wounds, betrayal, loss, and deep emotional pain; these topics can surface strong feelings.
You have permission to pause the reading or practice at any time and to prioritize safety and grounding.
If the material brings up traumatic memories or intense distress, consider reaching out to a trauma-informed therapist, trusted companion, or crisis resources in your area for support.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Vibrational Signature of Your Soul: Your Voice Speaks
teachings.title: The Vibrational Signature of Your Soul: Your Voice Speaks
teachings.summary: Susan explores the voice as the body’s vibrational signature — an instrument that carries emotion, history, and soul. She traces how childhood conditioning and fear can constrict the throat and silence authentic expression, describes the anatomy and nervous‑system links behind voice and feeling, and offers a gentle invitation to reclaim voice through small, somatic practices like humming and honest self-attention.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember the first time I truly heard my own voice. I don’t mean the sound of it, the one I’d recognized for decades in conversation or on a crackling answering machine message. I mean the *feeling* of it. The vibration of it in my own bones.

I was in a vocal toning workshop, of all places. A group of us, mostly strangers, were invited to lie on the floor and simply…sound. To let a tone emerge from our bodies without shaping it into a word or a song. At first, I was hesitant, my throat tight with a familiar tension. The thought of making a sound that wasn’t polite, that wasn’t language, felt terribly vulnerable. Who was I to take up that much sonic space?

But then, a woman across the room let out a low, resonant hum. It was a sound like the earth itself. It gave me a strange kind of permission. I took a breath, and on the exhale, I let a sound of my own emerge. It was shaky at first, a thin, wavering note. But as I stayed with it, as I allowed it to simply *be*, it deepened. It dropped from my throat into my chest, and I could feel the vibration spreading through my ribs, down my spine, into the floor. It was my own energy, translated into sound. It was the feeling of my own soul, vibrating. And in that moment, I understood something profound: my voice wasn
’t just a tool for communication. It was a direct line to the core of my being.

Have you ever truly listened to your own voice? Not just for the words, but for the music beneath them? The unique, unrepeatable frequency that is *you* and you alone. In a world of seven billion people, no two voices are exactly alike. Your voice carries your history, your joys, your sorrows, your unexpressed longings. It is, in the most literal sense, the vibrational signature of your soul.

It’s a tricky business, this human experience of being heard. From a young age, we learn to modulate our voices to fit in, to please, to avoid causing trouble. We learn to tighten our throats to hold back a sob, to swallow our anger, to pitch our words in a way that will be acceptable to others. We are told to “use our inside voice,” and often, that inside voice becomes the *only* one we feel safe using. The raw, untamed, fully expressed voice gets locked away. And when we silence the voice, we begin to sever the connection to the very truth it is designed to express.

## The Anatomy of a Miracle

The vocal cords themselves are a marvel of biological design. Two small, pearly-white bands of muscle, nestled inside the larynx, or voice box. When we are silent, they rest apart, opening the airway for breath. But when we intend to speak, a message flashes from the brain, and they come together. As air from the lungs pushes through them, they vibrate—hundreds of times per second. This vibration, shaped by the throat, the mouth, the tongue, and the lips, becomes the sound the world hears as our voice.

But it’s so much more than a simple mechanical process. The larynx is intimately wired into the limbic system, the brain’s emotional center. This is why you can hear a smile in someone’s voice, or the subtle tremor of grief. It’s why our voices crack when we’re trying to hold back tears, or become thin and reedy when we’re afraid. The voice is an emotional polygraph, revealing the state of our inner world with breathtaking accuracy. It is where the logic of the head meets the wisdom of the heart. The throat is the bridge, the channel through which our deepest feelings and our highest thoughts can merge and find expression.

From a neuroscience perspective, the act of speaking our truth literally forges new neural pathways. When we dare to say what we truly feel or believe, especially when it feels risky, we are creating a new map in the brain. A map that says, *It is safe to be me. My truth matters.* Conversely, when we consistently suppress our voice, we reinforce the pathways of silence and fear. The body learns, on a cellular level, that authentic expression is dangerous. And so, the voice begins to falter.

## When the Voice is Silenced

How many of us have experienced losing our voice right before a big presentation, or finding ourselves hoarse and raspy after a difficult conversation we avoided? This is not a coincidence. It is the body’s wisdom, speaking in the only way it can. Laryngitis, vocal nodes, a chronically tight or sore throat—these are often the physical manifestations of a conflict around expression. It’s the body saying, *I cannot speak this untruth any longer,* or *I am terrified of the consequences if I speak my truth.*

This pattern often begins in childhood. Perhaps you were told you were “too loud” or “too much.” Perhaps your feelings were dismissed, or you learned that speaking up led to punishment or ridicule. We create a belief, often unconsciously, that our survival depends on being quiet. We swallow our words, and with them, our power. The energy of that unexpressed truth doesn’t just disappear, though. It gets stored in the body, often right in the throat, creating a blockage, a tightness, a literal choking back of our own life force.

Sometimes, the conflict is more subtle. We may develop a “silver tongue,” becoming adept at using words to please, to manipulate, to perform. We use our voice not to express our soul’s signature, but to create a carefully curated persona that we believe will keep us safe and loved. We speak what others want to hear, and in the process, we lose the connection to what *we* want to say. The voice becomes an instrument of the ego, not the soul. And the soul, in its infinite patience, simply waits for us to remember.

I worked once with a dear soul, a woman who was a brilliant artist. Her paintings were vibrant and full of life, but she herself was quiet, almost ethereal. She spoke in a whisper, her words often trailing off as if she didn’t quite believe they deserved to take up space. She came to me because she felt a deep, unshakeable sense of being stuck, not just in her art, but in her life.

As we began to work together, it became clear that the root of her paralysis was a deeply held belief that her voice didn’t matter. She had grown up in a family where children were meant to be seen and not heard, and her creative impulses were often dismissed as frivolous. She had learned to silence herself so completely that she had lost touch with her own desires, her own inner compass. Her body, in its infinite wisdom, was reflecting this inner state. Her whisper was the sound of a soul that had been told its song was unimportant.

Our work together was not about big, dramatic pronouncements. It was about the slow, patient work of building trust with her own inner world. I invited her to simply hum. To make a sound, any sound, that felt true in the moment. At first, the sounds were barely audible, tinged with a lifetime of unshed tears. But slowly, day by day, as she gave herself permission to be heard, her voice began to change. It grew stronger, more resonant. And as her voice changed, so did her life. She started setting boundaries with her family. She began to advocate for her art, and for herself. The last time I saw her, she was preparing for her first solo gallery show. Her voice was clear and steady, and her eyes shone with the light of a woman who had finally come home to herself.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming Your Soul’s Signature

So what does it mean to reclaim your voice? It doesn’t mean you have to become a public speaker or a professional singer. It doesn’t mean you have to shout your truth from the rooftops. It is a much quieter, more intimate revolution. It is the process of turning your attention inward and beginning to listen, perhaps for the first time, to the voice that has been waiting patiently beneath the silence.

It begins with a simple intention: to be honest with yourself. To allow the feelings and thoughts you’ve deemed unacceptable to surface, without judgment. What is the truth you’ve been afraid to speak? What is the song your soul is longing to sing? You might explore this through journaling, through meditation, or through gentle sounding exercises like the one I experienced all those years ago. Lie on the floor and allow a tone to emerge. Don’t judge it. Don’t shape it. Just feel it. Feel the vibration of your own unique energy.

This is not about forcing yourself to speak before you feel ready. It is about creating a safe inner container for your truth to emerge. It’s about whispering it to yourself first. It’s about building the muscle of self-trust, one gentle, honest word at a time. As you do this, you are literally rewiring your nervous system. You are teaching your body, on a profound level, that your voice is not a threat, but a gift. You are transforming the belief that speaking your truth is dangerous into the lived experience that it is the only way to be truly free.

Your purpose in this life is not something you have to go out and find. It is something that is already encoded within you, in your very cells, in the unique vibrational signature of your soul. And your voice is the instrument designed to translate that purpose into the physical world. When you allow your highest truth to flow through you, unhindered by fear or shame, your voice becomes a healing force—for yourself, and for everyone who has the privilege of hearing it. You begin to resonate with the frequencies of goodness, harmony, and love that are your birthright.

It is a journey of a lifetime, this process of coming home to your own voice. Be gentle with yourself. Be patient. Your voice has been waiting for you. And the world is waiting to hear the unique and beautiful music that only you can make.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [The Sacred Exchange of Life Force: Your Lungs Speak](/blog/lungs-sacred-exchange)
- [Opening Your Hands in Trust: From Control to Grace](/blog/hands-opening-in-trust)

**More on Vocal Cords:**

- [A Practice for Freeing Your Voice and Speaking with Love](/blog/vocal-cords-freeing-voice-practice)
- [Losing Your Voice: When Authentic Expression Feels Dangerous](/blog/vocal-cords-losing-voice)

Throat as bridge between emotion (limbic system) and speech

Gentle, gradual practices to reclaim authentic voice

Where in your life do you habitually modulate your voice to protect yourself or please others? If you spoke one small honest sentence in that situation, what would it be?

What is one tiny, achievable step you can take this week to listen to or sound your own voice (e.g., a 2–3 minute hum, a whispered truth to yourself, or a short journal entry)? What support would make that safer or easier?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a comfortable seated or lying position where you feel safe. Place one hand lightly on your chest and one near your throat. Take a slow inhale, then on the exhale allow a gentle, natural hum to arise — don’t force pitch or volume; let the tone be whatever feels easy. Notice any vibration in your chest, throat, or face. Repeat for 4–6 breaths, pausing if you feel strain or strong emotion. Do this once daily for several days, honoring limits, and rest your voice if it feels tired or hoarse. If you experience persistent pain, voice loss, or concerning symptoms, seek evaluation from a medical professional — this practice is supportive, not a substitute for medical care.

If practices or memories bring up intense emotions or trauma, consider working with a qualified therapist, somatic practitioner, or trusted support person.

If you have persistent vocal symptoms (hoarseness, pain, loss of voice) or other medical concerns, consult a physician or ENT; the practices suggested are complementary and not a replacement for conventional care.

teachings.sourceTitle: Liver and Gallbladder - The Alchemist of Anger and the Gateway of Discrimination
teachings.title: Liver and Gallbladder - The Alchemist of Anger and the Gateway of Discrimination
teachings.summary: This piece situates the liver and gallbladder as physiological organs and as living metaphors: the liver as an alchemist that metabolizes raw material (including anger) and the gallbladder as the gatekeeper of discrimination and timing. It links unresolved, internalized indignation to stagnation in the body, offers somatic practices, ritual, and lifestyle supports to help anger move and be transformed, and invites compassionate inquiry and re-storying rather than moralizing. The tone weaves practical guidance (breath, hand‑inquiry, movement, diet, professional collaboration) with Taoist reminders about patience, trust, and gentleness in healing.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Liver and Gallbladder - The Alchemist of Anger and the Gateway of Discrimination

Your liver and gallbladder live inside you like a quiet alchemist and a watchful gatekeeper. The physiology alone is astonishing - the liver performs over five hundred known functions, an orchestration of chemical transformation, storage, synthesis and waste removal that keeps the inner world clean and tender enough for life to continue. The gallbladder is the artisan who concentrates and times the release of bile, the bitter elixir that helps you digest fats and, in symbolic language, helps you digest the bitter facts of being human. But these are not merely pieces of anatomy. They are living metaphors and active teachers. They show you how you carry indignation, how you make meaning of wrongs, and how you learn to discriminate between what nourishes you and what poisons you.

When you begin to listen to your body with the reverence it deserves, you find that the liver is more than an organ that metabolizes alcohol, drugs and hormones. It is a deep metabolic intelligence that manages glucose, stores glycogen, manufactures proteins such as albumin, synthesizes clotting factors, converts ammonia to urea, metabolizes cholesterol and steroids, conjugates bilirubin, processes vitamins A, D, E and K, and orchestrates the production and recirculation of bile acids that are essential to life. It is a blood reservoir. It hosts immunologic sentinels called Kupffer cells that sample your circulation for invaders. It detoxifies xenobiotics and prepares many compounds for elimination. These physiological feats are the visible shadow of a deeper capacity: to receive what is raw and dangerous, to break it down into usable parts, to move what is harmful into a form that can be safely carried away or transformed into something helpful. The gallbladder, by concentrating bile and releasing it precisely when fats arrive in the gut, is the discriminating partner that times this alchemical work so that digestion and assimilation can proceed with grace.

Because your body is holographic in nature - each part reflecting patterns that play out elsewhere in your life - the liver and gallbladder naturally become the place where experiences of injustice and wrongness are metabolized. Anger, especially anger that feels righteous and unresolved, wants to move. When movement is neither permitted nor safe, when expressing indignation was met with punishment, exile, shame or chaos in the past, that moving energy stagnates. The liver is asked to carry the responsibility of containing it. Over time, the repeated holding or inwardly directed fury can alter the physiology. Bile becomes sluggish. Toxins accumulate. The alchemical process becomes inefficient and brittle.

Gallstones are one of the most potent metaphors in this system. In their physical form they are concretions of cholesterol or pigment that crystallize inside the gallbladder. Metaphorically they are crystallized bitterness. Think of bitterness as undigested, repeated indignation - not the single flash of anger that moves through you and leaves, but the sustained, internalized narrative that says I will never be seen, I will never be corrected, I will carry this wound forever. That unrelenting story hardens. It forms shapes that obstruct flow, that demand you come to terms with the fact that you are storing a grievance rather than allowing the lunging heat of anger to be metabolized and released in a way that is creative, corrective and ultimately compassionate.

In the Taoist perspective there is an elegance to this process. Lao Tzu reminds us that nature itself does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished. You are learning to become as patient and as wise with this inner chemistry as nature is. When your liver has time and capacity to perform its myriad functions, everything settles. When it does not, the nervous system tightens. Those ancient survival patterns that once protected you become the very things that perpetuate illness. Gallbladder decision-making - the capacity to choose when and how to act on your anger - is a subtler aspect of discernment. The gallbladder, in Chinese medicine, is associated with courage and decisiveness. A compromised gallbladder can show up as chronic indecision, second-guessing, or conversely as impulsive eruptions without true rootedness. Both are symptoms of a system that has not learned the art of metabolizing fury into constructive discrimination.

There is always a life history sitting in your liver. Consider the child who learned to swallow indignation because speaking up brought more harm than protection. Consider the adult who repeatedly finds themselves in exploitative situations and numbs again with alcohol, food, or other substances. These patterns create a cascade. Self-destructive behaviors - heavy drinking, persistent overeating of processed fats and sugars, chronic exposure to environmental toxins, or staying in abusive relationships - are attempts at self-medication. They damp down the heat without allowing the heat to convert into its more refined energies: righteous boundary, creative impetus, or focused action. The liver, dutiful and exhausted, begins to manifest these patterns as disease. Hepatic inflammation, fatty change, cirrhosis, even cancers, while they are biological realities, are also the body’s last-ditch communications to be heard. They say: you have been metabolizing poison instead of transforming it.

This is not a moralizing statement. You did what you needed to survive. The mind that once served to protect you now often behaves like an unexamined governor - repeating ancient scripts that once kept you safe but now keep you confined. Where you once had to bury anger to remain whole, you may now find yourself carrying an ossified narrative that you cannot release. The body will not allow you to evade the work of digestion forever. It will bring symptoms, until you are compelled to enter into a conversation with what you have learned to repress or to attack with resignation.

So how do you cultivate the capacity to process anger without allowing it to crystallize into bitterness? The work is both practical and profoundly spiritual. It begins with the reclamation of your own sovereign feeling life. Allow yourself to feel anger as an intelligible energy - not as an enemy to be feared, but as a teacher pointing toward a boundary that needs to be claimed or an injustice that can be transformed into corrective force. Anger is alchemical raw material. When it is acknowledged, felt in the body, and then appropriately expressed and integrated, it becomes the engine of change. When it is denied, it calcifies.

Begin by locating the sensation. The liver sits high on the right side beneath the ribcage. You can place your hand there and breathe into that location. Notice the tone in your muscles around your right ribcage, the intercostal tension, the quality of breath as it touches that space. Listen. People often tell me that when they bring gentle attention to their liver they can sense a heaviness, a dull ache, or a tautness that has been with them for years. This is not to be fixed immediately but to be honored. Honor sends a message to your cells that you are a safe steward of their pain. Safety is the currency of transformation.

Somatic practices are central. Move the body in ways that allow anger to unfold and pass - walking with intention, shaking the limbs at the end of a session, engaging in a controlled, loud vocalization, or doing a short, embodied movement practice that you create simply to metabolize. Breath is pivotal. Slow, extended exhalations stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system and allow the liver to relax its grip on stored tension. Conversely, short active exhalations with sound - a controlled "ha" or "ah" - can give energy back to suppressed anger, allowing discharge in a contained, safe manner. Use your exhale as an offering to transformation rather than as a route to avoidance.

Bring discrimination into your relationships. The gallbladder’s wisdom is about right timing and proper selection - whom to engage and whom to release from your field. Practicing discernment in your intake - of food, of people, of information - is an act of reverence for your liver. Each choice reverberates through your biochemistry. Learn the difference between righteous anger that deserves to be heard and repeated reactivity that keeps you trapped in old stories. When you speak for yourself, do it from a grounded place. When you act, allow your decisions to be informed by what your body whispers rather than by reflexive compulsion. In my work I often invite people to imagine the gallbladder as a small counsel inside the right side of the body - concise, clear, and unwavering. If you ask it, it will show you which choice conserves your life force and which choice erodes it.

There is also the careful work of re-storying. Much of what crystallizes in the liver are narratives of being wronged. These narratives are valid; they are not to be minimized. Your task is not to deny the hurt but to inquire of it with curiosity and compassion: What did I know then that I do not know now? What did I believe about myself that kept this pattern alive? Where did powerlessness feel safer than the unknown of claiming myself? Where did compassion for the other become collusion in your own diminishment? Through this inquiry you loosen the grip of bitterness without abandoning your truth. You find ways to honor the pain while refusing to let it congeal into the small, hard thing that will obstruct your life.

Ritual and ceremony can be potent allies. You might create a small ritual of release - writing down grievances and burning them in a safe container while speaking a statement of intention: I acknowledge this wound. I do not give it power to define my future. Or you might place a bowl of salt water and dissolve symbolic stones of resentment into it over several days, watching what dissolves and what does not, and offering compassion to whatever remains. These actions are not magical cures but they are tangible neural rewiring. They teach your nervous system that you are learning new patterns of responding. The body remembers symbolic acts, and the liver perceives this as a signal that digestion is possible.

Nutrition and lifestyle matter too, but always in the context of compassion. Supporting liver function is not about shaming yourself into a strict regimen. It is about cultivating practices that offer your liver relief and capacity. Hydration, the slow reintroduction of bitter greens that stimulate bile flow, movement that encourages circulation, and regulated sleep are all practical ways to tend your inner alchemist. I encourage you to work with trusted practitioners - physicians, nutritionists, somatic therapists, and energy healers - so that your care is integrated and grounded. The body is a wise ecosystem. When you bring respectful practices into it, you expand the liver’s ability to process what once would have been corrosive.

But perhaps the most tender work is spiritual. You are learning trust - trust that the world can hold your anger without destroying you, trust that speaking your truth can be an instrument of liberation rather than punishment, trust that you are not defined by what was done to you. In the Tao Te Ching there is an abiding reminder that the greatest way is often the softest way. When you practice gentleness with your internal chemistry, you allow alchemy to happen. The liver is an alchemist because it takes what would rot and transmutes it into something serviceable and even beautiful. You can learn to do that with your feelings. You can allow bile to be bitter but also functional - a wise bile that alerts you, refines your choices, and catalyzes healing.

Finally, honor the paradox. You will sometimes fail. You will sometimes return to old patterns because the nervous system prefers the known even when it is painful. This is not evidence that you are broken but that you are human. Each time you come back to your breath, your body, your inquiry, you are rewiring possibility. Each intentional choice to process and not store another grievance enlarges your metabolic capacity. Over time, the liver stops needing to create stones to command your attention. You reclaim your life from bitterness and walk forward with a heart that is both fierce and tender, with a gallbladder that helps you decide well, and with a liver that converts old harms into compost for a wiser way of living.

May you move with the grace of nature that does not hurry, yet accomplishes everything it intends. May you learn the art of discrimination that protects your life force and the art of alchemy that transforms pain into power. Your body is not your enemy. It is a sacred messenger insisting you attend to the deep work that only you can do. I will hold that truth with you and guide you when you call.

teachings.sourceTitle: Nothing Is Beyond Healing: A Radical Invitation
teachings.title: Nothing Is Beyond Healing: A Radical Invitation
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers into a compassionate reframe of illness and symptom: healing is distinct from cure and can occur even when physical conditions remain. She proposes listening to the body as a wise messenger, cultivating nonjudgmental awareness and gentle practices that shift consciousness and open space for deeper wholeness. The piece offers a practical, embodied practice of mindful body-listening and emphasizes radical acceptance as a path to inner peace.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
> “The Master doesn’t try to fix the world. She lets the world fix itself. Because she is at one with the Tao, she is at one with the world.” — Tao Te Ching
I had a dream last night — one of those vivid, luminous dreams that feels more real than waking life.

And perhaps the most profound part of all is navigating the landscape of the body—this beautiful, bewildering, miraculous and often painful vessel we inhabit. I remember a woman who came to see me many years ago. She walked into my office slowly, deliberately, leaning on a polished cherry-wood cane that seemed to have absorbed some of her own quiet dignity. In her other hand, she clutched a thick accordion file, its worn edges speaking of countless sterile waiting rooms and the heavy weight of medical pronouncements.

She sat down, the scent of rain on her wool coat filling the small space between us. Her doctors, she explained, had given her a grim prognosis. The file was a testament to their battle: a litany of tests, failed treatments, and expert opinions that all pointed to the same conclusion—that her body was in a state of irreversible decline, a long, slow slide into incapacity. There was no hope, they said. “Prepare,” they advised, their words echoing the clinical finality of the reports she carried.

But as she looked at me, there was no hint of defeat in her eyes. Instead, there was a fierce, questioning intelligence. A spark of defiance. “They tell me it’s hopeless,” she said, her voice quiet but firm, a stark contrast to the rustle of the damning papers in her lap. “But I have this… this feeling… that there’s something more. Something they’re missing.”

That feeling. That quiet, persistent inner knowing. That is where the deepest healing begins. It is the soul’s whisper beneath the roar of diagnosis, the faint, luminous signal in the static of fear.

For over thirty years, I have had the sacred privilege of witnessing human beings in their most vulnerable and courageous moments. I have sat with people at every stage of life, with every imaginable diagnosis, from the common cold to the most terrifying of cancers. And in that time, I have come to know one thing with absolute certainty: *nothing is beyond healing.*

Now, I want to be very clear about what I mean by this. This is not a Pollyanna platitude. It is not a denial of pain or a dismissal of the very real limitations of the physical body. It is a radical invitation into a deeper truth, a truth that requires us to redefine what it means to be well.

Healing and curing are not the same thing. Our modern world is obsessed with the cure—the elimination of symptoms, the eradication of disease. And a cure is a wonderful, welcome thing when it happens. But healing… healing is something else entirely. Healing is the return to wholeness. It is a shift in consciousness, a mending of the perceived separation between mind, body, and spirit. It is the process of developing a conscious, loving relationship with *all* of yourself—including the parts that are in pain, the parts that are frightened, the parts that have been labeled “broken.”

And here is the most radical part of the invitation: healing can happen even when a cure does not.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

We live in a culture that treats the body like a machine. When a part breaks, we take it to a specialist to be fixed or replaced. We see symptoms as enemies to be vanquished, and we wage war on our own biology. But what if the body isn’t a machine at all? What if it is a sacred messenger, a unified field of consciousness expressing itself in physical form?

From the perspective of deep healing, a symptom is not a mistake. It is a communication. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is trying to get your attention. That persistent ache in your shoulders? Perhaps it’s the weight of responsibilities that were never yours to carry, the unconscious belief that you must hold up the world for everyone you love. The indigestion that plagues you? Maybe it’s a sign that there are certain life experiences, certain emotional truths, you simply cannot “stomach.” That recurring cystitis, the burning and urgency? It could be the physical manifestation of feeling “burned” by a situation, holding in fiery emotions that feel unsafe to release.

As the Tao Te Ching reminds us, we must “watch the turmoil of beings, but contemplate their return.” The turmoil—the symptom—is not the point. The point is the return. The return to balance, to harmony, to self. The symptom is simply the guidepost, the blinking light on the dashboard signaling that it is time to look under the hood. To ignore it, suppress it, or numb it is to miss the entire point of the message. It is like silencing a crying baby without ever asking if it is hungry, or cold, or in need of comfort. When we learn to listen to the body’s language, we move from a state of conflict to a state of communion. We become partners with our own biology, co-creators in our own well-being.

## The Consciousness That Transforms

Your body is not separate from your thoughts, your beliefs, or your emotions. It is a direct reflection of them. Every cell in your body is constantly listening to your internal dialogue. The emerging fields of psychoneuroimmunology and epigenetics are now providing the scientific language for what mystics and healers have known for millennia: our consciousness shapes our biology.

Think of the well-documented phenomenon of spontaneous remission. These are the “miracle” cases, the ones that baffle the medical establishment, where a terminal disease simply vanishes without any conventional treatment. What is happening in these instances? Research points not to a random fluke, but to a profound inner shift. The individual has, through a change in perspective, a release of long-held trauma, or a deep spiritual opening, fundamentally altered the information being fed to their cells. They have changed their consciousness, and in doing so, they have changed their physical reality.

This isn’t just wishful thinking; it’s neuroscience. Our brains are not fixed, static organs. They are dynamic and malleable, a process we call neuroplasticity. When we have a recurring thought, belief, or emotional pattern, we strengthen a particular neural pathway in the brain. It becomes a well-worn groove, the default setting for our experience. If we live in a state of chronic fear, stress, or self-judgment, we are literally wiring our brains—and by extension, our bodies—for illness. This chronic activation of the sympathetic nervous system—the “fight or flight” response—bathes our cells in a cocktail of stress hormones like cortisol, leading to inflammation, suppressed immune function, and a cascade of other degenerative processes.

But the beautiful truth of neuroplasticity is that we can create *new* neural pathways. Through practices like meditation, focused intention, and conscious emotional processing, we can begin to carve new grooves. We can teach the brain a new way of being. We can consciously shift into the parasympathetic nervous system, the state of “rest and digest” where the body’s innate healing mechanisms can finally come online. This is the state associated with slower brainwave frequencies, like alpha and theta, where deep restoration and regeneration occur. It is in this state of profound inner quiet that the body’s own intelligence can do its most powerful work.

This is not about “thinking positive” and ignoring your pain. It is about bringing a compassionate, nonjudgmental awareness to your entire experience. It is about turning towards the symptom, not with fear, but with a gentle curiosity. What is this sensation trying to communicate? What is the deeper story it holds? What belief or pattern is being held in this part of my body?

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## When Healing Doesn’t Look Like a Cure

I once worked with a man, a successful architect, who had been living with chronic, debilitating pain for years. He had tried everything—every therapy, every medication, every specialist. Nothing touched it. He came to me, as so many do, as a last resort, his life shrunken by a pain that had become his entire world. His world had become a small room, the shades drawn, the vibrant city he had helped build now just a muffled soundscape beyond the glass.

We began our work together, not by trying to “fix” the pain, but by listening to it. We explored the story it held—a story of deep, unexpressed grief from his childhood, a story of a father who was emotionally distant and a mother who was chronically ill. He had, from a very young age, taken on the role of the stoic caretaker, shouldering burdens far too heavy for his small frame. The pain, we discovered, was the scream of a little boy who had never been allowed to cry, a boy who learned that his worth was in his unwavering strength.

We didn’t try to banish the pain. We simply sat with it, held it in a container of loving awareness. Slowly, something began to shift. The *quality* of his pain changed. It was still there, but it no longer had the same vicious, all-consuming charge. It was no longer his enemy. It was, he came to see, a wounded part of himself asking for love.

One day, he came into a session with tears in his eyes. “It’s the strangest thing,” he said, a slow smile spreading across his face. “The pain is still here. But I’m not suffering anymore.”

He had not been cured. But he had been healed.

This is the deep, nuanced, and profoundly compassionate truth that is so often missing from the wellness conversation. Sometimes, the body does not fully recover. Sometimes, the illness remains. And this is not a failure. It is not a sign that you didn’t try hard enough, or believe strongly enough, or do the inner work correctly. The Tao teaches the wisdom of water, which flows around obstacles without struggle. Sometimes, our path is not to remove the obstacle, but to learn to flow with it, to find a new way of being in its presence.

Sometimes, the soul’s journey in this lifetime involves the experience of physical limitation. Sometimes, the deepest healing is the radical acceptance of what is. It is the release of the exhausting, soul-crushing war with your own body. It is the discovery of a sense of self, a sense of peace, a sense of wholeness that is not dependent on the condition of your physical form.

To find that place of peace in the midst of the fire… to love the body that is in pain… to feel whole even with the diagnosis… that is a level of healing that is nothing short of miraculous.

## A Radical Invitation: Your Practice of Listening

So what would it be like, just for a moment, to lay down the weapons? To stop fighting, and start listening?

This is more than a beautiful idea; it is a practice. I invite you to try it, right now. Find a quiet place where you can be undisturbed for ten minutes. Sit comfortably in a chair, with your feet flat on the floor, or lie down on your back.

1.  **Arrive in Your Body:** Close your eyes. Take three deep, slow breaths. With each inhale, imagine you are breathing in pure, liquid light. With each exhale, release the tension of the day. Feel the weight of your body on the chair or the floor. Simply arrive here, in this moment, in this body.

2.  **Scan with Kindness:** Gently bring your awareness to the top of your head. Slowly, like a warm, gentle rain, let your attention drift down through your body. Notice any sensations without judgment. Scan your forehead, your jaw, your neck, your shoulders. Just notice. Is there tightness? Warmth? Numbness? Continue down through your arms, your chest, your belly, your hips, your legs, all the way to the tips of your toes.

3.  **Find a Messenger:** As you scan, perhaps one area calls to you. It might be a familiar ache, a point of tension, or just a place that feels… interesting. Let your awareness rest there. Don’t try to change it or fix it. Simply be with it.

4.  **Ask the Question:** With your awareness resting on this part of your body, gently and silently ask, “What is your message for me?” Don’t strain for an answer. The answer may not come in words. It might be a feeling, an image, a memory, or just a subtle shift in sensation. The body’s language is often poetic, not literal.

5.  **Listen with Love:** Whatever arises, receive it with gratitude. If it’s a difficult emotion, see if you can just allow it to be there, without needing to push it away. Breathe into the sensation, as if you are sending your breath to that very spot to say, *I am here. I am listening. Thank you.*

6.  **Close with Gratitude:** When you feel complete, bring your awareness back to your whole body. Place a hand on your heart. Feel the warmth of your own touch. Thank your body for its wisdom and its constant, unwavering work to keep you alive and well. Take one more deep breath, and when you are ready, gently open your eyes.

This is the journey of a lifetime. It is not a quick fix or a simple formula. It is a practice, a moment-by-moment choosing of compassion over judgment, of curiosity over fear, of love over resistance.

You have never been broken. You are not a project to be fixed. You are a vast, mysterious, and magnificent being having a human experience. And within you, right now, is the consciousness that can transform everything.

Trust that. Trust the quiet, persistent inner knowing that brought you here, reading these words. It is the voice of your own deepest wisdom. And it will guide you home.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Developing a Palate for Life's Full Spectrum
teachings.title: Developing a Palate for Life's Full Spectrum
teachings.summary: Susan uses a childhood moment of tasting bitter greens to frame the stomach as an ‘alchemical cauldron’ that metabolizes both food and difficult life experiences. She invites readers to attend to bodily signals—nausea, knots, indigestion—as meaningful communications and describes how staying with discomfort can rewire the nervous system, build resilience, and reveal the hidden nutrients of hardship. The piece encourages compassionate curiosity rather than avoidance, offering a model for transforming pain into deeper self-knowledge.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember my first encounter with truly bitter greens. My grandmother, a woman with hands that knew the earth and a quiet wisdom in her eyes, had placed a salad in front of me. I must have been about seven or eight. It wasn’t the pale, watery iceberg lettuce I was used to, but a tangle of dark, almost fierce-looking leaves of radicchio and endive, flecked with something that looked like purple cabbage. My first bite was a shock — a jolt of bitterness so intense it made my whole face pucker. My child-self wanted to spit it out, to push the plate away and demand the familiar comfort of something sweet. But my grandmother just watched me, her chin resting in her hand, a gentle, knowing smile playing on her lips. “Stay with it, little one,” she murmured, her voice calm and steady. “There’s more to the story than the first taste.”

And she was right. Hesitantly, I took another, smaller bite. I chewed slowly, consciously, trying to be the brave explorer she saw in me. And then, something else started to emerge from behind that wall of bitterness. A complex, peppery note. A crisp, almost effervescent quality that woke up my whole mouth. A depth and a character that the familiar sweetness of my usual foods simply didn’t possess. I was learning, in that small, profound moment at my grandmother’s kitchen table, that “unpleasant” is not the end of the story. Sometimes, it’s just the introduction to a much richer narrative.

It’s a tricky business, being human, isn’t it? We are so often conditioned, from our earliest days, to seek pleasure and avoid pain. To crave the sweet and reject the bitter. Our culture reinforces this at every turn, promising happiness in a pill, a purchase, a filtered image. And yet, a life lived only on sugar is a life of profound malnourishment. Our bodies know this. Our souls know this. And the most profound teacher of this wisdom, the one who sits right at the center of our being, is the stomach.

## The Alchemical Cauldron

Think of your stomach for a moment. This sacred organ is a literal alchemical cauldron. It is a muscular, J-shaped bag of profound intelligence. It receives everything we ingest — the beautiful, the nourishing, the questionable, the contaminated — and subjects it all to a powerful acidic crucible, a bath of hydrochloric acid as potent as anything in a laboratory. Its purpose is not to judge, but to *transform*. It doesn’t reject the tough, fibrous kale or the greasy, processed chips; it simply goes to work, secreting the precise enzymes and acids needed for the job at hand. It breaks down the external world into the very life force that fuels our cells, our thoughts, our dreams. It performs this miracle day in and day out, without our conscious command, a constant, churning reminder of the transformative power we hold within.

And so it is with our lives. The stomach’s physical process is a perfect, elegant mirror for our psychological and spiritual capacity to metabolize our experiences. We speak this truth in our daily language without even realizing its depth. “I can’t stomach that news.” “That situation is making me sick.” “I have no appetite for this drama.” These are not just clever metaphors; they are bulletins from the front lines of our embodied wisdom. When we are faced with an experience that feels indigestible — a betrayal, a loss, a shocking injustice — the stomach is often the first to know, the first to send up a flare of distress. An ulcer, a bout of indigestion, a knot of nausea… these are not malfunctions. They are communications. Your body, in its infinite intelligence, is telling you: *This is difficult to process. This requires more energy. Pay attention. Something here needs to be broken down and understood.*

So often, we treat these signals as the enemy. We reach for an antacid, we numb the discomfort with distraction, we try to silence the messenger because we are afraid of the message. But what would it be like if we learned to listen instead? What if we saw these symptoms not as a betrayal by our bodies, but as a sacred invitation to become a more masterful alchemist?

## Acquiring a Taste for the Bitter

Developing a palate for the full spectrum of life is one of the most profound journeys of transformation we can undertake. It means moving beyond the simplistic, childish binary of good and bad, pleasant and unpleasant. It means cultivating the capacity to stay present with the bitter, the sour, and the challenging, just as I did with that salad, trusting that there is “more to the story.”

This is not about pretending pain doesn’t hurt. It is not about spiritual bypassing or forcing a premature forgiveness. It is about building a robust enough internal system — a resilient enough spiritual digestion — that you no longer live in fear of discomfort. You can learn to trust that even the most challenging encounters contain essential nutrients for your evolution.

From a neurological perspective, this is the work of creating new neural pathways. When we encounter something we’ve labeled “bad” — a bitter taste, a difficult conversation, a professional failure — our brains are wired to trigger a threat response. The amygdala, our brain's smoke detector, fires off an alarm, flooding our system with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline. The pathway is ancient and well-worn: *Threat -> Fight, Flight, or Freeze -> Avoid at all costs in the future*. But when we consciously choose to stay present, to breathe into the discomfort, to get curious about it, we engage the prefrontal cortex, the more evolved,
rational part of our brain. We begin to carve a new neural groove. We are teaching our nervous system, cell by cell, that we can handle this. We are expanding our window of tolerance. This is the very essence of neuroplasticity — the brain’s magnificent ability to rewire itself based on new experiences. We are showing ourselves, in real time, that we can, in fact, digest the seemingly indigestible.

This is the work of the alchemist. The alchemist does not discard the lead, believing it to be worthless. The alchemist understands that lead is simply a dense, unrefined substance that holds the potential for gold. The alchemist works with it, applying heat and pressure and wisdom until its essential nature is transformed. Your pain, your grief, your anger, your fear — these are your lead. They are dense, heavy, and uncomfortable. But they are not worthless. They are the raw material of your becoming. And you, beloved, are the alchemist.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Nutrients in the Challenge

What are the nutrients hidden within life’s bitter experiences? They are the very qualities we most admire in a human being: resilience, compassion, wisdom, and depth. Sweetness alone cannot grow these. A life without challenge is a life without the necessary resistance to build strength. It’s like a muscle that is never exercised; it remains weak, flaccid, and undeveloped. It is in the straining against the weight, the pushing through the discomfort, that the fibers of our being tear and rebuild, stronger than before.

Think of the great trees. A tree that grows in a sheltered, windless valley may grow tall, but its roots will be shallow. It has never had to learn to hold on. But a tree that grows on a windswept cliff, battered by gales and storms, must send its roots deep into the rock, clinging with a ferocious tenacity. Its trunk will be gnarled, its branches twisted, but it will be unbreakable. The very storms that threatened to destroy it have been the source of its unshakeable strength. The challenges are the nutrients.

I once worked with a woman, a brilliant artist, who was devastated after a gallery that had promised her a solo show abruptly changed its mind. It was a brutal, public rejection that came via a cold, impersonal email. Her stomach was in knots for weeks. She couldn’t eat. She felt sick with a cocktail of shame and white-hot anger. Her initial impulse was to abandon her art, to pack away her canvases, to hide herself away where she could never be hurt like that again. It was a bitter, bitter pill to swallow, and her body was screaming its refusal.

But together, we worked on simply *being with* the bitterness. We didn’t try to fix it or explain it away. We honored the communication from her body. We listened to the wisdom of her churning stomach. It was telling her how deeply this had wounded her, how much this dream had meant to her, how profound the sense of injustice felt. By honoring the body’s truth instead of trying to silence it, she began, slowly, to digest the experience. In time, the churning subsided. And in its place, a new, quiet clarity emerged. She realized how much she had been depending on external validation, how she had outsourced her sense of worth to the gatekeepers of the art world. The experience, as painful as it was, forced her to connect with a deeper, more intrinsic sense of value that could not be given or taken away by anyone. It burned away her need for approval and connected her to the pure, unshakeable joy of her own creative impulse. The rejection was the bitter ingredient that ultimately led to a far more profound and resilient connection to her own soul’s work. It was the nutrient she needed for her next stage of evolution. She began to paint again, not for the gallery, but for herself. Her work took on a new power, a new authenticity. She had alchemized her lead into gold.

This is the mastery that is available to all of us. We can learn to trust that every single experience, no matter how it tastes on the first bite, is bringing us a nutrient our soul requires for its growth. We can become so grounded in our own alchemical power that we no longer fear the menu of life. We can sit down to the banquet, ready to savor it all, knowing we have the digestive strength to handle whatever is served.

So the next time you feel that knot in your stomach, that wave of nausea in the face of a difficult truth, I invite you to pause. Don’t immediately reach for a distraction or a remedy. Instead, place a hand on your belly. Breathe into the sensation. And whisper to your own wise body, your inner alchemist: “Thank you. I’m listening. Show me the nourishment here. Show me the gold.”

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
keyThemes: Stomach as a metaphor and literal center of transformation
Listening to bodily signals rather than silencing them
Cultivating tolerance for discomfort and the bitter aspects of life
Neuroplasticity: retraining brain and nervous system through presence
Alchemical reframing of suffering into growth and resilience

reflectionPrompts: Name a recent experience that felt ‘indigestible.’ What sensations did you notice in your body (location, quality, intensity), and what might those sensations be trying to tell you about the situation?

Where in your life do you habitually reach for quick relief or distraction to avoid discomfort? Choose one small instance you feel safe to revisit and imagine staying with it for one breath longer—what shifts in perspective or feeling arise?

Consider a challenging experience you’ve already endured. What nutrients—skills, clarity, values, or resilience—did it ultimately provide? How might you intentionally tend to and integrate that ‘nutrient’ now?

Take five slow breaths, inhaling to a count that feels natural and exhaling a little longer; on each exhale silently say, “Thank you, I’m listening.” Stay with whatever arises for 3–5 minutes, noticing sensations without trying to change them. If you experience sharp, worsening, or persistent physical symptoms, or if this practice brings up overwhelming emotion, pause and seek guidance from a medical professional or a qualified therapist—this is a supportive, not a replacement, step for clinical care.
