You have full permission to pause any reflection or practice at any time; grounding, stepping away, or reaching out to a trusted friend is appropriate.
If the material touches on past trauma, sustained distress, or causes intense dysregulation, consider contacting a qualified therapist or support person for safety and processing.
If you are experiencing severe or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms or other medical concerns, consult a healthcare professional for assessment and treatment.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Alchemy of Grief: How Loss Becomes the Gateway to Deeper Love
teachings.title: The Alchemy of Grief: How Loss Becomes the Gateway to Deeper Love
teachings.summary: Susan describes grief as an embodied, sacred process rather than a problem to be fixed, inviting readers to stay present with loss with tenderness and courage. Using the alchemy metaphor, she suggests that attending to grief can transform pain into a deeper capacity for love and compassionate presence for others. The piece emphasizes there is no timeline and that integration — not erasure — is the goal.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a tender thing, this human heart. So vast, so resilient, and yet so very fragile. We move through our days, our lives, building connections, weaving our stories together with others, only to find that the very fabric of our reality can be torn by loss. And in that tearing, we are introduced to one of the most profound and misunderstood teachers we will ever know: grief. We are taught to fear grief, to see it as an enemy. A problem to be solved. A dark tunnel to rush through so we can get back to the light. We are told to “get over it,” to “move on,” as if the heart were a simple machine that could be reset. But grief is not a detour from life — it is a part of life itself. It is the sacred, aching echo of love. ## The Shape of Loss Grief arrives in a thousand different forms. It is the gut-wrenching emptiness after the death of a beloved one. It is the quiet sorrow of a dream that will never be realized. It is the slow, creeping ache of a friendship fading into the past. It is the loss of a version of ourselves we once were, or a future we had so carefully planned. Whatever its source, the experience is profoundly physical. It lives in the body. A tightness in the chest that makes it hard to breathe. A hollowness in the belly. A weariness in the bones that sleep cannot touch. Neuroscience helps us understand this. When we experience deep emotional pain, the anterior cingulate cortex — the same part of the brain that processes physical pain — lights up. Your heartbreak is not just *like* a broken leg; your brain processes it in a remarkably similar way. The pain is real. It is encoded in our very neurology. I remember when my grandmother passed. She was the anchor of my childhood, her home a sanctuary of unconditional love and the smell of baking bread. For months after she was gone, I would find myself reaching for the phone to call her, my fingers hovering over the familiar number before the reality crashed down on me again. The grief was a physical weight, a constant companion. I would be sitting in my garden, watching the sunlight filter through the leaves of the Japanese maple, and suddenly be overwhelmed by a wave of sorrow so immense it felt like I might drown in it. My body remembered her hugs, her laughter, the specific cadence of her voice. It was my body that was grieving, as much as my mind. ## The Alchemical Fire So what do we do with this pain? How do we navigate this territory that feels so desolate? The ancient alchemists sought to turn lead into gold. They worked with base materials, subjecting them to fire and pressure, believing that through this intense process, a transformation could occur. This is the perfect metaphor for the journey of grief. Our pain, our loss, our leaden sorrow — this is the raw material. And our willingness to feel it, to stay present with it, to tend to it with compassion… that is the alchemical fire. Grief is not something to get over; it is something to move *through* with all the tenderness and courage we can summon. It asks us to be still. To listen. To allow the waves to wash over us without resisting. It is in this surrender that the magic begins. > "The dark is not an end, but a beginning. It is the womb from which all things are born." - Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching When we allow ourselves to truly feel our losses, something remarkable happens. The heart, broken open, does not shatter. It expands. It becomes more spacious, more capable of holding both the sorrow and the love. We begin to understand that grief and love are not opposites. They are two sides of the same coin. Grief is simply love with nowhere to go. It is the shape of love in the absence of the beloved. ## The Gateway to Deeper Love This is the great secret of the alchemical process. The gold that is created from the lead of our sorrow is a deeper, more profound capacity for love. A love that is not dependent on circumstances. A love that is not afraid of the dark. When you have walked through the fire of grief and allowed it to transform you, you no longer fear the shadows. You know that you can survive loss. You know that your heart is more resilient than you ever imagined. This knowing changes everything. It allows you to love more freely, more fully, without the constant, subtle fear of the inevitable goodbyes that are a part of this human life. You become a safer harbor for others in their own storms. You can sit with a friend in their sorrow without needing to fix it, without needing to rush them through it, because you know that the only way out is through. You can offer the profound gift of your presence, a quiet testament to the truth that they are not alone, and that this, too, is a sacred part of the journey. This is the alchemy. The pain does not simply disappear. Rather, it is integrated. It becomes a part of the rich tapestry of who you are. The scars become reminders of your strength, of your capacity to love and to lose and to love again. You learn that the human heart is not diminished by sorrow — it is carved into a more beautiful, intricate vessel, capable of holding more light, more compassion, more love. So if you are moving through the landscape of grief right now, my friend, be gentle with yourself. There is no timeline. There is no right way to do it. There is only your way. Let the tears come. Let the anger rise. Let the weariness be there. Your only task is to be present with what is true in this moment. To honor the love that is at the heart of your pain.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
Your grief is a testament to your ability to love. It is a sacred fire. And if you can tend it with patience and compassion, it will transform you, leaving you not broken, but broken open — into a deeper, more expansive, more unconditional love than you ever thought possible. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan
keyThemes: Grief as an expression of love — not an enemy
Embodiment: grief shows up in the body and nervous system
Alchemical transformation: using presence and compassion to integrate loss
No timeline or single ‘right’ way to grieve
Expansion of capacity for love and compassion through loss
Being a present witness to others’ sorrow without fixing
reflectionPrompts: Which loss or longing feels most present for you right now, and what sensations or images arise in your body when you name it?
Where in your life do you habitually rush away from sadness, and what might tender, curious attention to that resistance reveal?
How has a past experience of grief changed the way you hold yourself or others — what did it carve open or teach you about love?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a quiet seat. Rest one hand over your heart and the other on your belly. Breathe slowly for three to five minutes, noticing each inhale and exhale and any sensations that arise without trying to change them. If emotions intensify, give yourself permission to pause, open your eyes, and reach out to a trusted person or professional. This brief practice is gentle and intended as supportive self-care, not a substitute for medical or mental health treatment.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article engages with grief, loss, and intense emotion; please move at your own pace and grant yourself permission to pause whenever needed.
If you feel overwhelmed, unsafe, or are experiencing thoughts of harming yourself, contact local emergency services or a mental health professional immediately.

Seeking qualified support (therapist, grief counselor, physician) is a valid and often necessary part of healing; compassionate presence and self-practice can complement but do not replace professional care.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Kidneys - The Alchemists of Emotional Balance
teachings.title: The Kidneys - The Alchemists of Emotional Balance
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard the kidneys as quiet alchemists that both literally manage bodily fluids and symbolically hold patterns of fear, will, and emotional retention. She links kidney symptoms to habitual avoidance, victim consciousness, and crystallized emotions, and offers somatic practices, ritual, and small boundary-based actions to help restore flow. Throughout, she emphasizes marrying soulful practice with appropriate medical care and choosing steady, compassionate agency over hurry or blame.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a quiet, uncelebrated alchemy happening inside you every single hour of every single day. The organ you most rarely think about - your kidneys - are master chemists of your internal ocean, guardians of balance that work in a silence both humble and profound. They filter roughly 200 quarts of blood each day, deciding with a wisdom that is at once physical and symbolic what to keep and what to release. If you listen with reverence, they will tell you the story of how you have learned to carry life - the burdens you have swallowed, the fears you have let settle like silt, the places where your will has been dimmed or deepened.

The kidneys as the internal ocean's alchemists

Imagine an inner sea that you carry with you. This ocean is not metaphor alone - it is the literal milieu of fluids that sustain your cells, dissolve nutrients, and dissolve away what no longer serves. Your kidneys are the tidemasters of this sea. They sieve, concentrate, dilute, neutralize, and calibrate. They take what has been poured into you - your meals, your relationships, your traumas, your unspoken resentments - and they work to render these into something that nourishes instead of corrodes. This is not a passive filtration. It is an active, discerning chemistry that requires strength, clarity, and a kind of moral intelligence. When your inner ocean is balanced, your days feel buoyant. When it tilts toward stagnation or hyper-reactivity, you notice it in the edges - fatigue, swelling, changes in appetite, recurring infections, or the shock of stones forming where water should have flowed.

You process more than blood. You process feeling. The ancient physicians of China knew this well. They linked the kidneys with fear and with willpower. They described the kidneys as the home of jing - your essence, your life seed. Weak kidneys in their view did not simply mean poor filtration; they meant a life lived under the tyranny of fear, a will that had been compromised by chronic surrender. Stones in this system were not just calcifications; they were crystallized patterns of unprocessed experience. When emotions are not metabolized, when fear becomes habitual and blame becomes the default explanation for what happens to you, feelings harden into substance - a literal, painful reminder that something needs to change.

Kidney issues as maps to your interior life

When you come to me in sessions or when you draw the kidney card in your practice, what I hear beneath the medical words is an invitation to reclaim agency. Kidney complaints often point to emotional overwhelm. You have been drenched in currents you did not choose and you have tried to manage by shrinking, by waiting for rescue, or by hoping that someone else will carry the load. Victim consciousness settles like silt because it is an energy of being buffeted rather than steering. It assumes that life happens to you rather than responds to your steady, courageous participation.

Victim consciousness is subtle and seductive. It offers a release from responsibility in exchange for the energy of helplessness. You may not realize how congenial it has become until your body objects - until the kidneys, those master alchemists, begin to cough up a warning. Kidney stones are a clarifying metaphor. They are the crystallized product of repeatedly retaining strong feelings - fear, resentment, shame - rather than transforming them through expression, boundary, ritual, or movement. They demand to be released. That release can be violent and painful if it is resisted. Or it can be gentle and dissolving, when you learn to become fluent in your own emotional chemistry.

Fear, willpower, and the Tao of the kidney

There is a Taoist way to look at the kidneys that invites a deeper relationship with fear. Lao Tzu wrote, "Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished." When fear governs you, there is a hurried contraction - a wasting of vital force that wants to be reclaimed. The kidney asks you to move away from frantic reactivity toward an unhurried strength. This is not stoicism. It is a poised receptivity - an inner posture that can face what is true and still remain unbroken. Willpower from this vantage point is not brute force; it is the disciplined softness that allows you to say no to what drains you and yes to what sustains you.

Fear has many faces. It can appear as freeze, as a numbing that prevents you from feeling and thus from processing. It can appear as avoidance, where you schedule your life around safety rather than meaning. It can appear as rage at those you perceive as taking from you - rage that masks a deeper trembling. Healing the kidneys means learning to recognize fear when it arises, to sit with it long enough to name it, and to choose a response that honors your dignity. Willpower is the muscle you build in that naming. It is the steady hand that returns to the task of filtering life without being swept away by every tidal surge.

The holographic body and the kidney's message

In holographic body wisdom, each organ is a mirror for wider themes in your life. The kidney does not only process fluid. It holds the story of your receptivity to support, of your capacity to stand firm when you are unmoored, and of your choice in the face of helplessness. If you grew up in circumstances where you needed to be small to survive - where asserting a need felt dangerous - your kidneys may have held the strategy of contraction in place so long that it became the norm. You learned to be vigilant, to conserve, to fear the expenditure of your own energy. You learned that trust is risky. Over time, those habits calcify.

But there is a path back. The holographic model tells you that when one place softens, the whole field changes. When you begin to cultivate trust in the small decisions - when you say no here and yes there, when you permit a small grief and then let it flow - you initiate a cascade. Your fluid systems respond. Your breath deepens. Your posture shifts. Your kidneys receive the message that the world is not an endless threat, and they relax into their luminous task of alchemy instead of siegecraft.

Practical somatic practices for kidney alchemy

You do not need to run from your fear or attempt to intellectually cajole it into submission. You can meet it bodily. Sit with me here in a practice that has helped many people reclaim kidney strength. Begin by placing both hands on your lower back, where the kidneys live beneath the ribs and behind the abdominal cavity. Let your palms rest there with gentle pressure. Close your eyes if that helps. Breathe down into the place where your hands sit. As you inhale, imagine drawing cool, clear water into your lower back. As you exhale, imagine any clouded, heavy feeling being dissolved and carried away by that inner current.

Do this for several minutes each day until your body remembers how to move fluid with intention. Add sound if you are called to - a low hum or the vowel "oo" drawn out on the exhale helps to engage the parasympathetic nervous system and to loosen held tension. Movement supports this work. Gentle hip circles, spinal twists, and slow squats help massage the internal ocean externally, reminding the kidneys to travail rather than accumulate. Warmth is a balm. Soaking in a bath with a handful of sea salt or taking short saunas stimulates circulation and invites deposits to soften. Hydration is literal medicine. Drink water as a conscious ritual - not hurried gulps, but steady sips that acknowledge you are replenishing life in your cells.

Equally important is expressive release. Learn pathways that allow feelings to move so they do not sediment into stone. This may be rhythmic dance, cathartic vocalizations, journaling that honors the impulse without judgment, or conversations where you practice naming fear without blaming. You will find the right methods for you when you approach the process with patient curiosity rather than urgency.

Shifting from blame to responsible power

There is tenderness required when you look at kidney-related patterns of victimhood. You did not choose many of the circumstances of your early life. Those who loved you did the best they could with what they had. Yet at some point you must choose to step out of the identity that says, "This is happening to me" as a perpetual condition. That choice is not cold or punitive. It is a re-membering - a reclaiming of the authority you always possessed but may have abandoned. Responsibility here is the power to respond with wisdom, not the weight of shame.

Begin with small acts. Re-establish boundaries that protect your energetic and emotional resources. Practice saying no when your body tightens at the thought of over-committing. Choose one micro-action each week that affirms your agency - perhaps returning a difficult email with clarity instead of silence, or declining an invitation that drains you. These are not grand gestures. They are kidney work. Each small act of integrity is water turned from stagnation into current. Over time the will grows supple and strong.

A ritual for dissolving crystallized emotions

If you suspect you carry crystallized emotion - the kind that rings like stone under the ribs of your life - consider a ritual that blends tenderness with will. Prepare a warm bath with mineral salts and perhaps a few drops of juniper, rosemary, or frankincense if they are appropriate for you. Sit beside the water with a journal. Begin by calling in a sense of safety - perhaps lighting a candle, perhaps placing a hand on your chest. Speak aloud what you have been carrying in the voice of compassion: "I have carried this because I did not know how to release it. I honor what that served me in our survival. Now I choose to allow this to move." Place a single seed of intention - for example, "May this soften and return to the current." Then allow tears or sound or silence to do their work while you soak.

When you are finished, write down anything that shifted. The next day, take one practical step that aligns with that shift - a conversation, a boundary, a check-in with a practitioner. Alchemy is not only internal; it requires a bridge into action. The Tao reminds you - paradoxically - that non-action through wise timing is often the greatest action. Yet the Tao also insists on simplicity and presence. In the kidney's work you will balance stillness with courage.

Honoring medical wisdom and the mystery

Be tender with yourself. Some kidney conditions need urgent medical intervention. Stones can be physically dangerous; infections can escalate quickly. Honor the medicine that modern science offers. Let your somatic, energetic, and spiritual work walk beside medical care rather than replacing it. In my own life and in the lives of those I have guided, the greatest transformations have happened when physical care and soulful practice were held together in reverence.

And remember that not every journey ends in the neat slippage of symptom-free perfection. There may be incarnational work you are doing that includes bodily difficulty as part of your growth. Approach this possibility with compassion. You are not a failure if your body resists simple change. You are a human being engaged in a deep transformation that spans systems and lifetimes.

Inviting the kidneys into partnership

To live in right relationship with your kidneys is to cultivate a daily dialogue. Offer them water, warmth, movement, and clear boundaries that preserve your emotional fluids. Practice naming fear without dramatizing it. Choose small, steady acts of will that direct your life toward integrity. Slow down so that you can sense what is lodged and what can pass. When you do this, you allow the kidneys to return to their vocation - to be wise chemists, translating the alchemy of your experience into circulating life instead of calcified pain.

I invite you, as a practice, to speak to your kidneys as you would to a devoted friend who has labored for you without complaint. Place your hands on your lower back. Whisper gratitude. Promise to listen when they have something to say. In the medicine of reciprocal relationship - the heart of Taoist practice - this simple act has the power to tilt your whole internal ocean back toward flow.

In the words of the Tao Te Ching, "Empty yourself of everything. Let the mind become still. The ten thousand things rise and fall while the Self watches their return." When you learn to be still and to trust in the competence of your own inner alchemists, you do not need to frantically control each wave. You become the patient steward of a living sea that knows how to balance itself when you give it space to be seen, heard, and honored.

May your kidneys be recognized as the humble sages they are. May you feel their wise chemistry working for you. May you reclaim your will, soften your fear, and allow the stones of old stories to be dissolved back into the river from which you came. This is not merely bodily healing. It is an initiation into a life lived with steadier nerve, keener clarity, and a tenderness that is fierce and sovereign at once.
keyThemes: Kidneys as both physiological organs and symbolic 'alchemists' of emotion
Fear, willpower, and the cultivation of disciplined softness
How unprocessed feelings can 'crystallize' into physical symptoms
Somatic and ritual practices to encourage fluidity and release
Small boundary actions as practical support for inner change
Respecting medical care while practicing soulful embodiment

Close your eyes if you can and take slow, attentive breaths for 3–5 minutes: inhale imagining cool, clear water moving into the space beneath your hands; exhale imagining clouded, heavy feeling dissolving and flowing away. If it feels helpful, soften into a low hum on the exhale. Pause immediately if you feel any pain or distress, and seek medical care for severe or acute symptoms.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article names childhood survival patterns, victimhood, and intense emotions; pause the reading or practice at any time if you feel overwhelmed.
If this material brings up trauma, grief, or strong reactivity, consider doing practices with a trusted therapist, somatic practitioner, or support person present.

If you experience acute physical signs (severe pain, fever, blood in urine, difficulty urinating) seek urgent medical attention—somatic practices are complementary and not a substitute for professional medical care.

teachings.sourceTitle: You Are Not Broken: A Love Letter to the Healing Journey
teachings.title: You Are Not Broken: A Love Letter to the Healing Journey
teachings.summary: Susan offers a tender reframing of the common sense of being “broken,” inviting readers to stop trying to fix themselves and instead to turn toward felt experience with curiosity and compassion. She names how cultural and neural habits keep us in the story of lack, points to the body as a wise messenger, and uses the kintsugi metaphor to celebrate cracks as places where light and meaning enter. A short, accessible body-centered practice is offered to begin shifting from analysis to embodied listening.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There are moments in life when a profound understanding arrives, not with a thunderclap, but with the quiet clarity of an ocean tide. It is the recognition of a feeling so many of us carry: the sense of being broken.

Isn’t it?

Consider the experience of holding something precious, something that represents a fragile perfection. It could be a relationship, a dream, or a sense of self. Many of us have known the sharp, definitive sound of that precious thing shattering. The impact is not just external; it creates a fault line that seems to run right through us. In the aftermath, well-meaning hands may offer to piece things back together, to make it all "good as new."

But it is never quite the same. The lines of the repair remain visible. The love for what was is mingled with a quiet, persistent grief for its lost perfection. The eye is drawn not to the wholeness, but to the evidence of the shattering. The object becomes a monument to a perceived failure, to an irretrievable loss of innocence.

For so many years, this is how so many of us relate to ourselves. And it is how so many of my friends who seek guidance relate to themselves. They come with their shattered pieces—the trauma, the grief, the chronic illness, the relationship that ended, the career that faltered—and they hold them out, hoping for the right kind of glue. Hoping to be made “good as new.” They see the cracks in their own stories as proof of irreparable damage.

And so, I want to write this love letter to you. Yes, *you*. The one reading this, with your own collection of beautiful, jagged fragments. I want to whisper this into the deepest, most tender parts of your heart, the places that have been convinced of their own deficiency: You are not broken. You have never been broken. You are a magnificent, whole, and holy being having a human experience.

## The Great Misunderstanding of the Healing Journey

We live in a culture that is obsessed with fixing. The entire wellness and healing industry, for all its good intentions, is often built on this very premise: you are sick, and you need to get well. You are wounded, and you need to be healed. You are broken, and you need to be fixed.

We are given ten-step plans to “heal” our anxiety, diets to “fix” our digestion, and spiritual formulas to “cure” our sorrow. We are told to raise our vibration, manifest our best life, and unlock our potential, as if our current state is a locked room and our inherent worth is something we must earn through diligent self-improvement.

This language, this entire paradigm, inadvertently reinforces the most painful story of all: *Something is wrong with me.*

And here’s a very good thing to know: the brain loves a familiar story. Our experiences, especially in early life, carve neural pathways that become our default operating system. Think of it like water flowing down a hill; over time, it creates a deep groove, a channel. If you were taught, through overt messages or subtle energetic cues, that you were too much or not enough, that your needs were an inconvenience, or that your sensitivity was a flaw, your brain diligently built a superhighway around the core belief: “I am broken. I am lacking. I must be fixed to be worthy of love.”

Your nervous system, the electrical network of safety and connection in your body, learned to operate from this premise. It organized your reality around it, constantly scanning the horizon for evidence to prove the story is true. Every mistake, every rejection, every failure becomes another piece of “proof.” It’s not a personal failing; it’s neuroscience. It’s the brain’s incredible efficiency at work. It’s a survival mechanism. But, beloved, survival is not the same as thriving. It is not the same as living from the radiant truth of your wholeness.

Many people walk this path for decades, feeling fundamentally flawed, like a precious object with visible cracks. The journey can become a relentless pursuit of ‘fixing.’ It’s common to become a master student, collecting healing modalities like charms on a bracelet—cranial sacral therapy, shamanic healing, homeopathy. Each one is held with the hope that it will be the magic glue. The thought process is often, "If I can just learn enough, I can fix myself. And by extension, I can fix others." Early work as a healer can be, with honest reflection, an extension of this. It can be like holding a tube of glue, desperately trying to hide the cracks in oneself and in the precious people who come for help.

Consider a common scenario in healing work: a client presents with a persistent issue, like debilitating migraines. A practitioner can become so sure they can “fix” the person. They might use every technique they know, offer remedies, suggest dietary changes, and perform energy work. And while the client may find some temporary relief, the issue often returns. The practitioner can feel like a failure, even becoming frustrated with the client’s stubborn refusal to be fixed. Then, a moment of insight might strike when the client says something like, “I feel like my head is screaming, and no one is listening to the words.” Wow. That can stop a practitioner in their tracks. It reveals a focus on silencing the scream, rather than asking what it is trying to say. It shows how easy it is to treat a person’s head as a broken object, not as a sacred messenger.

But the cracks are where the light gets in. The cracks are where our humanity lives. The cracks are the entry points for grace.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Sacred Shift from Fixing to Feeling

The turning point for many doesn’t come from a lightning bolt moment or a dramatic spiritual awakening. It often comes quietly, in the stillness of meditation, after years of running. It is the simple, profound, and body-centered realization that all efforts to “fix” oneself are just a more sophisticated form of self-abandonment.

So many people treat parts of themselves as problems to be solved. Anxiety is a problem. Grief is a problem. The tension in the shoulders—that familiar weight of responsibility—is a problem. This is a state of standing apart from one’s own experience, judging it, trying to manage it, trying to glue it into a more acceptable shape.

The shift comes when we stop trying to fix and simply… turn toward. When we dare to ask the question: *What if this anxiety isn’t a flaw, but a messenger? What if this grief isn’t a wound, but a testament to my capacity for love? What if this tension is just stored energy, a story my body is waiting to tell?*

This is the beginning of true healing. It is the shift from the head—the land of analysis, judgment, and fixing—to the body, the sacred vessel of feeling, wisdom, and direct experience. Your body has never believed you are broken. It is always, *always* working toward wholeness, toward homeostasis, toward life. The symptoms we pathologize—the pain, the inflammation, the fatigue—are not punishments. They are love letters from a body that is desperately trying to get your attention, trying to communicate an unmet need or an unprocessed experience. The ache in your lower back might be a story about feeling unsupported. The tightness in your throat could be the vibrational signature of years of unspoken truth.

The Tao te Ching says, “Do you have the patience to wait until your mud settles and the water is clear?”

We are so often trying to stir the water, to filter it, to purify it, to make it something other than what it is. The invitation of the healing journey is to simply sit with the muddy water. To bring a compassionate, nonjudgmental presence to our own inner chaos, and to trust that with stillness and with love, the mud will settle. The clarity we seek is already there, beneath the turbulence of our own self-judgment.

This isn’t a passive process. It is an act of profound and courageous love. It is the practice of meeting the tight knot in your stomach with a soft breath. It is the willingness to feel the ache in your heart without needing it to go away. It is the choice to listen to the story your body is telling, rather than trying to silence its voice. This is the work of neuroplasticity in action. Every time you meet a sensation with compassion instead of fear, you are building a new road in your brain—a road of safety, of self-trust, of belonging to yourself. You are, in a very real sense, creating a new mind.

Here is a small practice. Right now, as you read this, allow your eyes to soften. Take a gentle breath. Now, scan your body and find one place that is calling for your attention. It doesn’t have to be a place of pain. It could be a warmth in your hands, a tingling in your feet, a tightness in your jaw. Just choose one spot. Now, bring your full, loving attention to that spot. Don’t try to change it. Don’t judge it. Just… be with it. Offer it your presence as you would offer a cup of tea to a dear friend. Breathe into it. Imagine your breath is a wave of warm, liquid light, washing through that area. What do you notice? Is there a color? A texture? A temperature? A memory? Stay with it for three more breaths. Now, gently ask the sensation, “What do you want me to know?” Don’t search for an answer with your mind. Just listen with your whole body. The answer may come as a word, an image, a feeling, or just a subtle shift. This. This is the practice. It is this simple, and this profound.

## A Love Letter to Your Wholeness

So, my beautiful friend, I invite you to lay down the glue. Let the fragments lie there, in the soft light of your own awareness. See them not as evidence of your brokenness, but as the sacred mosaic of your unique and precious life.

That part of you that is terrified? It is not a flaw; it is the keeper of your safety. Can you thank it for its fierce protection?

That part of you that carries so much sorrow? It is not a weakness; it is the measure of your profound connection to life. Can you honor its depth?

That part of you that rages with anger? It is not a monster; it is a life force that knows the meaning of justice and boundaries. Can you listen to its truth?

That part of you that feels numb and disconnected? It is not a void; it is a brilliant strategy for surviving the unsurvivable. Can you marvel at its ingenuity?

You are not broken. You are a universe. You contain stars and supernovas, stillness and storms, light and shadow. Wholeness isn’t about eradicating the shadow; it’s about turning to embrace it with love, knowing it is just as sacred as the light.

Your healing journey is not a project of self-improvement. It is a journey of self-remembrance. A remembering of the magnificent, unbreakable wholeness that has been your true nature all along. It is the realization that a precious object was never more beautiful than when its cracks were filled with golden light, telling the story of its fall and its rising. The Japanese have an art form for this: *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted or mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. As a philosophy, it treats breakage and repair as part of the history of an object, rather than something to conceal. The breaks are highlighted, celebrated. They are a testament to the object’s resilience, its journey. They make it more beautiful, not less.

This is you. You are a masterpiece of living kintsugi. Your cracks and fissures are where the divine light shines through most brightly. They are the map of your soul’s journey, and they are breathtakingly beautiful. The gold that fills your cracks is the love, the compassion, the awareness you bring to the places that have hurt. It is the courage you show every time you choose to feel instead of fix. It is the wisdom you gain from having been shattered and having gathered yourself back together, not as you were, but as who you are now—more spacious, more compassionate, more breathtakingly whole.

May you be gentle with yourself. May you trust the wisdom of your body. May you see your own beautiful, resilient, and perfectly imperfect self through the eyes of infinite love.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: A Guided Practice for Tuning Into Your Nervous System
teachings.title: A Guided Practice for Tuning Into Your Nervous System
teachings.summary: Susan offers a gentle, step-by-step practice for tuning into the nervous system, beginning with recognizing fight/flight/freeze reactions and treating the body as a wise, sensing companion. The guided exercise invites curiosity rather than fixing, teaching you to notice physical sensations, emotions, and habitual reactivity and to allow natural movement and discharge. Regular practice is presented as a compassionate way to build new pathways of presence and self-understanding.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
*~ An adapted excerpt from my book "Elevating Origins to Love"*

Have you ever noticed how your body seems to know things before your mind catches up?

I remember sitting in a café once, years ago, waiting for someone I hadn't seen in a long time. Everything looked perfectly fine — the sun was streaming through the window, my coffee was warm in my hands, the hum of conversation around me was gentle and ordinary. And yet, somewhere deep in my belly, something was tightening. A quiet constriction, almost imperceptible at first, like a fist slowly closing around something tender. My shoulders had crept up toward my ears without my noticing. My breath had become shallow, almost held.

Nothing had happened yet. But my body already knew.

This is the extraordinary intelligence of your nervous system — a vast, intricate web of communication that is constantly reading your environment, your memories, your relationships, and your inner landscape, all at once. It's working tirelessly on your behalf, even when you're completely unaware of it. And here's the thing that took me years to truly understand: learning to listen to this intelligence — really listen, with curiosity rather than judgment — is one of the most profound acts of self-compassion you will ever practice.


**The Architecture of Your Inner World**


When we are in the grips of a stress or defensive response, we truly feel alone. There is no sense of safety, no relaxation, no feeling of belonging to a community — except, perhaps, with those who share our exact experience in that exact moment. It's an alienating state, and we aren't meant to stay in it for very long. Essentially, it uses all our resources — our energy is entirely consumed by mounting a defense against whatever is threatening us so we can escape.

The three main reactions of the stress-activated nervous system are ones you've likely heard of: fight, flight, and freeze. But knowing their names and actually recognizing them in the living tissue of your own body are two very different things.

**Fight** is an aggressive, hot energy — a rising up. You feel as though people or situations are against you, and something within you must rise to meet them with force. Your jaw might clench. Your fists might tighten. There's a forward-leaning quality to it, an urgency that says, *I will not be overtaken.*

**Flight** is more like the prey animal suddenly bursting into motion to escape the lion bearing down on it. It's the desire to get out — to leave the room, the conversation, the relationship, the situation. Your legs might feel restless. Your eyes might dart toward exits. Everything in you says, *I need to get away from here.*

**Freeze** is perhaps the most misunderstood of the three. It's the deer caught in headlights — so overcome with overwhelm that you cannot speak, think, or move. It can look like numbness, dissociation, or a strange blankness that descends like fog. People sometimes mistake freeze for calm, but it's not calm at all. It's a kind of paralysis born from a nervous system that has decided the threat is too great to fight or flee from.

Once the threat is over, our optimal human blueprint — our natural wiring — is designed to return us to a state of relaxation, rejuvenation, reconnection, and restoration. In that state, you feel at ease with others, your body can repair and rest, and you naturally return to activities that interest or inspire you. Your creativity flows. Your heart opens. You remember who you are beyond the emergency.

But here's where it gets tricky — and this is where so many of us live without realizing it.


**When the Thermostat Gets Stuck**


Your nervous system is like a sensitive thermostat. It's constantly calibrating, constantly seeking to protect you. And this is a beautiful thing — it's the reason you pull your hand away from a hot stove before you've even consciously registered the heat. It's the reason you instinctively reach out to steady a child who's about to fall.

But this same protective mechanism can also cause you to experience significant difficulty with situations that don't actually pose a threat. A critical email from a colleague. A certain tone of voice from your partner. A news headline that echoes something painful from your past. Your thermostat reads these as danger — and suddenly you're in fight, flight, or freeze, your body flooded with the same chemistry it would produce if you were being chased by a predator.

The stress response doesn't distinguish between a tiger in the jungle and a difficult conversation with your mother. To your nervous system, threat is threat.

And when we don't understand this — when we don't realize that our body is responding to a perceived danger rather than an actual one — we can spend years, even decades, living in a state of chronic activation. Our shoulders permanently raised. Our digestion perpetually disrupted. Our sleep fractured. Our relationships strained by reactions that seem to come from nowhere and everywhere at once.

Learning more about your inner wiring and design, and tuning into your own experience of reality, can help you gain essential understanding that allows you to navigate your life with greater peace and confidence. Not by overriding your nervous system — that never works — but by developing a relationship with it. By becoming a compassionate witness to your own inner landscape.


**The Practice: Tuning Into Your Nervous System**


What I'm about to share with you is a practice I've guided many people through over the years, and it's one I return to myself again and again. It's deceptively simple — there's nothing to achieve, nothing to fix, nothing to get right. You're simply turning your attention inward and observing what's already happening.

**Before you begin:** Find a quiet place where you won't be disturbed. Don't do this while driving or anywhere you need to be alert to the external world. Give yourself at least twenty minutes. You deserve that.

**Step One: Arrive**

Sit quietly, away from distractions. Let your body settle into whatever position feels most natural. Take a few breaths — not forced or dramatic, just easy breaths that remind your body you're here.

**Step Two: Invite the Stressor**

Think of a stressful situation you are currently dealing with in your life. You don't need to choose the most overwhelming thing — something moderately activating is perfect. Let it come to mind gently, as though you're opening a door just a crack.

**Step Three: Turn Inward**

Close your eyes and turn your attention inside, into your body. What do you notice? Where do you notice things? What kind of physical sensations do you feel? How do you experience them? Get specific.

Perhaps there's a tightness in your chest. A heaviness in your stomach. A tingling in your hands. A constriction in your throat. Whatever you find, simply name it to yourself. *There's a tightness here. There's a heaviness there.*

**Step Four: Explore with Curiosity**

Now explore your sensations further. Describe them to yourself in more detail. Their quality — is it sharp or dull? Their density — is it thick or thin? Do they stay static or change? Do they remain in one spot or radiate outward? Do they connect to other parts of your body, or remain separate?

Don't try to change anything. Simply tune in and observe whatever physical sensations you experience when you think of this stressful situation. You are being a gentle detective of your own inner world.

**Step Five: Meet Your Emotions**

Now tune into any emotions you may be feeling. Very likely, these are quite present to you — maybe even easier to identify than the physical sensations. As you name your emotions, ask yourself: *What is the sensation of this particular emotion within my body?*

Fear might live in your belly. Anger might burn in your chest. Sadness might pool behind your eyes. Each emotion has a physical signature, a way it writes itself into your tissue. Be an observant detective of whatever is happening within you.

**Step Six: Observe the Cycle**

Keep your eyes closed and simply remain focused on your inner experience. Notice whether you are experiencing any reaction not only to the situation, but perhaps to your own physical and emotional reaction itself. What is happening within your physical chemistry? Your neurology?

This is a profound moment in the practice — the moment you realize that you are not just reacting to the stressor, but often reacting to your own reaction. Layer upon layer. And each layer is worthy of your attention.

**Step Seven: Allow Movement**

You may notice a desire to move or shift a part of your body. Go ahead — let your body do anything it wants to do. Shift. Stretch. Shake. Vibrate. These are your nervous system's natural ways of completing the stress cycle, of discharging the energy that has been mobilized. Remain keenly present to every aspect of your body's movements, and follow any changes that occur as a result.

**Step Eight: Return to the Present**

Now see if you can let the image of the situation, or whatever has been causing you stress, fade away a bit. Remain very present to your inner experience as you remember that this isn't actually happening anywhere other than in your body and mind right now. Bring yourself back to the here and now — to sitting in your chair, to this moment where there is no need for you to take any action or solve any problems.

Continue to notice your physical sensations, your emotions, and any thoughts running through your mind. Don't buy into them, but don't resist them either. You simply want to be fully present to whatever is happening inside, watching without any resistance.

Notice how things may be shifting. Perhaps the sense of danger or anger or tightness or constriction begins to lessen a bit. Remember — you are simply sitting here. No one is threatening or disturbing you in actuality. It's all been an inner journey, and now you are letting it go.

**Step Nine: Gently Close**

Take a few deep breaths and let them out slowly... slowly. Open your eyes and see if you can find something soothing or enjoyable to look at. Notice any further internal loosening or relaxing that may be taking place.

Ask yourself: *Have I fully let go of any of the stressful feelings I conjured up? How connected to other people and the world around me do I now feel?*


**What You May Have Discovered**


As you thought of the stressful situation, you likely noticed tightening or constriction in your body — maybe your stomach, chest, shoulders, neck, or head. You may have experienced some unpleasant emotions — fear, anger, panic, frustration. And your mind was probably telling you in no uncertain terms all the things wrong with this situation.

This is your nervous system doing exactly what it was designed to do. There is nothing wrong with you for experiencing any of this. Nothing at all.

But here is what I want you to sit with, gently: the energy you were emanating during that activated state — that contracted, defensive, vigilant energy — is the energy you carry into your relationships, your work, your parenting, your creative life, every time your thermostat gets triggered. It shapes how you feel about yourself. It colors how you perceive others. It determines, in ways both subtle and profound, the quality of your lived experience.

And the beautiful thing — the truly miraculous thing — is that simply by turning your attention toward it, simply by being present to it without trying to fix or change it, you begin to shift it. Not through force. Not through willpower. But through the gentle, revolutionary act of awareness itself.


**An Invitation**


I encourage you to return to this practice regularly — not as a task to complete, but as a conversation with yourself. Each time you do it, you'll notice something new. Each time, your nervous system will reveal another layer of its extraordinary intelligence. And each time, you'll be building new neural pathways — pathways of presence, of compassion, of the kind of deep self-knowing that no external circumstance can take from you.

Your body is not your enemy. It is your most faithful companion on this human journey. And when you learn to listen to it — truly listen — it will show you the way back to yourself.

*With infinite love and support on your journey,*
*Susan*

teachings.sourceTitle: A Healing Practice for Your Hands and Heart Connection
teachings.title: A Healing Practice for Your Hands and Heart Connection
teachings.summary: Susan invites a gentle somatic practice to reconnect the hands with the heart, framing the hands as both sensory instruments and energetic extensions of our capacity to give and receive. She names how protective nervous-system patterns can close that flow and offers mindful attention, self‑massage, and a heart‑to‑hand visualization as steps to re‑establish trust and aliveness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was sitting in a circle of women, many years ago, in one of my first explorations of shamanic healing. The teacher asked us to extend our hands, palms up, to the person next to us, but not to touch. Just to hold them there, an inch or so apart. I remember the absolute terror I felt. My hands began to tremble. To receive from a stranger? To be that open, that vulnerable? It felt… impossible. My hands wanted to curl into fists, to hide themselves away in my lap, to protect the tender, uncertain heart they were connected to.

It’s a complex business, being human. And so much of that business is conducted through our hands.

Our hands are how we first learn the world. They grasp, they hold, they explore. They build, they soothe, they create. They are the instruments of our doing, the agents of our will. But they are also profound organs of perception, constantly sending information back to our brain about texture, temperature, pressure, and safety. And they are, perhaps most importantly, the extensions of our heart. In the energetic anatomy of the body, the pathways run directly from the heart, down the arms, and into the palms of the hands. They are the instruments of love’s expression.

So what happens when that expression has been thwarted? When we’ve learned that it’s not safe to reach out, or that what we receive will be painful? What happens when our hands have been taught to clench in fear, to defend, to push away? The connection between the heart and the hands becomes… congested. Muted. We may feel a longing to connect, to give and receive love, but our very bodies hold the memory of past hurts. Our hands literally stay cold, “out of touch,” as the old wisdom says.

This isn’t a failing. It’s a brilliant survival strategy. Your nervous system, in its profound wisdom, created a pattern to keep you safe. But what was once a necessary protection can become a prison. The good news—the beautiful, miraculous news—is that these pathways are not fixed. Through conscious, gentle attention, we can begin to restore the flow. We can re-teach our hands how to open in trust, and in doing so, create a new neural pathway… one that says *it is safe to connect. It is safe to love.*

## The Wisdom of Open Hands

Think of the 27 intricate bones in each hand, the complex network of nerves and muscles. They are designed for exquisite sensitivity, for both strength and tenderness. When we are anxious or feel we can’t “handle” life, our hands often reflect that conflict. We might get eczema, an itching to *do* something different. Or our hands might feel perpetually cold, a sign of the energy having withdrawn from this primary place of connection.

To handle life beautifully isn’t about controlling it more tightly. It’s about balance, sensitivity, and trust. It’s about learning to hold life with open palms, allowing it to be what it is, rather than trying to force it into what we think it should be. This is not a passive act. It is an act of profound courage and presence. It is the beginning of allowing our hands to become, once again, instruments of grace.

What would it be like to feel that grace flow through you, into your hands, and out into the world? To trust the wisdom of your own touch? To feel the warmth of your heart in the center of your palms?

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Guided Practice for Your Hands and Heart

This practice is an invitation to come home to your hands. It’s a gentle exploration, not a task to be achieved. Find a quiet, comfortable space where you won’t be disturbed for 15-20 minutes. You can sit in a chair with your feet on the floor or on a cushion. Allow your hands to rest gently in your lap, palms facing up in a gesture of receiving.

**1. The Hand Meditation: Arriving in Presence**

Close your eyes, or soften your gaze. Bring your awareness to your breath, just noticing the gentle rise and fall of your chest or belly. No need to change it. Just be with it.

Now, bring your full, compassionate attention to your hands. Don’t move them, just… feel them. Notice the weight of them in your lap. Notice the air on your skin. Are they warm or cool? Can you feel a tingling, a buzzing, a sense of aliveness? You may not feel much at first, and that’s perfectly okay. This is simply an act of showing up. Of bringing your awareness to a part of you that may have been quietly waiting for your attention.

Stay here for a few minutes, just being with the simple, direct sensation of your hands. If your mind wanders, gently guide it back. *Here are my hands. Here I am.*

**2. Self-Massage: The Gift of Loving Touch**

Now, let’s introduce the gift of your own touch. Pick up one hand with the other. Hold it as you would hold a precious object. Look at it. See the lines, the textures, the story it tells.

Using the thumb of your opposite hand, begin to press gently into the palm of the hand you are holding. Make slow, deliberate circles. Explore the fleshy part at the base of your thumb, the center of your palm. If you find a tender spot, don’t force it. Just pause, breathe into it, and offer it your silent, loving attention. You might even whisper, *“It’s okay. I’m here.”*

Slowly, methodically, massage each finger, from its base to its tip. Squeeze it gently. Roll it between your thumb and forefinger. Pay special attention to the fingertips, which are so packed with nerve endings.

When you feel complete with the first hand, simply let it rest back in your lap. Pause for a moment to feel the difference between your two hands. Notice the warmth, the aliveness, the tingling in the hand that has just received such loving attention. Then, when you are ready, repeat the entire process with your other hand.

**3. Heart-Hand Visualization: Restoring the Flow**

Once both hands are resting in your lap again, bring your awareness to the center of your chest, to your heart space. Imagine a beautiful, warm light in the center of your heart. It could be any color that feels loving and healing to you—a soft rose, a warm gold, a gentle emerald green.

With each inhale, imagine this light growing a little brighter, a little warmer. With each exhale, imagine this warm light beginning to travel. Picture it flowing from your heart, down your shoulders, through your upper arms, past your elbows, and down your forearms.

Feel—or imagine feeling—this warm, loving energy pouring into your hands. Picture it filling your palms, swirling in the center of them, and then extending out into each and every finger. Your hands are now filled with the light and warmth of your own heart.

Sit with this feeling for a few moments. Your hands, resting in your lap, are now radiant vessels of your own love. This connection has always been here. We are just gently, patiently, reminding the body of its own truth.

**4. The Practice of Trusting Touch**

When you feel ready, slowly open your eyes. Pick up a simple object near you—a smooth stone, a soft piece of fabric, a warm mug. Hold it in your hands. Feel it with the new awareness you have cultivated. Notice its texture, its temperature, its weight. Explore it not just with your mind, but with the full sensory capacity of your hands, now connected to your heart.

This is how we begin. We start with ourselves. We offer ourselves the loving touch we may have longed for from others. We re-establish the safety and trust within our own being. From this place, our interactions with the world begin to transform. We can begin to “handle” life not with a clenched fist of control, but with the open, sensitive, and responsive grace of a heart-connected hand.

This is a practice you can return to anytime you feel disconnected, anxious, or overwhelmed. It is a coming home.

May you trust the wisdom in your hands. May you feel the infinite love of your own heart. And may you remember that you are a channel for that love, in all that you do and all that you are.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Your Heart: The First Declaration of Your Existence](/blog/heart-first-declaration)

**More on Hands:**

- [Handling Life: When Grip Becomes Grasp](/blog/hands-handling-life)

teachings.sourceTitle: What Your Resistance Is Trying to Tell You
teachings.title: What Your Resistance Is Trying to Tell You
teachings.summary: Susan reframes resistance as a messenger from the body rather than an enemy to be fought, inviting compassionate curiosity about what refusal or procrastination is protecting. She explains how the nervous system can trigger a freeze response, invokes the Tao image of water to suggest a flowing approach, and offers somatic practices—body scan, journaling, and movement—to listen, learn, and move forward gently.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We long for growth, for change, for a deeper connection to ourselves and the world around us. Yet, when the moment of transformation arrives, we often find ourselves… stuck. Frozen. That thing you keep avoiding? The conversation you cannot seem to have? The change you know you need to make but somehow never do? That, beloved one, is resistance. And it’s not your enemy. It is a messenger carrying vital information about what lies beneath. We are taught to fight resistance. To “push through” and “just do it.” But what if that’s the wrong approach entirely? What if, instead of a battle, we saw resistance as a sacred dialogue? A call from the deepest parts of ourselves to pause, to listen, and to understand. ## The Wisdom of the Body I remember when I was writing my first book. The desire was there, a burning fire in my heart. But every time I sat down to write, a wall would go up. My body would tense, my mind would go blank. I’d find any excuse to get up—make tea, do laundry, organize my bookshelf. For months, I was in a state of profound resistance. I berated myself for my lack of discipline, my procrastination. I was at war with myself. One afternoon, sitting in my garden, watching a bee move from flower to flower, a thought drifted in. *What if this isn’t laziness? What if this is a message?* So I stopped fighting. I sat with the feeling. I closed my eyes and asked my body: *What are you trying to tell me?* And the answer came, not in words, but in a wave of feeling—a deep, primal fear of being seen, of being judged, of not being good enough. My resistance wasn’t trying to stop me from writing; it was trying to protect me from a wound I hadn’t even realized was there. This is the wisdom of the body. Our nervous system, in its infinite intelligence, is wired for survival. When it perceives a threat—real or imagined—it activates a protective response. This can manifest as the classic “fight, flight, or freeze” response. Resistance is often a form of freeze. It’s the body’s way of saying, “Hold on. This doesn’t feel safe.” ## The Science of Stuck From a neuroscience perspective, resistance is a fascinating dance between the prefrontal cortex—the part of our brain responsible for planning and decision-making—and the amygdala, our brain’s ancient fear center. When we contemplate a change that feels threatening, the amygdala sounds the alarm, flooding our system with stress hormones. This can override the rational, goal-oriented thinking of the prefrontal cortex, leaving us feeling paralyzed. But here’s the beautiful part. We can learn to work with this process. By bringing mindful awareness to our resistance, we can begin to soothe the amygdala’s alarm bells. We can signal to our nervous system that we are safe, that we are not in immediate danger. This is the work of somatic healing—of learning to listen to the language of the body and respond with compassion and care. ## The Tao of Resistance The Tao Te Ching teaches us about the power of water. It does not resist; it flows. When it meets a boulder, it does not try to smash through it. It flows around it, over it, under it. In time, with gentle persistence, it wears the boulder smooth. > “The supreme good is like water, > which nourishes all things without trying to. > It is content with the low places that people disdain.” What if we could approach our resistance with the wisdom of water? Instead of seeing it as a boulder in our path, what if we saw it as part of the landscape of our being? What if we could flow with it, around it, learning from its shape and texture? What if we could be content with the “low places” it reveals to us—the fears, the wounds, the unmet needs? This is not a passive process. It is an active engagement with the truth of who we are. It requires courage, curiosity, and a deep well of self-compassion. It asks us to trade our battle armor for a listening heart. ## How to Listen So how do we begin this dialogue with our resistance? Here are a few gentle invitations: * **Body Scan:** Find a quiet place to sit or lie down. Close your eyes and bring your attention to your body. Notice any areas of tension, tightness, or discomfort. Don’t try to change anything. Just notice. Breathe into those sensations. Ask them: *What do you have to tell me?* * **Journaling:** Take out a pen and paper and write a letter to your resistance. Start with “Dear Resistance…” and see what flows. Ask it questions. Express your frustration, your curiosity, your willingness to listen. You might be surprised by the answers that emerge. * **Movement:** Sometimes, the body needs to speak in its own language. Put on some music and allow your body to move in whatever way feels right. Shake, stretch, dance, curl up in a ball. Let your body express the feeling of being stuck, and then, perhaps, the feeling of a tiny bit of release. Remember, dear one, this is a practice. It is a journey, not a destination. There will be days when you feel like you are flowing, and days when you feel like you are hitting a brick wall. And that’s okay. That’s all part of the tricky, beautiful, messy business of being human.

Discover what your body is telling you

And on the other side of that threshold is a deeper, more authentic, more integrated version of you, waiting to be born. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: When Nurturing Becomes Depletion: Breast Health and Boundaries
teachings.title: When Nurturing Becomes Depletion: Breast Health and Boundaries
teachings.summary: Susan shares Claire’s story to show how persistent breast pain and benign lumps can be read as the body’s message about chronic over-giving and unmet inner needs. The piece links nervous-system patterns formed in childhood to energetic stagnation in the breasts and offers a compassionate, practical self-mothering practice and boundary work as part of a larger healing path. Healing is framed as re-patterning the nervous system, learning to receive, and creating sustainable nourishment rather than blaming caregivers. The article emphasizes gradual, gentle change—small promises to oneself that, together with conventional medical care, support embodied recovery.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman I’ll call Claire came to me once, a successful graphic designer in her late forties, with a story that is achingly familiar. She arrived in my office, elegant and composed, but with a shadow of exhaustion behind her eyes that told a story of its own. She was a mother to three, a devoted wife, the go-to person in her circle of friends, the one who remembered birthdays and organized meal trains. She was, by all accounts, a pillar of strength, a nurturer. A giver. And she was in pain.

Her left breast had been troubling her for months. A dull, persistent ache that sometimes sharpened into a stabbing sensation. Doctors had found a cluster of cysts—benign, they assured her, nothing to *worry* about. But Claire was worried. It felt, she said, like a stone in her heart. A heavy, unmovable weight.

“I feel like I’m giving and giving,” she told me, her voice barely a whisper, “and there’s nothing left for me. It’s like I’m a well, and everyone is drinking from it, but the water level is getting dangerously low. I think I'm broken.”

It’s a tricky business, being human. And it is an especially tricky business to be a woman in a world that so often equates our worth with our capacity to give. To nurture. To mother. The breasts, in their very design, are the sacred symbol of this nourishment. They are the biological wellspring, the first source of comfort and life for a newborn. But what happens when the well runs dry? What happens when the act of nurturing becomes an act of self-depletion? This is not a sign of being broken; it is a sign that something is out of balance.

This is a conversation we must have. It’s a conversation about breast health that goes beyond mammograms and self-exams, and into the very heart of our relationship with ourselves, our energy, and our deepest patterns of connection.

## The Energetics of Nurturing

In my three decades of work as a healer, I have sat with so many women like Claire. Women with breast pain, with cysts, with mastitis, even with the terrifying diagnosis of cancer. And so often, the physical symptoms are a messenger, a communication from a part of the self that has been long ignored. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is sending a dispatch from the front lines of the soul. It is asking us to pay attention.

Our bodies are not separate from our lives. They are the living, breathing record of our experiences, our beliefs, our joys, and our sorrows. The neural pathways in our brain, those intricate webs of connection forged by years of repeated thoughts and behaviors, have a direct and profound impact on our biology. When we consistently operate from a pattern of over-giving—of putting everyone else’s needs before our own—we are, in essence, programming our nervous system for depletion. We are sending a constant signal to our cells that our own nourishment is a secondary concern, an afterthought. This isn't a conscious choice, but a deeply embedded pattern, often learned in childhood, that equates self-sacrifice with love and safety.

The breasts, being so intimately tied to the archetype of the mother and the energy of the heart, are often where this imbalance makes itself known. They are the energetic heart of our feminine nature. When we are constantly directing our life force outwards, mothering our partners, our children, our friends, our colleagues, without replenishing our own source, the energy in this sacred center can stagnate. It can become dense, heavy, and painful. The flow of life force, which should be a radiant, circulating current, becomes blocked.

Think of it this way: a healthy river is one that both receives water from its source and flows out into the world. If the river only flows out, without being replenished, it will eventually become a dry and barren bed. So it is with our own capacity to nurture. We are designed to be source-fed rivers, not stagnant ponds that are slowly drained. The act of giving is meant to be an overflow of a cup that is already full.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Hard Lumps and Uncried Tears

When Claire and I began to explore the landscape of her life, a deeper story emerged. A story of a mother who was critical and demanding, a story of a childhood where love felt conditional upon performance. Claire had learned, from a very young age, that her value lay in her ability to please others, to anticipate their needs, to be the “good girl.” This pattern, so deeply ingrained in her neural pathways, had become the unconscious operating system of her life. It was a brilliant survival strategy for a little girl, but a devastating one for a grown woman.

Her over-investment in others was not simply a generous impulse; it was a deeply rooted strategy for seeking the love and approval she had never fully received. And the pain in her breast? It was the physical manifestation of a lifetime of unmet needs. The cysts, those so-called “benign” lumps, were something else entirely when viewed through the lens of the body’s wisdom. They were crystallized grief. Hardened resentment. The unshed tears for the mothering she had never received, and the self-mothering she had never learned to give.

This is a profound teaching that the body offers us. Those hard lumps, whether they are diagnosed as cysts, fibroadenomas, or even tumors, can be seen as the physical embodiment of crystallized emotional energy. Grief, resentment, loss, a deep and abiding confusion towards our own mothers—these powerful emotions, when left unfelt and unexpressed, do not simply disappear. They take up residence in our tissues. They become the stones in our hearts, the aches in our breasts. The body, in its incredible intelligence, encapsulates the overwhelming emotion to protect the whole system, but it comes at a cost.

To heal, then, is not simply to remove the lump. It is to begin the sacred work of thawing the frozen grief. It is to create a safe space within ourselves to finally feel the anger, the sadness, the longing. It is to learn, perhaps for the first time, how to mother ourselves. How to offer ourselves the unconditional love, the gentle compassion, and the fierce protection that we have so freely given to others.

## A Practice for Self-Mothering

This work is not abstract. It is a practice, a daily turning towards oneself with love. If this story resonates with you, I offer you this simple practice. It is a way to begin to repattern your nervous system and to offer yourself the nurturing you so deeply deserve.

1.  **Find a quiet space.** Sit or lie down comfortably. Close your eyes and take three deep, slow breaths. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing a layer of tension.
2.  **Place your hands on your heart.** Feel the warmth of your own touch. This simple action sends a powerful signal of safety and love to your nervous system.
3.  **Acknowledge the giver.** Silently, or out loud, say: “I see how much you give. I see how hard you work to care for everyone around you. Thank you.” Feel the truth of these words.
4.  **Invite the receiver.** Now, gently ask: “What do *you* need right now?” Listen. Don’t judge or edit the answer. It might be a need for rest, for a walk, for a glass of water, for five minutes of silence. It might be a need to cry.
5.  **Make a promise.** Whatever the need is, make a small, tangible promise to yourself to meet it. Not tomorrow, not next week, but today. It could be as simple as, “I will take a 10-minute break this afternoon,” or “I will allow myself to feel my sadness tonight.”
6.  **Breathe into your heart.** Spend another minute just breathing, with your hands on your heart. Imagine you are breathing in pure, unconditional love, and breathing out any sense of unworthiness or depletion.

This practice, done regularly, begins to carve new neural pathways. It is an act of neuroplasticity in motion. You are teaching your body and your brain that you are worthy of your own care. You are becoming your own mother.

## Becoming the Source of Your Own River

Healing is not about blaming our mothers or rejecting our desire to nurture. It is about bringing our lives into balance. It is about recognizing that we cannot give what we do not allow ourselves to receive. It is about transforming the pattern of depletion into a pattern of radiant, sustainable nourishment.

So how do we begin? We begin by listening. We begin by turning our attention inwards, to the quiet whispers of our own bodies. What is the pain in your breast trying to tell you? What is the exhaustion behind your eyes asking for?

Perhaps it is asking for a boundary. A gentle “no.” A moment of rest. Perhaps it is asking for you to receive. To allow yourself to be held, to be supported, to be nourished by others. For many of us, receiving is far more vulnerable than giving.

For Claire, the journey of healing involved learning to say no, and learning to be okay with the discomfort that arose. It involved carving out non-negotiable time for herself, for walks in nature, for quiet contemplation. It involved grieving the mother she had always wanted and forgiving the mother she had, understanding that her mother, too, was likely caught in a lineage of depletion. It involved, most profoundly, learning to place her own hand on her heart and offer herself the same love and tenderness she had so freely given to her children.

It was not a quick fix. It was a slow and gentle unfolding. A re-patterning of her nervous system, a rewiring of her deepest beliefs about her own worth. But as she began to fill her own well, the pain in her breast began to subside. The cysts, on her next scan, were smaller. She began to feel, she said, like she was coming home to herself. The light returned to her eyes.

This is the invitation that our bodies extend to us, always. The invitation to come home. To release the burdens of the past, to reclaim our own sacred energy, and to become the source of our own ever-flowing river. It is a journey of a lifetime, and it is the most worthy one we can take.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Dis-heartened: When Giving Depletes and Receiving Feels Impossible](/blog/heart-disheartened)
- [Reclaiming Your Creative Fire: Healing Reproductive Patterns](/blog/reproductive-reclaiming-creative-fire)
- [A Breathwork Practice for Lung Healing and Vitality](/blog/lungs-breathwork-practice)

**More on Breasts:**

- [Healing the Mother Wound Through Your Body's Wisdom](/blog/breasts-healing-mother-wound)
- [The Sacred Symbol of Nurture: What Your Breasts Are Telling You](/blog/breasts-sacred-symbol-nurture)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
