teachings.sourceTitle: The Courage to Be Seen: Vulnerability as the Path to Authentic Power
teachings.title: The Courage to Be Seen: Vulnerability as the Path to Authentic Power
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider that true power arises from vulnerability and embodied presence rather than from performed strength or armor. She describes how social threat activates the nervous system, how chronic self-protection fragments life and drains energy, and points to simple body-based practices as a path back to authenticity, connection, and resilient power. The piece encourages moment-by-moment choices to show up as imperfect, alive, and seen.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We spend so much of our lives building—our careers, our families, our homes, our identities. We construct walls and assemble armor, hoping to keep ourselves safe, to present a version of ourselves to the world that is strong, capable, and unflawed. But the deepest truth, the one that whispers to us in the quiet moments, is that our most authentic power doesn’t live in the fortress. It lives in the open field. It lives in the courage to be seen. There is a particular kind of bravery that has nothing to do with swords or shields. It is the raw, tender courage of vulnerability—the willingness to stand in the full light of day, unadorned and utterly real. It’s the courage to let the carefully constructed masks dissolve and allow our true selves to be witnessed, in all our messy, magnificent, and unfinished humanity. This is not an easy path. It goes against so much of our conditioning. From a young age, we learn to hide the parts of ourselves we deem unacceptable. We learn to perform, to please, to perfect. The fear of judgment, of rejection, of not being enough—it’s a primal fear, wired into our nervous systems for survival. To be cast out from the tribe, in ancient times, was a death sentence. And so, our bodies, in their infinite wisdom, learned to scan for threats, to adapt, to ensure we belong. ## The Neuroscience of Hiding Our brains are magnificent, intricate organs of survival. When we perceive a threat—and for our nervous system, the threat of social judgment is very real—the amygdala, our internal alarm bell, sounds off. It triggers a cascade of stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, preparing us for fight, flight, or freeze. In the context of being seen, this often manifests as a kind of "freeze" or "flee." We withdraw. We go quiet. We make ourselves small. We hide our true thoughts, our deepest feelings, our most passionate dreams. We become a carefully curated version of ourselves. But this state of chronic self-protection comes at a cost. It consumes enormous amounts of energy. It creates a constant, low-grade hum of anxiety in our systems. It disconnects us from our own vitality, from the very life force that longs to express itself through us. We end up living in a state of fragmentation, where our inner world is at odds with the face we show the world. This, beloved one, is the source of so much of our quiet suffering. > To be nobody-but-yourself — in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else — means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight; and never stop fighting. > — e.e. cummings I remember a client I worked with years ago, a brilliant and successful woman who, on the surface, had it all. Yet, she came to me with a profound sense of emptiness. "I feel like I'm an actress in my own life," she confessed, her voice barely a whisper. "I'm so good at playing the part that I don't even know who I am anymore." Her journey was one of peeling back the layers, of dismantling the persona she had so expertly crafted. It was terrifying for her. There were tears. There were moments she wanted to retreat back into the familiar comfort of her performance. But slowly, painstakingly, she began to let herself be seen—first by me, then by her closest friends, and eventually, in her work and in the world. What emerged was a woman who was not just successful, but powerful in a way that was deeply authentic and radiantly alive. ## The Body as a Gateway to Truth Our bodies hold so much of this story. They are the faithful keepers of our unspoken truths, our suppressed emotions, our hidden fears. When we numb ourselves to our vulnerability, we also numb ourselves to the wisdom of the body. We might experience this as chronic tension in the shoulders, a knot in the stomach, a tightness in the jaw. These are not random aches and pains. They are messages. Your body is speaking to you, always. One of the most profound practices for cultivating the courage to be seen is to come home to the body. To learn its language. To listen to its whispers before they become screams. Place a hand on your heart right now. Feel the warmth of your own touch. Take a deep, slow breath and feel your belly expand. This simple act is a revolution. It is an act of returning. You are signaling to your nervous system that you are safe, that you are present, that you are here. From this place of embodied presence, we can begin to touch into the tender places. We can ask, "What am I afraid of right now?" and listen for the answer without judgment. We can feel the flutter of fear in our chest and, instead of turning away, we can breathe into it. We can offer it our compassionate presence. This is not about eliminating fear. It is about expanding our capacity to be with it. It is in this compassionate holding of our own experience that we find the strength to be vulnerable. ## Vulnerability as Authentic Power The Tao Te Ching speaks of the power of water. It is soft, yielding, and yet it can overcome the hardest of substances. This is the nature of authentic power. It is not rigid or forceful. It is fluid, adaptable, and rooted in truth. Vulnerability is this kind of power. When we allow ourselves to be truly seen, we give others the gift of our authenticity. We create a space of permission for them to be real, too. Our courage becomes a ripple, a quiet invitation for others to lay down their own armor. This is how we build true intimacy, how we forge connections that are not based on performance, but on the shared ground of our humanity. It’s the artist sharing their unfinished painting. The leader admitting they don’t have all the answers. The friend confessing their loneliness. These are the moments that break us open, that shatter the illusion of separation and connect us heart to heart. This is where the magic lives. This is where we remember that we are not alone in our struggles, our fears, or our longings. Being seen is not a one-time act, but a moment-by-moment practice. It is a choice we make over and over again. The choice to speak our truth, even when our voice shakes. The choice to show our imperfections. The choice to let our hearts be known. It is the choice to stand in the open doorway of our own being and let the light stream in, illuminating everything. Yes, it is a tricky business, this being human. It is messy and unpredictable and often heartbreaking. But it is also breathtakingly beautiful. The courage to be seen is the courage to fully inhabit that beauty, to claim your place in the world not as a perfected ideal, but as a living, breathing, evolving work of art. It is the path to a power that no one can ever take from you—the power of your own authentic, undeniable self.

teachings.sourceTitle: Whole-Hearted Living: A Practice for Filling Your Own Cup
teachings.title: Whole-Hearted Living: A Practice for Filling Your Own Cup
teachings.summary: Susan offers a gentle, embodied practice to restore the balance between giving and receiving by tending the heart. Grounded in the metaphor and physiology of the heart as both receiver and giver, the article guides a five-to-ten minute Heart-Filling Practice to cultivate appreciation, receiving breath, and new neural pathways of self-compassion. The invitation is practical and sustainable: small daily acts of inner attention transform depleted giving into wholehearted, sustainable care.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember a time, years ago, standing in my kitchen at the end of a long day. The phone had been ringing with clients in need, my children were small and had their own endless wells of need, and the house itself seemed to be asking for something—tidying, organizing, tending. I felt a profound sense of emptiness, a hollow ache in my chest that was more than just fatigue. It was the feeling of being a vessel that had been poured out, with nothing left for myself. I felt like a dry riverbed, cracked and empty, where a flowing river once was. The world had received my water, but my own source was running dangerously low.

Have you ever felt that way? That your own heart—the very center of your being—is the last one to receive care? It’s a tricky business, this human life. We are taught so much about giving, about being of service, about showing up for others. And these are beautiful, essential things. But we are rarely taught about the sacred art of receiving, of filling our own cup so that our giving can be a genuine overflow, not a depletion.

In the miraculous journey of our becoming, from two cells to a fully formed being, the heart is the first declaration. Before the intricate universe of the brain is formed, before our limbs take shape, the heart begins its steady, rhythmic pulse. It is the central sun of our physiological being, and its primary action is a perfect, life-sustaining balance—a two-way pump. It receives, and it gives. It draws in, and it sends out. This is its fundamental wisdom. A wisdom we often forget in our eagerness to please, to serve, to be deemed 'good'. We forget that the giving and the receiving are not two separate acts, but two faces of the same coin. One cannot exist without the other. A heart that only gives will eventually have nothing left to offer. A heart that only receives becomes stagnant and isolated. The dance is in the balance.

When this balance is lost, the body, in its infinite intelligence, sends us a message. Issues with the heart often point to a deep, often unconscious, belief that we must sacrifice ourselves to be worthy of love and existence. We over-give, we people-please, we put ourselves last, all in an attempt to justify our place here. The heart, feeling this imbalance, can begin to protest. It’s not a punishment. It’s a desperate plea for attention, a call to return to its original wisdom: you must fill yourself to be a true and sustainable channel of love.

## The Practice of Filling Your Own Cup

Beginning to restore this balance is not a grand, complicated affair. It doesn’t require you to abandon your responsibilities or stop caring for the people you love. It begins quietly, inwardly, with a small, consistent practice of turning your attention and your compassion toward yourself. It’s about consciously creating new neural pathways, teaching your nervous system that it is not only safe to receive, but essential.

What would it be like to dedicate just a few minutes each day to your own heart? To intentionally fill your own cup before you pour for anyone else? Here is a simple, gentle practice I recommend to my clients—and practice myself—to begin this journey. It is not about adding another 'should' to your already long list. It is an invitation to come home to yourself, even for a few moments. I call it the Daily Heart-Filling Practice, and it is a radical act of self-love in a world that constantly asks us to look outside of ourselves for validation.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Guided Practice for Heart Healing

Find a quiet place where you can be undisturbed for five to ten minutes. Sit comfortably in a chair with your feet flat on the floor, or on a cushion on the ground. Allow your hands to rest gently on your thighs.

**Step 1: Find Your Stillpoint**

Close your eyes, or soften your gaze toward the floor. Take three slow, deep breaths. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing the busyness of your day… the to-do lists… the conversations… the worries. Just for this moment, let them go. Feel the weight of your body in the chair, the support of the earth beneath your feet. You are here. You are present. There is nothing else you need to do right now. Give yourself permission to fully arrive in this moment, in this body. It is a sanctuary, a safe harbor from the storms of life. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest with each breath. This is the rhythm of peace.

**Step 2: The Heart-Hand Connection**

Now, gently take your right hand and place it over the center of your chest, over your heart. Take a moment to simply feel the contact. The warmth of your palm against your body. You might feel the subtle movement of your breath, or even the faint, steady beat of your heart beneath your hand. This is the rhythm of your life. It has been with you from the very beginning, a faithful drumbeat in the symphony of your existence. Simply be with it for a few moments. No judgment, no agenda. Just feeling. Let the sensation of your own life force, your own aliveness, fill your awareness. It is a miracle, this beating heart.

**Step 3: The Appreciation Current**

Keeping your hand on your heart, bring to mind one thing about yourself that you can appreciate in this moment. It doesn’t have to be a grand accomplishment. Perhaps it’s the strength in your hands, the resilience that got you through a difficult day, your ability to listen to a friend, or simply the kindness you showed to a stranger.

Once you have it, allow yourself to *feel* the appreciation. Let the feeling be a warm, gentle current flowing from your mind, down into your chest, and out through your palm into your own heart. You are sending a wave of pure appreciation back to its source. Stay with this feeling for a minute or two. If other thoughts intrude, gently guide your focus back to the feeling of appreciation, to the warmth in your chest.

**Step 4: The Receiving Breath**

Now, shift your focus to your breath, but with a new intention. As you inhale, I want you to focus on the sensation of *receiving*. You are not just taking in air; you are receiving the gift of life force, of nourishment, of energy from the world around you. Feel your lungs gently expand, your chest softly rise. This is for you.

As you exhale, simply let go. Release the breath without effort. The inhale is for receiving, the exhale is for release. Continue this for a few cycles of breath, your full awareness on the gentle, life-giving act of receiving. You don’t have to earn it. You only have to allow it.

**Step 5: The Gentle Return**

When you feel ready, slowly release your attention from your breath. Let your hand rest back on your thigh. Sit for another moment in the stillness, noticing any shifts in your body, your energy, or your state of being. You might feel calmer, warmer, or more present. Whatever you feel is perfect. When you are ready, gently open your eyes, bringing your awareness back to the room.

## Living from a Full Heart

This practice, though simple, is deeply transformative when done consistently. It is a way of carving out a new neural pathway in your brain—a pathway of self-compassion, self-appreciation, and receiving. It is a declaration to your body, to your entire being, that you are worthy of your own care. And your body will listen. It is always listening. Every thought, every emotion, every intention creates a cascade of chemical and electrical signals that ripple through your entire system. When you consistently offer yourself compassion and appreciation, you are literally re-wiring your nervous system for safety, for connection, and for love. You are becoming a safe haven for yourself.

Living from a full heart changes everything. It doesn’t mean you stop giving, but the quality of your giving transforms. It comes from a place of abundance and genuine desire, rather than a sense of obligation or a desperate attempt to prove your worth. It becomes a joyful overflow, not a painful sacrifice. You will find you have *more* energy, *more* patience, and *more* love to share, because you are no longer running on empty.

This is the heart’s deepest wisdom. It is not selfish; it is sustainable. It is the foundation of a life that is not just about surviving, but about thriving in wholeness, in connection, and in love.

May you have the courage to fill your own cup, to tend to your own beautiful heart, and to know, in your bones, that you are worthy of all the love you so freely give to others.

teachings.sourceTitle: A Movement Practice for Hip Freedom and Grounded Stability
teachings.title: A Movement Practice for Hip Freedom and Grounded Stability
teachings.summary: Susan invites a compassionate, slow approach to freeing the hips and grounding the legs, framing tightness as meaningful communication rather than a flaw. The article offers a short, gentle movement sequence — grounding, hip circles, intuitive dance, a forward fold, and rest — and encourages small, consistent acts of attention to create new, safer neural pathways. The tone emphasizes listening, non‑forceful curiosity, and the body’s innate capacity for renewed fluidity and stability.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I've learned to trust the body's timing, even when my mind is screaming for a faster resolution.

I remember a client, years ago, a woman with a brilliant mind and a heart full of poetry, who told me her hips felt like they were encased in concrete. “It’s like I’m dragging this ancient history around with me,” she said, her hands resting on her thighs. “I want to move forward, I want to dance, but I can’t seem to find the rhythm.”

So many of us know this feeling. A deep, persistent tightness in the hips, a sense of being ungrounded, a feeling of instability in the very foundation of our being—our legs. We sit for hours, curled over computers, our bodies unconsciously folding into a posture of protection. We brace ourselves against the relentless pace of life, the endless demands on our time and energy. We hold, clench, and tighten, often without even realizing it. And our hips… our beautiful, powerful hips… they become the silent keepers of our unspoken stories, the storehouse of our unfelt emotions. They remember everything.

In the language of the body, the hips and legs are our foundation for the dance of life. They are our ultimate grounding rods, the very structures that give us both stability and mobility. They are meant to be our connection to the earth, our source of steadfast support, but also the initiators of our movement through the world. When we have issues here—stiffness, pain, a feeling of being disconnected—it’s often a mirror for an inflexibility in our approach to life. We may feel we don’t have a “leg to stand on” in our convictions, or we may be rigidly holding to old patterns, afraid to step into the unknown. The irony is that the hip joint, a magnificent ball-and-socket, is designed to move in every direction. It is built for fluidity, for circles, for expansion.

So how do we reclaim this innate freedom? How do we melt the concrete and rediscover our flow? It begins not with force, but with listening. It begins with the radical act of turning toward our bodies with compassion and curiosity, and offering them the one thing they have been craving all along: gentle, loving movement.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger

Before we move, we must first understand. Your body is not your enemy. That tightness is not a flaw; it is a communication. It is a sacred message from your deepest self. For years, perhaps decades, your nervous system has been learning a particular pattern of holding. In response to stress, to fear, to sitting in a chair for eight hours a day, it has created neural pathways of tension. It has learned that clenching the hip flexors is a way to stay safe, to brace for impact.

But here is the beautiful truth, a truth confirmed by the ever-evolving field of neuroscience: our brains are plastic. Our neural pathways are not fixed. We can, with gentle and conscious attention, create new pathways. We can teach our bodies a new language—a language of release, of safety, of freedom. A movement practice is not about forcing your body into submission. It is about entering into a loving dialogue with it. It is about sending new information, new signals of safety, up the spinal cord to the brain, letting your entire system know that it is safe to let go. It is safe to be fluid. It is safe to be grounded *and* free.

This is not about “fixing” yourself. You are not broken. You have never been broken. This is about coming home to the wisdom that already lives within you. It’s about recognizing that the body’s deepest impulse is always toward healing and wholeness. Our work is simply to create the conditions for that impulse to flourish. The hips, in many spiritual traditions, are considered the seat of our emotions, particularly the deep, primal emotions of fear and grief. When we experience trauma, or when we consistently suppress our feelings, that energy can become stagnant, creating the physical sensation of tightness and restriction. By bringing gentle movement and loving awareness to this area, we are not just stretching muscles; we are tenderly coaxing these stored emotions to the surface, allowing them to be seen, felt, and finally, released.

## A Gentle Practice for Hip & Leg Freedom

Find a quiet space where you can be undisturbed for fifteen or twenty minutes. Wear comfortable clothing. You can put on some soft, instrumental music if you like, or simply enjoy the silence. This is your time. A sacred appointment with your own body.

> **Step 1: Grounding and Arriving**
> Stand with your feet hip-width apart. Soften your knees. Feel the soles of your feet making contact with the floor. Imagine roots growing down from your feet, deep into the earth, anchoring you. Take three slow, deep breaths. With each inhale, imagine drawing energy up from the earth into your legs. With each exhale, release any tension, any holding, any story that you are carrying in your hips and legs. Just let it drain down, down into the earth. Simply be here, now.

> **Step 2: Awakening the Hips with Circles**
> Place your hands on your hips. Gently, slowly, begin to make circles with your hips. Imagine you are drawing a circle on the floor with your tailbone. Start small, and as you feel more comfortable, allow the circles to become larger. There is no right or wrong way to do this. Just feel the movement in your hip joints. Notice any areas of tightness or restriction, and breathe into them. Don’t force anything. Just invite the movement. After a minute or two, reverse the direction of the circles. Feel the ball of the femur rotating in the socket of the hip. This is a movement of pure nourishment for the joint.

> **Step 3: The Dance of Intuition**
> Now, let go of any structure. Allow your body to move in whatever way it wants to. Maybe you sway from side to side. Maybe you bend your knees and bounce gently. Maybe you want to stretch your arms to the sky. This is not a performance. No one is watching. Let your body’s innate wisdom guide you. If a part of you feels stiff, bring your awareness there and gently invite it to move. This is a dance of deep listening. What does your body want to express? Let it speak through movement. Let it be a meditation in motion.

> **Step 4: Releasing into Flexibility**
> After a few minutes of free movement, come to a comfortable seat on the floor. Extend one leg out in front of you, and bring the sole of your other foot to your inner thigh. Gently, leading with your heart, fold forward over your extended leg. Only go as far as you feel a gentle stretch. This is not about touching your toes. It’s about breathing into the back of your leg—your hamstring. With each inhale, find a little more length in your spine. With each exhale, soften and release. Stay here for five to ten breaths, then gently switch sides. This is an act of profound kindness to your body.

> **Step 5: Integration and Rest**
> Finally, lie down on your back. Let your feet fall open naturally. Rest your arms by your sides, palms facing up. Close your eyes. This is a moment of pure integration. Feel the energy you have stirred up settling in your body. Notice any new sensations of warmth, tingling, or spaciousness in your hips and legs. You don’t need to do anything at all. Simply rest. Allow your body to absorb the nourishment of this practice. Stay here for at least two to three minutes, simply breathing and being.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Weaving Freedom into Your Day

How do you begin to integrate this into your life? You don’t need to set aside an hour every day. The body responds beautifully to small, consistent acts of love. Perhaps you make a few hip circles while you wait for your tea to brew in the morning. Perhaps you take a moment to feel your feet on the earth before you step into a challenging meeting. Perhaps you put on a favorite song in the evening and allow yourself a two-minute dance of intuition in your living room.

This is a practice of remembering. Remembering that your body is a sacred vessel. Remembering that you are designed for both stability and flow. Remembering that you have the power to create new pathways, not just in your brain, but in your very experience of being alive.

Your foundation is not made of concrete. It is made of living, breathing tissue, infused with consciousness and wisdom. It is ready to support you, to ground you, and to help you dance your unique and beautiful dance through this life. The journey to hip and leg freedom is not a linear one. There will be days of openness and days of tightness. The invitation is to meet it all with the same gentle, loving attention. To keep showing up for your body, to keep listening to its whispers, and to trust in its profound capacity for healing and transformation.


---

teachings.practiceInvitation: Find 10–15 minutes in a quiet space. Stand with feet hip‑width and soft knees; take three slow, grounding breaths imagining roots from your feet into the earth. Place hands on hips and make slow hip circles for one to two minutes, then reverse. Allow two to three minutes of free, intuitive movement—sway, bounce, or stretch as feels natural—then sit and do a single gentle forward fold on each side (five breaths), finishing by lying on your back for two to three minutes of rest. Move gently, stop if you feel sharp pain, and consult a healthcare provider if you have recent injuries or medical concerns.
sensitiveContentNotes: This piece references stored emotions, trauma, and grief in the body; movement can sometimes stir strong feelings. You have full permission to pause the practice at any time.
If the practice brings up intense emotional material, consider reaching out to a qualified somatic therapist, counselor, or trusted support person rather than working through it alone.

If you have a recent injury, surgery, chronic condition, or are under medical care, consult your healthcare provider before trying new movement practices. This guidance complements but does not replace professional medical advice.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Ripple Effect: How Your Healing Changes Everything Around You
teachings.title: The Ripple Effect: How Your Healing Changes Everything Around You
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to see personal healing as a force that reshapes relationships and the wider field around us. Using a client's somatic story alongside neuroscience (neuroception) and Taoist imagery of water, she shows how tending body-held pain and calming the nervous system quietly creates a ripple effect that makes others feel safer and more alive. Healing is framed as both intimate work and a generous contribution to family, community, and future generations.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We walk around, carrying our histories in our cells, our stories in the very way we hold our shoulders. We believe we are islands, contained and separate, our inner worlds a secret known only to us. But what if that’s not the whole story? What if every internal shift, every quiet moment of self-forgiveness, every wound we bravely tend to, sends out ripples that touch everything and everyone around us? I remember a client I worked with years ago—let’s call her Clara. She came to me a woman folded in on herself. Her voice was a whisper, her shoulders were perpetually hunched, as if bracing for a blow. She spoke of a deep, pervasive sense of wrongness, a feeling that she was taking up too much space in the world. For months, we sat together. We didn’t talk about grand transformations or "fixing" her. We simply sat with the sensations in her body. The tightness in her chest, the knot in her stomach, the ache in her throat. We listened. Not with the ears, but with the whole of our beings. We listened to what her body had been trying to tell her for decades. One day, she came into a session and there was a new light in her eyes. She told me about a moment in her garden. She’d been weeding, her hands in the cool, dark earth, and she’d unearthed a tiny, perfectly formed snail shell. She held it in her palm, marveling at its intricate spiral. And in that moment, she said, she felt a profound sense of connection. Not just to the snail, or the garden, but to everything. She realized that her own "wrongness" was a story, a tightly held belief that had been passed down through her family line like a fragile, unwanted heirloom. In that moment of pure, embodied presence, the story began to unravel. It wasn’t a lightning bolt. It was quieter, more profound. A gentle unwinding. But the effects… the effects were anything but small. A few weeks later, she told me her husband had started painting again, a passion he’d abandoned years ago. Her teenage son, usually sullen and withdrawn, had started joining her for walks in the evening. Her colleagues at work commented on a new sense of calm and confidence she exuded. Clara hadn’t *done* anything to them. She hadn’t given them advice or tried to change them. She had simply, bravely, begun to heal herself. And in doing so, she had changed the very air around her. This, beloved one, is the ripple effect. It’s not a metaphor. It’s physics. It’s neuroscience. It’s ancient wisdom whispered down through the ages. ## The Science of Interconnection Neuroscience is beginning to catch up with what mystics have always known: we are wired for connection. Our nervous systems are not self-contained. They are constantly, unconsciously, in dialogue with the nervous systems of those around us. This is the principle of neuroception, a term coined by Dr. Stephen Porges. Our bodies are constantly scanning our environment for cues of safety or danger, and we are co-regulating with each other all the time. When you are in the presence of someone who is calm and grounded, your own nervous system naturally begins to settle. When you are with someone who is anxious and agitated, you may find yourself feeling a similar unease. When you do your own healing work—when you learn to soothe your own nervous system, to hold your own pain with compassion, to release the energetic charge of old traumas—you become a beacon of safety for others. You don’t have to say a word. Your very presence becomes a permission slip for others to feel more at ease, more authentic, more themselves. You become a source of co-regulation for your family, your friends, your community. You become the still point in the turning world. ## The Wisdom of the Tao The Tao Te Ching speaks of this in its own poetic way. It tells us that the supreme good is like water, which "benefits all things and does not compete." Water doesn’t force its way. It flows, it yields, it nourishes. It finds the lowest places, the places that are most in need of its life-giving presence. And in doing so, it changes the entire landscape. > "The gentle overcomes the rigid. > The slow overcomes the fast. > The weak overcomes the strong." When we heal, we are not engaging in an act of aggression against our pain. We are not "fighting" our demons. We are, instead, becoming like water. We are learning to be with what is, to hold it with a gentle, yielding compassion. We are allowing the rigid, frozen places within us to soften and melt. And as we do, we create a space for something new to emerge. We create a space for love to flow—not just for ourselves, but for everyone we touch. ## Your Healing is a Gift to the World It’s a tricky business, this healing journey. It can feel so personal, so private. We can get lost in the labyrinth of our own stories, our own pain. We can believe that our struggles are a burden, a sign of our own inadequacy. But what if we could hold it all with a different kind of awareness? What if we could see that our healing is not just for us? What if we could understand that every step we take toward our own wholeness is a step toward the healing of the world? Think of it. Every time you choose to respond with compassion instead of reactivity, you are breaking a cycle of ancestral pain. Every time you allow yourself to feel your grief, your anger, your fear, without judgment, you are creating a more emotionally honest and resilient world. Every time you choose to forgive yourself for your imperfections, you are giving others permission to do the same. Your healing is not a selfish act. It is the most generous, most radical, most world-changing thing you can do. It is a gift. A gift to your children, to your partner, to your friends, to your community. A gift to the ancestors who came before you, and to the generations that will come after. You do not heal alone, dear one. You are part of a vast, interconnected web of being. And when you tend to your own small corner of the garden, you are helping to make the whole world bloom.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Breathing Freely: Transcending Respiratory Patterns
teachings.title: Breathing Freely: Transcending Respiratory Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to explore how habitual breathing patterns—often formed in childhood or in response to stress—shape our nervous system, sense of safety, and capacity to receive life. She describes paradoxical, shallow breathing as a protective imprint, discusses how we can unconsciously carry others’ respiratory and emotional burdens, and offers a simple, compassionate practice to begin reclaiming the full, nourishing breath. The piece frames breathing as both physiological and symbolic: a bridge between effort and surrender, and a pathway to resourcing the nervous system and reclaiming space in the world.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember being six years old, sitting at the bottom of the public swimming pool, seeing how long I could hold my breath. The world went silent and blue. My own heartbeat was a drum in my ears. There was a strange peace in the pressure, a sense of control in the deliberate deprivation. Then, the inevitable, urgent burning in my chest, the desperate kick to the surface, the explosive gasp that was both relief and a kind of surrender. I was the master of my own little underwater kingdom, until I wasn’t.

It’s a complex business, being human. We learn so early to control our own life force. We hold our breath in moments of fear, clenching against the perceived threat. We breathe shallowly through days of low-grade anxiety, a subconscious strategy to feel less, to not be overwhelmed. We forget that the breath is a current, a tide that is meant to flow in and out, unimpeded. We treat it like a possession to be managed, when it is, in fact, a gift to be received.

The lungs, in their profound wisdom, are the most intimate interface between our inner world and the external atmosphere. With every single inhalation, we draw the outside world into the deepest parts of ourselves. And with every exhalation, we release a part of ourselves back into the world. It is a constant, sacred exchange. A conversation. But what are we saying?

## The Bridge Between Two Worlds

Your lungs are the perfect metaphor for the dance between effort and surrender. The breath is one of the few systems in the body that operates both automatically and consciously. It is a bridge between the unconscious and the conscious, the voluntary and the involuntary. You can hold your breath, as I did as a child, asserting your will. You can consciously slow it down, sending a signal of safety directly to your nervous system. And yet, the moment you stop paying attention, it continues its steady, rhythmic work without any help from you at all. It breathes you.

This is a very good thing to know. Because it shows us that we are designed for both doing and being, for effort and for grace. So many of us get stuck on one side of that bridge. We live in a state of perpetual, low-grade clenching. Our shoulders are tight, our jaws are set, and our breathing is a shallow, almost imperceptible movement in the very top of our chests. This is called 'paradoxical breathing,' and it's incredibly common. Instead of the diaphragm contracting and the belly expanding on the inhale, the chest and shoulders rise, and the belly might even pull in. It's an inversion of the natural mechanics of respiration.

This kind of breathing is the physiological signature of the sympathetic nervous system—the “fight or flight” response. It’s a state of readiness, of vigilance. And while it’s essential for genuine emergencies, many of us have neural pathways so deeply grooved that we live there 24/7. The brain, in its effort to protect us, learns from experience. If our early environment was chaotic or threatening, the brain creates a 'program' for survival that includes shallow breathing, a hyper-vigilant nervous system, and a tendency to brace against life. We are perpetually waiting for the other shoe to drop, and our bodies are paying the price.

When we breathe shallowly, we are sending a constant, subtle signal of danger to our own bodies. We are, in essence, telling ourselves that it is not safe to fully arrive in the present moment. It is not safe to take up space. It is not safe to receive the full gift of life. Depression and anxiety are not moral failings; they are often the logical conclusion of a nervous system that has been running on high alert for far too long. The body, in its wisdom, begins to shut down. It feels suffocated, not by a lack of air, but by a lack of safety.

## The Weight of What We Carry

We don’t just carry our own burdens. We are porous, energetic beings, and we often take on the emotions, beliefs, and fears of those around us, especially in childhood. We learn to constrict our own breathing to match the emotional atmosphere of our homes. If there was unspoken tension, we learned to make ourselves small and quiet. If there was explosive anger, we learned to hold our breath, bracing for impact. These patterns become so ingrained that we carry them into our adult lives, long after the original circumstances have changed.

We carry the weight of our ancestors’ traumas in our DNA. We carry the collective grief of the world in our hearts. And we carry it all in our lungs. We feel a responsibility to hold it all, to manage it all, to fix it all. And so we hold our breath, believing on some deep, unconscious level that if we just try hard enough, we can keep everything from falling apart. But the lungs are not designed for holding. They are designed for exchange. For release.

What would it be like to release what is not yours to carry? To take a deep, conscious breath and, on the exhale, to intentionally let go of the fear that was never yours to begin with? To release the grief you’ve been holding for your mother, for your father, for your entire lineage? I once worked with a woman, a successful lawyer, who suffered from chronic bronchitis. She came to me after her third round of antibiotics in a single year. As we talked, a story emerged. Her father had been a deeply anxious man, a chain-smoker who died of emphysema when she was a teenager. She had been his primary caregiver, and his labored breathing was the soundtrack of her adolescence. On some level, she had taken on his struggle to breathe as her own. Her body was playing out a story of loyalty and love, but it was suffocating her.

This is not an act of abandonment. It is an act of profound love. It is a recognition that your primary responsibility is to your own life force, to the sacred breath moving through you. It is about honoring the love you have for others without taking on their physical and emotional patterns as your own. You can love them, and still breathe.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Transcendent Power of the Full Breath

You deserve to inflate with the full gift of life. You deserve to draw in inspiration—*in-spirit-ation*—completely and without reservation. You deserve to feel the delicious, expansive stretch of your own ribs, to feel your belly soften and rise, to feel the air fill every last corner of your being. This is your birthright.

To breathe freely, deeply, and fully is a radical act of self-love. It is a declaration that you are worthy of nourishment. It is a claiming of your space in the world. It is a conscious choice to shift from a state of threat to a state of trust. With each conscious, deep breath, you are literally rewiring your own nervous system. You are strengthening the neural pathways of the parasympathetic response—the “rest and digest” state. You are toning your vagus nerve, that beautiful, wandering nerve that connects your brain to your heart, your gut, and your lungs, and tells them that you are safe.

Let’s try something, right now. You don’t have to close your eyes unless you want to. Just for a moment, bring your awareness to your breath, without changing a thing. Simply notice it. Is it shallow or deep? Fast or slow? Is your belly moving, or just your chest? There is no judgment here. Just gentle, curious awareness.

Now, place a hand on your low belly. And as you inhale, gently invite the breath to travel all the way down to your hand. Feel your belly soften and expand into your palm. And as you exhale, just let it all go. A soft, gentle sigh. Let’s do that again. A long, slow, deep inhalation, filling the belly, feeling the ribs expand. And a long, slow, complete exhalation, releasing everything. One more time. The deepest, most nourishing breath you’ve taken all day. And a full, complete, letting-go exhale.

Wow. What do you notice? Perhaps a little more space. A little more quiet. A little more *you*. This is the beginning of the conversation. This is how you start to build a new relationship with your breath, and with yourself. A relationship based not on control, but on trust. Not on fear, but on love.

To transcend the old, restrictive patterns of the breath is not about forcing anything. It is about creating the conditions for release. It is about making it safe for your body to let go of the armor it has been carrying for so long. It is about reminding yourself, breath by breath by breath, that you are held. You are supported. You are safe. And you are so, so worthy of the air you breathe.


---

teachings.title: The Belly of Trust: When Your Stomach Holds What You Cannot Digest
teachings.summary: Susan explores the stomach as a sacred messenger that stores not only food but emotional and ancestral material, illustrating how early experiences and lineage shape our capacity to receive. She describes how somatic awareness, gentle practices, and neuroplasticity can begin to rewire the enteric nervous system and restore trust in nourishment and life. Through clinical vignettes and personal reflection, the piece invites readers to attend to their belly as an ally in healing.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The phone rang at 2:47 AM, pulling me from deep sleep. My friend Maria's voice was tight with panic: "Susan, I can't stop throwing up. It started after I hung up from that call with my mother. I know this sounds crazy, but it's like my body is rejecting something that isn't even food."

I sat up in the darkness, immediately awake. After thirty years of working with the body as a sacred messenger, I've learned that our stomachs rarely lie — and they almost never speak only about what we've eaten.

"Tell me about the call," I whispered into the phone.

What Maria shared in those predawn hours illuminated something profound about the intricate relationship between our emotional lives and our digestive system. Her mother had once again dismissed Maria's career choices, invalidated her feelings, and ended the conversation with the familiar refrain: "You're too sensitive for this world." Maria's stomach, it seemed, had finally reached its capacity for swallowing what could not be digested — decades of criticism, invalidation, and emotional poison disguised as motherly concern.

## The Stomach as Sacred Keeper

Here's something remarkable to know: your stomach contains more nerve endings than your spinal cord. This dense network of neurons, known as the enteric nervous system, has been called our "second brain" — and for good reason. It processes information, makes decisions, and responds to emotional stimuli completely independently of your conscious mind.

When we say we have a "gut feeling" or describe something as "hard to stomach," we're speaking a deeper truth than we might realize. The stomach doesn't just break down food; it processes life experiences, relationships, and the constant stream of what we encounter daily. Some of these experiences nourish us. Others... well, others sit like stones in our belly, creating a different kind of indigestion altogether.

I remember working with a client — let's call him David — who'd been struggling with chronic gastritis for years. No medical intervention had provided lasting relief. During our first session, as I placed my hands gently on his solar plexus, he began to weep. "I've been angry for so long," he whispered. "I don't even remember what it feels like not to be angry."

The stomach, you see, is exquisitely designed to handle the acidic breakdown of food. But when we chronically swallow rage, resentment, or unexpressed grief, we create a different kind of acid — one that burns from the inside out, gradually eroding our capacity to trust not just others, but life itself.

## When Trust Turns to Stone

The belly holds our deepest relationship with trust. Think about it — when we feel safe, we say we have a "settled stomach." When anxious, our stomach "churns." When shocked, we feel "punched in the gut." The stomach is where we first learned whether the world was a safe place to receive nourishment, whether what was offered to us could be trusted.

This begins before we can even speak. As infants, we learned whether our cries for food would be met with warmth and presence, or anxiety and disconnection. We learned whether the milk that came carried love or stress, whether feeding time was sacred communion or rushed transaction. These early experiences create what neuroscientists call our "visceral blueprint" — a deeply embedded pattern of how our nervous system responds to the act of receiving.

Here's what's both fascinating and heartbreaking: the stomach retains these patterns with remarkable fidelity. A woman who learned as a child that expressing hunger was met with irritation may find herself unable to eat when stressed, even decades later. A man whose early feeding experiences were chaotic might discover that his stomach rebels against nourishment during times of emotional uncertainty.

But here's the crucial point — and this is where hope enters the picture — neuroplasticity extends to our enteric nervous system. The neural pathways in our belly can be rewired, just like those in our brain. We can literally teach our stomach to trust again.

I witnessed this transformation in my own body years ago. I'd been struggling with what doctors called "functional dyspepsia" — a clinical term that essentially means "your stomach doesn't work properly, and we don't know why." The symptoms were maddening: nausea after eating, a constant feeling of fullness, and a deep, gnawing sensation that no amount of food could satisfy.

One evening, while practicing cranial sacral therapy on myself, I felt my hands drawn to my solar plexus. As I settled into stillness, an image arose unbidden — myself at age seven, sitting at our kitchen table, my parents arguing in sharp, brittle voices. I could feel my small body contracting, my stomach clenching, as I tried to swallow my dinner along with the toxic energy that filled our dining room.

In that moment, I understood something profound: my stomach had learned to associate nourishment with danger. Every meal had become a battlefield, every bite a risk.

## The Alchemy of Undigested Experience

The stomach's role in processing undigested experience goes far beyond our personal history. As I've studied the intersection of trauma and healing, particularly through the lens of [spiritual guidance and ancestral healing](https://paulwagner.com), I've come to understand that our stomachs often hold what our lineages could not digest — generations of unexpressed grief, swallowed rage, and abandoned dreams.

This isn't metaphorical. Emerging research in epigenetics shows us that traumatic stress can literally alter gene expression in ways that affect digestive function across generations. The grandmother who survived famine may pass down a stomach that hoards every calorie. The grandfather who swallowed his tears during wartime may leave descendants whose bellies cannot relax into the simple pleasure of a meal.

But here's where the alchemy begins — when we bring consciousness to these inherited patterns, we can transform not just our own relationship with nourishment, but the template we pass forward. Healing your stomach is, in many ways, healing your lineage.

I think of Elena, a client who came to me with severe gastroparesis — a condition where the stomach essentially forgets how to empty properly. During our work together, she began to uncover stories of the women in her family: her mother, who never allowed herself to fully receive love; her grandmother, who'd fled her homeland with nothing but the clothes on her back; her great-grandmother, who'd learned to live on scraps and consider herself grateful.

"We're all women who forgot how to digest sweetness," Elena realized one day, tears streaming down her face. "We learned to survive, but we forgot how to thrive."

Elena's healing journey involved not just addressing her physical symptoms, but actively rewiring her nervous system's capacity to receive nourishment — both physical and emotional. She learned to eat in presence rather than rushing through meals while multitasking. She practiced receiving compliments without deflecting them. She allowed herself to be nourished by friendship, beauty, rest... all the forms of sustenance her lineage had taught her to view with suspicion.

## The Sacred Return to Trust

The path back to trust begins with the simplest of acts — placing your hand on your belly and breathing. Not the quick, shallow breathing of anxiety, but the deep, generous breathing that massages your internal organs with each exhale, that tells your nervous system: "We are safe. We can receive. We can digest not just food, but life itself."

Here's a practice that has transformed countless lives, including my own:

Begin each meal with thirty seconds of stillness. Place one hand on your heart, one hand on your belly. Breathe deeply three times. With each exhale, imagine releasing any stress, any hurry, any concern about anything other than this moment of nourishment. With each inhale, invite gratitude — not forced positivity, but genuine appreciation for whatever is about to sustain you.

This isn't about perfection. Some meals, you'll forget. Some days, your stomach will still clench with old memories. That's not failure — that's the honest, messy, beautiful work of healing. Each time you return to presence, each time you choose trust over the familiar patterns of contraction, you're literally rewiring centuries of conditioning.

What astonishes me is how quickly the body responds to this conscious choice. I've seen clients experience dramatic improvements in digestive symptoms within weeks of beginning this practice — not because they're forcing their bodies to behave differently, but because they're finally creating the internal conditions their stomachs have been longing for: safety, presence, and permission to receive.

The stomach, you see, is not just a digestive organ — it's a portal. When we heal our relationship with how we receive nourishment, we heal our relationship with how we receive life itself. We begin to trust that there will be enough, that we are worthy of sustenance, that the universe is not a place of scarcity requiring us to grab and hoard and protect, but a place of abundance inviting us to open and receive and digest the sweetness that surrounds us.

## Living from the Belly of Trust

As I write this, nearly five years have passed since that middle-of-the-night phone call from Maria. Her healing journey led her not just to resolve her physical symptoms, but to fundamentally transform her relationship with boundaries, with receiving, with her own worthiness for love and nourishment.

She learned to recognize when her stomach was responding to emotional toxicity rather than physical food. She developed the courage to have difficult conversations rather than swallowing her truth. She began to see her sensitive stomach not as a weakness, but as an exquisite guidance system — a sacred messenger alerting her when something in her environment was not truly nourishing.

"My stomach has become my ally," she told me recently. "It no longer feels like something happening to me, but something happening for me — a wise teacher showing me how to live in greater alignment with what truly serves my highest good."

This is the gift waiting in the belly of trust — not the absence of sensitivity, but the wisdom to honor what your sensitive system is telling you. Not the ability to stomach anything, but the discernment to know what deserves your precious life force and what does not.

Your stomach has been holding space for more than you realize. It's been carrying not just what you've eaten, but what you've experienced. Not just nutrients, but emotions. Not just food, but the entire question of whether life can be trusted to provide what you need.

The answer, beloved one, is yes. Life can be trusted. Your body can be trusted. Your stomach's wisdom — even its rebellion — can be trusted. Every sensation, every symptom, every moment of discomfort is a sacred communication from the deepest part of yourself, inviting you back into right relationship with the profound act of receiving nourishment.

In a world that often feels unsafe, uncertain, and overwhelming, your belly can become a sanctuary of trust — a place where you remember that you are held, you are worthy, and there is enough. Not just enough food, but enough love, enough beauty, enough grace to sustain you through whatever life brings.

This is the true healing of the stomach: not the elimination of all sensation, but the restoration of trust in the wisdom of sensation itself. Not the ability to digest everything, but the discernment to know what truly nourishes you — and the courage to choose that, again and again, as an act of sacred self-care.

With infinite love and support on your journey back to trust, Susan

teachings.summary: Susan reframes bodily symptoms as wise, communicative signals rather than mechanical failures, inviting readers to listen to their bodies with curiosity and compassion. She explains how experiences become embodied through the nervous system and neural pathways and shows how gentle, specific inquiry can reveal the emotions, memories, and unmet needs the body is holding. The piece emphasizes integration over fixing, honoring the body as a temple and an ally on the path toward healing and wholeness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You know that feeling — the one where your chest tightens and your breath catches and the world seems to narrow to a single, sharp point?

We arrive here, in these miraculous bodies, with no instruction manual. We learn to walk, to talk, to navigate a world of breathtaking beauty and bewildering complexity. And along the way, we learn to distrust the very vessel that carries us through it all. We are taught to silence its whispers, to numb its aches, to wage war against its cycles and seasons. We are taught to treat the body as a machine, something to be controlled, optimized, and fixed. But what if this is the greatest misunderstanding of all?

I remember a client from years ago, a woman I’ll call Elena. She came to me as a last resort, her life having been systematically dismantled by debilitating migraines. She was a successful architect, a mother of two, a woman who moved through the world with a sharp, competent grace. But when the migraines descended, she was lost. The pain, she described, was not just an ache; it was a thief. It stole light, sound, and days of her life, leaving her in a black fog of silent agony. She spoke of her body with a kind of cold fury, the voice of a betrayed commander. “I’ve done everything right,” she told me, her hands clenched in her lap. “I eat clean, I exercise, I meditate. But my body is fighting me at every turn. It’s sabotaging me. Why is it betraying me?”

Her question hung in the quiet space between us, a question I’ve heard in a thousand different forms from a thousand different souls over my thirty years of practice. Why the chronic fatigue that feels like walking through wet cement? Why the searing back pain that makes it impossible to stand tall? Why the skin that erupts in angry, weeping rashes? Why the stomach that churns with a relentless, nameless anxiety? Why, we ask, is my body doing this *to* me?

And here is a very good thing to know, a truth that has been the foundation of my life’s work, a truth I have seen transform lives, including my own: Your body is never, ever betraying you. It is not your enemy. It is not a faulty machine in need of a better mechanic. Your body, in its infinite and often mysterious wisdom, is speaking to you. The symptoms, the pain, the discomfort… these are not the problem. They are the sacred messengers. They are the exquisitely precise language of your soul, communicated through the magnificent, intelligent, and deeply feeling instrument of your embodied being.

## The Living Archive: How Your Biography Becomes Your Biology

This isn’t just a poetic idea or a spiritual platitude—it’s a reality grounded in the very architecture of our nervous system. Our bodies are living, breathing archives of our every experience, every thought, every emotion, every moment of connection, and every instance of overwhelm. The story of your life is not just a narrative held in your mind; it is a physical reality encoded in your cells. Your biography becomes your biology.

From the moment of conception, our nervous system begins its primary task: to keep us safe. It is a brilliant, lightning-fast communication network, constantly assessing the environment for cues of safety or danger. When we experience something overwhelming—a parent’s sudden anger, a frightening fall, a lingering sense of not belonging at school—and we don’t have the support or the internal capacity to process the immense energy of that experience, it doesn’t just vanish. The nervous system, in its profound intelligence, makes a decision. It contains the charge. The energy gets stored in the body’s tissues.

Think of it this way. A young child is terrified by a barking dog. The child’s body floods with adrenaline and cortisol, the fight-or-flight hormones. The impulse is to run, to scream, to be scooped up into a parent’s safe arms. But what if the parent says, “Don’t be silly, it’s just a dog. Stop crying.”? The child, needing the parent’s love and approval to survive, learns to override the body’s powerful impulse. The scream gets swallowed, the trembling gets suppressed, the terror gets locked away. But where does it go? It might go into the diaphragm, creating a lifelong pattern of shallow breathing. It might go into the legs, which wanted to run but couldn’t, leading to issues in the hips or feet years later. The body isn’t being “bad.” It’s being brilliant. It’s holding the story that the mind could not yet integrate, keeping a promise it made to you long ago to help you survive.

These moments create what we in the field of neuroscience call neural pathways. Imagine them as grooves carved into a landscape by the flow of water. The more a particular thought, belief, or emotional response is repeated, the deeper and more defined that groove becomes. If we grew up in an environment where it wasn’t safe to express our anger, we might develop a deep neural pathway that equates anger with the danger of rejection or punishment. To survive, the body learns to suppress that fiery, vital energy. Perhaps it manifests as a tightly clenched jaw, leading to TMJ pain. Perhaps the liver, which in many wisdom traditions is the seat of anger, becomes burdened, working overtime to process the “heat” of the unprocessed emotion. The body is simply running a program, an old survival strategy that was once incredibly useful. The miracle, of course, is that these pathways are not fixed. This is the beautiful, hope-filled promise of neuroplasticity. The brain can and does change, throughout our entire lives. We can carve new grooves. We can create new neural pathways. We can, through conscious, compassionate attention, teach our nervous system that we are safe *now*, even if we weren’t back then. We can learn to listen to the story the body is holding, not with judgment, but with immense compassion. We can, in essence, elevate our own biology to love.

## The Art of Sacred Listening

So how do we begin this sacred act of listening? How do we learn to decode these messages from the soul? It begins with a radical shift in perception. It begins with turning *towards* the body, not away from it. It begins with laying down our weapons and coming to the conversation with an open heart. It begins with asking a different question. Not “What is wrong with me?” or “How can I get rid of this?” but “What are you trying to tell me, beloved one? What wisdom do you hold for me?”

This is not a conversation of force, of analysis, or of trying to “figure it out” with the mind. The mind is a beautiful tool, but in this realm, it can often be the loudest voice in the room, drowning out the subtle whispers of the body. This is a conversation of gentle, patient, and loving attention. It’s about creating a space of profound safety within yourself, a space where the deepest, most vulnerable, and often youngest parts of you feel safe enough to finally speak their truth.

One of the most profound ways to begin this dialogue is to get exquisitely specific. To move beyond the clinical label of “back pain” or “anxiety” and into the direct, raw, sensory experience of it. Find a quiet moment. Close your eyes. And bring your awareness to the sensation. What does it actually *feel* like? Is it sharp, or dull? Hot, or cold? Is it a constant, grinding ache, or does it come in pulsing waves? Where, precisely, does it live in your body? If you were to trace its outline with your finger, what shape would it be? If you were to give it a color, a weight, a texture, what would it be?

As you sit with the sensation, simply bearing witness to it without needing it to change or go away, you might notice other things arise. An image might flash in your mind’s eye. A memory from long ago might surface. A wave of emotion—sadness, anger, fear—might wash through you. A name or a phrase might echo in your inner hearing. This is the language of the body. It speaks in symbols, in sensations, in the currency of emotion and memory.

My client, Elena, began this practice with her migraines. During a quiet session, I invited her to sit with the pain, not as an enemy, but as a messenger. As she brought her awareness to the crushing pressure behind her eyes, she began to notice a deep, profound grief that lived there. It was a grief she had never allowed herself to fully feel over the sudden loss of her mother years before. She had been the strong one, the organizer, the one who held everyone else together. She had never given herself permission to collapse, to weep, to be held. The migraine, in its own fierce and terrible way, was a communication from her soul, a desperate attempt to get her to pay attention to the ocean of unshed tears and the unexpressed sorrow she was carrying. The pain was not the enemy; it was a messenger of love, calling her back home to the abandoned places within herself.

This is the wisdom held within every system of your body. Your lungs, in their constant, rhythmic exchange of giving and receiving breath, speak of your capacity to receive the fullness of life and to release what is not yours to carry. Your hands, those beautiful and intricate instruments of love’s expression, reflect how you are “handling” the challenges and gifts of your life. Your spine, your sacred central channel, communicates the delicate and powerful balance between your strength and your flexibility, your courage and your grace. A recurring bladder infection might be the body’s way of expressing a “pissed off” feeling that you feel you’re not allowed to voice. Pain in your feet might be speaking to a deep uncertainty about your next step forward on your life’s path.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

When we learn to see the body in this way, as a sacred text filled with living wisdom, everything changes. We move from a state of war with ourselves to a state of profound and loving relationship. We begin to understand that healing is not about “fixing” a broken part, because you are not a machine. You are not broken. You have never been broken. Healing is about integration. It’s about the courageous and tender act of welcoming all the exiled parts of yourself back into the wholeness of your being. It’s about developing a conscious, compassionate relationship with the entirety of who you are—the light, the shadow, the joy, the sorrow, the strength, and the vulnerability.

## The Body’s Benediction: Coming Home to Your Temple

Your body has been with you from your very first breath. It has held you, carried you, and tirelessly worked, day and night, to keep you safe and alive. It has metabolized not just the food you eat, but your every experience. It has stored your most ecstatic joys and held your most shattering sorrows. It is the most loyal and devoted companion you will ever have, a constant, unwavering presence on this wild human journey.

What would it be like, just for this moment, to pause and feel into that truth? To place your hand on your heart, or on the part of your body that is calling for your attention, and to simply offer a word of thanks? To thank it for its incredible intelligence, its astonishing resilience, its unwavering and unconditional commitment to your life?

This is the journey. It is not a journey to a perfect, symptom-free, ageless existence. That is a fantasy that keeps us at war with the beautiful, messy, and sacred reality of being alive in a human body. The real journey is to come home. To come home to the sacredness of your own being, to recognize the divine intelligence that is expressing itself in every one of your sixty trillion cells. To learn to listen to your body’s whispers before they are forced to become screams.

Your body is not a battlefield to be conquered. It is a temple to be honored. And its messages are not a curse. They are a blessing, a constant invitation to come deeper into love, into wholeness, into the magnificent truth of who you are.

Listen closely. It is whispering the secrets of your own liberation.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard gratitude not as a quaint sentiment but as a measurable, rewiring practice that reshapes brain and body. She outlines the neuroscience of appreciation, the somatic shifts that follow genuine gratitude, and simple daily rituals that accumulate into lasting resilience and presence. The piece encourages small, embodied moments of noticing as practical gateways into a more expansive baseline of well-being.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are wired for connection, for joy, for a sense of wonder… and yet, we so often find ourselves tangled in the thorns of worry, comparison, and a relentless sense of not-enough. We chase after big, shiny goals, believing they hold the key to our happiness, only to find the lock has changed by the time we get there. But what if the key wasn’t a destination at all? What if it was a frequency? A resonance we could tune into at any moment, regardless of our external circumstances. A quiet power that could fundamentally rewire the very structure of our brains and transform our experience of reality from the inside out. This, beloved one, is the frequency of gratitude. It’s a concept that might sound simple, almost quaint, in a world that shouts for more, bigger, faster. But gratitude is not just a polite sentiment or a passive state of being thankful. It is an active, measurable energy. A form of appreciation so profound it creates a cascade of positive change throughout our entire nervous system. ## The Neuroscience of Appreciation For a long time, we believed our brains were fixed, that the neural pathways carved in childhood were the roads we were destined to walk for life. But the beautiful, hope-filled truth of neuroplasticity has shown us otherwise. Our brains are constantly changing, adapting, and creating new connections based on our thoughts, feelings, and experiences. When we intentionally practice gratitude, we are doing something remarkable. We are activating key areas of the brain, particularly the prefrontal cortex—the seat of our higher reasoning, decision-making, and social-emotional intelligence. Studies using fMRI scans have shown that when subjects focus on feelings of appreciation, these brain regions light up, bathed in a cocktail of feel-good neurochemicals like dopamine and serotonin. Think of it like this: every time you consciously choose to acknowledge something you’re grateful for—the warmth of the sun on your skin, the taste of your morning coffee, the sound of a loved one’s laughter—you are forging a new neural pathway. It might be a tiny, faint trail at first. But with consistent practice, that trail becomes a well-worn path. And eventually, it becomes a superhighway. This is not just positive thinking. This is brain training. You are literally teaching your brain to scan for the good, to default to a state of appreciation rather than a state of lack. Over time, this practice can lead to a lasting increase in your baseline levels of happiness, a greater resilience to stress, and a more profound sense of connection to the world around you. ## The Power of a Moment There are moments when we feel particularly stuck. A project we have poured our hearts into has fallen through, and a cloud of disappointment seems to follow us everywhere. It is common to sit, staring blankly, lost in a spiral of what-ifs and if-onlys. And then, a tiny finch might land on a branch, its chest a startling splash of red against the green leaves. It begins to sing—a clear, impossibly joyful melody that seems to pierce right through the fog of our mood. In that moment, something shifts. We are no longer thinking about our failed project. We are simply… there. Present to the bird, to the song, to the gentle breeze rustling the leaves. A wave of gratitude can wash over us, so simple and so pure. Gratitude for that tiny, vibrant life. For the beauty of its song. For the quiet sanctuary of a garden. It isn’t a big, dramatic epiphany. It is a quiet, internal pivot. A choice to tune into the frequency of what is *right* in that moment, instead of what feels wrong. That small moment doesn’t magically solve our problems. But it changes our energy. It reminds us that even in the midst of disappointment, there is always, *always* something to be grateful for. It is a lifeline, a single note of grace that helps us find our way back to a more expansive, hopeful state of being. ## The Body’s Wisdom: Gratitude as a Somatic Practice Our bodies are exquisite barometers of our internal state. When we are stressed, our bodies constrict. Our shoulders hunch, our jaws clench, our breath becomes shallow. We are in a state of fight, flight, or freeze—a primal response designed to protect us from perceived threats. Gratitude, on the other hand, invites the body to expand. It is a direct antidote to the stress response. When we feel genuine appreciation, our heart rate slows, our blood pressure lowers, and our nervous system shifts from the sympathetic (stress) to the parasympathetic (rest and digest) state. This is body-based wisdom at its finest. You can feel the shift in your own physiology. Try it now, my dear one. Close your eyes. Take a slow, deep breath. And bring to mind one thing—just one small thing—that you are truly grateful for. Maybe it’s the feeling of the chair supporting you. The quiet hum of your home. The simple fact that you are breathing. As you hold this gratitude in your awareness, notice what happens in your body. Do you feel a softening? A release of tension in your shoulders? A warmth spreading through your chest? This is not imagination. This is the physical manifestation of the frequency of gratitude, soothing and regulating your entire system. In the Tao Te Ching, Lao Tzu speaks of the power of water, which flows effortlessly and nourishes all things without striving. Gratitude is like this. It is a gentle, yielding force that, over time, can wear away the hardest stones of resentment, fear, and despair. ## Cultivating a Daily Practice Like any practice, the art of gratitude deepens with consistency. It’s not about grand gestures, but about the small, steady accumulation of appreciative moments. Here are a few simple ways to weave this practice into your daily life: * **Start a Gratitude Jar:** Find a beautiful jar and keep it somewhere you’ll see it every day. Each evening, write down one thing you were grateful for on a small slip of paper and place it in the jar. When you’re feeling low, you can reach in and read a few, reminding yourself of the abundance that is always present. * **Take Gratitude Walks:** Dedicate a walk each day to simply noticing the good around you. Pay attention to the details—the intricate pattern of a leaf, the way the light filters through the trees, the friendly nod of a stranger. Let your senses be your guide. * **Practice Appreciative Inquiry:** When you find yourself in a challenging situation, gently ask yourself: "What can I be grateful for here? What is the hidden gift or lesson in this experience?" This isn’t about bypassing the difficulty, but about finding a new, more empowered perspective. This journey of being human is indeed a tricky business. It is messy and beautiful, heartbreaking and breathtaking, often all at once. But we are not passive victims of circumstance. We are active creators of our reality, and the tools we use are our thoughts, our feelings, and our focus. By choosing to tune into the frequency of gratitude, we choose to align ourselves with the expansive, life-affirming energy of the universe. We choose to see the world not as a place of scarcity and lack, but as a field of infinite possibility and grace. And in doing so, we don’t just change our minds—we change our entire world.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan
