teachings.sourceTitle: The Immune System - The Guardian of Identity and the Master of Discernment
teachings.title: The Immune System - The Guardian of Identity and the Master of Discernment
teachings.summary: Susan frames the immune system as a lived intelligence — a vigilant guardian that maps the boundary between self and other and a physiological mirror of our inner story. She explores how auto-immunity and chronic inflammation can arise from exiled parts of the self and a nervous system stuck in readiness, and offers embodied practices (breath, gentle movement, boundary-work, mourning rituals, and nourishing social contact) to invite integration. Throughout she holds a pragmatic bridge between inner work and conventional medicine, inviting curiosity rather than blame.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a quiet army within you that never sleeps. It moves like a border guard and like a gardener, like a sentinel and like a midwife. It is vigilant and tender, fierce and discerning. This army is the immune system. It keeps you alive by naming what belongs and what does not, by deciding what to tolerate and what to remove, by remembering patterns of invasion and the recipes for repair. Yet at the deepest levels it is also the physiological expression of a story you have told yourself about who you are and who the world is. To listen to your immune system is to listen to a primordial conversation about identity itself.

The Guardian of Identity

Your body uses language that predates words. Cells speak in molecules, in electrical whispers, in inflammatory flares and quiet reconciliations. The immune system's vocabulary includes cytokines that call for reinforcements, antibodies that mark the familiar, and regulatory cells that lower the alarm when there is no longer a threat. Taken together, these instruments perform discernment - they map the boundaries of you. Where does your self end and the other begin? How do you preserve integrity without becoming walled off? The immune system lives inside this question, and its choices reflect the subtler decisions you make each day about how to engage the world.

When the immune system functions in graceful balance it is a teacher of wise limits. It allows you to move through life with a capacity to receive, integrate, and then release. It permits you to touch, to be touched, to be nourished, and to be protected. But when your internal narrative about danger becomes chronic, your immune responses move from rhythmic tending to perpetual guarding. The soft frontier between you and the world becomes rigid, and that rigidity shows up in labs, in swollen tissues, in pain, in fatigue. Your cells become the stage where old fears play out again and again.

Auto-Immunity as Crisis of Identity

There are few phenomena more paradoxical than auto-immunity, where the immune system turns its force inward and treats parts of your body as invaders. On the physiological level this is a failure of recognition - markers that used to signify "self" now appear foreign. Yet on the deeper level it is, as the ancient path-keepers would say, an identity crisis. Somewhere in the history of your being you exiled aspects of yourself - tenderness, anger, a need for care, an acceptable expression of desire - because to hold them felt unsafe. You learned to name those parts as not-me, or worse, as shameful. Those very exiles become haunted by their own energy. They cannot rest in exile forever. They press to return and to be integrated. If the welcome is not prepared, if recognition is withheld or feared, the body may meet them with force.

Auto-immune disease, in this frame, is not an accusation. It is a summons. It is the body's insistence that the borders you have drawn are harming the whole. When your tissues become sites of chronic attack, something profound is being asked of you - not to blame, but to remember. Who did you have to disown to survive? Which parts of your heart were declared foreign so you could keep breathing in a difficult world? These questions are tender. They require the soft courage of a healer who will sit with what is hidden and say yes to reclamation, even when reclaiming pain feels like opening a wound.

Chronic Inflammation - The Perpetual Perceived Threat

Inflammation is the body’s alarm system. It is a flash of heat, of redness, of swelling meant to corral danger and accelerate repair. But when the alarm persists, when inflammation becomes an ongoing background hum, your tissues are living inside a perception of perpetual threat. This perception can be seeded by real injuries and infections, but often it is nourished by less visible sources - unresolved grief, ongoing relational stress, an inner narrative that says the world is unsafe, a nervous system stuck in readiness. Chronic inflammation is the physical echo of a life that believes danger is around every corner.

In the Tao Te Ching you find the simple, luminous counsel: "By letting go it all gets done. The world is won by those who let it go." This is not a call to passivity, but an invitation to shift from the posture of attack-defend to the posture of discerning embrace. If your body is locked into inflammation, part of the work is to teach your physiology that the world is not always hostile, that you can afford to relax the guard, that repair will be attended to. That teaching happens in many small ways - in the way you breathe, in the way you allow grief its time, in the way you practice returning to safety after a stressor. Over time, those practices alter gene expression, recalibrate immune set points, and invite the inflammatory chorus to lower its volume.

Exhaustion from Perpetual Defense

Defense requires energy. Every antibody, every activated macrophage, every repertoire of inflammatory mediators consumes metabolic currency. When you live chronically in a defended state the resources of your immune system become depleted. What once was abundant vigilance becomes burn-out and immunodeficiency. You may feel clinically tired in ways words barely touch - a bone fatigue that conversation cannot soothe. This exhaustion is political and poetic at once. It shows you what it costs to live as if the world is a battlefield. The body that once sang with vigorous protection now whispers. It cannot maintain the same tempo when the battery is drained.

You can recognize this constraint not as failure but as an opportunity to change how you hold yourself in the world. When you stop recruiting every moment into defense, some of that energy becomes available for repair, for pleasure, for creative flourish. The invitation is to retrain the nervous system and the immune system together. They are allies. When the nervous system learns safety, the immune system will downshift. When the immune system finds rest, your capacity to love and participate in life returns. This is the medicine of integration - the reallocation of attention from constant guarding toward a spacious presence that welcomes life without ceding your sovereignty.

The Truth at the Heart - There Are Ultimately No Borders

Here is the teaching that quietly unthreads the whole drama: at the deepest level of being, there are no borders. The Taoist masters say that the great river does not cling to banks; it dissolves distinctions through its flow. When you drink from that river you begin to see that the separation you have defended yourself from is, in great measure, a story useful for survival but not final. You are both a distinct organism and a point of participation within a single vast field of life. Your immunity to others is necessary and beautiful for short-term survival, but ultimate healing calls for a different posture - one of discernment without irrevocable exile.

This paradox can be held in your body. You can have clear boundaries that do not require absolute borders. You can say no and maintain openness simultaneously. You can protect your integrity while allowing your exiled parts to return and be reintroduced into your wholeness. To live this way is to practice the Taoist art of yielding that preserves strength. As the Tao Te Ching gently offers, "True gentleness is invincible." When you practice gentleness with your immune self - not by letting everything in uncritically, but by learning discrimination that knows when to integrate and when to release - you become both safe and resilient, porous yet sovereign.

Listening to the Holographic Body

Your immune system is a hologram. Its rhythms and expressions encode information about your relationships, your childhood, your patterns of belief and your current environment. A skin rash might trace a story about exposure to harsh words. A persistent sinus congestion might carry the dust of unresolved grief. Auto-immune flares often bloom in moments when your life asks you to reengage with what you had shut down - an invitation to reclaim voice, intimacy, creativity, or grief. When you begin to treat symptoms as intelligent messengers, not as punishments, you are invited into the most intimate spiritual work of your life: the unification of what was once split.

Begin by listening. Place your hands where something hurts or where something feels tender and simply be. Allow the mind to be curious without rushing to explanation. Notice the felt sense of what arises. In the silence between observation and action you open a window through which integration can come. The immune system does not need your condemnation; it needs your attention. In attending you give it permission to change its mind about what is friend and what is foe.

Practical Pathways Toward Integration

Integration is not a single act. It is a series of small recoveries. You will require practices that recalibrate your nervous system so the immune system can relax. Breathing practices that elongate the exhale teach the vagus nerve to signal safety. Gentle movement that honors the capacity of your legs and hips to hold you tends to the root sense of support that the immune system reads as context. Rituals of mourning that make permission for grief explicit give the liver and kidneys spaces to process bitterness and fear that otherwise poison immune balance. Creative practices that allow the reclaiming of expression - humming, drawing, speech - invite parts of you back from exile in non-threatening ways.

Equally important is the art of boundary-making as an inner conversation, not a war. Notice how you feel when you imagine saying no. Where in the body is the breath held? Where does the chest constrict? Work there slowly. Speak the no in small pieces until your body practices the muscular memory of refusal without rupture. At the same time, practice saying yes to small gestures of tenderness toward yourself - a warm cup, a slow walk, a kind reflection in the mirror. These micro-yeses train your immune system to expect restoration as a part of life.

Do not forget the social web. Human contact that is safe and nourishing teaches your physiology that you are supported. Touch is a deep teacher. A hand on your shoulder, a hug that is yes to you, a voice that names you as belonging - these are the kinds of nourishment that reset immune trajectories more quickly than you might imagine. If you have been isolated, begin with small, trustworthy encounters. Let the immune system experience safety through another's presence. Let your cells remember that belonging is possible.

A Gentle Caveat

As you do this inner work, attend to your outer medicines and the wise counsel of practitioners who can help you decode complex immune dynamics. There are times when physiology must be supported with interventions that stabilize and protect. Integration and reclamation are luminous aims, but they are not a replacement for necessary care. Walk both roads - the inner and the outer - with humility and patience. I have seen individuals transform their health through embodiment practices and relational repair, and I have also witnessed the profound gift of modern medicine holding someone steady so they could do the internal alchemy that follows. Both are sacred.

Closing Blessing

In the tender work of reclaiming yourself, remember this: your immune system is not an enemy. It is a loyal friend that has done its best with the map you gave it. In the places it has guarded too fiercely there are lost children of your soul waiting to be welcomed back. When you learn to move from attack and exile to discernment and integration, the cells will re-learn recognition. Chronic inflammation will dim like a sky after rain. Exhaustion will lift as the economy of your attention shifts from fear to repair. The borders you once needed for survival can soften into wise boundaries that allow both integrity and flow. From that place you can live as the Tao suggests - with a heart that yields yet does not collapse, with strength that is gentle, and with a life that moves from fragmentary defense into luminous wholeness.

May you meet your immune system with reverence and curiosity. May you answer its summons with courage and tenderness. And may you come to know, in your bones and in your breath, that though you are distinct, you are never separate from the great web of life that holds you always.

If any practice increases distress or if you have medical concerns, pause and consult your healthcare provider or a trusted clinician.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Art of Holding Space: For Yourself and Others
teachings.title: The Art of Holding Space: For Yourself and Others
teachings.summary: Susan reminds us that holding space is a quiet, non‑fixing presence that nourishes belonging for others and for ourselves. The piece invites cultivating self‑compassion through body awareness — noticing sensations, pausing, and listening — and then extending that steady presence outward. It frames this practice as a nervous‑system‑soothing gift that gently opens possibilities for inner transformation.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We long for connection, for deep, meaningful bonds with others, and yet we so often find ourselves feeling utterly alone. We want to be seen, to be heard, to be held in our vulnerability, but the world seems to demand strength, certainty, and a polished exterior. So many people, particularly those with a fiery spirit, find themselves feeling depleted. They are the ones everyone turns to, the rocks, the fixers. They hold space for friends, family, and colleagues, but forget to hold it for themselves. Their bodies may begin to protest in the form of migraines and deep fatigue. Their shoulders might hunch, as if carrying the weight of the world. They can become a container for everyone else’s pain, with no room left for their own. This is the paradox of holding space. It is one of the most profound gifts we can offer another human being, and one of the most difficult—and necessary—to offer ourselves. ## What Does It Truly Mean to Hold Space? Holding space is not about fixing. It’s not about giving advice, or sharing your own story, or trying to cheer someone up. It’s about being present, fully and completely, without judgment. It’s about creating a container of safety and acceptance where another person can simply *be*. It is the quiet art of accompaniment. Think of it like this: you are walking with a friend through a dark forest. You don’t know the way out, and you don’t have a map. Your role is not to lead, or to pretend you have the answers. Your role is to walk alongside them, to be a steady presence in the darkness. To let them know, through your quiet companionship, that they are not alone. This requires a radical kind of presence. It asks us to set aside our own agendas, our own discomfort, our own need to *do* something. It asks us to simply witness. To listen not just with our ears, but with our whole being. To feel into the spaces between the words, the subtle shifts in energy, the language of the body. Neuroscience tells us that this kind of deep, attuned presence has a profound effect on our nervous systems. When someone holds space for us, it co-regulates our system. It sends a powerful signal to our brain that we are safe, that we belong, that we are not alone in our struggle. This is the foundation of all healing. > To hold space for another is to offer them the gift of your unwavering presence, creating a sanctuary where their soul can unfold. ## The Art of Holding Space for Yourself And what about holding space for ourselves? This, beloved one, is where the real work begins. We are so often our own harshest critics. We judge ourselves, we push ourselves, we abandon ourselves in our moments of greatest need. We have internalized the message that we must be strong, that we must have it all together, that our vulnerability is a weakness to be hidden away. To hold space for yourself is to turn towards your own inner world with the same compassion and acceptance you would offer to a dear friend. It is to create a sanctuary within your own being where all parts of you are welcome—the messy parts, the scared parts, the parts that feel broken and lost. Consider a moment of feeling stuck, perhaps on a quiet morning with a cup of tea. A familiar old story of not-enoughness might be playing on a loop in the mind. The first instinct is often to push it away, to get busy. But what if, instead, one were to practice self-compassion? To close the eyes, take a deep breath, and place a hand on the heart. To simply listen to the story without judgment. To feel the constriction in the chest, the tightness in the jaw, and allow the feelings to be there without needing them to change. This is what it means to hold space for one's own pain. And then, a funny thing happened. The story began to lose its power. The constriction in my chest began to soften. A sense of peace, of deep okayness, began to wash over me. In the quiet spaciousness I had created within myself, a new possibility emerged. A new way of seeing. This is the magic of holding space for yourself. It is in the allowing, not the resisting, that transformation occurs. ## The Body as a Gateway Our bodies are wise and faithful messengers. They are constantly speaking to us, in the language of sensation, of tension, of ease. To hold space for ourselves is to learn to listen to this language. To cultivate a deep intimacy with our own physical being. When you feel a difficult emotion—anxiety, grief, anger—where do you feel it in your body? Is it a tightness in your throat? A hollowness in your belly? A buzzing in your hands? Can you bring a gentle, curious attention to that sensation? Can you breathe into it? Can you allow it to be there, without needing it to go away? This is not about wallowing in our pain. It is about meeting it with presence. It is about honoring the wisdom of our bodies, and trusting that they know the way to healing. The Tao Te Ching says, “The supreme good is like water, which nourishes all things without trying to.” When we hold space, for ourselves or for another, we become like water. We are soft, yielding, and yet incredibly powerful. We nourish, we cleanse, we create the conditions for life to flourish.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
So today, my friend, I invite you to practice the art of holding space. Start with yourself. The next time you feel a wave of emotion, or a familiar old story begins to play, pause. Take a breath. Place a hand on your heart. And just be with what is. No fixing, no judging, no running away. Just a quiet, compassionate presence. And then, when you feel ready, extend this gift to another. Listen with your whole being. Be a sanctuary of acceptance. Walk alongside them in the darkness, and trust that in the shared space of presence, you will both find your way home. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a quiet seat for three to five minutes. Place one hand lightly on your heart, close your eyes if that feels safe, and breathe slowly in and out. As you breathe, notice any tightness, warmth, or movement in your chest or elsewhere — name the sensation or emotion silently (for example, “tension,” “sadness,” “tired”). Offer yourself a simple compassionate phrase on the out‑breath (for example, “I am here” or “It’s okay to feel this”). If you feel overwhelmed at any point, pause the practice and reach out to a trusted person or professional; if you have persistent physical symptoms (migraines, deep fatigue, chest pain), consult a medical provider.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article invites contact with vulnerability and difficult emotions; it’s okay to pause or stop if you feel flooded.
If practicing these invitations brings up intense pain, trauma, or persistent distress, consider seeking support from a qualified therapist, trusted caregiver, or crisis resource.
Allow yourself permission to take small steps and to return to practices only as they feel safe and manageable.

teachings.sourceTitle: How Beliefs Shape Your Biology
teachings.title: How Beliefs Shape Your Biology
teachings.summary: Susan explores how our beliefs, perceptions, and emotions actively influence our bodies — not by changing DNA sequence but by shaping gene expression, chemistry, and neural pathways. Drawing on epigenetics, placebo/nocebo research, and a clinical example, she invites a compassionate, curious dialogue with bodily symptoms as sources of information and possibility rather than enemies to be silenced.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was in a workshop once, years ago, when the facilitator asked a question that stopped the room cold.

We walk around in these miraculous bodies, these intricate webs of tissue and bone, electricity and fluid, and most of the time, we treat them like cars. We expect them to run perfectly, we get frustrated when a part breaks down, and we often ignore the warning lights on the dashboard until we’re stranded on the side of the road, bewildered and wondering how we got here.

But what if the body isn’t a machine at all? What if it’s a sacred messenger, a wise and constant companion, whispering—and sometimes shouting—the truths our conscious minds are not yet ready to hear? What if that persistent ache in your lower back isn’t just a sign of a bad mattress, but a physical echo of feeling profoundly unsupported in your life? What if the tightness in your throat, that feeling of a lump you can’t quite swallow, is more than just a seasonal allergy… what if it’s the weight of a thousand unspoken words, a lifetime of truths you’ve held back for fear of making waves?

I’ve sat with hundreds of dear ones in my healing practice over the years, bearing witness to the silent stories their bodies are telling. I have seen, with a clarity that leaves no room for doubt, a profound and undeniable truth, one that modern science is only just beginning to fully embrace: our beliefs, thoughts, and deepest feelings are not separate from our physical bodies. They are the architects of our biology. They are, quite literally, shaping us from the inside out, cell by precious cell.

## The Ghost in the Machine Is You

For a long time, we were taught to believe in a kind of genetic determinism. The idea that our DNA is a fixed blueprint, a life sentence handed down from our ancestors. You have the gene for this, the predisposition for that. It’s a story of powerlessness, really. A story that leaves us as victims of our own heredity, passengers in a biological vehicle we have no control over.

But a revolutionary field of science, known as *epigenetics*, is telling a much more hopeful, and far more interesting, story. Epigenetics, which literally means “above the genes,” is the study of how our behaviors and environment can cause changes that affect the way our genes work. It’s not about changing the DNA sequence itself—the fundamental code remains the same. It’s about the *expression* of that code. It’s about deciding which genes get turned on and which get turned off, which chapters of our genetic story are read aloud and which remain silent.

Imagine your DNA as a vast library, containing the potential for every human characteristic. Genetic determinism would say that the library is pre-selected, and you can only read the books that are already open on the table. Epigenetics, however, reveals that *you* are the librarian. Your experiences, your perceptions, your emotions… they are the signals that tell the librarian which books to pull from the shelves and which to put back. A stressful thought, a moment of pure joy, a deeply held belief—these are all instructions that send epigenetic markers, like little chemical sticky notes, to attach to our DNA and command our genes into action or silence.

The pioneering cell biologist Bruce Lipton, Ph.D., demonstrated this beautifully in his groundbreaking stem cell research. He placed genetically identical stem cells into different petri dishes, each with a unique culture medium—a different environment. In one dish, the cells became muscle. In another, they became bone. In a third, they became fat cells. The cells’ fate wasn’t sealed by their genes; it was determined by their environment. Lipton realized that for the cells in our bodies, the “culture medium” is the blood, and the composition of that blood is directly shaped by our brain’s perception of the world. Our beliefs, filtered through the brain, create the chemistry that either nourishes our cells into health or signals them into distress.

Every thought you think is not just an ephemeral wisp of energy. It becomes chemistry. It becomes an electrical signal. It becomes a vibration that your fifty trillion cells are constantly listening to, attuning themselves to the song you are singing with your mind.

## The Pharmacy of the Mind

We have all heard of the placebo effect. It’s often dismissed as “all in your head,” but it is perhaps the most potent and scientifically documented proof of the biology of belief. A patient is given a sugar pill, told it is a powerful new drug, and their symptoms miraculously improve. The body, believing it is receiving medicine, activates its own innate healing capacities. It produces its own painkillers, its own anti-inflammatories. It becomes its own pharmacy, dispensing the precise chemical compounds needed for healing, simply because it *believes* it is supposed to.

But we don’t often talk about its shadow twin—the *nocebo* effect. This is when a negative belief creates a negative physical outcome. A doctor tells a patient they have three months to live, and the patient dies in exactly three months, even if the autopsy later reveals the diagnosis was incorrect. A person believes they are allergic to a certain flower, and they break out in a rash when presented with a plastic version of it. The belief itself becomes the toxin, the self-fulfilling prophecy written into the language of our cells. The body, in its profound and innocent wisdom, simply follows the instructions it is given by the mind.

This isn’t about blame. It’s not about suggesting that people are “thinking themselves sick.” It is about reclaiming a power we have forgotten we possess. The power of consciousness to inform and transform matter. It is a sacred and awesome responsibility, one that invites us into a deeper relationship with ourselves.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Shifting the Blueprint

I remember a client I’ll call Diane. She came to me with debilitating pain in her right shoulder, a pain she’d had for years. She’d tried everything—physiotherapy, massage, medication—with no lasting relief. In our sessions, as we gently explored the landscape of her life, a theme emerged. As the eldest daughter in a large family with a chronically ill mother, she had been the designated caretaker since she was a little girl. She carried the weight of everyone’s well-being, the unspoken responsibility for everyone’s happiness. Her shoulder, the joint that governs our capacity to carry and to reach, was screaming the truth her conscious mind had normalized. It was literally buckling under the *weight of the world* she had placed upon it.

The work wasn’t about forcing the pain to go away. It was about listening to it. We didn’t try to violently uproot the belief that she had to care for everyone. Instead, we gently inquired. *What would it be like to set just one of those burdens down? What would it feel like to receive support, instead of always giving it?* At first, the very idea felt terrifying to her, a betrayal of her identity. But slowly, through breath and presence and a deep, compassionate listening, she began to create a new neural pathway in her brain. A new possibility.

She started to believe that it was safe to let go. That her worth was not tied to her endless doing for others. And as that new belief began to take root, her shoulder began to release its grip. The pain, which had been a constant companion for a decade, simply… dissolved. Her body, finally feeling heard, let go of the alarm bell. It had done its job beautifully, delivering the message she so desperately needed to hear.

This is the heart of the work. It is not about fighting with your body or your mind. It is about entering into a loving dialogue, becoming a student of your own inner landscape.

1.  **Listen Gently:** When a physical symptom arises, instead of immediately trying to silence it, get quiet. Place a hand on that part of your body. Breathe into it. Ask it, with genuine curiosity, “Beloved one, what is the message you have for me? What truth are you trying to show me?” You might be surprised by the answers that arise from the quiet wisdom of your cells.

2.  **Inquire with Compassion:** Notice the thoughts and beliefs that surface. Perhaps it’s “I’m not good enough,” or “I have to do it all myself,” or “It’s not safe to be seen.” Don’t judge them or push them away. Just notice them with a gentle curiosity. Ask, “Where did I learn this? Whose voice is this, really?” Often, these are the inherited beliefs of our family, our culture, our childhood experiences, running on autopilot in our subconscious mind.

3.  **Introduce a New Possibility:** You don’t have to believe it fully at first. Just open a window. *What if it were possible to feel supported? What if I am already worthy, just as I am? What if it’s safe to be my authentic self?* The science of neuroplasticity shows us that the brain is capable of changing and forming new connections throughout our lives. By repeatedly and gently introducing a new, more loving thought, you begin to carve a new riverbed for your energy to flow through. You create a new song for your cells to sing.

Your body is not your enemy. It has been on your side since the moment you were conceived, working tirelessly to keep you in balance, in health, in life. It is the most faithful friend you will ever have. Learning to listen to its wisdom, to honor its messages, and to consciously cultivate an inner environment of love and safety is the most profound healing journey you can ever take.

You are the artist, and your body is the canvas. Your beliefs are the brushstrokes. What masterpiece are you creating today?

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: A Somatic Practice for Calming Your Nervous System
teachings.title: A Somatic Practice for Calming Your Nervous System
teachings.summary: Susan invites a compassionate, body-led approach to calming chronic nervous system activation, reminding readers that the nervous system responds to sensation more than thought. She outlines a gentle practice—grounding into contact, vagal humming, pendulation between activation and ease, and self co-regulation by hand-on-heart—to teach the body it is safe and to strengthen pathways of rest through small, consistent rituals. The emphasis is on presence, patience, and daily repetition rather than fixing or forcing change.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There's a particular kind of silence that arrives just before dawn, when the world holds its breath between what was and what is becoming.

And one of the most profound aspects, I find, is navigating the sheer speed of it all. The other day, I was standing in my kitchen, holding a beautiful, ripe tomato I’d just picked from the garden. The sun was streaming through the window, my cat was purring on the rug, and by all accounts, it was a moment of perfect peace. Yet, inside my own body, a storm was brewing. My heart was thrumming a little too fast, my breath was shallow, and a familiar, low-grade hum of anxiety was vibrating just beneath my skin. Nothing was wrong, and yet… everything felt wrong.

Does this feel familiar to you? This sense of being internally revved up, even when your external world is calm. It’s a profound and often painful disconnect, a feeling of being a stranger in your own home, your own body. For years, I tried to *think* my way out of this feeling. I would reason with my anxiety, meditate for hours, try to force my mind into a state of peace. But it was like trying to tell a tidal wave to be still. The hum would only grow louder.

What I didn’t understand then, and what I have come to know with every cell in my being now, is that I was speaking the wrong language. I was trying to have a conversation with my nervous system using only my mind. But the nervous system, in its ancient wisdom, speaks a much older, more primal language. It speaks the language of sensation, of vibration, of felt safety. It is the body’s electrical network, its first responder, and its primary job is to answer one fundamental question, over and over again: *Am I safe?*

## The Body’s Electrical Network

Your nervous system is the fastest communication network in your body, a vast and intricate web of neural pathways that assesses every millisecond of your existence for signs of danger or safety. When it perceives a threat—a real one, like a car swerving towards you, or a perceived one, like a critical email from your boss—it kicks into the sympathetic state, the “fight or flight” response. Your heart rate increases, your muscles tense, your digestion slows. It’s a brilliant, life-saving mechanism designed to help you survive.

The problem, for so many of us in this modern world, is that our nervous systems learned that the world was not safe a very, very long time ago. Perhaps in childhood, when our need for connection and safety went unmet. Perhaps through an accumulation of losses, heartbreaks, or stresses that taught our bodies, on a cellular level, to be perpetually on guard. The neural pathways for “danger” became deeply grooved, while the pathways for “safety” and “rest” grew faint. We end up living in a state of chronic sympathetic activation, even when, like me standing in my sun-drenched kitchen, we are objectively safe.

This is where the profound work of somatic practice begins. “Soma” simply means “the living body in its wholeness.” Somatic practice is the art of listening and responding to the body’s native language. It’s not about fixing or controlling. It is about building a relationship. It is about gently, compassionately, beginning to teach your nervous system that it is safe *now*. That you are no longer that powerless child. That the threat has passed. And you do this not with logic, but with love. With your own embodied presence.

## A Gentle Practice for Nervous System Regulation

This is not another thing to perfect or achieve. This is an invitation to come home to yourself. Find a quiet space where you can be undisturbed for a few minutes. You can do this sitting in a chair with your feet on the floor, or lying down.

**Step 1: The Arrival**

Begin by simply feeling the points of contact your body is making with the world. Feel the weight of your body in the chair, the texture of the fabric against your skin. Feel your feet on the floor—the solid, unwavering support of the earth beneath you. Let your attention drop down, out of the busy-ness of your mind, and into the simple, physical reality of your body. This act of grounding is the first step in signaling safety. It communicates to your primal brain that you are held, that you are stable. You are not floating in a sea of threat; you are connected to the firm ground of the present moment. Don’t try to change anything. Just notice. You are here. You are held.

**Step 2: The Vagal Hum**

The vagus nerve is the main nerve of your parasympathetic nervous system, the “rest and digest” state. It wanders from your brainstem down through your heart, lungs, and abdomen, and it is the key to shifting out of a state of alarm. Gently toning this nerve can be a powerful signal of safety.

Take a comfortable breath in. As you exhale, begin to make a low, gentle humming sound. “Mmmmmmm.” Feel the vibration in your chest, your throat, your skull. It doesn’t need to be loud. The vibration itself is a form of internal massage for your vagus nerve. Imagine the vibration is a warm, soothing balm, spreading through your entire torso, calming the waters within. Do this for five to ten breaths. Notice any shifts, however small. A softening in your jaw, a deepening of your breath, a sense of quiet spreading through you. These are the first whispers of your nervous system beginning to down-regulate, to move from red alert to a gentle green.

**Step 3: Pendulation — Finding the Good**

Pendulation is a beautiful somatic concept developed by Dr. Peter Levine. It involves gently swinging your attention between a place of discomfort or activation in your body, and a place that feels neutral, or even pleasant. This teaches your nervous system that it can experience activation without being consumed by it. It builds resilience, the capacity to be with difficulty without becoming the difficulty.

First, scan your body and find a place that feels even a tiny bit activated or tense. Maybe it’s a tightness in your shoulders, a clenching in your gut. Don’t dive into the story of it. Just notice the pure sensation. Stay with it for a moment… just a moment. This is important. We are not wallowing in the pain, but simply acknowledging its presence with a gentle, curious attention.

Now, gently guide your attention to another part of your body that feels neutral, or even good. Perhaps your hands feel warm. Perhaps your feet feel grounded. Maybe you can feel the gentle rhythm of your own breathing. Linger here. Savor this sensation of okay-ness, of ease. Let it fill your awareness. This is your anchor in the present moment, your resource of safety.

After a minute or so, gently swing your attention back to the place of activation for just a moment. Then, swing back to the place of ease. You are the conductor of your own experience, creating a new neural pathway that says, *“Even when there is discomfort, there is also ease. I can hold both.”* You are teaching your body, in its own language, that it has the capacity to navigate challenge and return to a state of balance.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

**Step 4: Co-Regulation with Self**

As infants, our nervous systems learn regulation through the calm presence of our caregivers—this is co-regulation. When a baby cries, a loving parent picks them up, holds them close, and speaks in soothing tones. The baby’s nervous system, through the process of resonance, begins to mirror the calm of the parent. As adults, we can offer this same gift to ourselves.

Place one hand on your heart and the other on your belly. Feel the warmth of your own touch. This simple act is a profound signal of safety to your body. It says, *“I am here with you. You are not alone.”* Breathe into your own hands. Feel the gentle rise and fall of your chest and abdomen. Imagine your breath is a soft, loving wave, washing through you, cleansing, soothing. Stay here for as long as it feels good. You are, in this moment, becoming the compassionate caregiver your nervous system has always longed for. You are re-parenting yourself, not from a place of lack, but from a place of profound and gentle presence.

## Your Daily Practice

It is a practice, this journey of nervous system healing. It is not a one-time fix. The pathways of fear were laid down over a lifetime; the pathways of safety are built with gentle, consistent repetition. Neuroplasticity, the brain’s amazing ability to rewire itself, is on your side. Every time you practice these simple exercises, you are carving new neural grooves. You are strengthening the pathways of calm, of resilience, of self-compassion.

My invitation to you is to create a small, daily ritual of connection with your body. It doesn’t have to be long. Perhaps it’s five minutes in the morning before you get out of bed, placing a hand on your heart and simply breathing. Perhaps it’s a moment in your car before you walk into your home, humming to yourself to release the day.

What matters is the consistency of your return. You are showing your body, through sensation and presence, that you are a safe harbor. You are teaching it, with infinite patience, that the war is over. That it can finally, finally, come to rest.

It is from this place of inner safety that true connection becomes possible—connection with ourselves, with others, and with the great, mysterious flow of life itself. It is from here that we can begin to truly live, not just survive.


---

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [The Sacred Central Channel: What Your Spine Communicates](/blog/spine-sacred-central-channel)
- [Releasing the Ego's Throne: Your Head as Servant, Not Master](/blog/head-releasing-ego)

**More on Nervous System:**

- [The Electrical Network of Safety: Your Nervous System's Story](/blog/nervous-system-electrical-network)
- [Fight, Flight, Freeze: When Your Nervous System Runs the Show](/blog/nervous-system-fight-flight-freeze)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
keyThemes: Somatic attunement: listening to the body’s language of sensation
Grounding and felt contact as signals of safety
Vagal toning through gentle humming
Pendulation: oscillating attention between activation and ease
Self co-regulation and compassionate re-parenting
Neuroplasticity and building new pathways of calm
Practical, brief rituals for daily nervous system care
reflectionPrompts: Recall a recent moment when your body felt internally agitated despite an outwardly calm setting. Where did you feel that activation in your body, and what small contact or sensation could you offer that would signal safety right now?

Without needing to tell the whole story, notice early or repeated experiences that may have trained your nervous system to expect threat. What physical sensations arise as you hold that awareness, and how might a gentle, nonjudgmental presence shift those sensations over time?

Consider your daily rhythm: what is one very small, realistic ritual (2–5 minutes) you could do consistently to practice signaling safety to your nervous system? Where and when will you place it so it becomes a reliable anchor?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a quiet seated place with your feet on the floor. 1) Arrival (30–60 seconds): soften into the points of contact—feet on the floor, weight in the chair—simply notice without changing. 2) Vagal hum (5 gentle breaths): inhale comfortably; on each exhale make a low, soft “mmmm” and feel the vibration in your chest and throat. 3) Pendulation (2–3 cycles): briefly bring attention to a small place of tension (5–10 seconds), then shift to a neutral or pleasant place (20–30 seconds); alternate two or three times. 4) Co-regulation with self (1–3 minutes): place one hand on your heart and the other on your belly, breathe into your hands, and offer a kind, steady presence. End by widening your attention to the room. If you feel overwhelmed at any point, pause the practice and seek support as needed. This supportive practice is not a substitute for medical or mental health care.
sensitiveContentNotes: The article touches on childhood wounding, chronic activation, and emotional pain; these topics can bring up strong feelings. You have permission to pause, shorten, or stop any practice at any time.
If this material surfaces intense memories, dissociation, or distress, consider doing practices with a qualified somatic therapist or mental health professional and prioritize safety and grounding.

This practice is presented as supportive self-care and is not a substitute for medical or mental health treatment; consult your healthcare provider if you have significant physical symptoms, psychiatric concerns, or are in crisis.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Flow of Completion: Transcending Bladder Patterns
teachings.title: The Flow of Completion: Transcending Bladder Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan frames common bladder complaints as embodied expressions of long-held patterns of control, shame, and the learned habit of holding in bodily and emotional needs. She invites a compassionate, curious rewiring—through breath, somatic softening, and inner caregiving—to restore a natural capacity for release and completion.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a story I tell sometimes, about a woman who came to me convinced she was falling apart.

We learn so early to control ourselves, to hold it all in. Crying, shouting, laughing too loudly, even the simple, honest functions of our own bodies. I remember being a little girl, maybe four or five, at a large family gathering. The room was filled with the low hum of adult voices, the clinking of glasses, and the scent of my grandmother’s perfume. I had that sudden, urgent feeling. I needed to go. But I was shy, standing in the doorway in my patent leather shoes, and everyone seemed so important, so absorbed in their conversations. I didn’t want to interrupt, to be a bother. So I held it. I crossed my legs, I squeezed, I tried to will the feeling away, my small body rigid with the effort of containing a simple, natural truth. Of course, it didn’t work. The inevitable happened—a warm rush of shame that was far more disruptive than just quietly asking to be excused would have been. My mother was kind, but the feeling of failure, of my body betraying me in front of everyone, stayed with me for a long, long time.

How many of us have a version of that story? A moment where the natural, elegant function of our body became a source of shame or embarrassment? This is so often the story of the bladder—an organ system with the dual function of holding and releasing, and one that so often becomes a battleground for control, revealing our deepest conflicts around letting go.

## The Reservoir of Release

The bladder is a remarkable organ, a muscular reservoir designed to patiently collect what the kidneys have filtered from our internal ocean, and then, at the right moment, to release it completely. It’s a simple, elegant dance of filling and emptying, of gathering and letting go. Yet for so many of us, this dance is fraught with complication. We develop patterns of holding on, of clenching against the natural flow, not just physically, but emotionally and energetically.

In my work, I’ve seen it time and time again. The client with recurring cystitis, that feeling of being “burned” by life, by relationships, by unmet expectations. She’d spent years in a marriage where her needs were secondary, holding back her own desires to keep the peace, and her body was screaming the truth of it in fiery bursts of pain. Or the man with a constant, nagging urgency, a successful executive terrified of losing control in a board meeting. His entire life was built on a foundation of impeccable control, and his bladder was in open rebellion against the tyranny of his own mind. This isn’t just a physical issue; it’s the body speaking a profound truth. It’s the physical manifestation of a conflict that lives deep within our consciousness.

We hold in the tears that need to be cried after a loss, believing we must be strong for others. We hold in the anger that needs to be acknowledged when a boundary is crossed, fearing we’ll be seen as difficult. We hold in the words of love that need to be spoken, afraid of vulnerability. We do this because, at some point, we learned that letting go was not safe. We learned that our natural expressions were “too much” for others. We learned that to be loved, to be accepted, we had to control ourselves, to keep the messy, inconvenient parts of our humanity tucked away. This creates a tremendous amount of internal pressure, a constant, low-grade clenching in our systems. The body, in its infinite wisdom, reflects this back to us. The bladder, the very organ of release, becomes tight, irritated, and inflamed.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Tyranny of Control

This pattern of control is often rooted in our earliest experiences. As children, our survival depends on the love and approval of our caregivers. We are wired for connection. When our authentic expressions—our tears, our anger, our wild joy—are met with impatience, punishment, or withdrawal, we learn a powerful lesson. The brain, in its desire to keep us safe and connected, begins to build neural pathways of suppression. These are not conscious decisions; they are brilliant, adaptive strategies for survival. We become masters of holding it all in, experts in the art of self-containment.

The problem is that these neural pathways, once paved, become our default setting. We carry them into adulthood, long after the original threat has passed. We continue to clench and control, unconsciously expecting that this is what will keep us safe, what will earn us love. We might have a deep-seated belief that if we just manage ourselves perfectly, if we never let anyone see our mess, then we will finally be worthy of the happy ending we’ve been longing for. But life doesn’t work that way. And the body, our sacred messenger, will always, always tell the truth.

When we live in a state of chronic holding, we are essentially stuck in a low-level sympathetic nervous system response—the “fight or flight” mode. Think of it as driving a car with the emergency brake engaged. Our muscles are tense, our breath is shallow, and our bodies are flooded with stress hormones like cortisol. This is utterly exhausting. It creates a burnout that isn’t just mental or emotional, but deeply physical. The bladder, in this environment, can’t function optimally. The delicate balance of filling and releasing is disrupted. The tissues become irritated, leading to that burning sensation, that constant, anxious urgency. It’s the body’s way of screaming, “I can’t hold anymore! The pressure is too much!”

## The Flow of Completion

So what is the way through? How do we transcend these deeply ingrained patterns of holding and control? The journey begins not with more force, but with a radical act of compassion. It begins with turning towards the pattern, not with judgment, but with a gentle curiosity. To acknowledge that this pattern of holding, this clenching, has served you. It was a brilliant strategy that helped you survive. You can thank it for its service, and then, with love, you can begin to let it go.

The invitation here is to embrace the flow of completion. To understand that release is not shameful; it is essential to health. It is the body’s natural way of maintaining balance. This isn’t just about urination; it’s about the flow of life itself. It’s about allowing emotions to move through you without getting stuck. It’s about speaking your truth with kindness and clarity. It’s about letting go of the exhausting expectation that you must control yourself to be loved.

This is the work of neuroplasticity. We can, quite literally, rewire our brains. By consciously choosing to relax, to breathe deeply, to allow our bodies to soften, we begin to create new neural pathways. We can teach our nervous systems that it is safe to be in a parasympathetic state—the “rest and digest” mode. It is in this state of deep relaxation that the body can heal. The inflammation can subside. The elegant, simple function of the bladder can be restored: a timely and easy filling and releasing, a letting go without blockage or burn.

Let’s try a small practice right now. Find a comfortable seat. Close your eyes if that feels good. Place a hand on your lower abdomen, below your navel. Just feel the warmth of your hand. Now, take a slow, deep breath in, and imagine that breath traveling all the way down to your hand, creating space and softness. As you exhale, make a soft “shhh” sound, and with it, consciously invite the muscles of your pelvic floor to soften, to release, to let go. Imagine a gentle, flowing river, moving without effort. Inhale softness, exhale release. Stay here for a few breaths. This is a way to begin a new conversation with your body, a conversation of safety and trust.

This is about taking full and complete responsibility for your own happiness, your own well-being. It’s about understanding that no one outside of you can give you the love and acceptance you seek. That is an inside job. It is about learning to mother yourself, to hold yourself with the same tenderness and compassion you would offer to that small child in her patent leather shoes. It is about whispering to that part of you, “It’s okay, beloved. You can let go now. I’ve got you.”

As we learn to release the need for control, as we allow life to flow through us without blockage, something miraculous happens. We find a deeper sense of peace, a more authentic sense of power. We are no longer at war with our own bodies. We become a clear channel for life’s energy to move through us, to express itself through us. We return to our original design: a being of flow, of grace, of completion.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [A Practice for Kidney Healing and Emotional Flow](/blog/kidneys-healing-practice)
- [Shame, Sexuality, and the Silencing of Creative Power](/blog/reproductive-shame-sexuality)
- [Rewiring for Safety: The Neuroscience of Nervous System Healing](/blog/nervous-system-rewiring-safety)

**More on Bladder:**

- [When Holding On Hurts: The Emotional Patterns Behind Bladder Issues](/blog/bladder-emotional-patterns)
- [A Guided Practice for Bladder Healing and Release](/blog/bladder-guided-practice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you find the courage to let go. May you trust the wisdom of your body and the beautiful, elegant flow of your own being. And may you know, in the deepest part of you, that you are worthy of love, not because you are perfect, but because you are you.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Sacred Exchange of Life Force: Your Lungs Speak
teachings.title: The Sacred Exchange of Life Force: Your Lungs Speak
teachings.summary: Susan invites the reader to regard the lungs as a sacred, two-way doorway between inner experience and the wider world — a place where grief, childhood patterns, and the life force itself are held and exchanged. She explains, in accessible physiological terms, how conscious breathing can shift the autonomic nervous system and create conditions for restoration, and offers a gentle practice to begin reclaiming a fuller, more nourishing breath. The piece is both poetic and practical, calling for tenderness and patience rather than force.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember standing on the wild, windswept coast of Vancouver Island, the air thick with the scent of salt and cedar. For days, I had been carrying a heavy feeling—a dense, formless grief that wasn’t entirely my own. It felt ancient, a sorrow of the land itself, and it had settled deep in my chest. Each breath felt shallow, a sip of air when my body craved a gulp. It was a familiar feeling, this constriction, one I had known in different forms throughout my life. It was the tightness in my chest as a young girl, trying to be good, to be quiet, to not take up too much space. It was the breath I held waiting for a difficult conversation to be over. It was the shallow sips of air during times of deep stress, my body unconsciously preparing for a threat that was more emotional than physical.

Standing there, with the Pacific roaring in my ears, I consciously dropped my awareness into my body, into the twin sacs of my lungs. I imagined them not as mere organs, but as sacred chambers, the place where my inner world met the vast, untamed atmosphere. With my next inhale, I didn’t just take in air. I drew in the wildness of the ocean, the resilience of the ancient trees, the very life force of the planet. And as I exhaled, I didn’t just release carbon dioxide. I released the grief, the constriction, the story that I was separate from the world around me. I breathed out, and the wind carried it away.

It’s a tricky business, this being human. We walk around with these incredible bodies, these intricate systems of wisdom, and so often we treat them like machines. We forget that they are alive, that they are speaking to us, that they are constantly engaged in a sacred dialogue with life itself. And nowhere is this dialogue more intimate, more constant, than in our lungs.

## The Two-Way Door of Being

Your lungs are the only organ system in your body that operates both automatically and under your conscious control. All day, all night, they breathe for you, a faithful, rhythmic exchange that sustains your life without a single thought. Yet, at any moment, you can step in. You can deepen your breath, you can hold it, you can change its pace and its texture. This is a profound and often overlooked power. It is the key to shifting your entire state of being, from the biochemical to the emotional to the spiritual.

From a neuroscience perspective, this is because the breath is a direct line to the autonomic nervous system—the command center for your body’s fight-or-flight and rest-and-digest responses. When you are stressed, anxious, or frightened, your breathing automatically becomes shallow and rapid, signaling to your body that you are in danger. This is the sympathetic nervous system at work, preparing you to run or fight. But when you consciously slow and deepen your breath, you activate the vagus nerve, the superhighway of the parasympathetic nervous system. This sends a powerful, body-wide message that cascades through your entire system: *You are safe. You can relax. You can heal.* The heart rate slows, blood pressure drops, digestion comes back online, and the immune system can focus on long-term repair. It is a physiological sigh of relief, initiated by your conscious choice to breathe deeply.

Think about that for a moment. With something as simple as a conscious breath, you can guide your body out of a state of alarm and into a state of restoration. You can quiet the frantic mind, soothe the anxious heart, and create the internal conditions for healing. This isn’t just a nice idea; it’s a biological reality. The neural pathways of your brain, the very chemistry of your blood, all shift in response to the rhythm of your breath. It is a form of the most beautiful and intimate alchemy, turning the lead of anxiety into the gold of presence.

But the wisdom of the lungs goes even deeper than the nervous system. They are the intimate interface between your inner world and the external atmosphere. With every single breath, you are drawing the outside world into the deepest parts of you. You are taking in the air that has been breathed by the trees, that has traveled across oceans, that has been part of the wind and the rain. You are, in a very real sense, breathing the world.

And in return, you are breathing yourself back out into the world. You are releasing what is no longer needed, what is toxic, what is ready to be transformed. This is the sacred exchange. It is a constant, life-sustaining dance of giving and receiving, of taking in and letting go. It is the universe breathing you, and you breathing the universe.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Language of the Lungs

When this sacred exchange is flowing freely, there is a sense of ease, of vitality, of being at home in your own skin. But when it is constricted, the body speaks in a different language. So many of us walk around in a state of chronic, low-grade breath-holding. We are afraid to take up space, to fully inflate with the gift of our own life force. We have been taught, in subtle and not-so-subtle ways, that it is safer to be small, to be quiet, to not want too much.

This pattern often begins in childhood. Perhaps you grew up in an environment where it wasn’t safe to have big feelings. Perhaps you learned to hold your breath to stifle your sobs, to swallow your anger, to make yourself invisible. These patterns become etched into our neural pathways, into the very tissues of our bodies. As adults, we may find ourselves struggling with anxiety, depression, or a pervasive sense of being stuck. We may feel suffocated by our lives, our relationships, our own minds. And all the while, our breath remains shallow, a quiet, unconscious echo of that original, protective impulse. We live our lives in a state of subtle, chronic oxygen deprivation, wondering why we feel so tired, so disconnected, so joyless.

Chronic lung conditions, from asthma to bronchitis, can also be the body’s way of expressing a deeper conflict. They speak of a feeling of being smothered, of not having enough space to breathe, of carrying a grief that is too heavy to bear. The lungs are where we hold our sorrow, our unspoken pain. When we cannot cry our tears, the lungs weep for us, filling with fluid, becoming inflamed, struggling to perform their vital function. Grief, in the language of the body, is a liquid. When it is not allowed to flow through our tears, it can settle in the lungs, creating a damp, heavy environment where pathogens can thrive and the light of our own life force struggles to shine through.

What would it be like, beloved, to allow yourself to breathe again? To consciously, deliberately, take in the full measure of your life? To trust that you are deserving of this vital energy, this inspiration? And to trust, equally, in your capacity to release what is not yours to carry? To let go of the old stories, the ancient griefs, the accumulated toxins of a life lived in a state of contraction?

This is not about forcing or striving. It is about allowing. It is about creating a space of safety within yourself, a space where the breath can finally, gently, deepen. It is about listening to the wisdom of your lungs, and honoring the sacred exchange they so faithfully perform, moment by moment.

## A Practice for Reclaiming Your Breath

I invite you to try a simple practice. Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down. Close your eyes, if that feels good to you. And for a few moments, simply notice your breath, without trying to change it at all. Notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest, the sensation of the air at your nostrils.

Now, gently, begin to deepen your inhale. Imagine you are drawing the breath all the way down to the base of your lungs, allowing your belly to soften and expand. And as you exhale, let it go with a soft sigh, a sound of release. Do this for several rounds, just gently deepening the inhale and softening the exhale.

As you continue to breathe in this way, bring your awareness to your lungs. You might even place your hands on your chest, feeling the movement of your breath beneath your palms. Send a feeling of gratitude to your lungs, for their tireless work, for their constant, faithful exchange of life force.

With your next inhale, imagine you are breathing in a quality that you need more of in your life. Perhaps it is peace. Perhaps it is courage. Perhaps it is simple, uncomplicated joy. Breathe it in, and feel it filling every cell of your body.

And as you exhale, imagine you are releasing something that is ready to be let go of. A fear. A worry. A belief that no longer serves you. Let it go with the out-breath, offering it back to the world to be transformed.

Continue this for as long as it feels nourishing. Breathing in what you need, breathing out what you are ready to release. This is the sacred exchange, in conscious practice. This is you, remembering your innate power to partner with your own life force, to become an active participant in your own healing and evolution.

Your breath is your anchor, your teacher, your most intimate companion on this human journey. It is always with you, a constant reminder of your connection to the source of all life. May you learn to honor it. May you learn to trust it. And may you allow it to lead you home, to the spacious, sacred center of your own being.

teachings.sourceTitle: When Your Head Wars with Your Heart: Finding Peace Between Them
teachings.title: When Your Head Wars with Your Heart: Finding Peace Between Them
teachings.summary: Susan describes the familiar inner conflict between a protective, thinking mind and the quieter, somatic intelligence of the heart, tracing how survival wiring and childhood experiences often privilege thought over felt knowing. She offers a compassionate, embodied practice for acknowledging the head’s protective role, dropping into the heart, and listening for nonverbal guidance so these parts can inform each other rather than remain at war. The piece emphasizes tender curiosity for the inner critic and the slow work of rebuilding trust with one’s own body-wisdom.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The question is not whether you are strong enough. You are. The question is whether you are willing to be soft enough.

And one of the most profound aspects, I’ve found, is navigating the space between the neck and the crown. The head. That three-pound universe, as some have called it, where so much of our identity, our thoughts, and our fears reside.

I remember a time, years ago, when my own head was a battlefield. I can still feel the cold, smooth surface of the wooden desk in my office, my hands clasped tightly on top of it, as I stared out at the Vancouver rain. I was at a crossroads in my healing practice, a point where every external sign pointed toward a particular path. It was the “sensible” choice, the one my colleagues were making, the one that promised financial stability and professional recognition. My mind had gathered all the evidence, constructed flawless arguments, and presented me with a logical, bulletproof case. It was a fortress of shoulds and supposed-tos, complete with charts and projections. My head was *convinced*.

And yet… my heart was a quiet, persistent ache. It wasn’t loud or demanding. It was a gentle, gravitational pull in a completely different direction. A direction that made no logical sense, that felt risky and uncertain and utterly unproven. It felt like stepping off a cliff with only the faith that I might grow wings. To my head, it was foolishness. To my heart, it was the only way home.

This is a war so many of us know intimately, isn’t it? The constant, exhausting tug-of-war between the intricate logic of the mind and the deep, non-verbal knowing of the heart. The head, with its library of past hurts and future fears, screams for control. It builds walls of knowledge, not for the joy of wisdom, but for the illusion of safety. It memorizes the rules, internalizes the criticisms, and becomes a relentless prosecutor, judging our every move against a set of standards we never consciously agreed to.

## The Head as Battlefield

Why does this happen? Why does this beautiful, miraculous brain so often become a place of conflict rather than a throne of clear consciousness? Part of the answer lies in our wiring. Our nervous systems are ancient, designed for survival. They are brilliant at scanning for threats, and the thinking mind—the neocortex—gets recruited for this mission. It learns early on to equate “figuring it out” with being safe. If I can just think my way through this, if I can just accumulate enough information, if I can just make the “right” decision, then I will be okay. Then I will be loved.

This pattern often begins in childhood. When we don’t feel seen or safe, we retreat into our minds. We become excellent students, voracious readers, keen observers of others. We learn to perform, to please, to perfect. This isn’t a flaw; it’s a brilliant adaptive strategy. The head becomes a sanctuary, a place where we can feel a sense of control in a world that feels uncontrollable. The pain comes when this strategy becomes our only strategy. The neural pathways become deep, well-worn grooves, and the voice of the head becomes the only one we trust.

I worked with a woman once, a brilliant lawyer, who suffered from debilitating migraines. She came to me as a last resort, having tried every medical intervention available. As we began to explore her inner world, it became clear that her head was a fortress. She had built an incredible career through sheer force of intellect, but her body was screaming. Her migraines, we discovered, were the physical manifestation of a lifetime of suppressed intuition. Her heart had been whispering to her for years that she needed to paint, to create, to live a life with more color and less rigidity. But her head, the highly-trained lawyer, dismissed this as inadmissible evidence. The pain in her head was her consciousness literally pressing against the constraints of her own beliefs about who she was allowed to be.

We forget that there is another kind of intelligence available to us. A wisdom that doesn’t speak in linear arguments but in sensation, in imagery, in a quiet and profound sense of *rightness*. This is the body’s wisdom. The heart’s knowing. It’s the intelligence that beats our heart without instruction and guides the migration of birds. It is our birthright. But when the head is at war, its noise drowns out this subtle, essential guidance. The head becomes a crown of thorns.

## The Tyranny of the Inner Critic

Fueling this war is the voice of judgment. That relentless inner critic that sounds so much like us, but is actually a collage of every critical voice we have ever internalized—a parent’s disappointment, a teacher’s correction, a culture’s impossible standards. It’s the voice that says, *You’re not smart enough. You’re not ready. You’ll make a fool of yourself. Who do you think you are?*

This voice is the head’s most powerful weapon in its war against the heart. It uses shame and fear to keep us small and safe within the confines of what is known. It convinces us that the heart’s desires are frivolous, dangerous, or selfish. It makes us believe that self-worth is something to be earned through intellectual achievement or flawless performance, rather than something that is inherent and unconditional.

And so we live in a state of perpetual division. We walk through our days with a silent battle raging within, feeling exhausted and disconnected, wondering why life feels so hard. We judge ourselves for our indecision, for our lack of clarity, for the very war that is being waged within us. It’s a painful, lonely place to be.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Finding Peace: A Practice

My own journey out of that battlefield was not a single, dramatic event. It was a slow, tender turning-towards. It was the practice of learning to listen differently. When my head presented its logical, fear-based case, I learned not to argue with it. Arguing, I discovered, just gives the warring mind more ammunition. Instead, I learned to say, “Thank you. I hear you. I know you are trying to protect me.”

This was a revelation. To treat the fearful mind not as an enemy to be vanquished, but as a scared part of myself that needed compassion. I started to create a space for a new kind of dialogue. If you feel called, I invite you to try this practice with me. It is a way to begin brokering peace between your own head and heart.

1.  **Find a quiet space.** Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a few deep, gentle breaths. Allow your body to settle. Feel the support of the chair or the floor beneath you.

2.  **Acknowledge the Mind.** Bring your awareness to your head. Notice the thoughts, the chatter, the arguments. Don’t try to stop them. Just observe them with a gentle curiosity. Imagine you are sitting on the bank of a river, watching the thoughts float by like leaves on the water. Silently, or out loud, say to your mind: “Thank you for all that you do. Thank you for trying so hard to keep me safe. I see you. I hear you.”

3.  **Drop into the Heart.** Now, gently shift your awareness from your head to your heart space, in the center of your chest. You might even place a hand over your heart to help focus your attention. Breathe into this space. Feel the warmth of your own hand. Don’t search for anything. Just rest here.

4.  **Ask and Listen.** With your awareness still centered on your heart, gently ask a question. It could be about a specific decision you’re facing, or a more general inquiry. Something like: “Heart, what do you know about this?” or “Heart, what do you need me to know right now?” Ask, and then listen. The answer may not come in words. It might be a feeling—expansion, warmth, a sense of peace. It might be an image, a color, a memory. It might be a single word. Trust whatever comes. It doesn’t need to make sense to your mind.

5.  **Receive and Integrate.** Whatever you receive from your heart, simply receive it without judgment. Breathe it in. Let it settle into your being. You don’t have to *do* anything with it right away. The simple act of listening is the healing. You are re-establishing a connection, rebuilding a bridge.

Slowly, painstakingly, I chose the heart’s path. And it was terrifying. My mind screamed in protest. But with every step I took, the ground rose to meet my feet. The path wasn’t easy or linear, but it was alive. It was authentic. It was mine.

This is the invitation for all of us. Not to silence the head, but to gently dethrone it as the sole authority. The brain is a magnificent tool, a faithful servant, but it makes a terrible master. The true throne of our being is the spacious, unified field of our own consciousness, where the head’s logic and the heart’s wisdom can finally meet and inform each other.

What would it be like to honor the head’s desire for safety while also honoring the heart’s call to wholeness? To see your thoughts not as absolute truth, but as clouds passing through the vast sky of your awareness? This is not a battle to be won, but a relationship to be nurtured. It is the sacred work of coming home to yourself.


---

And may you discover the profound peace that comes from walking in alignment with your own deepest truth, feeling the wisdom of your heart and the clarity of your mind dancing together in beautiful, sacred partnership.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
