teachings.sourceTitle: Self-Mothering: The Deepest Healing Your Breasts Can Offer
teachings.title: Self-Mothering: The Deepest Healing Your Breasts Can Offer
teachings.summary: Susan frames breast tenderness and changes as wise, embodied signals that often point to chronic depletion from caregiving and unmet needs. She weaves attachment neuroscience and neuroplasticity with the practice of "self-mothering," offering an invitation to receive one’s own care through small, tender acts that retrain the nervous system toward safety and replenishment.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A friend of mine, a beautiful, fiercely loving mother of two, called me in tears the other day. She had found a lump in her breast. A small, hard, pea-sized thing that sent a jolt of pure terror through her system. Her voice was tight with panic. "How can this be happening?" she whispered. "I do everything for my kids. I pour everything I have into them. My life is for them."

I listened, my heart aching with her fear. And I heard the deep, unspoken story beneath the words. The story of the modern mother, the devoted woman, trying so desperately to be the perfect, inexhaustible wellspring of love and care for others… while her own well runs dangerously dry. We spoke for a long time, and as she talked, a familiar landscape emerged—one I have traversed with so many women in my healing practice. It’s a landscape of profound generosity and quiet self-abandonment. A place where the needs of children, partners, parents, and even pets, are placed on a high altar, while one’s own needs are left like small, hungry ghosts at the gate. She told me about her days, a relentless marathon of school runs, meal prep, work deadlines, and bedtime stories, all while ignoring the persistent ache in her shoulders and the growing feeling of being invisible in her own life. 'I feel like a ghost,' she said, 'just moving through the motions of a life that belongs to everyone but me.' Her words hung in the air between us, a testament to a silent epidemic of depletion.

It’s a tricky business, this dance of nurturing. Especially for women. We are conditioned to give, to soothe, to offer the breast, literally and metaphorically. But what happens when the giving becomes a depletion? What happens when we mother everyone but ourselves?

The body, in its infinite wisdom, will always tell the truth. And the breasts, those sacred symbols of nourishment and connection, are often the first to speak up. They are the first to send a signal flare when the balance of giving and receiving has gone askew.

## The Echo in the Cells

When your breasts hurt, or when cysts develop, or when the tissue becomes dense and tender, it is not a punishment. It is not a failure. It is a message. A deeply intelligent, compassionate message from your body, asking you to come home to yourself.

The body is speaking of an imbalance in the sacred art of self-mothering. It’s pointing to a pattern of trying too hard to be the perfect, endless source for others, a role none of us can sustain. Because here is a profound truth: you cannot give what you do not allow yourself to receive.

This pattern often begins with a wound that is almost archetypal, a wound of separation that echoes in our very cells. The moment we are born, we leave the perfect oneness of our mother’s womb. We are thrust from a world of warmth and constant nourishment into a world of separation, of hunger, of need. That initial shock, that first cry… it’s a cry for reunion. A cry to return to that state of perfect, unconditional love.

For the rest of our lives, a part of us is searching for that feeling. We look for it in our partners, our children, our work. We try to *become* it for others, hoping that if we are the perfect mother, the perfect giver, we will somehow heal that primal wound within ourselves. But it’s an impossible task. We end up exhausted, resentful, and our bodies begin to protest. The breasts, the very emblem of that maternal nourishment, begin to store the unprocessed grief, the silent resentment, the unshed tears of our own unmet needs. The hard lumps, the tender spots… they can be seen as crystallized sorrow.

## Rewiring for Self-Reception

Here’s a very good thing to know: our brains are wired for connection. The neuroscience of attachment shows us how crucial early bonding is for creating neural pathways that tell us we are safe, loved, and that the world is a benevolent place. When we receive consistent, attuned care as infants, our nervous systems learn to settle into a state of calm and connection—what is known as the parasympathetic state.

But for many of us, that early wiring was… incomplete. Perhaps our own mothers were stressed, depleted, or carrying their own unhealed wounds. They did the best they could, but they couldn’t give us the constant, perfect attunement our infant nervous system craved. And so, we may have developed a baseline of anxiety, a subtle, lifelong feeling of not-quite-safe, of needing to *do* something to earn love and security.

This is not a life sentence. Not at all. The beauty of neuroplasticity—the brain’s incredible ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections—is that we can consciously create *new* pathways. We can, with intention and practice, teach our own systems the language of safety, of unconditional love, of deep, internal nourishment. This is the essence of self-mothering. It’s not just a nice idea; it’s a biological imperative for true health and wholeness. Every time you choose a self-honoring action, no matter how small, you are a pioneer, forging a new trail in your own neural landscape. You are telling your body, on a cellular level, that you are worthy of your own care.

It is the act of turning your own warm, compassionate attention inward. It is the practice of listening to your own needs with the same tenderness you would offer a beloved child. It is the radical act of allowing yourself to *receive*—from yourself.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

When you place a hand on your own heart, when you speak to yourself with kindness, when you allow yourself to rest when you are tired… you are literally sending signals of safety to your brain. You are activating the vagus nerve, the superhighway of the parasympathetic nervous system, which wanders through the body connecting the brain to the heart, lungs, and gut. A calm, toned vagus nerve is the biological foundation of feeling safe and connected. Simple acts of self-care—a warm bath, a slow, deep breath, a moment of quiet—are powerful vagal toners. You are also releasing oxytocin, the “love hormone,” the same hormone that floods a mother’s system when she holds her baby, creating feelings of bonding and love. You are, in a very real, biological sense, mothering yourself. This isn't just a metaphor; it's a physiological reality. You are actively shifting your body out of the fight-or-flight state of the sympathetic nervous system and into the 'rest-and-digest' state of the parasympathetic. This is where true healing happens. It is in this state of inner safety that the body can repair, regenerate, and release the stored tension that manifests as pain and dis-ease.

## An Inquiry for Your Heart

So, beloved one, I invite you into a gentle inquiry. Not with judgment, but with a soft and open curiosity. This isn’t about adding another ‘to-do’ to your already overflowing list. It’s about subtraction. It’s about letting go of the crushing weight of self-expectation and opening up to a more tender way of being with yourself. What would it be like to mother yourself today?

What if, just for a moment, you let go of the belief that you must be an inexhaustible source for everyone else? What if you acknowledged the deep well of your own needs?

Take a breath. Place your hands gently on your breasts. Feel the warmth of your own touch. This is not a gesture of examination or fear, but one of reverence. Of listening.

Ask your body, ask your heart: *What do you need from me today?*

Perhaps the answer is a cup of tea in the quiet of the morning, before anyone else is awake, savoring the warmth of the mug in your hands. Perhaps it’s a walk in nature, without a destination, your only goal to notice the way the light filters through the leaves. Perhaps it’s five minutes of simply breathing, feeling your own life force, your own precious existence, without the need to be productive or useful to anyone. It could be buying yourself the flowers you wish someone would bring you, or taking a nap without guilt, or simply saying ‘no’ to a request that would drain you. These are not indulgences; they are sacred acts of self-preservation.

Perhaps it’s the permission to grieve. To cry for the mothering you didn’t receive. To acknowledge the exhaustion of always being the strong one. To release the resentment that may have taken root in your tender tissues.

Self-mothering is not selfish. It is the most generous act you can undertake. When you fill your own well, your giving becomes a joyful overflow, not a painful depletion. You become a source-fed river that never runs dry, nourishing all those you love from a place of wholeness, not sacrifice.

Your body is not your enemy. It is your most devoted ally, your most sacred messenger. The tenderness in your breasts is a call to tenderness for your whole being. It is an invitation to the deepest healing you can offer yourself: the profound, unconditional, and ever-present love of the mother within.

May you answer the call with courage and grace. May you learn to receive your own love as the sacred nourishment it is.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Tidal Pool Within: How Cranial Fluid Carries Your Deepest Healing Intelligence
teachings.title: The Tidal Pool Within: How Cranial Fluid Carries Your Deepest Healing Intelligence
teachings.summary: Susan describes cerebrospinal fluid as a living, tidal intelligence that carries bodily memory and supports regulation, creativity, and healing. She weaves personal clinical stories with anatomical detail and traditional wisdom to invite readers to listen to their cranial rhythm and to create spaciousness for the body’s own restorative intelligence.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was lying on the treatment table when my cranial sacral therapist paused, her hands cradled gently beneath my head. "Do you feel that?" she whispered. "Your fluid is... singing."

I didn't know what she meant then — fifteen years ago, when I was still learning to listen to the subtle voices of the body. But as I lay there, something ancient and wordless began to pulse through me, like the memory of being held in the first waters of my mother's womb. The cerebrospinal fluid that bathes our brain and spinal cord wasn't just fluid, I realized. It was liquid intelligence... a tidal pool of consciousness carrying messages I'd never learned to read.

Here's a very good thing to know: within your skull and spine, approximately 150 milliliters of cerebrospinal fluid ebbs and flows in a rhythm as old as the ocean itself. This isn't just anatomical housekeeping — though Western medicine has long dismissed it as such. This fluid carries your deepest healing intelligence, the whispered wisdom of your nervous system, the very essence of what makes you... you.

## The Ocean Within Your Bones

Your cerebrospinal fluid moves in what we call the cranial rhythm — a gentle, tidal pulsation that occurs 8 to 12 times per minute, completely independent of your heartbeat or breathing. When I first felt this rhythm under my hands as a beginning practitioner, I wept. Here was proof that the body holds its own sacred calendar, its own mysterious timing that has nothing to do with our busy, linear world.

The fluid itself is produced in the choroid plexuses — tiny, fern-like structures in your brain's ventricles that work like the most sophisticated water purification system imaginable. Every drop is filtered from your blood, infused with exactly the right balance of electrolytes, glucose, and proteins your nervous system needs to thrive. Your brain literally bathes in this liquid light, and every four hours, the entire volume is renewed. Wow.

But here's where it gets truly fascinating — and where neuroscience meets the mystical. This fluid doesn't just nourish and protect; it carries information. Recent research has revealed that cerebrospinal fluid acts as a communication highway, transporting growth factors, hormones, and even waste products through what scientists now call the glymphatic system. It's like having a postal service for your consciousness, delivering messages between brain regions that we're only beginning to understand.

Your cranial bones — those eight intricately fitted plates that house your brain — expand and contract in microscopic movements with each cranial pulse. The temporal bones widen, the occiput lifts slightly, the sphenoid rocks in its ancient cradle. These movements, barely perceptible to the untrained hand, create the pressure changes that drive cerebrospinal fluid through its sacred circuits.

When I learned to feel these rhythms, I discovered something profound: each person's cranial pattern tells a story. Some move like gentle ocean waves, others like choppy waters after a storm. The fluid might feel thick and sluggish in someone carrying old grief, or electrically charged in a nervous system on high alert. Your tidal pool within reflects not just your current state, but the accumulated wisdom — and trauma — of your entire life.

## The Sacred Messenger System

Here's the point: your body is a sacred messenger, and cerebrospinal fluid is one of its most eloquent voices. But we've forgotten how to listen.

In traditional Chinese medicine, practitioners speak of the "Sea of Marrow" — a concept that beautifully captures what Western anatomy calls the central nervous system. This sea, they understood, needed to flow freely for health and vitality to flourish. When the sea became stagnant, illness followed. When it flowed clear and strong, the person embodied their fullest potential.

Modern neuroscience is finally catching up to this ancient wisdom. We now know that restricted cerebrospinal fluid flow contributes to everything from headaches and learning difficulties to depression and chronic fatigue. The fluid's movement affects the Default Mode Network — that constellation of brain regions active during rest and introspection. When cerebrospinal fluid flows freely, our capacity for self-reflection, creativity, and emotional regulation expands. When it's restricted, we might feel stuck, foggy, or disconnected from our inner knowing.

I remember working with Maria, a teacher who'd suffered from debilitating migraines for twelve years. "It feels like my head is in a vise," she told me, pressing her palms against her temples. When I placed my hands on her cranium, her fluid felt almost... frozen. The gentle tide that should have been rocking through her nervous system was barely detectable.

As we worked together over several sessions, something beautiful began to happen. The microscopic movements of her cranial bones started to restore themselves. Her cerebrospinal fluid began its ancient dance again — slowly at first, then with increasing vitality. Maria's migraines didn't just improve; her entire relationship with stress transformed. "I feel like I'm thinking clearly for the first time in years," she marveled.

This is what happens when we honor the body as a sacred messenger. The symptoms that feel like enemies — the headaches, the brain fog, the inexplicable fatigue — are actually communications from our deepest intelligence. Your cerebrospinal fluid is trying to tell you something. Are you listening?

Many spiritual teachers, including [those like Paul Wagner who understand the body as a temple of consciousness](https://paulwagner.com), recognize that healing happens not when we override our symptoms, but when we create spaciousness for our body's own wisdom to emerge. Your tidal pool within holds this wisdom — the accumulated intelligence of millions of years of evolution, the memory of every ancestor who survived long enough to pass their gifts to you.

## When the Tide Gets Stuck

Sometimes, though, our internal tides get stuck. Birth trauma can compress the delicate bones of an infant's skull, creating restrictions that last decades. A car accident might jar the cervical vertebrae, disrupting the fluid's flow through the spinal cord. Even emotional trauma — that heartbreak at sixteen, the loss of a parent, the chronic stress of an impossible job — can create holding patterns in the cranial system that affect cerebrospinal fluid dynamics.

Here's what's particularly beautiful about this system: it remembers everything, but it also knows how to heal. Your cerebrospinal fluid carries not just the imprints of old injuries, but the blueprint for your restoration. Every cell in your nervous system is bathed in this liquid intelligence, receiving moment-by-moment instructions for repair, growth, and adaptation.

The key is learning to create the conditions for this natural healing to unfold. In cranial sacral therapy, we don't fix anything — we simply listen with our hands, offering a quality of presence that allows the body's inherent wisdom to express itself. It's like becoming a meditation partner for someone's nervous system.

I've felt cerebrospinal fluid that moves like honey — slow and golden in someone who's been holding grief for years. I've felt it sparkle like champagne in a child's system, effervescent with possibility. I've felt it nearly stop entirely in adults who've forgotten how to play, how to wonder, how to let life move through them with ease.

But here's the miracle: I've also felt these restricted patterns begin to shift the moment someone feels truly seen, truly held. The cerebrospinal fluid seems to respond not just to physical touch, but to the quality of attention it receives. When we approach the body with reverence, with curiosity rather than judgment, with the understanding that it holds our deepest wisdom... something sacred awakens.

## The Rhythm of Remembering

Your cranial rhythm is as unique as your fingerprint, yet it connects you to something universal. In those moments when I'm working with someone and their cerebrospinal fluid begins to flow with renewed vitality, I'm reminded that we're all part of one vast ocean of consciousness. The same minerals that flow through your nervous system once flowed through ancient seas. The same tidal forces that move the waters of the earth move the waters within your bones.

This rhythm — this gentle, persistent pulse of life — continues whether we're aware of it or not. But when we begin to attune to it, something profound shifts. We start to live in greater harmony with our own natural timing. We begin to trust the body's wisdom rather than overriding it with our busy minds. We remember that we are not machines to be optimized, but living systems designed to self-regulate, self-heal, and continuously evolve.

In my practice, I've noticed that people who develop a conscious relationship with their cranial rhythm often report feeling more grounded, more creative, more able to navigate life's challenges with grace. They sleep better. They think more clearly. They feel more connected to their intuition and less driven by anxiety or compulsion.

This makes perfect sense when you understand that cerebrospinal fluid carries not just nutrients, but information about your nervous system's state of regulation. When the fluid flows freely, it's constantly updating your brain about safety, connection, and possibility. When it's restricted, those same neural networks might default to patterns of protection, hypervigilance, or disconnection.

Here's a simple practice you can try: Place one hand on your heart and one on the base of your skull, where your head meets your neck. Close your eyes and breathe naturally. Don't try to feel anything specific — just rest in this gentle contact with your own nervous system. Sometimes, if you're very quiet and very patient, you might sense a subtle quality of movement, like the gentlest tide washing through you. This is your cerebrospinal fluid, carrying its ancient wisdom, whispering your deepest truths.

## The Intelligence of Integration

What continues to amaze me, after all these years of working with the cranial system, is how intimately connected it is to every aspect of our being. The same cerebrospinal fluid that bathes our brain also surrounds every nerve in our body. It's the medium through which our nervous system communicates with itself — a liquid network of consciousness that integrates sensation, emotion, memory, and insight into the coherent experience we call "self."

When this system is flowing optimally, integration happens naturally. We can feel our emotions without being overwhelmed by them. We can access our memories without being trapped in the past. We can sense the subtle energies of others without losing our own center. We become more ourselves — not because we've added anything, but because we've removed the obstacles to our natural radiance.

I think of cerebrospinal fluid as the body's meditation practice — a constant, gentle reminder to come back to center, to flow with life rather than against it, to trust the deeper rhythms that guide our healing and growth. In our culture of constant stimulation and perpetual hurry, reconnecting with this inner tide can feel like coming home to ourselves.

The neural pathways that govern our stress response, our capacity for joy, our ability to form secure attachments — all of these are influenced by the health of our cerebrospinal fluid system. When we create conditions for optimal flow, we're not just addressing physical symptoms; we're supporting our entire capacity for conscious, connected living.

## Trusting the Tide

Perhaps the most profound teaching of the cerebrospinal fluid system is about trust. This liquid intelligence knows exactly what it's doing, even when we don't understand its methods. It carries the accumulated wisdom of your entire lineage — not just genetic information, but the energetic imprints of every healing your ancestors achieved, every limitation they transcended, every moment of grace they embodied.

Your tidal pool within is ancient and eternal, personal and transpersonal, scientific and mystical all at once. It connects you to the first waters of creation while supporting the most sophisticated neural networks in the known universe. It carries your deepest wounds and your greatest possibilities in the same gentle embrace.

This is why cranial sacral work can feel so profoundly moving, so unexpectedly transformative. We're not just adjusting mechanical structures or manipulating fluid dynamics. We're entering into sacred partnership with the intelligence that created us, the wisdom that sustains us, the love that continues to heal us in ways our minds can barely comprehend.

Learning to listen to your cerebrospinal fluid is learning to trust your own deepest knowing. It's remembering that your body is not your enemy, but your most faithful ally. It's discovering that healing doesn't require you to fix anything, but simply to create spaciousness for your innate wholeness to reveal itself.

When I feel someone's cranial rhythm restore itself under my hands — when that sacred tide begins to flow with renewed vitality — I'm reminded again and again that nothing is beyond healing. We are not broken beings in need of repair, but whole beings temporarily forgetting our wholeness. Your cerebrospinal fluid never forgets. It carries the memory of your perfection even when you can't feel it, the blueprint of your healing even when you can't see it, the truth of your infinite worth even when you can't believe it.

In those quiet moments on the treatment table, when your inner tide is free to express its ancient wisdom, you might remember what you've always known: that you are held, you are loved, and you are exactly where you need to be in your journey of becoming fully, radically, beautifully yourself.

May you learn to trust the sacred intelligence that flows within your bones. May you honor your body as the temple it has always been. May you remember that your deepest healing wisdom has been with you all along, whispering its truth in the gentle rhythm of your own cerebrospinal tide.

With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Hips and Legs - The Foundation of Your Dance Through Life
teachings.title: Hips and Legs - The Foundation of Your Dance Through Life
teachings.summary: Susan invites you to regard hips and legs as both anatomical foundations and somatic metaphors: they ground you, translate intention into step, and hold stories of protection and stuckness. The piece maps how beliefs and survival strategies settle into tissue, offers gentle movement and inquiry practices, and emphasizes curiosity and compassion—especially when pain persists. It closes with a three-lens practice (purpose, inquiry, transcendence) to re-educate the nervous system toward fluidity and ethical action in the world.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Your hips and legs hold you in this world. They are the earth-facing edges of your human design, the bearing surfaces of courage and surrender, the arms with which your life reaches down and takes root. When you wake in the morning, before thought organizes itself into plans and duties, your hips and legs are doing something essential: they are trusting gravity, finding alignment, negotiating balance. They are silently declaring - I will stay here. I will move. I will bear weight. This simple, everyday dialogue between bone, muscle, tendon, and the earth is a sacred teaching if you are willing to listen.

The anatomy of a life lived on two feet

The hip is a marvel - a ball-and-socket union that invites freedom. It was not designed to be a hinge, narrow and single-purpose. It was conceived to move in every direction, to swivel and spin, to release and receive, to absorb shock and translate momentum into grace. Your legs are the foundation - long chains of osteo-muscular architecture that convert the pull of your deeper intentions into forward movement. From pelvis to toes, there is an economy of give and support that allows you to stand upright in your body and in your life. Consider how the hip can externally rotate to open to another, or internally rotate to pull back in; how the ankle subtly accommodates uneven ground so you can continue your path. These are not incidental features - they are metaphors made body.

Your body as a holographic map

Working with the body as messenger means you invite a different kind of intelligence into conversation. You know, at some level, that pain is information and restriction is a language. The same holographic principle described in the work you carry - that each part of your body reflects a pattern that reverberates through the whole - applies beautifully to hips and legs. Tightness in the hips often mirrors a life that has grown rigid in its stance. A limp can speak of shame that has become a hidden gait. Locked knees sometimes hold the posture of unyielding pride or a refusal to lower yourself in service, while swollen ankles may reflect the agitation of not feeling supported by your circumstances. In this way, your pelvis and lower limbs carry a ledger of your emotional and belief-based history, one written in muscle memory and posture instead of ink.

When you notice a physical theme - a chronic ache, a recurring injury, a subtle lack of mobility - it is less often an isolated defect and more often a message. The hips and legs, as the body's ultimate grounding rods, show you exactly where you have stopped dancing with life and begun to resist it. They tell you where you are over-weighted - not only with pounds - but with ideas, with "shoulds" and "musts," with negative beliefs that settle into tissue like sediment. Your legs speak to your ability to take the next step. Your hips speak to your capacity to pivot when the music changes.

Inflexibility in the body, inflexibility in life

Language gives you clues because idioms are distilled body wisdom. To have "no leg to stand on" names instability in argument and being. To "stand your ground" names resilience. To "bend the knee" names humility. When a body part articulates a phrase that becomes habitual in your life - when you habitually refuse to yield, or habitually fold in - the physical structure follows the narrative. The hip, so designed for rotation, will calcify into a narrower range if you insist on one way of being. It will tighten around habitual positions and refuse novelty. The legs will be reluctant to step into unknown ground if you have told yourself for decades that the world is unsafe, that you cannot trust others, that adventure is reckless. These beliefs do not float ethereally outside you - they weigh down like stones and are experienced by ligaments and fascia as load.

Because the hips are ball-and-socket joints, they offer you the possibility of spaciousness - to change direction without experiencing catastrophe. Yet the body will only give you that fluidity when your nervous system feels it is safe to do so. Many people who cannot pivot in life have hips that can hardly rotate a handful of degrees. This is not an accident. It is a living negotiation between past survival strategies and present possibilities. The legs become defensive columns when your inner world has learned to fortify itself against disappointment. The way you hold your pelvis when angry, or the way you tighten your quadriceps when anxious, are the somatic echoes of old paradigms that kept you alive when you were small - paradigms that now ask to be revisited and sometimes revised.

Negative beliefs - the invisible weights

There is a kind of weight that sits invisibly in the hips - a cultural, familial and personal burden that feels like gravity made personal. You may carry beliefs that your needs are a burden, that pleasure is indulgent, that to ask is to risk abandonment. Such beliefs gather momentum and density; they become chronic tension that calcifies into restrictions. You might notice this as difficulty in sitting comfortably, as a shallow stride, as back pain that traces up into the heart. The legs then work overtime to compensate, to provide a stable base for a torso that has learned to hunch and protect. Over time, this compensation becomes the story your nervous system auto-plays. It is what you reach for without thinking.

And yet your hips and legs are not merely containers of difficulty. They are also conduits of reclamation. Because these joints are meant to engage with gravity, they can teach you how to use weight instead of fight it. When you begin to interrogate the beliefs that act as ballast - when you listen with curiosity rather than condemnation - those same structures can become energetic levers. Imagine negative beliefs not as chains but as dense clouds that are visible when you practice discernment. Bring breath toward the hips and allow the inhale to expand the space around those clouds, the exhale to silently invite slight loosenings. Over time, with sustained, compassionate awareness, weight becomes manageable. You will learn to dance with it rather than be dragged by it.

Invitation to dance - not as escape but as integration

There is a Taoist teaching that I return to when the lower body feels rigid: "Nothing in the world is softer or more yielding than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong there is nothing better." Allow this image to sit in your bones. Water yields. Water moves, curving around obstacles, wearing down stone without force. Your hips and legs can be like water - holding you and moving you without unnecessary hardness. The dance I speak of is not performance. It is not about showing that you can be spry. It is an invitation to relearn fluidity in how you approach life - to relearn how to give way when required, and to stand firmly when needed, but without turning standing into stubbornness.

You can begin to practice this in small, embodied ways. Stand and feel your feet on the floor as if you are meeting an old friend. Notice the weight distribution between heels and balls of the feet. Allow your knees to micro-bend - not collapsing, not locked - but alive. Gently shift your pelvis forward and back, left and right, just enough to feel the hip sockets glide. Let your breath be slow and curious, the exhale softening whatever held tension arises. This is the dance of attunement - a tiny, reverent practice of registering what the ground offers and how your body receives it. Over weeks, these small acts accumulate into a new neurological narrative: you are allowed to move. You are allowed to change direction. You are allowed to keep going despite the music changing.

Listening through the three lenses - purpose, inquiry, transcendence

There is a gentle framework you can use to deepen this relationship, one that echoes the three-card process I have worked with in many practices - purpose, inquiry, transcendence. Begin with purpose: feel the hip, feel the leg, sense their physiological function and appreciate it. Place your hand there and say aloud, "Thank you for keeping me upright." Allow gratitude to be the first water poured onto hardened ground - gratitude is often the solvent that starts the loosening. Then move to inquiry: with tenderness and curiosity, ask the parts what story they are holding. Where does the tightness want to be seen? What memory surfaces when you release that muscle? You may notice an image, a phrase, a sense of déjà vu. Do not interpret quickly. Stay present. Finally, arrive at transcendence: imagine the healed possibility not as a fix but as an opening. What would it be like to move through life with hips that are supple and a stride that trusts the earth? Speak that possibility into being. Let your body rehearse it with small movements, each one a prayer for a new habit.

Rituals of practical tenderness

There are practices that invite the hips to soften and the legs to remember their purpose. Walk deliberately - not as exercise to punish the body but as an offering to re-educate the nervous system. In each step, sense the ankle giving slightly, the knee accepting a small hinge, the hip negotiating direction. Let your breath and your feet be in conversation - inhale to collect, exhale to forward. Move into gentle rotations from the hip joint, not forcing the range, only approximating and then returning with compassion to what is available. If pain spikes, do not push. Pain can be a guard, not an enemy; treat it as you would a trembling child who has learned to protect itself. Speak soothing words. Give it time.

Another tender practice is the dialog of the body. Place both hands on your pelvis and imagine the tissue speaking. Ask, "What do you need from me to feel safe enough to soften?" Listen without rushing to answer. You may feel warmth, a micro-sigh, or a sense of remembering. Sometimes the answer will be a tangible change to daily habits - release high heels if they compress the ankle, change sleeping position, allow longer warm-ups before strenuous movement. Other times the answer is invisible - forgiveness to a caregiver, a boundary you finally articulate to a partner, a decision to move in a new direction. The body knows these as they influence how it can breathe, rotate, and bear weight.

When limitation remains - compassion over guilt

I must also hold a space of compassion for those who, despite everything, still live with persistent pain. There are lives in which some physical challenges are part of the soul’s plan - not a verdict on your worth, but part of a larger trajectory of learning and devotion. If your hips or legs continue to restrict you, do not turn this into another failing to be corrected with will alone. Patience, wise medical support, and a loving relationship with your limits often create more liberation than fierce insistence. Remember, the healing path is not always linear; sometimes the deepest lessons come through the counterintuitive route of learning to love what is rather than only striving to change it.

The ethics of movement - how you meet the world

Your relationship with your lower body extends into the moral and relational. How you allow your legs to carry you into action is related to how you carry commitment and responsibility in life. Do you take a step when required? Do you stand for someone who cannot stand for themselves? Do you pivot when new information asks you to reorient? These are not abstract virtues; they are somatic habits. When you choose to soften the hip that had become rigid with righteousness, you are choosing to let go of a small tyranny of self. When you train the ankle to be responsive in unstable terrain, you are cultivating trust - trust in the ground, trust in the present, trust in your capacity to adapt. This is the moral life embodied: humility and courage in equal measure, practiced through footfalls and bone memory.

A final word - the dance continues

The invitation that your hips and legs extend is simple and radical at the same time: learn to dance with whatever life brings. This dance is not an evasion of difficulty. It is a reorientation toward flexibility, toward accepting gravity as teacher rather than enemy. It is an ethic of soft power - like water finding its way through stone - and a reclamation of the body as a partner in wisdom. Allow your hips to remember their design - ball to socket, moving in all directions - and let your legs be the rods of grounding that give you confidence to step into the world. Speak to them with gratitude, listen with steady curiosity, and move with tenderness. When you do, you will find that you have more room to receive, more capacity to pivot, and a truer freedom to dance your life in your own, sovereign rhythm.

And when you feel unsure, return to the simple line from the Tao: "By letting go it all gets done." Let the letting go be embodied - a release through joint and breath and step - and notice how your life begins, quietly and insistently, to rearrange itself into a new, more fluid form. I will be watching the earth in your footprints, and I will keep making space for you to learn the music.

teachings.sourceTitle: Becoming the Conductor: Orchestrating Your Entire Being
teachings.title: Becoming the Conductor: Orchestrating Your Entire Being
teachings.summary: Susan uses the image of a conductor to invite readers to unite the fractured parts of their inner life — mind, heart, body, and spirit — into a coherent, listening field. She names how modern life, stress, and even chronic illness can fragment our internal orchestra and offers a path back through mindful presence, somatic attention, and compassionate curiosity. The piece encourages a daily practice of returning to the podium: listening first, honoring each part, and collaborating rather than silencing what arises.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The velvet hush of the concert hall holds its breath. A thousand souls lean forward, a collective vessel waiting to be filled. From the wings, I watch the conductor stride to the podium—a small, still point in a sea of potential. With a flick of the wrist, a universe of sound erupts. The soaring cry of the violins, the deep heartbeat of the cello, the triumphant brass… each instrument a voice, a color, a world unto itself. But it is the conductor who gathers them, who weaves their individual truths into a single, magnificent tapestry of harmony. She doesn’t play a single note, and yet, she is the music itself. She is the space, the silence, the intention that allows the symphony to be born.

For so many years, I felt like a discordant orchestra. My mind, a frantic first violin, sawing away with worry and what-ifs. My heart, a muffled drum, beating a rhythm of old grief I couldn’t quite name. My body… my body was the forgotten instrument, the one left in its case in the dusty attic, its strings slack, its wood unpolished. I lived in a state of internal cacophony, a constant, low-grade static of disconnection. One part of me would be striving for success, another whispering of exhaustion. One part would crave connection, while another built walls of self-protection. It was a symphony of fragmentation, and I was a conductor who had long since abandoned the podium.

This is the reality for so many of us, isn’t it? We are taught to compartmentalize. We have our “work self,” our “parent self,” our “social self.” We numb the body’s whispers with caffeine, sugar, and endless scrolling. We silence the heart’s longings with logic and practicality. We allow the mind’s anxieties to drown out the soul’s quiet wisdom. Every pattern, every coping mechanism, has served a purpose—it has helped us survive. But what if we are ready for more than just survival? What would it be like to not just live, but to live in harmony? To become the conductor of your own magnificent, messy, miraculous being?

Quantum physics whispers a profound truth that ancient wisdom has always known: at the most fundamental level, we are not separate parts, but a unified field of consciousness. Think of it as the “Web of Your Being.” It’s not a single organ or system, but the miraculous totality of you—the energetic, emotional, physical, and spiritual threads woven together. This web is the silent, intelligent field that holds every cell, every thought, every memory. When this field is coherent, we experience flow, vitality, and a deep sense of wholeness. When it’s fragmented, we feel the familiar pangs of self-disconnection, dissociation, and that nagging sense that we are not quite “all there.”

Neuroscience offers us a beautiful map of this process. When we are stressed or traumatized, our brain patterns become incoherent. The amygdala, our internal alarm system, hijacks the prefrontal cortex, the seat of our higher reasoning—our inner conductor. We get stuck in fight, flight, or freeze. The different sections of our orchestra are no longer listening to each other. The brass section of anger might be blaring so loudly that we can’t hear the gentle flute of compassion. The somber cellos of sadness might overwhelm the playful piccolo of joy. The work isn’t to silence any of these instruments. Every single one has a place in your symphony. The work is to return to the podium.

Perhaps the first step is simply to listen. To pause, right now, and close your eyes. Can you hear the rhythm of your own breath? Can you feel the steady, faithful beat of your heart? These are the foundational rhythms of your orchestra. They are always there, a homing signal back to yourself. What if, for just a moment, you allowed yourself to be the space for it all? The anxiety, the joy, the fatigue, the hope. Not judging, not fixing, just… listening. This is the essence of mindfulness, of presence. It is the conductor turning to face the orchestra, baton in hand, ready to begin.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

Once you begin to listen, you might start to notice the more subtle players in your orchestra. The tightness in your shoulders—what is that telling you? It’s not just a physical sensation; it’s a voice. Perhaps it’s the voice of overwhelm, the part of you that has been carrying too much for too long. The flutter in your stomach—is it anxiety, or is it the thrill of a new possibility? We spend so much time in our heads, analyzing and interpreting, that we forget the profound intelligence of the body. Your body is a Stradivarius, a magnificent instrument capable of expressing the full spectrum of human experience. But you must learn to play it. You must learn its language.

I remember a time when my own body’s whispers had become screams. For years, I had ignored a deep, aching fatigue, pushing through with sheer force of will. I was a conductor demanding a relentless tempo, ignoring the exhausted musicians. Finally, my body put its foot down. I was diagnosed with a chronic illness that forced me to stop, to rest, to finally listen. It was a brutal, humbling, and ultimately… a sacred process. I had to learn to tune in to the subtlest of cues. A wave of dizziness was a signal to lie down. A feeling of warmth in my hands was a sign of gentle energy flow. Slowly, painstakingly, I began to rebuild the relationship with my own embodied being. I learned that my body wasn’t betraying me; it was desperately trying to communicate with me. It was inviting me back into wholeness.

This journey from fragmentation to unity is not a one-time event. It is a practice, a daily returning. It is choosing to hear the whisper before it becomes a scream. It is treating yourself with the same reverence and attention that a conductor gives her orchestra. What would it be like to ask your mind, “What beautiful thoughts do you have for me today?” To ask your heart, “What are you longing to express?” To ask your body, “What nourishment do you need?” This is not about control; it is about collaboration. It is about creating a space of infinite love and acceptance for every part of you.

You are the unified field of consciousness experiencing itself through the magnificent instrument of your embodied being. You are the music and the listener, the dancer and the dance. The symphony of your life is playing right now. The question is, are you at the podium? Are you ready to pick up the baton and lead yourself into the most exquisite harmony you have ever known? The world is waiting to hear your unique and beautiful song.

teachings.sourceTitle: Simplicity, Patience, and Compassion: Sitting With All of Who We Are
teachings.title: Simplicity, Patience, and Compassion: Sitting With All of Who We Are
teachings.summary: Susan reflects on a verse from the Tao Te Ching—simplicity, patience, compassion—and describes how these principles invite us to welcome the full range of our interior life, including the parts we habitually exile. She emphasizes somatic presence: that real understanding comes through the body as we learn to sit with difficult feelings rather than suppress them. The practice she offers is an ongoing, relational path that transforms reactivity into inner freedom and deep acceptance.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a verse in the Tao Te Ching that has lived inside me for decades. It has been a companion through my darkest nights and my most luminous mornings, a quiet thread woven through every session I have ever held, every hand I have ever placed on a trembling body. Lao Tzu writes:

> I have just three things to teach:
> simplicity, patience, compassion.
> These three are your greatest treasures.

When I first read those words, I was a young woman sitting cross-legged on the floor of a tiny apartment, surrounded by books and candles and a desperate hunger to understand why life hurt so much. I thought I understood them immediately. Simplicity — keep things simple. Patience — wait for things to get better. Compassion — be kind to others. Check, check, check. I could do that. I could *master* that.

Oh, how little I knew.

It has taken me a lifetime to begin to understand what Lao Tzu was actually pointing toward, and the understanding has not come through my mind. It has come through my body, through my bones, through the slow, sometimes agonizing process of sitting with everything I did not want to feel.

## The Tao Does Not Take Sides

There is another verse that cracks open the comfortable illusion most of us carry around like a security blanket:

> The Tao doesn't take sides;
> it gives birth to both good and evil.
> The Master doesn't take sides;
> she welcomes both saints and sinners.

Read that again, slowly. Let it land in your body, not just your mind.

The Tao — the great creative intelligence of the universe, the source from which all life springs — does not take sides. It does not sort the world into neat columns of acceptable and unacceptable, worthy and unworthy, light and dark. It gives birth to *all of it*. The saint and the sinner emerge from the same womb. The tenderness and the rage arise from the same source. The part of you that loves with fierce devotion and the part of you that wants to slam the door and walk away — they are both children of the Tao.

This is not a comfortable teaching. It is, in fact, deeply unsettling to the part of us that has spent a lifetime building walls between our "good" qualities and our "bad" ones. We have been taught, from the time we were very small, to identify with the saint and exile the sinner. To present our polished, acceptable face to the world and to lock the rest away in a dark closet, hoping no one — including ourselves — will ever look inside.

But the closet door never stays shut, does it?

It rattles in the night. It leaks. The exiled parts of ourselves find their way out through our sharp words, our sudden irritations, our inexplicable anxieties, our bodies that ache in places we cannot explain. They emerge in the friends who trigger us, the enemies who enrage us, and the quiet moments alone when we are flooded with feelings we cannot name.

## We Are All Both

I want to say something that may feel radical, though it is the simplest truth I know: *we are all both*. Every single one of us carries within us the capacity for extraordinary kindness and extraordinary cruelty. We hold tenderness and violence, generosity and greed, wisdom and foolishness. We are saints. We are sinners. We are confused, contradictory, magnificently messy beings.

And this is not a problem to be solved. This is the human experience to be *lived*.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

I have sat with thousands of people over the years — in my healing room, in workshops, in retreats around the world — and I can tell you that the single greatest source of suffering I have witnessed is not the external circumstances of people's lives. It is the war they wage against themselves. It is the relentless, exhausting effort to be only the saint, to banish the sinner, to present a version of themselves that is acceptable and safe.

A woman came to me once, a dear one who had spent her entire adult life in service to others. She was a healer, a caregiver, a devoted mother. And she was utterly depleted. When I placed my hands on her body, I could feel the tension — a deep, chronic holding pattern that ran from her jaw through her chest and into her belly. It was the tension of someone who had been holding her breath for thirty years.

"I don't understand," she whispered. "I do everything right. I meditate. I eat well. I serve others. Why do I feel so angry all the time?"

Because, my love, you have been trying to be only the saint. And the sinner — the part of you that is furious, that is exhausted, that wants to scream "What about *me*?" — has been locked in that dark closet for decades. And she is *done* being quiet.

## The Path to Peace

So how do we find our way to peace? Not the brittle, surface-level peace of pretending everything is fine, but the deep, unshakeable peace that can hold the full catastrophe of being human?

We begin with those three treasures Lao Tzu offered us. But we must understand them at a depth that goes far beyond their surface meaning.

**Simplicity** does not mean making your life simple. It means stripping away the layers of pretense, the masks, the stories you have told yourself about who you are supposed to be. It means returning to the raw, unadorned truth of this moment — including the parts of this moment that are uncomfortable, confusing, or painful. Simplicity is the courage to stop performing and to simply *be*.

**Patience** does not mean waiting for things to get better. It means being willing to stay present with what is, even when what is feels unbearable. It means sitting with your own confusion without rushing to resolve it. Sitting with your own anger without immediately trying to fix it or explain it away. Patience is the radical act of giving yourself permission to not have it all figured out.

**Compassion** does not mean being kind to others while secretly judging yourself. It means turning that same tenderness inward — toward the parts of yourself you have rejected, the feelings you have deemed unacceptable, the memories you have tried to bury. Compassion is the willingness to hold your own brokenness with the same gentleness you would offer a frightened child.

## Sitting With Our Own Good and Evil

Here is the practice, and it is deceptively simple: we have to be willing to sit with *all of it*.

We have to be willing to sit with our own good and evil. Our own saints and sinners. Our own confusion and anger. Our own jealousy and pettiness and fear. Not to wallow in them. Not to act on them. But to *acknowledge* them. To feel them fully. To let them move through us like weather moving through an open sky.

Because here is what I have learned, in my body, through decades of this work: what we resist, persists. What we exile, grows stronger in the shadows. But what we meet with presence — what we turn toward with those three treasures of simplicity, patience, and compassion — begins to transform.

This is not a metaphor. I have felt it happen under my hands, in the bodies of people who finally, *finally* gave themselves permission to feel what they had been running from. The jaw unclenches. The belly softens. The breath deepens. Something that has been frozen for years begins to thaw, and what flows out is not the monster they feared, but a river of tears, of relief, of homecoming.

## Our Friends, Our Enemies, Ourselves

This inner work does not happen in isolation. It plays out in every relationship we have — with our friends, our enemies, and ourselves.

The friend who irritates you? She is showing you a part of yourself you have not yet made peace with. The person who enrages you? He is holding up a mirror to the exile in your own closet. This is not to say that harmful behavior should be tolerated or that boundaries are unnecessary. Boundaries are essential. But the *emotional charge* — the intensity of our reaction — is always, always pointing us back to our own inner landscape.

When we can sit with our own darkness, we stop needing the world to be different in order to feel at peace. We stop needing our friends to behave perfectly. We stop needing our enemies to change. We stop needing *ourselves* to be flawless. And from that place of deep, embodied acceptance, something miraculous happens: we become genuinely free.

Not free from difficulty. Not free from conflict. But free from the tyranny of our own resistance to life as it is.

## The Cost of Abdication

If we cannot sit with our own inner storms — if we refuse to meet our own confusion, our own anger, our own shadow — then we are abdicating. We are handing over our power to every external circumstance, every difficult person, every piece of bad news. We are saying, in effect, "I will only be at peace when the world arranges itself to my liking."

And the world, as you may have noticed, has no intention of doing that.

This is the great trap. We wait for peace to arrive from the outside — from the right relationship, the right job, the right political outcome, the right spiritual experience — and it never, ever comes. Because peace is not a destination. It is a practice. It is the daily, moment-by-moment choice to turn toward ourselves with simplicity, patience, and compassion, and to welcome whatever we find there.

The Tao does not take sides. It holds everything. And when we learn to do the same — when we learn to hold our own saints and sinners with equal tenderness — we discover that we have been carrying the peace we were searching for all along. It was never out there. It was always right here, in the willingness to sit with the full, glorious, heartbreaking truth of who we are.

This is the path. It is not easy. It is not quick. But it is real, and it is yours.

---

teachings.bodyMarkdown:
We live in a world that loves a quick fix. A pill, a protocol, a five-step plan.

And perhaps nowhere is that complexity more potent, more charged, and more deeply felt than in the sacred center of our bodies: the reproductive system.

For so many of us, this is a landscape of profound contradiction. It is the source of our greatest creative power, the wellspring of life itself. It is the seat of our sexual energy, a force that can be a source of immense pleasure, intimacy, and connection. And yet… it is also a place where we hold so much of our shame, our wounding, our inherited silence.

I remember a client, a brilliant artist, who came to me feeling utterly blocked. Her canvases were gathering dust, her inspiration had dried up, and she felt a deep, gnawing emptiness in her womb space. She’d had a difficult relationship with her mother, a history of painful periods, and a sense that her sexuality was something to be managed, controlled, or even feared. She felt, in her words, “creatively and sexually constipated.”

Her story is not uncommon. For centuries, and particularly for women, this part of the body has been both revered and reviled, celebrated and controlled. We’ve been taught to disconnect from its wisdom, to numb its messages, to feel ashamed of its power. The result is a deep split—a chasm between our life force energy and our conscious awareness. We learn to live in our heads, disconnected from the very source of our vitality.

But what if we could begin to heal that split? What if we could reclaim this sacred portal not as a source of shame, but as a source of profound wisdom and creative power? This is the journey of honoring your reproductive system. It is the work of coming home to yourself.

## The Body as a Sacred Messenger

Your body is always speaking to you. Always. Every symptom, every sensation, every pattern is a form of communication. It is a message from your soul, delivered in the language of biology. When we experience challenges in the reproductive system—be it infertility, painful cycles, low libido, or creative blocks—it is not a sign that we are broken. It is an invitation to listen more deeply.

From a physiological perspective, the reproductive system is a marvel of design, a complex and beautiful dance of hormones and cycles. But from an energetic and spiritual perspective, it is so much more. It is the cauldron of creation. This is not just about creating babies, though that is one of its most miraculous expressions. It is about creating *anything*—a business, a work of art, a garden, a new way of being in the world. Your creative energy and your sexual energy are one and the same. When we stifle one, we stifle the other.

So many of the struggles we face in this area are rooted in old, inherited beliefs. Beliefs that our bodies are not our own. That our sexuality is dirty or dangerous. That our creative impulses are frivolous or unimportant. These beliefs become embedded in our tissues, creating patterns of tension, stagnation, and dis-ease. They become the neural pathways through which our life force energy struggles to flow.

But here’s a very good thing to know: those pathways can be rewired. The body, in its infinite wisdom, is always seeking wholeness. And with gentle, compassionate attention, we can begin to dissolve the old patterns and create new ones. We can learn to listen to the whispers of our womb, to honor the rhythms of our cycles, and to reclaim the full spectrum of our creative and sexual power.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Guided Practice for Reproductive Healing

This is not a quick fix. It is a practice, a returning, a slow and tender courtship with a part of yourself that may have been long neglected. I invite you to find a quiet space where you won’t be disturbed. Give yourself the gift of at least 15-20 minutes. You can sit or lie down, whatever feels most comfortable for your body.

**Step 1: Arriving in the Body**

Begin by closing your eyes and taking a few slow, deep breaths. With each inhale, imagine you are drawing your awareness down, out of your head and into your body. Feel the weight of your body on the chair or the floor. Notice the sensation of the air on your skin. Just arrive, here, in this moment. No need to change anything. Simply be.

**Step 2: Connecting with the Womb/Sacral Space**

Bring your gentle, loving attention to your lower abdomen, the physical location of your reproductive system. If it feels right, you can place your hands on this part of your body, a gesture of warmth and connection. This is your sacral center, your womb space (regardless of your anatomy, we all have a womb space energetically).

Don’t try to feel anything specific. Just rest your awareness here. Notice any sensations that are present—warmth, coolness, tingling, numbness, tension, softness. Whatever is there, just meet it with gentle curiosity. For so long, we have been taught to ignore this part of our body. Now, you are simply saying, “I see you. I am here with you.”

**Step 3: The Golden Light Visualization**

Now, imagine a beautiful, warm, golden light beginning to form in the center of your womb space. See it, feel it, sense it in whatever way is right for you. This is the light of pure, unconditional love. It is the light of your own essence.

With each inhale, imagine this golden light expanding, growing brighter and warmer. Feel it filling your entire pelvic bowl, bathing every cell, every organ, in its gentle, healing radiance. This light has the power to dissolve any tension, any holding, any old, stagnant energy. It is pure love, and in the presence of pure love, anything that is not love can begin to melt away.

**Step 4: Releasing Shame and Old Stories**

As you continue to breathe and allow the golden light to fill you, you might become aware of old feelings or stories that have been stored here. Shame. Fear. Grief. Anger. You might see images, hear words, or simply feel a wave of emotion. Whatever comes, your only job is to meet it with the same gentle, non-judgmental awareness.

See if you can simply name what you are feeling. “Ah, there is shame.” “There is grief.” You don’t need to analyze it or fix it. Just acknowledge it. And as you acknowledge it, imagine that golden light surrounding it, holding it, loving it. You can say to this part of yourself, “I see you. I hear you. Thank you for trying to protect me. You are welcome here.”

With each exhale, imagine you are releasing a layer of this old energy. You can visualize it as a grey smoke, leaving your body and being effortlessly transformed by the light of the universe. You are not pushing it away. You are simply letting it go, creating more space for your own radiant life force energy to flow.

**Step 5: Honoring Your Creative and Sexual Energy**

Now, as you rest in this space of golden light, I invite you to connect with the pure, positive essence of your creative and sexual energy. Feel it as a vibrant, life-giving force within you. It might feel like a gentle hum, a warm pulse, or a powerful current. This energy is your birthright. It is the energy of creation itself, and it is holy.

Take a few moments to simply honor this energy. You can say silently to yourself, “I honor my creative power. I honor my sexual energy. I honor my body as a sacred vessel of life.” Feel the truth of these words resonating in your cells. Feel the joy, the pleasure, the simple rightness of this energy flowing through you.

**Step 6: A Daily Practice of Reverence**

When you feel ready, slowly begin to bring your awareness back to the room. Wiggle your fingers and toes. Gently open your eyes. Before you move on with your day, take a moment to thank your body, and especially your reproductive system, for its wisdom and its messages.

This is a practice you can return to every day. Even five minutes of placing your hands on your womb and breathing with loving attention can be profoundly transformative. It is a way of saying to your body, over and over again, “I am on your side. I am listening. I love you.”

This is how we begin to heal. Not by forcing or fixing, but by listening, honoring, and returning, again and again, to the truth of our own sacredness. It is a journey of a lifetime, and it begins with a single, loving breath.


---

teachings.title: The Holographic Body: Why Healing One Part Transforms the Whole
teachings.summary: Susan presents the body as a holographic, unified field in which each part contains information about the whole. Symptoms and sensations are framed as meaningful communications—tissue-held memories and energetic ripples—that invite curiosity rather than purely mechanical fixes. She encourages listening practices, boundary-setting, and embodied inquiry as pathways to greater coherence and self-understanding.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We walk around in these bodies, so familiar and yet, at times, so utterly mysterious. We treat them like machines—a little creaky here, a bit of fuel there—and forget the universe of wisdom they hold. We see a sore shoulder as just a sore shoulder, a grumbling stomach as a dietary misstep. But what if it’s all connected? What if your body is speaking a language deeper than muscle and bone? Many of us have experienced a persistent pain that seems to have no physical cause. Consider a person with a demanding career and a chronic pain in their shoulder that resists all conventional treatment. In exploring their inner world, a narrative often emerges—one of carrying heavy emotional or familial burdens for years. The shoulder, in this context, is not merely a joint but a vessel for accumulated stress and responsibility. When these invisible weights are acknowledged and consciously released, through setting boundaries or speaking long-held truths, the physical pain can remarkably diminish. This is the secret of the holographic body. It’s a principle, rooted in both ancient wisdom and quantum physics, that suggests every part of a system contains the information of the whole. Just as a single fragment of a hologram can reconstruct the entire image, a single cell in your body contains the blueprint for all of you. Your shoulder holds the story of your responsibilities. Your gut holds the truth of how you digest life itself. ## The Body as a Living Hologram Think of it this way. When you look at a hologram, you see a three-dimensional image floating in space. If you were to shatter that holographic plate, you wouldn’t find tiny, broken pieces of the image. Instead, each fragment, no matter how small, would still contain the *entire* image, just from a slightly different perspective. Your body operates on a similar principle. It isn’t a collection of separate parts working in isolation. It is a unified, interconnected field of information and energy. This is why practices like reflexology—where applying pressure to points on the feet can affect organs throughout the body—can be so profoundly effective. The foot is a microcosm of the whole. The ear, the hands, the eyes… they are all portals to the entire system. > “The part is in the whole, and the whole is in the part.” — A fundamental concept in holographic theory. This understanding shifts everything. It moves us from a mechanical view of healing—fixing the broken part—to a holistic one. When we address a symptom with curiosity and reverence, we are not just treating a localized issue. We are entering into a conversation with the entire being. We are acknowledging that the ache in your lower back might be connected to a deep-seated feeling of being unsupported, or that the tension in your jaw might be the physical manifestation of words left unspoken. ## Ripples in the Energetic Pond There are moments in nature that offer profound metaphors for our own existence. Imagine a dew-covered spiderweb shimmering in the early morning light. When a single drop of rain falls onto a leaf, the vibration of that tiny impact sends ripples across the entire web. This is a perfect illustration of the holographic body. A thought, an emotion, a physical sensation—none of these exist in a vacuum. They are like that single drop of rain, sending ripples throughout your entire system. This is where the insights of neuroscience become so illuminating. Dr. Candace Pert’s groundbreaking research on neuropeptides showed us that the “molecules of emotion” are not just confined to the brain. They are found throughout the body, in the immune system, the endocrine system, and the gut. This means your body is constantly thinking, feeling, and processing information on a cellular level. There is no real separation between mind and body. There is only the bodymind—a single, intelligent, holographic system. When you experience a trauma, for instance, that experience isn’t just stored as a memory in your brain. It is stored in your tissues, in your posture, in the very way you breathe. Healing, then, is not just about talking through the past. It is about releasing the energetic imprint of that past from the body itself. It’s about allowing the ripples to settle, creating a new pattern of coherence and ease. ## The Tao of Wholeness The Tao te Ching, that ancient book of wisdom, speaks of the uncarved block—the state of natural, simple, and whole potential. Our modern lives, with their relentless pressures and fragmentations, carve us up. We become a collection of roles—the parent, the professional, the partner—and we forget the uncarved block that lies beneath. We identify with our pain, our diagnoses, our limitations, and we forget the wholeness that is our birthright. To heal in a holographic way is to return to the uncarved block. It is to see the body not as a problem to be solved, but as a sacred text to be read. Each sensation, each symptom, is a word on the page. It is an invitation to go deeper, to listen more closely, to understand the story that is being told. This is the work I do with my clients, and it is the work I invite you into, beloved one. It is the journey of decoding the messages your body has been holding, and transforming them into doorways of healing and self-discovery. It is about learning to trust the wisdom that is already within you, shimmering in every cell.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
Your body is not a battlefield. It is a field of intelligence, a holographic miracle. And by healing one part, with love and attention, you truly can transform the whole. With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan
