reflectionPrompts: Choose one persistent sensation or recurring pain you notice. What story or role in your life might that sensation be pointing to if it were trying to tell you something?

Recall a time when shifting an emotional pattern (setting a boundary, speaking a truth, or changing a routine) changed how your body felt. What changed first — the feeling, the thought, or the external situation?

Imagine the ‘uncarved block’ within you — the state of natural, whole potential beneath roles and symptoms. Where in your body do you sense fragmentation, and what small, compassionate action could help you tend that place?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Find a comfortable seated position and place one hand gently over an area of your body you want to listen to. Take five slow breaths, softening your attention into that place. Without trying to fix anything, notice sensations, images, words, or emotions that arise; name them silently (for example, “tightness,” “old worry,” “tired”). Stay with this curious, nonjudgmental attention for 3–5 minutes, then thank that part of your body for communicating. If you notice strong emotion or distress, pause and consider reaching out to a trusted practitioner or healthcare provider.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article references trauma and bodily storage of distress. If reading or practicing brings up strong feelings, you have permission to pause, step away, and seek a qualified mental health or body-oriented practitioner.
The practices suggested are invitational and should be approached gently; avoid pressuring yourself to produce insights or immediate change.

If you have a history of significant trauma, medical conditions, or are currently in active treatment, consider doing embodied inquiry with a trauma-informed clinician or supportive practitioner present.

teachings.sourceTitle: Saving Face: The Exhausting Art of Hiding Who You Really Are
teachings.title: Saving Face: The Exhausting Art of Hiding Who You Really Are
teachings.summary: Susan explores how early survival strategies become facial masks that both protect and exhaust us, showing how chronic tension and skin or head symptoms can be the body’s signal of inner conflict. She invites gentle, compassionate inquiry and small shifts—breathing into tension, softening the jaw, and allowing "cracks" in the facade—to free energy for fuller self-expression and deeper connection.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a garden in my neighbourhood where an old cherry tree blooms every spring with such extravagant beauty that it stops people in their tracks.

And perhaps nowhere is that business more revealing than on the small, expressive landscape of our own faces.

I remember being a young girl, maybe seven or eight, standing before the mirror in my mother’s bedroom. The air was thick with the scent of her Jean Naté dusting powder. I wasn’t looking at my reflection so much as I was studying it, practicing. I was practicing my “brave face” for school, my “happy to help” face for chores, my “everything is fine” face for when the familiar tension in our house grew thick and silent. I would pull the corners of my mouth up, widen my eyes just so, and try to smooth the worry from my brow, a furrow that already seemed to be making its home there. Even then, I knew, on some deep, cellular level, that my survival depended on successful facial management. It was a silent, intuitive understanding that love and safety were conditional, and my face was the passport.

It’s a skill we learn so early, isn’t it? The art of arranging our features into a mask that we hope will be acceptable, pleasing, or at the very least, safe. We learn to present a version of ourselves to the world, a carefully curated ambassador for the vast and often messy kingdom within. We put on a face to get the job, to keep the peace, to attract a partner, to hide our breaking heart. And my goodness, is it ever exhausting.

This isn’t just a metaphor. The body, in its infinite wisdom, doesn’t distinguish between the mask we wear emotionally and the physical reality of our face. The face *is* the presentation of the self, but it is also a mirror of the soul. It is the frontline of our identity, the place where our inner world and the outer world meet. And when there is a conflict between the two—between the authentic self that longs for expression and the persona we feel we must perform—the face becomes a battleground.

## The Topography of Inner Conflict

The body is a sacred messenger, and the face speaks its language with exquisite precision. Every chronic tension, every recurring breakout, every ache in the jaw is a communication. It’s a whisper from a deeper part of you, asking to be heard.

Think of the immense energy required to hold a smile when you are crumbling inside. That energy has to go somewhere. It gets stored in the masseter muscles of the jaw, leading to the grinding teeth and agonizing pain of TMJ. It’s the physical manifestation of biting back words, of clenching against the tide of what you *really* feel. It’s a conflict of identity—the identity that must appear capable and serene at war with the one that feels overwhelmed and inadequate. The jaw, a hinge joint designed for the vital functions of speaking and eating, becomes a prison for unspoken truths.

Or consider the skin—our largest organ and our most visible. When we feel a deep sense of shame about who we are, a feeling of being somehow “wrong” or unacceptable, the skin can erupt in a fiery protest. Acne, rosacea, eczema… these can be the outward signs of an inner inflammation, a conflict with the self that has become so hot it literally burns its way to the surface. We are trying to hide, to conceal what feels shameful, but the body, in its profound honesty, refuses to keep our secrets. It wears our inner state on our sleeve, or in this case, on our cheeks and forehead.

It’s a beautiful, if sometimes painful, paradox. We believe we are controlling the narrative, managing our appearance with such focus. But the truth has a way of leaking out. Neuroscience tells us about micro-expressions, those fleeting, involuntary flashes of emotion that cross our faces in a fraction of a second. A flicker of fear, a shadow of sadness, a tightening of contempt. No matter how practiced our mask, the limbic system—the ancient, emotional part of our brain—will not be silenced. It sends its signals up the neural pathways, and for a millisecond, the truth is written there for all to see, even if it’s only perceived unconsciously. The body’s wisdom will not be denied.

The sheer stress of this constant monitoring and controlling is enormous. It’s a full-time job, being the security guard of your own face. This vigilance keeps the nervous system in a low-grade state of fight-or-flight, simmering in a broth of stress hormones like cortisol. It’s a profound expenditure of our life force, all in service of hiding who we really are. This chronic state of alert can impact everything from our digestion to our sleep, all stemming from the face we present to the world.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Masks We Wear

I worked with a woman once, a brilliant and successful lawyer I’ll call Sarah. She came to me for debilitating migraines. In her professional life, she was known for her unshakable composure, her “poker face.” She could negotiate multi-million dollar deals without ever betraying a hint of doubt or pressure. But in our sessions, as she began to feel safe, her face would tell a different story. Without the mask of the powerful lawyer, her features softened into an expression of profound weariness and a deep, childlike grief.

Sarah had learned early on that her sensitivity was a liability in her family and, later, in her career. She had meticulously constructed a persona of invulnerability. The migraines, we discovered, were the scream of her silenced sensitivity. Her head was literally pounding against the constraints of the mask she wore. The pain was the only way her body could get her attention and say, *“This is not all of who you are. The pressure is too much.”* Through our work, she began to gently, carefully, allow small cracks in the facade. She started by simply noticing the tension in her jaw during a conference call, and instead of fighting it, she would breathe into it. A tiny act of kindness toward herself. Over time, these small acts of presence began to repattern her neural pathways. The migraines lessened in frequency and intensity as she learned to honor her sensitivity instead of banishing it.

Her story is not unique. We all wear masks. The “good girl” mask. The “tough guy” mask. The “spiritual, serene” mask. The “I have it all together” mask. These personas are not villains; they are often brilliant survival strategies developed by a younger part of ourselves to navigate a world that felt unsafe or conditional. They helped us belong, to get our needs met, to protect our tender hearts.

But a strategy that serves us in childhood can become a prison in adulthood. The mask that once protected us can begin to suffocate us. It keeps love, intimacy, and true connection out, just as it keeps our authentic self in. We become so identified with the face we present that we forget the radiant, multifaceted soul shimmering just beneath it.

I invite you to gently inquire, just for a moment. What is the primary face you show the world? What mask do you most often wear? Feel its shape, its weight, the subtle tension it requires. And then, with infinite compassion for the part of you that created it, ask: What am I afraid would happen if I let it slip, just for a moment? What is the truth it is working so hard to hide?

## The Radiance of Sheer Love

The path of healing is not about violently ripping the mask off. It is not another form of self-improvement or another face to perfect—the “enlightened” face. It is a gentle turning-toward. It is the process of extending compassion and understanding to the parts of you that have been in hiding.

It is about creating enough inner safety that the clenched jaw can finally soften. It is about tending to the inner fire of shame so the skin no longer has to carry the heat. It is about allowing the truth of your weariness, your grief, your joy, your anger to be felt, first by you, and then, perhaps, by a trusted other. This is the work of neuroplasticity in action. We are not just changing our minds; we are changing the very structure of our brains, creating new pathways that lead to self-acceptance rather than self-concealment.

When we stop pouring so much energy into facial management, a tremendous amount of life force is liberated. This is the energy of transformation. It’s the energy we can use to rewire those old neural pathways of inadequacy and fear, and to cultivate new ones of self-acceptance and grace. It is the energy to finally let the shoulders drop, to let the breath deepen, to let the heart feel what it feels.

The ultimate transcendence is to release the exhausting art of saving face altogether. It is to embrace *all* the faces you show—the brave one, the scared one, the messy one, the radiant one. It is to understand that beneath every expression, beneath every persona, you are the unchanging, unwavering light of consciousness itself. You are the radiance of sheer love.

What would it be like to let your face simply be a reflection of that love? To let it be a soft, open, expressive landscape, moved by the weather of your inner world but grounded in the bedrock of your being? This is not a destination, but a moment-by-moment practice of coming home to yourself. It is the most profound rest you will ever know. It is the quiet joy of letting yourself be seen, truly seen, perhaps for the very first time.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision](/blog/eyes-emotional-roots-of-vision)
- [Losing Your Voice: When Authentic Expression Feels Dangerous](/blog/vocal-cords-losing-voice)

**More on Face:**

- [The Face You Show the World: Identity, Masks, and Authenticity](/blog/face-identity-masks-authenticity)
- [Letting Your Soul Shine Through: Transcending Facial Masks](/blog/face-letting-soul-shine)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Bring awareness to where tension lives on your face (jaw, forehead, between the brows, throat). What emotion or need might that tension be trying to keep hidden, and how can you acknowledge that part with kindness?
Imagine the life force saved if you spent less energy policing your expressions. What could you do with even a small amount of that reclaimed energy—one tiny, realistic next step?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Try a 3–5 minute face-check: sit comfortably, soften your shoulders, close your eyes if that feels safe. Breathe slowly for three cycles, then gently scan from forehead to jaw, noticing areas of tightness without trying to change them. When you find a tight spot (e.g., jaw or brow), pause and breathe into that area for two to three slow breaths; on an exhale, allow a small, gentle softening. If you notice strong pain or intense emotion, stop, rest, and consider reaching out to a trusted practitioner or support person.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article touches on childhood survival patterns, shame, grief, and emotional pain; these topics can bring up strong feelings—you have permission to pause at any time.
If reflection or the practice raises intense memories or distress, consider reaching out to a qualified therapist, physician, or trusted support person for guidance and containment.

The piece references physical symptoms (jaw tension, migraines, skin conditions). These descriptions are experiential, not diagnostic—if you have persistent or worsening physical symptoms, please consult appropriate healthcare professionals.

teachings.sourceTitle: Slowing Down to Stay Safe: Hypothyroidism and Suppressed Aliveness
teachings.title: Slowing Down to Stay Safe: Hypothyroidism and Suppressed Aliveness
teachings.summary: Susan reframes hypothyroidism and the body’s slowing as a protective strategy rather than a failure, linking thyroid function to the throat’s role in voice and self-expression. She traces how childhood and intergenerational patterns can wire the nervous system to equate aliveness with danger, and invites a gentle, embodied inquiry to begin restoring safety between you and your body. The piece emphasizes compassion, listening, and small practices that support neuroplastic change.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember a client, years ago, a woman with a brilliant, crackling mind and a laugh that could fill a room. But when she came to see me, the laugh was gone. Her energy, which she described as once being a ‘wildfire,’ had dampened to a pilot light, flickering weakly against a persistent fog of fatigue. Her doctors had given her a diagnosis: hypothyroidism. She was given a prescription, but the feeling of being muted, of living life behind a thick veil, remained.

“It’s as if my body has put the brakes on,” she told me, her hands resting on her throat. “And I don’t know why. I feel like I’m failing at being alive.”

That phrase has stayed with me for years. *Failing at being alive.* It’s such a heartbreaking and common sentiment, and it speaks to a fundamental misunderstanding we have in our culture. We are taught to see the body as a machine that should perform on command. When it doesn’t, we think it’s broken. We see symptoms as enemies to be vanquished, flaws to be eradicated. We declare war on our own biology.

But what if, just for a moment, we laid down our weapons? What if we considered that the body, in its infinite wisdom, is never failing us? What if it is always, *always*, attempting to protect us in the only way it knows how, based on the information it has gathered throughout our lives?

What if the slowing down is not a failure, but a strategy? A profound, if painful, act of love.

## The Conductor of Your Pace

In the landscape of your body, the thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the base of your throat, the very channel through which your voice, your truth, emerges into the world. It is the master regulator of your metabolism, the conductor of your body’s pace. It dictates how quickly you burn energy, how fast your heart beats, how warm your body runs. It sets the rhythm of your life.

When the thyroid under-functions, as it does in hypothyroidism, it’s as if the conductor has instructed the entire orchestra to play in slow motion. The symphony of your biology becomes a dirge. You feel cold, tired, sluggish. Your thoughts move through molasses. Your hair may thin, your skin may dry, and a sense of deep, persistent melancholy can settle in your bones. The world sees lethargy; the body is in a state of profound conservation.

It’s a tricky business, being human. We are taught to push, to strive, to be more, do more, achieve more. So when the body insists on slowing down, we declare war. We fight it. We resent it. But the body is not a machine to be fixed; it is a sacred messenger. And the message of the underactive thyroid is one of the most poignant I have encountered in my work. The message is this: *Don’t be too alive. It’s not safe.*

This isn’t a conscious thought, of course. It is a deep, cellular belief, a pattern etched into your neural pathways long ago. It is the body’s memory of a time, or many times, when your full, authentic, radiant aliveness was met with a response that felt like a threat to your survival.

## The Danger of Shining Too Brightly

Think of a small child. A child is pure life force—loud, messy, curious, emotional, and utterly, authentically themselves. They have not yet learned to calibrate their energy for public consumption. When that child’s vibrant expression—their passionate storytelling, their uninhibited joy, their righteous anger—is met with disapproval, punishment, or simply being ignored, a devastating lesson is learned.

That lesson is: *Who I am is too much. My energy is dangerous. To be loved, to be safe, I must become smaller. Quieter. Less.*

This is not a failure of parenting; it is often the unconscious passing down of generational patterns. A parent who was taught to suppress their own aliveness will, without meaning to, teach the same to their child. The message is received not just in the mind, but in the body. The nervous system, that exquisite surveillance network, wires itself for this reality. It creates a neural pathway that equates authentic expression with danger. The body learns that shining brightly invites being shut down.

And so, in its profound and fierce love for you, the body devises a strategy. If being too alive is dangerous, then the body will simply… slow down the aliveness. It will instruct the thyroid to dial down the metabolic fire. It will conserve your energy, keeping you in a state of semi-hibernation, because the memory it holds is that the alternative—your full, blazing, magnificent self—is simply too risky. It’s a brilliant, if devastatingly costly, form of self-protection. The body, in its profound and fierce love for you, would rather you be tired and sad than annihilated. It chooses the lesser of two perceived evils.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Voice of the Throat

It is no accident that the thyroid resides in the throat. This is the fifth chakra, the energetic center of communication, truth, and self-expression. It’s the bridge between your inner world and the outer world, the place from which you speak your reality into being. When the thyroid is suppressed, it is intimately linked with a suppression of your voice.

How many times have you swallowed your words? How many times have you wanted to scream, or sing, or declare your truth, but held back for fear of the consequences? Fear of being judged, of being dismissed, of being unloved. Every time you silence yourself, you send a signal to your body, and specifically to this energy center. The signal says, *It’s not safe to speak. It’s not safe to be heard.*

Over time, this energetic suppression can manifest physically. The throat constricts. The thyroid, bathed in this energy of fear and silence, begins to down-regulate. It’s a feedback loop. The less you speak your truth, the more your physical energy wanes. And the less energy you have, the harder it is to summon the courage to speak. You become trapped in a cycle of silence and fatigue.

Healing the thyroid, then, is not just about a pill. It is about reclaiming your voice. It is about finding the courage to speak the truths you have swallowed, to express the feelings you have suppressed, and to allow your unique, authentic, and sometimes messy self to be seen and heard in the world.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## An Inquiry for Your Body’s Wisdom

If any of this resonates in you, beloved one, I invite you not to despair, but to get curious. This is not another reason to feel broken. It is an opening, a doorway into a more compassionate relationship with yourself. It is an opportunity to understand the story your body is telling.

Let’s try a gentle inquiry. There’s no need to force anything. Just allow the questions to land softly in your awareness.

Find a quiet moment. You might sit in a comfortable chair, with your feet on the floor, feeling the support of the earth beneath you. Place a warm hand over your throat, over that little butterfly gland.

Take a breath. And then another.

Now, whisper to your body, either aloud or in the quiet of your heart: *What if this slowing down has been a profound act of protection?*

Don’t search for an answer with your mind. Just feel the question in your body. Notice any sensation, any image, any feeling that arises. There is no right or wrong here. There is only listening.

Now, gently ask: *Where did I learn that my full aliveness was a threat? Where did I learn that it was safer to be small?*

Again, just listen. A memory may surface. It might be from childhood, or from a relationship, or from a workplace. It might be a feeling without a specific story. It might be a sense of ancestral grief you are carrying. Whatever comes, simply meet it with gentle awareness. You are not trying to fix it. You are simply bearing witness. You are letting your body know that you are finally ready to hear its story.

Finally, with your hand still on your throat, offer these words to your body: *It’s safe to be alive now. It’s safe to be me. I am here with you.*

Feel the vibration of those words under your palm. Breathe them into your cells. This is not a one-time fix. This is the beginning of a new conversation, a new relationship. It is the practice of neuroplasticity in action—the conscious creation of new neural pathways that associate your authentic self not with danger, but with safety, love, and belonging. It is the slow, sacred, and deeply rewarding work of earning your body’s trust.

The journey with hypothyroidism, from this perspective, is not about fighting your body. It is about creating such a profound and unwavering internal safety that your body no longer needs to protect you by keeping you small. It’s about gently, lovingly, coaxing your beautiful, wise system out of hibernation, letting it know that the long winter is over, and it is finally safe to feel the sun.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

I am here with you.” If you become overwhelmed, pause the practice and rest.

teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I remember standing in front of the mirror, my hand resting on the base of my throat, a place I’d never paid much attention to before. It felt… quiet. Too quiet. A deep, humming stillness where I sensed there should be a gentle vibration. Outside, the world was a blur of deadlines, expectations, and the relentless hum of a city that never slept. I was keeping up, or so I thought, but my body was telling a different story. A story of deep fatigue, a brain fog that felt like a constant veil, and a sense of being perpetually chilled, no matter how many layers I wore. My doctor had given it a name: hypothyroidism. But my soul knew it by another — a profound and persistent dampening of my own authentic purpose.

This delicate, butterfly-shaped gland at the front of our neck, the thyroid, is so much more than a master regulator of our metabolism. It is the conductor of our inner orchestra, setting the rhythm and tempo of our lives. It’s the energetic gateway between our heart’s desires and our mind’s expression. When it’s in balance, we feel it. There’s a flow, an ease, a sense of being perfectly in sync with the unfolding of our own journey. But when it’s out of balance, it’s a powerful messenger, asking us to pause and listen to the deeper story our body is trying to tell.

What if we saw hypothyroidism not as a failure of the body, but as a sacred invitation to slow down? For so many of us, especially women, we are conditioned to believe our worth is tied to our productivity. We push, we strive, we achieve. And when our body puts on the brakes, we feel a sense of panic, of falling behind. The fatigue and slowness of an underactive thyroid can feel like a betrayal. But perhaps… perhaps it is a profound act of self-preservation. It’s the body’s way of saying, “Beloved, you cannot keep going at this pace. You are burning out your inner light.” It’s a fear, often rooted deep in our ancestral or childhood experiences, of being ‘shut down’ if we dare to shine too brightly, speak our truth too loudly, or take up too much space. So we dampen our own fire, dim our own light, and our thyroid, in its infinite wisdom, reflects this inner state. It’s a call to reclaim our right to rest, to receive, and to simply *be*.

On the other side of the spectrum is the frenetic, racing energy of hyperthyroidism. This is the feeling of being on a treadmill that you can’t get off. Your heart races, your thoughts spin, and you feel a constant, humming anxiety beneath the surface. It’s the belief that your worth is directly proportional to your accomplishments. “If I just do more, achieve more, be more… then I will be worthy of love and belonging.” It’s an exhausting way to live, and the thyroid, in its overactive state, is screaming for a reprieve. It’s a pattern of running too fast, of trying to outrun a feeling of “not-enoughness.” The body is flooded with energy, but it’s a scattered, chaotic energy that doesn’t nourish, it depletes. It’s a call to find a different kind of worth, one that isn’t earned through doing, but is inherent in our being.

This is where the beautiful dance of neuroscience and ancient wisdom comes in. Every thought we think, every belief we hold, creates a neural pathway in our brain. These pathways are like well-worn trails in a forest. When we repeatedly tell ourselves “I’m not safe to be seen” or “I have to earn my worth,” we strengthen those trails. Our body, in its incredible intelligence, responds to these signals. The frequencies of these beliefs are broadcast throughout our system, and our thyroid, a highly sensitive gland, picks up on them. It’s not a one-way street, from gland to body; it’s a constant feedback loop. Our consciousness, our very awareness, is shaping our biology in real-time.

So how do we begin to shift these deeply ingrained patterns? We start by bringing gentle, compassionate awareness to them. We place a hand on our throat and we breathe. We ask, “What is the story you are trying to tell me? What is the rhythm you are longing for?” We begin to create new neural pathways, one conscious thought at a time. We introduce the possibility that it is safe to slow down, that our worth is inherent, that we can trust the timing of our own transformation. It’s not about forcing or fighting; it’s about creating a space of loving presence for what is.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

Transcending these patterns is not about ‘fixing’ the thyroid. It’s about coming into right relationship with ourselves. It’s about finding our authentic rhythm, the one that is uniquely ours. For some, this may mean embracing more stillness and learning to say ‘no’. For others, it may mean giving themselves permission to take bold, decisive action without the fear of judgment. It’s a process of unlearning the conditioning that tells us we must be a certain way to be safe or worthy.

Think of the butterfly, the very shape of the thyroid gland. A butterfly does not struggle to become. It surrenders to the process of transformation within the chrysalis. It trusts the timing. It doesn’t try to speed up the process or slow it down. It simply allows the unfolding. This is the wisdom the thyroid holds for us. It’s an invitation to trust the chrysalis, to know that even in the dark, a profound transformation is taking place. It’s a call to release the belief that we must slow down to be safe, or speed up to be worthy. It’s an invitation to find the delicate, powerful rhythm of our own becoming.

What would it be like if you allowed yourself to trust your own timing? If you knew, on a cellular level, that you are not behind, you are not ahead, you are exactly where you need to be? This is the journey of healing the thyroid on an energetic level. It’s about more than just medication or diet; it’s about transforming your relationship with time, with your purpose, and with your own precious self-worth. It’s about learning to listen to the whispers of your body before they become screams. It’s about coming home to the truth of who you are: a magnificent, unfolding being of light and love.

Your body is always, always speaking to you. It is the most faithful friend you will ever have. And the messages of the thyroid are some of the most profound. They are about the very essence of how we move through the world, how we express our soul’s purpose, and how we value our own being. By learning to listen with compassion and curiosity, we can begin to shift the energetic patterns that have held us captive. We can create new pathways of healing and wholeness. We can, like the butterfly, emerge from the chrysalis and fly.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Let’s go deeper into this connection. The thyroid is located at the 5th Chakra, the throat chakra, which is our center of communication and expression. It’s not just about the words we speak, but about how we express our truth, our creativity, our very essence in the world. When this chakra is blocked, we feel it as a lump in our throat, a hesitation to speak up, a feeling of being invisible or unheard. This energetic block can, over time, manifest in the physical body, and the thyroid is often where this imbalance shows up. It’s a beautiful and poignant example of how our energetic body and our physical body are inextricably linked.

Consider the quantum physics perspective. Everything is energy, and our thoughts and emotions are powerful frequencies that ripple out into the universe and also back into our own bodies. When we are living in alignment with our truth, our energy flows freely. But when we are suppressing our voice, our creativity, our desires, we create a dissonance, a static in our energetic field. This static can disrupt the delicate hormonal balance of the thyroid, which is so exquisitely attuned to the frequencies of our inner world.

So, what can we do to bring our thyroid and our throat chakra back into harmony? Here are a few gentle inquiries you might explore:

1.  **Journaling:** Take some time to sit with your journal and reflect on these questions: Where in my life am I not speaking my truth? What am I afraid would happen if I did? What does my heart long to express? Don’t censor yourself, just let the words flow. You might be surprised at what comes up.

2.  **Sound Healing:** The throat chakra is activated by sound. Chanting, singing, or even just humming can be incredibly powerful. You can find guided toning meditations online, or simply put on your favorite song and sing your heart out. The vibration of your own voice is a potent medicine.

3.  **Creative Expression:** Find a creative outlet that feels joyful and liberating for you. It could be painting, dancing, writing poetry, or anything else that allows you to express yourself without words. The goal is not to create a masterpiece, but to give your soul a voice.

4.  **Mindful Self-Compassion:** When you notice the familiar patterns of self-criticism or the pressure to perform, can you meet them with a moment of kindness? Place a hand on your heart and say, “This is a moment of suffering. Suffering is a part of life. May I be kind to myself in this moment.” This simple practice, developed by Dr. Kristin Neff, can begin to rewire the neural pathways of self-judgment and create a new habit of self-compassion.

Remember, this is a journey, not a destination. It’s a process of peeling back the layers of conditioning and coming home to the truth of who you are. It’s about learning to trust the wisdom of your body and to honor the messages it is sending you. Your thyroid, in its infinite wisdom, is not your enemy. It is your ally, your messenger, your guide. It is calling you back to yourself, back to your truth, back to the beautiful, authentic rhythm of your own life.

This journey of listening to your thyroid is a profound act of love. It is a commitment to honoring the sacred vessel of your body and the divine wisdom it holds. It is a path of returning to wholeness, not by fixing what is broken, but by embracing all that you are with compassion and grace. As you walk this path, know that you are not alone. We are all on this journey of becoming, of learning to listen to the whispers of our souls. And in this shared journey, there is infinite love and support available to us, always.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Embodied Compass: Navigating Life Through Your Nervous System's Wisdom
teachings.title: The Embodied Compass: Navigating Life Through Your Nervous System's Wisdom
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe intelligence as embodied rather than purely intellectual, proposing the nervous system as a continual, wise internal compass. Using polyvagal language, she describes the ventral (safe, social), sympathetic (mobilized), and dorsal (shutdown) states and highlights how habitual activation can persist after danger has passed. The piece offers gentle, practical practices—breath, sensation, mindful movement, co-regulation, grounding, and self-compassion—to cultivate felt safety and reclaim ease and creativity.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The other day, I was sitting by the window, watching a particularly blustery Vancouver rainstorm — the kind where the wind whips the branches of the old maple tree outside my studio into a frenzy, and the rain doesn't just fall, it *dances* sideways. I found myself humming an old tune, something from my childhood, and without even consciously trying, my breath deepened. My shoulders, which I hadn't realized were practically up around my ears, softened. It wasn't a grand meditation; it was just a moment of quiet observation, a noticing of the storm outside and the subtle shift within. And that, beloved one, is often how our nervous system speaks to us — in whispers, in sensations, in the gentle pull of a memory or a melody.

For so much of my life, like many of you, I lived mostly from the neck up. My brain was the CEO, the strategist, the problem-solver. I thought if I could just *think* my way through things, if I could analyze enough, understand enough, then I would find peace, find solutions, find my way. And while our minds are magnificent tools, they are only one part of the symphony that is us. What I’ve come to understand, through decades of working with bodies, with energy, with the subtle currents of human experience, is that our truest compass isn't lodged in our prefrontal cortex. It's woven into the very fabric of our being — our nervous system. This intricate, intelligent network is constantly receiving, interpreting, and responding to the world around us, and more importantly, the world *within* us. It’s our primal intelligence, our ancient wisdom, and it’s always, always speaking. We just haven’t always been taught how to listen.

### The Unseen Language of Your Inner World

Think of your nervous system as an exquisitely sensitive antenna, constantly scanning. It's not just about "fight or flight" — though that's certainly a crucial part of its repertoire. It's about a vast spectrum of states, from deep rest and connection to playful engagement, from focused concentration to profound grief. Polyvagal theory, a brilliant framework developed by Dr. Stephen Porges, helps us understand this spectrum with such clarity. It tells us that our nervous system isn't just a simple on/off switch. It's a hierarchy, a beautifully complex system that prioritizes safety.

At the very top, the newest part of our vagal nerve — the ventral vagal complex — is all about connection, safety, and social engagement. This is where we feel calm, curious, compassionate, and connected. This is the state where our digestion works optimally, where our immune system is robust, where creativity flows. When I’m in this state, I feel a warmth in my chest, a sense of ease in my breath, and my eyes feel soft, taking in the world with gentle interest. This is our home base, our optimal state of being.

Below that, when we perceive a threat, our sympathetic nervous system kicks in. This is our familiar "fight or flight" response. Our heart rate increases, our muscles tense, our senses sharpen, ready for action. It’s a powerful, necessary response designed for survival. We’ve all felt this — the sudden jolt of adrenaline, the quickening breath, the urge to run or confront. It’s not "bad"; it’s simply a protective mechanism.

And then, at the very bottom, the oldest part of our vagal nerve — the dorsal vagal complex — comes into play when the threat is overwhelming, when fight or flight isn't an option. This is the "freeze" response. Here, our system essentially shuts down, conserving energy, numbing us to pain. It's a brilliant survival strategy when facing inescapable danger, but it can also become a default pattern when we've experienced chronic stress or trauma. In this state, we might feel numb, disconnected, hopeless, or invisible. Our energy drops, our voice might become quiet, our eyes might lose their sparkle.

Here's the point: none of these states are inherently "wrong." They are all intelligent responses to perceived circumstances. The challenge arises when we get *stuck* in a state that no longer serves us, when our nervous system continues to perceive threat even when the actual danger has passed. This is where our inner compass can feel jammed, sending us signals that lead us astray, or keeping us frozen when movement is what we need.

I remember a period in my life when I was constantly feeling on edge, perpetually bracing for something bad to happen. My sympathetic nervous system was in overdrive. I’d wake up with my jaw clenched, my shoulders tight, a low hum of anxiety always present. I was "functioning" — going to work, seeing clients, being a parent — but I wasn't truly *living*. I wasn't experiencing joy or ease; I was just surviving. It felt like walking through life with a constant, low-grade alarm blaring in my ears. My mind was trying to "fix" it, to understand *why* I felt this way, but the answers weren't in my thoughts. They were in the persistent tension in my belly, the shallow quality of my breath, the way I flinched at sudden noises. My body was screaming for attention, but I was too busy listening to the frantic chatter of my mind.

### Listening to the Body's Whispers and Roars

So, how do we begin to listen to this embodied compass? It starts with presence. It starts with a gentle curiosity about what's happening *right now* in your internal landscape. We often spend so much time outside of ourselves — focused on external demands, on what we *should* be doing, on what others think. But the wisdom we seek is always available, always present, if we simply turn our attention inward.

One of the simplest, most profound ways to tune into your nervous system is through your breath. Your breath is a direct, immediate conduit to your autonomic nervous system. When you're stressed, your breath becomes shallow, quick, often held high in your chest. When you're calm, it deepens, slows, and moves into your belly. Just noticing this — without judgment, without trying to change it — is a powerful first step. Perhaps you might simply pause right now, wherever you are, and take three slow, deep breaths. Feel the air enter your nostrils, fill your lungs, expand your belly, and then gently release. Notice what shifts. Even that small act can send a signal of safety to your system.

Another key is sensation. Our bodies are constantly providing us with information, but we've often been taught to ignore it, to push through discomfort, to intellectualize our feelings. What if we started to treat these sensations as messengers? That knot in your stomach — what is it trying to tell you? That tension in your jaw — what emotion is it holding? That sudden wave of warmth or coldness — what does it signify?

I remember a client, a brilliant artist, who came to me feeling utterly stuck. She couldn't paint, couldn't create, felt a pervasive sense of dread. Her mind was racing with self-criticism and fear of failure. When I asked her where she felt this in her body, she initially said, "Nowhere, it's all in my head." But as we gently explored, she noticed a persistent, icy coldness in her hands and feet, and a feeling of immense weight on her chest, as if a stone were pressing down. We didn't try to "fix" these sensations. We simply acknowledged them, gave them space, and breathed into them. Over several sessions, as she learned to simply *be* with these bodily experiences, the coldness began to thaw, the weight began to lift. And as her nervous system started to feel safer, her creativity, which had been frozen, began to flow again. Her body, in its wisdom, had been communicating a deep need for rest, for safety, for permission to simply *be* without the pressure to produce.

Here's a very good thing to know: Your nervous system is not broken. It is always, always trying to keep you safe. If you find yourself in a state of chronic anxiety, or feeling numb and disconnected, it's not a failure on your part. It's your nervous system doing its best to protect you, based on past experiences and current perceptions. The work, then, isn't to fight it, but to gently guide it, to offer it new information, new experiences of safety.

### Cultivating a Sense of Safety: Your Daily Practice

So, how do we cultivate this sense of safety, this ventral vagal state, more consistently? It’s not about grand gestures; it’s about small, consistent practices that send reassuring signals to your system.

**1. Mindful Movement:** Our bodies are designed to move. Gentle movement, like walking in nature, stretching, or dancing to your favorite music, can be incredibly regulating. When you move, pay attention to the sensations in your body — the feeling of your feet on the earth, the stretch in your muscles, the rhythm of your breath. This mindful connection helps to bring you into the present moment and signals safety. I find that even a short walk around my neighborhood, really *feeling* the air on my skin and the ground beneath my feet, can shift me from a state of overwhelm to one of gentle presence.

**2. Co-Regulation and Connection:** We are wired for connection. Safe, authentic connection with others is one of the most powerful ways to regulate our nervous systems. This could be a warm conversation with a trusted friend, a hug from a loved one, or even simply making eye contact and sharing a genuine smile with someone. The presence of another regulated nervous system can help to soothe and calm our own. This is why I emphasize the importance of community and genuine relationship in my work — we heal in connection.

**3. Sensory Soothers:** What brings you a sense of calm and pleasure through your senses? Is it the scent of lavender, the feel of a soft blanket, the sound of gentle music, the taste of a warm cup of tea? Intentionally engaging your senses in ways that feel good sends powerful signals of safety and well-being to your nervous system. For me, it’s often a particular piece of classical music, or the feel of my cat purring on my lap, or the earthy scent of rain after a dry spell. These small moments are not luxuries; they are necessities for nervous system regulation.

**4. Orienting and Grounding:** When we feel overwhelmed or disconnected, our gaze often becomes fixed, or we might stare blankly. Orienting means gently looking around your environment, noticing what’s safe and present. Take in the colors, the textures, the shapes. This simple act helps your nervous system register that you are here, now, in a relatively safe space. Grounding involves bringing your awareness to your body’s contact with the earth — feeling your feet on the floor, your sit bones on a chair. It’s a way of saying, "I am here. I am supported."

**5. Self-Compassion:** Perhaps most importantly, approach yourself with immense kindness and non-judgment. When you notice your nervous system in a state of activation or shutdown, resist the urge to criticize or shame yourself. Instead, offer yourself the same gentle understanding you would offer a beloved child. "Ah, I see you're feeling anxious right now. That makes sense. What do you need?" This compassionate inquiry is a powerful act of self-regulation. It tells your system, "You are not alone. I am here with you."

I often think of our nervous system as a wild, beautiful creature — sometimes skittish, sometimes playful, sometimes needing deep rest. It doesn't respond well to force or criticism. It responds to gentle reassurance, to consistent care, to the feeling of being truly seen and understood. As we learn to listen to its subtle cues, to honor its wisdom, we begin to navigate life not from a place of frantic striving, but from a deep, embodied knowing. Our inner compass becomes clear, guiding us towards what truly serves our highest well-being, towards connection, creativity, and profound peace. Nothing is beyond healing, beloved one, and your body, your nervous system, is always ready to show you the way home.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.title: The Gentle Current: How Water's Wisdom Soothes a Strained Nervous System
teachings.summary: Susan uses the Taoist metaphor of water to offer a gentle, practical framework for soothing an overactive nervous system. She explores yielding, flow, and humble persistence—inviting simple sensory practices with water and moments of rest to support regulation and deeper integration. The piece emphasizes small, consistent acts rather than dramatic fixes and reminds readers that nervous-system re-patterning is a gradual, embodied process.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The other morning, I found myself standing at the kitchen sink, watching the water fill my kettle for tea. It was a simple, everyday moment, yet something about the steady, unhurried flow caught my attention. The water wasn't rushing, wasn't forcing – it was simply *being*, filling the space it was given with a quiet, persistent grace. And as I watched, a subtle shift happened within me. The low hum of a busy mind, the faint tension in my shoulders – they began to soften, just a little. It was a whisper of peace, a gentle reminder that sometimes, the most profound healing comes not from striving, but from yielding.

This quiet observation brought me back to a core teaching that has guided my life and work for decades: the wisdom of water, so beautifully articulated in the Tao Te Ching. Lao Tzu, that ancient sage, spoke of water as the ultimate teacher – yielding, yet powerful; soft, yet capable of wearing away stone. He observed its humility, always seeking the lowest places, and its incredible adaptability, taking the shape of any vessel it enters. For those of us navigating the choppy waters of a modern life – with its relentless demands, its constant pings, its subtle and not-so-subtle pressures – this ancient wisdom offers a profound balm, especially for a nervous system that often feels perpetually on high alert.

## The Nervous System: Our Inner Ocean

Think of your nervous system as an intricate, intelligent ocean within you. It’s a vast network of electrical and chemical signals, constantly receiving information from your internal and external worlds, then orchestrating your responses. We have the sympathetic nervous system – our "fight, flight, or freeze" response, like a powerful current that surges when danger is perceived. And then there's the parasympathetic nervous system – our "rest and digest" or "tend and befriend" mode, a gentle, restorative tide that brings us back to equilibrium.

In our contemporary world, many of us find ourselves caught in a perpetual sympathetic surge. The constant stream of information, the pressure to perform, the underlying anxieties about the future – these are like relentless storms, keeping our inner ocean turbulent. Our bodies, designed for short bursts of stress followed by long periods of rest, are often stuck in a state of chronic activation. This isn't a moral failing, beloved one; it's a physiological reality. Our brains, brilliant as they are, often can't distinguish between the roar of a saber-toothed tiger and the ping of an urgent email at 10 PM. Both can trigger the same cascade of stress hormones – cortisol, adrenaline – keeping us wired, tired, and often, unwell.

Here's a very good thing to know: your nervous system is not broken. It's simply doing what it's designed to do – protect you. But when it's overstimulated, it loses its fluidity, its ability to move gracefully between states of activation and rest. It becomes rigid, stuck in patterns of tension, anxiety, and even physical pain. This is where the wisdom of water – and the profound teachings of the Tao – can offer a pathway back to balance.

## Embracing Water's Qualities for Nervous System Regulation

Lao Tzu said, "The best man is like water. Water benefits all things and does not compete with them. It dwells in lowly places that men disdain. Therefore, it is near to Tao." What does it mean for us, in our modern lives, to be "like water" when our nervous system feels frayed?

First, consider water's *yielding nature*. Water doesn't resist. It flows around obstacles, finds the path of least resistance, and adapts to whatever container it's in. When our nervous system is activated, our natural inclination is often to *resist* the uncomfortable sensations – the racing heart, the tight stomach, the anxious thoughts. We try to push them away, to control them. But resistance, as any river knows, only creates more turbulence.

What if, instead, we could learn to yield? Not to surrender in a defeated way, but to *allow* what is present. This is a profound practice. When anxiety arises, instead of fighting it, can you simply notice it? Can you feel the sensations in your body without judgment? This isn't about liking the feeling; it's about acknowledging its presence, just as water acknowledges the rock in its path. This act of allowing – of yielding – sends a powerful signal to your nervous system: "It's okay. I'm safe enough to feel this." This subtle shift can begin to dial down the sympathetic response, inviting the parasympathetic system to gently re-engage.

I remember a time when I was going through a particularly challenging period – a confluence of personal and professional stresses that left me feeling constantly on edge. My sleep was disrupted, my digestion was a mess, and I felt a persistent knot in my stomach. I was trying everything I knew to "fix" myself – meditating harder, exercising more, pushing through. But the more I pushed, the more resistant my body became. One day, sitting by the ocean, watching the waves endlessly roll in and out, I had a moment of clarity. The waves weren't fighting the shore; they were simply arriving, receding, arriving again. They were yielding to the natural rhythm. And in that moment, I felt a deep invitation to yield to my own inner tides, to allow the discomfort without trying to force it away. It wasn't a magical cure, but it was the beginning of a profound shift, a softening that allowed healing to finally take root.

Second, think about water's *flow and adaptability*. Water is never stagnant for long. It moves, it transforms – from liquid to vapor to ice, and back again. Our nervous system, too, is meant to be fluid, to move between states of activation and rest. When we get stuck in sympathetic overdrive, it's like a dam has been built, blocking the natural flow.

How can we invite more flow? Simple, sensory experiences with water can be incredibly powerful. Taking a warm bath or shower – feeling the water cascade over your skin – can be a deeply regulating experience. The warmth and the tactile sensation stimulate the vagus nerve, a key player in the parasympathetic nervous system, signaling safety and relaxation. Spending time near natural bodies of water – a lake, a river, the ocean – has a scientifically documented calming effect. The rhythmic sounds, the vastness, the gentle movement – these sensory inputs help to quiet the busy mind and soothe the nervous system.

Even just drinking water mindfully can be a practice in flow. Instead of gulping it down, notice the sensation as it moves through your body. Hydration itself is crucial for nervous system health; our brains are mostly water, and even mild dehydration can impact mood, focus, and energy levels. It’s a simple act, yet when approached with intention, it becomes a powerful invitation to bring more fluidity and ease into your internal landscape.

Third, consider water's *humility and persistence*. Water always seeks the lowest place. It doesn't strive for grandiosity; it simply does its work, patiently and persistently. When our nervous system is overwhelmed, we often feel a strong urge to *do more*, to *fix it now*. We can fall into the trap of believing that healing must be a dramatic, uphill battle.

But what if healing, like water, is often about gentle, persistent, downward-flowing movements? What if it's about returning to the basics – the "lowly places" – that we often disdain in our pursuit of bigger, faster solutions? This might look like prioritizing simple moments of rest, even just five minutes of quiet contemplation. It might mean choosing a gentle walk in nature over an intense workout when your body is signaling exhaustion. It might be about allowing yourself to cry, to express the emotions that water up from within, rather than holding them back.

These aren't dramatic interventions, are they? They are humble, persistent acts of self-care that, over time, can profoundly re-pattern your nervous system. Just as a tiny drop of water, over millennia, can carve a canyon, these small, consistent acts of yielding and flowing can create deep, lasting shifts in your internal landscape. It's about trusting the natural intelligence of your body to find its way back to balance, much like water always finds its way back to the sea.

## The Tao of Deep Rest: Beyond Sleep

One of the most profound gifts of embracing water's wisdom is the invitation to deep rest. In our culture, rest is often seen as a luxury, something to be earned after all the "important" work is done. But for a strained nervous system, rest is not a luxury; it's a necessity. And I'm not just talking about sleep, though sleep is absolutely vital. I'm talking about a quality of rest that allows your nervous system to truly downshift, to move into those slower brain wave frequencies – alpha and theta – where deep healing and integration occur.

Think of a calm lake – its surface still, yet beneath, there's a vibrant ecosystem thriving. This is the kind of deep rest we're aiming for. It's a state where your body feels safe enough to release tension, where your mind can quiet its incessant chatter, and where your internal resources can be replenished.

Practices that embody water's qualities can facilitate this deep rest. Gentle, restorative yoga, where you hold poses supported by props, allowing gravity to do the work – this is yielding. Mindful breathing, where you simply observe the ebb and flow of your breath, like waves on a shore – this is flow. Spending time in nature, especially near water, without an agenda, just *being* – this is humility.

Here's the point: your nervous system is always listening. It's constantly scanning for cues of safety or danger. When you consciously choose practices that embody the qualities of water – yielding, flowing, humble persistence – you are sending powerful signals of safety. You are communicating to your body, "It's okay to relax. It's okay to let go. You are supported." And as your nervous system receives these signals, it gradually learns to release its grip, to soften, to return to its natural state of fluidity and balance.

This isn't about forcing relaxation; it's about *inviting* it. It's about creating the conditions for your body's innate wisdom to re-emerge. Just as water doesn't *try* to flow, it simply flows, you don't *try* to relax, you create the space for relaxation to arise naturally.

## The Ripple Effect: Healing Ourselves, Healing Our World

The Tao Te Ching reminds us that we are not separate from nature; we are an integral part of it. When we align ourselves with the wisdom of water, we are not just healing our individual nervous systems; we are participating in a larger pattern of harmony and balance. When we bring more fluidity, adaptability, and gentle persistence into our own lives, that energy ripples outwards. It affects our relationships, our communities, and ultimately, the world around us.

Perhaps this is the ultimate lesson of water: that true strength lies not in rigidity or control, but in adaptability and yielding. That the most powerful force is often the one that moves with the least resistance. And that healing, like water, is a continuous, gentle process of returning to our natural state of flow.

So, beloved one, I invite you to consider where in your life you might embody more of water's wisdom. Where can you yield instead of resist? Where can you invite more flow instead of stagnation? Where can you embrace humble persistence over frantic striving? Trust that your body, your nervous system, holds an innate intelligence, a deep knowing of how to return to balance. All you need to do is listen, and allow the gentle current to guide you home.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Heart's Inner Compass: Navigating Life Through Its Neural Wisdom
teachings.title: The Heart's Inner Compass: Navigating Life Through Its Neural Wisdom
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider the heart as a neural, sensing organ that communicates continuously with the brain. She explains how cultivating heart coherence through simple somatic practices such as slow breathing and heart-focused attention can clarify intuition, steady emotion, and become an inner compass for decision-making and flow.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The other day, I was sitting by the window, watching the rain — that soft, persistent Vancouver rain that seems to wash the world clean. My cat, Luna, was curled on my lap, a purring warmth, and I was just… being. No agenda, no to-do list humming in the back of my mind. Just the sound of the rain, the feel of Luna’s fur, and a quiet sense of presence. And in that stillness, a memory surfaced, unbidden, from years ago. I was in my early twenties, fresh out of university, and utterly lost. I’d followed all the “right” paths — good grades, a respectable degree — but my heart felt like a hollow drum. I remember standing in a busy street, the noise and rush of people swirling around me, and feeling an almost physical ache of disconnection. I kept asking myself, “What am I supposed to do? Where am I supposed to go?” And the answers that came from my mind were always logical, sensible, and utterly devoid of spark. It felt like trying to navigate a dense forest with a map drawn by someone who’d never actually been there.

It took me years — decades, really — to understand that the map I needed wasn’t in my head at all. It was in my heart. Not the romantic, sentimental heart, though that’s beautiful too, but the deep, intuitive, intelligent heart that speaks in whispers and sensations, in subtle shifts of energy and knowing. This heart, I’ve come to understand, is our most profound inner compass, a sophisticated neural network far more intricate than we’ve often given it credit for. It’s a wisdom that transcends logic, a knowing that precedes thought. And learning to listen to it, to truly *feel* its guidance, has been the most transformative journey of my life.

### The Heart's Brain: More Than a Pump

For so long, we’ve been taught to view the heart primarily as a pump — a vital, muscular organ that circulates blood, keeping us alive. And of course, it *is* that. But modern science, in its beautiful unfolding, is revealing something far more profound: the heart possesses its own intrinsic nervous system, often referred to as “the heart brain.” This isn't just a metaphor; it’s a tangible network of approximately 40,000 neurons, neurotransmitters, proteins, and support cells — a complex mini-brain that communicates with the cranial brain in a continuous, bidirectional dialogue.

Here’s a very good thing to know: this communication isn't one-way, with the brain dictating to the heart. In fact, the heart sends more signals to the brain than the brain sends to the heart! These signals profoundly influence brain function, affecting our perceptions, emotions, decision-making, and even our cognitive abilities. Think about that for a moment. The rhythm, the coherence, the very *feeling* of our heart space is constantly shaping our experience of reality.

When I first learned about this, it was like a light switch flicked on. It suddenly made sense why, when I was lost in my twenties, my logical mind felt so inadequate. My heart, though beating, wasn't speaking in a coherent way to my brain. It was likely sending signals of stress, confusion, and disconnection, which then amplified those very feelings in my mind. It wasn't until I started to consciously cultivate practices that brought my heart into a state of coherence — practices like deep breathing, meditation, and simply spending time in nature — that I began to experience a shift. My thoughts became clearer, my decisions felt more aligned, and that hollow drum began to resonate with a quiet, steady hum.

This heart-brain connection is powerful. When our heart is in a state of coherence — a rhythmic, harmonious pattern of heart rate variability — it sends signals that promote optimal brain function. This state is associated with increased emotional stability, enhanced cognitive performance, greater intuition, and a stronger sense of inner peace. Conversely, when our heart rhythms are chaotic, often due to stress, fear, or anger, it sends signals that can impair cognitive function, fuel anxiety, and make it harder to access our innate wisdom. It’s a feedback loop, you see. Our emotional state influences our heart, and our heart’s state influences our brain, which then reinforces our emotional state. The good news is, we can consciously intervene in this loop.

### The Language of the Heart: Sensing Beyond Words

So, if the heart has its own intelligence, how do we listen to it? What is its language? It’s rarely in words, beloved one. The heart speaks in sensations, in subtle shifts of energy, in gut feelings, in an inexplicable pull or push. It’s that feeling of expansion when something feels right, or a tightening, a contraction, when something feels off. It’s the quiet knowing that settles within you, even when your mind is still wrestling with pros and cons.

I remember a time when I was considering a significant career change. My mind had a meticulously crafted list of reasons why it was a good idea — financial stability, prestige, all the external markers of success. But every time I imagined myself in that role, I felt a subtle but undeniable constriction in my chest, a faint sense of dread. It wasn't a panic attack; it was far more subtle, like a quiet alarm bell ringing deep within. My rational mind tried to override it, to dismiss it as fear of the unknown. But my body, my heart, kept sending that signal. I listened. I chose a different path, one that initially seemed less "sensible" but resonated with a feeling of spaciousness and joy. And that path, though it had its challenges, ultimately led me to the work I do today — work that fills my heart and soul.

This is the language of the heart: a somatic intelligence, a felt sense. It’s why practices that bring us into our bodies are so crucial. When we are deeply present in our physical form, we become more attuned to these subtle signals. Meditation, conscious breathing, walking in nature, gentle movement — these aren’t just “wellness trends”; they are profound tools for recalibrating our internal compass, for quieting the incessant chatter of the mind so that the heart’s wisdom can rise to the surface.

Here's the point: your body is a sacred messenger. It’s constantly communicating with you, offering wisdom and guidance. Symptoms, discomfort, ease, joy — these are all communications. And the heart, with its intricate neural network, is a central hub for this communication. When we learn to interpret its signals, we unlock a profound source of self-guidance.

### Cultivating Coherence: Harmonizing Your Inner World

So, how do we intentionally cultivate this heart coherence? How do we strengthen our connection to this inner compass? It’s simpler than you might imagine, though it requires consistent, gentle practice. It’s about creating an internal environment where the heart can thrive and communicate clearly with the brain.

One of the most powerful tools is conscious breathing. When we breathe slowly, deeply, and rhythmically, we directly influence our heart rate variability. Try this: Inhale slowly to a count of five, feeling your breath expand your chest and abdomen. Then, exhale slowly to a count of five, feeling a gentle release. Do this for just a few minutes, and notice what happens. You might feel a subtle shift — a softening, a sense of calm. This isn't just anecdotal; it's a physiological response. Slow, deep breathing activates the vagus nerve, which in turn signals the heart to enter a more coherent rhythm.

Another practice I find incredibly potent is heart-focused attention. This involves simply placing your attention in the area of your heart, perhaps even placing a hand gently over your chest. As you breathe, imagine your breath flowing in and out of your heart space. As you do this, recall a feeling of genuine appreciation, gratitude, or love. It could be for a pet, a loved one, a beautiful sunset, a warm cup of tea — anything that evokes a true feeling of warmth and expansion in your heart. Hold that feeling for a few moments. This isn't about intellectual gratitude; it's about *feeling* it in your body.

This practice, often called "heart coherence training," has been extensively studied. Research shows that even short periods of intentionally evoking positive emotions while focusing on the heart can significantly improve heart rate variability, reduce stress hormones, and enhance cognitive function. It’s like tuning an instrument — bringing your internal symphony into harmony.

For me, this practice has become a daily ritual. In the mornings, before the day fully begins, I sit quietly, often with Luna purring beside me, and I breathe into my heart. I call to mind the things I genuinely appreciate — the warmth of my home, the beauty of the trees outside my window, the love in my life. And I feel my heart soften, expand. It sets a different tone for the day, a tone of grounded presence and openheartedness. It’s not about ignoring challenges; it’s about meeting them from a place of inner strength and clarity.

### The Tao of the Heart: Trusting the Flow

The wisdom of the heart, like the wisdom of the Tao, is about flow, about effortless action, about trusting the natural rhythms of life. It’s about letting go of the need to control every outcome and instead, aligning with the deeper current that moves through all things. When our heart is coherent, when its neural wisdom is clear, we become more attuned to this flow. Decisions feel less like battles and more like gentle nudges. Opportunities appear as if by magic. Synchronicity becomes a common occurrence.

This isn't woo-woo or magical thinking; it’s the natural outcome of an integrated inner system. When your heart and brain are communicating harmoniously, you are simply more receptive to the subtle cues and opportunities that life is constantly presenting. You’re less likely to be caught in the grip of fear or doubt, which can blind us to possibilities.

Think of it like a river. When the river flows freely, unblocked by debris, it carves its path with grace and power. When our inner river — the flow of energy and information between our heart and brain — is clear, we too navigate life with greater grace and power. We are less likely to get stuck in eddies of anxiety or dashed against the rocks of self-doubt.

My journey has been one of continually learning to trust this inner compass, even when my mind screams otherwise. It’s about honoring that subtle contraction, that gentle expansion, and knowing that these are messages from a deeper, wiser part of myself. It’s about understanding that I am not broken, that you are not broken, and that within each of us resides an extraordinary capacity for healing, for knowing, for transformation. The heart, with its intricate neural wisdom, is a key to unlocking that capacity. It’s a reminder that true guidance comes not from external maps, but from the sacred landscape within.

So, perhaps, as you go about your day, you might pause for a moment. Place a hand on your heart. Take a slow, deep breath. And just listen. What is your heart whispering to you? What does it feel like to simply be present, in this moment, with the incredible intelligence that resides within your own chest? Trust that feeling. It is your most reliable guide.

With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan
