teachings.sourceTitle: Left Shoulder, Right Shoulder: The Feminine and Masculine of Carrying
teachings.title: Left Shoulder, Right Shoulder: The Feminine and Masculine of Carrying
teachings.summary: Susan uses a clinical story of a frozen right shoulder to explore how our bodies encode patterns of doing and receiving, associating the right side with duty/action and the left with receiving/emotional labor. She links these patterns to neuroplasticity — explaining how long-held beliefs and responsibilities become bodily habits — and offers a gentle somatic practice of mindful attention and breath to begin unburdening the shoulders and rebalancing giving and receiving.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A client, let’s call her Sarah, came to me years ago with a frozen right shoulder. She was a successful lawyer, a mother of three, and the primary caregiver for her aging parents. She described her life as a series of responsibilities she shouldered with grim determination. Her right arm, the one she used to write legal briefs, to carry her children, to support her mother, was locked in a painful, rigid state. “It’s like my body is refusing to do one more thing,” she told me, her voice a mixture of frustration and despair.

It’s a complex business, being human. We are born into a world that asks so much of us, and we so desperately want to be good, to be helpful, to be loved. We learn early on to carry things. We carry our schoolbags, our siblings, our parents’ expectations, our own dreams. Our shoulders, these marvelously complex joints, are the physical embodiment of this capacity. They are the cradle of our responsibilities, the gateway through which we extend ourselves into the world. Each shoulder is a marvel of engineering, a meeting point of three bones, allowing for a remarkable range of motion. This flexibility is not just physical; it is energetic. It is the capacity to hold, to release, to reach, to embrace. Our shoulders are designed to be in a constant, fluid dance with life.

But what happens when the carrying becomes too much? What happens when the weight of our perceived burdens begins to crush us? The body, in its infinite wisdom, will always tell us the truth. And when it comes to our shoulders, the story is often one of imbalance, of unconscious beliefs about responsibility, and of the delicate dance between giving and receiving.

## The Two Sides of the Story: Feminine and Masculine

In the language of the body, the left side is often associated with the feminine, with receiving, with emotional and relational burdens. The right side is associated with the masculine, with doing, with duty, protection, and the burdens of the external world. When I see a client with left shoulder pain, I often find a story of carrying the emotional weight of their family, of feeling responsible for everyone’s happiness, of an inability to receive support and nourishment for themselves. When the right shoulder is in distress, as it was for Sarah, I often find a story of over-doing, of a relentless drive to achieve and protect, of a belief that their worth is tied to their productivity.

Sarah’s frozen right shoulder was a classic case of the masculine side in overdrive. She was a master of doing, of providing, of protecting. But she had completely forgotten how to receive. Her left shoulder, while not in acute pain, was weak and underdeveloped. She had no capacity to take in the love and support that was offered to her, because she didn’t believe she deserved it unless she was carrying the world on her right shoulder. Her body, in its wisdom, had finally said, “Enough.” It had frozen her “doing” arm to force her to confront the imbalance in her life. I remember another client, a man this time, who came to me with chronic pain in his left shoulder. He was a stay-at-home father, a deeply sensitive and empathetic man who had taken on the emotional labor of his entire family. He absorbed his wife’s work stress, his children’s anxieties, his parents’ marital problems. His left shoulder, the feminine side, was screaming under the weight of all this emotional baggage. He had forgotten how to set boundaries, how to discern what was his to carry and what was not. His healing journey was about learning to honor his own emotional needs, to create a container for his own feelings, and to release the emotional burdens of others.

We are not meant to be creatures of pure doing or pure receiving. We are designed for flow, for the beautiful, rhythmic exchange of giving and taking. The heart, the central sun of our being, models this for us with every beat. It expands to receive, and it contracts to give. It is a perfect, life-sustaining rhythm. Our shoulders are meant to participate in this dance. They are designed to be a stable foundation from which we can reach into the world, and a soft place upon which we can receive the world’s gifts.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Neuroscience of Burden

Our beliefs about responsibility are not just abstract concepts. They are wired into our nervous system. From a young age, our brains create neural pathways based on our experiences. If we grew up in an environment where we were praised for being “a little helper,” for taking on adult responsibilities, for never complaining, our brains learned that this was the way to be safe and loved. These neural pathways become deep grooves, and we continue to play out these patterns long after the original circumstances have changed.

Sarah’s childhood was one of immense responsibility. Her mother was chronically ill, and Sarah, as the eldest daughter, became a surrogate parent to her younger siblings. She learned that her value lay in her ability to care for others, to be strong, to never falter. This belief became a core part of her identity, a deeply ingrained neural pathway. Her brain, in its attempt to keep her safe, continued to fire along this pathway, even when she was a grown woman with a family of her own. The result was a nervous system in a constant state of high alert, a body braced for the next burden, and a right shoulder that finally gave out under the strain.

But here is the beautiful, hopeful truth: our brains are not fixed. They are capable of profound change, a process known as neuroplasticity. We can create new neural pathways. We can teach our nervous system that it is safe to rest, to receive, to let go of the burdens that are not ours to carry. This is the work of transformation. It is the work of coming home to ourselves. Every time we choose a new response, every time we interrupt an old pattern, we are literally forging new connections in our brain. It is like creating a new path in a dense forest. At first, it is difficult, and we may stumble. But with each repetition, the path becomes clearer, wider, and easier to travel. The old path, the one of over-responsibility and self-neglect, begins to fade from lack of use. This is not about forcing or striving. It is about gentle, consistent redirection. It is about choosing, again and again, to move towards self-compassion and balance.

## The Practice of Unburdening

So how do we begin to unburden our shoulders? How do we create a new relationship with responsibility, one that is based on balance, discernment, and self-compassion? It begins with awareness. It begins with listening to the whispers of the body before they become screams.

Here is a simple practice you can do. Find a quiet place to sit or lie down. You can be in a chair with your feet on the floor, or lying on your back with your knees bent. Allow your body to be comfortable and supported. Close your eyes and bring your attention to your shoulders. Notice any sensations you feel. Is there tension? Tightness? Pain? A sense of weight? Don’t judge what you find. Simply notice. Be curious. What is the quality of the sensation? Is it sharp or dull? Constant or intermittent? Does it have a color? A texture? A temperature?

Now, imagine that you can breathe into your shoulders. With each inhale, imagine you are bringing in a sense of spaciousness, of light, of ease. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing the burdens you have been carrying. You might even want to name them silently to yourself. “I release the burden of my mother’s happiness. I release the burden of my children’s future. I release the burden of my own perfection.”

As you continue to breathe, you might notice a shift in the sensations in your shoulders. They might feel lighter, more relaxed. Or you might feel a wave of emotion. Sadness, anger, grief. This is all part of the process. These are the crystallized emotions that have been stored in your tissues. Allow them to flow. Allow them to be released.

This is not a one-time fix. It is a practice, a way of being in a new relationship with yourself. It is a commitment to honoring the wisdom of your body, to creating a life where you are both strong and soft, where you can both give and receive with grace and ease.

For Sarah, the journey of healing her shoulder was a journey of healing her life. She learned to delegate at work, to ask for help from her husband, to allow her children to be responsible for their own lives. She started taking pottery classes, something she had always wanted to do, but never felt she had the time for. She learned to use her hands not just to carry, but to create. Her left arm, the arm of receiving, began to awaken. Her right shoulder, slowly, miraculously, began to thaw.

Your shoulders are not your enemies. They are your faithful servants, your sacred messengers. They are telling you a story. A story of what you have carried, of what you have held, of what you are ready to release. Listen to their story. Honor their wisdom. And allow yourself to be unburdened. This is a journey, not a destination. There will be days when you feel the old weight settling back on your shoulders. And on those days, you will meet yourself with compassion. You will remember that you are learning a new way of being. You will breathe into your shoulders, and you will release. You will remember that you are worthy of a life of ease and grace, a life where you are both a powerful giver and a joyful receiver. A life where your shoulders are free to dance.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Letting Go Without Shame: What Your Bladder Is Teaching You
teachings.title: Letting Go Without Shame: What Your Bladder Is Teaching You
teachings.summary: Susan explores how bladder symptoms can be a somatic expression of long-held emotions—particularly shame, suppressed anger, and grief—using a client story of chronic cystitis to illustrate the point. She links these patterns to neurobiology (Polyvagal Theory) and invites a non-forcing, compassionate practice to listen to the bladder and nervous system. The piece reframes release as a gradual reclaiming of unmet needs and safety rather than a demand for immediate catharsis.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
>
> The nervous system remembers everything. This is both its gift and its burden.

We are wired for connection, for love, for belonging. And yet, so often, we find ourselves tangled in the very emotions that seem to push love away: fear, resentment, and that most painful and isolating of all human experiences—shame.
>
> I remember a client, a woman I’ll call Josephine, who came to me with chronic cystitis. She was a successful lawyer, a mother of two, a woman who seemed to have it all together on the surface. But her body was telling a different story. It was screaming, in fact. A fiery, urgent, relentless burning that no amount of cranberry juice or antibiotics could permanently quell. “I feel like I’m on fire,” she told me, her voice tight with a mixture of frustration and despair. “It’s like my own body is attacking me. I do everything right, I eat all the right things, I exercise… why is this happening?”
>
> As we began to work together, a deeper narrative started to emerge. It wasn’t one of a body gone rogue, but of a lifetime of holding in. Holding in her anger at a partner who didn’t see her, who dismissed her needs with a casual wave of the hand. Holding in her grief over a childhood that was far from the “happy ending” she was taught to expect, a childhood where her sensitivity was treated as a flaw. Holding in her own deep needs for rest and care while she endlessly poured herself out for her family and her career, running on a fuel of sheer willpower. She was holding it all in, creating a pressurized reservoir of unspoken emotion. And her bladder, that beautiful, sensitive organ of release, was simply reflecting the truth of her inner world. The urgency she felt was the urgency of her soul’s need to let go. The burning was the friction of her resistance against that essential release.
>
> ## The Myth of the Happy Ending
>
> So many of us are raised on a diet of fairy tales, stories that promise a neat and tidy resolution if we just follow the rules. If you’re a *good* girl, if you work *hard*, if you put others *first*, you will be rewarded. You will be rescued. You will live happily ever after. We internalize this script, believing that our goodness is a currency we can use to purchase a life free from pain and disappointment.
>
> Josephine had followed the script to the letter. She had been the perfect daughter, the perfect student, the perfect wife and mother. She had held herself in, controlled her natural impulses, and presented a flawless facade to the world. But the promised happy ending never materialized. Instead, she found herself in a life that felt profoundly inauthentic, simmering with a quiet resentment for all the ways she had abandoned herself in the pursuit of an illusion. Her body, through the persistent fire of cystitis, was burning away the fantasy. It was demanding that she look at the truth of her own experience, a truth that was messy, complicated, and anything but a fairy tale. That burning sensation she described so vividly was the physical manifestation of feeling *burned* by others, by life, by the promises that had gone unfulfilled. It was the heat of her own held-in anger and resentment, an internal fire that had nowhere to go.
>
> This is a profound teaching. The body is not interested in our fantasies. It is interested in the truth. When we hold onto rigid expectations of how life *should* be, we create a tremendous amount of internal conflict. The bladder, in its wisdom, asks us to release not just our emotions, but our attachment to outcomes. It invites us to let go of the need for a happy ending and to find peace in the unfolding reality of our lives, with all of its imperfections and unresolved chords.
>
> [PROMO_SESSIONS]
>
> ## The Neuroscience of a Shame Shutdown
>
> It’s a very good thing to know that shame is not just a feeling; it’s a neurobiological state. From the perspective of Polyvagal Theory, developed by Dr. Stephen Porges, shame is the signature of the dorsal vagal state of the parasympathetic nervous system. This is our most ancient survival response, a primal strategy of immobilization or feigning death in the face of an overwhelming threat. When we experience shame, our nervous system perceives a profound threat to our belonging—a fear of being cast out, which for our ancestors, was a literal death sentence.
>
> In these moments, the dorsal vagal branch of the vagus nerve can trigger a shutdown response. It’s a physiological freeze. Our heart rate and blood pressure drop, we may feel dizzy or disconnected, and a heavy, leaden feeling can settle in our limbs. We feel numb, collapsed, heavy, and disconnected from ourselves and the world. It’s the body’s attempt to help us survive an experience that feels unsurvivable, to play dead in the face of overwhelming social danger. This is why shame can feel so debilitating, so utterly isolating. We are, in a very real sense, *offline*.
>
> This is why letting go can feel so terrifying. If you have a lifetime of associating authentic expression with rejection or punishment, the mere thought of releasing your held emotions can trigger this dorsal vagal shutdown. The body braces for impact. The urgency of the bladder—the *need* to let go—collides with the terror of what that release might cost you. The result is this intolerable burning, this sense of being trapped in an impossible bind. You’re damned if you do, and in agony if you don’t. The way through is not to force the release. It is not to shame yourself for the shame. It is to bring a gentle, loving presence to the part of you that is so terrified. It is to begin to create a new neural pathway, one that whispers: *it is safe to feel. It is safe to release. You are not wrong for what you feel.*
>
> ## A Gentle Inquiry for Reclaiming Your Flow
>
> I invite you to try a small practice. This isn’t about fixing or forcing, but about listening and befriending. Find a quiet moment where you won’t be disturbed. Lie down comfortably and place a hand on your lower belly, over the space of your bladder.
>
> 1.  **Arrive in Your Body:** Close your eyes and take three slow, gentle breaths. With each exhale, imagine you are releasing a layer of tension. Feel the weight of your body on the surface beneath you. Just be here, now.
>
> 2.  **A Gesture of Kindness:** Feel the warmth of your hand on your belly. Let this touch be a message of pure kindness, of loving presence. You are not here to judge or demand anything. You are here to listen.
>
> 3.  **The Gentle Question:** Now, you might gently ask, internally: *Beloved body, what am I holding here? What is needing to be released?* The question is an invitation, not an interrogation. Let it float in your awareness.
>
> 4.  **Listen with Compassion:** Don’t search for an answer with your mind. Just listen with your body. You might feel a sensation—a tightness, a flutter, a warmth. An image might drift into your mind’s eye. A word or a phrase might echo in your inner ear. It might be a flicker of anger. A wave of sadness. A deep well of unspoken need. Whatever arises, can you meet it with compassion? Can you whisper to it, *I see you. I feel you. You are allowed to be here. You are welcome here.*
>
> 5.  **The Possibility of Release:** As you continue to breathe, you might imagine a tiny, gentle stream of energy flowing from this area, down through your legs, and out the soles of your feet. It doesn’t have to be a flood. Just a trickle. A single drop. Imagine this release being met by the earth, received without judgment. With every exhale, you can silently affirm: *I am allowed to let go.*
>
> This is not about a dramatic catharsis. It is about the slow, patient work of building trust with yourself. It is about learning, moment by moment, that your inner world is not a source of shame, but a source of sacred information. Your body is not your enemy; it is your most devoted ally, constantly speaking to you, guiding you back to wholeness.
>
> The journey of letting go is not about becoming perfect. It’s about becoming whole. It’s about reclaiming all the parts of yourself you were taught to hide. It’s about understanding that your needs are not a liability, but a vital part of your humanity. And it’s about discovering that true safety doesn’t come from controlling yourself, but from learning to love and trust the magnificent, messy, sacred truth of who you are.
>
>

---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

**More on Bladder:**

> Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Silver Tongue and the Silent Scream: Two Sides of Vocal Wounding
teachings.title: The Silver Tongue and the Silent Scream: Two Sides of Vocal Wounding
teachings.summary: Susan describes two embodied patterns of vocal wounding: the Silver Tongue—an articulate, performative voice that disconnects from inner truth—and the Silent Scream—a suppressed voice that the body protects by constricting expression. She traces how these patterns form in early life, show up as neck tension, headaches, hoarseness or fatigue, and invites a gentle, somatic path back to authentic, resonant speech through presence, small acts of expression, and neuroplastic practice. The piece emphasizes listening to the body’s messages and relearning safety for voice without forcing or shaming the process.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
He came to me for his chronic headaches, but within ten minutes on the table, I could feel the real story wasn’t in his head at all. It was in his throat.

This man was a master communicator—a celebrated litigator, in fact. His words were his trade, his art, his weapon. He could spin arguments from thin air, charm the most hostile witness, and deliver a closing statement that could bring a jury to tears. A true silver tongue. Yet, as my hands rested gently on his neck, I felt a constriction that was profound, a deep and ancient tension around his larynx. It felt like a fortress.

When I mentioned it, he was dismissive. “My voice is my greatest asset,” he said, his tone smooth as polished stone. But the energy in his body told a different story. It spoke of a lifetime of saying the right thing, the effective thing, the winning thing… but rarely, if ever, the *true* thing. His asset was also his cage.

It’s a tricky business, this human need to express. Our vocal cords, those two small, miraculous folds of mucous membrane, are the primary bridge between our inner universe and the world outside. They take the silent, invisible energy of a thought, a feeling, or a knowing, and translate it into a vibration that can be heard, felt, and received by another. They are the instruments of our soul’s signature song. But what happens when that song gets distorted?

In my years of working with the body and its sacred messages, I’ve seen two primary, and seemingly opposite, distortions of this vocal energy. They are two sides of the same wound, the wound of believing that our authentic voice is either not enough, or far too much. I call them the Silver Tongue and the Silent Scream.

## The Polished Cage of the Silver Tongue

The Silver Tongue is the voice of performance. It’s articulate, often brilliant, and incredibly persuasive. It’s the voice that has learned, usually very early in life, that love, safety, and success come from saying what others need or want to hear. It’s the voice of the pleaser, the performer, the salesperson, the politician, the advocate who has become disconnected from the heart they are meant to be advocating for.

This isn’t about conscious manipulation in a villainous sense. It’s a survival strategy, a neural pathway carved deep into the brain’s terrain. A child who learns that parental approval only comes when they are charming, quiet, or agreeable will learn to sever the connection between their messy, authentic inner world and the words that leave their mouth. The voice becomes a tool for managing the outside world, rather than an expression of the inner one.

The body, however, never lies. While the silver-tongued among us may win arguments and close deals, the body keeps the score. The unexpressed truths, the swallowed disagreements, the unheard feelings… they don’t just vanish. They crystallize. They become the fortress of tension in the neck, the grinding of the jaw at night, the chronic headaches that seem to have no source. The throat, which is meant to be a wide, open channel between the heart’s wisdom and the head’s articulation, becomes a tightly controlled checkpoint. Only the most carefully vetted words are allowed to pass.

To have a silver tongue is to live in a polished cage. It looks beautiful, it sounds impressive, but it is a profound form of self-imprisonment. The soul’s true, unvarnished, and sometimes inconvenient song remains unsung. The body, in its infinite wisdom, bears the resonant ache of that silence, hoping one day we will finally listen.

I once worked with a woman, a CEO, whose migraines were legendary. She had a classic Silver Tongue. She could command a boardroom, negotiate multi-million dollar deals, and deliver keynote speeches that received standing ovations. But in our sessions, her body told the story of a little girl who had to be the perfect, high-achieving daughter to a demanding and critical father. Her voice became her armor. The migraines were the cracks in that armor, the pressure of a lifetime of unexpressed feelings—of not being good enough, of anger at the constant pressure, of a deep yearning to just be held and loved for who she was, not what she accomplished. The pain in her head was the physical manifestation of the battle between her authentic self and her carefully constructed persona.

## The Suffocating Weight of the Silent Scream

On the other end of the spectrum is the Silent Scream. This is the voice that is lost, suppressed, or chronically weak. It’s the experience of the woman I worked with who would get laryngitis before every single family gathering. It’s the artist who feels a lump in his throat whenever he tries to talk about his work. It’s the feeling of having a thousand words to say, but an absolute inability to push them out.

Where the Silver Tongue learns to perform, the Silent Scream learns to disappear. This pattern often comes from an environment where speaking one’s truth was met with punishment, ridicule, or danger. The nervous system creates a powerful association: *My voice = Unsafe*. To protect the self, the body wisely and brilliantly begins to shut down the mechanism of expression. The throat constricts, the vocal cords become inflamed or hoarse, and the voice literally vanishes.

This is the body’s wisdom at work. It is saying, “I will not let you put yourself in danger again.” The symptom is not the enemy; it is a message from a deeply loving and protective part of your own consciousness. It is the echo of a past reality where your truth was not welcome.

The tragedy is that this pattern continues long after the original danger has passed. The neural pathways of suppression become so automatic that we find ourselves unable to speak up in a loving partnership, to ask for a raise from a reasonable boss, or to set a boundary with a friend. The throat becomes a graveyard of unspoken truths. The energy of all that wants to be said—the anger, the grief, the joy, the fierce love—gets trapped. This is the silent scream. It’s not silent because there’s nothing to say; it’s silent because the body believes, based on past evidence, that the cost of saying it is simply too high. The nervous system, in its primal role as our protector, makes a calculation: survival is more important than expression. The throat becomes the chokepoint, the place where the impulse to speak is physically halted.

Think of the sheer amount of energy this requires. To constantly suppress the life force that wants to move through you and be expressed as sound takes a tremendous toll. It can manifest as chronic fatigue, thyroid issues (the thyroid gland sits right at the base of the throat, the butterfly of transformation), and a persistent feeling of being disconnected from oneself and the world. It is a profound and exhausting form of self-gaslighting, where the body is screaming a truth that the conscious mind has learned to deny.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Reclaiming Your Vibrational Signature

Whether you find yourself in the polished cage or the suffocating silence, the path to healing is the same. It is the journey back to authentic expression. It is the process of gently, compassionately, re-establishing the sacred connection between your heart, your mind, and your voice.

This isn’t about suddenly speaking every thought that enters your head. Authentic expression is not brutal honesty. It is *resonant* honesty. It is learning to feel what is true in your body, to allow it to be met with the wisdom of your heart, and to express it with a clarity that is both kind and true.

We begin by honoring the body’s message. If your throat is tight, if your voice is gone, the first step is not to force it. It is to listen. Place a hand on your throat. Breathe. Hum gently, feeling the vibration under your palm. What is the quality of that vibration? Is it buzzing with unexpressed anger? Is it trembling with fear? Is it numb with grief? You don’t need to have the words yet. You just need to be willing to feel the energy.

This is neuroplasticity in action. We are consciously creating a new experience, a new memory for the body. We are laying down a new neural pathway that says, *"Feeling in my throat is met with presence."* We repeat this, day after day. A hand on the throat while humming in the car. A moment of silence before a difficult conversation, just to breathe and feel. We are teaching our nervous system, breath by breath, that it is safe to feel, and eventually, it will be safe to speak.

For the Silver Tongue, this practice is about learning to tolerate the discomfort of not performing. It’s about allowing a pause, a moment of silence, before answering. It’s about asking, “What do I *really* think? What do I *really* feel?” and waiting for the quieter, less-polished voice to emerge from beneath the performer. It’s about risking being less charming in order to be more true.

For the Silent Scream, it’s about starting small. It might be saying “no” to a small request. It might be stating a simple preference: “I’d prefer the window seat.” It might be writing down the words you’re afraid to say in a journal. Each small act of authentic expression is a victory, a signal to the nervous system that the world did not end, that you were not abandoned, that you are, in fact, still safe.

From this place of embodied presence, we can begin to allow the soul’s true signature to emerge. It may be a whisper at first. A single, true word. A boundary spoken with a trembling voice. A declaration of love that feels terrifying and exhilarating. Each time you speak from this place of integrated truth, you are reclaiming your voice. You are telling your body, your history, and the universe that you are ready to let your own unique and sacred frequency be heard.

This is the transcendence of vocal wounding: to release the deeply held belief that your truth is dangerous or inadequate. It is to allow the highest frequencies of your being—the frequencies of goodness, harmony, and love—to flow through the channel of your throat and into the world, not as a performance or a plea, but as a simple, resonant offering of who you truly are.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [A Breathwork Practice for Lung Healing and Vitality](/blog/lungs-breathwork-practice)
- [Handling Life: When Grip Becomes Grasp](/blog/hands-handling-life)

**More on Vocal Cords:**

- [A Practice for Freeing Your Voice and Speaking with Love](/blog/vocal-cords-freeing-voice-practice)
- [Losing Your Voice: When Authentic Expression Feels Dangerous](/blog/vocal-cords-losing-voice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: The Supreme Good Is Like Water: What the Tao Teaches About True Strength
teachings.title: The Supreme Good Is Like Water: What the Tao Teaches About True Strength
teachings.summary: Susan draws on Chapter 8 of the Tao Te Ching to offer a gentle reframe of strength as fluidity, surrender, and humility rather than forceful striving. She links the Tao’s water metaphor to contemporary understandings of the nervous system, and invites small, body-based practices that help us move from habitual 'trying' into a more restful, receptive way of being. The piece honors the value of low places—grief, rest, uncertainty—as fertile ground for integration and renewed resilience.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We are coached to be strong, to strive, to push, to *win*. We are taught that strength is a kind of rigidity, an unyielding force against the pressures of the world. But what if true strength isn’t about force at all? What if it’s about fluidity, adaptability, and the quiet power of surrender? The ancient wisdom of the Tao Te Ching, in its gentle and profound way, offers a different perspective. In Chapter 8, Lao Tzu whispers a truth that can unravel a lifetime of conditioning: > The supreme good is like water, > which nourishes all things without trying to. > It is content with the low places that people disdain. > Thus it is like the Tao. Water. It is the most powerful and yielding substance on Earth. It carves canyons out of stone, not through brute force, but through persistence and flow. It nourishes all of life, from the smallest seed to the mightiest forest, without ever asking for anything in return. It flows to the lowest places, the places we are taught to avoid—the places of humility, of not-knowing, of being rather than doing. This, the Tao tells us, is the nature of true strength. It is the path of *wu wei*, of effortless action. It is the grace of moving with the current of life, rather than fighting against it. ## The Tyranny of "Trying" So many of us are caught in the exhausting cycle of *trying*. Trying to be better, trying to heal, trying to fix our relationships, trying to force life into the shape we believe it should take. We clench our jaws, tighten our shoulders, and brace ourselves for the next battle. This constant state of tension, this internal bracing, is the opposite of the water-like state the Tao describes. I remember a client I worked with years ago, a brilliant and successful woman who felt like she was drowning. "I'm doing everything right," she told me, her voice tight with frustration. "I meditate, I journal, I eat clean, I say my affirmations... but I still feel so anxious and empty." Her body told the story. Her shoulders were hunched up to her ears, her breath was shallow, and her whole system was humming with the high-frequency buzz of a nervous system on high alert. She was *trying* so hard to be well that she was making herself sick. Our work together was not about adding more techniques or strategies. It was about subtraction. It was about gently, tenderly, helping her to *un-try*. We worked with the body, with the breath. We invited her to notice the tension, not as an enemy to be vanquished, but as a messenger. We explored what it would feel like to let go, just for a moment. To soften. To allow herself to be in the "low place" of not having it all figured out. It was a slow process, like the melting of a glacier. But little by little, she began to find the flow. She discovered that beneath the armor of trying was a deep well of wisdom and resilience she never knew she had. She learned to trust the current. ## The Neuroscience of Flow This ancient wisdom finds a beautiful echo in modern neuroscience. When we are in a state of stress and striving, our sympathetic nervous system—the "fight or flight" response—is in overdrive. Our bodies are flooded with cortisol and adrenaline, preparing us for a perceived threat. While essential for survival, living in this state is profoundly depleting. It shuts down our creativity, our capacity for connection, and our ability to heal. The state of being like water, on the other hand, corresponds to the activation of the parasympathetic nervous system—the "rest and digest" response. This is the state of flow, of deep presence, of *safety*. When our nervous system is in this state, our bodies can repair, our minds can quiet, and our hearts can open. The practice is to learn how to consciously shift from the sympathetic to the parasympathetic. This is not another thing to *try* to do, but a gentle allowing. It can be as simple as feeling your feet on the earth. Taking a slow, deep breath and making the exhale longer than the inhale. Placing a hand on your heart and feeling its steady beat. These small, body-based practices are anchors. They are invitations to the nervous system to come back to its natural state of rest and flow. They are reminders that we don’t have to carry the weight of the world in our shoulders. We can let the river carry us. ## The Wisdom of the Low Places We live in a culture that worships the peak. The promotion, the award, the public recognition, the perfect family photo. We are taught to scramble for the high places and to fear the low ones. The valleys of grief, of uncertainty, of failure, of rest—these are seen as places to be avoided at all costs. But water knows the secret. The low places are where the nourishment is. The low places are where the soil is fertile, where the seeds of new life can germinate. It is in the quiet valleys of our lives that we can truly integrate our experiences, heal our wounds, and gather the strength to continue our journey. To be like water is to have the courage to be with what is, without needing to change it or fix it. It is to trust that even in the darkest, most difficult moments, there is a current of grace that is holding you. It is to know that your vulnerability is not a weakness, but a doorway to the deepest kind of strength. Beloved one, if you are feeling tired of striving, if you are weary of the fight, I invite you to consider the way of water. What would it feel like to soften, just a little? To let go of the shore and trust the flow? To allow yourself to rest in the low places and be nourished? This is not about giving up. It is about giving *in*. It is about surrendering to a power that is infinitely greater than our own small, striving self. It is the supreme good. It is the way of the Tao.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

Which small, body-based cue (feeling your feet, a longer exhale, a hand on your heart) might you try for one minute today, and what difference do you notice in your shape or mood?

Soften your shoulders, close your eyes if that feels safe, and take five slow breaths, making each exhale slightly longer than the inhale (for example: inhale 4 counts, exhale 6 counts). After the fifth breath, rest for a moment and notice any shift. If you feel lightheaded or unwell, stop and sit quietly; consult a healthcare professional for persistent symptoms.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Head - The Crown of Consciousness and the Throne of Identity
teachings.title: The Head - The Crown of Consciousness and the Throne of Identity
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reconsider the role of the head: it is a brilliant instrument that too often becomes the sole storyteller, creating habitual neural grooves that harden into anxiety, control and physical symptoms like headaches. She offers somatic pathways — breath practices, soft gaze, naming thoughts, humming, felt-futures and ritual — to rebalance the intellect with heart and gut intelligence so the brain serves rather than rules. The aim is practical remapping through small, repeatable practices that re-establish embodied guidance without abolishing thinking.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You carry within your skull a three-pound universe - a trembling, incandescent organ that both fashions the story of you and receives the deeper currents that seek to move you. The head sits at the apex of your anatomy like a crown of light and a throne of identity. It organizes, it remembers, it predicts, it protects. Yet it also, often without your permission, insists upon a single story about who you are and how life must be managed. This insistence becomes habit. Those habits become grooves. Over time the grooves harden into neural highways that the river of your attention will follow without thought, making the cerebral world feel less like a servant and more like a master.

The Three-Pound Universe and Its Habit-Making Ways

The brain is exquisite in its economy. It learns by repetition. Each emotion you loop through, each interpretation you rehearse, each strategy you deploy to stay safe, lays down a synaptic trace. These are not metaphors alone - neurons that fire together wire together, and what is wired becomes the default. You feel the world, you think about it, and the thinking becomes the felt field that confirms itself. The mind becomes a groove-making machine, smoothing over novelty so you can conserve energy. That conservation was once protective. As an infant you learned quickly which facial expressions invited nourishment and which invited withdrawal. Those adaptive strategies became neural templates and they layered into the architecture of your head like sedimentation.

But the head also loves narrative. It will tirelessly choreograph reasons and justifications, loop future catastrophes as a primitive vigilance system, and try to negotiate safety by predicting outcomes. It can be generous and creative and brilliant. It can also become compulsive. What begins as helpful patterning can calcify into overthinking, rumination, strategizing, rehearsing and controlling. The more you rely upon the head as primary authority, the more disconnected you can become from felt experience, from the quiet intelligence that pulses in the heart and the somatic knowing that lives in the tissues. You lose access to the bodily guidance that once informed your choices with subtlety, and instead live by the loudness of thinking.

Headaches, Migraines and the Tyranny of Control

When your head aches it is not only a physical symptom. It is a punctuation mark. Tension, pressure, throbbing and the knives of migraine often mark a mind that has carried too much responsibility for outcomes, too much insistence on certainty, too much insistence on being correct. Headaches are frequently the body’s blunt instrument - a way for the deeper self to say stop. When you try to control life through mental gymnastics, the muscles of your jaw, neck and scalp tighten. The breath moves shallow and high. The nervous system remains in sympathetic tone. Blood vessels constrict and dilate unpredictably. The brain that was meant to be your tool becomes a battleground between the ego that wants to prove itself and the inner intelligence that seeks to return you to balance.

Imagine a head that is constantly rehearsing possible failures. Each rehearsal attracts cortisol, adrenaline, and a shrinking of attention. You may find yourself replaying conversations, re-editing what you said, imagining responses that will never happen. Or you may try to pre-plan every social, work or intimate contingency so tightly that spontaneity becomes a liability. The result is a clenched face, a neck like a drawn bowstring and headaches that demand you stop and attend. The pain is literal. It insists that you feel what you are doing with your attention and your life force.

When Inner Guidance Is Unheard

The head insists because it fears chaos. Its logic is: if I figure everything out, if I predict risk, then I can keep myself safe. Yet this makes you small. The head is not intended to be the sole source of counsel. Within your body there exists a vast intelligence - a holographic knowing that speaks through heart rhythms, gut sensations, skin temperature, the way your breath finds a new cadence when you are leaning toward truth. When you are disconnected from this somatic guidance, decisions are made in a conceptual vacuum. You may arrive at outcomes that look right on paper but feel dead in your bones. Or you may be paralyzed because the head cannot reconcile competing narratives with the agility of embodied wisdom.

There is another voice inside you that is quiet and not interested in debate. It is not impressed by logic. It does not persuade by argument. It meets you in sensation and in silence. If you are only listening to thought, you will miss those softer cues. The Tao sagely teaches that the deepest knowledge is not spoken. "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao," it says. This is not to demean the mind; it is to remind you of a larger field where wisdom arrives without being manufactured. You cannot think your way into every sense of rightness. You must learn again how to tune into your felt self.

The Myth of Mind as Monarch

Part of the suffering of the head arises from the myth that the intellect should be monarch. In many cultures the cognitive mind is equated with maturity and authority. If you can explain it you have mastery. If you can justify an action you own it. Yet this is a partial truth. The intellect is one faculty among many and when it rules without counsel it becomes bureaucratic, risk-averse and often cruelly blind to the nuances of life. Identity becomes conflated with thought. You equate yourself with your opinions, your history, your achievements and your fears. The ego sits upon the throne in the skull and elaborates a self-image that must be defended at all costs.

Defending identity requires endless mental labor. It requires comparing, measuring, retrofitting experience to maintain coherence. This mental labor costs physical energy because the nervous system believes the threat to identity is an existential threat. Headaches, insomnia, brittle concentration and a chronic sense of smallness are common companions. The antidote is not to abolish the mind but to remap its relation to you. Let it be a crown that adorns your sovereignty rather than a tyrant that demands homage.

How to Release Mental Gymnastics and Trust Wisdom Beyond Intellect

You do not need the head to stop thinking completely. That is unrealistic and not even desirable. Your thinking mind is a glorious instrument - capable of exquisite analysis, art and invention. The practice is to stop revering thought alone and to develop an ongoing conversation between your mind and the rest of your intelligence. Begin by listening to the head with curiosity rather than with fear. When a wave of anxious planning rises, say to yourself: Ah, there you are, old friend. Thank you for protecting me. Then gently ask: What would we learn if we slowed down and felt this through?

Bring the breath into the equation. The breath is the bridge between thinking and feeling. When you allow your exhales to be longer than your inhales you signal safety to your nervous system. The head relaxes. A simple practice is to lengthen the exhale by a count of two relative to the inhale - for example inhale four, exhale six. Do this several times and notice the change in the musculature around your jaw and neck. Notice whether the headache softens. Pair this with an embodied inquiry: place your hand at the base of your skull or at your sternum and feel. What is here? What wants to be said without words?

Another doorway is to name the repetitive thoughts as if they were weather patterns, not you. "There is thinking." "There is planning." "There is fear." Distancing language allows you to recognize the mind as phenomenon rather than identity. When you do this, you create a small space where the body can speak. The heart rate may settle. The gut may unclench. In that space, intuition can arise and your decisions can be informed by embodied knowing.

You can also retrain the neural grooves. Neuroplasticity is the proof that your brain is malleable. Each time you intentionally bring awareness into sensation and then act from that felt-sense rather than from thought alone, you carve a new path. Practice choosing one small decision each day that comes from felt guidance. Notice how your body responds before you rationalize. With repetition you will create new synaptic highways that support a different way of being - a head that learns to listen as well as to think.

Rituals of Reconciliation Between Head and Body

Create rituals that honor the crown but also invite it to be a servant. You might begin your morning with a short sitting that includes a bow - not apologetic but reverent - toward your body. Thank the brain for its service. Then place your attention into a region below the collarbone and ask that region what it needs for the day. Let the head be the steward who carries out the body's intentions with discernment and skill.

Another practice is the 'soft gaze'. So often you clamp your eyes tight in concentration and then scramble your thoughts like ants. Instead, soften your sight, allow peripheral vision to open and let your attention rest in open awareness. This simple change sends signals to your brain that you do not need to hyper-focus to survive. The muscles around your eyes and face will loosen and the jaw will unclench. Tension headaches will often yield when the face can relax.

Humming is a somatic tool you can use in moments of over-activity. The vibrations of a low hum stimulate the vagus nerve and increase parasympathetic tone. Hum while you breathe and feel the resonance in the skull and chest. The hum is an audible way to align brain rhythm with bodily rhythm, to remind the cerebral throne that it serves a larger chorus of intelligence.

Listening Practices That Invite Inner Counsel

Make space each day for silence that is not anxious or performance-driven. Sit quietly and ask a simple question: What is seeking me now? Then listen not with your thinking mind but with your interior senses - with subtle changes in the throat, a shifting in the belly, a throat-catch, a longening behind the eyes. These are the ways your inner guidance speaks. Sometimes the answer will come as a clear sentence. More often it will be a sensation that points you toward what feels aligned.

When you are at a crossroads, try the practice of 'felt futures'. Close your eyes and imagine each possible path briefly. Notice the somatic reaction to each image. One path may feel open in the chest. Another may make the stomach sink. You can name these sensations and let them inform your choice. Over time you will develop trust in this method because the body remembers what the head forgets - the taste of ease versus the cost of a choice that demands resignation.

Embodied Reframing and the Taoist Way

In Taoist language this is learning the art of non-doing - not as passivity but as aligned responsiveness. Wu wei is often mistranslated as inertness. In truth it is the intelligence of acting without contrivance, of letting action arise from an integrated field rather than from frantic mustiness. "When nothing is done, nothing is left undone." In other words, when you allow alignment to lead, you discover a different efficiency. The head still thinks, but thinking follows resonance rather than command. This way of being invites the crown to sit lightly and the throne to be occupied by a sovereign that includes heart and belly.

Practice the Taoist art of beginning small. Let small acts of surrender gather authority. When you experiment with trusting somatic cues on modest decisions and you see the world unfold, you gain evidence that wisdom beyond intellect is reliable. You do not have to leap from full control to complete surrender. You can walk there by foot, guided by felt-sense footsteps. The Tao reminds you that the valley receives and the mountain stands. Both are needed. Your head need not be diminished; it must be recontextualized into a fuller map of intelligence.

Moving from Identity to Presence

The final teaching I offer is this: your identity is not a static edict written in bone. It is a story that breathes and can be updated. When you begin to meet your head with compassion and curiosity, you free the throne from fear. You let the crown be a conduit of clarity instead of a coronation of self-judgment. You will still think, analyze and choose. But you will do so from an embodied platform that knows it belongs to more than argument and opinion. You will begin to taste the serenity of decisions that come from both wise mind and wise body in concert.

Return often to silence, to breath, to the simple practices that reestablish contact between your skull and your bones. Honor the three-pound universe for its service and ask it to loosen its death grip on identity. Invite your heart and gut to sit at the council. Learn the practice of listening as if life itself is offering counsel. Slow down the mental gymnastics, place your hand on your head and on your heart, and feel the difference. The crown will remain. The throne will become a seat of service rather than an altar of control.

You are more than the narrative that lives in your head. You are the living field that contains heart intelligence, gut wisdom and the subtle, luminous guidance of presence. When the head becomes a loving instrument again, instead of the sole storyteller, you reclaim the freedom to be guided by a wisdom that surpasses words. In that reclaiming you feel both small and vast, fragile and indestructible, humble and fully awake.

May your crown sit gently. May your throne be supple. May your head learn the art of listening and the world will follow.
keyThemes: Mind-body integration: bringing the head into dialogue with heart and gut wisdom
Neuroplasticity and habitual thinking: how repetition carves neural grooves
Somatic practices for regulation: breath, soft gaze, humming, and felt-sense
Headache and tension as embodied messages rather than only pathology
De-identifying from thought: language that creates space between you and thinking
Taoist-inspired wu wei: non-doing as aligned responsiveness
Ritual as a tool to recontextualize the intellect into service
reflectionPrompts: Notice a recent decision made primarily from thinking alone. How did your body respond before, during and after that choice? Describe any sensations in the chest, belly, throat or jaw.
When repetitive worry or planning arises, try the distancing phrase 'There is thinking.' What shifts in tone, posture, or facial tension occur when you treat thought as weather rather than identity?

Imagine two possible next steps for an upcoming choice; briefly visualize each and record the felt difference (openness in the chest, sinking in the belly, tightening in the neck). Which felt-sense more closely aligns with a sense of ease or integrity?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Practice a three-minute head-to-heart check-in: sit comfortably, soften your gaze, place one hand at the base of your skull and the other on your sternum. Inhale for a count of 4 and exhale for a count of 6, repeating for one to two minutes; notice jaw, neck and chest softening. Hum low on an exhale once or twice and name aloud or silently, 'There is thinking' when stories arise, then return attention to bodily sensations. If you feel lightheaded, increased pain, or any worsening symptoms, pause and, for persistent or severe headaches or other medical concerns, consult your healthcare provider—this practice is supportive, not a substitute for medical care.
sensitiveContentNotes: If identity, anxiety or chronic pain themes feel intense, you have full permission to pause the practices and return when you feel steady.
These somatic invitations can surface strong emotions; if you become overwhelmed, consider reaching out to a trusted mental health professional or support person.

This editorial content and the invitation are not a replacement for medical evaluation or treatment; for persistent or severe headaches, migraines, or other physical concerns, seek conventional medical advice.

teachings.sourceTitle: Putting Down What Isn't Yours: Transcending Shoulder Patterns
teachings.title: Putting Down What Isn't Yours: Transcending Shoulder Patterns
teachings.summary: Susan explores how shoulder tension often reflects the invisible burdens we absorb—felt physically as pain or tightness—and invites a practice of discernment to distinguish responsibilities that belong to us from those we’ve taken on by habit. She weaves anatomy, embodied attention, and neuroscience to encourage gentle self-inquiry, compassionate boundary-setting, and small, repeatable practices that support letting go and learning to receive.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The air in the high alpine meadow was thin and sharp, smelling of pine and damp earth after a morning rain. I sat on a smooth, grey boulder, the kind that has been warmed by a thousand suns. For years, I had been coming to these mountains to walk, to breathe, to simply be. But on this day, I was carrying something heavy. Not in my pack, which was light with just water and a small snack, but in my body. A familiar ache had settled deep into my shoulders, a tense, burning line from the base of my neck out to each joint. It was the weight of a choice that wasn't mine to make, a responsibility I had absorbed from someone I loved, believing my carrying it could somehow lighten their load.

Our shoulders—the cradle of responsibility, the gateway of extension. Anatomically, they are marvels of engineering, the most flexible joints in our entire body. Three distinct bones meet there, creating a complex articulation that allows us to reach, to pull, to push, to embrace. They are the physical foundation from which we extend ourselves into the world. But what happens when the extension becomes overextension? What happens when the embrace becomes a stranglehold of perceived duty?

This is where the deeper teachings of the body begin to speak to us, often in the language of discomfort and pain. When our shoulders begin to ache, to freeze, to burn, it is an invitation to look at what we are carrying. We often speak of “shouldering a burden” or “carrying the weight of the world on our shoulders.” These are not just metaphors; they are energetic realities. Our bodies, in their infinite wisdom, become a physical record of our energetic and emotional lives. The strain we feel in our shoulders is often the direct result of the invisible burdens and responsibilities we’ve taken on, consciously or unconsciously.

There’s a subtle distinction the body makes, a polarity of energy that can offer us clues. The left shoulder is often associated with our emotional burdens, the weight of our relationships, and the feminine principle of receiving. An ache on this side might be asking you: Where are you carrying the emotional weight of others? Where are you struggling to receive support, love, or care for yourself? The right shoulder, in contrast, is often linked to the burdens of duty, protection, and the masculine principle of doing. A strain here might be a sign of over-giving, of pushing too hard in your career, or of feeling an overwhelming need to protect and provide for everyone around you.

I remember a client, a brilliant and compassionate woman who came to me with chronic right shoulder pain. She was the CEO of a successful company, a mother of three, and the primary caregiver for her aging parents. She was, by all accounts, a pillar of strength for everyone in her life. As we worked together, she began to see that her shoulder pain was the physical manifestation of a deeply ingrained belief that she had to *do it all* herself. The weight of her "doing" was crushing her. The healing wasn't about her abdicating her responsibilities, but about learning to discern which ones were truly hers and which were born of a conditioned pattern of over-functioning. It was about learning to delegate, to ask for help, to allow herself to be supported. It was about the radical act of receiving.

These patterns are not our fault. Every pattern has served you. Perhaps taking on the weight of the world was a strategy you learned in childhood to feel safe or loved. Perhaps over-giving was how you learned to prove your worth. There is no shame or blame here, only a gentle, compassionate curiosity. What would it be like to simply notice the tension in your shoulders without judgment? To breathe into it, and ask, “Beloved, what is this? What part of this is mine, and what is not?”

This is the beginning of transcendence. It’s not about suddenly dropping all our responsibilities and running for the hills (though some days that might sound tempting!). It is a much more subtle, and ultimately more powerful, process of discernment. Transcendence, in this context, is the practice of putting down what isn’t yours to carry. It’s about cultivating the wisdom to know the difference between healthy, chosen responsibility and the unconscious absorption of others’ energy and burdens.

From a neuroscience perspective, these patterns of over-responsibility are deeply grooved neural pathways in the brain. We’ve fired and wired them for years, even decades. The thought “I have to handle this” automatically triggers a cascade of stress hormones and muscle tension, particularly in the neck and shoulders. The practice of discernment begins to create new neural pathways. The simple, conscious act of pausing and asking, “Is this truly mine?” introduces a moment of spaciousness. In that space, we can make a new choice. We can choose to not pick up the burden. We can choose to consciously release the tension in our shoulders, sending a signal back to the brain that we are safe, that we are not under threat.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

This process is a dance between giving and receiving. A healthy shoulder girdle is one that can do both with ease. It can reach out and give from a place of fullness, and it can also soften and open to receive. When we are out of balance, stuck in over-giving, we are essentially operating from a place of energetic deficit. We are pouring from an empty cup. Learning to receive—whether it’s a compliment, a helping hand, or simply a moment of quiet stillness—is what refills our cup. It is what creates a stable foundation from which we can then authentically and sustainably give to the world.

Think of your shoulders as the anchor points for your wings. If they are weighed down, constricted, and tight, how can your wings possibly expand? How can you soar? The journey of healing the shoulders is the journey of lightening the load so that you can reclaim your innate capacity for flight. It’s about understanding that your greatest gift to the world is not your martyrdom, but your wholeness.

What would it be like to let your shoulders soften, just for a moment? You might place a hand on each shoulder, offering a bit of warmth and gentle pressure. Breathe into your hands. With each exhale, you might imagine the heavy, dense energy of accumulated burdens beginning to dissolve. You might visualize it flowing down your arms and out through your fingertips, returning to the earth. You are not rejecting or pushing anything away. You are simply allowing what is not yours to fall away, with grace and with gratitude for the lessons it has taught you.

This is not a one-time fix. It is a practice, a moment-by-moment returning to awareness. You will pick up old burdens again. You will find yourself tensing your shoulders in familiar situations. And when you do, you can meet yourself with compassion. “Ah, there it is again. Hello, old friend. Thank you for trying to protect me. But right now, in this moment, I am choosing to put you down.”

As I sat on that mountain boulder, the sun warming my face, I began to breathe into my own aching shoulders. I acknowledged the love that motivated me to take on that weight, the fierce desire to protect someone I cared for. And then, with each exhale, I consciously offered it back to the universe, to the great mystery. I didn
’t have to carry it for them. My love was not contingent on my suffering. A profound sense of release washed over me, more expansive than the mountain vista before me. The ache in my shoulders began to subside, replaced by a feeling of lightness, of spaciousness. Of freedom.

This is the invitation for you, beloved. To find your own mountain, whether it’s a physical place or a quiet corner of your own heart. To become a student of your own body, listening with reverence to the stories it is telling you through its aches and pains. To cultivate the courageous discernment to put down what is not yours, and to embrace with your whole being the responsibilities that are. This is how we build a stable foundation from which to reach into the world, not from a place of strain, but from a place of grace.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you walk your journey with shoulders that are light and free, strong enough to carry your true purpose and soft enough to receive the boundless support of the universe. May you learn to discern what is yours to hold, and release the rest with love.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
keyThemes: Shoulders as embodied record of responsibility
Discernment between chosen duty and absorbed burdens
Balance of giving and receiving
Neural habits and neuroplasticity
Self-compassion and nonjudgmental awareness
Practical somatic practices for release
Boundary-setting and delegation
reflectionPrompts: Notice any habitual tension in your shoulders: what specific responsibility, relationship, or belief does that tension seem to be connected to? Name it without judgment.

Scan left and right shoulders separately. Which side feels heavier or tighter? Reflect on whether that side relates more to emotional/receiving burdens (left) or doing/protective responsibilities (right) in your life.

Trace the origins of one persistent ‘I must handle this’ belief: when did you first learn it, and what is one small, practical boundary or delegated task you could try this week to test putting that burden down?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Sit comfortably with a straight spine. Place your fingertips lightly on the tops of your shoulders and take five slow, intentional breaths: inhale to expand the chest and soften around the neck, exhale and consciously let the shoulders melt down a fraction, imagining any heavy, borrowed energy easing out through your fingertips. Repeat this cycle 3–6 times, pausing whenever you need to return to neutral. If the movement or sensations increase pain or emotional overwhelm, stop and rest; consult a healthcare professional or qualified somatic therapist as needed—this practice is supportive but not a substitute for medical care.
sensitiveContentNotes: This piece references childhood patterns, emotional burden, and strong caring responsibilities; these themes can surface intense feelings—give yourself permission to pause at any time.
If the material brings up significant distress, trauma, or grief, consider reaching out to a qualified therapist, trusted support person, or crisis resource for safety and containment.

If you experience persistent or worsening physical shoulder pain, please consult a medical professional; somatic practices here are complementary and should not replace conventional assessment or treatment.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Alchemy of Compassion: Transforming Pain into Presence
teachings.title: The Alchemy of Compassion: Transforming Pain into Presence
teachings.summary: Susan invites a reframe of pain from enemy to messenger, proposing compassion as a practical, nervous-system–wise way to transform relationship with physical and emotional suffering. She blends personal narrative with accessible neuroscience and offers simple practices—touch, curious inquiry, and loving‑kindness—to cultivate presence and soften habitual resistance. The piece emphasizes listening to the body and letting compassionate attention shift experience rather than promising instant cures.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The ancient healers knew something that modern medicine is only beginning to remember.

And perhaps one of the most profound parts of this human experience is how we relate to pain.

I remember a time, years ago, when a sudden, searing pain shot through my lower back. It wasn’t from a dramatic fall or a heavy lift. It arrived unannounced, a sharp, unwelcome guest that took my breath away and brought me to my knees on the cool kitchen floor. My first reaction was a wave of pure resistance. *No. Not this. Not now.* I was angry at my body, frustrated by the interruption, and terrified of what this pain might mean for my life, my work, my ability to simply *be*.

For days, I fought it. I tried to ignore it, to push through it, to medicate it into silence. I treated the pain as an enemy to be vanquished, a flaw to be fixed. But the more I fought, the louder it screamed. The more I resisted, the more it consumed my awareness, casting a long, dark shadow over everything. The pain in my back became a pain in my soul.

What if our pain—whether it’s the searing ache in a body, the deep throb of a broken heart, or the quiet despair of a spirit that feels lost—isn’t an enemy to be defeated? What if it’s a messenger?

And what if the secret to hearing its message isn’t to fight it, but to meet it with the transformative power of compassion?

## The Language of the Body

In our culture, we’ve been taught to see pain as a problem. A signal that something is broken. We are masters of the quick fix, the immediate silencing, the numbing. We want it to go away, and we want it to go away *now*. But in my three decades of work as a healer, I have learned a profound truth: the body never lies. And its symptoms, especially pain, are a sophisticated form of communication. They are the whispers—and sometimes, the desperate screams—of a part of ourselves that needs our loving attention.

When we only ever try to silence the pain, we miss the message. It’s like turning off a fire alarm without checking for the fire. The noise stops, but the danger, the underlying imbalance, remains. To truly heal, we must learn a new way of relating to our pain. We must learn the language of compassion.

It’s important, here, to clarify what compassion truly is. It is often confused with its cousins, sympathy and empathy, but it is a profoundly different energy.

> Sympathy says, “I feel sorry for you.” It creates a distance, a hierarchy of the well and the unwell. It looks down from a safe remove.

> Empathy says, “I feel your pain.” It’s the ability to resonate with another’s emotional state. It’s a vital human connection, but it can also be overwhelming. If we simply feel another’s pain, we can drown in it with them.

> Compassion, however, is something more. The word itself means “to suffer with.” But it is not about joining in the suffering. It is about bringing love *to* the suffering. Compassion is empathy plus action. It’s the ability to be present with pain—our own or another’s—without being consumed by it, and to respond with kindness, care, and a desire to help. It is the alchemical agent that doesn’t just witness pain, but actively transforms it.

## The Brain on Compassion

This isn’t just a beautiful spiritual idea; it’s grounded in the very wiring of our nervous systems. When we experience pain, our brain’s threat-detection system—the amygdala—goes on high alert. It floods our system with stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, preparing us for a fight-or-flight response. Our muscles tense, our heart rate increases, our focus narrows to the source of the threat. This is an ancient and brilliant survival mechanism. But when the “threat” is chronic pain or emotional suffering, we can get stuck in this state of high alert. The nervous system becomes locked in a pattern of defense, which, ironically, can amplify our experience of pain.

Compassion is the key that unlocks this prison. When we practice compassion, we activate a different set of neural pathways. Neuroscientists have found that the act of generating compassionate thoughts stimulates the prefrontal cortex, the brain’s center for higher-order thinking, emotional regulation, and empathy. It also activates the reward centers of the brain, releasing oxytocin, often called the “love hormone,” which promotes feelings of bonding, safety, and well-being.

Furthermore, compassion has a profound effect on the vagus nerve, a critical component of our parasympathetic nervous system—the “rest and digest” system. A healthy vagal tone is associated with better emotional regulation, lower inflammation, and a greater sense of calm. Practicing compassion, particularly self-compassion, strengthens this vagal tone, effectively telling our body, on a deep physiological level, that we are safe. The threat has passed. We can release the armor.

In this state of safety, the body can finally begin its own innate healing process. The pain may not vanish in an instant, but its *quality* changes. The sharp, terrifying edges soften. The resistance melts. The pain is no longer an invading enemy, but a part of our experience that is being held, seen, and cared for. It is being bathed in the light of our own loving presence.

## My Own Alchemical Experiment

Lying on my kitchen floor all those years ago, I finally surrendered. My strategies of fighting and ignoring had only led to more suffering. So, I tried something new. I stopped. I breathed. And instead of sending anger and frustration toward the pain in my back, I sent it a different message.

I placed a hand on my lower back, and with a tenderness that surprised me, I whispered, inwardly, *“I’m here. I’m listening. What do you need me to know?”*

I didn’t demand an answer. I simply stayed present. I breathed into the sensation, not trying to change it, but just… being with it. I offered it the warmth of my hand, the gentle rhythm of my breath, the quiet attention of my awareness. I offered it my compassion.

And then, a shift. The pain didn’t disappear, not at first. But the panic did. The anger did. The terror did. In their place, a deep, aching grief began to surface. Grief for all the ways I had pushed my body too hard, ignored its signals, and demanded it perform for me without rest or gratitude. The pain in my back, I realized, was the culmination of a thousand tiny moments of self-abandonment. It was a cry for rest. A cry for presence. A cry to be treated not as a machine, but as a sacred, living being.

In that moment of compassionate presence, the pain was transformed. It was no longer just a physical sensation; it was a wise messenger. And by listening to its message, I could finally give my body what it truly needed. The healing that followed was not about “fixing” my back; it was about transforming my entire relationship with myself.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Practical Compassion: Three Ways to Begin

Cultivating compassion is a practice, not a perfect. It’s a muscle we strengthen over time. It begins with the simple, radical act of turning toward our own suffering with kindness. Here are a few ways you might begin:

**1. The Compassionate Touch:** The next time you feel a pang of physical or emotional pain, try this. Place a hand over the area of your body where you feel the sensation most strongly—your heart, your stomach, your aching shoulder. You don’t need to fix anything. Just let your hand rest there, a simple gesture of presence and warmth. Feel the contact of your skin. Breathe. And perhaps offer a few words of kindness, as you would to a beloved friend: *“This is a moment of suffering. It’s okay. I am here with you.”*

**2. The Compassionate Question:** When you are in the grip of a difficult emotion—anxiety, anger, sadness—instead of pushing it away, get curious. Ask it a gentle question. *“What are you trying to protect me from?”* or *“What do you need right now?”* You may be surprised by the wisdom that arises from the depths of your own being when you approach it with genuine curiosity instead of judgment.

**3. The Loving-Kindness Meditation:** This is a classic practice for cultivating compassion. Find a quiet place to sit for a few minutes. Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you love easily and unconditionally. Feel the warmth of that love in your heart. Then, offer them these phrases: *“May you be happy. May you be healthy. May you be safe. May you live with ease.”* After a few moments, turn that same loving attention toward yourself, offering the same phrases: *“May I be happy. May I be healthy. May I be safe. May I live with ease.”* Finally, extend this loving-kindness outward to all beings everywhere. This practice rewires the neural pathways of the brain, making compassion a more accessible and natural state.

## The Ripple Effect

As we learn to meet our own pain with this gentle, loving presence, something miraculous begins to happen. Our capacity for compassion for others expands exponentially. The judgments we held against ourselves begin to soften, and so too do the judgments we hold against others. We begin to see that everyone is carrying their own invisible burdens, fighting their own silent battles.

We understand that a harsh word may come from a place of deep pain, that defensiveness is often a shield for a tender heart. Our relationships transform. We become a safe harbor for others, not because we have all the answers, but because we are no longer afraid of the dark. We have learned to sit with our own pain, and so we can sit with theirs, offering the simple, profound gift of our compassionate presence.

This is the alchemy of compassion. It doesn’t erase our pain, but it transforms it. It takes the lead of our suffering and, through the gentle heat of our own loving attention, turns it into the gold of presence, wisdom, and a deeper connection to ourselves and all of life.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
