teachings.sourceTitle: Grounding Into Trust: Healing Through Your Feet
teachings.title: Grounding Into Trust: Healing Through Your Feet
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider the feet as a somatic archive of early life experience, showing how patterns of mistrust and hypervigilance can become held in posture and foot pain. Through narrative, anatomy, and a gentle grounding practice, she offers a compassionate pathway back to felt safety and the possibility of letting weight rest into the earth. The piece emphasizes slow, embodied listening rather than quick fixes, and frames pain as a messenger inviting inquiry and tenderness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The morning light was filtering through the blinds, casting long golden stripes across the treatment table, when she finally said it.

We are born into this world utterly dependent, wired for connection, and yet we so often find ourselves feeling profoundly alone, untethered, as if we’re walking on shifting sands. We learn to hold ourselves up, to brace against the unknown, to manage a world that feels unpredictable. And the whole story of this effort, this deep and often unconscious questioning of whether we are truly supported, is written in the body. Especially, I’ve found, in our feet.

I remember a client from years ago, a brilliant woman named Claire. She came to me for a series of sessions, complaining of chronic plantar fasciitis. The pain was sharp, relentless, a cry for attention first thing in the morning and a dull ache by day’s end. She had tried all the things — the special socks, the ice packs, the stretches, the orthotics. The relief was always temporary, the pain always returning, a faithful companion she had come to despise. As she spoke, I noticed she held her body with a kind of rigid grace, her shoulders perfectly set, her spine straight. She was a woman who knew how to hold herself together. Her whole life was a testament to her strength, her resilience. But the body, in its profound wisdom, keeps an honest score. It doesn't care about our carefully constructed personas. It simply reflects the truth of our lived experience.

But as we began to work, to listen to the deeper story her body was telling, something else emerged. Claire had grown up in a home where the ground was never truly solid. Her father’s moods were erratic, her mother’s love conditional. Support was a currency that had to be earned, and even then, it could be withdrawn without notice. She learned, as children in such environments do, to rely only on herself. She became hyper-vigilant, her nervous system a finely tuned instrument always scanning for the next potential threat, the next reason the floor might fall out from under her. She never, ever fully relaxed. She never trusted that the ground would simply be there to hold her.

Her feet, in their wisdom, were simply telling the truth of her experience. They were the interface between her being and the ground of physical reality, and they were screaming, *I don’t feel safe. I don’t trust that I will be held. I don’t know where I’m going, and I’m terrified to take the next step.*

## The Anatomy of Trust

Our feet are masterpieces of engineering. Each one contains 26 bones, 33 joints, and a network of more than 100 muscles, ligaments, and tendons. They are designed to be both incredibly strong and exquisitely sensitive, providing a dynamic foundation for our every move. They are our grounding point, our connection to the earth. But they are more than just physical structures; they are carriers of our deepest beliefs about safety and support.

When we experience early life environments where support is inconsistent or absent, our neural pathways wire for survival. The brain, in its magnificent effort to protect us, creates a map of the world that says, *It is not safe to let go. You must hold on, be ready, stay vigilant.* This isn’t a conscious thought; it’s a deep, cellular knowing, a pattern etched into our nervous system. We hold this tension in our tissues, in our posture, and especially in the parts of us that are meant to connect us to the ground. We literally forget how to put our full weight down.

This can manifest in a myriad of ways: foot pain, bunions, collapsed arches, chronic ankle instability. We might find ourselves perpetually “stuck,” unable to move forward in our lives, or we might rush ahead, never truly landing in the present moment. We are walking, but we are not grounded. We are moving, but we are not home. The foot, this incredible instrument, becomes a source of pain not because it is flawed, but because it is faithfully reflecting our inner state. It is the loyal soldier standing guard, long after the war is over, still braced for a threat that lives only in the echoes of the past.

The body, in its infinite compassion, is not trying to punish us with these symptoms. It is trying to communicate. It is waving a flag, sending up a flare, inviting us to look at a deeper pattern that is no longer serving us. The pain in our feet is a sacred messenger, asking a profound question: *Beloved one, what would it be like to trust that you are held? What would it be like to believe that the earth, and life itself, is here to support you?*

## A Practice for Grounding

This journey of coming home to the body is not a one-time event, but a practice. It is a conscious turning-towards, again and again. If you feel called, here is a simple practice you can do right now to begin to cultivate a new relationship with your feet and the ground that holds you.

> Find a comfortable place to sit or stand. If you can, take off your shoes and socks. Feel the floor or the earth beneath you. Take a few gentle breaths, not trying to change anything, just noticing the air moving in and out of your body.
>
> Now, bring your awareness to your feet. Simply notice them. You don’t have to judge them or fix them. Just feel them. Are they warm or cool? Tense or relaxed? Can you feel the points of contact between your soles and the surface beneath you? The heel, the ball of the foot, the toes.
>
> Imagine, just for a moment, that you could let your weight drop a little more fully into your feet. Imagine the bones of your feet, all 26 of them, resting, supported. Imagine the muscles softening, letting go of even 1% of their holding.
>
> Now, picture roots growing from the soles of your feet, down into the earth. See them extending deep into the rich, dark soil, anchoring you, holding you. Feel the steady, unwavering support of the planet rising up to meet you. You don't have to hold yourself up. The earth has you. Stay with this sensation for as long as you like.
>
> When you are ready, gently bring your awareness back to the room. Notice how you feel. Is there any change in your body, your breath, your sense of presence? This is the beginning of a new conversation. A conversation of trust.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Path Back to Ground

Healing this fundamental lack of trust is not about forcing ourselves to think positive thoughts or ignoring the very real fear that lives in the body. It is a gentle process of repatriation, of coming home to ourselves. It is about creating new experiences, new neural pathways, that teach the nervous system that it is finally safe to let go.

I worked with Claire for months. Our sessions were quiet, slow. We didn’t focus on “fixing” her foot pain. Instead, we focused on creating a space where her body could finally feel safe enough to speak. Through gentle touch and deep listening, we invited the stored tension in her feet, her legs, her spine, to begin to unwind. We didn’t try to get rid of the fear; we met it with compassion. We acknowledged the incredible intelligence of the pattern she had developed to survive.

Slowly, something began to shift. As her nervous system moved from a state of sympathetic dominance—the “fight or flight” response—to one of parasympathetic restoration, her tissues began to soften. She started to feel her own weight differently, to sense the support of the table beneath her, the ground beneath the building, the earth beneath it all. It wasn’t a concept; it was a felt sense, a physical reality that her body could register.

One day, she came into a session and told me she had been walking in the park and had, for the first time she could remember, felt the sensation of the grass beneath her feet. She had stopped and stood there for ten minutes, just feeling. Tears streamed down her face. They were not tears of sadness, but of a profound, quiet joy. The joy of coming home.

This is the journey. It is the path from the head to the feet, from the story of fear to the felt sense of support. It is about learning to inhabit our bodies with a new quality of presence, to listen to their wisdom, and to trust the ground of our own being. Your feet know the way. They remember the feeling of being held, and they are inviting you, with every ache and every pain, to remember it too.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [No Leg to Stand On: The Emotional Roots of Hip and Leg Pain](/blog/hips-legs-emotional-roots)
- [The Sacred Central Channel: What Your Spine Communicates](/blog/spine-sacred-central-channel)
- [A Practice for Kidney Healing and Emotional Flow](/blog/kidneys-healing-practice)

**More on Feet:**

- [Your Feet and the Ground Beneath You: The Foundation of Your Journey](/blog/feet-foundation-of-journey)
- [A Grounding Practice for Feet and Foundation](/blog/feet-grounding-practice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you walk in trust, feeling the solid ground of love beneath you with every step. May you know, in your bones and in your soul, that you are and have always been, completely and utterly supported.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

If you feel pain, dizziness, or strong emotion, pause, open your eyes, and rest your hands where they feel soothing. This is a gentle, invitational practice and not a substitute for medical care — if you have persistent foot pain or medical conditions consult your healthcare provider before trying new practices.

teachings.sourceTitle: Handling Life: When Grip Becomes Grasp
teachings.title: Handling Life: When Grip Becomes Grasp
teachings.summary: Susan uses the hands as a living metaphor and somatic entry point to explore how holding, control, and anxiety show up in the body. She invites attentive, nonjudgmental noticing of hand tension and offers a short, gentle practice of opening the palms as a way to train the nervous system toward receptivity and connection. The piece weaves embodied observation, simple neuroscience, and compassionate instruction to suggest new possibilities for how we handle life.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a particular quality of attention that heals. Not fixing. Not analyzing. Just… attending.

And sometimes, the most profound part is simply…handling it. All of it. The relentless flow of tasks, the emotional currents, the people we love, the challenges that arise like sudden storms. How do we hold it all without losing ourselves?

I was in my garden the other day, a simple, grounding task I’ve done a thousand times. The late afternoon sun was warm on my back, the scent of damp earth rising to meet me. I was tackling a patch of stubborn dandelions, their roots sunk deep into the soil. But as I worked, I noticed something. My hands were not simply weeding; they were waging a war. They were clenched into tight, rigid claws around the dandelion roots, my knuckles white with strain. I was pulling with a furious, desperate force, my jaw locked, my breath held tight in my chest. It was as if the fate of the world depended on eradicating this single patch of weeds. And I had to stop. I dropped the mangled root, sat back on my heels, and just…breathed. I placed my soil-caked hands, palms up, on my knees, and I asked them, *What is this about, beloveds? What are we trying so hard to control?*

Our hands are such exquisite instruments, a miracle of design. An extension of our heart’s energy into the world. With them, we create, we soothe, we build, we gesture, we give, we receive. They are our primary way of interacting with the material world, of quite literally *handling* our lives. So, what happens when the very act of handling becomes a source of pain? When our grip, meant for connection and creation, becomes a desperate, fearful grasp?

## The Eloquent Story in Your Hands

In my three decades of work as a healer, I’ve come to see the body as a sacred messenger, and our symptoms are its primary language. It never lies. And the hands, with their twenty-seven intricate bones and dense network of nerves, are particularly eloquent storytellers. When they begin to speak through pain, stiffness, numbness, or inflammation, it’s an invitation to listen on a much deeper level. It’s rarely just about the hands.

Think about the neurology of it. When we feel overwhelmed, when life feels like it’s slipping through our fingers, what is our instinct? We clench. We grip. We try to get a better handle on things. This isn’t a conscious decision; it’s a deeply ingrained neural pathway, a survival response hardwired into our nervous system. The brain’s ancient amygdala, constantly scanning for threats, perceives a looming deadline, a difficult conversation, or a global crisis as a predator. It sends a signal through the nervous system: *Hold on tight. Don’t let go. Danger!* The muscles in our hands, arms, and shoulders obey, tensing in preparation for a fight that never comes. When this becomes a chronic state, the body begins to cry out. The arthritis that stiffens the joints, the carpal tunnel that sends shooting pains up the arm, the mysterious aches that doctors can’t explain… they are often the body’s way of showing us where we are holding on too tightly in our lives.

This is the body’s wisdom. It is reflecting our inner state back to us. Are you being ‘heavy-handed’ with yourself or others, forcing outcomes instead of allowing them to unfold? Are you wrestling with a situation that is truly ‘out of your hands,’ yet you keep trying to manage it through sheer force of will? That inward curling of the fingers, a common pattern I see, is the body’s posture of defense and anxiety, a pulling away from the world. It’s a story of conflict in managing, or being managed by, life itself.

Even the temperature of our hands tells a tale. Cold hands can speak to a feeling of being ‘out of touch,’ disconnected from our own heart’s warmth or from the world around us. And skin conditions, like the eczema that makes us want to scratch and claw, can be a sign of a deep, unmet ‘itching’ to *do* something, to create, to change a situation we feel utterly stuck in. The body is so beautifully, heartbreakingly literal.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Grace of the Open Palm

It’s a very good thing to know that these patterns are not a life sentence. Here is where the modern understanding of neuroscience becomes a sacred text. Thanks to the principle of neuroplasticity, we know that our brains are malleable, capable of creating new neural pathways at any age. We can, with conscious and compassionate attention, teach our bodies a new way to be. We can learn to soften the grip, to release the grasp, and to open our hands to a different way of being in the world.

This isn’t about passivity or giving up. It’s about shifting from the illusion of control to the reality of connection. Control is rigid, brittle, and fear-based. It’s the white-knuckled grip on the steering wheel in a snowstorm. It’s exhausting, and ultimately, it’s a fantasy. We control so much less than we think we do. Connection, on the other hand, is flexible, resilient, and love-based. It’s the sensitive, responsive touch of a potter shaping clay. The potter doesn’t force the clay; she listens to it, feels its capacity, its moisture, its limits. She guides it with a firm but gentle presence. She is in relationship with it.

What would it be like to enter into that kind of relationship with your own life? To meet your challenges not with a clenched fist, but with an open palm?

An open hand is a posture of receiving. It is vulnerable. It is trusting. It cannot control, but it can *feel*. It can sense the texture of the moment, the temperature of the emotional landscape. When our hands are open, we are open. We can receive support, we can receive guidance, we can receive the unexpected grace that is always available when we stop trying to force everything. The tight fist of anxiety, which thinks it is protecting us, actually cuts us off from the very resources that could help us navigate the storm.

I worked with a woman once, a brilliant executive who came to me with debilitating pain in her hands. She was at the top of her game, known for her ability to “make things happen.” But her hands were so stiff and painful she could barely type. As we worked together, she discovered that her entire life was a clenched fist. She was holding her company, her family, and her own emotions in a tight, controlling grip. The idea of “letting go” terrified her; she thought everything would fall apart. Slowly, through gentle practice, she began to experiment with opening her hands, both literally and metaphorically. She started delegating at work. She started listening to her children without trying to fix their problems. She started allowing herself to feel her own sadness and fear, without judgment. It was not easy. But as she learned to open her hands, the pain began to subside. She hadn’t lost her strength; in fact, she discovered a deeper, more resilient power. The power of connection, not control.

## A Practice for Releasing the Grasp

I invite you to try a small practice. It’s not about fixing anything, but simply about listening. Find a quiet place where you can sit for a few moments without interruption.

Close your eyes, or soften your gaze toward the floor. Bring your awareness to your breath, just noticing the gentle rise and fall of your chest or belly. No need to change it. Just let it be your anchor to this present moment.

Now, bring your attention to your hands. Don’t judge what you find. Simply notice. Are they open or closed? Are they resting, or are they holding tension? Is there a tingling, a numbness, an ache? Be curious. What is the story they are holding right now?

Consciously, deliberately, open your hands and rest them on your lap. Turn them so the palms face upward, a gesture of receiving. Feel the air on your skin.

Take a deep breath in, and as you exhale, imagine you are releasing all the things you’ve been trying to handle all on your own. The worries, the to-do lists, the difficult conversations, the burdens you’ve been carrying. Let the weight of them fall away, just for this breath. With your next exhale, imagine a wave of softness washing down your shoulders, through your arms, and into your hands, all the way to your fingertips. Let your fingers gently curl, not in a clench, but in a soft, receptive repose.

Stay here for a few more breaths. Simply being. Noticing. Allowing. You are not solving anything. You are simply creating a small space of peace in your own nervous system. You are reminding your body that, in this moment, you are safe. You are teaching it a new possibility beyond the clenched fist of fear.

This is the beginning of a new conversation with your body. A conversation of trust. It’s a shift from seeing life as something to be wrestled into submission to seeing it as a dance to be entered into with sensitivity and grace. Your hands, these beautiful, capable instruments of love, are not meant for grasping. They are meant for creating, for holding, for healing, for opening. They are meant to be instruments of grace, extending the love from your own heart out into the world.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Whole-Hearted Living: A Practice for Filling Your Own Cup](/blog/heart-whole-hearted-practice)
- [The Vibrational Signature of Your Soul: Your Voice Speaks](/blog/vocal-cords-vibrational-signature)
- [A Somatic Practice for Calming Your Nervous System](/blog/nervous-system-somatic-practice)

**More on Hands:**

- [Cold Hands, Warm Heart? The Emotional Truth in Your Fingers](/blog/hands-cold-hands-warm-heart)
- [A Healing Practice for Your Hands and Heart Connection](/blog/hands-healing-practice)

Susan

teachings.title: When You Cannot Breathe: Suffocation, Grief, and Your Lungs
teachings.summary: Susan reflects on breath as both a physiological exchange and an energetic language, exploring how grief and held emotion can lodge in the lungs and constrain breathing. She traces shallow, contracted breathing to survival patterns around deserving and presence, and offers a gentle, invitational practice to begin reclaiming spacious, nourishing breath.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a question I've been sitting with for decades, and I still don't have a tidy answer.

We arrive with this incredible instrument—the body—and no instruction manual. We learn to walk, to talk, to navigate the world, but so rarely are we taught to listen to the body’s own language. And it is always, always speaking to us.

I remember being a little girl, maybe five or six, and discovering the game of holding my breath. I’d sit at the bottom of the public pool, the water a muffled blue world around me, and see how long I could last. There was a thrill to it, a sense of control. But then would come the inevitable, desperate bursting for air, the gasp back into the world of sound and light. It was a game, but it was also my first lesson in the body’s non-negotiable need for breath. That frantic, full-bodied gasp was pure instinct, a life-force override. It wasn't a thought; it was a cellular command. And it taught me something profound: the body will always, always fight for its own life, for its own breath.

As I’ve journeyed through life and sat with hundreds of clients in the sacred space of healing, I’ve come to see that so many of us are playing a version of that game. We are holding our breath, not in the playful way of a child, but in a quiet, chronic, and often unconscious way. We are living in a state of subtle suffocation, our lungs contracting in response to a life that feels too heavy, too fast, too much.

## The Sacred Exchange

Your lungs are the most intimate interface between your inner world and the outer atmosphere. Think about that for a moment. With every single breath, you are drawing the outside world *into* your body. You are taking in the very air that has passed through the leaves of trees, that has traveled over oceans, that has been breathed by every other living being. It is a constant, profound exchange. A sacred communion.

Physiologically, this exchange is about oxygen and carbon dioxide. It’s about fueling your cells and releasing metabolic waste. But on an energetic and emotional level, it’s about so much more. Breath is life force. It is *prana*, *chi*. It is the vital energy that animates you. When you breathe deeply and freely, you are drawing in inspiration, vitality, and the full gift of life. When you exhale completely, you are releasing what is no longer needed, what is toxic, what is complete.

So, what happens when that exchange is constricted? When the breath becomes shallow, tight, or held? This is where the body’s wisdom begins to speak. Chronic lung conditions, from asthma to persistent coughs, often reflect a deeper feeling of being suffocated by life—by a job, a relationship, a family dynamic, or a set of expectations. Depression and anxiety are almost always correlated with shallow, apical breathing, where the breath barely moves beyond the upper chest. It’s as if the body is saying, *I cannot take in any more. I cannot bear it.*

## Where Grief Comes to Rest

In the landscape of the body, grief has a particular affinity for the lungs. It settles there, heavy and dense. When we experience a profound loss—the death of a beloved, the end of a marriage, the shattering of a dream—the natural response is to weep, to sob, to wail. And what is that, if not a powerful, full-bodied exhalation? It is the body’s instinctive way of moving the energy of grief out.

But we are often taught to be strong, to hold it together, to not make a scene. We swallow our tears, stifle our sobs, and in doing so, we trap that immense energy of grief within the delicate tissues of our lungs. It becomes a silent, heavy presence. The breath, which should be a flowing river, becomes a stagnant pool.

I once worked with a woman, a dear one in her late fifties, who came to me with a persistent, dry cough that had plagued her for years. Doctors could find nothing wrong. As we began to work together, she spoke of her mother’s death, which had happened over a decade earlier. She had been the “strong one” for her family, organizing the funeral, managing the estate, comforting everyone else. She never gave herself permission to fall apart. Her lungs, in their infinite wisdom, were still trying to release the unshed tears of that profound loss. The cough was a decade of grief, asking to be heard. Energetically, that unexpressed sorrow had become a kind of density in her lung field, a weight that her body was trying to physically expel. The healing wasn't in a remedy for the cough, but in creating a safe space where the grief itself could finally be breathed, sobbed, and released from her tissues.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Courage to Take Up Space

Perhaps the most profound pattern I have observed around the lungs is the connection between breath and deserving. When you feel, on a deep, often unconscious level, that you do not deserve to be here, that you are too much, that you must make yourself small to be loved or safe, your lungs will contract. You will literally and metaphorically shrink, refusing to take up your rightful space in the world.

This is not a conscious choice. It is a neural pathway, a pattern of survival carved out in early childhood. Our infant nervous system, in its brilliance, is constantly scanning the environment for cues of safety or danger. If we learned, through a million micro-interactions, that our full expression—our loud cries, our big needs, our uninhibited joy—was met with stress, disapproval, or overwhelm, we adapted. We learned that being quiet, being good, being small, was the best way to maintain connection and safety. The body, in its wisdom, found a way to help: it constricted the breath. A shallow breath keeps feelings down. It numbs. It makes a small space feel manageable.

But that pattern, a brilliant survival strategy for a dependent child, becomes a prison for the adult. That old neural pathway continues to fire, telling your nervous system to stay small, to stay quiet, to not take up too much space, even when the original danger is long gone. It keeps you from inhaling the full, glorious, and sometimes messy experience of being alive. The good news? Because of neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to change and rewire itself, we are not stuck with these patterns forever. We can, with conscious and compassionate attention, create new pathways.

To breathe deeply is an act of profound self-worth. It is to declare, with your whole body, *I am here. I deserve to take up space. I am worthy of receiving the full gift of life.* It can feel vulnerable, even dangerous, to let the breath drop deep into the belly, to allow the ribs to expand fully. It can bring up all the old stories of being too loud, too needy, too much.

## An Inquiry for Your Lungs

So, I invite you into a gentle practice. You don’t need to change anything forcefully. This is an exploration, an act of listening.

Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Close your eyes if that feels safe.

For the first minute, just notice your breath as it is. Don't alter it. Simply be the observer. Where do you feel the breath most distinctly? In your nostrils? Your chest? Your belly? Is the texture smooth or rough? Is the temperature cool on the inhale and warm on the exhale? This is the practice of simple presence.

Now, gently place one hand on your heart and one hand on your lower belly.

Without forcing, simply invite the breath to meet your lower hand. Imagine your lungs extending all the way down into your pelvic bowl. As you inhale, feel your belly soften and expand into your hand. As you exhale, feel it gently recede.

Stay with this for a few rounds. This simple act sends a powerful signal of safety to the nervous system. It says, *You are safe enough to be here, in your body. You are safe enough to breathe.*

Next, bring your awareness to your ribcage. Imagine your ribs expanding not just to the front, but to the sides and even to the back. With each inhale, feel a sense of three-dimensional expansion. With each exhale, feel a gentle gathering back to center. You are creating space. You are, quite literally, taking up more space.

Finally, allow the exhale to become a full and complete release, a letting go. Let it out with a sigh if that feels good. Let it carry out any tension, any old stories, any constriction that is ready to be released.

As you do this, what do you notice? What sensations arise? What feelings? Is there a flicker of fear? A wave of sadness? A sense of expansion? Just be with whatever is there, with gentle, compassionate awareness. Your body is speaking to you. It is telling you its story.

This is not about forcing yourself to breathe “correctly.” It is about developing a loving relationship with your breath, and through it, with yourself. It’s about creating new neural pathways in the brain, pathways that say, *It is safe to breathe. It is safe to feel. It is safe to be fully here.*

Your breath is your most constant companion, your most faithful guide. It is with you from the moment you are born to the moment you depart. It is the rhythm of your being, the sacred exchange between your inner and outer worlds. By tending to your breath, you are tending to the very essence of your life.

May you have the courage to inhale the full measure of your existence, and the grace to release all that is not yours to carry. May you find the space within you to breathe, and to be.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


---

Then, invite the inhale to soften the belly into your lower hand, allowing the ribs to expand front-to-back and side-to-side. Follow each inhale with a full, unhurried exhale—an audible sigh if that feels relieving. Continue for 3–5 slow rounds, pausing anytime you feel lightheaded or distressed.

teachings.title: Kidney Stones and Crystallized Emotions: When Feelings Harden
teachings.summary: Susan frames kidney stones as a potent bodily message—an image of unprocessed, crystallized emotion lodged in the body’s watery systems—and invites a compassionate turn toward inner listening rather than blame. The piece traces a path from victim consciousness to gentle inquiry, offering a simple breath-and-touch practice to begin meeting fear, grief, and powerlessness with presence. The tone is invitational and emphasizes ongoing, patient relationship with the body as the work of emotional alchemy.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
T# Kidney Stones and Crystallized Emotions: When Feelings Harden

A client, years ago, told me about a kidney stone she had passed. She spoke in a hushed tone, as if recounting a visitation from a strange and terrifying deity. She described this thing that her own body had created—this tiny, jagged crystal that had brought her to her knees, pacing the floor for days in a state of agonizing, relentless pain. “It was like a piece of gravel made of lightning,” she said, her eyes wide with the memory. And then, after a long, contemplative pause, she whispered a question that has stayed with me ever since: “What part of me made *that*?”

It’s a question that cuts right to the heart of the body’s mysterious wisdom, isn’t it? When our soft, fluid, miraculous bodies produce something so sharp, so crystalline, so profoundly *hard*… it is an invitation. It’s a message, delivered in the body’s most elemental and undeniable language, asking us to pay attention.

Our kidneys, those two brilliant, bean-shaped organs nestled in the soft tissues of our lower back, are the master alchemists of our internal ocean. They are the silent, tireless guardians of our equilibrium. Day in and day out, they filter nearly 200 quarts of fluid—the equivalent of 50 gallon jugs—sifting and sorting, cleansing and balancing the very essence of our physical waters. They meticulously decide what nutrients to return to the bloodstream, what waste products to send away for disposal. Their intelligence is staggering. But their sacred work isn’t just physical. They are also, and this is a very good thing to know, constantly processing our emotional lives.

## The Emotional Filters

In the vast and ancient wisdom of Chinese medicine, the kidneys are considered the seat of our deepest life force, our *Jing*. They are the home of our ancestral reserves, the battery pack of our vitality. They are also intimately connected to the emotion of fear. When we are in a state of flow, of trust, of feeling capable of meeting life’s challenges, our kidneys are strong and resilient. But when we are chronically overwhelmed by fear, when we feel like a victim of our circumstances, the kidneys bear the brunt of that emotional load.

Think about what it feels like to be truly overwhelmed. It’s a visceral sensation. There’s a sense of being flooded, of drowning in feelings or situations that are simply too much to handle. The phone calls with bad news, the unexpected diagnoses, the shattering heartbreaks, the gnawing financial fears… it all comes rushing in, a relentless deluge. And the kidneys, our sacred filters, can become clogged by the sheer volume of it all. They can no longer efficiently sort what is life-giving from what is toxic. The whole system becomes sluggish, overburdened, and saturated.

When this state of emotional overwhelm becomes chronic—when the feelings aren’t processed, acknowledged, and allowed to move through us—they don’t just disappear. Energy cannot be destroyed; it can only be transformed. If that emotional energy is not transformed through conscious awareness, it begins to harden. It crystallizes. Just as minerals in a supersaturated solution will precipitate into solid form, unprocessed emotions can precipitate in the body. And in the delicate, watery environment of the kidneys, this can manifest as stones—tiny, jagged crystals of solidified feeling. A kidney stone is a crystallized tear that was never shed, a shard of terror that was never allowed to tremble and release.

I have observed this pattern over and over in my three decades of practice. It often appears in individuals who hold a deep-seated, often unconscious, belief that life is happening *to* them. It’s a state of victim consciousness, a profound feeling of powerlessness in the face of external events. The narrative is one of “I can’t handle this,” or “It’s not fair,” or “Why is this always happening to me?” This is not a judgment; it is a deeply human response to pain, trauma, and conditioning. But when that story becomes the primary lens through which we view our reality, our bodies listen. The kidneys, flooded with the biochemistry of fear and powerlessness, begin to reflect that state of being. The unprocessed grief, the unexpressed anger, the terror that was never given a safe space to be felt… it all congeals into a hard, painful, physical reality.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## From Victim to Alchemist

So what do we do? How do we begin to dissolve these hardened places within us, both physically and emotionally? The journey, like all true healing, begins not with a fight, but with a gentle, compassionate turning-towards. It begins with the courageous choice to shift from a consciousness of victimhood to one of quiet, empowered inquiry.

Instead of asking, “Why is this happening *to* me?” we can begin to tenderly ask, “What is this asking of me? What is this revealing within me?” This is not about blaming ourselves for our physical ailments. It is never, ever about blame. It is about reclaiming our partnership with the body. It is about recognizing the body as a sacred messenger, a wise and loving friend who is doing its absolute best to get our attention.

A kidney stone is a very loud message. It’s a scream, really. It’s the body saying, with all the force it can muster, “I can no longer filter this overwhelm for you. I can no longer hold this much unprocessed fear in my delicate tissues. Please, beloved one, you must learn to feel and release in a new way.”

This is the sacred work of emotional alchemy. It’s the practice of developing our emotional literacy, of learning to sit with the intense discomfort of our feelings without being consumed by them. It’s about creating a safe inner container—a space of unconditional presence—where fear, anger, and grief can be held, heard, and honored without judgment. When we do this, we take the burden off our physical organs. We become the primary filters of our own emotional lives.

One of the most powerful practices I know for this is simple, yet profound. It requires no special equipment, only a willingness to be present with yourself. Find a quiet moment and a comfortable place to sit or lie down. Place your hands on your lower back, over the area of your kidneys. Close your eyes. Take a few deep, slow breaths, imagining you can direct the breath into this space beneath your hands. Feel the warmth of your palms, a gesture of pure, loving attention.

And then, simply begin to listen. You might ask, silently, from your heart, “What fear is here? What story of powerlessness is ready to be heard?”

Don’t search for an answer with your analytical mind. That part of you can rest. Just listen with your whole being—your felt sense, your intuition. A memory might surface from long ago. A sensation of heat or cold might arise. An image, a color, a single word might float into your awareness. Your job is not to analyze it or fix it, but simply to receive it. To breathe with it. To offer it the warmth of your own compassionate presence. You are letting the hardened places know that they are seen, that they are allowed. You are bringing the gentle, healing waters of your own awareness to the crystallized shards of your past.

This is not a one-time fix. It is a practice, a relationship you are building with the deep wisdom of your body. It is the slow, patient, and deeply loving work of dissolving a lifetime of unprocessed experience. But with each moment of conscious, loving attention, you are fundamentally changing your internal chemistry. You are rewriting the neural pathways of fear. You are shifting from a state of contraction to a state of flow. You are reminding your body, on a cellular level, that you are no longer a helpless victim of your history. You are the alchemist of your own healing.

This journey of alchemy is not about forcing the stones to disappear. It is about changing the inner environment that allowed them to form. It is about cultivating a state of being where such hardness is no longer necessary. As you practice this deep listening, you may find that your relationship with your body begins to change. The pain may still be there, but your relationship to it shifts. It is no longer an enemy to be vanquished, but a messenger to be honored. You are learning to meet your own suffering with a profound and unwavering kindness. And in that kindness, the deepest healing begins.


---

May you learn to flow with the great river of your life, trusting its currents and honoring its mysterious depths. May you have the courage to feel what has been hardened within you, and the boundless compassion to allow it to dissolve back into the loving, fluid waters of your own being. May you come to know yourself not as a victim of circumstance, but as the tender, powerful alchemist of your own beautiful life.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

After a few breaths, silently ask with kindness, “What fear is here?” and listen with your felt sense for a memory, image, word, or sensation; when something arises, breathe with it for 5–10 minutes without trying to fix it. Pause at any time if you feel overwhelmed; this practice is gentle self-awareness and is not a substitute for medical care—seek professional help for severe pain or medical concerns.

If memories or emotions feel too intense, consider pausing and reaching out to a qualified therapist, support person, or crisis resource.
This portal practice is an inner, contemplative support and does not replace medical evaluation or treatment for kidney-related symptoms or severe pain.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Hands - The Instruments of Love's Expression
teachings.title: The Hands - The Instruments of Love's Expression
teachings.summary: Susan invites you to regard your hands as expressive instruments of the heart — anatomically precise and energetically bound to how you give, receive, trust and set boundaries. Physical sensations and common hand complaints are read as meaningful signals about patterns of holding, grief, work and protection, and she offers gentle embodied practices to restore warmth, openness and a balanced rhythm of giving and receiving. The piece blends physiology, metaphor and practical ritual while urging patient, kind attention to limits and healing.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
You carry the world in your hands and you carry your heart there as well. When you rest your palm on something - a child, a table, your own face - you trace the boundary between inside and outside, between tenderness and action, between the invisible current of love and the visible work of living. The hands are not mere tools; they are the language by which the heart speaks, the grammar of intimacy, labor and grace. You have twenty-seven bones working in exquisite coordination in each hand, a small cosmos of carpals, metacarpals and phalanges that articulate intention into form. They are a marvel of mechanics and wisdom, a living choreography that can cradle a newborn and carve a rock, that can produce a lullaby on a piano and write a last letter. Watch them closely and they will tell you what your life has been asking you to learn.

The Anatomy of Tenderness

Notice the precision of those twenty-seven bones nested like promise into flesh. Notice the tendons and ligaments that translate a decision into movement, the complex networks of nerves that carry the warmth of a touch and the fine discrimination of texture. This anatomy is not incidental to your inner life; it evolved to be an extension of your relational intelligence. In Chinese energy maps and in many wisdom traditions the hands are literally tied back to the heart center - not as poetic metaphor only, but as an energetic reality. When you reach out you do more than grasp an object - you extend the field of your loving attention, and in doing so you shape the world around you.

Hands are the first instruments of reciprocity. They give food, steady a shoulder, caress a brow. They also receive: coins, apologies, a damp towel, the warmth of another palm. The balance between these two motions - giving and receiving - is the most intimate physics of your life force. When that balance is off, when you habitually give more than you take or when you hold back from offering what is yours to give, your hands will often remember and then speak the truth in their own language.

When Hands Hurt They Are Speaking

Your body is a hologram - each part reflects the whole. So the hands, being directly involved with how you handle existence, carry messages about your relationship to life itself. Hand issues are rarely only local. They reveal conflicts in how you are managing, avoiding or embracing your circumstances. Arthritis may be the slow narration of a life of long-standing rigidity - the tissues stiffen as a mirror of a habitual clenched response to challenge. A bent finger may echo a time when you could not straighten yourself publicly in the face of shame. Eczema on the hands is an itch that reminds you of something you cannot quite get your hands on - an ongoing irritation with life as it was handed to you. Carpal tunnel speaks to repetitive pattern and narrowness of movement - the body compresses because your nervous system has been compressed by long hours of forced posture or long-held tasks that were never nourished by rest or by right relation.

Cold hands are a particularly distinct language. To have cold hands is to be out of touch - not merely physiologically but symbolically. The world arrives to you and you respond with a slight frost. Coldness in the hands can indicate disconnection from the flow of giving and receiving. It can reveal a nervous system that holds its warmth close, fearful to extend its heat where it might be unreturned or exploited. You may have been taught that warmth is dangerous - that to reach is to lose yourself. Cold hands can be the body’s way of preserving itself. They are a tender alarm, asking you to notice where your warmth has been withheld and why.

When your hands clench into fists, the image is archetypal. The fist is the body’s cultivation of certainty and armor. Clenched hands are often the echo of a heart that has learned to protect itself by gripping. The grip is efficient, even righteous, but it cuts circulation. It isolates. The work of transformation is often to learn to open that fist - not as a surrender to imposition but as an act of trust that life can be held without strangulation. In Taoist language this is the cultivation of softness over hardness. As Lao Tzu taught in the Tao Te Ching, "Nothing in the world is as soft and yielding as water. Yet for dissolving the hard and inflexible, nothing can replace it." You practice becoming water in your palms - fluid, adaptive, able to flow into the contours of circumstance while carrying your center with grace.

Hands as Hologram - Professions, Identity and Longing

Look at what your hands do across days and years and you will find a biography. The hands of a baker carry the palimpsest of flour and warmth, shaped by dawn and devotion. The hands of a nurse hold both instruments and hearts at the bedside, alternating between meticulous skill and quiet compassion. The hands of a writer have a different wear - small gestures repeated over an ocean of time, precision and impatience braided together. Injuries to hands so often begin as betrayals between identity and action. If your hands are sore because they are overused in work that does not nourish you, your body protests. If you cannot engage in your craft because of pain or numbness, you grieve the loss of an aspect of yourself. The hands become waystations where identity and duty negotiate their terms.

There is another narrative that hands will tell - the story of consent and boundary. Nails are small edges that protect, yet they also mark where you end and another begins. Cuts and calluses are signatures of labor or of defensive habit. If you habitually smooth the surface of things in order to avoid the discomfort of confrontation you may find soft callused pads where there should be gentle skin. If you protect too much, the texture of your fingertips becomes a map of separation. This is not blame - it is evidence. Your hands are simply faithful recorders of how you have learned to negotiate your safety in the world.

Cold Hands and the Art of Returning to Touch

When your hands are cold you learn how to meet yourself with curiosity rather than judgment. Begin by naming what you feel. Bring breath to the tips of your fingers and imagine warmth as a river from the heart traveling down your arm to the palm. This is not magical thinking alone; breath regulates your autonomic nervous system. Naming does not fix everything in one moment, but it invites the nervous system to relax and to receive. Place your hands, palm to palm, and breathe steadily into the space between them. You will often notice that simply acknowledging the chill and offering warmth with intention alters the physiology. Your hands will unfurl like a flower toward the sun.

If cold hands are frequent, ask where your heat has been spent. Perhaps you have been giving without replenishing. Perhaps you hesitate to take warmth because it has been withheld in the past. The remedy is a twofold practice. First, cultivate a small domestic ritual of return. Warm your hands deliberately - soak them in warm water, press them to your chest beneath clothing, hold a warm cup and feel the heat move into your bones. Second, practice the art of receiving. Let another person hold your hand for a few breaths. Say aloud, "I receive." The voice is a vector for acceptance. If words are difficult, let the silence between palms be your transmission. Pleasure is allowed. Warmth is a right. You are not greedy when you reclaim your warmth - you are simple and necessary.

The Balance Between Giving and Receiving

There is a rhythm to life that the hands model when they are healthy. One hand gives, the other may receive. One hand pushes, the other supports. When both hands are active in balance, you move through the world with grace. When one hand is always giving and the other always receiving, imbalance becomes chronic. Many of us are taught that virtue lies only in the giving, and from that mistaken altar we impoverish our ability to receive. You may recognize this as emotional exhaustion, resentment or the bodily collapse of an overworked heart. The hands will show you where you have been keeping that ledger.

You can practice re-calibrating with a simple ritual. Sit quietly and rest your right hand on your lap. With the left hand take a small stone, or a leaf, or a coin. With great tenderness offer it to your right hand as if offering yourself a kindness you have been avoiding. Notice how each cell of your hand responds. Now reverse roles. Let your right hand place that small object into your left palm and receive it. Say the words "I give" and "I receive" or simply breathe into the exchange. Notice any resistance. This is not metaphysical only - it is training for your nervous system and for your relational muscles. Your hands will learn a new choreography. Over time, the gesture becomes a habit that extends into how you allocate time, attention and affection in life.

On Trust and the Open Palm

Trust is embodied in the open palm. When you extend an open hand you risk. You relinquish the illusion of control. You say in a bodily language that you are willing to be seen, to be altered by another, to be given to and given back. The open hand is paradoxically the most powerful posture - powerful because it refuses force. It invites response rather than demands compliance. As Lao Tzu reminds us in the Taoist way - yield and flow are forms of deep power. To carry this simplicity into your hands is to practice a kind of non-doing that actually accomplishes what force never can.

There are times when opening the hand must be accompanied by fierce discernment. Openness does not mean naivete. You will need boundaries - lines of skin and heart that say what you will accept and what you will not. Use your hands as instruments of wise boundary. A gentle but firm palm on a shoulder can stop a pattern of intrusion. A clasp of fingers across your own chest can return you to center when you feel scattered. The highest mastery comes when you can be both soft in touch and unambiguous in your direction. Hands that love well are not limp - they are alive, present and well-hinged by clear intention.

Practical Embodied Practices

Practice is the way you teach your body a new language. Begin with awareness. Sit quietly and fold one hand into the other. Feel the weight, the warmth, the ridges of skin, the pulse under the wrist. Breathe into your hands. Imagine each inhale as a small sun that travels from the chest, through the forearm and into the palms. Exhale and allow the hands to release any tension into the earth. Repeat this for several minutes and then open each hand slowly as if unveiling a treasured object. Watch how the fingers orient themselves. Do they curl or spread? Do your hands hesitate to open fully or do they bloom easily? The answers are information, not verdicts.

Another practice is to use touch as a ritual of integration. At the beginning and end of your day, place your right hand over your heart and your left hand over your belly. Breathe there. Speak a simple vow to yourself - to give what is yours to give and to receive what is yours to receive. Let your hands rest there for several breaths and allow the body to reorient. Do this for a month and you will notice subtler shifts - less hurry in your fingers, softer grips, warmer palms.

If your hands are injured or chronically painful, honor the limits. Healing sometimes means temporary slowing, not only exercise. Tend to them with patience and curiosity. Seek medical counsel when necessary and then bring the inner work alongside the outer care. Say to yourself often: I am learning to handle my life with greater tenderness. This statement alone changes micro-muscular patterns; it reshapes how you begin the day.

A Blessing for Your Hands

Receive this as a blessing. The hands that have shaped bread and soothed fever, that have written painful letters and held a dying arm, that have waved with joy and also waved farewell - these hands are holy. They are archives of both hurt and healing. Make of them not an object of judgment but a sacred instrument of repair. As the Tao Te Ching teaches, there is a power in returning to what is simple and small - "the one who knows others is wise, the one who knows himself is enlightened." In your hands you know both your world and your willingness. When you touch with intention you transform the ordinary into an altar.

I invite you to listen to your hands. Let them be the first place you turn when you are uncertain about how to act. Let them teach you how much warmth you can give and how much you must receive in order to be whole. Practice opening slowly until the motion becomes effortless. Allow tenderness to replace default force. Trust that when you hold the center of your life in a palm that is willing to both give and receive, you will not lose yourself - you will become more of who you are meant to be.

May your hands be instruments of love's expression - steady, warm and free. May they teach you how to hold what is sacred and how to let go when letting go is the only true kindness. In the soft yielding of your palm you will find both power and peace, and through that opening you will touch the world into greater wholeness.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Crown of Consciousness: What Your Head Is Really Telling You
teachings.title: The Crown of Consciousness: What Your Head Is Really Telling You
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to reframe the head as both a biological command center and a sacred crown of consciousness, showing how habitual thought patterns and an over-identified ego can trap awareness and sometimes show up as headaches or migraines. She offers an embodied pathway — returning awareness to bodily sensations and listening to heart and gut intelligence — so the brain can shift from tyrant to collaborator and receive deeper knowing.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a river that runs through all of us — a current of life force that connects every cell, every thought, every breath.

And perhaps one of the most profound parts of this human experience is lived entirely within the space between our ears. I’m talking about the head — this beautiful, heavy, miraculous sphere that we carry around each day. Have you ever stopped to truly consider it? Not just as the thing that holds your brain, but as the seat of your consciousness, the throne of your identity, and the command center of your very survival.

I remember a time, years ago, when my head felt less like a crown and more like a cage. I was living in a small apartment with a window that looked out onto a brick wall, and the view felt like a metaphor for my life. I was plagued by a series of migraines that would arrive like a storm, forcing me to retreat into darkness for days. The pain was a relentless, throbbing pressure behind my right eye, a physical manifestation of the mental gymnastics I was performing at the time. I was trying to *think* my way out of a difficult life situation, analyzing every angle, running every scenario, convinced that if I just found the right logical solution, the pain in my life — and the pain in my head — would cease. My mind had become a tyrant, and my body was screaming in protest. It was a profound, and profoundly uncomfortable, lesson in the dual nature of the head: it is both a magnificent tool and a potential prison.

Our heads house the most complex and mysterious organ we know of: the brain. This three-pound universe, as some have called it, is responsible for creating our entire experience of being ‘you.’ It’s a biological marvel, a network of billions of neurons firing in intricate patterns, creating thoughts, feelings, memories, and perceptions. These neural pathways, over time, become well-worn grooves through which our consciousness habitually flows. Think of it like water carving a canyon into rock; the more a particular thought pattern is repeated, the deeper that channel becomes, and the more likely our awareness is to travel down that same path again and again. This is the basis of neuroplasticity, the brain’s incredible ability to reorganize itself, but it’s also how we can become stuck in loops of anxiety, self-criticism, or fear. A thought like "I’m not good enough" can, through repetition, become a deep, reflexive groove in our consciousness, a belief that feels as solid and real as the ground beneath our feet.

## The Command Center and the Ego’s Throne

From a survival perspective, the brain is an unparalleled command center. It’s constantly scanning the environment for threats, making split-second calculations to keep us safe. This is the ancient, reptilian part of our brain at work, the part that governs our fight-or-flight response. It’s a necessary and brilliant function. Yet, in our modern world, this survival mechanism can become chronically over-activated. The "threats" are no longer saber-toothed tigers, but deadlines, social pressures, and the relentless influx of information. The result is a state of low-grade, persistent stress, where the head is constantly ‘on,’ trying to manage, control, and predict everything.

This is where the head also becomes the throne of the ego. The ego, that sense of a separate ‘I,’ loves to live in the head. It thrives on analysis, on judgment, on being right. It constructs elaborate stories about who we are, what we’re capable of, and what we must do to be worthy of love and belonging. And while the ego is a necessary part of our psychological structure, when it reigns unchecked from the throne of the head, it can disconnect us from the deeper wisdom of our bodies and our hearts. It convinces us that we *are* our thoughts, that our mental chatter is the ultimate reality. The pain I experienced with my migraines was a direct result of an over-identified ego, one that believed it could and should control everything through sheer force of will and intellect.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Neuroscience of a Deeper Knowing

What neuroscience is now revealing is what mystics and wisdom traditions have known for centuries: the head is not the only source of intelligence in the body. The heart has its own complex neural network, often called the "heart-brain," which sends more signals to the head than the head sends to it. The gut, too, is lined with an extensive network of neurons — the enteric nervous system — and is responsible for producing a significant amount of the body’s serotonin, a key neurotransmitter for mood regulation. There is a constant, flowing conversation happening between our head, our heart, and our gut. The problem is, most of us have been conditioned to only listen to the loudest voice in the room: the one in our head.

When we experience headaches, mental fog, or that feeling of being ‘stuck in our heads,’ it is often a sign that our consciousness is pressing against the constraints of our limited belief systems. The energy of our awareness, which is vast and limitless, is being forced through those narrow, habitual neural pathways. The pain is a messenger, asking us to expand. It’s an invitation to let go of the need to figure everything out, to release the mental gymnastics, and to drop into a different kind of knowing. This is the purpose of the head, not just to think, but to be a receiver for a higher consciousness, a crown that can attune to the wisdom of the entire body and the universe itself.

This is where we can begin to understand the head not just as a biological organ, but as a sacred center of energy and awareness. In many spiritual traditions, the crown of the head is associated with the seventh chakra, the point of connection to the divine. It is the place where our individual consciousness meets the universal consciousness. When this center is blocked — by fear, by rigid beliefs, by the tyranny of the ego — we feel disconnected, anxious, and alone. But when it is open, we experience a sense of purpose, of belonging, of being part of something much larger than ourselves. We begin to understand that our purpose is not something we need to *figure out* with our minds, but something we must *allow* to unfold through us.

## Reclaiming Your Crown

So how do we begin to shift this relationship with our heads? How do we transform it from a prison of overthinking into a crown of consciousness?

It begins with presence. It begins with the simple, radical act of bringing your awareness out of the stream of thought and into the sensory reality of the present moment. Feel the weight of your head on your shoulders. Notice the subtle sensations in your scalp, your jaw, your forehead. Can you soften the space behind your eyes? Can you allow your tongue to rest gently in your mouth?

This is not about stopping your thoughts; it’s about shifting your identification with them. You are not your thoughts; you are the awareness *behind* the thoughts. By consciously placing your attention on the physical sensations of your head, you begin to create a new neural pathway — a pathway of embodied presence. You signal to your nervous system that it is safe to move out of the realm of abstract analysis and into the grounded reality of your body.

From this place of presence, you can begin to listen differently. You can start to notice the subtle whispers of your heart’s wisdom and your gut’s intuition. What would it be like if you didn’t have to *think* your way to the right answer, but could *feel* your way forward? What if you trusted the intelligence that beats your heart and digests your food to also guide your life?

This is a practice, a gentle and continuous returning. It’s the practice of noticing when you’re caught in a mental loop and choosing, with compassion, to guide your awareness back to your breath, back to your body, back to this moment. It’s about developing a relationship with your head that is based not on control, but on collaboration. The brain is a magnificent tool, but it is not the sole authority on your life. When it is in service to the heart, and in partnership with the body’s wisdom, it becomes what it was always meant to be: a radiant crown of consciousness, connecting you to the vast intelligence of life itself.

Your purpose is not a problem to be solved by the mind. It is a truth to be felt by the heart, and expressed through the unique and beautiful instrument of your being. The head, in its highest expression, is the antenna for this truth, the crown that receives the signal and allows it to flow through you, into the world. It is the bridge between the infinite and the finite, the spiritual and the material. It is the place where the universe comes to know itself, as you.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Nearsighted, Farsighted, Insightful: The Emotional Roots of Vision](/blog/eyes-emotional-roots-of-vision)
- [A Practice for Spinal Freedom and Authentic Uprightness](/blog/spine-freedom-practice)
- [Fight, Flight, Freeze: When Your Nervous System Runs the Show](/blog/nervous-system-fight-flight-freeze)

**More on Head:**

- [Headaches, Migraines, and the Prison of Overthinking](/blog/head-headaches-overthinking)
- [A Practice for Quieting the Mind and Trusting Deeper Wisdom](/blog/head-quieting-mind-practice)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

May you wear your crown with grace, and may you trust the deep wisdom of which it is a part.

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

Finish with one gentle neck roll. If any movement or attention increases pain or distress, pause the practice and reach out to a healthcare or mental-health professional as needed.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Holographic Body: How Every Part Reflects the Whole
teachings.title: The Holographic Body: How Every Part Reflects the Whole
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard the body as holographic: each symptom or sensation carries information about larger emotional, relational, and ancestral patterns. Drawing on clinical experience and neurobiological metaphors, she offers the Elevated Body cards as a tool to listen to the body’s messages and to explore the wider stories that symptoms may be reflecting. The piece encourages gentle, nonjudgmental inquiry into whatever part is speaking and emphasizes compassionate, embodied listening as a pathway toward greater insight.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
A woman came to see me years ago, wrestling with a persistent, sharp pain in her left shoulder. On paper, she was the picture of health. She ate well, she exercised, she had a successful career. But for months, this sharp, insistent pain in her left shoulder had become her constant companion. She’d been to doctors, physiotherapists, all the experts. They’d X-rayed and MRI’d and prodded. No one could find a thing wrong with the joint itself. The structure was sound, the muscles strong. Yet the pain remained—a hot, insistent ache that radiated down her arm and made it difficult to sleep, to work, to even lift a coffee cup.

“It feels like I’m carrying something,” she told me, her voice tight with frustration. “A heavy, invisible weight I can’t put down.”

As we began to work together, a story emerged. It wasn’t a story about her shoulder at all. It was a story about her mother, who had been chronically ill for years, and for whom my client was the primary caregiver. The weight she felt in her shoulder was the emotional weight of that responsibility—the unspoken grief, the exhaustion, the feeling of being tethered to a situation she could not change.

This is the profound truth I’ve come to witness again and again in my three decades of healing work: the body is holographic. Every single part, from the smallest cell to the most complex organ system, reflects the patterns of the whole. Your shoulder pain is never just about your shoulder. Your digestive issues are never just about your stomach. They are messengers from a deeper place, echoes of a larger story that is asking to be heard.

## The Science of the Whole in Every Part

The concept of a hologram is a beautiful scientific metaphor for this principle. In a hologram, if you cut the image into tiny pieces, each piece still contains the entire image, just at a lower resolution. The whole is encoded in every part. Your body operates on a similar principle. It is a unified field of consciousness, and the story of your life—your beliefs, your traumas, your joys, your ancestral patterns—is not stored in one single location. It is distributed throughout your entire being.

Neuroscience is beginning to catch up to this ancient wisdom. We now know that memories are not filed away in a single brain region like books on a shelf, but exist as distributed networks of neural pathways that fire together. The brain itself is holographic in its organization. And this extends to the body. Dr. Candace Pert’s groundbreaking research on neuropeptides showed that these “molecules of emotion” are found not just in the brain, but throughout the body—in our organs, our immune cells, our gut. Your gut, in fact, has its own complex neural network, often called the “second brain,” which is in constant communication with the brain in your head. This is why you feel “butterflies” in your stomach when you’re nervous, or a “gut feeling” about a person or situation. It’s not just a metaphor; it’s biology. Your body is thinking, feeling, and experiencing right alongside your brain.

The Tao Te Ching speaks to this beautifully: *“The universe is a perfect whole. The part is not separate from the whole.”* This is the essence of holographic consciousness. There is no separation between mind and body, between emotion and physical sensation. It is all one unified field of information and energy.

What does this mean for you, in your lived experience? It means that the tension in your jaw is connected to the way you hold your feet. It means the anxiety in your chest has a relationship with the way your liver processes your experiences. It means that when we work with one part of the body, we are—if we listen closely enough—working with the whole. The body is not a machine with separate, replaceable parts. It is a sacred, interconnected ecosystem of intelligence.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## A Conversation with Your Holographic Self

This understanding of the body as a holographic system is what led me to create The Elevated Body cards. For years, I had been listening to the stories my clients’ bodies were telling. I saw the undeniable connection between a client’s grief and their lung issues, or between a deep-seated fear and the state of their kidneys. The patterns were so clear, so consistent. I began to map them, to document this language of the body.

I wanted to create a tool that would allow people to have this conversation directly with their own bodies—to bypass the analytical mind and access the body’s deep, intuitive wisdom. The cards are an invitation to do just that. Each card represents a different body part or system, and each one offers a doorway into the specific emotional, energetic, and ancestral patterns associated with it.

When you pull a card—perhaps for the Feet, or the Liver, or the Spine—you are not just looking at an isolated part. You are inviting a holographic conversation. You are asking, “What is the larger story that my feet are trying to tell me right now? What pattern in my life is my liver asking me to metabolize?”

For example, I worked with a man who was struggling with chronic foot pain. He drew the Feet card, which speaks to our foundation, our ability to move forward, and the support we feel on our journey. As he sat with the card, he began to talk about his childhood, about feeling unsupported by his parents, about a deep-seated fear of taking the next step in his career. His foot pain wasn’t just a physical problem; it was the embodiment of a core belief that he was walking through life alone. By bringing compassionate awareness to that old story, by consciously working to build a sense of inner support, the pain in his feet began to soften. He was healing the whole by tending to the part.

I remember another client, a woman with chronic laryngitis. She would lose her voice for weeks at a time, and it was impacting her work as a teacher. She pulled the Vocal Cords card, which is all about authentic expression and speaking one’s truth. As we explored this, she realized she had a deep-seated pattern of silencing herself to keep the peace, a pattern that began in her conflict-avoidant family of origin. She was terrified of confrontation, and so she would swallow her words, her needs, her desires. Her body, in its infinite wisdom, was creating a physical manifestation of this emotional pattern. The healing for her was not about vocal exercises; it was about finding the courage to speak her truth in small, safe ways. It was about learning that her voice mattered. As she began to do this, her laryngitis simply… fell away. The symptom was no longer needed, because the message had been received.

We see this everywhere. Someone with persistent bladder issues might be holding onto old resentments, unable to “let go” of a past hurt. The healing isn’t just about the bladder; it’s about learning the grace of release throughout their entire life. Someone with thyroid imbalances might be caught in a conflict between their authentic desire to speak up and a learned fear of being silenced. Healing the thyroid means reclaiming their voice and their truth in all areas of their existence.

## Your Body is Speaking. Are You Listening?

This is the magic of the holographic body. You don’t have to have it all figured out. You don’t have to understand the entire, complex web of your being. You can simply start with the part that is speaking the loudest—the ache in your back, the flutter in your stomach, the tension in your neck. You can bring your gentle, loving attention to that one place, and trust that the healing will ripple outwards, touching every aspect of your life.

Perhaps you can try it right now. Take a moment to close your eyes and take a soft, easy breath. Let your awareness drift through your body. Is there a place that is calling for your attention? A place of tension, of numbness, of discomfort? Don’t judge it, don’t try to fix it. Simply… arrive. Bring your awareness to that place as if you were visiting a beloved friend.

Ask it, gently, “What do you have to tell me?”

And then listen. Listen with your whole being. Don’t expect a clear, linear answer. It may come as a feeling, an image, a memory, a single word. It may be a whisper, a nudge, a subtle shift in sensation. The wisdom of the body is not loud. It is quiet, and deep, and profoundly intelligent. The more you practice this kind of listening, the more fluent you will become in your body’s unique language. You begin to realize that your body has been your most loyal and constant companion on this journey. It has been trying, in its own way, to guide you back to yourself all along.

Your body is not a problem to be solved. It is a sacred messenger, a wise and loving guide. It is constantly speaking to you, offering you a pathway back to wholeness. All it asks is that you listen.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan
