teachings.sourceTitle: Illuminated Vision: Seeing the World Through the Light of Love
teachings.title: Illuminated Vision: Seeing the World Through the Light of Love
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to consider the eyes as both sensors and storytellers — bodily messengers shaped by fear, habit, and love. She offers a gentle breathing and visualization practice to soften ocular tension, access the "inner eye," and begin to rewire habitual patterns of perception from vigilance to kindness. The piece frames seeing as a bodily, emotional, and spiritual practice rather than a mechanical problem to fix.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The first client I ever saw — over thirty years ago now — taught me more about healing than any textbook ever could.

And part of that complexity business involves how we see the world—or perhaps, how we *think* we see the world. I remember a time, years ago, when my eyes felt perpetually tired. Not just sleepy, but strained, as if they were carrying a heavy weight. I’d find myself squinting at things, both near and far, a constant, low-grade tension humming behind my temples. My optometrist told me my prescription hadn’t changed, that my eyes were physically healthy. Yet I was experiencing the world through a subtle, weary filter.

It wasn’t until I was deep in a meditation one afternoon that a quiet question surfaced: *What are you so afraid of seeing, Susan?* The question didn’t come with an immediate answer, but it loosened something in me. It was the beginning of a profound realization: the tension in my physical eyes was a direct reflection of a tension in my inner world. My eyes were not just passive cameras recording reality; they were active participants, gates of perception shaped by my beliefs, my fears, and my history.

Our eyes are the primary way we receive the external world, the famous “windows of the soul.” But they are not just windows; they are projectors. Our brain, that three-pound universe in our head, doesn’t just see what’s out there. It takes in billions of bits of data and, based on a lifetime of experience stored in our neural pathways, it constructs a story of reality. It tells us what is safe to see, what is too painful to look at, and what we must keep a close watch on. And our precious eyes… they obey.

## The Body as Sacred Messenger: What Your Eyes Are Telling You

In the language of the body, every symptom is a communication. A sacred message from a part of you that needs to be heard. When it comes to vision, the messages are often profoundly insightful. Do you find the future blurry, indistinct, a little frightening? This can manifest as nearsightedness, a conflict about seeing what lies ahead because the present feels like the only safe harbor. Or is the present moment too painful, too overwhelming to fully look at? Farsightedness can emerge from this, a way of keeping the immediacy of your life at a distance, focusing only on a far-off horizon that feels less threatening.

This isn’t about judgment. It’s about compassion. Every pattern has served you. That tension in your gaze, that need to keep the world at a distance or pull it in close—it was a brilliant strategy your nervous system developed to help you feel safe. But what if that old pattern is no longer needed? What if you could begin to release the tension, to soften the gaze, and to see not just with your physical eyes, but with the illuminated vision of your heart?

This is not about striving for perfect 20/20 vision, as if our bodies were machines to be calibrated. It is about developing a conscious, loving relationship with your own perception. It is about learning to see the world, and yourself, through the light of love. And that is a practice. It is a journey, not a destination. It’s a commitment to meeting yourself, right where you are, with tenderness and curiosity. What a relief. We don’t have to be perfect. We just have to be present. This presence is a form of deep listening, a turning inward to the quiet wisdom of the body that is always available, beneath the chatter of the mind. It is in this space of presence that true healing begins, not as a fixing of something broken, but as a remembering of the wholeness that was never lost.

## A Guided Practice for Illuminated Vision

I would like to offer you a practice. A gentle, guided journey into the landscape of your own vision. This isn’t about forcing anything; it’s an invitation to soften, to open, and to listen. Find a comfortable place where you can sit quietly for a few minutes without being disturbed.

**Step 1: Softening the Gaze**

Begin by closing your eyes. Or, if that doesn’t feel comfortable, simply lower your gaze and let it rest softly on the floor a few feet in front of you. Take a deep, slow breath in… and as you exhale, let go of the day. Take another breath, and this time, bring your awareness to the tiny muscles around your eyes. The muscles at the corners, between your brows, the ones that hold your eyeballs in their sacred sockets. You don’t have to do anything at all. Just notice. Notice any tension, any holding, any tightness.

Now, imagine that with every exhale, you are breathing a soft, warm mist into this area. A mist of pure relaxation. Feel the muscles begin to soften, to release their grip. You might even feel a gentle warmth spreading from your temples, across your eyelids, and deep into the eyes themselves. Stay here for a few breaths, just savoring this feeling of release.

**Step 2: The Healing Light Visualization**

Now, keeping your eyes softly closed, imagine a point of warm, golden light shimmering in the space right in front of you. It could be the color of sunlight, of candlelight, or any color that feels healing to you. See it, feel it. This light is the essence of pure, unconditional love.

On your next inhale, imagine drawing this beautiful, healing light in through your eyes. Feel it bathing your retinas, nourishing your optic nerves, filling the entire globe of each eye with its gentle, radiant energy. As you exhale, imagine any tension, any strain, any old ways of seeing that no longer serve you, dissolving and flowing out of you, carried away on the breath. Continue this for several cycles. Inhaling the golden light of love. Exhaling the residue of fear and tension. Let your eyes drink in this nourishment.

**Step 3: Inner Seeing Meditation**

As you continue to breathe, allow your awareness to drift to the space between your eyebrows, the location of what many wisdom traditions call the “inner eye.” Let your attention rest here, gently. There is nothing to force, nothing to *try* to see. You are simply opening to a different kind of perception, one that is not limited by the physical senses. This inner eye, or ajna chakra in Sanskrit, is the seat of intuition, of insight that arises not from logical deduction but from a direct knowing. It is the part of you that sees the energetic truth of a situation, the part of you that can feel the resonance of love and the dissonance of fear. By resting your attention here, you are gently awakening this dormant faculty.

Ask this center of wisdom within you a quiet question: *What would it be like to see with new eyes?* Or, *Show me what it looks like to see through the light of love.* Don’t search for an answer with your thinking mind. Simply hold the question in this space and be open to whatever arises. It might be a feeling. It might be a color, a memory, or a sense of deep peace. It might be a subtle shift in the energy behind your closed eyelids. Whatever it is, just receive it without judgment. This is your inner wisdom speaking to you in its own language. Rest in this awareness for as long as you feel comfortable.

When you are ready, slowly begin to bring your awareness back to the room. Wiggle your fingers and toes, feeling your connection to the ground beneath you. And when you feel ready, gently, slowly, allow your eyes to flutter open. Don’t immediately focus on anything specific. Just allow the light, colors, and shapes of your environment to enter your awareness softly, without striving or labeling. It’s like letting your eyes be kissed by the world. Notice if anything feels different. Is the world a little softer? A little brighter? Is your own gaze a little more relaxed, more spacious? There is no right or wrong way to feel. Simply notice what is true for you in this moment.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

This practice is a way to begin rewiring those ancient neural pathways. It’s a declaration to your body and your consciousness that you are ready to see differently. You are ready to release the need to “keep an eye on” everything, to let go of the vigilance that exhausts your spirit and strains your beautiful eyes. You are choosing to see from a place of trust, not fear.

To see with illuminated vision is to recognize the sacred in the mundane. It’s to look at a loved one and see not just the person you know, with all their history and habits, but the radiant, eternal soul shining through them. It’s to look at a challenge and see not just an obstacle to be overcome, but a sacred invitation into deeper wisdom and resilience. It’s to look in the mirror and see not a collection of flaws to be fixed, but a being worthy of infinite love and compassion, exactly as you are. This is the vision that heals. This is the vision that transforms. It doesn’t require you to go anywhere or achieve anything. It is available to you, right here, in every moment. All you have to do is soften, breathe, and open your eyes to the love that is already and always here, waiting patiently for you to see it.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Tricky Business of Being Human
teachings.title: The Tricky Business of Being Human
teachings.summary: Susan names the everyday paradox of being human — holding joy and grief, hope and despair — and reframes that contradiction as evidence of a living, transforming soul rather than brokenness. She explains the brain’s survival-driven negativity bias, invites gentle awareness and neuroplastic practices, and describes challenges as a "birth canal" through which new ways of being are born.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I was standing at my kitchen sink this morning, washing a bowl, and I was ambushed by two completely contradictory feelings at once. The morning light was streaming in, catching the dust motes dancing in the air, and I felt a wave of the most profound, simple joy. The beauty of it all… the quiet of the house, the warmth of the water on my hands. And in the very same breath, a deep, aching grief for a friend who is struggling, for the state of our world, for a loss I thought I had long metabolized.

I want to ask you something, and I want you to answer honestly, even if only to yourself.

*

Isn’t it? This beautiful, messy, magnificent, and often maddening experience of having a soul, a spirit, housed in a body, walking this earth. We are creatures of immense contradiction. We can hold soaring hope and deep despair in the same heart. We can be breathtakingly kind and shockingly cruel. We build cathedrals and we start wars. We are capable of infinite love and yet we wound the ones we love the most.

It’s so easy to feel like we’re doing it wrong. To look at the mess and the contradiction and think, *I must be broken.* We get the cultural message constantly that we should be happy, sorted, successful, and ever-ascending. But what if the mess isn’t a sign of failure? What if the trickiness is the whole point?

## The Brain’s Beautiful, Terrible Job

Here’s a very good thing to know: your brain is not designed to make you happy. It’s designed to help you *survive*. That’s its number one job, a job it has been perfecting for a couple of hundred thousand years. And to do that job well, it has developed some very particular, and very tricky, habits.

One of its most powerful habits is a negativity bias. Your brain is like Velcro for bad experiences and Teflon for good ones. It scans the horizon—and your inner landscape—for threats. It remembers the time you were embarrassed in a meeting far more vividly than the ten times you were praised. It replays the argument, the mistake, the moment of fear, because its primary directive is to ensure you don’t let that happen again. It’s not trying to make you miserable; it’s trying to keep you safe.

This ancient wiring, while brilliant in its evolutionary purpose, creates so much of our modern-day, quiet suffering. It builds and reinforces neural pathways—literally, connections between brain cells—that become our default settings. Think of it like carving a path in a forest. The first time you walk it, it’s slow and difficult. But the more you travel that same path, the wider and clearer it becomes, until you can walk it without thinking. This is how our patterns of anxiety, self-criticism, or fear become automatic. We create entire identities around these well-worn grooves of suffering, believing the stories our survival-brain whispers to us in the dark. *See? You failed again. You’re not lovable. It’s all going to fall apart.* The brain chemistry of this is real—cortisol and adrenaline flood our systems, preparing us for a fight that exists only in our minds, and this chronic state of low-grade alarm is utterly exhausting.

But here is the miracle, the beautiful truth that changes everything: *you are not your brain.* You are the consciousness that is aware of your brain. You are the sky, and the thoughts are just the weather. And with that awareness, you gain the power to build a new relationship with this magnificent, and sometimes maddening, three-pound universe in your head. This is the essence of neuroplasticity. The brain can change. It is designed to change. When you bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your patterns, you activate the higher, more evolved parts of your brain, like the prefrontal cortex. You can acknowledge your survival-brain’s intention to protect you—'Ah, thank you for trying to keep me safe'—and then gently, lovingly, choose a different path. You can consciously choose to focus on a moment of beauty, to practice gratitude, to place a hand on your heart and breathe. Each time you do this, you are beginning to walk a new path in the forest. You are forging a new neural pathway, one of peace, of self-compassion, of groundedness. It feels effortful at first, but with practice, it becomes the new default. This is the sacred work of transformation.


## The Birth Canal of Transformation

I’ve come to see our challenges not as interruptions to our lives, but as the very fabric of our becoming. Every struggle, every dark night of the soul, every place where we feel stuck and lost… it is a birth canal. It is a sacred, and often painful, passage from one way of being to another.

Think of the seed. For the shoot to emerge, the seed must be completely undone. It must break apart in the dark, damp earth. It doesn’t look like progress. It looks like destruction. And yet, it is the only way for the new life to begin. Our human journey is so often like this. The moments that feel like the end are so often the beginning.

The Tao te Ching, that beautiful wellspring of ancient wisdom, speaks to this constantly. It reminds us that the softest thing in the universe overcomes the hardest. That the valley, the empty space, is what makes the bowl useful. It whispers of a reality where yielding is strength, where darkness is the womb of light, and where the greatest journeys are made one small step at a time.

When we are in the tight, dark passage of a challenge—a health crisis, a relationship ending, a career implosion—it feels like we are being crushed. It feels like a mistake. But what if it is simply the pressure of new life? What if the discomfort is the force of your own soul, pressing against the constraints of your old beliefs, your old identity, your old way of being in the world? The pain is the signal that a transformation is underway.

It’s not about figuring it out. It’s about *being with* it. It’s about allowing the process to unfold, trusting that the pressure is purposeful, even when you cannot see the light ahead. It is the tricky, tender work of letting yourself be remade.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## My Own Tricky Business

I have spent a lifetime navigating this tricky business. For years, I lived in a state of quiet, chronic anxiety, my nervous system wired for high alert from a childhood where it learned that the world was not a reliably safe place. I became a master of control, of performance, of trying to be perfect and good enough to finally earn a sense of safety. My body was screaming at me for decades, through migraines and exhaustion, but I didn’t yet know how to listen. I thought my body was the problem.

My own birth canal was a long and winding one. It wasn’t a single, dramatic event, but a slow, patient, and often deeply uncomfortable turning towards myself. For years, I lived in a state of quiet, chronic anxiety, my nervous system wired for high alert from a childhood where it learned that the world was not a reliably safe place. I became a master of control, of performance, of trying to be perfect and good enough to finally earn a sense of safety. My body was screaming at me for decades, through migraines, digestive issues, and a profound, bone-deep exhaustion, but I didn’t yet know how to listen. I thought my body was the problem, a betrayer to be managed and overcome.

The real shift began not when I tried to fix myself, but when I started to listen. It was the slow, patient work of sitting with the discomfort. Of learning to meet the churning anxiety in my stomach not with resistance, but with a gentle curiosity. *Hello there. What are you trying to tell me?* It was the radical act of placing a hand on my own heart in the middle of the night and whispering, *I am here with you. This is hard. You are not alone.* It was the work of tracing the patterns back to their roots, not to create a story of blame, but to cultivate a field of profound compassion. To see the little girl who learned she had to be vigilant to survive, and to wrap her in the love and safety she always deserved.

It was, and still is, the work of neuroplasticity in action. Every time I chose to pause instead of react, to breathe instead of brace, I was carving a new neural pathway. I was telling my brain, my body, my entire being, that a new reality was possible. A reality where I could be both strong and soft, where my worth was not tied to my doing, and where my body was not an enemy to be conquered but a sacred messenger to be revered.

There is such an exquisite beauty in this. The beauty is not in arriving at a place of perfect, perpetual peace. The beauty is in the relationship you build with your own messy, magnificent self. It’s in the moment you can look at your own contradictions—your fear and your courage, your doubt and your faith—and hold them all with love. It’s in the growing trust that you can handle the trickiness, that you have the resilience to navigate the birth canals, and that you are held by a love that is so much bigger than your mind can comprehend.

This human experience is a profound gift. It is a chance to feel everything—the heart-stopping joy and the heart-wrenching sorrow. It is an invitation to transform our deepest wounds into our greatest wisdom. It is a journey of coming home to the truth of who we are, beneath the stories, beneath the patterns, beneath the noise of the survival-brain.

You are not broken. You have never been broken. You are a soul on a magnificent, and yes, a very tricky, journey. Be gentle with yourself. The mess is part of the magic.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.sourceTitle: Your Bladder Speaks: The Reservoir of Release
teachings.title: Your Bladder Speaks: The Reservoir of Release
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to hear the bladder as a living metaphor for what we hold and what we need to release, connecting pelvic tension and bladder distress to patterns of emotional control, shame, and learned neural habits. Through a client's story and gentle somatic guidance—breath, hand-on-belly presence, and visualization—she encourages compassionate curiosity rather than shame-driven control. The piece offers short, accessible practices to begin retraining the nervous system toward softness and trust while honoring that change is gradual and non-linear.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
What if everything you've been through — every heartbreak, every disappointment, every dark night of the soul — was not punishment, but preparation?

We are asked to hold so much. The joys, the sorrows, the mundane logistics of a life. We are also asked to let it all go. To release, to forgive, to flow with the current of what is, rather than what we think should be. And nowhere in the body is this paradox more exquisitely held than in the bladder.

I often begin my day in quiet contemplation, a cup of tea in my hands, watching the light change over the water. It’s a time for gentle listening. And one morning, a thought arose with such clarity: our bodies are living metaphors. They are constantly speaking to us in a language of sensation, of symptom, of pure, unvarnished truth. If we can learn to listen, not with fear, but with a reverent curiosity, a whole new world of wisdom opens up. This is especially true of the parts of ourselves we’ve been taught to ignore or even feel ashamed of—like the bladder.

I remember a client, a woman I’ll call Claire, a gifted architect with a razor-sharp mind and a life that looked perfect on the outside. She came to me suffering from chronic, painful cystitis. She felt, in her words, “constantly burned.” By her colleagues, by her partner, by a world that seemed to take and take and never give back. Her bladder was, quite literally, on fire. As we began our work together, peeling back the layers of her story, a deeper truth began to emerge. It wasn’t just about being burned; it was about the immense, crushing pressure she felt to *hold it all together*. To be the perfect professional, the unflappable partner, the ever-capable daughter. She had built an entire identity on controlling her responses, tamping down her needs, and managing every conceivable outcome. Her bladder, this beautiful, humble organ, was simply screaming the truth she couldn’t yet voice: *I can’t hold anymore.*

## The Sacred Reservoir

Let’s speak for a moment about the physiology of this incredible organ, this sacred reservoir. The bladder is, in essence, a muscular, hollow sac. It sits patiently in the pelvic basin, collecting the filtrate from the kidneys—the waste products, the excess salts, the things the body has used and is now ready to discard. It is designed to stretch, to expand, to accommodate. It holds what is no longer needed until the moment of release. It’s a final gateway. A threshold between what we keep and what we let go.

This dual function—the holding and the releasing—is a profound metaphor for our emotional and spiritual lives. Think about it. How often do we hold on to things long past their expiration date? An old hurt from a thoughtless comment, a lingering resentment toward a family member, a story about who we are that no longer fits but feels terrifying to release. We clench, we tighten, we resist the natural flow of completion. We believe, on some deep, often unconscious level, that letting go is a form of failure. That it’s shameful, or embarrassing, or simply not safe.

This is a pattern I see so often in my work. The belief that if we can just control ourselves, our emotions, our natural expressions, we will finally earn the love or approval we seek. We hold our breath when we feel tears coming, we hold our tongues when we long to speak our truth, we hold in the very life force that wants to move through us. And the bladder, in its infinite wisdom, often reflects this tension back to us. The urgency, the pressure, the fear of a leak… it’s the body’s way of saying, *Beloved, this is becoming intolerable.*

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Neuroscience of Holding

When we live in a state of chronic holding, it’s not just a psychological experience; it’s a physiological one. Our nervous system learns this pattern. The sympathetic branch, the one responsible for our “fight or flight” response, becomes dominant. It’s as if the body is in a constant, low-grade state of alarm. This sends a cascade of signals throughout our entire being. The muscles of the pelvic floor, the very hammock that supports the bladder, can become chronically tight. This isn’t a conscious choice; it’s a deeply ingrained neural pathway. The brain has learned that clenching equals safety.

This creates a vicious feedback loop. The tight muscles put pressure on the bladder, creating a sensation of urgency. The brain interprets this as a threat—*Oh no, I might leak!*—which reinforces the original pattern of clenching. And so it goes, a self-perpetuating cycle of tension and fear. We are literally clenching against the flow of our own lives.

What would it be like, just for a moment, to soften? To introduce a new possibility into this ancient wiring? To allow the idea that release is not shameful, but essential? That it is not a sign of weakness, but of profound trust in the cycles of life and your body’s innate intelligence?

This isn’t about forcing yourself to “let go.” That’s just another form of control, isn’t it? It’s a much gentler, more compassionate process than that. It’s about developing a conscious, loving relationship with the parts of you that are holding on so tightly. It’s about bringing a warm, curious attention to the fear that underlies the control. Perhaps that pattern of holding everything in served you once. Perhaps it was a brilliant strategy for surviving a childhood where your authentic feelings weren’t welcome or safe. Our brains are wired for survival, and they will adopt whatever strategy is necessary. But now? Now, you are no longer that powerless child. Now, you have a choice.

## The Wisdom of Release

Here’s a very good thing to know: your body is a sacred messenger. It is always, *always* communicating with you, guiding you back to wholeness. The discomfort in your bladder is not an enemy to be silenced or a problem to be fixed. It is a call to attention. An invitation to explore what you are holding, and why. It’s a chance to rewrite the old story that says you must contain yourself to be loved.

For my client Claire, this was the turning point. When she began to see her cystitis not as a random affliction, but as a message from her own deep wisdom, everything started to shift. She started to notice the moments when she would physically clench her jaw or hold her breath. She began to connect the flare-ups in her bladder with the times she felt most pressured to perform. Slowly, gently, she started to practice a different way of being. She started to take small moments to consciously soften her belly. She started to ask herself, *What is the truth that wants to be expressed right now?* She started to trust that she could handle the outcome, even if it wasn’t perfectly managed.

It wasn’t a linear process. There were steps forward and steps back. But over time, she began to build a new neural pathway—one of trust, of flow, of self-compassion. Her bladder, in turn, began to quiet down. The fire subsided. She was no longer at war with herself.

Here is a simple practice you can try. Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down. Close your eyes if that feels good to you. Bring your awareness to your breath, without changing it. Just notice the gentle rise and fall of your belly. Now, imagine a beautiful, soft light filling your pelvic bowl. A warm, golden light. See it surrounding your bladder, infusing it with ease and peace. With each exhale, imagine that you are releasing a little bit of the tension you’ve been holding. You don’t have to know what it is or why it’s there. Just intend to let it go. Let the light dissolve it. Do this for just a few minutes each day. It’s a way of communicating a new message to your body: *It is safe to release. It is safe to be in the flow.*

## A Blessing for the Flow

So, I invite you now, wherever you are, to place a hand on your lower belly, over the space of your bladder. You don’t need to press, just rest your hand there. Feel the warmth, the simple connection of your own touch.

Take a slow, deep breath. And as you exhale, imagine a wave of softness moving through your body. Soften your jaw. Soften your shoulders. And see if you can invite a sense of gentle release into your pelvic bowl.

And perhaps, you might offer a small blessing to this part of your body, this faithful reservoir.

>*Thank you, bladder. Thank you for your patience, for your resilience. Thank you for holding what I was not yet ready to release. And thank you for showing me, with such clarity, when it is time to let go. I am listening. I am willing to learn a new way. I am willing to trust the flow.*

Stay with this for a few more breaths. See if you can feel a subtle shift. A gentle, internal permission to release the tension you’ve been carrying. This is the beginning of a new conversation with your body. A conversation grounded in reverence, in listening, and in the profound wisdom that knows, without a doubt, that you are not broken. You have never been broken. You are a magnificent, flowing river of life.

teachings.sourceTitle: The Soft and Supple: Why Flexibility Is the True Strength
teachings.title: The Soft and Supple: Why Flexibility Is the True Strength
teachings.summary: Susan returns to a teaching from the Tao Te Ching to illuminate how softness — not hardness — is the truest form of strength. She traces how we build protective armor in response to hurt, how that rigidity becomes stored in body and relationships, and offers an invitation to practice gentle awareness and yielding as a pathway back to resilience and relational openness.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
There is a teaching in the Tao Te Ching that I return to again and again — one that has quietly reshaped the way I work with the human body, the human heart, and the mysterious territory where the two meet. Lao Tzu writes:

> Men are born soft and supple;
> dead, they are stiff and hard.
> Plants are born tender and pliant;
> dead, they are brittle and dry.
> Thus whoever is stiff and inflexible
> is a disciple of death.
> Whoever is soft and yielding
> is a disciple of life.

Consider the image of a windy autumn afternoon. Maple trees bend and sway, their branches dancing with the gusts rather than fighting them. In this, we can see the whole teaching embodied right in front of us.

Softness is life. Rigidity is death. It sounds so simple. And yet, so many of us have spent a great deal of our lives learning to be hard.

## The Armor We Build

We come into this world soft. Have you ever held a newborn? That impossibly tender body, those tiny fingers that curl around yours with a grip that is fierce and gentle at the same time. There is no rigidity in a baby. There is no holding, no bracing, no armor. There is only openness — a complete, breathtaking willingness to receive whatever life brings.

And then life brings things that hurt.

A sharp word from a parent. A playground rejection. A moment of shame so hot and sudden that our little bodies don't know what to do with it. And so we do the only thing we can: we tighten. We brace. We build walls around the soft places, because the soft places are where we got hurt, and we are determined — with the fierce, wordless determination of a child — to never be hurt like that again.

This is not a failure. This is intelligence. This is the body's brilliant, instinctive response to threat. The armor we build as children is not a mistake — it is a survival strategy, and it works. It gets us through.

But here is the thing that Lao Tzu understood, and that we can witness in body after body: the armor that once protected us eventually becomes the thing that imprisons us.

## The Stiff and the Inflexible

Many of us have encountered people who seem to command every room they enter. They may appear to be pillars of strength, but their bodies can tell a different story. You might see shoulders pulled up around the ears like a permanent flinch, a jaw so clenched that the muscles bulge at the temples, or a lower back that is a solid wall of tension.

Such a person might say, "My back pain is stress-related, but that's ridiculous. I handle stress perfectly well."

It is common to hear this sentiment. What it often means is: *I have become so rigid that I can no longer feel what is happening inside me.*

When we place our hands on a back like that, we can feel it — layer upon layer of holding, decades of tension compressed into tissue that has forgotten how to let go. The body is not handling stress. The body is *storing* stress, packing it away like bricks in a wall, and the wall is getting so high and so heavy that it is beginning to collapse under its own weight.

This is what rigidity does. It does not protect us. It calcifies us. It turns the living, breathing, responsive tissue of our bodies into something brittle and dry — exactly as Lao Tzu described. And what is brittle, breaks.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Way of Water

Lao Tzu had a great love for water, and it appears throughout the Tao Te Ching as the supreme teacher of the soft way. Water does not fight. It does not resist. It flows around obstacles, finds the lowest places, and yet — over time — it carves through solid rock. It is the softest thing in the world, and it overcomes the hardest.

> The soft overcomes the hard.
> The slow overcomes the fast.

This is a powerful lesson for those in the grip of a life crisis — a divorce, a diagnosis, a loss that has shattered their world. The instinct, always, is to harden. To clench. To *hold it together*. This instinct is deeply human and understandable.

But holding it together is not the same as being whole. Holding it together is rigidity wearing the mask of strength. True strength — the strength that Lao Tzu points us toward — is the willingness to soften. To bend. To let the grief or the fear or the confusion move through us like water, rather than building a dam against it.

When people finally allow themselves to soften, it is a beautiful thing to witness. For the executive mentioned earlier, after several sessions, something might begin to shift. His shoulders could drop, just a fraction of an inch. His jaw might unclench. And in that tiny opening, tears can come. Not dramatic, wracking sobs — just a quiet stream of tears that had been waiting behind that wall for thirty years.

He might whisper, "I didn't know that was in there."

It is always in there. The softness never leaves us. It just gets buried under all that armor.

## Flexibility in Our Relationships

This teaching does not apply only to our bodies. It applies to every relationship we have — with our partners, our children, our friends, our colleagues, and perhaps most importantly, with ourselves.

How many of our conflicts arise from rigidity? From the insistence that we are right and the other person is wrong? From the refusal to bend, to see another perspective, to allow for the possibility that our way is not the only way?

So many people describe couples sitting across from each other with arms folded and jaws set, each one locked into their position like a fortress. There are moments, however, when one of them softens. When one of them lets the wall down, just enough to say, "I'm scared," or "I miss you," or simply, "I don't know."

That is the moment everything changes. Not because the problem is solved, but because the rigidity is broken. And in the space that opens up, something new can grow.

Lao Tzu tells us:

> The stiff and unbending is the disciple of death.
> The soft and yielding is the disciple of life.

In our relationships, rigidity looks like: *I will not apologize first. I will not be the one to reach out. I will not show vulnerability because vulnerability is weakness.* And this rigidity, over time, kills the relationship as surely as frost kills a flower.

Flexibility looks like: *I can hold my truth and still make room for yours. I can be hurt and still stay open. I can disagree and still love.* This is not weakness. This is the deepest strength there is.

## The Body Remembers

In healing work, it is understood that the body is the most honest teacher we have. It does not lie. It does not rationalize or justify or explain away. It simply holds the truth of our experience, written in the language of tension and release, contraction and expansion, rigidity and flow.

When we are rigid in our thinking, our bodies become rigid. When we are inflexible in our emotions — refusing to feel grief, or anger, or fear — our tissues become inflexible. The fascia tightens. The joints stiffen. The breath becomes shallow. We become, quite literally, hard.

And when we begin to soften — when we give ourselves permission to feel what we have been avoiding, to bend where we have been bracing, to flow where we have been frozen — the body responds with an intelligence that can be astonishing. Muscles that have been locked for decades begin to release. Breath deepens. Pain that seemed permanent begins to dissolve.

This is not magic. This is the Tao at work in the body. It is the natural movement of life toward softness, toward openness, toward the supple aliveness that is our birthright.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

## The Practice of Softening

So how do we practice this? How do we, in a world that rewards toughness and punishes vulnerability, learn to be disciples of life rather than disciples of death?

We begin, as always, with awareness. Notice where you are holding right now, as you read these words. Is your jaw clenched? Are your shoulders lifted? Is your belly tight? These are the places where your armor lives. These are the places where your body is saying, *I am bracing for impact.*

And then, gently — with the same tenderness you would offer a frightened child — invite those places to soften. Not to collapse. Not to give up. But to *yield*. To let go of the grip, just a little. To trust that you do not need to be hard in order to be safe.

This is a practice, not a destination. You will tighten again. Life will bring you moments that make you want to build the wall higher and thicker than ever before. And that is all right. The practice is not about being permanently soft. It is about noticing when you have become rigid, and choosing — again and again, with infinite patience — to soften.

The maple tree does not resist the wind. It bends. And because it bends, it survives the storm. The oak that refuses to bend is the one that breaks.

You are not an oak. You are something far more alive, far more resilient, far more beautiful than anything that is stiff and unyielding. You are a living, breathing expression of the Tao itself — and the Tao, as Lao Tzu reminds us, is always flowing, always yielding, always soft.

May you find the courage to let your armor down. May you discover that your softness is not your weakness but your greatest power. May you bend with the winds of your life and find, in that bending, a strength you never knew you had.

---

teachings.summary: Susan offers a compassionate, body-centered practice for reclaiming your voice, describing how throat tension often represents long‑standing survival patterns formed in childhood. The practice blends gentle humming, vowel toning, timed freewriting and loving touch to retrain the nervous system and restore resonant, authentic speech. It emphasizes consistency, non‑forcing, and the energetic dimension of the throat as a bridge between inner truth and outward expression.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Something remarkable happened in my practice last month that I haven't been able to stop thinking about.

We long for connection, to be seen and heard in our fullness, yet so often we find ourselves swallowing our words, a lump forming in our throats where a clear, true sentence was meant to be. I remember a time, years ago, sitting on a plush rug in a circle of women, the air thick with the scent of beeswax and earnest intention. One by one, they spoke their truths, voices raw and shaky and breathtakingly real. Tears flowed freely, met with knowing nods and gentle hands on shoulders. When the talking stick finally came to me, a familiar vise gripped my throat. My heart hammered against my ribs. The words I truly wanted to say—words about a deep ache of unworthiness I’d carried since childhood—felt like jagged stones in my mouth. They felt… dangerous. Too much. So, I offered a polished, palatable summary instead, a story that skimmed the surface. I left that circle feeling a profound and hollow loneliness, a disconnect not from the compassionate women around me, but from the deepest part of myself.

That feeling, that ache of the unspoken, is a deep and ancient one. It lives in the body, specifically in the delicate, powerful tissues of our vocal cords. These twin bands of mucous membrane, stretched across the larynx, are more than just the architecture of sound. They are the vibrational signature of your soul, the bridge between your inner world and the outer one. When they are free, your voice is a clear channel for your truth. When they are constricted, it is a sign that a part of you has gone into hiding.

So many of us have learned, often in the tender years of childhood, that our authentic voice is not safe. Perhaps you were told you were “too loud,” “too sensitive,” or “too much.” Perhaps your truth was met with anger, dismissal, or punishment. The nervous system, in its incredible wisdom, creates a strategy for survival: it constricts. It learns to hold back the tide of authentic expression to keep you safe in your environment. The throat becomes a gatekeeper, and the message it sends is, *it is not safe to speak*. This isn’t a conscious choice. It’s a deeply embedded neural pathway, a pattern of protection that can persist for a lifetime, long after the original threat is gone.

What does this feel like in a body? It can manifest as a chronically hoarse voice, a tendency to lose your voice entirely when you have something important to say, or even physical issues like nodules or polyps on the vocal cords. It can feel like a constant tension in the neck and shoulders, a sense that you are physically holding yourself back. Emotionally, it’s the frustration of being misunderstood, the sorrow of not being fully known, the exhaustion of performing a version of yourself that feels acceptable to others.

But here is a very good thing to know: you are not broken. You have never been broken. These patterns of constriction, these habits of holding back, were born of a deep intelligence. They served you. And now, with compassion and gentle awareness, you can begin to create new patterns. You can rewire those ancient pathways. You can teach your body, on a cellular level, that it is now safe to be seen and heard in your wholeness.

## A Practice for Reclaiming Your Voice

This is not about forcing your voice or pushing through the fear. It is a gentle practice of befriending your throat, your breath, and your sound. It is an invitation to come home to yourself. I recommend finding a quiet space where you won’t be disturbed for 10-15 minutes each day. This consistency is key—it’s how we create the new neural grooves of safety and freedom.

**Step 1: The Releasing Hum**

Begin by finding a comfortable seated position. Close your eyes and bring your awareness to your breath. Don’t change a thing, just notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest and belly. After a few moments, begin to hum on your exhale. It doesn’t need to be a particular note, just a low, gentle vibration. As you hum, place your fingertips lightly on your throat. Feel the resonance there. Imagine that sound is a warm, golden honey, gently loosening any tension, any constriction. Let the vibration be a massage from the inside out. Do this for 2-3 minutes, allowing the hum to be soft, easy, and full of kindness.

**Step 2: Vocal Toning with Vowels**

Now, we will move from humming to toning with open vowel sounds. These sounds resonate in different areas of the body and help to open the energy centers. We’ll use the sounds: *Ahhh*, *Ohhh*, and *Eeem*.

*   **Ahhh:** This is the sound of the heart, an opening and a release. Take a gentle breath in, and on the exhale, release a soft, open “Ahhh” sound, like a sigh of relief. Imagine your heart space is a wide, open meadow, and this sound is a gentle breeze moving through it, carrying away any old grief or tension. Feel the vibration resonate in your chest, right behind your sternum. Let it be as long and gentle as your breath allows. Repeat 3-5 times.
*   **Ohhh:** This sound resonates in the lower belly and pelvis, your center of gravity and creative power. It is grounding and centering. Take a breath in, and on the exhale, create a round, resonant “Ohhh” sound, as if you are marveling at a beautiful sunset. Feel the vibration deep in your core, a sense of being deeply rooted and stable in your own body. This sound connects you to the earth and your own foundational strength. Repeat 3-5 times.
*   **Eeem:** This sound vibrates in the head and the space between your eyebrows, the third eye. It is clarifying and illuminating. Take a breath in, and on the exhale, let a gentle “Eeem” sound buzz behind your closed lips. Feel the vibration in your sinuses, your forehead, your entire skull, like a gentle inner tuning fork. Imagine it clearing away mental fog and confusion, bringing a sense of clarity and focus to your mind. Repeat 3-5 times.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

**Step 3: The Truth-Speaking Exercise**

This is a powerful practice for aligning your words with your inner knowing. You will need a journal and pen. At the top of the page, write the prompt: “What is true for me right now?”

Set a timer for 5 minutes. For those 5 minutes, write continuously, without stopping to edit or judge. Let your pen move. It might be, “What is true for me right now is that my throat feels tight.” or “What is true for me right now is that I am afraid of what my boss will say.” or “What is true for me right now is that the sun on my face feels wonderful.”

There is no right or wrong answer. The goal is simply to create a direct line from your inner experience to its expression on the page. When the timer goes off, read what you have written out loud. Just once. Hear your own truth in your own voice. Then, close the journal. This is not for analysis. It is for the simple, profound act of speaking what is true.

**Step 4: The Gentle Throat Release**

End your practice with a moment of gentle, loving touch. Using the pads of your fingers, gently massage the muscles on the sides of your neck, your jaw, and the base of your skull. Use slow, circular motions. Yawn if you feel the urge. A yawn is one of the body’s most effective ways of releasing tension in the throat and jaw. Finally, place one hand over your heart and one hand over your throat. Breathe into this connection. Send love and gratitude to your voice, to your body, for its wisdom and its unwavering commitment to your survival.

## The Throat Chakra: Your Energetic Center of Expression

In many ancient wisdom traditions, the throat is seen as the home of the fifth chakra, Vishuddha. This energy center governs not only our vocal cords but our ability to express our inner truth, to communicate with clarity and integrity, and to listen as well as we speak. When this chakra is balanced, our words are aligned with our hearts, and we can express ourselves creatively and authentically. When it is blocked—often by fear, shame, or unspoken grief—we experience the very symptoms we’ve been exploring: a constricted throat, a hesitant voice, a feeling of being unheard.

The practice of humming, toning, and speaking your truth is a direct way to work with this energy center. The vibrations you create are literally tuning your throat chakra, breaking up stagnant energy and restoring its natural flow. Think of it as clearing a blocked channel. As the energy begins to move more freely, you may find that not only does your voice change, but your entire relationship with expression begins to shift. You might feel more creative, more confident in sharing your ideas, more able to set clear boundaries, and more willing to have the conversations that matter most.

This is the profound connection between the physical and the energetic. By working with the tissues and structures of the body—the vocal cords, the breath, the muscles of the neck—we are simultaneously tending to the subtle energy that flows through them. It’s a holistic approach, honoring the beautiful, intricate way that our body, mind, and spirit are woven together. You are not just freeing a voice; you are liberating a vital part of your life force.

## The Journey of a Thousand Words Begins with a Single Sound

Freeing your voice is not a one-time event, but a tender, ongoing homecoming. It is a journey of returning, again and again, to the quiet, unshakable truth of who you are. It is a practice of cultivating a deep and loving relationship with every part of yourself—the parts that are loud and clear, and the parts that are still whispering. Some days, your voice will feel as clear and strong as a ringing bell. Other days, it may feel shaky and small, a mere flicker of a flame. That’s okay. That’s human.

The point is not perfection. The point is presence. The point is to meet yourself, in each moment, with radical compassion. To honor the wisdom of your body’s contractions, and to gently, lovingly invite it into a new possibility—the possibility of a voice that is free, a heart that is open, and a life that is an authentic expression of your beautiful, unique soul.

Your voice is a gift. Not just to the world, but to you. It is your connection to your own heart, your own wisdom, your own truth. May you have the courage to listen to it. And may you have the grace to let it be heard.


---

## Explore Related Systems

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to notice how the nervous system constantly scans for safety or danger, describing its three guardians: sympathetic (fight/flight), parasympathetic (rest/digest), and the enteric or “gut” brain. She normalizes chronic hypervigilance as an adaptive response to past threat and emphasizes neuroplasticity: with compassionate, embodied attention we can slowly rewire toward safety. A brief, practical practice (hands on heart and belly, gentle words, five–ten breaths) offers a way to begin befriending the body’s signals and creating new experiences of safety.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Close your eyes for a moment — just a breath or two — and notice what your body is telling you right now.

And one of the most profound aspects is navigating the world with a nervous system that is constantly, tirelessly, and often unconsciously scanning for one of two things: safety or danger.

I remember a time, years ago, when I was walking down a familiar street in my neighbourhood. The sun was warm on my shoulders, the scent of roses from a nearby garden was thick in the air, and the distant sound of children's laughter was a gentle melody. It was, by all accounts, a perfect, peaceful afternoon. And yet, my heart suddenly began to pound, a frantic drum against my ribs. A wave of cold anxiety washed over me, so potent it nearly buckled my knees. I stopped, leaning against a maple tree, my breath catching in my throat.

I looked around, my eyes darting, trying to find the source of this sudden alarm. There was nothing. A child on a bicycle, a woman watering her petunias, a ginger cat sunning itself on a white porch railing. The world was exactly as it had been moments before—peaceful, ordinary. And yet, my body was screaming *danger*. My palms were sweating, my vision had narrowed, and a single, primal thought echoed in my mind: *run*.

It took me a long time, and a lot of gentle, compassionate inquiry, to understand what had happened that day. It wasn’t the street, or the child, or the cat. It was the particular slant of the late afternoon light, filtering through the leaves of the maple tree. That specific quality of light had unconsciously reminded my body of a long-forgotten moment in my childhood—a moment of profound fear and helplessness. My nervous system, in its infinite wisdom and unwavering dedication to my survival, had stored that memory not as a story with a beginning, middle, and end, but as a raw, visceral, felt sense. And on that sunny afternoon, it had reacted as if the past were happening right now.

This is the power and the mystery of our nervous system. It is the body’s fastest communication network, an intricate web of electrical and chemical signals that operates largely outside of our conscious awareness. It is the silent guardian that stands at the gate of our experience, constantly asking, *“Are we safe?”* It is the storyteller of our lives, but it tells its stories not in words, but in the language of sensation, impulse, and emotion.

## The Three Guardians Within

From a neuroscience perspective, our nervous system has three main branches, each with its own distinct role in this ongoing assessment of safety. You might think of them as three guardians, a family of protectors living within you, each with a different strategy for keeping the kingdom of You safe and sound.

First, there is the **sympathetic nervous system**. This is our “fight or flight” guardian, the hyper-alert, action-oriented protector. When it perceives a threat—a real one, like a car swerving into our lane, or a perceived one, like a critical email from our boss—it sounds the alarm. It floods our system with adrenaline and cortisol, the hormones of stress. Our heart rate increases, our breathing becomes shallow and rapid, and blood is diverted from our organs to our limbs, preparing us to either fight for our lives or run for the hills. It’s a powerful and essential system, designed for short-term, acute emergencies. It is the guardian that says, “Get ready! Something is wrong!”

Then, there is the **parasympathetic nervous system**, our “rest and digest” guardian. This is the gentle, soothing hand that calms us after the danger has passed. It is the guardian that says, “You can rest now. You are safe.” It slows our heart rate, deepens our breath, and brings our body back into a state of equilibrium, or homeostasis. It’s in this state that we can heal, digest our food, build relationships, and feel a sense of connection to ourselves and the world. It is the state of safety, of coming home to ourselves.

And finally, there is the **enteric nervous system**, often called our “second brain,” located in our gut. This system is a vast network of neurons lining our digestive tract, and it is in constant, intimate communication with the brain in our head. This gut-brain axis influences our mood, our intuition, and our overall sense of well-being. That “gut feeling” you get about a person or a situation? That’s your enteric nervous system speaking to you, offering its own unique brand of ancient, primal wisdom. It is the guardian that whispers, “Pay attention. Something feels… off.” Or, “Yes. This feels right.”

For many of us, however, especially those who have experienced developmental trauma, chronic stress, or overwhelming events in childhood, the sympathetic nervous system can become chronically activated. The “fight or flight” guardian, in its zealous effort to protect us, can get stuck in the “on” position. We live in a state of low-grade, or even high-grade, anxiety, our bodies constantly braced for a threat that may no longer be present. The neural pathways for danger become deeply grooved, like well-worn paths in a forest, while the pathways for safety and connection can feel overgrown and inaccessible.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Rewiring Your Inner World for Safety

Here’s a very good thing to know: *you are not broken*. Your nervous system is not malfunctioning. It is doing exactly what it learned to do to keep you safe in a world that, at one time, may have felt very unsafe. The patterns of anxiety, of hypervigilance, of feeling “on edge” all the time—these were brilliant adaptations to your early environment. They served you, perhaps for a very long time.

But what happens when those patterns are no longer serving you? What happens when the old wiring is keeping you from the very connection, joy, and peace that you so deeply crave? The beautiful truth, supported by the science of neuroplasticity, is that we can create new neural pathways. We can, with conscious, compassionate attention, begin to rewire our nervous systems for safety and connection. We can, in essence, teach our inner guardians new strategies.

This is not a quick fix, or a matter of simply thinking positive thoughts. It is a deep, embodied process of befriending your nervous system, of learning to listen to its signals with curiosity rather than judgment. It is about creating small, consistent experiences of safety in your daily life, and allowing your body to truly register them, to soak them in like a healing balm.

I learned this myself, not just through study, but through practice. For years after that experience on the street, I would notice a subtle tension in my body in the late afternoon. Instead of ignoring it or pushing it away, I learned to turn towards it. I would pause, take a breath, and place a hand on my heart. I would say to my body, silently or out loud, “I feel you. I know you’re trying to protect me. But right here, right now, in this moment, we are safe.” I would then intentionally look for evidence of that safety—the feeling of my feet on the ground, the sound of my own steady breath, the sight of a bird on a wire. Slowly, gently, I began to carve a new path in my own neural forest. A path of presence. A path of safety.

### A Simple Practice: Coming Home to Safety

I invite you to try a simple practice right now, to begin this conversation with your own nervous system.

1.  **Find a comfortable position**, either sitting or lying down. Allow your eyes to gently close, or soften your gaze towards the floor.
2.  **Bring your awareness to your breath**, without trying to change it in any way. Simply notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest or belly with each inhale and each exhale.
3.  **Now, place one hand on your heart and one hand on your belly.** Feel the warmth of your own hands on your body. Feel the gentle pressure. This simple act of touch can be incredibly soothing to the nervous system.
4.  **Silently, or in a soft whisper, offer yourself a few words of comfort.** You might try: “I am here.” “I am safe in this moment.” “May I be at ease.” Find the words that feel true and gentle for you.
5.  **Stay here for five to ten breaths**, simply receiving your own touch and your own gentle words. Notice any shifts, however small, in your body. A softening in your shoulders, a deepening of your breath, a sense of quiet in your mind.

This is the work. It is small, it is quiet, and it is profoundly powerful. This is how we begin to show our inner guardians that we are no longer that helpless child. We are the loving, attuned adult who can now provide the safety we have always longed for.

Your nervous system is not your enemy. It is your most loyal and devoted protector. And as you begin to build a relationship with it based on trust, curiosity, and deep compassion, you will find that it can also become your greatest ally on the path to wholeness, and your most trustworthy guide on the journey home to yourself.


---

teachings.sourceTitle: The Feet - The Grounding Point of Your Journey
teachings.title: The Feet - The Grounding Point of Your Journey
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to regard the feet as both anatomical foundation and somatic oracle, holding memories and beliefs about support, trust and readiness to move. The piece offers embodied questions, simple grounding and walking practices, and small rituals (like anointing or the 'step of witness') to retrain the nervous system toward trust. It emphasizes gentleness, adaptation for injury, and the idea that walking with attention is a neuroplastic, sacred inquiry.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
The soles of your feet hold a kind of quiet intelligence that you rarely invite into conversation. They are the first organs to meet the ground when you arrive into this life and the last to release you from it at the end of the day. Each foot contains twenty-six bones, an architecture of delicate interdependence that makes possible astonishing feats of balance, movement and subtle sensation. Feel into that number for a moment. Twenty-six bones in a single foot, articulating with tiny joints, ligaments and muscles so that you may walk, run, dance, kneel, stand and whisper your presence into the world. This is not incidental design. It is a choreography between you and the earth, a constant dialogue between inside and out.

In Taoist language you might say your feet are the place where your life force anchors itself into form. Lao Tzu reminds us that "a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step". There is a deep paradox here that Taoist practice highlights again and again - you do not need to see the whole road to travel it. The feet, by their nature, ask you to trust the next step without requiring the entire map to be visible. When the feet ache, when walking becomes hesitant or impossible, something more than tissue is speaking. The body is teaching a form of listening you have not yet practiced.

The Feet as Holographic Map

Your body is holographic. That is not a metaphor I use lightly. Every tissue holds memory, and every organ has a governance beyond its mechanical role. The feet carry beliefs about whether life will support you, about whether the ground beneath you is reliable, about whether you have permission to move toward your desires. Foot pain - whether it shows as plantar fasciitis, bunions, neuropathy, arthritis, or chronic soreness - is often a messenger about how you relate to direction and support. When a foot becomes stiff and unwilling to flex, your nervous system is rehearsing an old story: better not move, better stay where you are because moving might endanger you.

Consider the child who learned early in life that the world was unpredictable - a caretaker's presence unreliable, resources scarce, safety conditional. That child does not outgrow the memory of instability. It continues in the tissues as a hypothesis about the world. The feet, which literally carry you through life, hold that proposition stubbornly close. They will test it by creating conditions that force you to examine whether it is still true. Chronic immobility is one of the body’s gentler interventions - it asks you to look, to inquire, to question the assumptions you have been living from.

In this way, the feet are both foundation and oracle. They do not simply support you. They narrate your readiness to step into the unknown. They are sensitive to the tiniest tremor of doubt and can translate that doubt into guarded posture, altered gait or withdrawal. When you study your own feet with reverence you begin to see an inner geography of courage and fear. You begin to decode the idioms they use to speak about your life.

What the Body Asks You to Know

There is a series of questions your feet carry, held in bone, tendon and skin: Do you trust the earth will carry you? Can you allow yourself to be supported without controlling it? Are you willing to move knowing the next step will reveal itself only as you go? These are not philosophical riddles. They are somatic inquiries, intended to be answered in the language of sensation rather than thought. When you respond by shifting posture, softening tension, or placing weight differently, you are teaching your tissues a new grammar for relating to the world.

Foot conditions often arise in correspondence with specific life themes. A bunion can speak to overcompensation in meeting expectations, the grinding pressure of trying to fit into a shape that does not serve you. Neuropathic numbness can mirror an emotional numbness - a survival strategy developed to avoid pain but which also dulls joy and curiosity. Stiff ankles can insist that you slow down where you have been rushing to prove yourself. Even the pattern of wear in the soles of your shoes can tell a story about the direction you habitually favor, the old paths you circle and the edges you never visit.

Your feet are intimately connected to questions of worthiness. If you were taught, explicitly or implicitly, that life is conditional - that care, attention and belonging must be earned through performance - this becomes a somatic pattern. Your feet will ask: if I lift myself to step ahead, will the ground be there to receive me? The answer your nervous system expects is often no. The practice is to gradually teach it otherwise.

Listening Practice - An Invitation to Your Feet

You can begin a conversation with your feet in simple, sacred ways. The invitation is not to fix them intellectually or to force change by sheer will. It is to listen, to witness, and to move with gentleness. Start by sitting with them at the end of the day. Remove your shoes and socks and place the soles on the earth if you can - grass, soil, stable wood. If you are indoors, place them on the cool floor and feel the minutiae of texture. Notice any sensations - warmth, tingling, heaviness, lightness. Notice where your attention wants to rush away. Bring it back. Breathe into the places that feel tight. Let your exhale soften whatever is holding you back.

Ask your feet a question. Keep it simple and present-focused. What would you like me to know about my next step? Wait. The body answers not in words but in pictures, urges, a wish to move, tears, a sudden memory, a shift under the heel. Stay patient. Notice the stories that arise in your mind and do not conflate them with somatic intelligence. Thoughts are not the only voice here.

As you become more practiced at listening, you can introduce a small ritual before you walk. Stand still and ground. Bring your weight into the arches of your feet. Imagine your roots extending into the earth like tree roots, subtle and patient. Feel the gravitational exchange - the earth holding you, you being held. Then lift one foot slightly and sense the invitation to move, trusting you will be supported. Take three slow, deliberate steps. Let each step be a sacrament - an offering and an experiment in trust.

Walking as Alchemy

Walking with intention transforms ordinary travel into embodied inquiry. When you walk as if the feet are teachers, each step becomes a chance to re-pattern fear. You do not need to walk far. You do not need to perform. You simply bring attention to the act of placing heel, then ball, then toes, and feel how the body responds to being supported. Over time the nervous system learns that ground can be reliable in the moment. This small neuroplastic rewiring is sacred. It takes the habitual expectation of betrayal and replaces it, step by step, with evidence of support.

If you are dealing with injury, this practice must be tender. Healing is not a race. The Tao teaches that nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished. You may need to adapt posture, use props, or walk shorter distances. Let gentleness be your method. I have seen that even tiny triumphs - lifting an ankle an extra centimeter, allowing a toe to unfurl - become thresholds of new possibility. They signal to the body that the world can be trusted a little more than it was yesterday.

Beliefs Underneath the Bones

Our earliest paradigms form in the years when we are most helpless and impressionable. Children who felt the ground shift beneath them when a parent left, when resources disappeared, or when love was inconsistent, often embody a chronic hypothesis about existence: the earth may not keep me. This is not a moral failing. It is an adaptive strategy that once preserved you. But it can calcify into limitation if unexamined.

Working with the feet invites you to question these old paradigms. Are you still operating from rules that no longer apply? Do you continue to tighten your toes in anticipation that the ground will recede? Are you waiting for conditions to be perfect before you move? The practice is to hold these questions without blame and to experiment with alternatives. Walk when you might once have stayed put. Take a risk calibrated to your capacity. Notice what your feet say. If they tremble, breathe. If they relax, acknowledge the truth of that new evidence.

There is also a subtle spiritual invitation in all of this. To be grounded does not mean to be stuck. The Tao encourages you to be like water: yielding enough to fit through cracks, persistent enough to shape stone. Your feet teach you that movement and grounding are partners. The foot that trusts the earth becomes an organ of exploration, not escape. It knows that the next step will be revealed when needed, that the path is built underfoot rather than planned in its entirety ahead of time.

Rites for Regrounding

Over the years I have guided many people back into their feet with practices both somatic and ritual. One simple rite that can be done nightly is to anoint your feet with oil as you listen to your breath. Use a warm, gentle oil - olive, sesame, or coconut - and massage the sole with slow, circular motions. As you do this, name an intention aloud: "I am supported. I am safe to move." Let the words feel true in your mouth even if they are not yet entirely accepted in your heart. The ritual is not spiritual bypass. It is a physical and energetic rehearsal of new truth.

Another practice is the "step of witness." When you are at a crossroads in a decision, rather than weighing every possible outcome in your mind, take a literal step. Step outside and place your bare foot forward. Feel the weight shift. Ask the foot to tell you, through sensation, where your body inclines. You may be surprised by how often your first embodied impulse is wiser than any prolonged mental debate.

Grounding can also be communal. There is medicine in shared walking, where bodies move together in a rhythm that supports individual courage. When others are moving nearby, your nervous system reads social safety. Group walks, pilgrimages or even synchronized steps in a small circle can calibrate your tissues toward trust. The collective earth-holding is a powerful antidote to the solitary stories of abandonment that might have taken root early in life.

Transcending Through the Feet

The ultimate work of the feet is not merely to heal pain or restore mobility. It is to help you cultivate a way of being in the world that is both soft and resolute, patient and adventurous. When your feet reclaim their function as trusted allies, your life shifts. Decision-making becomes less a battleground of fear and more a choreography of clear impulses. You stand in your commitments without rigid bracing. You move forward with curiosity and a deepened capacity to return to center when the terrain changes.

This is the promise of transcendence the cards call you toward when you work with the feet as a system. Purpose is recognized - the architecture of twenty-six bones meant for flexible grounding. Inquiry follows - what stories about support and direction have your feet been carrying? And transcendence arrives not as an escape from difficulty but as an embodied reconciliation with it. Your feet become instruments of your soul's journey - a bridge between heaven and earth guiding each step into wisdom.

A Blessing for Your Feet

Place your hands under your feet and feel the small, enormous intelligence that has carried you this far. Speak to them as you would to a beloved friend. Tell them of the roads you have traveled, of the times they have trembled and of the times they have soared. Offer gratitude for the fidelity they have shown even when you doubted them. Promise them you will listen more closely. Promise yourself you will honor the next step as a revelation not a test.

In the words of the Tao, move like a good traveler - not attached to arrival, but skillful in each step. Let your feet be the witness and the teacher. Let them remind you that grounding is not a static thing. It is a living conversation between your inner certainties and the earth's patient generosity. Each day you may practice this conversation again, and in doing so you slowly re-sculpt the body’s tale to match the new truths you choose to live by.

May your feet carry you with grace, and may each step be a prayer. May you learn to trust the ground beneath you and the guide within you. Step forward, beloved. The earth is waiting with an embrace.

If it feels safe, stand, ground into the arches, imagine gentle roots into the earth, and take three slow, deliberate heel–ball–toe steps.
