teachings.title: A Practice for Integrating Body, Mind, Emotion, and Spirit
teachings.summary: Susan offers a concise, three-part daily practice to restore cohesion among body, mind, emotion, and spirit. The practice combines a gentle body scan, a guided systems dialogue (inviting messages from heart, stomach, head, etc.), and a coherence visualization that reunites the felt-sense of the whole self. She frames the work in the context of neuroplasticity and invites a steady, compassionate return to wholeness rather than perfection.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
I want to invite you into a different kind of conversation today.

Have you ever had one of those days where your mind is racing with a to-do list, your heart is aching with an old sadness, your body is screaming for rest, and some deeper part of you is just… gone? It feels like you’re a committee of warring factions, each pulling in a different direction. Your head says, “Get to work.” Your heart says, “I need to cry.” Your body says, “I’m exhausted.” And that quiet, essential self? It’s drowned out by the noise.

Many of us have experienced moments of profound internal fragmentation. It can happen on an otherwise peaceful day, where the external world is calm, but inside, a storm is raging. One part of the mind might be replaying a difficult conversation, another part is consumed with worry, and the body holds the tension in tight shoulders and a clenched jaw. We can feel scattered, pulled in a dozen different directions at once. In these moments, a fundamental question can arise: *Who is the one living this life? Who is the conductor of this chaotic orchestra?*

This question is at the very heart of healing. We are not meant to live as a collection of disconnected parts, each vying for control. We are designed to be a unified whole, a luminous web of being where body, mind, emotion, and spirit are in constant, loving communication. The body is not a machine to be fixed, the mind is not an enemy to be silenced, and the emotions are not inconvenient interruptions. They are all sacred messengers, vital threads in the intricate tapestry of you.

## The Symphony of You: Your Web of Being

In the work I do with The Elevated Body cards, we explore 21 different systems of the body—from the grounding wisdom of the Feet to the crown of consciousness in the Head. But the final “card,” the one that holds all the others, is the Web of Your Being. This isn’t a physical system you can point to. It is the unified field of consciousness that orchestrates the entire symphony. It’s the miraculous, intelligent awareness that knows how to beat your heart, digest your food, and heal a cut on your finger without any conscious instruction from “you.”

When we feel fragmented, it’s because we’ve lost our connection to this unifying field. We’ve started identifying with one part of ourselves over the others. We live in our heads, ignoring the body’s whispers until they become screams. Or we get swept away by a powerful emotion, forgetting the grounding presence of our physical form. The journey of integration is the journey back to the conductor’s podium. It’s about learning to listen to, honor, and guide all the different instruments in your orchestra so they can play in harmony.

This isn’t just a beautiful metaphor; it’s grounded in neuroscience. Our brains are constantly forming and reforming neural pathways based on our focus and experiences. When we repeatedly focus on worry, our “anxiety pathways” become superhighways. When we consistently ignore our body’s signals, the connection between the brain’s awareness centers and our physical sensations weakens. The beautiful news of neuroplasticity is that we can consciously create *new* pathways. We can train our brains and nervous systems to listen inward, to foster communication, and to create a state of whole-being coherence.

So, how do we begin? How do we move from being a warring committee to a harmonious symphony? It begins with a simple, dedicated practice. Not another thing to perfect or get “right,” but a loving, daily ritual of checking in with your whole self.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## The Integration Practice: A Daily Return to Wholeness

I want to offer you the practice that I have shared with hundreds of clients and that I return to myself, day after day. It’s a simple, three-part process for orchestrating your entire being. Find a quiet place where you can be undisturbed for 15-20 minutes. Sit comfortably, with your spine tall but not rigid, and your feet on the floor. Close your eyes, and let’s begin.

### Part 1: The Body Scan of Presence

Start by bringing your awareness to your breath. Don’t change it, just notice it. Notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest, the cool air entering your nostrils, the warm air leaving. This is your anchor to the present moment.

Now, slowly, begin to scan your awareness through your body. Start with the tips of your toes. Can you feel them inside your socks or shoes? Wiggle them gently. You don’t have to feel anything spectacular. Just bring your quiet, loving attention there. Slowly, move your awareness up to your feet, your ankles, your lower legs. Notice any sensations—warmth, coolness, tingling, pressure, perhaps nothing at all. Continue this slow journey up through your knees, your thighs, your hips.

Move your attention to your spine, feeling its connection to the chair and the earth. Scan your belly, your chest, your shoulders. Are they tight? Are they relaxed? No judgment. Just notice. Travel down your arms to your fingertips. Finally, bring your awareness to your neck, your jaw, your face, the top of your head. For a few moments, simply sit with the full, tingling, alive sensation of your entire body. You are here. You are embodied.

### Part 2: The Systems Dialogue

Now, from this place of embodied presence, we’ll begin a gentle dialogue. You are the conductor, and you are going to greet the different sections of your orchestra. You can pick one or two systems that you feel drawn to, or you can move through a few key ones.

Let’s start with the Heart, the first declaration of your being. Place a hand over your heart center. Breathe into this space. Silently, or out loud, you might ask, *“Beloved Heart, what is your wisdom for me today?”* And then… you listen. Don’t search for an answer. Just create a space for a feeling, an image, a single word to arise. Your heart’s wisdom is not about overthinking; it’s about receiving.

Now, move your awareness to your Stomach, the alchemical cauldron of experience. Ask, *“Dear Stomach, what have I been struggling to digest in my life?”* Again, just listen. Perhaps a situation or a person comes to mind. You don’t need to solve it right now. The simple act of acknowledging what is difficult to stomach is a profound act of self-compassion.

Finally, bring your attention to your Head, the throne of your identity. Ask, *“Wise Mind, how can you serve my wholeness today? How can you be a partner to my heart and body, rather than the sole authority?”* Feel the possibility of your brilliant mind becoming a trusted advisor, rather than a relentless master. You can do this with any of the 21 systems—the Lungs, the Kidneys, the Shoulders. You are simply asking, listening, and acknowledging.

### Part 3: The Coherence Visualization

To close the practice, you will bring it all together. Imagine a beautiful light in the center of your chest, at your heart. This is your central sun, the core of your being. With each inhale, imagine this light growing brighter, warmer, more radiant. With each exhale, imagine this light expanding, sending beautiful rays of coherence and love to every single cell in your body.

Visualize this light flowing down your spine, illuminating the central channel of communication. See it flowing into your shoulders, down your arms, and out through your hands. Imagine it flowing down through your hips and legs, grounding you to the earth through your feet. See it flowing up into your head, bathing your brain in calm, clear, loving awareness.

Feel all the systems of your body—your Nervous System settling into safety, your Lungs breathing in the fullness of life, your Heart beating in a steady rhythm of self-love—all working together in perfect, effortless harmony. You are not forcing this; you are simply remembering the wholeness that is your natural state. You are the Web of Your Being, a unified field of consciousness experiencing itself through this magnificent, sacred body.

Sit in this feeling of integrated wholeness for a few final moments. This feeling is your truth. The fragmentation is the illusion. This practice, this gentle return, is always available to you.

It is a way to come home.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Whole-Hearted Living: A Practice for Filling Your Own Cup](/blog/heart-whole-hearted-practice)
- [Standing Tall in Your Truth: Transcending Spinal Patterns](/blog/spine-standing-tall)
- [A Somatic Practice for Calming Your Nervous System](/blog/nervous-system-somatic-practice)

**More on Web of Your Being:**

- [Becoming the Conductor: Orchestrating Your Entire Being](/blog/web-of-being-becoming-conductor)
- [Fragmentation and Wholeness: When Your Inner Orchestra Plays Off-Key](/blog/web-of-being-fragmentation)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan

teachings.title: From Surviving to Thriving: Rewiring Your Nervous System for Safety
teachings.summary: Susan describes how chronic stress and early-life experience can lock the nervous system into survival states and introduces polyvagal theory as a useful map for understanding ventral (safe/social), sympathetic (mobilize), and dorsal (immobilize) responses. She emphasizes neuroplasticity and offers gentle somatic practices (orienting the eyes, lengthening the exhale, grounding through the feet) alongside the relational work of co-regulation. The piece invites patient, compassionate repetition rather than quick fixes, and highlights that healing is both individual and social.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
Every cell in your body is listening. Right now. In this very moment.

Especially now.

We are swimming in a sea of information, of stimulation, of constant, low-grade activation. The phone buzzes. The headlines scream. The unspoken demands of modern life press in. And through it all, a very ancient part of our biology is working tirelessly, asking one simple, relentless question: *Am I safe?*

For so many of us, the answer that echoes back from the deepest recesses of our being is… *no*. Not really.

It might not be a conscious thought. It’s more of a feeling. A hum of anxiety beneath the surface. A tightness in the shoulders. A shallow breath you don’t realize you’re holding. It’s the feeling of being perpetually braced for impact, even in moments of relative peace. This, my dear one, is the signature of a nervous system stuck in survival mode.

I know this landscape intimately. For years, my own nervous system was wired for high alert. A difficult childhood, layered with the ambient stress of a fast-paced world, had taught my body that danger was always lurking just around the corner. I was successful, functional, even outwardly calm. But inside, my internal engine was perpetually revving in the red. I was surviving. But I was not thriving.

The journey from that state of chronic activation to one of grounded safety has been the central transformation of my life. It’s a journey that has taken me deep into the elegant wisdom of the body, the astonishing plasticity of the brain, and the profound truth that we are not doomed to repeat our patterns. We can, in fact, rewire ourselves for a new way of being.

## The Body’s Electrical Network

To understand this shift, we first have to understand the nervous system itself. Think of it as your body’s electrical wiring and communication network. It’s the intricate web of nerves, brain, and spinal cord that receives information from the world, processes it, and decides how to respond. Its primary job, above all else, is to keep you alive.

At the heart of this system is the polyvagal theory, a beautiful map of our inner landscape developed by Dr. Stephen Porges. In accessible terms, this theory shows us that our nervous system has three primary states it can be in, each with its own logic and purpose.

There is the state of **safe and social connection**, governed by the ventral vagal part of our parasympathetic nervous system. This is our thriving state. When we are here, we feel grounded, open, and connected to others. Our heart rate is regulated, our breathing is deep, we can digest our food, and we feel a sense of ease. This is the state of restoration, of creativity, of love.

Then, there is the state of **mobilization**, or the classic “fight-or-flight” response. This is governed by the sympathetic nervous system. When the nervous system perceives a threat, it floods the body with cortisol and adrenaline to prepare you to fight or run away. Your heart pounds, your muscles tense, your digestion shuts down. This is a brilliant and necessary state for acute danger, but it was never meant to be a long-term residence.

And finally, there is the state of **immobilization**, or the “freeze” response. This is the most ancient part of our nervous system, the dorsal vagal part of the parasympathetic system. When a threat feels so overwhelming that we can’t fight or flee, the system slams on the brakes. We shut down, disconnect, numb out. It’s the possum playing dead. It’s a state of dissociation, of feeling not-quite-here. It’s the ultimate survival strategy when all else fails.

For many of us, our systems learned—often in very early life—that the world was not a safe place. Through trauma, neglect, or chronic stress, our nervous system became conditioned to live primarily in the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) or dorsal vagal (freeze) states. We became stuck in survival mode. Sympathetic dominance looks like chronic anxiety, irritability, and restlessness. Dorsal dominance looks like depression, exhaustion, and disconnection. Many of us learn to oscillate between the two, bouncing from anxiety to collapse and back again, rarely touching the shores of true safety and connection.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

## Learning the Language of Safety

For years, I lived in a state of sympathetic dominance. I was always on. Always scanning the horizon for the next problem. My mind was a master strategist for anticipating worst-case scenarios. It was exhausting. My body was paying the price with digestive issues, sleep disturbances, and a constant, underlying hum of tension.

The turning point for me wasn't a grand epiphany, but a quiet, internal whisper. It was the recognition that my body was not my enemy. It was, in fact, my most devoted ally, doing its absolute best to keep me safe based on a set of outdated instructions. The threats of my childhood were no longer present, but my nervous system hadn’t gotten the memo. It was still running a program for a world that no longer existed.

This is where the beautiful concept of neuroplasticity comes in. Our brains and nervous systems are not fixed. They are constantly learning, adapting, and creating new pathways based on our experiences. This means that just as we learned patterns of danger, we can learn—and embody—new patterns of safety. We can, quite literally, rewire our nervous system.

This is not a process of thinking your way into calmness. You cannot command your nervous system to relax. It doesn’t speak the language of logic; it speaks the language of sensation, of breath, of movement, of connection. This is somatic work. It is the work of the body.

Here are a few gentle, somatic practices that became my anchors in this journey. They are not quick fixes, but invitations into a new relationship with your body.

> **The Orienting Practice:** When you feel a wave of anxiety or a sense of being ungrounded, pause. Let your eyes slowly scan the room you are in. Don’t just look, but truly *see*. Notice the color of the wall. The texture of the chair. The way the light falls on the floor. Let your head and neck turn gently. This simple act sends a powerful signal to your brainstem: *I am here, in this moment, and I am safe enough to look around.* It interrupts the tunnel vision of the threat response.

> **The Power of the Exhale:** Your breath is the most direct and accessible tool for communicating with your nervous system. Inhaling is linked to the sympathetic system, and exhaling is linked to the parasympathetic. When we are stressed, our exhales become short and clipped. To shift the balance, consciously extend your exhale. Breathe in gently for a count of four, and then breathe out slowly, as if through a straw, for a count of six or eight. Do this for just a minute. Feel the subtle shift in your body. This is you, actively guiding your system back to a state of restoration.

> **The Gravity Anchor:** Place your feet flat on the floor. Feel the points of contact. Feel the solidity of the ground beneath you. Imagine roots growing down from the soles of your feet, deep into the earth. Feel the pull of gravity, holding you, supporting you. The earth is always here, stable and unwavering. Let your body borrow that stability. This practice is a profound antidote to the feeling of floating or being untethered that often comes with anxiety or dissociation.

These practices are not about achieving a perfect state of zen. They are about tending to your inner world with compassion and consistency. They are about showing your body, through direct experience, that it is safe to let down its guard. It is safe to rest. It is safe to thrive.

It’s a slow and tender process, this rewiring. It requires patience. It requires immense self-compassion. There will be days when the old patterns feel strong. But with each conscious breath, with each moment you choose to orient to the safety of the present, you are laying down a new neural pathway. You are casting a vote for a new reality.

Your body has an infinite capacity to learn, to heal, to find its way back to wholeness. It has never been broken. It has only been doing its best to protect you. And now, you can begin to offer it the safety it has been longing for all along.

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


## The Co-regulating Field

While these personal, somatic practices are the bedrock of rewiring, there is another layer that is just as crucial: co-regulation. We are social creatures, and our nervous systems are designed to attune to one another. From the moment we are born, our sense of safety is shaped by the nervous systems of our caregivers. A calm, regulated parent helps a baby’s nervous system feel safe. A dysregulated, anxious parent communicates danger, even without a single word.

This dynamic continues throughout our lives. Being in the presence of a calm and grounded person can have a profoundly settling effect on our own system. Their regulated state acts as a resonant field that our own nervous system can tune into. This is why therapy, deep friendships, and loving partnerships can be so healing. We are not just talking; we are communicating safety, nervous system to nervous system.

Part of the journey of thriving is consciously choosing to cultivate relationships that feel safe and supportive. This doesn’t mean finding “perfect” people. It means finding people who are also on a path of awareness, who are willing to be present with you, and whose presence helps your body feel at ease. It means learning to recognize the difference between relationships that activate your survival patterns and those that nourish your ventral vagal state of connection.

As you heal, you also become a source of regulation for others. Your grounded presence becomes a gift to the world, a small anchor of peace in a turbulent sea. This is the beautiful, reciprocal nature of healing. As we find our way home to ourselves, we make it a little easier for everyone else to find their way home, too.

reflectionPrompts: Notice your baseline: when you feel stressed or low, what are the first three bodily sensations, postures, or breathing patterns you observe? Where do you most commonly feel activation or shutdown in your body?

Who in your life reliably helps you feel calmer or more present? Describe a recent moment when someone’s presence shifted your state — what changed in your breath, face, or shoulders? What small, realistic step could you take to cultivate more of that co-regulating presence?

Which of the somatic practices offered here (orienting the eyes, lengthening the exhale, or grounding through the feet) feels most approachable right now? Commit to trying it for one minute a day for a week and note any subtle changes; what supports or boundaries would help you keep that promise to yourself?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Try a 3-minute safety check you can do anywhere: 1) Pause and allow your eyes to slowly scan the room for 20–30 seconds, taking in color, texture, and light; 2) Rest your feet flat on the floor and notice points of contact for 20–30 seconds; 3) Breathe gently for one minute with an inhale to a comfortable count of four and an exhale through pursed lips for a count of six, returning to natural breath when you finish. If you have significant medical or mental-health concerns, consult a qualified provider before beginning and pause the practice if you feel overwhelmed.
sensitiveContentNotes: This article includes references to childhood stress, trauma, dissociation, and intense emotional states. These topics can be activating; you have permission to pause or step away at any time.
If reading this material brings up strong memories or distress, consider reaching out to a trusted friend, clinician, or crisis service. You do not need to do this work alone.
If you are in immediate danger or experiencing thoughts of harming yourself, please seek emergency help or your local crisis resources right away.

teachings.title: A Guided Practice for Bladder Healing and Release
teachings.summary: Susan offers a short, compassionate somatic practice that invites gentle breath, curious inner inquiry, and visualization to bring attention and safety to the bladder and pelvic bowl. She frames bladder sensations as meaningful bodily messages shaped by patterns of holding, and connects the practice to vagal regulation and neuroplasticity without promising medical outcomes. The tone emphasizes nonjudgment, presence, and small, repeatable steps toward trusting natural release.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
In my years of practice, I have come to understand that the body speaks a language all its own.

We learn so early to hold things in. To hold our tongues, to hold back tears, to hold our bodies still when they want to dance or tremble or run. We learn that control is often rewarded, that a tidy appearance is preferred over a messy truth. And our bodies, in their infinite wisdom and loyalty, learn to do the same.

I remember being a little girl, sitting in a circle on the scratchy rug of my kindergarten classroom. The teacher was reading a story, and I was utterly captivated. But a familiar pressure was building in my lower belly. I knew I should raise my hand, ask to be excused. But I couldn’t bear to miss a single word of the story. And a deeper, quieter part of me felt a flicker of shame—a sense that my body’s needs were an interruption, an inconvenience. So I held it. I crossed my legs, I wiggled, I clenched, and I held on, believing that my stillness, my control, was the most important thing.

Of course, the inevitable happened. A sudden, warm release. A puddle of shame on the floor. My teacher was kind, but my own hot-faced embarrassment was a lesson I wouldn’t forget. I had failed at control. And for years, that pattern echoed—a belief that I had to hold myself in, emotionally and physically, to be good, to be loved, to be safe.

Our bladders, the beautiful, resilient reservoirs of our pelvic bowls, are masters of this very dance. They have a dual function, a sacred rhythm of holding and releasing. They are designed to patiently contain what is no longer needed, and then, when the time is right, to let it all go. Completely. But when we live in a state of chronic holding—of our feelings, our words, our true selves—the bladder can become a vessel for this conflict. It can begin to speak to us, sometimes in whispers, sometimes in screams.

## The Language of the Bladder

When the body speaks, it doesn’t use words. It uses sensation. For the bladder, that language can be one of urgency, of pressure, of the burning heat of a urinary tract infection. In my work, I’ve come to see conditions like cystitis as the body feeling “burned” or inflamed by a situation or relationship. There’s an intolerable quality to it, isn’t there? That combination of urgency, fear, and shame can feel like a five-alarm fire in the soul.

This isn’t a punishment. It’s a message. The body is a sacred messenger, and it is asking for our attention. It might be revealing a deeper pattern—a pattern of holding onto expectations of how things *should* have turned out. A quiet resentment for all the times you held yourself in for the comfort of others. A deep-seated belief that your natural, spontaneous expressions are somehow wrong or shameful.

What would it be like to stop seeing these signals as an enemy to be defeated, and instead see them as a loving call home to yourself? What if you could learn to listen, to enter into a gentle dialogue with this part of your body, and to support its innate wisdom of release?

This is not about forcing or fixing. It is about creating a safe space within your own being for a new kind of conversation. A conversation grounded in compassion, curiosity, and the profound truth that you are not broken. You have never been broken.

## A Guided Practice for Bladder Healing

I invite you to find a quiet, comfortable space where you can be undisturbed for the next ten to fifteen minutes. You can sit in a chair with your feet on the floor, or lie down on your back with your knees bent. Let this be a time just for you.

**Step 1: The Breath of Welcome**

Begin by closing your eyes, or softening your gaze toward the floor. Take a few slow, gentle breaths. Don’t try to change your breath or force it. Simply notice it. Notice the air entering your nostrils, filling your lungs, and the gentle release as you exhale.

Now, invite your breath to travel deeper into your body. Imagine you could breathe all the way down into your lower belly, into your pelvic bowl. With each inhale, feel a gentle expansion in this area. With each exhale, feel a soft release. Let your belly be soft. Let go of any tension you might be holding there. This breath is a message to your nervous system that you are safe. You are here. You are present.

**Step 2: The Gentle Inquiry**

As you continue this deep, gentle breathing, bring your awareness to the physical location of your bladder, resting in the front of your pelvic bowl. You don’t need to have a perfect anatomical map; just bring your loving attention to that general area.

Without judgment or expectation, simply notice what is there. Is there warmth? Coolness? Numbness? A sense of holding, or perhaps a feeling of ease? Whatever you perceive, just meet it with kindness. *Ah, there you are.*

Now, I invite you to silently, from your heart, ask your bladder a question. You might choose one of these, or one that feels more true for you:

> *Beloved bladder, what are you holding for me?*
> *What do you need me to know?*
> *What does release feel like for you?*

Ask gently. And then, listen. The answer may not come in words. It might be a feeling, an image, a memory, or just a subtle shift in sensation. Don’t search for an answer. Simply create a space of loving silence and be willing to receive whatever arises. Trust the wisdom held here.

**Step 3: The Visualization of Release**

Continue to breathe into your lower belly. Now, begin to imagine a beautiful, soft, healing light filling this space with every inhale. It could be a warm golden light, a soothing blue, or a shimmering silver. See this light surrounding your bladder, infusing it with safety, peace, and unconditional love.

With each exhale, imagine a gentle, effortless release. You might visualize a stream of clear water flowing out from you, carrying away anything that is ready to be let go—old fears, resentments, the pressure of unmet expectations, the shame of not being “perfect.” See it flowing away from you, back to the earth to be composted and transformed.

Feel the relief in this release. It is not forced. It is not shameful. It is the most natural thing in the world. Inhale love and safety; exhale and let go. Stay with this for several breaths.

[PROMO_SESSIONS]

**Step 4: The Integration of Transcendence**

As you bring this practice to a close, rest for a moment in the space you have created. Feel the gentle rhythm of your breath, the quiet presence of your body.

The ultimate teaching of the bladder is this: *natural release is not shameful, but essential.* The healing journey is not about achieving perfect control. It is about releasing the *need* for control as a way to earn love or safety. It is about trusting the natural, intelligent flow of your own life force.

Your body knows how to heal. Your path is to create the conditions of safety, presence, and compassion that allow that healing to unfold. This practice is a way to begin building that trust, that conscious, loving relationship with yourself.

You might choose to do a shortened version of this practice each day—perhaps just a minute or two of breathing into your pelvic bowl and sending love to your bladder. It is a way of reminding this part of yourself that you are listening. You are here. And it is safe to let go.

This is the work of transformation. Not a violent overthrow of old patterns, but a gentle, persistent turning toward love. It creates new neural pathways in the brain, pathways of safety and self-compassion that, over time, become your new default. You are rewiring your being for peace, one gentle breath at a time.


---

## Explore Related Systems

Your body is an interconnected web of wisdom. Each system speaks to and through the others. Continue your exploration:

- [Flowing with Life: Transcending Kidney Patterns](/blog/kidneys-flowing-with-life)
- [The Sacred Portal of Creation: Your Reproductive System Speaks](/blog/reproductive-sacred-portal)
- [From Hypervigilance to Peace: Transcending Nervous System Patterns](/blog/nervous-system-hypervigilance-peace)

**More on Bladder:**

- [When Holding On Hurts: The Emotional Patterns Behind Bladder Issues](/blog/bladder-emotional-patterns)
- [The Flow of Completion: Transcending Bladder Patterns](/blog/bladder-flow-of-completion)

[PROMO_BODY_CARDS]

With infinite love and support on your journey,
Susan


## The Neuroscience of Letting Go

It’s a remarkable thing to consider that this simple practice of breath, attention, and visualization is actually remodeling the architecture of your brain. For years, perhaps a lifetime, your nervous system may have operated from a place of hypervigilance. A perceived threat—whether it was the fear of a teacher’s disapproval or the more complex dynamics of a painful relationship—triggered your sympathetic nervous system, the body’s “fight or flight” response. Adrenaline and cortisol flood your system, your muscles tense… and you hold on. This becomes a deeply ingrained neural pathway, a well-worn groove that your energy automatically flows down.

When you consciously bring your awareness to your breath and send it into your pelvic bowl, you are activating the vagus nerve, the superhighway of your parasympathetic nervous system—the “rest and digest” state. This is the state where healing happens. You are, in a very real sense, telling your body, on a cellular level, that it is safe to stand down. It is safe to release. It is safe to let go.

With repetition, you are not just having a momentary experience of peace; you are engaging in neuroplasticity. You are building a new neural pathway, one of safety, self-compassion, and release. It may feel like a tiny, overgrown footpath at first, while the old highway of holding and fear is wide and paved. But every time you choose this practice, you are clearing that path. You are making it wider, smoother, and more accessible. Eventually, it becomes the new default. Your nervous system learns that it can return to a state of balance and flow, and the bladder, as a loyal messenger, no longer needs to scream for your attention.

This is the beautiful intersection of ancient wisdom and modern science. The mystics and sages have always known the power of presence and intention. Now, neuroscience shows us the tangible mechanisms at play. You are not just wishing for healing; you are actively participating in its creation, co-creating a new reality within your own sacred body.

reflectionPrompts: Recall a time you were taught to ‘hold’—how did that experience shape the way you respond to bodily signals now? Notice images, feelings, or physical sensations that arise.
If you were to ask your bladder, in a soft, non-demanding way, what it needs from you now, what form does the reply take (word, image, sensation)? Stay with whatever appears for a few breaths.
Where in your life do you still hold for others as a way to feel safe or loved, and what is one small, practical sign you could offer yourself that it is okay to let go?
teachings.practiceInvitation: Set aside 5–10 minutes in a quiet place where you won’t be disturbed. Sit with feet on the floor or lie on your back with knees bent. Rest your hands on the lower belly and take slow, gentle breaths, guiding the breath down into the pelvic bowl. Silently, with kindness, ask one simple question (for example, “What do you need?”) and, as you inhale, imagine a soft healing light filling the area; as you exhale, imagine a gentle, effortless release. Stay curious, stop anytime it feels uncomfortable, and treat this as a gentle, complementary practice — not a substitute for medical care. If you are experiencing pain, infection, or persistent symptoms, please consult a qualified healthcare provider.
sensitiveContentNotes: The article includes childhood shame and other emotionally intense material; you may feel strong emotions during or after the practice — it is okay to pause.
If you have a history of pelvic or sexual trauma, chronic pelvic pain, or PTSD, consider doing this work with a trusted somatic therapist or clinician and keep a safety plan in place.
If you become overwhelmed, stop the practice, ground with the breath or a trusted person, and seek qualified emotional or medical support as needed.

teachings.sourceTitle: Reclaiming Your Story: How to Rewrite the Narrative That Holds You Back
teachings.title: Reclaiming Your Story: How to Rewrite the Narrative That Holds You Back
teachings.summary: Susan invites readers to recognize that the stories we carry are lenses—not immutable facts—and offers an embodied pathway to reclaim authorship of our lives. She guides readers to listen to the body as a living archive, to compassionately witness entrenched narratives, and to cultivate new neural pathways through small, sustained practices of naming, finding feeling, and gathering evidence. The piece blends practical steps with evocative imagery to support a steady, gentle shift from being the character to being the author of your story.
teachings.bodyMarkdown:
It’s a curious thing, this human experience. We walk around carrying worlds inside of us—entire universes woven from memories, beliefs, and the quiet whispers of our ancestors. We believe these worlds are fixed, immutable landscapes. We believe the stories they tell are *us*. But what if they are not? What if we are the storytellers, not just the characters? Many of us have experienced feeling utterly stuck. We speak of our lives as a series of unfortunate events, a narrative of "not-enoughness" that has been a constant companion. This story is a heavy cloak we wear, so familiar we no longer notice its weight. It is the water we swim in, the air we breathe. We believe it is reality. But a story is not reality. A story is a lens. And we, beloved one, have the power to change the lens. ## The Tyranny of the Old Story We all have them—the old, dusty narratives that play on a loop in the back of our minds. *I’m not good enough. I’m unlovable. I’ll always be alone. I’m not creative. I’m destined to struggle.* These are not harmless thoughts; they are the architects of our reality. Neuroscience teaches us that every time we repeat a story, we strengthen the neural pathways associated with it. We are, quite literally, wiring our brains to believe it. It’s a process called Hebbian learning: "neurons that fire together, wire together." The more the story of "not enough" plays, the more the brain becomes ruthlessly efficient at finding evidence to support it. This is not a personal failing. It’s a survival mechanism. Our brains are designed to create meaning, to find patterns and make sense of the world. Stories are the most ancient and powerful tool we have for doing this. They helped our ancestors understand the changing seasons, the behaviour of animals, the mysteries of the stars. But when a story is built on a foundation of fear, trauma, or limiting beliefs, it becomes a cage. The tricky part is that these cages are often invisible. They are constructed from the half-forgotten words of a parent, the sting of a childhood rejection, the inherited anxieties of our lineage. We mistake the bars for the horizon. We forget we are the ones holding the key. ## The Body as a Compass So how do we begin to see the cage? How do we find the key? We must turn away from the noisy chatter of the mind and listen to the quiet wisdom of the body. Your body, dear one, is a living library of your entire history. It holds every joy, every sorrow, every unspoken word. It is the most honest storyteller you will ever meet. When you feel that familiar knot of anxiety in your stomach as you think about a new project, that is your body telling you a story. Perhaps it’s a story about a time you failed, a time you were judged. When your shoulders ache with a familiar tension, that is your body whispering a narrative of carrying too much, of bearing the weight of the world. Consider a moment in a garden in spring, watching the first tender shoots of the peonies push their way through the dark, cold earth. One might feel a familiar pang of sadness, a story of loss and the fear of new beginnings. For a moment, one can let it wash over them. It isn't necessary to fight it, or to "think positive." One can simply place a hand on their heart and breathe. Acknowledge the story. *Hello, old friend. I see you.* And in that moment of gentle, compassionate witnessing, something can shift. The story loses its power. It is just a story—not the truth of the peonies, not the truth of the spring, and not the truth of oneself. This is the first step: to listen. To get quiet enough to hear the stories your body is telling. Where in your body does the story of "not enough" live? Is it a tightness in your chest? A clenching in your jaw? A hollowness in your belly? Breathe into that space. Offer it your gentle, loving attention. You don’t need to fix it or change it. Just be with it. This is the beginning of reclaiming your story. ## The Quantum Leap of a New Narrative Once we have witnessed the old story with compassion, we create a space for a new one to emerge. This is where the magic happens. This is where we step out of the role of the character and into the role of the author. And this is not just a metaphor—it has roots in the strange and wonderful world of quantum physics. In the quantum realm, reality is not a fixed, determined thing. It is a shimmering field of infinite possibilities, a sea of potential that collapses into a single reality only when it is observed. Your attention, your focus, your *story*—this is the act of observation that collapses the wave of potential into the particle of your experience. As long as you are observing your life through the lens of "I am broken," you will continue to create a reality that reflects that belief. But what if you were to choose a different story? What if, instead of "I am not enough," you began to whisper a new narrative: *I am whole, just as I am. I am learning and growing every day. I am worthy of love and belonging.* At first, it might feel like a lie. Your brain, so accustomed to the old neural pathways, will resist. It will show you all the evidence to the contrary. This is normal. This is the old story fighting for its life. Your job is not to argue with the old story. Your job is to gently, persistently, and lovingly introduce the new one. Write it down. Speak it aloud. Find evidence, no matter how small, to support it. Did you make a healthy meal for yourself? *See? I am capable of caring for myself.* Did you have a moment of connection with a friend? *See? I am worthy of love.* You are literally building new neural pathways, wiring your brain for a new reality. You are choosing a new possibility from the quantum field and calling it into being with the power of your attention. > "The world is full of magic things, patiently waiting for our senses to grow sharper." — W.B. Yeats This is not about "positive thinking" in the superficial sense. This is about a deep, embodied shift in your perception of yourself and the world. It is about understanding that you are not a victim of your history, but the creator of your destiny. It is about reclaiming the pen. ## Writing Your New Chapter So how do we begin to write this new chapter? It begins with a single, conscious choice. A choice to no longer be defined by the old story. A choice to become a curious and compassionate observer of your own inner world. Here are a few gentle practices to begin your journey of reclaiming your story: * **Name Your Old Story:** Give your old narrative a name. "The Not-Enough Story." "The I’m-Always-Left-Out Story." "The I-Have-to-Do-It-All-Myself Story." Giving it a name separates it from you. It is a story, not your identity. * **Find the Feeling:** Where does this story live in your body? When you think it, what do you feel? Get to know its physical signature. This is your internal compass, letting you know when the old story is running. * **Craft a "Bridge" Thought:** It can be hard to jump from "I am worthless" to "I am magnificent." A bridge thought can help. Something like: *\"I am willing to consider that I might have worth.\"* Or *\"I am open to the possibility of being loved.\"* Find a thought that feels true-ish, even if it’s just a little bit. * **Gather New Evidence:** Actively look for proof of your new story. Keep a journal. At the end of each day, write down three pieces of evidence that support your new narrative. This trains your brain to start looking for what you want to see. * **Embody the New Story:** How would the person who lives this new story walk? How would they breathe? How would they speak? Spend a few minutes each day embodying this new way of being. Feel it in your bones. Let it become your new normal. This is not a one-time fix. It is a practice, a journey, a returning-home to yourself again and again. There will be days when the old story feels overwhelmingly real. On those days, be gentle. Place your hand on your heart. Breathe. Remember the peonies pushing through the dark earth. Remember that you, too, are a force of nature. You, too, can begin again.

Discover what your body is telling you

Explore the Elevated Body Cards

A holographic body-mind-spirit healing tool that helps you decode the messages your body has been holding — and transform them into doorways of healing and self-discovery.

EXPLORE THE BODY CARDS
You are the storyteller. The pen has been in your hand all along. What new story are you ready to write? With infinite love and support on your journey, Susan

The body as a compass and repository of memory
